This little game actually surprised me.. Quite a bit so.. It's very simple, yet complex enough to be fulfilling. It has done an excellent job of finally satisfying that craving for a simple space empire/fleet building game.
There are a few things that I feel could have been done better, and i'll cover those second.. But first, onto the positives!
1- Simple and effecient!
This is where this game surprised me. I am really impressed with the control and management given to the players in this form. Want to play rpg style with a single ship as your own? Or have a small fleet of escorts? You can do that. Want to play rts style where you tell a few ships, or large quantities of ships to perform specific actions? You can do that too. Want to just sit back, and stare at a spreadsheet and operate your vastly growing empire without directly controlling any ships? You can do that too, All the while not being hassled to mine/farm repetatively for 20 hours before you start your own empire. You can do that right off the bat. Additionally, while you do have control over your own faction ships and structures, civillian activity is present aswell. The structures you build will automatically spawn civillian ships which will act like free-willed npcs to participate in the growth of your empire. Whether that be mining, trading, or even bounty hunting. You do not need to manage them on your own, and there is no loss when they get their little pea shooter box-car bounty-hunter blown up by a dreadnaught pirate.
Unending Galaxy has managed to mash all this together in one simple and efficient design where one method of play does not clash with another, all in the same game session. Nor are you required to do one over the other. The controls are simple and straightforward enough, without the hassle of selecting gamemodes or setting things up. Simply generate your world, and off you go.
The AI works. You can assign different roles and goals for all your ships individually, or in groups, and the optional automation is self-sufficient.
Now. There is one thing need to be aware of though, and that is the graphics. While this does not hold a huge impact on my judgement for this game (as i've all but been able to see past it all), the game does not use original assets, and the most beautiful visuals are the planets. (Like, really beautiful!).. Some assets are open source assets, which included a ship i used to make my first mod in Endless Sky (That was amusing to see!)
One final note, is that when I first got this game, I was not able to launch it. I was having issues that was ultimately determined to be my AV.. But before that was figured out, the dev was very helpful in trying to get my issue resolved, and even offered that if my attempts to make the game work went past the refund policy for steam, he would send them an exception to allow me to refund it. I'm glad that it was not necessary, as I've had a lot of enjoyment with this game.
Reminds me of X3 but 2D. Its a great game and highly addicting. Some may not like it, but I'd recommend trying it. Also the developer cares, and he has a very good track record with devlopment.

Oh wow, does this poor game have issues.
It doesn't know what it wants to be, and it doesn't know who it's trying to appeal to.
At its core, this is effectively Mass Effect, but set in a weird alternate 60s XCOM universe. As a Third Person Shooter, it's too derivative and rough to appeal to TPS fans on its own merit. As an XCOM game, it deviates too much from the XCOM canon and gameplay for it to have much appeal to die-hard XCOM fans either.
Where it racks up credit is in its story... however, that isn't plain sailing either. Essentially a story about a secret war against an Alien invasion that took place in 1962, it covers your perspective as Agent William Carter, as he gets sucked in to the conflict and finds himself on the frontlines. While it starts off great, the dev's complete boner for setting the game in the 60s and the general confusion of whether this game is a prequel or an alternate reboot create a number of issues and inconsistencies that the devs didn't have either the time or the skills to iron out. For instance, the game makes a big deal out of the 60s paranoia, in this case about alien infiltration... but when your own character starts manifesting paranormal abilities like levitating opponents and healing critical injuries, no-one bats an eyelid. It's not even brought up. Later on, the game tries to claim XCOM managed to cover up a countrywide alien invasion - complete with kilometre-tall alien citadels and whole fleets of UFOs - with some radio operators, a couple of helicopters and a few good men. Yeah, sure thing.
From a technical and gameplay standpoint, it's a bit shaky. Weapon balance and challenge is all over the place, with the game insisting on limiting your ammo and dropping aliens behind you. Level design and graphics aren't bad, but rough edges are everywhere - e.g. lip syncing is weird, with everyone looking like they're speaking through gritted teeth.
So the story is a bit sketchy, it can't work out what it is, and plays like a beta version of Mass Effect 1. Why did I give it a thumbs up?
Because it does an amazing job of translating the tense, creepy atmosphere of XCOM into a TPS. There are very few games that try to depict an alien invasion as an X-Files style approach, and this actually manages it. Some of the missions actually felt like they'd directly transplanted some of XCOM:Enemy Unknown's levels directly into a TPS. The game feels like it runs a checklist of X-Files-style sci-fi - alien viruses, abductions, gadgets, government agencies, saving the world, paranormal abilities - it's all here, and the devs clearly enjoyed themselves weaving everything together. Despite it's rough edges, the story is
good - you genuinely don't see some of the twists coming and the finale is pretty spectacular. About the worst I can say is that it deviates so much from the XCOM canon that it might as well be unrelated. Still, if you're generally a fan of sci-fi, it shouldn't be an issue.
If you're a fan of Mass Effect, XCOM, and X-Files.... then consider grabbing this in a sale. Just don't expect an XCOM:Enemy Unknown prequel (even though it starts playing the EU theme at end cinematic).

This isn't a proper XCOM game. Get Enemy Unknown if that's what you're looking for. Instead, this is a third person, squad-based shooter that takes a few elements from those other games, like the organization itself, enemies and things like that. Overall playing this was a nice experience for me, although the difficulty curve (at least on Commander difficulty) is a bit messed-up: Because much of your effectiveness depends on the level of your characters, your squadmates and you can't do much in terms of special abilities at the start. Some encounters early on are incredibly difficult and frustrating because of this, while the game actually gets much easier once your buddies gained a few levels. Those special abilities are spread out across five distinct character classes (squad leader plus four different squadmate types) with slight customizability. The game also follows a lot of typical videogame and console tropes, such as cover-based shooting and sticking to walls, regenerating health (to a degree), checkpoints instead of proper savegames and arena-like combat zones with enemies spawning or teleporting in. While I dislike some of these tropes, it's all competently done at least. Even the ridiculously gravelly voice actor for the protagonist is alright, especially considering this game is clearly inspired by pulp scifi and B-movies. There's even a clever twist about the character you're playing as towards the end of the game, which I won't spoil here, but let me just say that I was genuinely surprised by it, in a good way. In conclusion, this game is not one of the greats, but it's very enjoyable once you get past a slightly slow start and can actually play around with the varied special abilities of your team. At a $20 budget price, even without an ongoing sale, this game is worth the price, I'd say.

Fantastic stealth game. Bloody fantastic.
The game is extremely fluid and smooth, and the abilities, movement, and actions are so precise and satisfying.
The powerups and the unique elements of this game compared to other games makes it fun to play and learn, and if you decide to learn how to do stuff like attatching a spring razor to a rat while freezing time and escaping the scene by posessing a rat, you can make yourself feel like a badass assassin.
Another amazing feature of Dishonored is the replayability.
Not only are there multiple endings and small but satisfying details you can change, but the amount of ways to approach a level with different powerups and different postitioning makes the game fun to play every time you play through it, despite reinacting the same storyline over again.
One flaw of this game however, is the storyline.
The lore and concept of a plague ridden steampunk era is certainly quite interesting, but the way the game tells it's story is quite lacking.
For some the characters and the plot might not be that appealing or memorable, which makes sense because the devs seemed to focus more on the mechanics of the game rather than the story. This is not necessarily a bad thing mind you, but it makes the story element of the game suffer as a result.
The concept of multiple endings based on your actions is quite neat, but the way the endings play out and are shown to you are extremely dissatisfying and can make you feel a sense of incompletion, or emptyness.

The difficulty isn't too high (in fact there are multiple difficulty sliders), but the game is randomly unfair regardless of the challenge level you choose. I'm a fan of Darkest Dungeon, so believe me - I think there's a place for crushingly punishing random events in my games. But you have to be able to adapt or recover; that's where the challenge lies.
There is no recovering in Billions. You're either prepared for attacks or you're not, and an overlooked threat results in immediate and total devastation. (A rewind feature might mitigate some of the frustration of watching 2 hours of work undone in literally 10 seconds by a randomly spawned runner.)
There is no tech tree, just a progression of buildings you must construct in the same order each game.  That's not a problem, but it makes every game very same-y.
The art is gorgeous.
The voiceover is embarassingly amateur (clearly the devs or their friends, hopefully will be professionally re-recorded before release).
As is, definitely not worth the $25 price tag.

For a long time I have been looking for a modern colony/ base building game with resources and defense.  I loved the old settlers games and was looking for a modern equivalent with increased difficulty.  This game hits the nail on the head and is about as addictive as opioids.
As a veteran strategy gamer, I was surprised at the difficulty of this game, but also find it quite refreshing.  Many modern games are set at a difficulty level to appease the masses.  First time players want to be able to win and not have to repeat a map.  They Are Billions does not hold your hand.  It does everything it can to swamp your base with diseased man-eating mutants.  A primary difference between They Are Billions and a standard RTS is that you are not directly fighting a standard enemy who is playing by the same rules as you.  The zombies are not building up a base and they can attack from any direction at any time.  This means you cannot just "learn the AI" and be able to conquer any difficulty.
There is definitely room for improvement to They Are Billions, but this is certainly the best Early Access game I have purchased.  I am excited for the future of this game!

The game is incredibly fun and addictive for the first 20-30 hours due to the novelty the game presents you with. After the initial adrenaline rush, it shows it's apparent flaws, which aren't many but they are very serious, making the game just a good game.
The voice overs and the unit AI pathfinding are horrible. Often there is a delay between issuing and executing orders (move->hold takes a second or a couple of seconds) and that can be the difference between a Harpy outright killing a low HP unit, because the delay causes the unit to keep moving until the order is executed, so any units that don't stop move further away from your unit group thus becoming isolated.
The music of the game, while initially gives you a sense of dread and impeding doom quickly becomes annoying. All of the music tracks are 2-3 minutes long with the same dark drone ambient theme. While the tracks themselves are good they quickly become annoying, especially if you do really big game sessions. The game desperately needs more tracks of also bigger variety of music genre.
The graphics are good for what the game is. The details in the building models are great and there've been a lot of times where I zoomed in just to check them out. The terrain - especially the ground- needs to be more detailed, with more decals. The game also needs a rotating camera. Like, now. Nothing is more frustrating than trying to build a wall behind your command center.
The gameplay is good and addictive. Obviously the game needs more balance and more content but the developers are aware of this so I won't delve into it much.
Special mention must be given to the game's random map generation. You are effectively at the mercy of your map layout and a good vs bad layout (fewer resources, resources farther from your starting point) can be the difference between a win or a loss. If the developers want this to be randomly generated, then it would only be fair to allow the players to also generate any resources or terrain qualities randomly with a percentage slider. They could also tie these percentages to the map's final score, so a map with more resources will obviously give you a lower final score.
All in all, a refreshing change to the triple A+ copypasta games with BILLIONS of money to spend on marketing. This game is indicative of what indielike games stand for; addictive gameplay and game genre advancement. Keep up the good work.

I'd like to say this is a standard RPG and reminds me of Neverwinter, but aside from the appearance that is a lie.
The story is pretty typical where you have an evil god and the rest are fighting against him. The 'chosen' humans get involved and do the work for the good gods and defeat the evil god. And then plot twist. I didn't run into any bugs or plot holes, but the character builds are skewed badly. I don't regret kickstarting this but I do regret not cheating earlier.
Pros:
- Details of expected plot twist are unexpected
- No bugs
- Shop prices are typically good
- Scrolls and skill books to offset magic uselessness
- Going over the weight limit doesn't actually cause any problems
- Skills (eventually) become available to help(-ish) offset the stat issues
- Multitudes of skills
- Pretty graphics
Cons:
- Character stats are unbalanced (SPD and AGL should have just been rolled into DEX. And why would CON affect your carry weight instead of STR?)
- Magic is useless - persistently low MP pool on all characters, high MP costs for low damage. And the only thing the 'magic' stat affects is the MP pool
- Predictable plot twist
- Preachy and obedient main character (I really hate zealots)
- Not enough skill points per level - when skills can cost 4+ and you only get 4/lvl?
- Skill point trainers instead of skill trainers, and the gold requirement rises exponentially
- Food - I like being able to rest and heal, but you lose food too quickly to make later (mandatory) areas anything but a grind
Recommendations to anyone playing:
Use the editor to do the following:
- Drop the magic costs, and up the power
- Up the Divine Prayer, Energy Absorption, Exploration and Hunting level limits
- Up Divine Prayer secondary power rate and Energy Absorptions primary rate
- Increase the random encounter rate to 10 - this way you'll be able to actually clear an area without running out of food 6+ times
- Increase the food limit and drop the food consumption
- Up the Skill Points gained per level

This visual novel feature a male protagonist Kirill who ran errands for his brother Shrapnel. With his father Shatalin, a long-time communist party leader busy in his work amidst the backdrop of a revolution and change in leadership, Kirill is constantly harassed by thugs. While helping Shrapnel buy beer one day, Kirill happens to encounter Doc Ippolit, an eccentric scientist from another time period. After helping Doc Ippolit with several heavy sacks of grain, Kirill will also get to know Doc Ippolit's granddaughter Slava.
I have mixed opinions on this visual novel. Having played through and reached all endings in Dagestan Technology's first visual novel on Steam
, I would definitely say this visual novel is an improvement over the first visual novel. This game still has translation errors for those playing the game in English and the sprites for each character could definitely need more improvement (Slava looks more like a frump than a pretty girl). I also checked with a Russian friend in Steam and he complained that many of the negative reviews on this game were somewhat justified as it had a lot of inaccurate historical references.
On the plus side, I would definitely say that the game by using licensed music from Artek Elektronika is a great improvement and probably saved this visual novel from being just another forgettable visual novel I would uninstall after finishing this game. By also doing away with the arcade game in
, this game is also a short and easy visual novel to finish and get all achievements in less than 10 hours. I managed to get the game with soundtrack on discount in a bundle and I liked the soundtracks in this game enough to give this game a recommended review.
Overall, this game is recommended only for those who like or follow Artek Elektronika and the nice, uplifting techno music in the soundtrack DLC or for those who like a short easy game to finish and get all achievements in about 1-3 hours of reading. In which case, this game and soundtrack DLC bundle is recommended only when at large discount of approximately $1-2.

I played To The Moon- which is one of my favorite games of all time- before playing this game. So bear with me that I will be comparing the two, since the two games are based in the same universe.
A Bird Story is worth playing for the ending. It's heartfelt and has that same feel-goodness at the end that To The Moon had. And before I get to the negatives, bear in mind that my experience with this game as a whole was not negative.
A Bird Story had so many cutscenes that it can hardly be considered a game. It was an hour long but I felt like I interacted as the character for MAYBE ten to twenty minutes of that. I'm not even sure what the characters name was- I felt unattached. You aren't given any backstory.
I also disliked that the (small spoilers ahead for both games) memories the character in A Bird Story experiences are unrealistic. I may be nitpicking, but it's something that ruined it for me. At one point, the child flies away on a paper plane. In To The Moon, every memory given to Johnny was at least mostly realistic. It makes it seem like the two games should be in two different worlds, not the same.
As I said earlier, I enjoyed A Bird Story for the ending and also the soundtrack was lovely. It's one of those games you wouldn't reccomend to your friends but you'd probably give them a summary of the story over tea.
I'm going to say I reccommend this for those of you interested in the style of Freebird Games, but on terms of gameplay- it doesn't even shine a light on To The Moon. Expect more of a show than a game and- if you can find the patience to get through it- don't expect you'll ever play it again.

This game can get very repetitive and the rig battles take a lot of the enjoyment out of the gameplay. Completing missions often involves following guided points to a location, completing the objective, and then walking all the way back to base for the next mission. Returning back can take as much as 10-15 minutes sometimes. Getting fast travel at base helps this some, but does not completely deal with this problem. Combat is farily repetitive and enemies are rarely unique in form or attacks. Once a boss encounter occurs you often fight the same boss 2-4 times in a row to complete the objective. Rig battles consist of your character moving around in a mech without any guns. You claw, punch and drill enemies to kill them. The problem lies in the slowness of the mech unit with its attacks. Often times an enemy can get in 2 or 3 attacks before you can effectively get in a single blow. These battles often consist of QTE (quick time events) to beat the enemy which means you can't just pummel the enemy into submission despite having the tools to do so; it requires a certain repeatable pattern for each enemy type. I often found it easier to get out of the mech and fight on foot. I got this game for $0.25 as part of a bundle, but I wouldn't recommend it because it is too repetitive to get enjoyment out of.

First off I recommend to anyone to play the demo/old versions which are availible for free before making this purchase, keep in mind those versions are really buggy.
Arts design is great in my opinion factions are varied enough to distinguish one faction from another, however UI leaves much to be desired and becomes hard to manage later on when you have an empire of ships. Events are well thought out, and provide good universe story telling I haven't seen all of them but I hope there are more in future updates. Music is fine I personally am not crazy about it, but I see it's appeal. Stability wise I've run into a crash or an error for every 4ish hours of leaving the game running since the last patch.
Focusing on the 4 x aspects:
Economy in the game is modelled pretty well and tied to the questing system and the player feels like you are actually a part of the economy, however some factions feel too player dependant and fail to keep up with other factions unless actively supported. Automation makes it easy to manage your faction and allows you to work on a variety of tasks as the player without having to micro every ship.
I really enjoyed combat, once familiar with the controls battles become much easier but still manage to stay interesting. Combat requires skill, I was able to take down 2 capital ships, a carrier and it's escort with a single fast cruiser, and I have lost player controlled capital ships to fighters.
I recommend tutorials for empire building if you are new to these types of games,I jumped right in because I am used to space 4x games and it took me an hour to figure out that I needed to transfer funds from trades into other parts of the economy to build stations. Empire building is also interesting.
If you want to play a rags to riches game and stay fairly neutral, you want to focus on taking an open system as soon as possible peacefully, as the other empires grow fast. However pirates and the antagonst faction grow too fast in my opinion.
Exploration leaves much to be desired, which ties into the event/questing systems. More unique events triggered by exploring a certain number of places or finding artifacts, would really serve this game well. There is so much potential for exploration that the dev has not yet explored in the current version, scouting/exploration quests would be really nice.
Game of the year for me. This is probably my favorite game. I will be playing this game years.

Review as of patch 1.2.0.5 at 29.02.2016:
Hey, I am not a native english-speaker so please go easy on any typos you may find :-)
I bought the game at the initial steam release and had a lot of crashes. Then I set the game to run in Direct X 9 Legacy mode which helped a lot for me and I get barely any crashes at all.
The good about the game is... if you can run it, its pretty fun. The price tag of 11,99 Euro atm is in my opinion set too high, since the game has still some serious crashes (can still not go to game settings from ingame and have to use the game settings out of game before starting the game to change things). Also the economy and number of ships is not nearly as complex as for example a X-series game (which the game creator is a modder of). I think the game still lacks a lot of content and it could need a more fleshed out economy. Also the battles are a lot too fast... sure there is a combat mod that makes some changes, so that combat is slower and more meaningful than just pewpew boom battleship gone, but I think the core game should also lean a lot more in such a direction, basically more away from that arcady feeling and more to a full-scale 4x where you have a slow build-up and your bases and economy has a bigger meaning. It would be also nice to do more with your own sectors when you have some... as far as it is atm you build stations into your sectors and thats pretty much it... I would like to have more defence structures, maybe even minefields and such... I would like to be able to customise the automated patrolships in my sector (amount and kind of and such) maybe that could be also imbued by adding for example a fleet headquarter for stronger patrols and fighter bases for more smaller patrols or something like that.
All in all the game has a good idea behind it. The technical execution is not that good atm, it needs quite more polishing.  Also it needs a lot more base game content, sure the game is heavily modable and modders already did come up with smaller mods but to get more people into the game (and more bigger mods in the end) it would be good to lure in a bigger audience with more and of course more fleshed out content. What would also help to make the economy more meaningful... make ship building for the own faction and the AI more complex and as I said combat slower and more meaningful. Give players and AI more tools to protect their assets and add more content in general (would like a lot more ship types like corvettes, cruisers with different niches and something bigger than a battleship maybe to have as a flagship). Thats in my opinion what would help this game a lot and take it from "oh a small nice game that I play for a few hours" to "WOW... and its also heavily modable... I am so gonna make a mod for it and play that game forever".
I know as a user its always kind of easy to point out the weaker parts of a game and say "oh that needs more work" and all. Still keep in mind this is a one man show and he is fixing as fast as possible and will add more content to it as far as I did read on the forums (and I believe him). The game will get there to be that masterpiece we all would like to have, but it still needs time and some deep balancing changes.
So... why a positive review?
If you want to help a dev in getting the game to a broader audience and dont mind the 11,99 Euro price tag you should jump in with both feet. If you have a lot of crashes and graphical odd behavior like me, try the Direct X9 legacy mode, helped me. Also I think you have to see this kind of game here as some kind of early access and not as finished triple A title.
So If you have no problem to get a game thats not labeled Early Access but should be, then buy... help the dev make it bigger and better with your money, feedback and maybe even mods (as far as I did read he also needs more ship models and stations and such, if you have some or know how to make some, maybe contact him?)
If you mind buying a game for 12,99 Euro that needs quite some work (not meaning the content and content balance here, but especially the technical side), then wait a while and see how it turns out.
I think the game is worth playing. If you want to have a more polished experience its worth having it on your radar for a while and then jump in.

Unending Galaxy is a Sandbox RTS and Top-Down Shooter made by a former X series modder.
This description alone made me wanted to try it out over a year ago, and I've been coming back to it every few months since then. Mind that most of my play time wasn't logged on Steam.
In UG, you're free to pick your goal, map, gamestart and playstyle, or you can jump-in on the default settings and try to take over the galaxy!
On default, you start with one Transport (Trader) ship and one Cruiser (Combat) ship. This gives you a few opportunities:
- Automate your Trader (to trade automatically or to mine), and hunt bounties with your Cruiser.
- Automate your Cruiser (to hunt for bounties or raid ships), and perform trade and missions with your Transport.
- A few other options.. ;)
The game is full of such choices. When it comes to diplomacy, you could choose to turn a Galaxy full of hate in one full of peace, or simply turn it all into a free-for-all warzone!
As you build up your credits as an independent pilot and fleet commander, you'll eventually have enough money to buy a Dock Builder (Construction Ship), which will enable you to start your own empire, produce your own goods, own territory and construct ships for free with the Ship Parts you've produced yourself.
And again, you can choose wether to start taking over other empires through war, backstabbing or diplomacy.
Therefore, the strengths of the game really lie on its freedom, and on the ability to assign different roles to your ships by automating them with different AI modules (Trader, Miner, Police, Bounty Hunter, Military, Pirate Raider, Scavanger and maybe others). Building your empire and evading difficult situations through diplomacy is also fun, and finding different ways to deal with the challenges the game pit you against.
The problems lie at the fact the game is a niche game. There IS a learning curve, the controls and UI are not 100% intuitive to people who are not used with this genre and, even though the game has a very wide scope, it was and is being developed by a single person - so bugs and issues were probably going to exist.
However, the developer has a great habit of fixing critical things first, listening to suggestions and continuously improving and polishing the game.
As you may've noticed, there were three patches in the first week after release, and the developer has plans for the future and planned improvements for different areas of the game, and will probably release a roadmap in a few days.
If you enjoy Sandbox, Empire-Building or Space-themed games, UG is a keeper!

Osiris is a beautiful game, with a dedicated development team. I played before some of the newer features, but unfortunately the game has surpased what my potato of a PC may produce.
That being said, when I got to play, the immersion was amazing. The team tried very hard on making sounds indicate things happening around you, while filling the inactive times with sounds that make sense. (Though when some new elements are added, their audio tends to initially be rough). It's hard to describe the first feeling of getting caught in the shadow of a towering monolith, getting scared of the sudden change and running into a crater just as a dust storm hits. Then you hear the roar.
The planet to planet system is awesome. The spaceship is by far my favorite vehicle. Plenty of times I left the infested planet surface, just to relax and hover around in space, or swing by Aziel for new sights (I hadn't ever built a permanent base there).
The native animals and battle are cool as well. Each animal you come across has a unique way of fighting. I love shooting the legs off a giant space crab/spider, but then having to turn around an jump on a container because something burrowed from below.
This game is awesome, and I'm very jealous of those of you who get to keep following the updates!

I've always liked the XCOM games but not to the point of obsession or lionization. That's why the initial negative hype before this came out never really phased me. In finally diggging into the meat of the game, I found something else - third-person tactical action in the vein of Rainbow Six/Ghost Recon, but with an environment that's personally a lot more appealing (especially as personal politics shifts to the point of not being able to enjoy Tom Clancy games for the subtext, but I digress).
There's some excellent design choices here too, with the UI, the period sets, the characters (even though your starting mission characters look like three older John Cenas), and the Sectoids and Outsiders and related technology. Some Mass Effect aesthetic in the dialogue wheels and some of the specificities of the tactical layout is welcome as well. Overall, it's worth checking out, especially if you liked the Clancy tac-action games, Hidden & Dangerous, or SWAT 4 and want something similar that's just divorced enough from military tropes.
Surprisingly good story, gameplay is decent characters (for the most part) are interesting.  Good game, recommend.

As an Avid Enemy Unknown and XCOM 2 player, I picked this game up because I had always thought an XCOM shooter game would be way cool. I was not dissapointed. BUT, it's imperative that you know that going into it, this is not so much an XCOM game as it is a shooter Stylized to be LIKE XCOM. Also it's in the 60s because why not. The story was alright, and explains how it *could* be part of the new XCOM universe, but honestly if you're looking for story driven games, there's much better out there (and if you're not, you can essentialy skip through the entire story part by just mashing the skip button and always choosing the lefternmost response). Listening to your squadmates talk gives a humerous aspect to the game, and although I've seen many complaints about it I had very few problems with the squadmate AI on my own run through the game. A few times they would find weird paths to do what I ordered them, or get stuck on a wall for a few seconds, but no serious problems. The gameplay is interesting enough that I could see myself replaying it eventually. Very fun, but a pretty short game (get it on sale unless you REALLY want it). All in all, a very fun time and worth the price.
I'd also like to mention, I played this game entirely with a USB ported XBOX-360 controller, NOT a keyboard and mouse. I've heard terrible things about how the game handles with those, so be forwarned you might have to rebind some stuff to get a good control scheme on Keyboards.

Dishonored is one of the best games to come out this decade. In fact, if it wasn't for the Deus Ex Series, it would be my favourite game ever, and I was actually quite blown away by how good it was when I first played it.
Speaking of the Deus Ex series, there are many similarities between Dishonored and the Deus Ex games. The game is meant to be played stealthily, with minimal casualties, but you can play the game like John Wick if you really want. Another similarity between Dishonored  and the Deus Ex games are the RPG elements that the game includes. Neither of these games are outright RPGs, but they both allow you to upgrade your abilities through Augmentations or, in Dishonored's case, Rune Powers. Rune Powers can be unlocked by finding Runes in the gameworld, similar to Praxis kits in Deus Ex: Human Revolution, which is a nice touch and does a lot to encourage exploration, which is one of the game's most enjoyable elements. Thanks to the Blink power, you can teleport over short distances and climb onto almost any surface, which I spent hours doing, and often find multiple ways into the same building. One memorable moment featured  the player being able to run across the top of a very high bridge, and the whole experience is the sort of thing Assassin's Creed developers wish they could emulate.
When you're not exploring the world of Dunwall, you'll be completing mission objectives in a multitude of different ways. If you are required to bypass a Wall Of Light, you could climb over it, disable it, or even stop time and walk right through it. This sort of variety carries over to enemy encounters. If you're going for a non-lethal stealth playthrough, you could sneak past the guards, distract them by throwing something or knock them out silently for a harmless takedown. If you're playing lethally, you can stealthily assassinate them or confront them in open combat. Every aspect of the gameplay is very polished and fluid, making it very satisfying.
The story is a classic revenge plot. You play as a guy called Corvo Attano, who's just come back from an important diplomatic mission asking for help about a devastating plague that has swept across Dunwall, and just as you've delivered the results to the empress, she's murdered and you get framed for it while the people who had her killed take power. What follows is a dramatic prison escape before you begin a relentless, revenge-fueled crusade to bring the true villains to justice. I won't spoil any more because there's a significant plot twist halfway through the game, but the plot isn't the most original in the world. What is original, however, is the setting. The city of Dunwall is like a Victorian Steampunk Naval-themed place and the aesthetic is like a moving painting. This setting is very similar to the Thief series, which was made by a lot of the same people who made Dishonored, and the Thief influences can be seen everywhere, from the mumbling guards to the made-up swear words. In fact, during the section where you're escaping from a group of assassins who just captured you, there's a room where a trainee assassin is being instructed in the art of stealth using EXACTLY THE SAME WORDS as Garrett's mentor uses in the training section of Thief: The Dark Project, which was a nice touch. The soundtrack is decent as well and the voice acting is very good and features some notable actors.
Overall, Dishonored is easily one of the best games in recent memory. Is it worth a purchase? Never doubt it.

While my initial Impression of Lords of Xulima was not positive as there didn't seem to be much Role Playing aspect to it my opinion of it kept improving as I played the game. The game is a roguelike “auto-battle” RPG. Each floor is procedurally generated with a random placement of monsters and treasures. The monsters don’t move and you simply move into a monster to begin fighting it.
This may seem shallow at first but very quickly becomes addicting as the real depth of the game comes from customizing your equipment set and its enchantments. Stats such as bonus damage, health regen, mana regen, and resistances have to be balanced appropriately to play the game effectively.
The game is fairly simple but despite this remained very engrossing for a long time. I always wanted to push farther to see what better gear would drop.
-Playtime-
I think a good 10 hours before completing it the first time. The game has an infinite New Game+ which can be completed and then started again at an even higher difficulty each time.
-Achievements-
The biggest achievement was getting Completionist where you have to fill in the museum with every artifact piece of equipment. This took quite a bit of farming but I found it fun as it was just a perpetual treasure hunt and it was always exciting to open an artifact chest to see if it had an item I was missing. If you are trying for this achievement however I highly recommend that you don’t start the New Game+ as it brings a pretty large difficulty spike and will greatly slow down your farming time, especially on the lower levels. There are also achievements for maxing each of the 3 skill trees but I would recommend getting the 3rd one on a new character, otherwise be prepared for a massive grind as the exp needed to level scales up quite a bit toward the end.
Recommended at full price.

The Enchanted Cave 2 is a light, fun dungeon crawler. Your quest covers 100 levels, and you can only save certain gear as you progress. You make multiple runs of the cave, and you get different loot as you go. The loot can be nicely customised by other items that you find as you travel. Those items can either enhance gear, or be turned into potions. That's an excellent feature, and it means you're rewarded by using different combinations of ingredients. If you're on level 80 and you have a ton of starting ingredients, you can just turn them into potions and get some good effects.
If you're careful, you won't die in the game and your character just keeps getting better and better. It took me 25 hours to play through the game and I haven't had a character die. Since then, I have started the new game + mode, but the gear all seems really basic so I'm not sure if there's much point continuing.
I certainly enjoyed the game. It's a simple game at its core, but it has enough customisation of gear, and enough skills, that the game has a surprising amount of depth.

Although the learning curve on this game is somewhat high due to a lack of current or complete documentation (still in devlopement), I find Unending Galaxy (UG) to be a refreshing 4X game with a challenging AI, broad spectrum of potential scenarios and replayability, and just plain fun to play.  Once a player understands the controls, it is comparitively quick to play compared to other 4X games and yet still has a great deal of depth and a range of options for playability for various styles.    For a person like me who has a lot of personal demands upon my time, this has been a great way to feed my 4X game appetite.    I feel like in my dozens of hours of game play that I have hardly hit the surface of the game on many levels, and yet, the economic system and combat are straightforward and fast.  At times, I micromanage as much as possible while at others, I put my ships on autopilot and sit back and watch the action.    It has the feel of a universe which I am still exploring...and a game which will occupy many hours and days of my time.

This game reminds me a lot of how the X series games play along with some Distant Worlds and some top down space shooter added in.  It doesn't have cutting edge 3D graphics, but the aesthetic still feels great, the art is smooth yet crisp.  While it does use a lot of the ship assets from AI War, they still manage to feel fresh and don't detract from the value of the game at all.
From starting with a full empire to play it as a 4X strategy game, to starting with a small fleet or even a single ship to make it feel more like a sim, there is something here for you if you enjoy these types of games. There are 11 Starting Scenarios, 7 total handcrafted non-tutorial maps, a procedural map generator and a faction customizer which ends up offering a lot of replayability.  You can have a small knife fight galaxy or a huge 1800+ sector sandbox universe plus many other variable to fine tune how you want the universe to ultimately run.
I feel the music is standard for a small indie studio and I feel the sound effects could be better, but neither really detract from the gameplay and they are satisfactory.  Not too much to suggest here as I know how expensive these assets can be to acquire if you want superb and unique non-library music/effects.
To me, the game is great, I've had quite a bit of fun just trying out different starts and seeing what the gameplay has to offer both on the 4X end and the sim end.  At the basic level, it's very much trade, fight, build, think with the opportunity to play it as a nearly full featured 4X.  I say nearly because obviously some things are missing, like a researchable tech tree.  Your tech is actually pre-determined while setting up the game.  I do not feel that this takes away from the experience whatsoever, but it could for you if you prefer the traditional research trees.
One of the great aspects of the game is, like Distant Worlds, you can automate a lot of tasks and though it does not reach the level of Distant Worlds, it's not as complicated as that game either so it does not need as much.  For me, it is the right amount.  If you don't like all that automation, you can of course control everything yourself, you can even create control groups and play it as a typical RTS, right clicking your attack groups to wherever you like.
The biggest common complaint that I see popping up is the depth of the tutorial.  While for me personally, I felt it was fine and was able to easily figure out whatever was not answered in the tutorial simply by playing, I do understand that this is an issue for those not used to this type of gameplay.  It's important to note that this is on the list of things to fix along with the other issues.
Aside from the readability of the text font on my screen (which I have been able to work around thanks to some help), I do not have any big complaints about this game that would warrant a thumbs down.  In fact, quite the opposite as you can see.  The sheer fun of the game, the option to play it in different ways, the helpfulness of the developer, and the price (a steal in my opinion), this is a fine entry to the 4X Strategy/Space-Sim market.

My reviews are quite simple. I take all the aspects worth noting and just discuss them without any bias or long lists of pros and cons. Now, This game is EXACTLY what ive been looking for in modern space sims, This is what so many have wanted and finally theres a game where you can start off as a merchant flying one ship, and eventually play the game like an RTS once youve built a huge empire. Your decisions you make when trading, being a pirate, building stations, it all matters, because you can become a major player on the stage and interact with the other huge factions. Were you a pirate near the federation territory? Well theyll probably declare war on your affiliated faction. The frontlines will move from sector to sector as you see actual soverign territory being claimed by the stronger of the factions. As for the economic side, Im familiar with making money and managing assets but have not had an extremely long and drawn out game to see if it has any kinks, so far, so good in that aspect. The state of the game, is moderately buggy, but its not unplayable. The occasional crashes/freezes happen, but my autosave saves the day and theres already been a number of patches out since release. I could go further in depth about this game, but ill simplify it questions. Do you like X3? Do you wish that X3's universe would actually change? Do you wish you could have an impact on politics after youve become a quintillionaire? Do you want youre grinding as a trader/mercenary/bounty hunter/etc. to mean something? If you said yes to all these questions, then BUY THIS GAME.

Portal is an incredible journey through Apeture Science Laboratories. I know who you play as, and I know many facts about this game, but for the sake of reviewing just THIS game, I will review this as if I've only played through the first game.
You are a new test subject in Apeture Science Labs, testing the Portal gun (which is worth more than all the people in Subject Town 1 combined!) You will be going through 19 incredible puzzles, while being accompanied by GLaDOS, a computer/robot that appears to be in charge of running the experiments.
For those looking for a quick review, here you go. Portal is funny, entertaining, challenging, but not too difficult to the point you get angry. It's got a small story to follow, it's not too long, and the music is incredible. You will love this if you're even slightly a fan of puzzle games.
Now, for those looking for the full review, let's get into it.
One quick thing to note: I love first-person Valve games like Half-Life and Portal because they contain environmental puzzles, and I absolutely love these. They are far more entertaining than puzzles normally found in games. I struggle to explain this, but if you've played through Half-Life/Half-Life 2, you'll know what I mean. The puzzles are built into the area around you, and the puzzle is trying to get past an obstacle.
Now, I don't have a bunch to say about this game, because it is a rather short game (unless you attempt the Bonus Maps, which I'll talk about later). Still, this game is incredible for a few reasons. This game is humorous. GLaDOS is a very strange, creepy companion-ish robot that guides you through the puzzles. As you progress through, she begins to sound more corrupted and strange, and you'll learn what's going on once you reach the end of the game, which I am not spoiling. Even when she does sound more distorted, she has satire comments to give you, and it's all hilarious.
The puzzles themselves are a blast, and are the highlight of this game. There are multiple types of puzzles, and the obvious thing that makes this game different than others is the fact that you have a Portal Gun. This weapon allows you to create two portals, which connect to each other. This leads to a lot of physics-based and momentum puzzles. The puzzles are rather easy, while still being challenging in the sense that you will have to think about some, but not to the point that you get frustrated with it.
There's 19 test chambers, not counting the multiple puzzles within the innerworkings of the lab. There's plenty of hidden secrets and references in this game. There's secret areas where a mysterious man tries to explain how the cake that GLaDOS taunts the player with is a lie, in the sense that she is trying to kill you. He's a crazy man who managed to break into the innerworkings of the test chambers. While doing this, he had a Companion Cube with him, which he fell in love with. So clearly, he's crazy, and it's up to you whether or not you believe him when his scribbles say that GLaDOS is lying to you.
I didn't go in depth on the puzzles for the simple fact that they're all unique, and it's something better experienced, rather than read. The same goes for the music, which is absolutely amazing. The highlight song of the game though is "Still Alive" which plays during the credits, and reveals more information about GLaDOS. This song is catchy, and sounds incredible.
Now, as far as completion rewards, there's achievments, which are always satisfying. You get a new Main Menu scene for when you beat the game, which is nice. You also have access to all of the Bonus Challenges, which is where most of your time in this game will come from.
The Bonus Challenges come in three catagories- Least Portals, Least Steps, and Least Time. You can do these challenges for Chambers 13-18, and earn all Gold rankings on them, which gives you some more achievments. I personally haven't finished completing them all, but it's something fun to do if you really love this game.
To conclude, I loved this game from start to finish. There was never a dull moment, or a time where I was getting bored. I also like the fact that it's short enough to complete in one sitting. The puzzles are a blast, GLaDOS is hilarious, and the music is great. I'd gladly give Portal a
.

I've replayed this game more than I'd like to admit. It's one of my favourite games.
You play as Corvo Attano, the personal Bodyguard of the Queen of Dunwall.
After being attacked by assassins, she gets killed, her daughter kidnapped and you get blamed for it.
The game revolves around rescuing little Emily, taking over the Empire and taking revenge on those who caused the Queen's death to begin with.
The gameplay is split into two parts, Stealth and Action.
You can just run in and kill everyone or you can just avoid conflict altogether,
however the game punishes you for killing people by giving you a bad ending.
Killing everyone stealthily is probably the most fun play-style, because of the different abilities that Corvo can learn by using Runes, which are scattered all over the levels.
It's kind of weird that they give you a cop out for killing,
even though they provide you with so many options on how to kill more effectively.
Combat is simple and fairly easy. Even on harder difficulties, you mainly just block and spam the left mouse button.
There are Gadgets that can break up the monotony though, like Grenades, Guns and Traps.
Your abilities also come in handy, as you can stop time itself, spawn rats and shoot gusts of wind out of your fingertips.
I wouldn't recommend it for the combat though. The stealth part is the clear focus of this game.
The AI can be wonky at times, but the higher difficulties help fix that.
A big element of this game is teleporting, and although it doesn't sound that important, trust me, it is.
Not only does the teleport give you a vertical approach (meaning that you can quickly climb onto rooftops by teleporting on to them), but it also provides you with extra mobility on how you approach things.
Something that has always bothered me in Stealth games is how slow they can be sometimes.
In this game, you dont slowly sneak up to a guard. No.
YOU TELEPORT BEHIND HIM. YOU CHOKE HIM UNCONSCIOUS. YOU GRAB HIM AND ZOOM THE HELL OUTTA THERE.
It works so well. Taking out guards one by one feels fantastic. Not only does the protagonist's walk speed matter into this, but not having to carry a guard for 300 miles into a hiding spot feels so good. In most stealth games, well, "stealthing" feels like a burden. Arkane Studios completely nailed it here. It's the game's major strength.
The game's story has a few twists and turns, but is mostly forgettable.
Something that it does wonderfully though is setting up setpieces.
A really cool level, for example, is the Masquerade Ball.
In this mission you have to assassinate one of three sisters, only problem is, they wear matching costumes.
You walk into the mansion and everything is filled with color. The floor's marble-white, the walls are golden, plastered with paintings. It's such a contrast from the gritty, dark and diseased outside world.
So you walk these golden halls, talk to guests and sneak into forbidden territory trying to find out which sister you're supposed to kill. Or you can just kill all of them. Or you can just kill everyone. Or you can spare her.
This is just one of many. There are also some side quests you can do for some extra loot.
The soundtrack isn't very memorable, however it isn't annoying and there just isn't much room for a lot of melodies in a game about being sneaky.
The graphics, well. Faces look... bad. I generally do like the whalepunk aesthetic though and the game runs fantastic (unlike its successor, smh).
Replayability is there, since trying out different playstyles on various difficulties is a blast...
If there weren't those intro sequences. Let me elaborate.
Every time you start a mission you have to watch the boatsman sail you to the level while he chats with you for a little bit.
After replaying the game for the, what I can only assume, 10th time, these get really annoying.
That's my only gripe with the replayablity though. There aren't any cutscenes during gameplay. No QTEs, No Dialog. Only pure game.
Another thing that gets really annoying is the hubworld. After every mission you're transported back to the hubworld (and yeah, you also have to watch the boatsman sail you there. By the way, have I mentioned that these scenes are unskippable?). Here you have to talk to some dudes who mostly repeat themselves after every mission ("You did good, Corvo. We're one step closer to taking over the Empire!"). Sometimes you have to do some dumb sidequests there too, like jumping in a sewer and killing two zombies. These parts not only slow the gameplay down, but they're not very fun or engaging. You mainly just talk to people until they let you play the next mission.
The only really interesting thing there is the shopkeeper. Here you can buy Weapon upgrades, potions, ammunition and runes. However, in the DLC, they got rid of a hubworld altogether and literally just give you the shop screen before starting a mission. I don't understand why they didn't do that in the main game. Maybe they learned from their mistakes, I don't know.
Mentioning the DLCs, I've only played one of them. It was kinda cool, but not as interesting as the main game, since it didn't really provide any interesting levels or locations.
If you're really interested in the DLCs, go look at some Steam Reviews on their respective store pages, can't really help you with that, sorry.

Wow, just finished my first (and probably last *cough*) playthrough of Lords of Xulima. Took me about 80 hours of my lifetime, spread over like, eeeh, 9 months or so... I had abandoned this game multiple times due to unbearable frustration caused by, well, you will see :D
I'm gonna start with some basic stuff about the
: you play "Gaulen, the Explorer" and his five ever loyal companions (which can be predefined or custom made). Gaulen is chosen by some god-dude to go on an epic quest to... urgh, jeez, go read some wiki or whatever -.-' Just be assured that the plot could hardly be any more all-out and important and epic and fate determining and... monotonous :\ Did you ever watch any crime series on TV? There's always a murder at the beginning, 40 Minutes later justice is spoken, episode's over, see ya next time. Ah yes, and of course there is some super-important plot swirling around in the background, like the inspector, who's actually a writer, is in love with his female partner or something! Thats pretty much how Lords of Xulima feels: do the same thing over and over, watch some storypieces drop by every now and then. So if you are into unforeseeable plottwists and non-linear stories, don't expect too much here! Don't get me wrong, the game does have a really nice handcrafted lore in which the story takes place, it's just your activities in it which are rather repetitive.
Mentioning the lore leads me to tell you about the
. Xulima is an island, it can be traveled in its entirety and is devided into several regions. Despite its size Xulima shows a lot of diversity, from icy snow lands, over lush meadows to dried sand deserts, everything's there. Each region has its own map and is connected to neighbouring ones. Traveling between regions can be done via those connections or through portals, which of course have to be activated before they can be used. Your party, represented by Gaulen, is moved around the maps by clicking or by use of the arrow keys. Talk to NPCs, explore dungeons, collect treasures and do all the other fancy RPG-stuff, but always watch your food supplies! Food adds a strategic element to traveling the world of Xulima, as it is needed to replenish your party after a though fight, or simply to travel the world without an empty stomach (which otherwise causes debuffs and over-time damage, jeey ^^). Xulima is not all open-worlded though, while you could theoretically go anywhere you want to from the very beginning, the game prevents you from doing so by placing undefeatable enemy squads in your way. Sounds cheap, but this is actually a major part of the challenge posed by the game. Finding your way around and opening new paths is one of the dominant early game activities (and really really sucks at some times, you gonna want to quit, believe me).
Now enough about exploration, let's face
! Might! Magic! Hit chances! Critical fails! Spell failures! Over-time damage! Action modifiers! Inabillity to act! Curses! Death! Frustation! Fighting is a big part of Lords of Xulima. You will have to fight handplaced enemy parties as well as random encounters. The battle system is actually quite simple: every fighter takes his turn in order of the action que and can then perform a single action, like attacking, casting a spell or using an item. "Buh, lame!" , ok wait, wait, theres more to it. This game has the most exaggerated amount of bad status effects and things that could possibly go wrong I have seen in any video game yet. Well, of course there's poison and bleeding and burning doing some nice over-time damage, stun or freeze to prevent combatants from acting, or maybe one of your heroes just goes crazy and clobbers his allies, thats of course only if he's not too heavily wounded to get anything right in the first place! And then there are critical fails, actions that fail so hard, that the character attempting it actually hurts himself. Imagine your mage spent a huge amount of power points (thats what you need to perform skills and spells) to cast his most deluxe spell, that would turn the tides of battle in your favor and then it just... FAILS! ... *fizzle*, power points gone, caster takes damage, battle is lost, hurray! Even your bard tends to fail singing songs so hard that he manages to hurt himself (go find an other job pal)! But at least once the battle is over, all the pain is forgotten, well except for lost health and power points, wounds, critical wounds, sicknesses and curses... take a 24h rest, not like food is rare and expensive, and don't mind those sicknesses and curses, the kind priestesses will glady lift them from you for, like, all of your money -.-
I don't want to say a lot more about this game, these were the crucial aspects that come to my mind when I think back on my playthrough. But wait, this review sounded quite negative so far, still I'm recommending Lords of Xulima! Why? Here goes the
:
It is an excellent video game! Period! Maybe I'm not the most representive gamer on earth, but thats how I feel about it. If you like games that hold your hand, show you your way around with questmarkers and let you swap difficulty if a boss is too hard, Lords of Xulima is not for you. This game hates you! It hates you and it lets you know! You will have to think about how to set up your party and how to skill them, farm for level-ups to get bosses down, solve puzzels connected to the games lore and endure a lot of frustration. But to manage your way through all those seemingly undeaftable bosses and unsolveable puzzles feels so incredibly rewarding, that you will not want to miss the experience of having played Lords of Xulima!!!1one11!!eleven1!

just completed this game logging 134 hours on normal  difficulty, which was, believe me, tuff enough. LOX is like a  90's style  turn- based combat RPG; Wizardry, Baldurs Gate, Disciples and Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick come to mind, but Lords of Xulima is its own thing-unique in many ways,  Don't be to put off by the trailer video...You can toggle run, which is a good thing because there is a much to explore and many secrets to discover on the huge and colorfull maps. The graphics are not the trendy low res look-more like medium res, highly stylized and artfully done. The combat is simple, fun and highly tactical. Your party of 6 is represented by their portraits arranged in battle postions at the bottom of the screen, with the enemy troops arrayed above. Each combatant's turn is determined by their speed, or if they are stunned or frozen, etc.  Chose your unit's spell or potion or by default their weapon and select an enemy unit that is within reach to attack. Resource management is crutial. Your gold, loot, food iand experience is hard earned. A few times during the game I thought I might actually lose, because I did not fully understand the ecomomy of the game so wasted too many resourses, thus was too weak to defeat powerfull enemies that blocked my progress. Struggle on and you wil be rewarded in the end.

Checking the steam score I had very low expectations with The Bureau. However, after finishing the game the final impression is positive. For sure it is not an excellent 3rd-person tactical shooter but also not a fiasco. If someone expects stratetic elements of the original Xcom titles he/she will be underwhelmed. But from my perspective the same is more or less true for the new Xcom games: while very good turn-based strategy titles they are nowhere near as perfect as the original masterpiece of the 1994.
Pros:
+ excellent graphics for models and environment, very concincing lighting effects
+ very good soundtrack
+ variety of skills, weapons and team members to choose from
+ nice recreation of the sixties
+ interesting idea to walk/interact inside the base you build in the Xcom games
+ story is, on average, good with some nice twists
+ cover seems to work, same of team coordination although player actions have a much greater role than companions`.
Cons:
- I did not quite liked the introduction with the alien invasion and the plot seems to be played in fast forward at some instances. From the story perspective it feels like a sequel to a game we never played. I would prefer much more focusing on "first contact", i.e. early missions from the very beginning of the alien attack, searching crashed or landed ufos. The game starts from the middle or from near the end of the plot. Xcom organization gets hold of very advanced alien tech too early and too fast in the game.
- some important pacing issues. Parts in the missions include lots of walking without doing anything. A lot of back and forth is happening inside the base without any obvious reason. Running inside the base could be a good idea.
- Some ideas/concepts seem incomplete. For example there are dialogue options without changing something in the main story line. You find some logs, infos etc but again they play little to no role.
- Alien environment seems a bit repeated and boring compared to the earth setting.
- sometimes AI players seem to follow strange paths leading to suicide.
- veteran difficulty seems quite steep especially in confined environments (but you can change it).
- some aspects of the main plot are left unexplained (what happened to Carter?) or are not very believable (the whole USA got invaded and almost obliterated by the aliens but eventially the goverment managed to cover everything up?)
No comment on the DLCs as I have not bought/played them. DLCs with weapons etc leave me completely uninterested.
All in all a flawed but still interesting squad-based action game. It plays in the Xcom universe but is very different from the turn-based strategy games. Recommended, especially at discount.

Like many, I was touched by Freebird Games' first game 'To The Moon', one of the most emotional games I have ever played. So how does "A Bird Story" stack up compared to that game?
As you have probably already seen in the screenshots, both games are made in RPGmaker. Most people either love or hate RPGmaker games, personally I do not really care as long as the game is good.
Aside from the graphics, A Bird Story does differ a lot from To The Moon. The first difference is the length of the game, To The Moon was not a very long game but it still was a lot longer than A Bird Story, which only should take you one hour to complete. Second difference is there are no conversations, unlike To The Moon where you would get sucked in the story, A Bird Story takes on a different, more art-like story.
The third difference is that A Bird Story is a 'feel good' game and no tearjerker like To The Moon.
So yes, both games differ quite a lot from each other, which is not a bad thing. Both games are good in their own way, you just should not expect a game like To The Moon, even though it has some moments that reminds you of To The Moon.
Overall 'A Bird Story' is recommended to anyone who enjoys 'art' games and want a nice 1-hour experience.

To get this out of the way in advance- I don't know how I spent 20+ hours on this game. I took a lot of time trying to justify this purchase and find something good in this game but I instead burned out fast. Also I left it running in the background while I did other stuff, but we'll get to that later.
Apparently, this game has gotten a little better than when it launched, as it's at least a stable, running program that does what it's meant to with some degree of consistency. This has had the unfortunate side effect of revealing it to be a poorly designed and thought out game on several other levels. A lot of things in this game, from the stock Unity pregame config menu to the bizarre use of the English language, lead me to believe that this is less a project someone worked on because they wanted to and more a product hastily thrown together for commercial release.
Character creation is arguably worse than nonexistant. There is a character creator at game start, but you just shuffle through random selections until you find the one you want. This is made a little easier by how limited the selections are, and also how little they matter, as you'll see little of your own character in this game. You have direct control of where the Captain goes and who they attack and that's about it. You need the captain nearby to open chests and dig holes but they're otherwise a regular crewmember. If your Captain dies, they're unceremoniously replaced by another nearby crewmember. You might not even realize it happened, and realistically, even if you do it won't notice unless you were particularly attached to your starting character.
The central idea is that you build a ship and sail around, destroying other ships, looting and generally doing pirate-y things. There are towns, islands and other ships scattered around the world, and as you sail further towards the edges of the world, enemy encounters increase in difficulty. The problem is that this "difficulty" is entirely contrived. Enemies get bigger ships and more crew members for the first few levels, but around rank 5 the ships start to get samey. Coincidentally, this is the rank at which cannon combat becomes a major factor, necessitating a 30-second wait before boarding can begin. The fact that you can't control your gunners' targets and that their AI occasionally locks up for the entire phase doesn't help. Eventually all that increases is the level of the enemies you fight, and by that I mean their HP- and, more troubling, their tendency to know a skill that causes them to violently detonate on death. Otherwise they're not much of a threat- a team of four with decent stats and good weapon experience can handle most ships in the game with no meaningful injuries.
In combat, you have almost no control. You can try to direct your captain and crew to attack specific enemies, but they seem to just do as they please, usually aggroing onto enemies that attack them. Since ranged weapons can hit through walls, this means they get juggled between targets a lot and spend much of a boarding operation pathfinding up and down ladders. Trying to watch what's actually happening is meaningless, because the already tiny characters will bunch onto the exact same location. It's actually easier to just watch the equally tiny readout at the bottom of the screen to see if any of your crew has died, and wait for the sound that indicates that all the enemies are dead.
There's also islands, and that's about all I can say about that. They have enemies on them and items you can activate. There is one that can be exploited to gain a ton of TP over and over, but for the most part the gains are miniscule. Having to kill thirty natives just to get to two coconuts and a chest with 15 gold in it is less than busy work. A few interesting things are set to happen on islands, but few actually do because of how badly optimized the game is. Far too many times I fought an islander, reduced them to near-death and saw the screen go dark with the prompt for them to surrender and join your crew, only for them to die because the prompt took ten seconds or more to appear. Islands also have treasure that you can dig up with a shovel that costs more than several cannons. Most of these treasures are garbage, but using treasure maps you can dig up some interesting equipment, and in attempting to use it you'll have to do battle with the game's interface.
So much of the game is reliant on your pirates, so the menu for equipping and leveling them shouldn't be so much of a mess. All pirates are sorted manually into groups that determine how they're used- the player can never select individual pirates other than the Captain, only entire groups at once. Your crew also never use their skills naturally, as their AI is entirely determined by what group you put them in. This almost entirely means that Ship Crew is the only useful group, as they prepare food and clean♥♥♥♥♥♥off the decks, which is 90% of sailing really- the Training, Gunnery and Boarder groups are only useful if you have a handful of specific items placed on your ship, and presumably Custom 1 (of one) just idles until they get hungry or given a kill order. The problem is that these groups can only be changed by going into the crew management menu, which is a hot mess to say the least. The biggest problem by far is that after selecting a crew member, the only way to go back to the list of crew is to close and reopen the menu. There's no way to sort your crew at all, and the game's internal sorting seems arbitrary- your captain will often end up somewhere in the middle of the top row, even if they're consistently the highest leveled among your crew. This same menu is also how your crew uses items, and between the battle interface being literally unreadable and the menu being difficult to navigate, healing mid-fight is an impossible task.
So much of this game seems to have been added in because it was a popular game mechanic and not because it was actually considered in terms of meshing with the game. You can "plunder" towns by killing NPCs, but shopkeepers have normal pirate drops, so you're really just locking yourself out. Ships take damage from cannon fire, but enemy crews will just board you well before you deal enough damage, and when they're all dead you can blow the ship up automatically anyway, so really the damage to ships only affects the player ship. There are many different island types and a lot of rare encounters you can find, but they all boil down to "bump weapons with enemy until death".
By far, what sealed this for me- not just "this game is bad" but "I need to tell people this game is bad" is that this is all there is. The objective of the game is to defeat the four legendary pirates. They are placed at the corners of a square world, surrounded by rank 9 encounters. Sailing in this game is tedious- the game loads an empty encounter, adds a percentage to the top corner of the screen and makes you wait while it counts up to 100. Nothing happens while you sail but eating and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Events take place in between this, not during. Everything between point A and B is skipped. Enemy ships can interrupt your travel, but there's no pursuit or retreat, just an optional 60% chance to attempt to evade before you're stopped dead and forced to fight. You do this until you reach the corner and meet the game's final bosses- ships at about level 4, with the exception of a single pirate with 600+ HP. They die the same as any other enemy, and you're left in the far corner of the world with the knowledge that you have to do this all three more times.
Normally people say this kind of thing with hyperbole, but I entirely and earnestly mean it when I say that this game has caused deep levels of personal regret through my time with it. Looking for improvement made a passable game seem dry and tedious instead. If it were free, I would still not recommend it.

From the developers who brought the absolutely beautiful experience that was To The Moon, A Bird Story was set to be my next favorite narrative in gaming. Sadly, I found that it didn't live up to my own hype I had built for it.
When I finished To The Moon I was emotionally aching and affected to a degree I had not felt since Brothers. I expected the same thing from A Bird Story but the narrative just wasn't there. In a literal sense, the narrative was absent; the entire story is only told through visuals, music and the occasional thought bubble Sims style. One could easily (and justifiably) argue that Brothers also had no vocal narrative, but the difference is that A Bird Story’s story is either a bit too subtle and abstract or else is just overall very weak. The prior could be my own fault for not being able to pick out the nuances of the characters actions, but the latter felt like it was more the case. I want to love this game as much as I did To The Moon, but the narrative of this narrative only game is just not strong enough.
For a buck, A Bird Story is a cute little adventure with a boy and a bird, but I really don’t think the majority of players will get the quality of enjoyment out of it as they should.

A Bird Story is... well... a story... about a kid who befriends... a bird. It would be hard for me to say more without spoiling the story, which is the selling point of this game.
I love To the Moon, the previous game in this style by Freebird Games. It will hold a special place in my heart and I'll never forget my playthrough of it. I feel like A Bird Story aims to be just as emotional, but there is a simple fact that it simply cannot ignore: it's too short and does not have enough character development.
The necessarily slow transformation of humor into seriousness just doesn't have the time to occur, and the game feels like it doesn't know which way to go. The other thing that made To the Moon's formula special is the spot-on writing, which doesn't even have the chance to shine in A Bird Story because of how it's insistent on not containing a single piece of dialogue. The thing it does get right is the music.
The game also barely feels like a game. What little interactivity it offers boils down to moving your character, usually very, very slowly. It is truly difficult for me to write like this about a game that clearly evokes a touching story, but you cannot forget that a game should have a reason to be a game. The hinting that this was just a chapter of the protagonist's story makes me hope for more, but I urge the developer not to release every chapter separately for the same price.
In any case, it pains me greatly to say that I do not recommend this game. Pick it up only if you yearn for more in the style of To the Moon. If you haven't yet played To the Moon, play that instead.
