Portal is a first-person puzzle game developed and published by Valve and released in October 2007. You play as Chell, a female protagonist that completes testings for Aperture Science Laboratories. The game features a nineteen level campaign that allows you to solve puzzles. Solving each puzzle progresses you further into the story. This review will discuss the campaign, the levels, and gameplay.
Portal features a solid campaign that provides a good introduction to the world of the Laboratories. The game begins with an in-game tutorial introducing you to the portal gun, the tests and Glados, the antagonist AI computer. Portal excels at storytelling through the slow burn approach to the story. Certain sequences in the story subtly reveal major plot points such as what is Glados planning to do to Chell once she has completed her tests. These subtle hints provide excitement for those who have noticed them as it foreshadows the final scenes in the game. Portal 1 is less about story and more about introducing you to the environment. I get the vibe that this game is more like a prologue to Portal 2 because comparing Portal 1 to Portal 2, P2 expands on the gameplay and environment and emphasises the story whereas P1 introduces you to the setting, the characters, the type of gameplay, and the story. In saying that, I do really like the introduction to the characters as Glados is a refreshing computer personality in which gives the impression that robots control humans, or Glados controls Chell.
The campaign as mentioned includes nineteen levels and these levels are basic. It promotes creativity as the levels progressively become more difficult. However, I feel the majority of the levels are simple and relatively easy compared to the final five levels. The final five levels are challenging and they require more thinking, meaning they encourage more exploration on how to complete it. The levels are of good length. About 10 out of the 19 levels took some time to complete and it lengthened the game and made it more enjoyable because the overall campaign was short at under three hours. Portal features an 'advanced levels' mode which takes the final six levels of the campaign, reworks them and makes them much more difficult to complete. I did not play this mode because I prefer not to replay the same levels with no end goal. Generally though, it does add some variety and lasting appeal to the game for players.

The sad thing here is that, if you squint and look at the game just right, you can see its incredible potential. Unfortunately, that potential is currently unfulfilled. Several features that should have been in at launch, such as upgrading/refitting/converting naval vessels, military chains of command, ability to coordinate battle plans with allies, etc., are, at the time of this review, completely missing. The AI is badly incompetent, in both the grand scale and management of combat. While micromanaging your own troops alleviates some of that, it also results in constantly fighting the game, as it tries to send your troops around helter-skelter, and, obviously, does nothing to help the armies of the actual AI. And so on. All of these issues are representative of a game that badly needed several more months of development before release, and, somehow, still needs those same months of work after being released for over a year. The potential is there, but is not even close to being realized. Therefore, I, very sadly, cannot recommend purchasing this game at this time.

TL;DR: An Eastern-styled rogue-like, simple in design but engaging. Good for a playthrough, but late game and NG+ are heavily unbalanced.
The first thing to note about the Enchanted Cave is it is available for free as a flash game. That version of the game stops at level 80. The version on steam is the equivalent of the 'Premium' flash version, with steam achieves and trading cards added. The second thing to note is this is not what most modern people would consider a 'rogue-like' in the traditional sense. I would call this an Eastern rogue-like, closer to Shiren the Wanderer or Azure Dreams. Each run is not separate from the others, you play the same character, with certain things getting reset on the run while keeping others.
Gameplay wise, the game is about delving into a randomly generated dungeon. The end goal is to reach level 100 and defeat the boss there, but individual runs are about either collecting gear, levels, money, or making progress to a checkpoint. Every ten levels has a checkpoint available that can be warped to after you find it. The rogue-like part comes in that every new run has you lose all gear gained. You keep levels and money, and certain pieces of gear called 'artifacts', but generic gear and items such as healing potions and alchemy ingredients are lost. You finish a run by using a special item that exits the dungeon. If you die on the run, you are reverted to before you started the run, losing all progress made. In essence, the game is about knowing how far you can push a run before you need to leave. There is really very little luck-based about this, as you can look at monster stats before engaging them, and they stay in one place, never moving to engage you first. The main randomness is in criticals. Basically, you do runs at a level, until you acquire artifacts that let you start comfortably at a later level, making gradual progress until you win.
There is a sort of class system, with every level letting you apply points to features that either boost your warrior abilities, alchemy, or magic. Levels also raise a stat by one rank, as do crystals found in the game or later on purchased from a merchant. Gear found improves stats, and can be enchanted with items to give additional effects that aren't gained by levels, such as elemental damage/resistance and dodge chance. All of the paths seem a bit balanced, but warrior seems to coast through on minimal effort, only needing to dab in mage for a bit to grab healing until they finish that route and can do another. By the time you finish the game, you should have one path finished, and be most of the way down another.
The faults start to show when you reach the end of your first run of the game, and in NG+. Notably, levels don't scale, so you are still getting +1 attack at level 2 all the way to level 50. Notably, with gear, crystals, and the like, that means that levels mean way, way less as you go on. Raising your attack from 2-3 has more impact than raising it from 90-91. Once you get near the end, you'll pretty much have the best gear, have it enchanted the best, and find that you barely get stronger than that. This isn't a problem really, it leaves the final boss still challenging (albeit with spamming healing potions in combat, nothing is challenging). It becomes extremely broken in NG+, as you don't get any stronger gear, monsters just get much stronger, leaving your only way to advance being the less and less effective stat ups. Enchants get better, but the only enchantment worth anything by that point is instant death chance. You can easily break the game by stacking instant death and dodge, and relying on the RNG for most enemies.
As such, overall it is a well done game, and the cracks only start to show in the late game with scalability of stats. It is still worth a play through, though perhaps better to catch on sale than pay full price.

Unending Galaxy is a crazy ambitious game that melds many different elements from different genres. Despite all this ambition and the uncharted territory, Unending Galaxy is easily one of the best 4X games I’ve played in a while.  The learning curve can be kind of extreme, and the documentation is somewhat sparse.
Rating: 4 out of 5
Full review at:

Unending Galaxy promises real time 4X with a cool twist - build up from one ship, to a mighty galactic spanning empire.
However, the details of executing this promise are frustrating to accomplish - all from a lack of information given to the player to the lull of getting from one ship to an empire.
The game has some great stuff in it from the X universe, which the creator is a modder of. The good stuff is : the ability to make ships auto-trade and auto-mine asteroids to start building you a nest-egg for your future empire. Getting this is no problem at all and is very nicely done.
The combat however is very break-neck speed in my opinion. Big ships that cost quite a bit of money can die if you dont immediately start evasive maneuvers to get out of combat and kite enemies...that is unless you grossly outnumber the enemy, which can take a bit of time, even for small pirate factions.
Couple this with the fact that the game never tells you what weapons do differently than each other(even trying to guess visually is very rough), the one dimensional defense modules that just add shields: which all seem to get blown away with very little effort...and this makes managing a small combat fleet disappointing.
Building an empire is fun in this game. You get to build a lot of trade infrastracture that spans the entirety of a galaxy. But the lack of information on which ships have enough cargo room to build can set the player back at least 10-20 minutes of game time if they do not guess right. On top of this, there is a big system of infrastructure required to get ship parts and supply. which is also not that well explained in the game. This really stops you from enjoying the fun nature of this game for another couple of hours.
Overall, this game has potential to be a very fun 2D , real time 4X, that gives us what we want - adventures in a big galaxy on a small scale that lead to massive galactic warfare in the end. But getting to the end is a big pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and is just not as fun as it sounds when you see what is happening in the game and know what it takes to get there.

Putting those issues aside I love this game, I absolutely love it.
It's a large 4X RTS where you can play as a single ship or up to an entire empire. You can scavage battlefields for parts, you can hunt bounties, you can be a trader, you can claim territory, colonize planets, be a pirate, bring down empires, build them, create a space industry of your choice with factories ranging from farms to computers, to fire arms, fight rogue AI or space monsters, and a lot more.
You are placed in a simulated galaxy and then told to do whatever you want, that's what Unending Galaxy is, and it will likely become one of my new favorite games.
As for the dev they seem great, I've asked a few questions and put a few issues on the forum already and the dev was just about the first person to answer all of them, even more so he's already making changes in the next patch based on a couple issues I had, rare to have that kind of on-point activity.

Utilizing your enemies shipyards to create a fleet to destroy them is always fun. Actually controlling your forces is tedious and feels wonky most of the time. I easily got my budget wrong by not putting enough money into trading, and it took forever to get a ratio I liked.
I think its a great core game, especially since I dumped alot of time into X2, but it needs to be bug stomped and flesh out the user interface.

I've previously owned this game before on PS3, so I decided to give the game another chance on PC.
Personally, I like the artstyle, its fairly unique and sets the game apart from other run of the mill shooters. Although it is what you'd expect, everything for the resistance is improvised and gritty, everything for the security forces is shiny, white and looks brand new, etc. The soundtrack is also decent, the main menu theme is currently stuck in my head as I write this review.
The gameplay is class based, the game requires a large degree of teamwork to accomplish any of the objectives, this isn't really a game where you can be the lone wolf and decimate everything in your path. Anyone familiar with games such as TF2 or star wars battlefront, will feel right at home with the gameplay. The only aspect of the gameplay I don't like is the parkour, its very jerky, sometimes unresponsive, and difficult to pull off in certain situations due to the 1st person view limiting your perspective of the surrounding environment, it feels like the parkour was an afterthought and was wedged in at the last minute in order to attract the Mirrors Edge crowd. However, I've found that parkour isn't particularly usefull in all the missions anyway, so the clunkyness isn't really a problem as I rarely used parkour to its full extent.
Character customisation is rather good. By leveling up you unlock different outfits for your character, allowing you to personalise him as you see fit. Anyone wishing to play as a female character may be slightly dissapointed as you can only play as a male character. You can however choose from three different body types, Light, medium and heavy. all with their own advantages and drawbacks. e.g Light characters can run very fast but can be killed in only a few hits, wheras the heavy characters take more damage, but move slower. There are also perks and abilities for each class, with the Medic being able to upgrade his healing abilities, the engineer can gain a sentry gun upgrade, the soldier can dispense more ammo to comrades and the operative can genrally become more sneaky. More weapons and attachments for said weapons can be unlocked through the completion of individual challenges, separate from the main game. Most of these challenges are fairly easy, and don't require a great deal of effort, allowing you to unlock all the weapons and attachments somewhat quickly. The game has a wide variety of weapons to choose from, allowing for a good variety of playstyles.
Sadly, the multiplayer is fairly dead. Whenever I try to search for a match, there's no one else playing. This means you're left with the single player mode. However, those familiar with Star Wars battlefront's 'instant action' feature, will feel right at home as the 'free play' mode allows you to jump into any mission of your choosing, and apply custom mutators to that mission. Unfortuntely, the AI is not the best feature of this game as it is very temperamental. Sometimes the friendly AI will be as stupid as a sack of hammers and at others it will be flawless, the same can be said for the enemy AI, sometimes it wrecks you and your team, sometimes it just sits back and takes whatever beating you're giving it.
In conclusion, the game is fairly solid but is held back by the lack of an active multiplayer scene, the temperamental AI and the clunky parkour.

As of now it belongs in the $4.99 - $9.99 category for what you get in terms of quality of gameplay and content. Player doesn't get too much flexibility on their choices, especially in the early and mid game. However, it is still a great game and I do recommend it for anyone who wants to try out something new and see it grow into a better game.
A few things I'd like to see come into fruition:
1. Add a restart button in-game so you don't have to exit and create a new game. Keeps the settings and only shuffles the map seed.
2. Have a less steep learning curve:
- No tutorial whatsoever
- 2-3+ hours is a lot of time to waste only to have one zombie ♥♥♥♥ up your entire base. They 'turn' buildings too fast and by the time you have a troop there they've already multiplied into 100 zombies destroying your entire base.  All because you left ONE tile open where a wall should have been but you couldn't see it because it was at the corner of a forest/hill/lake.
3. Grammar fixes, but I can only speak for the English version. No big deal but also an easy fix.
4. More defensive and econonomic buildings to add more variety to your strategies
5. There is a pretty strict early game order of operations. As in you should do X first, then Y, then Z. Only took me a few games to realize the most efficient routes. I want to see greater flexibility in your choices.
Again, this feels like it belongs in the $4.99 - $9.99 category right now.

A depressingly mediocre game.
Instead of being about the over-the-top arcadey shooter giant monster action that the series is known for (and was cranked to 11 in LP2), Lost Planet 3 is instead an uninspired, "character-driven", "shoulder-hugging" TPS that feels like a bootleg version of Dead Space in more ways than one.
Gunplay is surprisingly decent. But the way the single-player campaign is formatted hurts it a great deal. You spend a lot of time trundling from point A to point B (either in your giant, slow - but still faster than on foot- robot, or through a myriad of bland contextual actions in caves), then pressing a button. Maybe shooting a handful of things along the way.
If it had instead been structured as stand-alone missions with non-stop action a-la Lost Planet 2, I might've been able to stomach more of this game. But the crappy open-world elements are just too clunky and uninteresting to hold my attention.
The fact that this game bears the Lost Planet name personally disgusts me. Literally every link it has to the franchise could be replaced with an original equivalent and the game would suffer nothing for it.
The Akrid could've just been generic aliens.
Thermal Energy could've just been a generic resource; it doesn't even function in the same way as it does in the previous games.
NEVEC could've been replaced with a generic corporation.
People looking to get into the Lost Planet franchise, stay away. Play Lost Planet 1 if you're looking for an atmospheric experience, or Lost Planet 2 if you're looking for an over-the-top shooter.
Existing Lost Planet fans, stay away from this game unless you wish to experience for yourself the bullet that killed the franchise you loved.

I'll keep this short, and to the point.
This is a decent, if not terribly inspired group based cRPG that is mostly bug free. It allows people to play both pregenerated and individually created characters in the party. Solid game, for a fairly cheap price.
The biggest negative for me was that compared to many other games of this type, it is VERY linear. There is basically one path to advance through the story and game. This is done through content being tied very closely to party levels, and ability. Sure, there is the illusion of "sandbox" or non-linear questing, but in reality, you can go to the various places whenever you want, but the enounters there will wreck your party if they try to do things in the "wrong" order.
Pros:
- Few bugs
- Decent UI
- Reasonable graphics
- Decent if fairly generic gameplay
- Reasonable sales price
Cons:
- Very linear in playability
- Some quests not explained well or have misleading instructions
- Wide disparity in usefulness of character classes (some are very powerful, others nearly useless)
Overall it gets a positive rating, it is a good game for what it is and what it is sells for. But Pillars of Eternity it is not.

Very decent indie rpg. Combat is deep and there's a ton of exploration. Game actually rewards clever item use. Beautiful world design. Everything is very well balanced early on- balanced so that everything is a major pain in your side. Don't expect much from the story, but this isn't a game that's about story. The game is a bit linear than I'd like, there's a number of spots where you can't move on until you go somewhere to get a specific item, but at each general stage of the game there's usually quite a few areas to explore at once.
There's a few balance issues (HINT: level up speed every level) and one of the classes is a little on the weak side (The Divine Summoner, though min-maxers love it for the ability to turn enemies into gold sources) but otherwise it's very well balanced, with no class being unplayable and only one class is consider "essential"- the Cleric. As it turns out, in these types of games, the healer is usualy pretty essential, and there ARE ways to avoid having to use one, it's just going to be much trickier. There's one guy you have to take along with you every game, Gaulen the Explorer, thankfully he actually isn't that terrible of a character and can fill a couple roles depending on the rest of the party. The rest of the party is up to the player, and it's very possible to make Combat Bards and Tank Clerics and other strange character types. Characters that entirely focus on out of combat utility (like Gaulen, in some teams) aren't completely a waste either, thanks to the decent item system.
It does drag towards the end, however. I feel this is a game that was actually a tad bit *too* long, and there's some pacing issues- 4 of the 8 temples are at the very, very end of the game. This is a problem, because the only things you fight in the temples are Undead, and you almost only fight them there, so there's suddenly a huge spike of Undead at the end of the game. Being undead, they are immune to fun things like mental attacks, bleeding, and poison, which makes fights against them a little dull. There were also a few puzzles in the temples that I probably would have enjoyed more if I wasn't fatigued from a 90 hour game. You also get a huge power boost, so very little things are actually a danger at the end of the game, but to make up for that power boost the enemies get tons of HP- not enough to actually make them dangerous, but enough to make battles drag.
Still. While I feel compelled to mention those endgame problems, that's a very small portion of the game, one that realistically many players will never reach (only 4% of players have gotten the endgame achievement). The rest of the game is very entertaining to play. I wouldn't say it's an amazing game, but it's a decent one, and it's very much worth the price.

Lords of Xulima certainly delivers on its promise to be difficult.  As many have pointed out, it definitely caters to a more "hardcore" fan base. In this day and age that means wiki, guide, and forum reading, rather than the previous trial and error systems, to hammer out the workings of your characters.
But skipping over all the debates of sleeping off death but not disease, low drop rates, or finite xp, it boils down to seeing Lords of Xulima like this:
If you believe "hardcore" means the game has a million ways to 100% screw you based off one decision you make, this game is for you.  If you believe "hardcore" means the game gives you a 1% chance of beating it and you have to figure out how you want to make that 1% happen, then this game isn't for you.

Pros:
1: Art Direction
Of all the many settings for many games ive explored, none is as masterfully crafted as Dunwall. Dunwall is a grim place, a plague ravages the population, and It's allies have left it for dead. The sick roam the streets, shunned and ignored by all, aside from those poor souls commissioned to have them killed. Walls of light divide society both physically and literally, the aristocrats feasting while the poor starve and die, kept in check by the city watch, who want nothing more than to gather for whiskey and cigars.
2: Corvo and 'Morals'
In amongst all this is you, Corvo Attano, the 'Dishonoured' royal protector, framed for the murder of empress Jessamine Kaldwin, imprisoned by the corrupt royal spymaster for your crimes.
As you escape from your prison and see the ruinous streets of Dunwall for the first time, you have to wonder how your crusade of justice is affecting the lives of the people of Dunwall. Even if you complete your quest leaving without killing anyone, for a society living on a knife edge your threatening presece could be enough to tip them over the edge.
The chaos system refelcts this, and while not perfect (I doubt one guardsman thrown in the ocean will make the difference between mass death and heroics), it still provides the player an incentive to consider the lives they affect as they hunt down their targets.
3: The gameplay and powers system
In the early stages of the game your are visited by the outsider, who grants you supernatural abilities. With these you can 'teleport' short distances, slow, and even stop, time, posses people and animals, and many more things. The powers and there respective upgrades are handled in such a way that they do not feel intrusive, but just enhance the way you play the game, openiing up new avenues of attack or escape .
TL;DR
It's ♥♥♥♥ing great and you should play it

Not nearly as bad as people make it out to be.
The story is good if... somewhat unbelievable.
Still there are some fun plot twists that imply that the main character may in fact be THE commander in Xcom 1 and 2.
There are a bunch of weird cases where the storyline is challenged by the gameplay like when your engineer buddy in the prologue can build LASER turrets before you even reclaim a single alien laser gun.
Still you get to walk around the base do some side quests and read up the research notes that the eggheads at the research lab scribble up.
The controls feel weird at first because the game was obviously made with consoles in mind so the mouse is not used much beyond aiming and shooting but the system that's in place is intuitive enough to work with even with a mouse and keyboard once properly introduced.
And if a person like me whose last physical contact with consoles was playing on an N64 can get used to it then so can you.
The squadmates are a mixed bag as they try to follow your orders AND follow you at the same time leading to weird situations where someone you send to flank proceeds to just sit there plinking away ineffectually at the exposed enemies or worse if you changed position he will try to run back and join you.
In the end the player character is the one doing the bulk of the killing.
There is also very little attachment you form for to your squadmates since they all speak and act the same. Even a russian who supposedly can't even speak english suddenly goes full on native when he's on your squad and speaks fluent english which is sad really since the game could use stronger squadmates you'd actually care about when they die.
On the upside you don't bring in your squadmates for their direct firepower but for their abilities which are usually pretty powerful and useful for crowd control or straight up killing the ayyy lamao's.
Everything aside... well it's a cover shooter with some tactical elements similar to Mass Effect.
While it might not be the best game in the genre it's certainly a 6/10.
There is some jankyness to it but it's still worth a look if you want to play everything that's related to Xcom or just like TPP tactics.
Especially if you grab it while it's on sale.

The game itself is a very decent third person shooter with tactical elements. The gameplay is a lot of fun and the world in which the game takes place in feels fleshed out and wholly realized. It has elements derived from the other XCOM games in here as well, although this should be looked at as an offshoot of the series and not as a main entry. The gameplay is inherently different from the other XCOM games, but still provides a good bit of tactical fun.
Pros
+Fun, tactical cover based shooting
+1960s setting, fleshed out world
+Voice acting
+Can pick your own squad
+Can pause and issue orders to your squad
Cons
-Level design is a bit flat and leaves wanting for more
-I've heard the game is short
-Physx integration in this game is very spotty
All in all, it's a competent third person, cover based shooter in the vein of Gears of War with added tactical elements (think like the first Gears of War squad commanding but waaaaay more fleshed out). Not sure about the $20 price tag, but the game does often go on a deep discount during sales and is definitely worth picking up on sale. As a fan of XCOM and X-Files, this game scratched an itch that other games really haven't been able to with the combination of the setting and world. If you're a fan of XCOM, Sci-fi, and tactical cover based shooting, give it a try!

Customisation is meh for your squadmates' apparel, but the extensive backpack; perk system and character skill pool is great.
Minro graphical and audio hickups here and there and maybe some kore explanation into the tech on your arm and how everything else works would be nice. But hey, you are not the commander afterall, meaning not everything is supposed to be known to you.
Overall: 8.5/10

Quake. This is the greatest FPS game of all time. Even all of these years later, this holds up like nothing else quite does.
Of course, now that it's been over twenty years since the game was released, some new technology is around, and using modern Quake clients is the best way to play it now. For a singleplayer experience as close to the original as possible, get QuakeSpasm. For a more modern look to singleplayer, check out DarkPlaces. For QuakeWorld multiplayer, get ezQuake.
Quake has a style to it that no other game has really tried to capture, although that is being changed as of the time this is being written with the development of DUSK. Not even any of the other games in the Quake series are like Quake. Every aspect of the game is incredibly gothic, which is a good thing, seeing as this game was inspired heavily by gothic literature. Quake is a realm in which the overall atmosphere feels undeniably... wrong. Every environment is dark and covered in filth. Every creature in the game would love nothing more than to tear you to shreds. Every area teems with life, yet the ever-looming presence of death is inescapable. Every structure feels alien in nature, yet somehow so human. The walls are filled with their own secrets. Any doorway could be an ambush. All objects metal are rusted. All structures built are falling apart. And all creatures moving are mortal. Even you.
This game (when properly configured) feels amazing to play. The levels are chunky, the controls are tight and smooth, and when you're bunnyhopping all over the place, it's incredibly fast. Seriously, if you only play QuakeWorld multiplayer for about a month straight and try to play any other multiplayer FPS game, they will feel clunky and slow. Even Quake 3/Live and Quake Champions feel slow after lots of QW.
The singleplayer levels are fun and have lots of replay value. Bumping up difficulty levels, speedrunning, and secret hunting means that you can run through them many times without getting bored. Heck, when I test to make sure that I have Quake working on a new system, I test by playing throught E1M1, and then I generally wind up playing through the first couple of levels of E1 because I enjoy it every time.
Multiplayer is fantastic. deathmatches, duels, and team games are all insanely frenetic, and take mountains of skill to get good at. Adrenaline will flow through you the whole way through. When you want to wind down and relax with all two of your friends (may or may not be counting yourself in that number) who play Quake still, coop is a fun way to play without constantly being 95% of the way to having a heart attack.
This game also has an enourmous number of maps, mods, and other goodies to keep both singleplayer and multiplayer fresh. No need to worry about running out of things to do in Quake.
Now for some of the cons of multiplayer. Weapon balance doesn't exist in this game. The rocket launcher and lightning gun beat out all other weapons always. Also, most of the people still playing QW have been playing it for years, if not decades, so they'll be seven gazillion times better than any new player could ever hope to be upon entry. If you stick to it and ask around for help (most of the guys in the QW community are nice and will give new guys a hand), you will get better. You just have to give it some time.
...Oh, singleplayer flaws? Quake doesn't have any of those.
Seriously, If you haven't already bought at least a couple of copies of Quake already, get one! Right now! Do it! It's worth more than Steam is ever going to charge you for it!

The next thing you know, you've been sucked into a desperate obsession with romancing every single bird because you're just dying to find out their story... and then... and
...
...the entire game turns upside-down, and kicks you right in the gut.
You think it can't possibly get any worse than this... but it
. The storyline unfolds right before your eyes, and you're helpless to do anything except keep playing, keep making choices, because you have to
. And while you're floundering there drowning in your own tears, the game just keeps kicking you. Again and again and again.

Portal is a first-person puzzle game developed and published by Valve and released in October 2007. You play as Chell, a female protagonist that completes testings for Aperture Science Laboratories. The game features a nineteen level campaign that allows you to solve puzzles. Solving each puzzle progresses you further into the story. This review will discuss the campaign, the levels, and gameplay.
Portal features a solid campaign that provides a good introduction to the world of the Laboratories. The game begins with an in-game tutorial introducing you to the portal gun, the tests and Glados, the antagonist AI computer. Portal excels at storytelling through the slow burn approach to the story. Certain sequences in the story subtly reveal major plot points such as what is Glados planning to do to Chell once she has completed her tests. These subtle hints provide excitement for those who have noticed them as it foreshadows the final scenes in the game. Portal 1 is less about story and more about introducing you to the environment. I get the vibe that this game is more like a prologue to Portal 2 because comparing Portal 1 to Portal 2, P2 expands on the gameplay and environment and emphasises the story whereas P1 introduces you to the setting, the characters, the type of gameplay, and the story. In saying that, I do really like the introduction to the characters as Glados is a refreshing computer personality in which gives the impression that robots control humans, or Glados controls Chell.
The campaign as mentioned includes nineteen levels and these levels are basic. It promotes creativity as the levels progressively become more difficult. However, I feel the majority of the levels are simple and relatively easy compared to the final five levels. The final five levels are challenging and they require more thinking, meaning they encourage more exploration on how to complete it. The levels are of good length. About 10 out of the 19 levels took some time to complete and it lengthened the game and made it more enjoyable because the overall campaign was short at under three hours. Portal features an 'advanced levels' mode which takes the final six levels of the campaign, reworks them and makes them much more difficult to complete. I did not play this mode because I prefer not to replay the same levels with no end goal. Generally though, it does add some variety and lasting appeal to the game for players.
All in All

I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that the original Enchanted Cave is not only one of my favorite Flash games of all time, but one of my most-played games of all time.
I spent a good 50 hours or so with the original version on Kongregate and would come back to it periodically. When I saw that a sequel had not only been made, but had a Steam version too, it became one of the few times I've instabought a new release sight-unseen.
The Enchanted Cave 2 is very similar to its predecessor. You play as a rogue adventurer who journeys deep into a 100-level dungeon in search of loot, monsters and glory. Along the way, you find relics, potions and new items, and if things get too dangerous, you can always "escape" with a pair of magical wings and try again with the gear you collected on the way. Combat is done automatically by just walking into enemies, and there's a semi-randomized aspect to the floors you visit - no two are the same.
It's pretty impressive what the creator, one-man dev studio Dustinaux, upgraded in the interim between games. Chief among the improvements is a massive skill tree system that has three distinct sectors. You can choose to upgrade physical skills (combat, defense, experience boosts and HP), magical skills (MP, new skills) or a general utility set (gold earned, potion efficiency). It actually gets quite challenging in later floors as you gain levels, because XP gains become minimal and you have to prioritize what you want to upgrade.
Instead of a simple splash screen in the original, there's now a town that you can visit in between runs, which has NPCs, shops and more. It even incentivizes the plot by making it possible to rescue NPCs trapped in the dungeon, who escape and become shopkeepers or bar patrons afterwards.
From a story standpoint, things haven't changed much. The story is pretty much exactly the same as before - there's an evil sorcerer who lives at the bottom of the dungeon and is trying his best to kill you, via subterfuge and the numerous enemies he summons on each level. The only difference now is that he isn't so blatant about his intentions, and you can find journal entries written by him in secret areas littered throughout the dungeon.
The one thing that makes the game so good is that it's addicting as hell. There's a definite sense of "one more run", and you're constantly on the lookout for better gear, relics and potions. You can craft your own upgraded gear with special attributes, pick one of four character skins to use when raiding and try to fill out the "Museum" (a place that houses all of your duplicate relics).
There are a couple problems of note as well. Despite the inclusion of Grant Kirkhope (Banjo-Kazooie, Donkey Kong Country) as composer, the music is... underwhelming, considering his pedigree. Likewise, it can take hours to finish a run. Don't be deceived - there are enemies you physically can't pass without significant grinding.
That being said, the Enchanted Cave 2 is just as immersive and enjoyable as its predecessor. While it's not necessarily a true roguelike, it offers enough fun for anyone who's looking for an adventure with lots of variety and grinding. There's even a New Game Plus mode once you complete the dungeon for the first time.
Definitely check this one out.

- If you play single player, you will find the AI is on par. They have their weak moments, most definitely. But overall, they function fairly well.
- Actual gameplay is more "shoot everything that moves" rather than being on the tactical side. If you like to sit on your laurels and snipe people, this game will not be your favorite. If you generally play a tank-like character who rolls in to battle and blows up everything that breathes, you will love this game.
- Sometimes has the feel of a FPS tower defense game. Especially if you play as an engineer. But I don't mind that aspect, and actually enjoy it.
- Multiplayer is well developed, but could use more maps and the entire game could use more weapons. You can at least unlock attachments for your guns through the challenge mode included in the main game.
- Campaign is interesting. You can play as radical terrorists on the Resistance side or as the grounded Security. There is no advantage or disadvantage to the sides. Weapons are the same. Appearance is only slightly tweaked (different jackets, hair styles, etc etc). I prefer the Security story line only because I like the appearance and dialog better. The story could have been more developed and more levels included, but I can't complain that much. I completed the campaign in a few hours. Replaying it has kept me occupied for a good while, however. Maybe it's jsut because I'm a simple person. My favorite aspect of the entire campaign and story is that you can play both sides and see how the story develops and progresses as you complete levels and objectives. Save the "Ark" or destroy it.
OVERALL RATING: 8.8 out of 10. Polished game. Few bugs. Keeps you occupied for a while. Would have liked it to be longer and more in depth with more variation in gameplay. Brink is a good game for a good price.

I bought this game a year ago way before it was on Steam. It was a lot of fun then, and since then it has had numerous improvements and fixes and extra features added.
It's a sandbox top down space shooter with both manual and RTS controls and empire management. You can pilot your ship and go bounty hunting, fight pirates, or trade. As you get money you can buy more ships, set up automated traders, build stations of your own, and even start your own empire that can compete with and conquer the AI empires. You can fly your ships manually, or just tell them what to do and watch. In combat you can just give orders to your fleet, or hop around controlling ships willy nilly if you like. Or play a single ship and have the rest following your orders.
What I really love about it is what you do actually affects the universe.
If you're a bounty hunter, you aren't hunting randomly generated quest opponents - you are actually hunting threats to that empire - pirate and other ships (like Swarm) who have been destroying their ships and earning a bounty. You also have competition - other bounty hunters are actively hunting the same list of bounties.
If you do trade missions to bring supplies to end a shortage at a station, you actually supplied that station - which will then start producing stuff.
If you pirate ships carrying supplies for ship part factories for a faction, that faction will not only be out the ships you blew up in the process - but it will have less parts to build new ships.
If you blow up a big military fleet of a faction, that faction will be weakened against both you (if you're running an empire of your own) and other AI empires until it can rebuild that fleet.
If you set up stations to bolster a faction's economy, not only will you make money - the faction will be better off.
Plus there is a huge appeal to me with starting as a single ship and working your way up to conquering the map as a faction.
Starting options lets you get into the game how you like it - as a single ship, as a pre-existing empire, and a lot of options in between (like being in charge of a small pirate fleet). You can also select from any of the technology groups in the game, which influences what ships and factories you can build.
I definitely recommend this game. The game has a free version available too to make sure you like the basic premise, albeit with less features (totally worth buying the full version). So give the free version a try - if you like it, buy it.

Developer:Anarkis Gaming
Genre:Strategy, 4X-lite, Trading, Space
Unending Galaxy [UG] is a 1 man game about intergalactic trading, empire building, trading fleet management all in a top down 2D view. It basically plays like the X series except well its 2D, the pace is faster, and it could use some polish in certain part of the gameplay.
Anyways lets get on with the review! There's not really much to talk about in the intro section.
Lets get this out of the way first, it uses asset packs from the AI war series.  So don't go in expecting fancy graphical settings and so on. But at least its not terrible to look at for one thing. Ok it might be a little be bad if you're not used to it but for a heavy space simulation game like this graphics would be a little be a little be lower on the list.
Just your average typical synth space music for the ambient that you might want to mute off and put on something else after 5 continous hours of pay because eventually they grate on your ears like cheese grater at the end of it. Meanwhile the average sound effects are just pew pew pew for guns and lasers and muted boom for explosion.
Nothing really impressive here but hey it works. Kinda.
And here's my favourite part of it. You see you can adjust most things from interpolation, resolution, some settings to set compatibility and increase FPS but if you happen to have an anamolous configuration like me the game will be very finicky. As in it will randomly throw out issues at you at random time. I had sprites corrupted, game crashes, spike lags, and so on. It even hates my mobile Radeon graphic card for some reason so I had to disable that and use my intel integrated graphics.
But when it does work it works very well at 60 fps and almost no lag. But do note the most important part of your configuration will be your processor. The graphics may not be pretty but a lot of process are running constantly in the background and for the largest map it taxed my i5 processort to 100% usage for all 4 core pretty much all the time. Smaller map while... less fun do offer slightly better performances.
That said it does depend on your final configuration setup so you might get a lot more mileage with it than me with the game.
The gameplay in UG is pretty simple. At the start of the game you can choose a list of preset maps [that are pretty resource heavy] or from the randomly generated maps that way less fun than the preset maps but will not set your computer on fire from the sheer amount of background processing. Then you choose your starting type ship type and empire affinity. You pretty much immediately start off as an empire in this game and everybody will treat you as such [even though you might only have 1 ship].
So assuming you pick the default starting merchant class there are a few things you can do in UG. First you can configure your drone ship to start trading supplies for you autonomously while you lay back and watch as the money increases in the background or you can also do a few jobs while the drone does its job that ranges from killing people, ferrying supplies, to destroying bases and these missions are dependant on which faction and base you pick them off from. Drones [and other ships] can also be set to autonomously patrol, hunt for bounties, and a few other things and task that you can set them with.
You can interact with the faction and improve your standing with them by doing missions but faction relationship can be improve simply bribing a lot of money if you wish although there's a hard cap to how much you can do this.
Maps are divided into sectors, wormholes provide quick transportation from one point to another while jump drive provide localize instant transportation between close nearby sectors. Late in the game you can make your own wormhole but as of early point you will be most likely be
The end goal of this game can be freely decided by you but assuming you want to 'win' the game sort of to speak you need to obliberate every factionand come out on top. To do so you need money to build builder ships which will build space stations that allows other factions to trade with you and generate more income. Once you build up a sizeable base you can then start to build military bases and shipyards outside of enemy control point, this will allow you to finally claim a sector for your own and begin your first foothold in conquering the universe. Pumping out fleets of ships while setting their AI, declaring war on other factions and ruthlessly destroying would then be your main objective and at that point you can simply start building your own wormhole that will not allow others to travel into. A true empire so as to speak from a lowly beginning so as to speak.
That said money isnt too terribly hard to earn and a typical game will just be over in 5-8 hours [I had half the galaxy conquered in 5] which makes it a lot more fast pace that most other space empire simulation game out there. Being a trader only is also viable and fun since you have to acquire bodyguards and make your own trade and space stations to maximise the amount of profit that you will get.
Randomly to mix things up a few random event might happen to you and it is up to you to adapt to their coming.
At this present time UG is a completely playable game, you can start from a humble beginning and end as an empire and the speed in which you do so is rather addicting with few downtime in between. That said a lot of things could use a little bit more polish to it which includes the UI, the trade section, more automation stuff, and further faction interaction but that could all come afterward.
For now its a pretty fun space empire management game [especially the trading screen watching the money go up cha ching cha ching cha ching] and since its feature complete and fully playable at the moment that is all fine for now. Although, people who had never play this kind of game should note that the learning ladder is rather steep but once you are at the top its easy to do a checklist.
Forgot to mention, the game does have a built in game editor so you can make up your own sector and adjust parameters for the ships. It's also rather easy to make up your own mod for it if you want to.

Pixel Piracy is a great concept for a game but currently there are a lot of problems that makes it difficult to enjoy. The biggest problem is a lack of any useful tutorial in a game that is moderately complicated. There isn't a lot of helpful tooltips or anything useful on the help page and 4 hours in I still find myself search for answers on the internet to find out what is wrong constantly or how to do things I should be able to do, such as firing a cannon after buying cannons, ammo and using the cannon firing skill.
Another huge problem is large portions of this game involve doing nothing. Everytime you have to sail somewhere which is very often you merely watch your pirates sail on their ship with little to no involvement. This plays itself like an extended loading screen every 2 minutes in game.
The last problem that is that controls are very minimal in this game and I find myself at the hands of the AI constantly even during battles. A battle can vary wildly from complete victory with almost no health lost to my captain dieing because he decided to fight on the edge of the ship and got pushed off. There are of course smalls ways to remedy these things however a better remedy would be having the player be far more involved in battles.
Overall the game is complex and engaging but has some major problems. It is definitely worth trying for cheap or worth revisiting later.

Basic Map layouts: Most areas are tight corridors with every bit looking the same as the other. More to that on another point. This is the best (free) single player game I have ever seen on Steam. I am only about three hours in but the depth of this game is already blowing me away. The gameplay and mechanics of this game are simple when viewed one at a time but come together to create a game that requires a lot of strategy and intelligence to get good at.
Imagine Zelda like puzzles in a large open world mixed with turn based battles along the way. The puzzles are difficult and meaningful but not so much that you want to smash your keyboard.
The battles are not random and act more as obstacles blocking your path. You can vie the enemies you will battle beforehand and choose not to fight if you don't mind leaving that path blocked for awhile longer. When you do choose to fight, the battle itself relies more on strategy than most other games as it is important that you know the strengths and weaknesses of your enemy.
Additionally, your characters grow not by levelling up but by taking on the properties of defeated enemies. You have full control over this transformation and whether it will happen or not. This creates a surprising amount of customization and it becomes important not only to know how you would like each of your characters to grow but also how absorbing a particular enemy will help you achieve that goal.
My advice (with my admittedly limited knowledge) is to pick one or two strengths for each character and focus mostly on increasing them when you transform.

This game is a weird piece of something. If the premise wasn't great on its own, the game itself is rather... crunchy.
I totally didn't expect these kinds of strategizing in battles trying to cover one party member's weakness with the other, the active switching and the overall trying to find the logic and memorize each foe's weakness/resistances through such simple and effective mechanics.
While I haven't played much, I've been to three very interestingly designed areas that got me hooked right away. I absolutely loved how it keeps itself extremely simple, clear and relies totally on great game and level design to keep things together.
Pros:
>Progress system based on transforming into defeated opponents, with the ability to keep some of their skills to create a nice and balanced party. This is done in a very clear way and everything you need to know is displayed in a direct manner.
>Battles are interesting, foes can be easily beat through knowledge and good transformation planning.
>Combat system fully explained through itself. No wondering if this stat does that as EVERY skill has on its description what stat it uses and its element/cooldown/power/effect.
>You can play as a spider.
>Map design is well made, with several shortcuts and small puzzles to keep travelling interesting.
>Music is a plus.
>Writing is intricate. Dialogues kept me wondering every time someone had something to say. I look forward to find new NPCs to talk to even though I don't really understand much yet.
Cons:
>It's not the prettiest thing out there, even with its own aesthetics taken into account, it does get somewhat hard to discern what is there and what isn't. I like how a detailed lamia lady turns into a small snake when you get her as a party member, though.
>It can get very confusing though it's very simple.
>Lack an Options menu. Can't even change the sound/music volume or pick a resolution.
>Whatever there is for a story isn't clear at all, though amusing due to its style.
Neutral:
>The game requires a lot of attention and memory. It doesn't hold your hand and expects a lot of the player, especially on the travelling side, as map design is far from straightforward. It's very easy to get completely lost.
>I miss health bars.
Overall, it makes up for a fun but demanding time and its a steal to be completely free. Just go and play it regardless.

All in all, if you liked the first mass effect you will probably like this one well enough.

I am mainly a strategy gamer coming from a background of playing Civ “X”, Gal Civ “X”, EUIV, M&B Warband, Matrix/AGEOD games, X-Com, etc.. I was in between games & looking for something different to play when I ran across this game in a thread about good RPG-Tactical Games. I am glad I gave Xulima a try. It has a nostalgic feel to it and that old fashioned D&D appeal (I date back to the white box/3 booklet early D&D Pen and Paper Days) that some of us old timers still remember. This feel though, is coupled with some very nice (albeit very basic) game mechanics that just simply work for the type game it was designed to be. At first glance, I thought that the combat mechanics were a little “hokey” but they work and they work elegantly. I look forward to the battles and they make you think and plan each combat turn. In addition to the combat and questing, there are some nice surprises in your exploration & adventuring. For us old schoolers that enjoy some logistics, there are some simple but elegant food & rest requirements that work without being tedious. To me, the best part of the game is the old school leveling up and making hard choices in your skill & attribute allocations as you advance. If you are a “instant gratification / pew-pew” gamer that needs high end graphics and action, stay away. But if you can use your imagination a bit and want a nicely done, old school adventure game, Xulima is your ticket. I hope they follow with a sequel…The game is quite addicting....buy the Golot Treasure DLC...its worth it....
Pros
Old School Nostalgic Feel
Nicely Done Game and Combat Mechanics
Immersion
Elegant Logistics, basic but not tedious
Nicely done advancement system
Challenging (recommend the medium or hard settings, don’t play on “normal”)
Overall game package just works – good feel, fit and finish
Hours and Hours of RPG Adventure Fun
Cons
Simple but elegant graphics – no huge explosions or 3D action here
Is grindy at times
Some might miss the “follow the green arrow” tips of other games ie., this is a thinking persons game…
Combat system may be too quirky for some (again, no “pew-pew” here)
Some may miss the “Monty Hall” feel of other titles…you work for your loot here…
Some of the game can bog down w/ tedious puzzle like problems to solve
You sometimes get stuck w/out any clear route to proceed, which can be tedious to figure out what to do next

It's worth the price of admission as long as you know what you're getting. If you've played any endless cavern concept like Lufia 2's endless cave, or the game Azure Dreams, you might find this game enjoyable.
For anyone new to this concept, the idea is simple. You enter a cave that's 100 floors deep, you can't go back up, you can only go down and your only way out is an escape item you will find fairly early on. Some items you find, you can keep when you leave, others you lose. The cave will get progressively harder as you run out of ways to stay alive, and eventually you find yourself in a risk vs. reward scenerio. Keep going, or be happy with what you've got? If you die, you lose everything from the run.
I personally always liked the idea and had fun with it so when I saw a game that was obviously based on the idea, I didn't hesitate to pick it up, especially for the whole whopping $4.99 that he's asking for. So, the question is, do I like it?
Yes, over all I do enjoy the game and would recommend it but be advised, this game is heavily automated. There's tons of loot and a fairly big (albeit simple) talent tree for you to fill out but combat will consist of you repeatedly and automatically attacking any enemy you walk up to. You could use the various elemental strikes you learn but I just kept my mana/MP for Healing and I was deep in the cave by the time I got any of those offensive abilities and wanted my Heal alot more than I wanted a small damage boost. You can also burn alot of mana enchanting gear and items you might want to keep when you leave.
If you find any item that's white, you lose it upon leaving the cave. If you find any item that's yellow, you keep it. You learn a spell that lets you turn items to yellows if you choose, so that's a good way to burn tons of your mana/MP.
As I said, the game is very simplistic, very click friendly and very automated. I think I saw that this game is or was planned for mobile devices, so if it was, I understand why he made it the way that he did, to keep it simple for those types of platforms.
I just wish it had a bit more involvement. Some input during combat, and in Azure Dreams, any action you take .. be it taking a step, attacking an enemy, or using an item lets every other enemy around you take one step or action too. So it made you consider your moves and decisions like a chess game when you were low on HP but not ready to give up yet. This game could have benefitted alot from that. The enemies are totally stationary and only fight you one on one.
Overall the game is a great little time killer when your attention span is low and you want something just simple to do. I found myself playing it mostly inbetween conversations with friends via instant messages, or other activities that I had to tab back to. This game is a perfect little filler activity.

Quick Summary: Lost Planet 3 is a Third Person Shooter with sci-fi weapons on a frozen alien world. There are some RPG elements such as weapon and suit upgrades and fast traveling to revisit prior areas, but it’s definitely more of an action shooter than anything else. I never played Lost Planet 1 or 2 and had no trouble following the plot. Don’t let that hold you back if you’re wondering whether or not you should try the game.
You play the character James Peyton, a new arrival on the planet EDN 3, an ice planet packed with T Energy, which is supposed to be the solution to Earth’s energy crisis. The entire EDN 3 research expedition is funded by the Nevec Corporation, who will do whatever it takes to make sure Earth gets the energy it needs. Unfortunately for both you and Nevec, the T Energy is sort of hard to acquire since it’s mostly found running through the veins of the alien creatures inhabiting this frozen world. The creatures aren’t the only threat around here, as you’ll find right from the start Nevec is as shady as they come.
As mentioned earlier, the game is played in third person over-the-shoulder most of the time, but you do spend a lot of time in your Utility Rig, which is a big mech with a drill arm that you can occasionally battle giant monsters with. Mostly the Rig is for story-based missions though, and for getting around the various environments with your winch (like a grappling hook). The health system for the game is basic regenerating  life where you just need to take cover for about 10 seconds and you’ll be back to full health. There aren’t that many weapons to choose from but if you’re like me you’ll probably be using the same ones most of the game anyways (assault rifle + sniper rifle). You can only carry 2 weapons at a time + your basic infinite ammo pistol. Throughout your game you can use the T Energy you collect as money, purchasing upgrades for your weapons (including specialty ammo) and upgrades for your Utility Rig (such as improved armor).
Pros:
+Decent story and “modern” graphics.
+Giant monster bosses, which is always nice.
+The specialty ammunition adds some variety, though you really won’t use it very much.
Cons:
-This is a console port and a couple things (such as opening large doors with your Rig) are not well implemented. It tells you to press the WASD buttons to open the giant gates, but really you just mash the “f” key.
-Moving between the various “areas” of the game is kind of tiresome because your Rig really doesn’t walk very fast.  You can probably get out and run just as quickly but then you wouldn’t be able to transition areas.
-Multiplayer is completely dead. Nobody’s playing online so you can’t get the multiplayer achievements.
Overall the game is fun enough to consume 10 hours if you enjoy shooters. As I’ve said, I haven’t played the previous 2 Lost Planet games so I couldn’t say how they match up. If I had to compare Lost Planet 3 with any other games, I’d say it’s more like Red Faction Armageddon than anything else (without the destructible environments).

You do not talk about the history of FPS games without mentioning Quake. The first real 3D game where the dead bodies of fallen enemies did not consist of sprites and you could actually circle around them and you could see these corpses from all angles. It was a big deal back then at a time where hardware accelerators were at our doorstep (instead of AMD Radeon and Nvidia GeForce people kept 3dfx Voodoo in their mind).
Quake 2 had a lot of sci-fi in it but the 1st in the series still had demons and pentagrams, so, essentially, the creators stuck to the concept of Doom. They applied a lot of dark fantasy, though, with chainsaw-wielding ogres and knights and zombies. The title is a reference to the entity that is tampering with the teleportation technology our government is experimenting with. You know the drill from Doom already: 4 chapters, lots of levels (including a secret at the end) and a boss fight at the end of each.
It is nice to see this classic in a digital form and that it runs well. Soundtrack was a major part of these games and neither the 1st nor the 2nd episode have them included. I'm not sure if there's a manual workaround for this but with some mods such as ezQuake you can make sure the game can be played on higher resolutions so that you can enjoy the convenience of modern PCs. A must have for fans - would love to see an "HD remaster" one day.

Ok, waited for 2nd playthrough, w/ mostly new classes (I've now played every class) and a higher difficulty level before writing a review.
Loved this game, and hope the developers are hard at work on the sequel! This was a Kickstarter homerun for me, and I'm glad I got the physical edition (very nice fold-out map, among other things).
This game can be quite challenging, especially in the early parts of the game, if you don't know what you're doing. There's very little handholding, so check out the community guides for some very helpful advice on builds and classes etc.
My favorite type of game tends to be turn-based strategy games w/ a fantasy setting. This game has that, a decent story, some interesting classes and synergy between them, tons of things to do, and a lot of gameplay and replayability on top of that.
If you want to grind (to get "area cleared" bonuses, along w/ normal xp, loot, etc.), you can, but the game doesn't force you to. In fact, the lead PC has specific skills to avoid combat altogether (not sure why you'd want to, but it's a nice option at least).
I highly recommend taking very good notes on the various maps; especially if you plan on playing a 2nd time (e.g., locations of secret doors, switches that open them, that kind of stuff).
This is a game that shows what you can do w/ a modest budget and a love for what you're doing. The only negative thing I could say about it is that the English translations (mostly spellings) aren't always perfect. Most people won't even notice...
One piece of advice (I should have followed in the 1st game). Don't pick any herbs (fruit is ok) until Gaulen has maxed out his Knowledge of Plants skill. It will require backtracking on the various maps, but after they're cleared anyway, that doesn't take too long, and the benefits are definitely worth it.

Before I get into things, I want to say that I really, really wanted to rate this game up.  I love the approach Freebird is taking to games, and To the Moon is still one of the most sobering games I've played in a long time.  That being said, a Bird Story does some pretty unique and awesome things, but it falls short of the mark.
I'll try my best to go into detail without spoiling anything.  Firstly, A Bird Story is marketed as an interactive story.  It's really not either of those.  The interactive scenes are 'move around, maybe press a button'.  They're largely irrelevant, but that doesn't really detract from the story that's being told.  The story itself does that.  The scenes are fragmented and disjointed, and where To the Moon went to painstaking lengths to confuse and confound the audience  purely to suckerpunch the player with deep and profound realisations, A Bird Story just... is.  It just exists, and that's about all I can say about its impact.  There are a few heavy themes introduced quite quickly, and then they're just... not there anymore.
The areas transition seamlessly together in a unique and very effective "abbreviation" of the real world, and I absolutely love the style.  There's a nice mix of reality, fantasy and memories (again seamlessly interwoven), and most characters appear as faceless shadows (which no doubt is a metaphor for something).  But therein lies the problem.  The game immediately establishes some heavy themes with a lot of potential to explore, but it doesn't even remotely scratch the surface of any of them.  Then it throws in its disconnected fantasy/reality/memory narrative and nothing makes any sense anyway. Add in some drawn out 'go from a to b' scenes, and there isn't really a whole lot to say about the game. It doesn't particularly leave a sour taste in the mouth, so much as an acknowledgement that there just isn't anything to really understand about it (apart from some basic themes).
I was really hoping to experience the roller coaster of emotions A Bird Story sets up, but it just isn't at the top of its game.  It does have a few scenes that do hit the mark (and hit it quite well), but they're very few and far between.
Quick and linear.  Emotional story.  Definitely recommend.

It's kinda like a cross between Desktop Dungeons and other Roguelikes. Enemies stay in place, and you can challenge them as you please, though obviously some you NEED to fight in order to get to the next floor. Along the way, you'll earn gold and experience as you gain levels and kill enemies, and you can loot bags/crates/chests for items and equipment along the way, and collect Stat Gems that permanently increase Stats. When it comes to equipment, they come in 2 type: regular and artifact. Normally when you die in the dungeon, you'll lose ALL progress you made on that run. However there's an item called the Escape Wings, which will not only return you to the town, but will let you keep all experience and levels earned, along with all gold and Artifacts and Stat Gems collected. When you escape, all regular items are lost/destroyed, while Artifacts are kept.
Whenever you gain a level, you get to choose 1 stat to permanently increase, and recieve 3 skill points to spend on the Skill Tree. The Skill Tree for the most part are passives, like increased damage, defense, magic, mana, health, etc.. Though there are Spell to get on the Skill Tree that are kept between dungeon runs. Spells like fireball and the like, though there's a few other utility spells, like one that will turn a regular item into an Artifact.
There are 100 levels in the dungeon, and every 10 levels is a shop to sell your stuff. When you make it to a shop, you'll be able to start your next run on the
shop. So, if I made it to the shop on Dungeon Level 20, that means all future runs I have the option of starting on Dungeon Level 10. There's are pluses to starting at the beginning or an earlier level, like having time to collect money and items, which is useful if you're low on gold.
There's some other side stuff to do, like quests and secret areas that I won't go anymore into. My only real gripe is that you can't rebind keys. It's just a personal preference, but I like to keep my fingers planted on the WASD area, so being able to put the Inventory key on "F" instead of "I" would be a nice touch. You can also play the game using only the mouse, which works great, though Keyboard works just as nicely.
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants a casual roguelike and/or RPG.

I didn't pick up this game until I heard that Re-Logic got some help from another developer and started fixing up some of the problems that the community had with this title and overall making this game great.
That said, it's definitely worth playing.
I was surprised at how deep the game is.  Each pirate you recruit, including yourself, can level up which allows you to allocate stat points on them, give them certain skills or jobs like fishing or cleaning up the ship, as well as giving each pirate a unique personality and a little bit of backstory.  There's a ton of weapons, skills, little gimmicks that you can add on to your ship to boost certain attributes or your pirates' abilities, and a lot of customization when it comes to building your ship.
The UI, menus, and the controls maybe take a little bit to get used to.  It's all cluttered and hard to figure out how to navigate through them, and it's hard to know how exactly to take off blocks and add blocks to your ship.  There's also not much explanation on items in the stores so you won't really know how skills work until you spend the gold on them and try them out.  After some time with the game, this all becomes easy to deal with.
When you make your world, you choose what kind of history it has and what kind of pirate you'll be, and then the world is randomly generated.  Each town and island offers something different, although it starts to get a little repetitive as an island will usually just have hostile inhabitants and maybe a treasure chest.
Battles are pretty difficult at times, but rewarding whenever you get an opportunity to capture a cooler ship than the one you currently have or to blow it up and gain the loot.  The game starts to get easy once you hire a bunch of pirates and level up their stats to crazy levels to where you'll almost never lose.  It does start to become a problem as there is too much crew management rather than actually playing the game, since you have to level up each individual pirate as well as equip them with the best weapons and passive items you've got.  This starts becoming time consuming once you get to a crew size over 10+ pirates, and would maybe benefit from an auto-level up and auto-equip feature.
I'm happy with this game and would love to see some more updates to it with more exciting content.  I know there's still a lot for me to see and a lot more challenges to come my way.

Ahh Quake. The underrated child of the iD FPS family. The eldest brother - Wolfenstein 3D - got himself some glory living off welfare for the first few parts of it’s life but bounced back being a partner with the 2nd oldest one, which is Doom. Who shared the story of Wolfenstein with more mistakes but a bigger boom at the start. Of course, Rage - the little brother - is the most popular new franchise for iD. But am I missing someone? Yes. Quake was the one that came between Rage and Doom. For this entry had some really interesting things about it. Let me tell you, it’s a great game.
Quake’s aesthetic is actually all dark and gloomy. Not satanically evil but kick♥♥♥♥♥in a sense - like Doom. This stuff - if it was a modern game - could be as terrifying as Call of Duty: World War 2’s ‘Zombies’ mode. The theme is Lovecraftian. Monsters from the most disrupted and broken of minds; beasts that wouldn’t just scare or harm you, but cause you to kill yourself as soon as possible to alive your being from any possible notation of that thing existing. It’s also never too dark; preventing a case of the “3Dg3Z” - a design condition that causes a game to be overly intense in lower light usage in order to try to scare the player. This usually fails and makes it look stupid. Henceforth: the 3Dg3Z.
The gameplay of Quake makes sense - a Doom-like game with some tweaks - but it’s actually pretty important. First of all; the new Quake engine - iD Tech 2 - is fully 3D! Doom was 2.5D. It was on the cusp of being fully 3D, but it retained sprites and couldn’t have rooms-over-rooms. These problems and limitations to the Doom engine made iD create iD Tech 2. Actual 3D models were used and rooms-over-rooms were used. Finally, fully 3D rooms could be used. This changes everything. On the flow of movement, moving in this game is fluid and dare I say it, fun!! You can jump left and right without limits. The controls are smooth.
On the end of how level progression works, it’s the standard for shareware games at the time - I’ll get into that later, 4 episodes with 7 levels each. But unlike Doom, the episode kinda cuts off. It’s kinda sad that iD didn’t have a boss at the end of each level. But the creativity of the final boss makes up for it.
The story of Quake is simple. A lovecraftian beast named Shub-Niggurath, y’know, the ‘Goat of the Black Woods With a Thousand Young?’ And her thousand young are taking over the land of Quake. You - which is named “Ranger” and is voiced by Trent Reznor - have to stop this invasion by collecting the four runes of Quake’s magic. Earth, Hell/Fire, Elder, and Dark. Once you collect all four you will finally be rewarded with fighting Shub-Niggurath which looks more like an uprooted tree. So that’s that, you kill Shub-Niggurath. The game is now over. It’s kinda disappointing. No real story post-game. Just “You win ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.”
Shareware Bliss
The thing is that Quake happens to be a game with a shareware episode. What’s shareware? Well, it’s a distribution method where a version of your game that doesn’t contain ⅔ or ¾ of your game that can be legally pirated. I can go ahead and give everyone a shareware copy of Quake and I wouldn’t be legally fined! Hell, I’ll do it right now. In the description there’s a link to get Quake’s shareware episode.
Quake is the basis of all multiplayer shooters. It refined deathmatch causing a classic arena shooter. And while the game may be difficult to set up, once you get it going it’s a blast. Seriously. Try it out!
Quake is a great game, no excuse. With multiplayer, singleplayer and even mods to boot you’ve got a great game. An instant 9/10 due to it being great on almost all aspects.
