As someone who never put a lot of time into turn-based RPGs in my youth, I found Lords of Xulima made me want to go revisit the games I may have overlooked. It's super accessible without being shallow, and even though I needed to pick through the forums for help early on due to my poor sense of direction, when the game opened up I found little need for outside help. Also, the game's really good at making your progress feel like an accomplishment, and makes figuring out certain tricks incredibly rewarding. Like, to the point where I pumped my fist when I got a permanent buff from doing a specific task. My only real complaint is that it ends kind of abruptly, but not so abruptly that I'd say it sours the experience.
Long story short is that I highly recommend this game. It's good fun and even approachable for folks like me who never really got into old school RPGs.

Positives:
Combat
Turn-based combat is well done and uses the melee in the front row and mages, archers, and pole arms in the back row concept (like Might and Magic). Only mages and bards have multi target offensive effects that can hit multiple foes in the front or back lines. Archers and thieves with shuriken can hit front or back lines, but only 1 foe at a time.
Story
As these games go I thought the story was well done and there was an entertaining twist that I didn't expect at the end
Length
You'll definitely get your money's worth, you could easily spend over 100 hours to finish this game. That said it can become a bit of a grind at times, but I always looked forward to playing even with over 100 hours of play time. I definitely recommend it.
Neutral:
Graphics and Sound
Good (for an old-school CRPG) but not great graphics and sound, but you don't play these type of games to show of your $500 video card or sound setup. That said the graphics weren't bad but definitely had a 2000-2005'ish feel to them, and the sound was ok including the voice acting which wasn't bad but went a little high on the cheese factor
Bad (for some)
Difficulty
I thought the difficulty on the Veteran level was perfect, but the game can be unforgiving to those new to CRPGs and even for rusty veterans. Many people on the forum have commented on the difficulty level playing on Veteran (and you can play on Hardcore which is even more difficult). There is definitely a significant difference in this game in terms of difficulty if you choose a suboptimal party or don't level your team with the right skills. The game does little to help here, so you'll either need to learn by trial and error restarting a few times until you figure out the right party mix and how to level your skills. I would suggest that you check the forums and online guides to get some ideas on what parties and classes are most useful and which are least useful.
I will give the following advice for new players. If you want a party that will do well in the early game and all the way through the end consider the following.
Gaulen (axe), Arcane Soldier (sword), Soldier (flail)
Thief (bow, shuriken), Cleric (pole), Mage (pole)
Make sure to get 10 levels of Power and Wound attack for the Soldier and at least 8 levels of Fire/Frost attack for the Arcane Soldier. Get 5 levels of Blizzard early for the Mage to give your group some early AOE. Get the Brittle Armor spell late in the game for the Mage. Get Mass Regen for the cleric (it's OP).

Just finished the game on old-school veteran. This is a rare gem.
My score: 9/10.
The world is vibrant, the mechanics neat. There are a few nice tricks, like limited random encounters (you can clear an area completely if you're persistent, and you get bonus exp for that), additive statuses like Bleeding, Burning or Poisoned (which are a real game changer), Speed is extremely important, as it in effect influences the number of attacks, etc. Exploring new areas was a load of fun, especially with collecting plants and mushrooms. The food mechanics makes you always on edge, planning and logistics is essential. It is just refreshing.
Some people don't like the story. I do. It was solid, nicely done, and the climax is well worth it. All things converge plotwise, the world of Xulima feels very detailed and well-thought.
The graphics and sounds were the thing that I didn't like all that much. Animations for monsters and creatures are... well, a bit dated, and it can be seen. But the sheer power and fun I had with Xulima made me overlook it. I'd rather play  a fun game with great mechanics than a lame pretty game with boring or stupid ones. If this game ever gets a remake...

This is an old school tactical RPG. It is hard. It makes you think hard to beat the next fight and it makes you manage your resources (food and wounds). Every decision you make impacts your success or failure, including where to travel next and whether you will fight or flee. If you loved the unforgiving games of the 80's, this is for you. Each turn is a chess move that can mean the difference between success and failure. Save often! Like Dark Souls, this game gives you the feeling of victory when you finally beat that enemy that blocks your way. If you like easy games, look elsewhere.

I started playing "A Bird Story" a few days after I finished "To the Moon." A lot of people have been comparing the games, and when I first started "A Bird Story" I can't say I didn't do the same. After having finished the game though, I don't really think they should be compared on the same level. "To the Moon" is a dialogue driven novel-like game which spans an entire lifespan, while "A Bird Story" is meant to be a short story about a particular time in a young child's life.
It was difficult at first to become immersed in "A Bird Story" but as I played I became more invested in the story. I liked the the game can translate into lots of cultures due to no language barrier. I think the lack of dialogue adds to the experience because it makes you focus on the emotions of the child. Just like with "To the Moon," the soundtrack is lovely (and contains the songs from "To the Moon" Holiday Special episode) and I cried profusely near the end for a good chapter long. If you want to play this game, but don't want to be dissapointed by it not being just like "To the Moon," I would try to play this game first, or wait a little longer until the memory of "To the Moon" fades a bit before starting this game. The game should be judged on its own rather than in comparison to another game. I recommend this game espcially to anyone who loves animals and can understand the world through a child's eyes.

This is pure narrative experience,  you go where the game wants to, no side trips, no secrets, nothing like that.  It's all about the story here.  A story told totally without words, actually. Ok, with that out of the way, there's the big question, is it worth it?  Is it good?  Yes, it is, absolutelly.  This game isn't To the Moon (by the same creator), it isn't its sequel, it's a separate thing, its own story that's obviously shorter and less ambitious in scope, but it's similar in feel, and just like To the Moon, worth playing. This is one of the best purchases that I've made on steam. The game is very simple in combat and very rewarding in exploration. Picture the concept of dark souls, where you lose souls every time you die. Well if a certain area in Lordran is tough, you go somewhere else and farm some souls, level up and gain new items and abilities until you are ready for the next area/ boss fight. Well in this game, you run around collecting loot in the various generated dungeon levels. Gold items you keep with you for the rest of the gme while white items dissapear once you leave the cave. The only way to leave the cave, however, is with a certain warping item you pick up. Once you warp out, you are returned to the town and all the gold items you've collected remain with you for the rest of the game but all the white ones will dissapear on return to the hub. If you die in the cave, however, you will lose all gold and white items that you have collected and then you will be transported back to the entrance of the cave. It's a very rewarding system and it made me feel like I progressed through each level of the dungeon and it caused me to actually manage my health and magic and make sure I could take down a certain foe. Whenever I felt a little overwhelmed, I would transport out of the cave (to make sure I kept my gold itmes) then I would re-eneter to go to the mercahnt and upgrade my weapon, buy health and magic potions, some armor and anything else I needed then I would venture back into the cave. If an area was too tough, I would go and revisit certain areas to level up on XP and upgrade weapons. What makes this different from needless grinding of XP through less tough enemies is that the loot respawns. I mentioned Dark Souls earlier and this is where these two mechanics differ drastically. See in dark souls (and other games, I'm not just singling out dark souls (I love the game)) loot doesn't respawn on corpses so it makes revisiting other areas much more of a hastle/ tedious rather than something you think you should do and even want to do. While they share the same risk and reward style, they differ drstically here. Now in this game, there is always the chance of finding an awesome gold weapon hidden in a secret area of the cave or in a chest guarded by some enemy. This the game feel fun and refreshing from a stale ginding mechanic you find in a lot of other games. The music in this game is also fantastic. Grant Kirkhope composed it so obviously its going to be good. I usually hate how the indie game scene sometimes rely heavily on a good musical soundtrack and then the game ends up being subpar, but the game and music are both good! One complaint I do have about the game is that there is sometime a lack of gold itmes. You can't purchase gold itmes from the merchant (at least as far as I've gotten) so you have to rely on purchases of white itmes prior to venturning forth and the itmes you find in the cave. But when you do stumble upon a gold item, it becomes your new baby. The crafting system is also very lack luster. It doesnt have the appeal that many other RPG smilar to this one have. You collect different items in the cave or buy the from the merchant but you don't really get to use them quite often and it makes them seem rather useless sometime, but the core game design is more revolving around exploration. Even though it explorartion heavy, it still doesn't excuse these two flaws to the game. This game has great replay value since it's dungeons are random, something you don't see much of now a days. Overall, this is game is right for the price and I would highly recommend it!
+Superb Exploration
+Easy Combat and Health/Magic Management
+Great Music
+Grinding made rewarding
+Random dungeons keep the game fresh
+High replay value
-Lack luster craft
-Shortage of gold itmes in cave
-Can't purchase gold itmes

I've put in enough hours to merit my review, as I am for most games that I play, so trust me when reading this when I say that I know what the game has going for it.
Here's a quick overview of a TL;DR before I get all crazy with my review:
They are Billions is a RTS Base Builder with Tower Defense themes. You gather resources, build defenses, expand, and essentially build a self-sustaining colony. You need houses for people and workers, you need workers to build , you need energy and gold for buildings. It's a fantastic cycle that plays off itself. You can build units, upgradable defenses and walls, and an ever increasing difficulty that, I feel, scales pretty well with you depending on how you play. You learn from each restart [And you -will- restart quite a lot when new, or your colony will perish and you'll start over] and develop skills that will perfect your play style until, like me, you beat your very first level.
Pros:
- Artstyle. Artstyle in this game is minialistic, but fits with what it's giving you. It seems simple, but when you have BILLIONS of zombies rushing at your colony... looking at it from a 'planes-eye-view' is beautiful. I personally adore it.
- Music. Holy christ this music. It's so amazing, dramatic and epic that it makes every wave feel intense. Espcially the final wave [Yes, there is EXTRA dramatic music for the final wave.]... it will have you on the edge of your seat as you watch your colony fight for survival.
- Gameplay. The gameplay is, obviously, a star here, no matter what some say. It progresses fantastically with the difficulty given to you at the start, and the waves grow harsher with every day you survive. The control of your units is fluid [However, there are some janky moments, none to really hinder my enjoyment of the game] and the controls given to you fit well for what the game demands.
- Pausing. In a game like this? Pausing is a fantastic tool to have, and always good to give you some breathing room should you want to perfect your colony.
- Basebuilding. The basebuilding in this game is fantastic. You can turn any start you have from a horrible run to a fantastic base. Of course, there will be bumps with the randomly generated maps... and some maps might require a restart should you feel it, but I always enjoy trying to survive with what's given to me.
- The threats. The zombies in this game, UNLIKE A LOT OF ZOMBIES IN OTHER GAMES, feel truly 'zombie'. The masses are slow walkers that take some time to get to you at the start... then as your colony grows, the threats adapt. Faster runners with more health, then the mutations come with the dangerous zombies. All while coming to you in HORDES... some might even say BILLIONS.
- Replayability. Perhaps it's just personally, since some reviews attack the game for NOT being this... but it's very replayable. I logged 24 hours in the game and every run felt completely different. Not to mention that you can alter various means of the game [Zombie population, game length, etc] to change how you experience every game you play.
Cons:
- Voice-acting. As I'm sure you've read, the voice-acting is... pretty not-so-good. They sound forced and the roles, while sterotypcical and fitting at times, the actors themselves truly feel like they aren't into it.
- Confusing U.I. At times, the games U.I can be a tad confusing. I get lost in various buttons or feel like it's a tad locked up when I'm trying to do something.
- Rough Micro. When you're trying to control your army, it's a tad rough to try and move SPECIFIC units away from the group, or try and split them when being attacked by some special zombies. Perhaps this will come in later development, but still.
Overall? Much more Pros than Cons.
Currently, 23.4 hours into They are Billions, I JUST beat the very first area that you can play on, and what a experience. This game has consumed me like several other games, but in a completely different way. A basic game (100 days) will take you at least 3 hours of gametime... that is, if you can even survive to the final rush. It progressively gives you harder and harder rushes testing and reminding you how, and where, to fortify your colony. One open spot that you aren't focusing on can lead your well established city into another infected den should you not be careful...
If you've read all the way through, then I'm sure there's enough information to sway you to buying They are Billions. The game is fantastic and well done for an early access title, and enjoyable if you're an RTS nerd such as me!

In 1996, even at 4 years old, I was introduced to Quake. It was burned into my mind from watching it; from the 3D visuals, sounds of and atmosphere of the world & the rush of speed! I had seen Doom and Doom II by the time, but Quake was unlike anything I had seen before on the computer. A world of fantasy and horror that made my little brain obsess and fear Quake.
Forwarding years later It can be said Quake even by today (2017) is still a ton of Fun. It's a Fast & Moody Shooter that takes wits and quick reaction time. Although the game isn't as scary to me now as it was then, there is something to be said about Quake's world that feels strange & out of place, encased in darkness and dread that still lingers since 96. Quake to me is a game that still fuels my obsession playing it and it holds true to the legacy Id software had brought with it.
I'd fully recommend this version as most of the old physical copies (mostly the Mission packs) have issues on later systems and hardware (That ain't Win95!) may require 3rd party software to run. But for the Steam ver. it's just a simple download, that's it! : ]
So If one has never played a shooter, Love Doom and Doom II, or are sick of the bleak modern military wantabe shooters, Quake+Mission packs I & II is interesting option. :3 An awesome & classy shooter that kickstarted the 3D FPS craze!
Note aside: Really hoping for a new Quake game in the style of the single-player in this game with Ranger, much like how Doom 2016 reboot did, just putting out that suggestion... C:

This has been a tough game to decide on whether to give it a positive or a negative, but after some thought I have to go with negative.
I was a huge fan of the Might and Magics growing up (World of Xeen was one of my favorite games) and saw this was recommend as a similar type of game. While it might be similar, it simply isn't as good.
The biggest flaw of this game is the ridiculously spikey difficulty. I am playing on the recommended difficulty (classic) and find playing it an act of willpower.  First, the early pacing is horrific.  Honestly, I wouldn't be surprised to see how many people quit this game by level 5.  The combat is simple in terms of mechanics, but dirt cheap in terms of enemies.
You are the chosen of the gods, well get use to being horribly murdered by bees and spiders.  Sure there are other enemies, but the poisons in the game are obscenely strong and will wipe your party.  I have found countless encounters where the game tells me it's a "balanced fight" that are totally unwinnable.  Why not go somewhere else? Well sometimes you simply can't, especially early on. That area is the one you have to suffer through so get use to constantly loading and hoping you get some rolls in your favor.  By the way, the poison isn't even really curable until you get a priest to 15 which is WAY too late in the game.
The difficutly is further inflated by the way random encounters work. Basically, any time you can get jumped and have a chance to flee or fight, but sometimes it just means load. This is because your chance to flee is based on your party speed, which if it is lower, will be a small chance of fleeing. Meanwhile, this same stat determines how easily you can hit things, so the same stat that determines if you can run away determines if you would hit the mobs (except casters).  That doesn't really make a whole lot of sense. It really means you will die and load.  While this is happening, you have to wait for your party memeber to get a turn before you can load.  Well guess what, some of the mobs are so cheap they will chain sleep, mind control, stun, etc affects to the point where you never actually get a turn before you die.  I have found it faster to alt f4 if i fail the flee role than to wait for my first turn.
This random difficulty seems to calm down some after about level 10, but you will still find poison mobs to be the most frustrating in the game.  In general, the monsters stack way too many of their conditions on a single apply and often to multiple party memebers.  You often feel as you need to win the fight as fast as possible, because you have no way of winning a long fight and some of the effects do not persist outside of combat.
There are some effects that last outside of combat and are only curable by the town healer for a ridiculous price until MUCH later in the game, or unless you buy a more expensive potion. I am currently 45 hours into the game and still cannot cure curse, which is unavoidable after certain events. Typically, after you get this cured, the next mob will reapply it and just suck away more of your money.
Aside from the combat, that game loves to throw ridiculous puzzles at you and disable saving just to make you restart them from the beginning.  Failed to weave inbetween those mobs 10 levels higher than you? Watch your whole party die in combat and reload and do better next time.  That's not the way you should go based on random art in the background? Have fun back at the beginning.  After a while, you'll just get sick of it and probably google the answer because you don't like having your time blatently wasted.
The game does have interesting pick lock and disarm trap mechanics that are difficult, but pretty fair.  However, the detection system is pretty wonky.  You have to level up detection to see the traps, but even with it the appropriate level, you will not always see the closest trap in a timely manner.  Get use to quick saving every few steps in a dungeon because if you set off a trap, you will either die or be on the brink of death.  Since trap detection is only on movement, you will find yourself saving before a trap and just walking back and forth in front of it until your detector randomly decides to see it.
Overall, I've had a lot of fun with this game but much more frustration and aggravation, which is why I chose to give it a negative review.  The game itself isn't bad but feels like it screws you over just a little too much. I haven't encountered any bugs in the game or had any crashing.  If you decide to pick it up here is some  advice for you:
1. Wiki your party. Some classes are totally useless and will only take a spot.
2. Get use to saving and loading a lot.
3. Mark food on the map. This will help save early game costs.
4. Prices at the first town for food, sleep, and healing seem to be cheaper.
5. The towns sell a one time use portal device for immediate return.
6. The bosses are pretty unfair and may require you to leave the dungeon and do something else for a few more levels.
7. You can determine the difficulty of a fight by right clicking on a monster. The game never told me this and it is pretty useful but don't take it as gospel.
8. The game doesn't tell you where to go next so if all the new places seem too difficult, see if there is a spot in the old zone you missed.

One of the most awkwardly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ RPG's I have played.
When I buy a game advertised as 'turn based RPG' I expect three things: Character development (the 'role play' aspect), story and (tactical) combat/gameplay
Lords of Xulima fails to deliver on each of these three pillars.
CHARACTER
Roleplay: There is none- you choose your 'character' from 20ish predefined portraits and a name, and thats about as 'deep' as any development of any of your own characters will go.
Advancement: A new defintion of the term liniar character development. No choice, no flavor. Adds absolutely nothing to the genre and the game seems proud of it.
STORY
The dialogue is longwinded. Walls and walls of unvoiced text from the moment you boot up a game.
The story-arch just dumps you into the deep from the very beginning. There is zero introduction of what appears to be the main character. It leaves you wondering wether you missed half of the story before even starting the game. To be fair, I didn't get past the first chapter- maybe it picks up and intentionally overwhelms you seemingly random, self made fantasy lore.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is repetitive and frustrating (you miss a good 50-75% of the time, your opponents hit 90% of the time). These odds trump any 'tactical' play and leaves you to either outlevel/gear the units you fight, or simply die and reload.
As I normally thouroughly enjoy turn-based RPG's of any kind, this was a disappointing experience. Surprised it got so many up votes.

TL;DR: My favorite visual novel game, period. I consider it a must-play for VN/otome fans.
---
: It took me awhile to get past, "Oh, Japan... dating birds?" to try it out. I had resolved I'd heard enough to give it a go, but it took watching Dodger's (presshearttocontinue) Let's Play to actually buy it. It made me laugh and it made me genuinely cry. It's probably best if you are familiar with otome game tropes, but a good background in anime/manga might do to pick up on all the jokes. Even if you only come at the game for the "weirdness", I hope you stay to see its real charm.
: Don't get me wrong - Hatoful Boyfriend may be silly and weird and cute on the surface and once you dig past it, well, it's
silly and weird... But it also brushes along some really dark and heavy stuff. The list that follows will contain content spoilers, though if you have issues, it's better to have mild spoilers than be upset.
SPOILERS: There is violence. Death - lots of death. War. Genocide. Murder (including of children). Suicide.
: I think the translation is fantastic.
: A few very minor issues, but overall, I had no complaints. I can't even remember any specific issues.
: Let's get real here... there's really not a lot of "art" here! Unlike many VNs, there are no "event" CGs. Each character really gets one sprite with no changes of expression and the human portrait you see once
you turn on the human portrait option. In the end, it honestly adds to the absurdity, so I have no complaints. The backgrounds are pretty gorgeous, though. And the ending slates are really cute. The artist has done comics with the gang and sometimes does artwork of the characters, which she posts to her Tumblr and Deviantart accounts. If you want art, check those things out, because they're great!
: On the surface, you're sold on, "Oh, Japan!" - just the absurd premise of a human girl going to a school for intelligent birds and falling in love with one of the birdie boyfriends available in typical "school romance" style.
You dig a little deeper and you see the tropes being made fun of (gently, and with love).
Then you start caring about these "dumb birds".
Then you're hit with something heavy. If you get to the point of caring, it's pretty much guaranteed it'll hurt. The author skillfully manipulates you to this point and I admire her greatly for it.
I honestly find myself at a loss to describe the story in any other way. I don't really see the birds as "bachelors to be wooed", though technically they are. They are, however, characters to fall in love with, and I do. I love every one of them, faults and all.
: She's kind of a meathead, honestly! (The creator also uses a cartoon piece of meat to represent her in the comics.) She's weird and maybe not entirely bright on the surface - but she's probably much smarter than she lets on. She definitely has a personality of her own! (She just has no official character design!) There's something subversive about her that the more I get to know her, the more I appreciate her.
I really, really hope you pick it up. I enjoyed it enough I own the Collector's Edition (something I wouldn't necessarily recommend at full price unless you're already a fan - the comic and yearbook aren't that many pages). I also own all the comics and the sequel game, Holiday Star, from purchasing them from the creator's homepage. I'll also be purchasing a new copy of Holiday Star when it it comes to Steam. I'm a super fan! Complete with fanart! It's often on discount, but even at full price is cheap for such a great game.
EDIT: Just adding that Holiday Star is out on Steam and I hope you pick it up too!
EDIT2: Should also note that Holiday Star is what I'd probably call a "fandisc". It adds content to the universe, but isn't entirely canon. Still quite worth picking up, though!

The Enchanted Cave 2 is an RPG rogue-like developed by dustinaux. In The Enchanted Cave 2 you, an adventurer with your eyes on the prize, enter an enchanted cave and travel through it taking all the loot you can find while taking down or avoiding the many monsters you'll find on your journey in the cave. As you fight monsters and search for loot you'll level up your character, making him more powerful and more able to take on the monsters.
One thing I'd like to address before I get to my review is that this game, despite being called a rogue-like, is not really a rogue-like. Sure it has procedural level generation but it lacks perma-death, when you die you keep all of your EXP and skills that you've collected.
+Great pixel graphics
+The cave consists of 100 levels so there's a fair amount to do unless you blaze through all 100 levels in one run
+Lots of different weapons and items for you to loot along the way
+Good variety of enemies, new enemies are introduced the further you get in the cave
+As well as finding loot you also have the ability to create potions and craft your own gear
+Four playable characters though as far as I can tell the only difference between them is their appearance
+It's simple and easy to get into, not something that can be said for many games similar to this
+Great soundtrack which fits well with the game
-While the skill tree is huge it's far too simplistic. The tree itself is split into three sections: warrior skills, mage skills and alchemist skills. Each section of the skill tree then has about four different skills/upgrades which just get repeated over and over again
-The combat is again, far too simplistic. Unless you try to use the weaknesses of the enemies against them combat consists entirely of walking up to an enemy and watching your character fight it, no input from the player is required
-The simplicity mentioned above leads to very little replayability in the game unless you're a perfectionist
Verdict:
Wait for a sale (7/10)
The Enchanted Cave 2 is a good RPG game with rogue-like elements that has great pixel graphics, a large cave to explore and lots of items and enemies that falls somewhat flat due to it's simplicity.

Intricate puzzles, clunky user intereface, spend lots of time Googleing for clues. But it's cheap and has a walkthrough guide.
TL;DR -- It's worth getting, but don't expect to spend an evening (or several) playing it through. You'll probably start a puzzle and spend the next hour Googleing for possible solutions (or just setting it aside and mulling the problem over).
I'm barely into chapter two and I have mixed feelings about this one. The price is cheap. There's  a bit of a quirky plot reminiscent of the stories like the X-Files. The puzzles are on the obscure side (there's a steep increase in difficulty after chapter one). You absolutely need to be googleing for leads during the game. The user interface is not well designed.
There are a series of discrete puzzles (seems like close to 100) with a vague plot thread connecting them. You get a clue from your online contact and you might have to do some sort of image manipulation or other thing to decipher the clue. You'll probably need to check online for what the clue might mean. What could have made this easier is to cut and paste text from the game and use it in a browser window for the searching, instead of having to retype everything out.
To solve a puzzle, you type the solution and send your contact a message through the faux computer desktop the game provides. The solution has to be exact, which is the frustrating part. Early in the game you have to wait a minute or so for your him to email you back and tell you wether you're right or not. Realistic but frustrating. There seems to be little tolerance for pattern-matching for the solution. It would be a little nicer to get something better than a yes/no on the solutions, like "that was close, but can you give me X's more common name". The reason is that the clues you find might only point in a vague direction to a possible answer to the puzzle, and it's frustrating to try loads of different dead ends before realizing that I should have typed in a person's given name instead of the name he's commonly known by.
The bright side is that there is a full walkthrough in the Community Guides, and several people have play-throughs up on youtube. There's at least one puzzle that I had no idea how to solve, looked up the solution, and still had no idea how I was supposed to have gotten there.
One of the cool ARGs available on steam, those who love solving puzzles and mysteries should try this.

I finished first 2 of 10 chapters but I won't be coming back. This game should be right in my alley but I did not like it for several reasons.
First problem was the clunky UI. It is competently made and looks good but there are several things that make the experience lacking. For instance you receive notifications for messages you've already read making you go back and forth between the screens. As the transition is not instant you are clicking around a lot for no reason. Adding sliders in image app for zoom instead of buttons would help. What I am missing the most is 'reply' button since the mailing app does not remember your email contacts. 'Copy to clipboard' button would not hurt either, especially since for some of the UV solutions you need to flip the image or copy a link.
Biggest issue I had with puzzles where you have to respond with a string is the pattern matching. Without spoiling the concrete puzzles: for instance Louie and Louis are considered different even though it is supposed to be a test challenge and could as well be accepted. I assumed since that puzzle that the verification is pedantic but that was wrong. Case in point being that in other puzzle I tried several entries and variations on a middle name (initial, initial with dot, full middle name) but it turned out the correct answer was a name without the middle one. In some puzzles abbreviation is accepted but not the full writeout or the name of the place/location (school). Similarily name of a place was not enough in other puzzle, location and country was wrong as well, in the end the correct answer was name of a place and 'dessert' behind it.
This issue is magnified by the fact that the verification of your input is not instant and you don't know if what you sent was correct so you just try a bunch of versions every time you send something. Match verification makes sense when you enter codes or passwords but all locations and names should have fuzzy match instead.
Some of the UV light puzzles don't make sense - for instance when the UV is usable on the photo that was supposedly taken by the quest giver. I can live with that. In some of the puzzles it's not a problem to find a solution but rather figure out where to send it. New email contacts could just automatically be added to your email client - it feels like unnecessary busywork to type stuff out all the time.
In a puzzle where password hint is in catalan (?) the answer is not the words in English which would make sense within the game. Not even in Catalan which would make sense in context of the puzzle. Not even in cyrrilics which would make sense in context of the answer. The answer is English transcription of Russian words. Odd. By that point I knew I just have to try all versions because I can't infer the solution from the game.
In a puzzle where I was supposed to look on a website of an island that does not exist I went off to look around the site not knowing I have a new message in the game client. The problem is that if you want to run the game on one screen and search on the other you have to play with a borderless window but you don't have the option to have the game client take your whole screen so the game was minimized while I was trying to call a number on said website.
Somehow all contact exist on the same domain even though naratively it does not make sense. The narrative was overall strange and could use some update. I would love to go on wiki binge across various subjects but the game did not feel like any of the tasks were thematically matching.
Overall - good puzzle game should let you have the 'a-ha' moments. After you figure a solution you should be able to finish a puzzle in a straightforward way. With TTI I had to try bunch of different variation of each solution and that takes the moment from you. Naratively it makes sense that the email is delayed but when the IM is introduced it should be possible to send solutions through it where possible and get an instant reply.
I suspect this was not playtested on an audience because these things would come up pretty fast.
The price of 5EUR is fair if you manage to stick with the game but I had more fun with The Black Watchmen.

In Pixel Piracy you play the role of a dashing pirate of your own make. You can choose parts of your history, but what it really comes down to is your infinite hatred for poop.
Left on his/her own with a boat in a land where everyone has been cursed to poop at any given moment for no reason and no matter where they are, it is up to you to establish the greatest poop cleaning ship in all the land.
Our hero must go to great lengths to train his/her crew in the art of poop cleaning or even improving their skill at controlling their poop.
Aside from the awesome storyline, the player is left with a lot of moral decisions like, do you go all genocide on the natives on some island just in case there might be a cleaning training book on the island? Do you attack the boat that is minding it's own business for the same reason plus a chance at taking a ship that might have more space for poop clearing facilities?
If taking ships doesn't shiver your timbers, you can also build your ship up to your liking. There's a lot of value in building the ultimate ship for combatting the poop menace.
All of that aside, here are some other miscellaneous features of the game that haven't been discussed above:
-Have your crew poop on the enemy ship!
-Watch your crew poop mid-combat!
-Hire awesome warriors to defend your poop cleaning guys. (The latter are the real heros)
-Defeat four major pirate bosses to distract yourself from the real war. (Talking about the war on poop)
-Keep the poopdeck clean, have your men and women wear diapers!
-Bras increase morale!
-Mount cannons and swivel guns onto your ship and shoot at stuff! (Mounted weapons can't shoot poop though)
-Be a badass!
-Ignore the war on poop and watch morale drop like poop in a vacuum!
-Pirate stuff! (Not really a major feature, it's more about the poop)
-Scurvy!
10/10 Would die of scurvy aboard a shop covered in poop again.

Had this on 360 and pc (not EX version) and mostly ignored the game.
Finally gave the EX version a go and I gotta say I'm very pleased with it. The one thing they fixed with this version is they simplified the currency (original game had three types- think nuts, bolts and screws). That for me made it more enjoyable because not having to worry about three different parts to have was a relief.
The second character Tarus is (surprisingly) fun to use... So much so that I completed his campaign, (and Btw I LOVED that ending).
Another thing I really like is the soundtrack. Heavy, crunchy guitar with some really catchy riffs and awesome solo work. This combined with some light electronic music thrown in is by far one of my favorite game soundtracks. I found myself at work whistling some of the tunes even!
Being able to go back to earlier stages with newly gained abilities to access new areas/collectibles /powerups is ALWAYS a plus in my book. So I guess it's *kind of* a metroidvania type game in this sense, but it's not open world. Instead of select the level you want to go to (there's 7 levels). Just think of it as warp spots. :)
I also liked how the cutscenes aren't voiced at all. I know I'm weird but Im the type of person who gives them my own voice.
Only a couple of things I didn't like but these are small nitpicks- every time a boss or miniboss is introduced you have to wait some seconds for an introduction (show off) before fighting.
Also the game is a bit short BUT as you can see I have almost 10 hours having played both campaigns and collecting and upgrading just about everything.
Also I found myself ditching the traditional x to shoot in favor of using the right stick instead. It's something I'm usually against for this genre but it feels much more natural and flows way better.

Lost Planet 3 is a third person shooter, that combines onfoot action with being in a giant mech. It's not quite the same as the previous games, which had much bigger bosses and coop gameplay, but sadly it does share the trait of being a slightly dull shooter.
As someone who enjoyed the developers earlier game (the very underrated 'Legendary') I had hoped to see them move onto bigger and better things. It's a real shame then that LP3, despite some neat touches and decent boss battles, is a bit plodding in general. I still give it a thumbs up because Steam is stupidly unflexible about it's recommendations, and the game is far from awful, but there are issues that drag it into mediocrity.
While your character isn't unresponsive to input he is sluggish when it comes to running, and when in the mech it moves very slowly too - which makes getting around in it a chore. The guns are unsatisfying, and combat just doesn't have the oomph to match a game like 'Deadspace' - it's not absolutely terrible, indeed none of the game is, but it's just so average.
This is at it's worst when they throw lots of enemy at you (and they do as it goes on), yet the bossbattles are actually quite enjoyable, whether they are onfoot or in the mech - or mixing both. That's what makes it so disappointing though - seeing that they are capable of decent gameplay, yet the main mechanics are a bit off, and the level design doesn't recognise this weakness, so compounds it further by upping the amount of shooting you have to do.
At the time of writing this review I haven't finished the game, and am losing patience with it. Admittedly some of the issue is playing it on hard - more than a few sections have been the wrong side of tricky, and not helped by the lumpy feel to the combat.
I wouldn't be surprised if there's a good bossbattle at the end of this, but whether I play through to see it is another matter. LP3 is pretty nice graphically, has excellent voice acting and a decent story - it's a pity that the gameplay isn't nearly as strong. I paid a couple of quid for this, and it's not hugely disappointing, but even reduced you might find it tiresome despite a couple of decent bits. Also I would say don't play it on hard - it's quite annoyingly tough, and saps the fun out of it. If I'd done that this review might be a bit more positive.

It is really well written. The dialogs, the videos from and to your family, the logs you find around the planet, everything is well written. The problem is the tedious gameplay.
This game starts with a very good setting, a sci fi story in an alien environment, the characters have a personality (not just cardboard characters), not the most original kind of characters but really well written. And the non playable characters have meaningful chats with or without you, while they play cards or try to fix a machine. It feels like a real mining facility, filled with people that really live and work there, not just stands there for the player to see something else than the walls.
But then it turns into a cover based shooter, a long and boring cover based shooter with long corridors filled with boring beasts to kill and QTEs. And when you go back to base, all those extra characters disappear, rooms are empty, tables are empty, the guy who was watching a pipe and talked to you three times before with different dialogs (all coherent and with meaning), all gone (maybe there is a reason, maybe later in the story this is explained, but it feels like the base was emptied).
Binary Domain is a cover based shooter, but the pace is fast, it moves forward the whole time. Lost Planet 3 is not a fast paced game, it has a good story and well written dialog, it could take it's time telling the story, building the characters and their relationships, making the player care about the main character and his family, but it chose to be a cover based shooter. And a very boring one.

This game seems to have a really rich story and setting, but after 6 hours of play I gave up.
Combat is, essentially, RNG-based. My main damage dealer, a berserker with no skills besides your basic attack, has 66% chance of hitting the big orc in front of him. if your rolls succeed, you will win the fight. If your rolls fail, you will lose, and there is no way around this.
Most RPGs take a different approach: in FF series, Baldur's Gate and others, a "miss" is a rare thing. Victory is often achieved through management of your  character's health bars, and through the knowledge that there is a constant outgoing and incoming stream of damage.
Other games which have high "miss" chance, such as XCOM, rely on tactical choices and calculated risks: you can move your assault in closer to the enemy, in order to have a higher hit chance, and expose yourself in the process.
This game, though, is the worst of both worlds: battle is an unpredictable RNG-fest. In a "balanced" fight, according to the game, the two enemy archers took out my backline before I had a chance to act (that was my summoner and rogue, 1/3 of my party). I can see why the enemies make such poor choices in combat, such as focusing on my paladin: because if they made the right choices, it would become obvious how unbalanced and broken combat is.
I am currently awaiting a refund request.
PS: after 8 hours of gameplay, I have no direct heal spells. It seems only one of the classes of the game have an ability of this type.

Difficulty: Old school veteran
Hours played: 90
Having completed the game on old-school veteran, here is my take:
I like the fact that you are not given loot frequently, as it A) makes it exciting when you do receive some and B) you don't spend ages sifting through the good/bad loot every 30 minutes. Also, I found gold never lost its value, you never became wealthy to the point that gold became worthless, there was always a nice balance. The visuals are nice, sharp and vibrant but here we move onto some negatives.
Some of the monsters look almost Disney like. At times, I found my party of 6 armed heroes taken out by a couple of Ravens. The villages you come across are almost clones of one another which doesn't offer much excitement and there are few people to interact with. At times the voice acting and dialogue is cringeworthy. I guess these points can be subsumed under immersion, in that they reduce the immersion of the game. Other annoyances for me were things like traps going through walls or being unfair. I remember many times walking slowly through a hallway with my perception being high and still not detecting a trap until it was too late. Repetition was also an issue sometimes with fighting similar groups of monsters, or disarming traps, picking locks that were similar throughout the game.
Back on the positive however, combat was always good and never ceased to be challenging. It was a good experience when you make it through a battle by the skin of your teeth or get defeated and try to work out what needs to be done differently for next time. The music is good and I thought the levelling system worked well. Overall, it was good enough to keep me playing for over 90 hours and if you are willing to overlook the flaws, there is a really solid game just beneath.
Rating: 7/10

This game definitely has a very "old school" RPG feel to it.
The art work is in a very original style, and the combat system allows for several different party formations and strategies.  The story is good, and has an ability to make you want to keep playing to see what you'll unlock next, and where the narration will take you.  Some have described the game as "too linear", but I didn't feel that much.  At the beginning, yes, but it allows you to get a feel for the game play, and get used to managing your party.  Soon players will find that the world begins to open up to them, and the whole set up makes discovering a new area to explore all the more exciting.  Puzzles abound, with many in game clues that are obvious once you discover their secrets, but you will have to read.  Find a random note on some dead adventurer's body?  It's not by chance.
One thing to note:  Level 1 is VERY difficult.  If you're not careful with encounters, and keeping your characters fully rested, some of your party members will die.  That said, there are in game mechanics to over come this, and make the early game difficulty a non factor.
I've played several RPGs that started out great, and then begin to lose their luster mid game.  Not so with Lords of Xulima.  I find myself wanting to continue on to the next quest, and unlocking the secrets of the next area.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes old school, turn based RPGs and is looking to recreate that feel without going back to "retro" graphics and game play.  Lords of Xulima provides that feeling, while keeping a fresh perspective on how a modern RPG should play.
One of my favorite games to play, and sure to be a future classic.  Definitely a world worth visiting, and revisiting.

Now that I have finished this game, can I recommend it?
You play through the game in increments where you go down into the cave, kill a bunch of monsters, get a bunch of loot, and then exit the game through the usage of an item which you always find. If you die, you lose all progress since you last exited the cave, if you leave, you only keep special, golden items. If you have played through the ancient cave in Lufia 2, this is exactly that.
This game is incredibly easy, and has little in the way of customizing your character in way of skills or items. As you start to get towards the end of the game, it turns into a bit of a grindfest, making sure you have enough gear and consumables to beat the end boss.
The game is also pretty short, it would probably have taken about 3-4 hours if I hadn't died on a mini-boss after a couple of hours of play without exiting the cave.
The replayability is limited in that there is a New Game+ option, allowing you to go back to the start of the game with harder enemies, but keeping all your character progression from your previous game.
The problem is that after the grind at the end of the game, I'm not really interested in playing through it again as a New Game+.

Loved the original, love this one even more. The first game felt more like it was about health management than anything else, lacking rewards other than gold when enemies are defeated. The added features of more loot, gold and now experience dropping from enemies changes up the game along with a graphical facelift from its previous incarnation to make a smooth game for a more casual dungeon crawling experience. My only complaint is that the shop UI and the process of getting items onto your hotbar are unintuitive.

I started playing this game via the Free Flash Version found on Armor Games. I was looking for something that provided a mix of challenge without having to over think things. It is something of a puzzle game as well as you decide is it worth fighting a creature to get to a new section of the level or should you work around it.
The broad array of equipment choices, the ability to enchant equipment, and potion making allow you to try out a variety of combinations to find one that works for your play style. The paid version has some nice new content including new side quests, more equipment, more levles, new shop options, and new NPCs. It is well worth the $4.99 price tag. You will find yourself replying and starting over just to try new strategies. For collectors there is even an in game muesum where you can store examples of all the Artefacts you find. Completely your Artefact collection is a nice personal challenge.
Some people might be turned off by the old style graphics, but as a child of the 80s I like the retro look. One other issue that might turn people off are the fact that the monsters don't move around or chase the player, but to offset that monsters often block your path and there are no ranged attacks. So unless you use magical pickaxes to tunnel around them you often have to go through a monster by killing it to get to treasure or the next floor. If they moved you could possible avoid them altogether.
Finally buy the game so that the developer can make more like it!

The summary of the review:
The Enchanted Cave 2 is very solid small dungeon crawler with some very interesting features. Despite some small annoyances I mentioned earlier the game delivers what it promises, which is a fun game. Of course, it doesn’t actually reach the quality of more complicated games developed by bigger companies, but then again it also doesn’t have the problems those game have, like wide variety of bugs. In fact, I haven’t encountered any bugs so far, which is very good thing. Still, a good game for what it is.
Now, the question whether to go with paid version or free to play version. I honestly see no reason why you shouldn’t buy this. The game is cheap, the paid version actually contains noteworthy improvements like more music and items, and honestly developers like the one who is behind this game actually deserve the support they can get.

This is a review of Cases 1-5 of this game, 6-10 have yet to be released.  This is a pretty good game if you enjoy puzzling things out.  Will definitely exercise your brain.  There's a variety of different things you will do to solve puzzles including but not limited to...
Googling
Reverse image searching
Deciphering morse code
Deciphering other kinds of code
Using your smart phone as a QR reader
Logical deduction
Scanning documents with UV light (in-game)
Manipulating photos' colors to find hidden messages (in-game)
Manipulating audio files to find information (in-game)
Other things...
The storyline is definitely a sci-fi/horror B-movie type of plot.  A stronger, more cohesive plot certainly would have helped but that wasn't as important to me as the puzzles, which this game mostly gets right.
Some of the puzzles are seemingly impossible to figure out without strong hints, but the answers to each puzzle are available in the Steam discussion thread if you get stuck.  It definitely seemed like the puzzles got harder as you went, and especially in Case 4 of 5 they were very frustrating at seemingly arbitrary.  Even after cheating and getting the answers to some of them I still couldn't figure out how someone came to those answers.
Overall this is a must buy for $5 if you enjoy these kinds of games.  Looking forward to the second half when it gets released.  These kinds of games are very few and far between so support this developer and pick it up!

I noticed around the beginning to middle of the story i got crippling framerate issues when events would be triggered. They lasted less than a minute and fortunately not during combat. It may have just been something with my computer but that being said I have a beefy PC.
Some of the logistics and story elements don't make sense. Reccomended, but not if you get frustrated by plot holes and only under $15 standalone.

The Bureau may not sport the best visuals, controls or AI out there, it may not have the most length or game depth, hell it may sometimes even be outright stupid, senseless or steal ideas or concepts from other games (we remember Cmdr. Shepard - right?) or media. HOWEVER, I had a blast playing this game 3 (!) times. There is a lot to like here if you don't take every little, tiny bit too serious and just enjoy the dark feeling of an alien-invasion in the 1960's. People are smoking and drinking all the time (which just suits the setting), there is a somewhat creepy Roswell-feeling all the time, the locations are designed really well and the action is likeable, also I like Carter (the protagonist) who constantly stumbles between being a total ***** and a soft-hearted human being. All in all I'd say that if you like cover-based third person shooters, sci-fi settings (and if you wait to get it on a sale), you'd probably get yourself 20+ hours of 1960's fun... ;)

An underated gem, The Bureau does an excelent job of making you feel like one of the expendible grunts you send out as an XCom Commander - and I mean that in a good way! A nice 50s atmosphere and a suprisingly interesting storyline. No, it's not a 'real' XCom game, but taken for what it is - an alternate look at an alien invasion - it does what it does extremly well.

I am going to begin this review by saying it is the first and only game I have ever bought pre-release. I read some interesting thoughts about it on the RPG Codex and snapped it up.
What does Old School RPG mean? If you think it means I played RPG back in the day and therefore fully capable of playing this one on Difficult - you won't get very far. Back in the day a bunch of us played RPG like Bards Tale 1, Wasteland 1, Ultima IV etc. They were not easy games. Try playing them now.
So my first tip is to play this game on normal difficulty and save yourself some angst - unless - unless you can remember all the mantras from Ultima IV and know the optimum party build for each Wizardry and Might and Magic.
The game - it's a blobber. Party based turn based combat. It is better than M&M X Legacy.
It's a beautiful little gem developed by this small group of people that obviously love RPG games. It comes through in the design and gameplay.
I was exploring and came across this structure and went inside. I found a talking skull that asked me its name. How would anyone know that. I was stuck. There are a few teleports around so I explore - going from place to place and mapping as I go. Still stuck. Frustration time right? I look at the overhead map and my poor old brain tells me the different sections sort of look like letters. If you look down from above like a map does. I have letters - but what is the order? Each section has candles - leading from 1-6. I solve the puzzle and progress.
I found the puzzle unique and amazing.
The game is not linear. But that does not mean you can go where you want. The trick is navigating a pathway through the dangers and my path was different from others. For example, I did not tip toe around the sleep causing mushrooms heavily cursed by all the frustrated players giving negative views. When I finally came across them I ate them for breakfast.
Some players get stuck because they do not pay attention to the text. Unlike M&M X, you need to pay attention. Pathways previously blocked open up as you progress. You need to backtrack. The game is not linear.
You need to use strategy in this game. RPG Strategy? What is this game some sort of RPGS - never heard of that. SRPG?
Off course you can run around and eat mushrooms and pick flowers. Your bard can sing 80s pop music. Can you manage assets? What the heck will your mage do when he runs out of magical energy - defend every turn? Maybe take a short tea break? You stock up on health potions but what are you going to do when you know someone in your party is likely to die because four spiders have their turn in combat before they get a chance to gulp down a potion? Damn healing scrolls - stock up.
Are you stocked up on torches and lock picks? Buy food and explore and then come back. Push your limits before heading back. Usually about five days is enough because after that the cost gets prohibitive. Don't rest after each fight like some weakling. Man up.
The combat is complex. I could write pages about it. Bleeding, Burning, Burping, Stunning, Wounding, Sleeping.
Your little thief from only doing 1 damage per turn with his little dagger becomes the best fighter in the game if you train him on Shurikens. Pointy ninja weapons that disappear after you throw them. Apart from the basic damage they do they also do Bleeding damage that stacks over time. STACKS OVER TIME. Remember that. You can only buy three of these at a time before the shopkeeper runs out - come back tomorrow! Keep all of these until you really need them. I had around 100 in stock before I came across some badass that would not go down.
Stacking works on your party as well.
Stunning. Some weapons don't do bleeding damage or cause wounds. They stun your opponent. I came across this evil looking Emerald Wyvern who basically could not get an attack in. That was amazing. Makes me ponder a STUN + STUN + BLEED front three. I came across this little Imp guarding a treasure chest who would not get out the way unless I answered a little riddle. Get lost you little squirt. He then grew to a gigantic size and nearly polished of my party as none of the bleed or stun effects worked on him. Eventually I figured out he was weak to burning and basically went into defensive mode apart from my Mage throwing fireballs like a maniac.
I could tell you lots of amazing stories about the game. The time I went through the desert and came across a kebab vendor. I will just say Buy It and support this little company.
Tips for beginners unless you want to learn the hard way.
Harvest those little wheat plants in the first town and sell for profit. That little money will help pay for food or blessings.
Blessings - get them for Speed increase and Resistance and Evasion - you get the idea
Skills - train up as many skill points as you can afford - you get four per level up but what would you do with 6 or 8 or 12?
Yes. Spend that cash mate. Your thief can pick locks better, train weapons, improve immunity and gain experience faster. They can even do some body building in the local gym.
Don't waste your Mage's time training his little puny staff fighting skills or trying to buff his muscles, maximise his potential in magic. He don't need the ability to wear Steel Armour as if everything goes correct - he won't never be in the front row.
That little twerp Gaulen - try waiting on picking flowers until he can get 3 herbs per pick. Train his hunting and exploring skills. People complain about the food requirement all the time. With hunting your whole party can transverse many maps with animals without losing food - you gain it!
Your Bard - he ain't a fighter - he is a pansy artiste. Stun music, music that make you angry, music that inspires you is the way to go.
You don't have to rest 8 hours after each battle to heal up - your cleric can do that - just make sure you have mana potions in stock
It's a charming little gem of a game. Don't think you know it all cos you played Baldur's Gate back in the day.
Support these guys and let's look forward to Xulima 2

Normally, when a game costs 1 euro it's rare for me to give it a negative review, because I tend to believe that at this price a lot can be forgiven. Psychocat, however, managed to step on my toes in all the right ways for that to not happen.
The game consists of you hurtling down a winding tunnel, having to jump over obstacles or duck underneath them at high speeds. To win (find the answer) you have to survive 175 seconds of that, but every 25 seconds the (randomly generated) obstacles get a bit harder. There are no checkpoints so any failure resets the playthrough. There is one, short musical track which is cute for about 30 minutes tops and the game is visually poor despite being colourful on the surface.
This game is
too difficult. The "difficult = good" meme has been going on for a few years now, and I still despise it. It is also too low on content. It feels like a tech demo or an alpha version of something that ended up not taking the shape it should down the road. The most fun I had with Psychocat was attacking it with tools, looking for solutions to the problem that this game is. Unless you are willing to do the same I definitely don't recommend it.

Hidden Folks is a hidden object game, akin to the old Where's Wally books. Unlike the old Where's Wally books though, Hidden Folks doesn't have a recurring character, like Wally, that you need to find on each page. The game has a very nice atmosphere to it, and the gameplay is amazingly fun!
Hidden Folks does not copy the typical hidden object book/game in a lot of aspects though, sound has become a major part of the game, not being essential, but adding so much more personality to the game. All the sounds in the game can be reproduced by the mouth, giving it a very childlike feeling to it, which accompanies the feelings of nostalgia (for the old hidden object books) quite well. Along with the design of the characters possessing a hand-drawn aesthetic, this creates a very comforting world to find hidden people in! (quite child friendly, with the exceptions of a couple minor characters in the game). You can change the atmosphere of the game majorly by selecting different colours for the game to be in. You can choose the average white background, and black lines, a light brown tea-stained look, or black background with white lines. I personally like the light brown look better, as it is easier on the eyes, so your eyes can focus on more important things, such as finding hidden folks!
The gameplay is very much what you'd see in a hidden object book, such as Where's Wally, with a lot of differences, mainly the game does not try to blind you with colours such as many hidden object books at the time did (especially Where's Wally), instead many of the people you need to find can be found through interacting with the environment (ah, the wonders of video games!), as well as reading the hints of the listed characters/objects you need to find, which changes in every scene. The game shakes it up as you progress the level area change, from forests to deserts, and change in difficulty, from small little maps, to huge ones! Many of the hidden folks at first are quite easy to find, but eventually you'll have one left, and for the life of you, you still can't find them! This game provides quite the challenge sometimes! But the game never gets too frustrating, it's hard to stay too angry at such an adorable game!
In short, although there is not much to say about this game in general, most of the charm and fun of this game cannot be explained, more of have to be experienced. The real hidden object game is really Steam, and trying to find a game that is amazing, and this game is that hidden gem. A game that's so enjoyable that it even makes the credits fun to read!

If you ever played Lufia 2 - Rise of the Sinistrals on the SNES you should know the Ancient Cave - the optional dungeon of that game. Enchanted Cave follows the same principle. You explore a cave with 99 floors where you will only be able to go further down, not up again. Every floor is filled with monsters and treasure and you must try to find good equipment and fight you way through. If monsters get to strong you can teleport out of the cave with a special item you have to find - but you will lose all equipment you found except for special artifact gear which you are allowed to start with at your next run.
Every 10 floors you reach a checkpoint, meaning you can start your next run from there once discovered. Occasionely you will find a shop (usually on said 10th floors) where you can sell your crap and buy useful stuff.
What i really enjoy compared to the first game is the implementation of a crafting system. You can't craft your own gear but improve the stuff you found for some extra stats or nice things like life regen.
I also like the new dungeon layout. The floors are no longer plain squares with walls drawn within them which is nice. There is also some sort of skill tree now which i guess could have been more interesting than it is. The magic path is nice since you learn your spells there now instead of finding them but everything else is just minor stat improvment.
Some of the villagers will give you quests that so far only consisted of finding specific things in the cave. Not the most interesting thing to do but it's alright for a little extra stuff to do.
Summary:
Some nice improvements over the first game. If you like rouge-lite dungeon crawling i highly recommend this one to you. The price tag is fair since i think you will at least get 10-12 hours out of it to complete it once and replayability is given for perfectionists.

So I write this review after playing through the base game only.  And I've only done my first playthrough, and am starting my second.  This doesn't take into account any DLC or the effects of a high chaos playthrough.  But I felt I could safely recommend the game after one low-chaos run.
The gameplay is just fun.  There's lots of fun ways to approach stealth, and lots of fun ways to approach combat, which means both styles of play have plenty of fun options.  The "good" ending requires more stealth than combat, and can be tracked with the "chaos level" indicator at the end of each level.  You CAN go back down to low chaos if you murder hobo everything in sight on a single level, but there is a point past which you're stuck in high chaos.  Basically, just kill nobody if you want low chaos.
The lore is amazing.  Read every book.  Listen to every audio log - and note that any time you rest or revisit a location, an audiobook might have new content despite being in the same spot!  Use the heart on everybody with a name and in every new location.  Listen to ambient conversations.  It makes the game so much more real and immersive, and gives a lot of believability to everything going on.  It also sets up some of the most fantastic plot moments later that otherwise would not be nearly as hard-hitting.  Take your time with this one, and really explore it as much as you can.
I wish I'd bought this and played it sooner.  The only complaint I really have is that some mechanics are poorly explained, and that leads to some frustration on occasion.  If something seems off, or if you don't understand, look it up.  You'll appreciate this masterfully done game more for it.

This is probably one of the most underrated games of the 21st century. I picked it up back on the PS3 originally, and despite it's flaws at launch such as mediocre AI and minor lag, (issues that were improved later into the games life) it was an absolute blast to play. The varying levels of customization were great, spanning all the way from weapons to the character itself. Not only that, but all the maps played well and looked absoulutely georgeous. The gameplay was a refreshing change to what you experienced in most FPS games at the time, with fun and flamboyant free running moves that not only looked great but were simple to execute. However, because Brink was developed by 'Splash Damage' and not 'Infinity Ward' websites such as IGN and Gamespot gave it a 6, slamming the game for it's poor AI and repetition. Sure I'd accept that if this was a game that based itself around singleplayer rather than multiplayer gameplay, but marking it down for repetition when video games such as Modern Warfare 2 get given 9's is ridiculous.
At the end of the day, this was a game that had it's head put on the block before it even got released. Sure, it's far from perfect, but it's as good as your going to get if your looking for a multiplayer FPS that's a little different from the norm.

My updated review for Pixel Piracy
------
4/26/2015
------
It's finally happened. This has become an actual game.
However, I still give it a "Does not reccomend".
-----------
Pros:
-----------
+The concept is pretty neat; there aren't enough 2D pirate games out there.
+The micromanagement system is alright (More on that later)
+It's pretty decent fun in small doses
+So, So much poop.
-----------
Cons
-----------
-The menus are fairly clunky, mostly in part due to a lack of a hotkey system
-There is little to no direction. They've recently added a tutorial to the game, but it still doesn't help all that much.
-The GUI can be pretty bad at points
-The Pirate AI is only customizable to a certain extent, based on what one of six or seven preset categories.
The game is to a point where I personally feel it could
feel good about calling it a finished product, but that's only in regards to a "Competed game design document" standard. There's still a TON of room for improvement.
With the kind of game this is, I'd expect you would be able to micromanage your crew all the way down to their very priorities of things that need to be done.  Unfortunately, I've had to keep all of my crew in the "Ship Crew" AI group because if I put them on Boarders like I would want to, they shirk their other duties like cleaning and repairing the ship.  I want to be able to create my own group types, create as many of them as I want, and get to customize EXACTLY what each of them does. There's also some problems with them only eating fruits rather than anything else on the ship, which is really frustrating because the fruit is only there to prevent scurvy, not so you can stuff yourself with it every single bloody meal.
I'll probably finish my playthrough, but until they add hotkeys to everything, improve the micromanagement, and make the pirates less stupid, It's gonna be a down-vote from me.

Pixel Piracy Review:
In this fantastic game, the graphics are in an 8-bit style. The devs of this game have actually done their job on this topic very well, they have added some cool effects, hundreds of weapons, a massive map and lots, lots more. The water is beautiful, the effects are awesome, the island / cities are not too interesting though. The start-game islands are very dull and boring, but once you go further into the game, they become a lot better, sometimes they have an interactive item (such as a banana tree). The animations are not too bad for an 8-bit style game, but they could've been improved. The weapons look very cool once you go further in the game. In fact, there's two different weapon types, melee and ranged and both look like they could do quite some damage.
This is a rouge-like game, so if you die once, you're out (unless you save your game). You will not get bored, even if you just came for the ship-building! Anyway, I'll tell you what you can do, from start to finish. Choose how your story started (it affects your gameplay) . Hire shipmates. Get weapons. Upgrade weapons. Kill enemy pirates / ships. Get quests. Build a might ship. Raid an island. Get companions. Level up. Make your mates learn skills. Cheat. And way, way, way more!
Pixel Piracy has some very good sounds, the muic is even better,though. Most things have their own sound, even the voices of pirates sound completely different from eachother! The quality isn't that bad, especially for an 8-bit game that is still quite early in developement. Apart from that, there is no more to talk about in sound.
Pros:
Replayability
Fun to play
You won't get bored quick
Tons of things to do
It's a rouge-like game with a twist
Character Creator
Cheats
Thousands of things to collect
Quests that aren't boring
Good community
Beautiful graphics
In depth settings
Cons:
Bugs
In conclusion, this is a fantastic game that's still being developed and doesn't cost much. So pick this up if you love pirated, 8-bit games or superb cheap games.

Originally I wasn't exactly happy with a lot about this game. A friend of mine wanted to play multiplayer in this though, said it was a lot of fun. In all honesty, I was surprised at how much he was right. The supplies mechanics are somehow both simplified and more complicated at the same time, while the way events are triggered and take place allows a somewhat historical game while events depend on your decisions, rather than an arbritrary start date as they were in Hearts of Iron 2.
The main downside of this game is the short period of time it covers. CK2, EU4, and even Victoria 2 all cover extensively longer time frames and have more overall replayability. The modding community of HoI4 helps to some degree, but this game could really do with an expansion of the timeline into the Cold War. The games are significantly shorter, but they're still fun while it lasts.

Do you remember
? It was game from 2001 by EA, back when EA was still a decent publisher that didn’t pump out repetitive trash. It was basically an augmented reality game. It lasted maybe a year, as it was commercially a failure. But it utilized the real world to solve problems. You could work with other players. There were phone numbers you could call, and you could receive phone calls with clues. There were videos to watch, and full websites made specifically for the game. It wound up being pretty fun, and I had a blast with it.
reminds me of
. It’s far less interactive, in that you search for already existing information, and it utilizes a sandbox email and internet system (so no actual access is required), but it has all the makings of a pretty fun, albeit exceptionally hard, game.
I’ve never had to use my brain as much as I did this one, nor have I had to confer and talk with people and work together as much as I have on this (not including obvious multiplayer games).
The game starts you off easy enough, with a couple of very easy riddles that everyone will get, even if one of the events took place half a decade ago. But the difficulty ramps up quickly, requiring you to change the coloring of an image to find hidden symbols, which might be from a cipher last used in the Roman era, to then convert to English which will reveal the coordinates of a location, having you use Google Maps (or some other subpar mapping service) to find the location, to then finally provide the answer to Dr. Quantum, who is your main contact throughout the game.
Puzzles, as partially explained above, will consist of: using a UV light, manipulating pictures, scrubbing audio, watching videos, translating ciphers (both real and fictional), figuring out non-typical alphabet systems, Wiki’ing, and more. Unless you’re a genius with an intimate knowledge of history, geography, cryptography, and television shows, you will be frustrated, but that frustration will pay off.
is a unique game. It gives you clues you need to find in the real world, to present to the game in hopes of figuring out just what is going on. The difficulty ramps up to the extreme not too far into it, and requires you to be either very knowledgeable in every subject the game touches on, or has you talking with people to figure out the clues.
Even if not on sale, there is a decent amount of content for the price, part two is actively being worked on (as of this review), and the developer has said corrections are coming to the grammar to make it both easier to understand the clues, and less trial and error for accurate answers (also being worked on as of this review).
It’s well worth your time. It is also a very small game, and one that should have no issue sitting on your drive should you take a break from it and revisit it a few days later, a week, or a month down the line.
