Lost Planet 3 is a good game that gets completely ruined by an excessive amount of padding and uneven pacing. If this game had been cut down to 5 or 6 hours, it would have been great, unfortunately it's twice that length, meaning almost everything gets stretched beyond enjoyability. Everything gets repeated over and over again in an MMO like grind. You fight a boss once, you'll fight him two more times. You drill a well, you'll drill three more. You fix one broken switch, five more await. All while being forced to stagger in your helpless Mech from location to location in excruciatingly slow fashion because fast travel doesn't open up until you're a few hours into the game, and even then it only works half of the time. And that is the real shame of this game, it wastes your time to such an insane degree that it becomes almost insulting; why do I need to take three different elevators to visit the labs? And the worst part is that, in truth, none of it was needed. The story was great, until the bad ending, the mechanics and gameplay were varied and enjoyable, the devs didn't need to inflate the run time. Paired with its multiplayer component, a shorter campaign would have been fine. Instead you have three, maybe four hours worth of quality gameplay and two-ish hours of cutscenes, stretched out to span twelve or so hours. Resulting in what could have been an amazing game, being rendered a complete waste of time.

Really good game ! Perfect for anyone wanting a modern turn based RPG old school adventure. A few points:
1) It's challenging. You need to think. There are times when things seem impossible - but there is always a way around.
2) Not every monster you come across must be fought then & there. Some are too hard and must be revisited later.
3) This game requires a lot of 'path finding' - finding alternate ways to reach your destination (walking around traps, tough mobs, thickets of trees etc).

5) Prioritise purchasing of mana potions.
6) Use the blessings from the town spiritual healer as often as possible - they make a huge difference.
7) The talisman of Golot DLC is worth it. The gold giving ability it provides is a massive help.

A Bird's Story is a charming experience that explores a brief time in the life of a young boy who one day discovers a wounded bird. He is imaginative and isolated, and the story that unfolds from his time caring for the bird is thought-provoking and heart-warming. This is, essentially, a feel-good game, but there are heavier undertones present that minimally occupy the story.
With a poignant soundtrack and characters that express themselves without dialogue, Freebird Games has accomplished something significant. It could be said that A Bird's Story is more visual novel than game, but that doesn't lessen the experience. This is a story, and it is the story of a tragically alone child who grows throughout the course of his time caring for the bird. Whether the bulk of the experience is purely in his imagination is of little merit: by the end of the story, he is more whole.
Absolutely recommended. This is a brief game, and it is entirely worth your time.

This is another example of a game that you have to play for what it is. If you leave a negative review for this because of its graphics or its length, you're an idiot and you're wasting everybody's time. With that in mind, I feel fairly confident that there isn't really a valid reason to give this game a negative review at all - for what it is, it's about as good as it can possibly be.
What it IS, is a very minimalistic little game with old SNES-era graphics that focuses on telling the best story that it can in its weird little medium. If you like games where the priority is the quality of the story and that premise sounds interesting to you, you will absolutely enjoy this game. Some more direct thoughts on the game itself - I really enjoy how it tells its story with surreal transitions that don't waste any time. The game is incredibly short because it
wastes your time - it is very efficient story telling. I think a big part of why it packs such an emotional wallop is because of how efficiently the story unfolds. You should be warned though that the story can be a little surreal and hard to follow at times. This does seem to be intentionally done, however. The point is worth considering though if you really don't like stories that aren't crystal clear. Ultimately, this is a great story in a plain looking package - it's very short, very cheap, and it's worth your time and money.

Enchanted cave 1 and 2 are the ultimate Dungeon Crawler/Rogue Like experience for
me, and with enchanted cave 2 compared to 1 the experience went to a whole new level.
The sequel adds better graphics, a larger, more interesting dungeon to explore, and a improved inventory screen and special attack system. The story is more interesting and we
have a town with NPCs.
The progression tree will allow you to become a mage, warrior, alchemist, or a mix of skills.
Craft potions, enchant your equipment and discover secret areas, all while learning more about the cave.
And you can now step over empty cloth sacks!
The most unique and fun feature in the game, in my opinion is the fact that you have to go in the cave several times to get deeper each time using the escape wings at the right time.
All floors are randomly generated so not 1 run will be the same.
The feeling of getting further each time you enter is a very good experience for me.
After you beat the game NG+ will offer a new challenge.
Having played the flash and android version for dozens of hours I highly advice anyone who loves rpg/rogue like games to give it a try.

The Enchanted Cave 2 comes to Steam, after a premium version of the game made it's way to the mobile platform a while ago. While the game isn't overly complicated in its mechanics, it's able to mix things up with resistances and other types of challenges to fully take advantage of risk/reward gameplay, where you have to question attacking an enemy and what benefits it gets you. The crafting system 2 attribute system does add a layer of choice that's appreciated, and while the combat is rather simple, it can work over the long haul. The music by Grant Kirkhope does stand out and was able to be listened to repeatedly over a period of time, and honestly, it's just a solid title all around, where you want a little bit more of a thinking roguelike more then anything else.

Evolve Stage 2 is is a truly unique multiplayer experience. Four Hunter players must track and hunt one Monster player, who must grow strong enough to beat the Hunters or destroy their base in a limited amount of time.
In an industry where most games shamelessly repeat the same old formula, and every multiplayer deathmatch is basically the same game, Evolve is a light in the dark.
Pros:
- Free to play
- Appeal to wide variety of play styles
- Each character/monster has unique play experience
- Each role has distinct job
- Dynamic, interactive gameplay
- Complex mechanics that are satisfying to learn and master
- Skill and teamwork are highly encouraged and truly matter
- Strong character designs (monsters look very alien, Hunters are all distinct and have unique personalities)
- Engaging sci-fi setting behind the game
Cons:
- Game takes patience to learn
- Visually busy
- No longer being patched
Just because a player is good at shooters or familiar with 4v1 gameplay does not mean they will master Evolve immediately. It requires some degree of patience and active learning to get a feel for how each role and character fit into the flow of the game. Like any game, it takes practice.
However, once you get a gauge for that flow, this is a very satisfying game to master. The mechanics are deep and complex to explore. The gameplay is dynamic, engaging, and involves constant adaption to the scene. Characters have a range of precision and burst abilities to use in combat, appealing to different player preferences. Successful moments are earned by skillful play and strong teamwork. The multiplayer component and variety of character interactions make for fun, different experiences every match.

A.R.E.S. Extinction Agenda EX is a side-scrolling mecha shooter game, safely to say a Megaman clone.
You have 2 mechs to choose from Ares and Tarus, similar to the roles how X and Zero in Megaman series.
Each has different set of weapons and abilities and both have different storyline, though same levels and objectives.
The game technically and visually is good, however the soundtrack doesn't fit and really boring.
The story in general is generic, although it has few cool twists. But it's nothing special at all. You go on levels, destroy bots to save humankind. That's it.
You have also a human female as an assistant that communicate with you throughout your mission and develop new upgrades for you suit.
During the levels there are database cubes and upgrade units to collect, the former for expanding game lore to read and the later allow you to upgrade weapons and abilities.
Each character has 7 levels, which are exactly the same but different dialogues.
And you can beat the entire game in few hours (took me 5 hours).
Let's switch to the cons:
- Level designs: Some areas can be really frustrating, designed to hinder your movements limits to your demise.
- Unskippale scenes: This really made me mad, because checkpoints happen before a hard part, which forcing me to watch the same scene over and over and over until I successfully pass the area. Boss Battles has the same problem.
- Checkpoints sometimes are set far from each other, again due to some areas being frustrating, having to run through many rooms/traps/enemies before you getting to a new checkpoint isn't really a nice idea if you want to put a challenge in the way. I really don't like repeating the same steps for 5~10 times before I figure out a solution.
- The Ending (both endings), although are good, end abruptly. It would be better to see at least a glimpse of the aftermath.
6.5/10

I'll be honest, I wasnt a big megaman fan back in my youth but metroid always was fun when I was able to borrow it from a friend. that being said: I want to like this game. I really really do! it's been on my wishlist for what feels like forever. it's been on here for so long that I didnt even know that they made this "EX" version of it until this very summer sale.
now that we have the intro out of the way:
+the visuals are really nice and pretty. the interface is clean, easy to understand and doesnt interfere or hinder gameplay in any way.
+the soundtrack is awesome and gets you pumped, wanting to keep charging in, dodging and weaving while dishing out your own punishment.
+it has that fun factor that you want in an arcade-style game in the vein of megaman, metroid, I'll even throw in contra and metal slug.
+the level up system is simple
+the upgrade system is simple as well and clearly meant to foster replayability (and done right, I'd say)
+enemies are cool looking and there's enough of them to present a challenge as well as allowing for satisfactory accumulation of your currency/resource. BUT!
and here's where we get to the cons:
-the hitboxes seem off to me. maybe I'm crazy but there are times where I've gotten so frustrated when I analyze a bosses pattern, go to dodge and watch myself still get hit.
-that also being said, the controls are definitely sluggish (using a mechanical keyboard). input lag is a very real and very deadly thing in this game, especially in boss fights and even more so when it comes to platforming puzzles where timing is key.
again, I really really really want to like this game. it's got that something that really helps scratch that arcadey-classic side-scrolling shooter itch and does a lot of things right that other similar games dont (level up, upgrades, interface, soundtrack, etc). but the fact that the controls are so slow and the hitboxes dont really seem to match the visuals sometimes just weighs so heavily upon this game since it's fairly fast paced. you're not sure why you didnt dodge that thing when it looked like you did on the screen, and you're pretty sure that you tried to 2xjump+air dash up, but instead you just headbutted the edge of the platform. I'll admit, I'll still keep playing this game and try to "get gud" but as it stands now, I cant recommend this game on the grounds of its combat and controls. if one was spot on accurate, the other wouldnt matter as much. but the fact that both of these major issues  are in the game just make it incredibly frustrating to make it past battles/platform areas. one last plus side though is that you dont really loose anything other than distance when you die

Before we get to the PRO's, let's get to the CON's first. Why? We'll diacuss that later.
CON's
1. Physics are garbage
2. Game doesn't launch frequently when booted
3. Multiplayer server is dead, so if you go with the online mode, you'll be stuck at nighttime since day and night cycle also stopped some time ago. You can't use online features either (e.g. casinos, clubs)
4. You can't add your own music into the game
Now, let's discuss the tasty spicy bits!
PRO's
1. Graphics are pretty beautiful.
2. Inbefore, in TDU1, we only had Hawaii. Now, we have Hawaii AND Ibiza!
3. Offroad races and cars!
4. More avatar and house customizations!
5. You can now apply car stickers!
Sure, the PRO's aren't really significant, but why do I still recommend this game?
1. The physics are moddable. Look for CTR handling mod and install it right away. This will make the handling physics a whole lot better. So that's the first CON countered, which is a big deal.
2. Download Knyazev's universal launcher for TDU2 and launch the game via that. You can also choose to go online or offline now. This will counter the second CON and enable the day night cycle. Keep in mind that CTR handling mod requires this launcher too. Otherwise, the game won't launch at all.
In conclusion, TDU2 sure has its flaws, but the player communities have managed to counter the significant ones. To be able to play and get as much good experience as possible, a little bit of modding is required and the process isn't complicated.
Should you buy this game?
Yes, but only when it's on sale.

Hidden Folks is not exactly a bad game but it is a disappointment. Everything I read about this game and everything people told me about it made it sound like it was Where's Waldo but for the modern era. It's not. I used to love hidden stuff books when I was a kid so this should have been perfect but the thing that those books had that Hidden Folks does not is simply visually interesting stuff.
Let's try something: I want you to go to google and just search for a page out of a Waldo book. You don't even have to bother looking for the guy, just look at the pages. You'll quickly notice that they are full of gags and interesting stuff happening, things that are not related with Waldo at all but simply happening in the scene. It is dense with fun things to see because the creator of Waldo would start each scene with a list of jokes or other visually interesting things that he wanted to draw and THEN he'd put Waldo in the scene once he had an interesting setup to show. Hidden Folks doesn't do that nearly as often. Instead it hides those little interesting things (a lot of times not that interesting either) within a massive scene of mostly copy-pasted and just slightly tweaked assets meant to hide what you are looking for, nothing more. That's just a bummer when it could be so much more if they focused on scene composition rather than having huge, sprawling screens full of little guys doing this wavey motion with their arms. It's why the tiny puzzles within Hidden Folks work better than the rest, I think: Less repetition, more unique and interesting stuff.
Get it if you like finding random stuff but don't expect a ton of clever or amusing things outside the cute noises and kind of cute graphics.

This is another solitaire game by the developers who made Chef Solitaire. So if you enjoy that one, you're bound to like this too. Actually, I like this one MORE but that's because of the theme. Graphics - Beautiful. Christmasy. Will make you smile.
Music - Great selection of different Christmas tunes. I often turn music off but these songs are quite fun and add much to the mood so I shall be keeping them on.
Gameplay - Basic solitaire where you're looking for one number higher or lower. There are 24 levels (in an advent calendar style) with multiple hands in each. At the beginning of each level, you'll play a very short hidden object scene. Then during play, little mini games will pop up. They're actually cute but I don't like being pulled from the main game so I turned them off in options. And you can play them separately from the menu whenever you wish. You earn gold from doing well in the game and you spend those coins in a shop to buy (uber cute Christmas) powerups and other passive abilities that make playing easier. There are also 3 levels of difficulty to choose from. If you've played any solitaire games (and especially if you've played Chef Solitaire), you know what to expect.
Bottom line is, this is a WONderful solitaire game for those in need of some Christmas spirit. There's a story told with cutscenes and voice acting between levels. Though in this case I can't tell you if it's any good because I haven't gotten very far. But I'm definitely going to keep playing. I'm sad about the lack of cards and achievements but this game is just plain fun so I'll get over it. :)
Two thumbs-up from me.

Let me start by saying this is not your traditional run and gun mega action Lost Planet game. If that is a major turn off I would not reccomend getting this. Lost Planet 3 is an interesting case where the devs decided to take a more story driven approach. You play this game for its story, and that's about it. It has this interesting quest system that made me feal as if I were playing an rpg game, and to be honest I liked it. I believe the game has a great story, one that really wrapped me into to it. But now lets talk about the gameplay itself. Lost Planet 3 takes a Dead Space approach to over-the-shoulder third person view, unlike other Lost Planet games. I'd forgotten how fun good old fashioned RTS games could be.
I used to love Age of Empires and Empire Earth back in the day, but more "realistic" games like Total War have since put me in a mindset that "real time strategy" means superb graphics, sprawling terrains and unit-based tactical maneuvering. My friend mentioned "They Are Billions" as a game on her list as we were skimming for last-minute deals before the big sale ended, and it had just enough of interest that I gave it a try.
The game is wonderful. It's reminded me that the old school RTS formula is still plenty fun. It's very reminiscent of Age of Empires, but with a twist: Your enemy is a semi-intelligent zombie horde, and you only have a limited time before... possibly literal billions of them come for you in a massive horde. Several other interesting elements are in play, such as the ability to stretch a power grid in order to build. I also appreciate the game's macro-management aspects: the ability to repair all your buildings with a click, and the fact that your workers are a resource rather than individual units to be commanded are both examples of ways the game makes it easier to manage your entire settlement.
This may sound like a watering down of the tried and true formula, but trust me, it's not. You'll CONSTANTLY be poked by zombies as your borders expand, and waves of hungry infected will occasionally swarm you long before the aforementioned time limit. You'll be constantly needing to repair buildings and elaborate upon your defenses, and micromanaging every settler is definitely not conductive to that.
Just one more interesting twist to watch out for, by the way: If you lose a building, it spawns several more fast, hungry zombies. Buildings have never been so important. Protect them at all costs!
Highly recommended, great game.

A Bird Story is a brief interactive story about a lone child saving and befriending a bird from the same developers of To the Moon.
One thing that you must get as soon as possible is that this game isn't a proper sequel to To the Moon: think of this title has just a taste of the things to come (as to say, the proper second episode of the series, Finding Paradise). A Bird Story is therefore a lot shorter (roughly one and half an hour of gameplay), features no dialogues whatsoever and is far less tasking from the player (you are rarely asked to move the protagonist around for more than two minutes between scenarios).
On a brighter side, A Bird Story's locations are far more complex and dreamy than the ones from To the Moon.
To sum things up, A Bird Story is just a little gem from Freebird Games to display once again their great writing abilities. Keep this in mind and don't expect anything else (or longer) before the release of Finding Paradise

I'm writing this as I felt I have seen an overwhelming amount of negativity towards this game,  so I thought I'd give a bit of input towards it.
First of all DO NOT buy this expecting to get another To The Moon, it is very very different in a number of ways.  There is no dialogue whatsoever and its a short prequel story so don't expect any more than an hour and a half out of it.
This seems to be the problem with most reviews is that they're comparing the two constantly (so treat it as its own game).
Another thing you might want to do is treat this more as an interactive story rather than a game.  You can't at any point die or fail it and most of the interaction involves walking around and touching things or using the arrow keys as the on screen directions tell you to.
So yeah, if you are looking for an action packed emotional TTM sequel then you might want to wait for Kens next game...
Now I'll explain why the game IS worth buying for those who want to try it for its own merits!
The music (like to the moon) is awesome, and of course the visuals are pretty too in their own simple way.  The story itself while very simple (as there is no dialogue like I mentioned) will still give you those feels at certain points and can still be entertaining.  While I wouldn't call it gripping and engaging I will definately say it does enough to keep you occupied for the short duriation of the game.
Many people have said they its confusing/makes no sense and in some ways it won't if you view it literally;  from what I can gather the story tries to see the world in a simple childlike view.  It uses a lot of environment merging to create a continuous effect (I suppose to create a time passing effect?).  It's definitely different and unusual but I would say for the asking price you can do a lot worse!  There is also the fact that this story may have some effect on the next proper sequel, so it may be worth buying it to get the full picture?
So in summary -
Pros: Great music, visuals and a unique style of story telling
Cons: Not going to interest you if you're expecting TTM2

A Bird Story is an interactive story from Freebird Games. You play a little boy with his head in the clouds and get to see his story about a bird.
A Bird Story is one hour of beautiful gameplay. The game has a railroad plot and no real options, but the story is great and the scenes are very well done. It is cleverly made and does a perfect job taking you into the imaginative mind of a child. After I finished playing I was completely relaxed and in a wonderful mood.
There are no real gameplay mechanics, inventory or dialogue; You just move around in the scenes and interact with some objects. Much of the time in-game are spent watching cutscenes.
If you have played To The Moon by the same developer, there are some differences between the games. To The Moon is a game with clear gameplay while A Bird Story really is not more than an interactive story. Still, both games have the same “aura” around them and you can tell that they are both made in the same spirit. (The developer has even said that the boy in A Bird Story grows up to be the patient in Finding Paradise, which is the “second episode” in the To The Moon-series.)
If you liked To The Moon or if you enjoy seeing a slow-paced beautiful story, A Bird Story is definitely worth playing.

Sat down and according to my played time, it took 1.2 hrs or ~72 minutes to beat this game. Let me preface my review with the fact I am a "To The Moon" fan even though I had my criticisms of the game, the emotional pulls and twist near the end of To The Moon turned me around. Feel free to explore my account for my To The Moon review, as well as other game reviews. I am a very big fan of story based games.
This game uses the exact same game mechanics as To The Moon, which is to say, they're very weak. You have your basic movement (arrow keys, not WSAD) with Space Bar interaction options. There is really no engagement or creative use of these basic controls like there is in the game "Brothers" for instance.
The game is fully on rails which I do not hate, not one bit. I don't mind a bit of exploring here or there, games like Uncharted, Tomb Raider, and FarCry 3/4 come to mind here, but I really dislike open world sandbox'ish games- GTA, Skyrim, etc. The game gives you absolutely no choices, again I'm ok with this, and gives you occasional pop-ups as to where you should be going or what you should be doing, also, not a negative criticism.
Where do my negative recommendation come from? Well, without compelling game play mechanics, and with a weak story, it just isn't worth a recommendation, even at the sale price I got it for ($3.78 w/soundtrack because I thought it was going to be good). The story follows a rebellious young boy rescuing and kinda nursing back to health an injured bird. They search for the bird's home, play together, yadda yadda, stuff happens, no spoilers, the end-- it's only 70 minutes long. So why is the story not engaging? It could be from the lack of any dialogue, text or spoken, and the fact there's no growth or character development. To The Moon suffered from the same lack of compelling game play mechanics and weak story, but with time and build up, it turned itself around.
Also to note another negativity with both this game and To The Moon- they both have issues running smoothly. A Bird Story took 3 tries to start up, twice it froze on launch, and had horrible screen tearing because there are no resolution or AA options. To The Moon suffered from ghost controller input: those with certain brands of computer peripherals, such as Saitek, the keyboard I previously used, installed certain gaming controller drivers which interfered with the gameplay (character always ran left, non stop).
Bottom Line: Cute game, definitely in the "spirit" of To The Moon, but with weak gameplay mechanics and a weak story, it's not worth the purchase- check out some other game series for strong stories like Telltale's games, specifically Walking Dead & The Wolf Among us, The Longest Journey trilogy, or Brothers, all of which I strongly recommend.

A Bird Story - A Short Review (no spoilers)
This brief work of interactive fiction explores the emotive spectrum contained within a child's small world of fantastic realism. There were moments in which I couldn't help but smile and laugh to myself, there were moments in which I found myself fighting back tears. Just as in To The Moon, the atmosphere of whimsy and levity complements the melancholy and moments of sorrow perfectly. As a caveat, if you have never had a close connection with a loved animal, you may find this game uninteresting or slow. Which brings us to a brief breakdown of "the game" itself.
While it does not follow traditional game structure or exhibit a high level of gameplay, I found the minor engagement of the user through simple controls to actually add to the game's tension towards the end of the story. First, you're using arrow keys to walk and enter to interact in basic ways with the world. Before you know it, you're using those same arrow keys to... do things that make you rethink what "controls" really entail. The simplicity is necessary to maintain the spotlight on the story itself. This title is worth every cent of the $5 you spend on it. Have you checked cinema ticket prices lately? And even if you regret your purchase, the developer has a 100% money back return policy. Look it up.
In terms of content, let me be very clear: it is A Bird Story. It is a story first and foremost and the key plot device is a bird. Or more particularly, the player's relationship with a bird. This is no aspiration for a new To The Moon, although a few not-so-subtle references did make me smile. What it is, however, is a very unusual work of fiction that explores themes such as social isolation, adolescence, moral culpability, and relationships. We've all experienced the confusion, reckless emotions, and hardships that accompany growing old. In this context, A Bird Story bears a good deal of symbolism that can only grow in meaning as we evolve as individuals.
A Bird Story is a poignant diversion into a realm of nostalgia.

The Temporal Invasion was released July 4, 2016 from indie developer Hybriona Labs on Steam. Currently, the developer only has a Windows version up, but promises iOS and Linux within the week. It's been on my Steam wishlist for a couple of weeks now, following some of the hype coming out of E3.
I was pleasantly surprised and delighted by the quality of this game. The price point is an extremely reasonable $3.99 (on sale for $2.39 through 7/11).
I occasionally play puzzle games like 100 doors or various hidden object games on my iOS devices while killing time, say, in an airport. So, when I got the email yesterday that The Temporal Invasion was coming up, I downloaded it with a subset of expectations that were wildly off course.
Firstly, this game is hard. It more closely resembles a virtual treasure hunt of information throughout history than any puzzle games I've played lately. The game gives you a few sandbox tools, but is designed for the player to utilize external internet searches (or other resources, if you have them) to fact-find through multi-step complex riddles and produce an answer for each case that moves the player through the story.
The premise of the story involves being contacted for help by the mysterious "Dr. Quantum." As the protagonist, you've already identified that occasionally your memories are out-of-sync with reality, but are completely unprepared to be whisked on a journey through the past and future to uncover the truth behind a massive conspiracy perpetrated by a mysterious group of scientists from the future.
Actual graphics in the game are just what the screenshots in the post show, no flashy graphics or crazy cut scenes, but the story holds your attention and the difficulty level is phenomenal. Some puzzles are intuitive and you only need a google search or two to find where you're going, while others are positively confounding. As yet, very few hint posts or walkthroughs are up, so you're completely left to your own devices to work through the puzzles and riddles.

Overview
This game has absolutely no redeeming qualities - the plot is bland, the character creation leaves a lot to be desired and the gameplay contains only the bad parts of old rpgs.
After the TL;DR part, here's me explaining the bad things more in-depth:
-Plot
"Hey, it's me, god. Some dude beat up all of us, can you beat him up for me?" That's literally all there is to the plot. Gaulen also has no personality beyond fulfilling this mission. Since the game wipes out your party for trying to not follow the red line, you have no means to influence that, either.
-Character Creation
Even if there's nine classes in total, I can't help but feel there was no balancing involved. I haven't played all of them yet (not that I want to waste any more time with this than I need to), but I'll give a brief overview of each of chars:
Gaulen the Explorer
Main character. He's basically a fighter, but also has a bunch of overworld boons. Not that interesting, but at least the only forced character is not a liability.
Azura the Paladin
Standing in the middle to heal. The only problem with that is that I need to invest into the healing aura to keep it useful, making its skill cost creep up faster than my maximum PP, so that I can use it less often. At least she has enough armor to keep herself alive (tough luck for her fellows in the front row)
Kallindra the Arcane Warrior
She has what I'd like to call the Black Mage problem. As her only skill is one that does damage, in addition to being not as strong as a true fighter, she must spend PP to accomplish what a fighter can do without spending PP. While she isn't weak when just hitting things, her skill is pretty mediocre and quite frequently fails (reminds me of random tripping in SSBB).
Boreas the Thief
I believe any group without a thief is weaker than one that has him. He can pick locks and detect traps, which allows you to get loot without massive wounding and also not taking humongous damage in dungeons. Furthermore, he even gets a skill to lower buy prices and raise sell revenue (which is crucial given how scarce money is). The bow sucks at Level 1, but as he skilled it, it gains wounding that cripples strong enemies.
Mike the Wizard
He has the Black Mage problem I mentioned with Kallindra. The game keeps the oldschool idea of a damaging mage while most modern games make spellcasters focus on crowd control. While I don't oppose this idea, the scaling of PP makes it really hard for him to do his job right.
Maia the Divine Summoner
The only class with any form of originality in it. She summons creatures that are the avatars of the gods to help you for a few turns. Her energy growth was decent enough that I could have her help out in tight battles, too. I'd love to have a better explanation for what the summons are for, though (I had a tank beast and a healer chick at my disposal).
-Enemies
This is the number one point where most RPGs fall flat - no matter how unique and interesting a game makes the character creation, enemies seem to solely consist out of HP and Attack values and maybe a status problem or a multi-hit ability. Lords of Xulima is no different. Enemies generally have no more than two actions and have little variety in how they're arranged. Success solely depends on you having higher numbers or, if the numbers are roughly even, that you roll better on hitting than the opponents do. An example how I'd do encounters (an example):
Front Row:
Worker Bee, Monster Rose, Worker Bee
Back Row:
Monster Lily-of-the-Valley x2
The worker bees have high evasion, but low HP and are weak to lightning. Their main action is gathering pollen (which recovers the HP of the rose or the LotV), which they can throw at your dudes for little damage and stun. Provoking them makes them sting you, which does quite a bit of damage and poison, but instantly kills the worker bee.
The monster rose mainly shoots spikes to do low-medium damage to the entire front row. Hitting it in melee makes your attacker take damage in retaliation. At lower health, it uses a single target petal shot that does shadow damage and can wound. It's health is quite high and it's weak to fire and resists light/divine.
The LotVs have rather low health and poison melee attackers. They shoot pollen at you that can cause stun, dealing medium-high damage. They swing their blossoms in melee if forced into the front row, dealing less damage and removing the chance to stun. A friendly LotV can force them to go into the back row if there's someone to stand behind. Immune to poison, resists shadow and weak to fire.
This is a battle where you can strategize - do you blast the worker bees with lightning so they can't heal? Or do you save  the magic for the melee-punishing rose? Pick apart the LotVs with ranged strikes to keep them from murdering your group? Or do you neuter them by provoking the bees with your tank? Protect your group from poison or rather stun?
If I can think of creative enemies without any drafting, the maker sure as hell can.
-Other things
-Having a tight food clock and constant expenses punish exploration and cripple you for looking into old places, forcing you to use a guide to know where to go at all times.
-No custom portraits? Acceptable, but disappointing.
-It's amusing that the game lets you access quickload in the middle of a battle. Did the maker expect savescumming the encounters?

Lords of Xulima (pronounced as 'Shoo-lee-mah') is a 2D isometric old-school role playing game from Madrid-based developers Numantian Game Studios.  The game is a ‘Kick starter’ success story that, as far as I know, had an original goal of only $10,000 but managed to reach a grand total of $35,657 by its end.  The game features a world map gameplay similar to that of Heroes of Might and Magic and King's Bounty, but has a combat mechanic that is more akin to the Might and Magic series with certain areas of the game being blocked off by monsters until you're powerful enough to defeat them or find a way around them.
The game places you in the boots of Gaulen, an adventurer summoned by one of the nine (9) gods to go to their divine homeland of Xulima where a civil war has broken out when the god of death declared war against the other eight (8) gods.  Gaulen sets sail with five (5) other companions but to their dismay, upon reaching Xulima, the gods had already left and in their place, terrible lords have taken power who will stop at nothing to keep Gaulen from interfering with the on-going war between the gods.
+ Good 2D graphics and art style but... (See CON #4)
+ Well implemented gameplay that is reminiscent of old CRPG titles
+ Helpful first mission tutorial and tool tips that covers the game's basic elements
+ Challenging difficulties
+ Good class system with different skills and abilities but… (See CON #2 and #3)
+ Good atmosphere for a CRPG with day and night cycles as well as weather effects on some maps
+ Healthy game time
+ Large world with a lot of room for exploration
+ Good story worthy of a sequel but… (See CON #5 and 6)
- The main character cannot be customized to have another class or portrait
- Some classes are almost indispensable for a successful campaign (ex. Cleric)
- No skill overview or mapping: This means you can not plan out your builds if it is your first play through unless you look it up in the internet or you're already familiar with the skill system.
- Portrait selections as well as some cinematic art works could use a bit more work
- The game's story (not gameplay) is linear because there are little choices to be made during important dialogue with the story NPCs
- Plot twist was a bit predictable
- Difficult early game
- Score system that is best ignored if you want a fun rather than competitive experience
- Game gets a bit boring at the end but that depends on you as the player
Lords of Xulima is a surprisingly
and I have no trouble giving it my full recommendation especially with Classic RPG fans.

Play With:Keyboard and Mouse, Windows 10
Level Design: Each level has a multitude of paths that you can use to approach your target; each loop onto themselves so that it’s a small maze that you will master as you explore. It encourages explorations as every inch of the level is covered in loot and upgrades, and side objectives that can be easily missed if you just rush for the target.
Actions Matter: The game is very adamant about you choosing to either kill or knock out everyone you approach and depending on how you deal with your enemies it will result in different endings and different enemies in future levels. If you mow down your enemies you will spread the plague which will increase the number of rats swarms and weepers that exists in the city of Dunwall. If you chose to stealth your way and knock out enemies you’ll encounter more of the city watch which are easier to outsmart and don’t travel in huge swarms.
Story/World Building: The story is a joy; you, the Empress’ protector, come back to report that no other place has dealt with such calamity that has befallen Dunwall and as you return she is assassinated and you are blamed. Now you must escape, clear your name and put down all that conspired against you. This simple plot is greatly shown off in this vibrant world filled with magic and steampunk accomited by good characters that stand on their own motivations.
Feeling of Progress: At the start of the game I had such a hard time traversing the level and dealing with the City Guards, by the time I’ve reached the last level I’d take out half the guards by zipping around their compound knocking everyone out and running around without sound of footsteps. The game really makes you feel as if you’ve grown and become stronger through your journey.
Save Scum: If you are doing a non lethal playthrough you will have to save, a lot, there are tons of chances when you clear a whole area and then by accident run into a guard and now everything went in the dumps especially when you are at the start with very few options to escape and you’re forced to fight them back. Once you’re spotted you have to blink away for them to lose you, there’s no way of knocking them out once you’re in combat; something that the second game has added in.
Jank: The game can glitch out, the frame rate swings up and down causing audio to glitch with it and at one point it even crashed. Sometime if you don’t aim at the exact pixel of the guard you can’t knock him out. At one point a person I had to save would fall out of my hands as I walked into a cut scene and they would die in the middle of the cut scene counting them as assassinated. There’s a lot of minor problems, but thankfully they don’t ruin the game.
This game is great, the stealth, the world, the plot, it’s all great and you have to give it a shot. Whether you chose to to let Dunwall burn or you save it you will have a great time.

I picked up this game at a considerable discount, thanks to the developer's decision to "celebrate" the release of Mighty No. 9. I played the original version of this game some years ago, but didn't get around to playing this version until today.
At the end of my run as ARES, I was ready to give Extinction Agenda EX a thumbs down, and maybe I still should: It's one of the jankiest run-and-gun games I have ever played. Asthetically, it's fine: The music is excellent and the sprite work fairly appealing. Aiming and shooting is just fine thanks to the mouse, but the jumping controls are uniquely unresponsive and occasionally just fail to work at all. ARES' air dash move is especially difficult to use properly. I must have wasted an hour of the two hours it took to finish the game just falling into pits. It's also rather difficult to avoid damage, and if not for the in-built repair ability, I probably would not have gotten anywhere. I imagine I had a similar experience playing the first version of this game, but that was back in 2011 so I don't remember for sure. Nostalgia makes every game seem better I guess, because I gave that game a positive review just yesterday. But playing it again was not nearly as fun.
Then, I played Tarus, the new playable character to this version of the game. And let me tell you, playing Tarus is like playing a different game entirely, and a better one at that. ARES' unwieldy air-dash is replaced with a much simpler to use mid-air hover move, which allows you to fly around for a short duration. At least once jump segment that gave me no end of trouble with ARES can be bypassed using Tarus entirely: Though Tarus' cutscenes differ from ARES, the levels do not. His "limit break"-type move, instead of a smart bomb like ARES, is a invulnerability shield. His weapons, while shorter-ranged and slower then ARES', do considerably more damage. All this meant that my run as Tarus took about half the time, give or take a few minutes. I've never seen a disparity between two characters in the same game this huge before. If you get this game, get it on sale like I did, and don't even bother playing as ARES- Tarus is your bot.

Pro's;
- Storyline was good (main reedemable feature)
- Voice acting (although some was terribly cliche)
- Not a bad shooter
- Variaty of weapons
- Artwork and level design was good
- Loved the 60's vibe
Cons;
- Not challenging
- Too short
- Too linear
- Empty (RPG and Game-wise)
Pros explained;
The storyline was great IMO, without ruining too much the start of the game starts out slow but then there is further development in the later stages of the game (although you do have to get to the end practically). It fits in with the universe, to an extent, and it ties itself off whilst still connecting itself to future game. Spoiler:
The voice acting was decent but I did get bored of Carters cliche 60's American hero, they tried to falw him and they did a good job, I hated the guy up until the end,
. The only other issue was Angelas character (Her emotions are warranted but she is suppose to be a CIA Operative, Comeon)
It isn't a bad shooter either for the price (if it's on sale i'd easily say £10 is worth it) for what it has, so long as you dont have any high expectations. Combat is pretty much whack-a-mole style (duck when they fire and shoot when they've stopped/or have your teammates shoot them) still there is some tactics involved. The variaty of weapons are good but only being able to carry two is a drawback but neccessary (as you do need to conserve ammo and adds more realism and for the player to use tactics). But there are plenty of games that are worse than this as a fps.
The artwork and design of the entire game I loved, there really isnt much I can critisise (unless we include Carters really annoying animations for hand gestures, where you just see him tapping his fist into his hands every second of the conversation) But overall they looked alien and i loved the contrast of America - Alien.
Con's Explained;
This game is not long. 20 hours on hardest difficulty and 30%-40% of that was the last mission, the long ending though did leave it enjoyable rather than alot of newer games with anti-climatic endings. But they really could of fleshed out more missions or longer ones. This leads to it not being difficult as enemies typically come in waves, which once you're behind cover you can pretty much eliminate 3-4 enemies before they position themseleves. I wish they used some of the more advanced units earlier or put more together so i felt pressured, like the end mission. (Permadeath on your agents really shouldnt be an issue so long as you keep together) I didn't lose a single agent on the hardest difficulty. I admit I was close a few times on the end mission.
Xcom's I know arent linear games, but what i mean by this, especially stating it as empty, was there wasn't many side missions or consequences of certain missions like in the others (which would of been nice). To top it off the missions were linear and there wasn't try this approach or go down this way to get to the objective (unless you call using a different hallway that) the most detailed areas were the combat areas. (understandably) The few areas in a mission you can go another way they're dead-ends to pick up lore (scraps of paper or audio reels), nice but they could of added more. To add to the lore it was a shame they didnt have more for the "scan", yes you can scan enemies and it details them and weapons for you which was pretty unique but it was a shame (part from one side-mission) that scanning wasn't used to find hidden things in the campaign or to research enemies or something similar.
Lastly the second point of it being or feeling empty is the RPG portion, although you have 4 types of squad mates and yourself you're probably only going to use the engineer and scout class (they have the best abilities by far deploying turrets and mines added with diversion and airstirke) the other two feel lackluster compared (the engineer was only redeemable for the turrent TBH). Adding to that they only have 5 levels, of which each class usually has three abilities and two upgrades for said abilities, YOU HAVE TO USE THESE ABILITIES, it's not a choice between two abilities, its a choice between two classes pretty much. The same thing applies to the protagonist.
If youre a fan of Xcom its good for lore and a chnage of pace, just dont think it's going to be as great as the traditional ones.
If not and you're looking for a casual gears of war/mass effect Third-Person (which the emphasis on cover, abilities and ammo conservation) This is pretty decent, Unless you fall into one of the two categories I wouldn't buy it.
Overall 7/10 Because of the gameplay and I didn't have my hopes up (I expected it to be terrible) But the gameplay aint bad. Then again I paid like £5 for this and i played 30+ hours, deffo worth it for that.

Gunplay in this game was really good. I found there were some great effects for bullets hitting enemies and in addition, there were nice modifications to buy with in-game points for weapons. One thing I did notice though was a lack of weapons. I found I was limited as to what weapons I could choose from, which limited my expectations of the future gameplay. However, they totally won me over with many boss battles that took a long time to conquer if I had picked the wrong weapon. Weapon customisations are vital to the harder enemies towards the end of the game.
Also, there were customisations for what the character calls his Rig. It is the vehicle you play a lot of the game in and customisations for that are not vital, but are pretty cool. In order to customise your Rig, you have to collect special parts that are scattered around the game. I found this was a good opportunity that the creators added in to really get the gamers to explore their full creation. Not only were there those collectibles, but there were audio logs and text logs scattered around the map as well, which you could then listen to on your menu screen. I found that this gamification really was a good thing to add to the game for some real emotional intensity to the game.
The storyline of this game is really long. I had idled for 6 hours on this game, and so my play time is an exceedingly long play time - but no worries, take 6 hours off of my game time and you have your result for how long it took me to complete this game. It has taken me around 11 hours to complete the campaign. Personally, I found this game droaned on with the same stuff up until around 3/4 of the way through. Things then got a lot more interesting, unexpected twists happened in the game which really gained my interest and I was hooked to the game.
While playing this game, it has made me laugh at some points where the creators have used a touch of humour to the conversations in the game. I think this is really cool, because that adds extra audience attraction, adding to the matter of how much we enjoy it.
The end of the game made me cry for about 30 seconds. Any game that makes me cry is automatically classed - to me - as a game with effective emotion. This game conquered my emotions. Good job to the creators!
This game looks beautiful. On the maximum graphics setting, it really is a stunner, bearing in mind this game was made in 2013. I really like the gunplay in this game, and the 3rd person point of view has a good camera angle. The reason why I mention the camera angle is because some 3rd person shooter games have some dodgy angles, which furthermore makes it hard to actually play the game comfortably.
There are very few cutscenes in the game. This, for some, may be an issue. However, for others this may be great news. Personally, I quite like cutscenes and - although this game doesn't have many - the cutscenes in this game really are relatable and gain my full interest. The creators of the game have thought about emotion well as they have used a wide range of emotion and expressions throughout the game.
They have effectively created a strong link between the player and the main character, which is always a bonus to the entire effect of the game. The end of the game was really good and is something that nobody wants to miss.
Just another thing to add in, there are side missions that you can complete throughout this game for more in-game points. I didn't do many of them, but they are good ways to gain yourself some points towards weapon modifications.
===================================================================

Note: I have not completed the game yet or played the previous titles so take this review with a grain of salt. I only review games before completing because I end up with a better review this way.
A third person shooter with some RPG elements. You are in a ice planet to harvest a new efficient energy source. However this planet is inhabited by aliens called akrid who spend most of their time killing anyone in their path. You get to kill the akrid and ride a mecha specifically designed for construction called the utility rig.
First of all you need a controller to play this game. The game allows you to play with keyboard and mouse but some parts of the game do not work without a controller. In particular when you're in your rig you need the analog sticks to turn valves and it is a lot easier or even only possible to defeat some large aliens with the controller.
This is one of those games that the developers spent too much time trying to make a movie rather than a game. In the first couple of hours you get very tedious cutscenes and very little gameplay. This can turn the impantient right off the bat. Gradually you get some decent gameplay but you are constantly interrupted by either cutscenes or quick time events. I feel like the developers should have spent more time tunning gameplay and level design instead of trying to make a movie.
Overall the game is kind of bland. The graphics are nice but repetitive. Most of the time you are either outside facing extreme cold weather or inside abandoned dark places. The aliens look generic, uninspired and without graphical quality. Most look like something from the Alien franchise but less detailed. The characters aren't very interesting and stereotyped. In particular the main character is a doofus often mumbling something irrelevant. They're not annoying but not interesting either. The story is very movie like and personally I find it unexciting and redone a million times but it does get a lot better over time. Expect lots of unnecessary family moments (just like movies).
When you're outside the rig you only need basic third person shooter skills. These parts work fairly ok with keyboard and mouse but are too easy. I've started the game in normal difficulty but if I knew I would have chosen hard instead. I felt most of the time not even bothered if I died or not because it was easier to just run around killing things and pay a little more attention in certain parts were you can die. Unlike small aliens, where you just shoot anywere to kill, large aliens and bosses require you to figure were to shoot and timing. Figuring out where to shoot is not always obvious but most time you just have to shoot the red part.
Using the utility rig is clunky and painful. The rig can be used to do small tasks such as turning valves, drilling ice or throwing a grappling hook to reach some places. The other use for the rig is to kill aliens. Small and medium aliens are easy to kill with the rig, you just stomp them, fire the grappling hook or grab them. Large aliens however are a big pain and sometimes you are forced to use the mecha when it would be easier to just not use it at all. To kill large aliens you need timing, patience and figuring out what the heck were the developers thinking. Don't forget to use the controller in boss sections, it is much easier.
Even though the game is bland it isn't a bad game either. Overall the game starts off very tedious but gets a lot better over time. I recommend this game for those are expecting something just to kill time.

The story takes a back seat and you just blow stuff away. Lost Planet 1 had amazing boss fights, but was repetitive in the gameplay department and the story stopped making any sense halfway through. Lost Planet 2 forget to implement a story and instead gave us an intense, action packed kill fest that we could play with friend. Mindless, but fun.
Then developer Spark gave us Lost Planet 3. Finally we have a logical and coherent story with characters that don't feel like they have jumped out of a bad anime. The story is a prequel to the first Lost Planet and follows the original colonists sent to explore E.D.N. III.
The gameplay is nothing special at all. Just another run-of-the-mill third person shooter in a sort-of open environment. You fight enemies, earn money, upgrade your weapons and your RIG, which is your giant mining mech you use to traverse the hazardous landscapes of the planet. There are some sidequests to earn a little extra cash, and the game itself is a decent length at about 15 to 20 hours depending on how much you want to explore. The graphics are decent, and some of the outdoor environments are gorgeous, but some of the character models are rather bland and the animations can be spotty.
The story manages to stay very interesting throughout, and unlike it's predecessors, makes sense. There are a few jumps in the plot here and there, and the game ends with a few questions still unanswered, but the result is still satisfying. What makes Lost Planet 3 great is it's main character, Jim Peyton.
Jim Peyton is a simple man who takes a mining job on E.D.N. III to support his family. Jim isn't special in any way, has no mysterious past, or any special skills or attributes, he is just a guy who travels halfway across the galaxy out of love for his wife and son. Throughout the game, Jim receives audio and video transmissions from his wife, and he sends some of his own in return. The two are just so damn adorable to watch and every message between them just makes their characters that much stronger and more interesting. His love and devotion gives him the drive to survive and keeps him smiling and helping those around him. Jim is not a battle hardened warrior or brooding anti-hero, he is a human being like you and me. You want Jim to succeed. You want Jim to see his family. You can't help but get engrossed in his journey from the very beginning and pray for a happy ending for the two.
The gameplay may be standard, but the story of Jim Peyton is a damn good one. In my opinion, he ranks up with some of the best video game protagonists like John Marston and Nathan Drake. Lost Planet 3 came and went with minimal fanfare, which is sad. Because under a by-the-numbers shooter lies a fantastic, character-driven story that 90% of games fail to achieve.

This game isn't perfectly polished by any stretch of the imagination, but I can't dislike it no matter how much I want to at times. The setting sucked me in instantly, and roaming around on foot or in my hulking rig instills a sense of isolation and feels authentically cold. The characters are all well developed and interesting, even the Nicholas Cage look alike you play as. The missions themselves are interesting for the most part, especially the facility you explore that takes a more horror centric approach. Really the game's trouble lies in its combat. The guns feel underpowered most of the time, and the knock down hits you take from bosses feel cheap. The QTEs are also strange, you are forced to wait until the last moment to dodge or block, rather than using quick reaction time. For example I see an enemy telegraphing a hit, if I roll as soon as he starts his cue I'll get hit. You're supposed to dodge at the EXACT moment his fist is about to clobber you, not before. All in all a little disjointed, but for 2 dollars (bundle price) I am enjoying the heck out of it. It's a great narrative focused game

A Bird Story - A Short Review (no spoilers)
This brief work of interactive fiction explores the emotive spectrum contained within a child's small world of fantastic realism. There were moments in which I couldn't help but smile and laugh to myself, there were moments in which I found myself fighting back tears. Just as in To The Moon, the atmosphere of whimsy and levity complements the melancholy and moments of sorrow perfectly. As a caveat, if you have never had a close connection with a loved animal, you may find this game uninteresting or slow. Which brings us to a brief breakdown of "the game" itself.
While it does not follow traditional game structure or exhibit a high level of gameplay, I found the minor engagement of the user through simple controls to actually add to the game's tension towards the end of the story. First, you're using arrow keys to walk and enter to interact in basic ways with the world. Before you know it, you're using those same arrow keys to... do things that make you rethink what "controls" really entail. The simplicity is necessary to maintain the spotlight on the story itself. This title is worth every cent of the $5 you spend on it. Have you checked cinema ticket prices lately? And even if you regret your purchase, the developer has a 100% money back return policy. Look it up.
In terms of content, let me be very clear: it is A Bird Story. It is a story first and foremost and the key plot device is a bird. Or more particularly, the player's relationship with a bird. This is no aspiration for a new To The Moon, although a few not-so-subtle references did make me smile. What it is, however, is a very unusual work of fiction that explores themes such as social isolation, adolescence, moral culpability, and relationships. We've all experienced the confusion, reckless emotions, and hardships that accompany growing old. In this context, A Bird Story bears a good deal of symbolism that can only grow in meaning as we evolve as individuals.
A Bird Story is a poignant diversion into a realm of nostalgia.

I was among the first people to be sceptical of Evolve. Seeing another 60$ DLC store being sold on steam? The red flags went up, and I was cautious. Then I come to find out my scepticism was justified? Yep, and witht that, I threw the game under the bus and forgot about it.
Fast foreward to about a year later. I had all but forgotten about Evolve, and so had the rest of the world. But suddenly, Turtle Rock announces stage two, and a new free to play model. I was suddenly interested. I mean, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ a developer somehow had the smarts and/or the balls to convince a major publisher to drop the price down, rework the game, and give the devs a chance to make the game actually fun? I was suddenly interested, and so I eventually gave the game a try.
And somehow, I got hooked. It was surprising just how much character and charm the game had, and the core of the game was actually changed to become much more solid and enjoyable. It was fun to unlock things now instead of a waste of time. It was fun to play, and it didn't cost me a cent. I was enjoying myself, which was the last thing I expected. Suddenly, I was invested, and I was hopefull for the future.
But sadly, with the end of the Shear horror event, comes the sad news: All development has officially ceased.
And frankly, that disgusts me. It disgusts me to see that a game with so much love and passion behind it just crumple into nothing. it disgusts me to think that people who worked so hard now have had all their efforts go to waste. And most of all, it disgusts me to see that the ONE TIME someone is actually able to swollow their pride and admit their mistakes, then try again with a real sense of decency, they still fall right back on their face.
And that's sad, really. I wanted to see a surprise success story from a game developer actually treating it's fans and players with some real respect (or at least a lot more respect than before). Having the game fail means people are going to be less likely to try this kind of stunt in the future. It's another sad story that ends with a crying gasp and a whimper of defeat.
As my final thoughts come out for this review, I want to end with this:
Thank you Turtle Rock, for having the passion, dedication, and hope to keep on trying. Thank you for believing in us, and believing in the game. If nothing else, you people have my upmost respect. I hope your future is brighter than the one you leave with this game.
And for everyone else, give the game a try, at least once; if only for the sake of experiencing a little bit of gaming history with me.

If you're a diehard fan of hidden object games, then rejoice; someone made a game just for you, and this is it.
Now, you may have found Waldo or any of a number of other clone characters during the Waldo/Wally craze in the '90s, but make no mistake: this game is NOT your old Where's Waldo. Martin Handford never went for this level of detail. Depending on your threshold for where detail gives way to far too much detail, that may be a good thing.
So what *is* Hidden Folks? It's a hidden object game, requiring you to seek out little people and objects in scenes that vary from small and simple to positlvely enormous and exceptionally detailed. There isn't a gradual ramp up, either, so expect to go straight from "hey, this is easy!" to "how am I going to find *ANYTHING* in this?!" in one step. But stick with it; while initially overwhelming, there's a lot of logical consistency in the scenes. Paying attention to the description of each person and item you're supposed to find and an eye for picking out context in the scenes serves you well. You can find your selected items just casting around randomly, but it will take just this side of forever.
This is a game where patience is a key element. If you're impatient, need things to happen quickly and regularly, and can't handle delayed gratification, this is not a game for you; boredom and frustration will reign in short order. But for true hidden object fans, this game is just about ideal.
So why "just about?" The artwork is first class, the puzzles creative and complete, and the environments are extremely interactive. Where's the gap? The audio. All of the sound in this game is vocalized sound effects, and there's not much of it. You will hear the same noises again and again until they grind themselves into your brain. Cute for the first couple minutes, grating from that point on. Turning off your PC's audio may well be in your future; it was here.
Put together, the extremely impressive visuals far outweigh the nearly-infuriating audio by a wide margin, so this game still easily earns a thumbs-up recommendation. For the patient object hunter, this game is practically a love letter.

The Temporal Invasion is a story-driven, riddle-based game that encourages the player to utilize any available resource needed to solve the provided puzzles. This may involve fine-tuning your Google searching skills, gathering friends, or even renting books at the library if you’re that desperate. Be prepared to ALT-Tab a lot in this immersive puzzle hunting game that does an eerily great job at making you feel like a conspiracy theorist.
The story involves you, the puzzle hunter, living a life where your memories differ from that of reality. For example, the POV protagonist truly believes that “The Chinese” started WWII. A letter from Dr. Quantum informs you that you are not insane. In fact, you are immune. Seeking the truth will reveal everything.
There are a total of 10 Puzzle Hunt challenges (Cases) in the game. Each puzzle contains 10 “Check Points” where the solution of each will be a clue for the next. Everything must be solved in order; no skipping is allowed, nor will "Hints" be provided. A prologue for each Case is provided, detailing the motivation for the upcoming Puzzle Hunt and summarizing the important objectives that need to be achieved. It may be important to note that the Computer and Sandbox E-mail App do not interact with anything outside of the game. They are tools provided to help solve Cases and increase immersion. Many of the clues can be solved using one or two tools, with most of the answers being relatively straightforward and simple. Some will require two or more steps to solve, but with a fine use of out-of-the-box thinking coupled with strong Google searching skills, nothing is ever
difficult. If you ever find yourself spiraling into a frenzy of trial and error submissions thinking that maybe the solution is, for example, not precise enough/in the wrong language/missing accent marks, etc., you are thinking too deep. The submissions are generally not case-sensitive, unless obviously presented as such.
In the above video, an image is provided as a clue that needs solving. Upon closer observation in the Photo Editor, the quote
is shown across the center, and a seemingly indecipherable message is written below it:

It is already somewhat apparent that the jumble of letters is an encoded message. The clue to solving this message lies in the quote, specifically the portion “The Truth got shifted by Two Pushes…” This provides the hint that the message is encoded with a Caesar Cipher (also known as a Shift Cipher). This means that if letters in the phonetic alphabet are assigned sequential numbers, the encryption process involves replacing the original letter of the message with a new, encoded letter shifted by two numbers. For example, A > C, X > Z. Decoding it will requiring moving it backwards or forwards (shifting) by two letters. A simple Caesar Cipher Decryption Tool on the internet will easily break this for you. Although this may have seemed easy, especially with the solution presented immediately below the image, there are many much more difficult puzzles left to solve.
There are a few suggestions that may improve gameplay; these are listed below.
The Temporal Invasion definitely feels cheesy at times, especially when it tries to connect so many different ideas and conspiracy theories; however, after puzzle hunting for a while, it does a great job making you feel like a detective. There is always a connection from one clue to the next, which gets really creepy if you think about the possibilities. Even though this game relies on storytelling through an alternate history, it only does so in between nodes of historically accurate content. With a unique approach on player interaction, along with fun little puzzles to solve, The Temporal Invasion is recommended to any fans of puzzle games or conspiracy theories. If you want to try out this game for yourself, there is a free, official downloadable demo (pre-release version) of this game at itch.io (website).

In Lords of Xulima you control a hero called Gaulen the Explorer and his five friends (these five can be completely created by yourself, with 9 additional classes at your disposal). Guided by a dream sent by the gods of his world, Gaulen sails to a forgotten continent. During exploration, the game is very similar to classics like Baldur´s Gate, but once combat begins, it will look like a mixture of Dragon Quest, Final Fantasy 10 and the newer Etrian Odyssey series. It is also often compared to the Wizardry-series.
Major Features:
- A charming atmosphere, travel through a mystical world and explore secret graves, forsaken temples and more.
- Challenging and strategic combat. Very original due to the elaborate debuff system.
- Character skills and equipment management are rich and rewarding.
- Recaptures the feeling of oldschool rpg series like no other game
Possible weakpoints (depending on your taste):
- Story plays only a secondary role. Exploration, combat and character management take the main spotlight.
- Recaptures the feeling of oldschool rpg series like no other game. You wonder why this is repeated in the negatives list? Because nowadays we are so accustomed to arrows that point where we have to go and other such luxuries that the transition can be very rough.
- Hard to get going. You have to manage the party, food reserves and find your way in a huge non-linear world. (If you have troubles, try the easiest difficulty. There you can learn the basic game mechanics without getting your head chopped off for every mistake.)

The only fact I've managed to declassify from The Bureau is that the game suffers from repetitive combat sequences with poor incentives to progress. Team AI and coordination is clunky and far from intelligent. I spent most of my time spamming squad regroup while just taking on everything by myself. There isn't a diverse array of weapon options, with no customization options.
While I'm sure that this game has a great deal of content in terms of its side quests and collectable discussions, there's just nothing wonderful or immersive about the story that grabbed me. Yes, the allure of a top secret agency is there and the core conflict is imminent. But what has always killed a narrative for me was how predictably static and hollow the protagonists were. Rather than present their information throughout the story, you have to go the extra mile and read about it from dossiers on their desks. As edgy as Carter comes across through his backstory, he loses all his charm when he begins to speak lines you've heard a million times before.
The Bureau miscarried the merge of a tactical third-person shooter in what appeared to be a promising premise. It's tepid mechanics and bland characters justify the game's ranking of being mediocre to poor. Don't be fooled by it, even in a humble bundle.

So, I believe this game has this huge stigma against it that it's a bad game because it's not a "Lost Planet" game. It's become a bit of a circlejerk, and a little unfair.
I should start with agreeing with the main stigma against it, it's /not/ the same as the other two games in the series, that being said it's not a terrible game. It has it's flaws, but all things considered still quite enjoyable. Though, maybe not for the full price of £20.
The combat is fairly decent, a little buggy in moments, and the shotgun has this weird little delay after evading/reloading, but all in all, nothing's seriously awful and it gets the job done.
The music in the game is.. Well, decent. It's nothing groundbreaking, but it's still an enjoyable listen. The Voice Acting, however, is absolute garbage, and you're probably going to want to turn that audio slider way down. The main character is decent, as with a few sides. But some of the key characters are just painful.
Storyline is albiet, quite cliche, but again, not too awful. The intro sequence was definitely intriguing, and got me surprisingly well immersed.
Control scheme is pretty janky, some keys just plain don't make sense. P, E, V and T are all different action keys, and it can get a little infuriating. They're rebindable, though. So all's good.
Honestly, despite the big flaws as they are. It's a buggy game, for sure. But nothing game breaking. It's a fun little game to kill some time in, and I came out rather happy with it.
I'd give it an honest 6/10. Pick it up on sale, you'll enjoy it.

The first thing to know is that this isn't XCOM.  It is made by the same company, but it is a spin off that is attempting to break new ground and take the tactic and strategical components from the main franchise and transition them to a first person shooter.
It... I mean it exists.
To be frank, this is neither a good nor bad game.  It's just kinda there.
The Buereau ends up being a third person shooter with strategic elements tacted on.  Playing on the lower levels, there was zero motivation to even utilize these strategic options.  There are a couple side quests at the hub and some very light rpg elements, further muddling what this game is.
I'm forced to ask who this game is made for.  It does everything. A fan of just about every genre could be it up and say, "this is... okay?"  This is a simple case of trying to please everyone resulting in inability shine any one area to an acceptable quality.
Like I said, it is niether bad nor good.  But is that really worth your time?

Let me start by saying that I am *not* a "purist" when it comes to the XCOM franchise.  I didn't play the originals and only started playing XCOM when I played the initial reboot from 2013 (which is an amazing game).
I looked at a number of the reviews of this game and saw a lot of anger about it that seem to sound off more about what it isn't rather than was it is.
What it is not:
-It's not the classic XCOM style of play.  Know this first.  Go in knowing that, and you're off to a good start.
-It's not turn-based
What it is:
-About the closest I can come to describing it is that it plays a lot like "Mass Effect" using the XCOM universe's storyline
-It's a prequel to the classic XCOM games that occurs in the 1960's.
-It's like "Mad Men" but with guns
-It's third-person real time squad based combat.
-It's a definite challenge
This game isn't as engaging as the 2013 XCOM reboot, but it's still a boatload of fun.  I haven't fully completed it at the time of writing this review, but I'm truly enjoying "nibbling" on it a couple of times a week.  I play a mission or two at a time, then come back to it later.
I am using Xbox One controller with my PC configuration and this game makes excellent use of full controller capability.
If you're a fan of Mass Effect style games and like the XCOM storyline, this game is a real gem to own.  Again...judge it for what it is, not what it isn't.
