A Bird's Story is less of a game and more of an interactive short story.  But anyone who has played To The Moon, the creator's previous work, knows that this is not necessarily grounds for criticism.   Any fan of classic 16bit Japanese RPGs could tell you that simpler graphics, animations and musical phrases, when used correctly, take on a metaphoric quality that can be more effective at communicating concepts and emotions than the most detailed scripts, character models, animations, and fully orchestrated scores ever could.
This is a director who demonstrates not only an understanding of this type of restraint, but a mastery of its employment.  Here, as in To the Moon, Kan Gao is able to get a lot of mileage out of lovingly drawn 16 bit pixel art and a beautiful miminalistic piano score.
A Bird's Story is a much simpler narrative than To The Moon, but it is no less elegant.  It is a deeply sentimental story, but also one with restraint, two characteristics rarely found in the same work.  The entire story is told, quite effectively, without a single word and the ending hints that this narrative serves as a small teaser for the creator's next big project, something undoubtedly to be anticipated.  But in the meantime, if you have an hour and a couple of bucks to spare, this is beautfully rendered little story.  Nothing pretentious enough to pretend profundity, just a lot of heart and beautiful craftsmenship. 4/5

There's two aspects that seem to be the options to go with any video game. 1 half is the gameplay aspect, the other is the story aspect. In this case, there really is no gameplay at all, simply walking between cutscenes and the slowest quicktime events ever. As far as a game, it's entirely unengaging.
That leaves it with if the story is strong enough to offset it, but I really don't think it is, certainly not for over an hour of game time. The idea is a 'cute' idea, but it could be done in a 5-10 minute short film far more effectively. Because of the choice to put this in 'game' format, the story progresses at a very slow pace, and the time it takes to wait for things to happen, even things like transitions from one scene to the next, is so long that I simply lose interest. There's about 30 seconds 2/3rds of the way in that were pretty entertaining, but the rest is just a slog through the story.
Without good gameplay or good storytelling, there's really not much to go on, and I rather regret the purchase. To be fair though, the developer has some good work with To The Moon, so I'll still give their next thing a try, I just hope that it's closer to To The Moon (with a strong story that offsets the low gameplay) than it is to this.

This effectively stops players from getting really overpoowered too early on. Third, there are some reworked levels. Those can be good or bad depending on your opinions. Finally, there's the added character Taurus.  He's more tanky than ARES, and all of his weapons are shorter ranged, but with more area of effect and a slightly different story line. Overall, this game is on par with the original, if not a little bit better. However, it would be definitely better if they would add in the Berserker suit and soundtrack already!

This is an updated version of A.R.E.S. Extinction Agenda. It's basically the same game, but with extra chapters and some minor tweaks.
For those unfamiliar with the game, it's a platformer action game, in which you control a robot exploring a space station that has suffered a mysterious accident. There's plenty of enemies to fight in the form of robots working on the station that went rogue due to an unknown contaminant.
The story remains pretty much the same, although now there's the possibility to play as either Ares or Tarus. Ares retains the story of the first game, with some additions; as for Tarus, he has his own story, although you'll find yourself playing the same levels as with Ares, including several of the cutscenes.
As far as gameplay changes, the scrap you used to collect in the previous game has been unified under a single type, but the crafting menu is still there. Upgrades to your weapons and abilities need to be found before you can unlock them. Each character has his own weapons and abilities.
My opinion: if you liked the original, you're going to enjoy this one as well. Recommended.

Lost planet 3 is a really good third person shooter but there are some really annoying things that hold it back from being great.
Starting with the positive: the combat is great, it's exciting and dynamic; the enemy variety is good enough but some bosses were reused too many times in my opinion, for the most part though I enjoyed boss fights; the atmosphere is excellent, the planet looks beautiful and resembles dead space 3 a bit; gotta mention a pretty good soundtrack too, certain enemies' screams literally sent chills down my spine and I loved it!
Now moving on to what could've been done better: the game has a really slow start so try to stay patient; lost planet 3 attempts to be some kind of open world but it fails miserably at that. The map is broken into approximately 10 areas which lead to smaller areas and until you unlock fast travel you'll have to walk all the way through multiple ABSOLUTELY empty areas to get where you need. And even fast travel doesn't really help a lot since it's garbage and yes it will save you some time but you'll still have to spend a lot of time walking in your "Rig" and trust me it becomes a chore before long. The worst part is that you always have to come back to your base to get a new assignment, this is absolutely unnecessary and it would've been soooo much better if it was simply linear and you received your new orders via radio or something so you could move on without backtracking cuz you spend way too much time walking and it's depressing at times, trust me. Not to mention how freaking slow your robot is...
Despite all that pros still far outweigh the cons and I do recommend this game. 7.5/10

This is the pure, uncut and unadulterated cocaine of FPS games. The genesis of skill based 3D FPS games. This is the grandaddy of practically every FPS we have today. Very small community if you want to play multiplayer but if you want to explore mods and single player campaigns this game has a lot to offer. Mods are still being released for this game 20+ years after it's release. In single player and especially multiplayer this game provided the framework and set the bar for the golden age of FPS games. Quake World Team Fortress (the original Team Fortress) lives on thanks to a small community that refuses to let the mod die.

vkQuake (rename vkQuake.exe to Winquake.exe so you could play in Steam) + vispatch + fog 0.04 + r_wateralpha 0.5  + host_maxfps 250. Use command-line options -zone 2048 and -heapsize 192000. Don't forget to copy the original NIN soundtrack to Id1\music. Finish the game and try frikbot_quickstart.zip for some bot action. Then play the two official mission packs. Now you are ready to download even more high quality single player mods! This game has been around for so long, you wouldn't know where to start. Finally, just for fun, why don't you dabble in some private modding and/or mapping yourself? By that time you'll love the original Quake without any doubt in your mind that this is one of the all time classics.

You better believe I took the god damned balista. I built so many god damned balista my accountants were screaming the entire game because we were barely pulling 100+ gold per 8 hours. It looked like I was trying to perform the ol Protoss Cannon strat on the entire map, but you know what! I held the god damned horde off and with the help of my Titan/Thanatos special forces unit we held back the horde and won the game.
After 4 tries I managed to defeat the massive zombie horde and I feel like a god! Next I will have to try and play on the level above cupcake and see how I do.
As for the game itself. It is very satisfying and quite fun. The visuals are basic, but rewarding. The backround music feels like it came directly from the Bloodmoore in Diable 2, which I absolutely love. The challenge is definitely there, so even though we only have survival mode at the moment it feels like I have plenty of game to play. My system is capable of running most any game at 144 FPS, so I don't know if it will be a resource hog on lower end machines, but it certainly runs smooth and doesn't seem to excessively draw uneeded power like many other early access games, so that's a big win for it in my opinion as well. I am excited to see how this game develops out as it goes through early access, but if you like Tower Defense, RTS, Survival, build em up games this is your go to for 2018. The only thing I really think is needed currently is a tutorial. I mean, I like jumping in and learning as much as the next person, but it took me longer then I want to admit to figure out that things like hunter cottages and fishing cottages can vary in their production based on the number that is showing when you are picking a spot to build it... Don't even get me started on the tech tree progessions. Also, building can be a bit of a pain due to terrain, and the edges of the map being restricted even though zombies can still spawn off those restricted edges, so you need to really pay attention, or else you will have a horde blasting through the west and you had no ability to build defenses their since it was restricted...
Still, if these are my only complaints then this game is winner! I give it 8/10 after 7 hours, and I expect the more comfortable I get with the game the higher that score will go. Great job!

Gotta say I loved this game when it first came out.  Loved playing the monster, loved playing the hunters, and even when they started remaking things I still loved it.
Now when it first came out it was all about the hunt.  The hunt being where the monster tried to be as any animal being hunted and knowing about it might be, being sneaky, staying out of sight, eating.  And a lot of people said this was a boring part of the game.  If you didn't have a great tracker on the team I can see how that would be the case, but being the monster it was always tense because when I played the monster it was only a few times when I absolutely lost the hunters.
So they've remade the game, free to play, and much much shorter matches with the maps being smaller and EVERYONE having a way to figure out where you are as a monster at almost any given moment.
Now that wouldn't be too much of a problem if you get a good enough head start, and there in lies the problem.  This time around there is no sneaking, except in a few varied cases.  If you slow down at all, any hunter can catch up to you and find you within the first minute or two of the game, and since EVERYONE can dome now, if you get caught early you are screwed.
Now the next problem is that there are several team comps now that even if you last long enough to get to stage two will be invincible no matter what monster or perks you have.  There are comps for infinite flying out of range for melee attacks and abilities.  Comps for infinite shields.  Comps for infinite healing.  Comps for infinite movement and attack to a crawl for the monster.
The only times I ever have a chance at winning now are against new players, or people trolling their teams.
All those one sided problems aside, that could still be fixed one way or another, I still love this game.  The atmosphere, the scifi, the monsters, the wildlife, and a way to blow of steam sometimes.  And when you win it feels damn good.
So I gotta say if you are competitive, like the look, and love a really hard chalange.  This is a game you'd love.  Also is great when you have enough friends and can just mess around on the maps for a while.
But if you don't like feeling paranoid about being hunted or loosing often, one side or the other, then I'd say look for something else.

Portal is a smart and witty puzzle game that takes place in the Valve-verse, the fictional universe occupied by the two Portal games and the Half-Life series.
In Portal, the player takes on the role of Chell, a silent protagonist who must solve a selection of puzzles based around the Aperture Science Portal Device, a gun that can fire up to two portals at once, one blue, one orange. If Chell walks through one, she comes out the other, and layered over this simple mechanic are buttons, weighted cubes, turrets, and all sorts of other objects. Each room makes up a puzzle, with the aim of each one being to leave the room and enter the next one. The execution of this differs from test to test, however, resulting in the game never feeling repetitive or dull. The satisfaction that comes with solving these puzzles is always rewarding.
Portal also uses a style of storytelling often praised in video games for separating the medium from other mediums of storytelling- environmental storytelling. Scattered throughout the Testing Facility are messages scrawled on walls, and even the occasional picture. This makes the story feel almost like another puzzle, further adding to the experience as the player must piece together exactly what's happening.
Apart from Chell, the only other true character to speak of is GLaDOS, an AI that leads you through the Testing Facility. For much of the game, GLaDOS is just a voice, and her dialogue is a joy to listen to, often funny, elevating GLaDos to one of gaming's best characters.
Though shorter than most games, Portal is a charming and clever package that is more than the sum of its parts, and once completed, will leave you wanting more. Thankfully, Portal 2 offers just that...

I'm going to "recommend" this game, only because I feel you'll probably get different feelings from it than I did. For me, it was a decent story, however, it was not nearly affecting enough. As a huge fan of To The Moon, I was looking forward to Gao's next project, and while this may hold me over a little while until his next full-length project, I can only hope his next game comes soon.
Firstly, the graphics. The sprites and pixel art are beautifully done, a huge improvement over To The Moon. Not only that, but other visual design elements in the world and storytelling have substantial meaning, and it feels like everything is done deliberately.
The soundtrack is also fantastic. Lighter and more subtle than To the Moon, it fits the feeling of each scene, even heightening the emotions. I would say it's the strongest part of this piece, and could probably be listened to separately from the game itself (though I did not buy the soundtrack bundle).
The gameplay is incredibly linear, as expected of an interactive story, and that's not a bad thing. Simple controls makes telling the story much easier, and the lack of dialogue removes any distracting "press this to continue" to remove you from the story. I'm glad with this choice, as it pushes the player to pay more attention to what's actually happening between the characters.
The story, without giving away spoilers, is my biggest problem. I didn't feel nearly as much emotion as I did during parts of To the Moon. While I think it is a good story, the entire time I was thinking "this would make a great indie movie," rather than "this is a great interactive story experience." There's immense amounts of character development, but due to the length (approximately an hour), I didn't become as attached to the characters as I feel I should have been. Maybe that's my problem, but I think a bit more length to the story would have helped a lot.
Give it a shot. It's a good interactive story, and if you're a fan of To the Moon, you'll likely like it a lot. If you're interested, give it a go, for $5 it's a great deal, and if it goes on sale again, you have no reason not to try it out. I know I said a lot of negative things, but it's a geniunely entertaining story, if not as much of a tear jerker as I was expecting.

Well, this game was awful. Which is a shame because it had so much potential. I would love to play a cold-war era third person shooter where I am defending the world against an alien invasion. Even more so if it involves building the organization I work for and uncovering the true motivations behind the invasion. XCOM does all of these things, and it is a very conceptually strong game. Where it fails is... well, everywhere else.
Let me explain. The core gameplay mechanics are a disaster. The controls are awkward and even moving around is a chore. Most guns do pathetically small amounts of damage, and result in you being quickly overrun. The command mechanic is prehistoric. Freedom Fighters and Brothers in Arms had more solid command systems, and they were developed over ten years ago. Here, the orders enable powers but allow for very little actual tactical command. Which is bad because the AI for your teammates is beyond worthless. They will break cover right into withering crossfire from turrets for no reason at all so they can be cut to ribbons. Oh, and if the scatter laser is any example of the alien tech you discover, they actually are worse than the human weapons.
The storyline is also pretty bad. The invasion is happening with alarming speed and the aliens identify XCOM's headquarters very quickly, but don't wipe it out. The main character, Carter, is completely unlikable. He's supposed to come off as a lone-wolf tough guy, but really is just a jerk with no real motivation. If they wanted to try that, they should have looked at Red Dead Redemption, which pulled off that character very well.
The game has some interesting visuals, but that is downplayed by the ridiculously simplistic level design. They reminded me a lot of the original Dead to Rights game or XCOM: Enforcer. Additionally, expect frequent crashes and bugs, even three years after its release.
I think XCOM fans everywhere wanted this one to work really badly. We held our breath for an XCOM shooter since XCOM: Alliance was cancelled. But no matter how much we wanted to like this one, it will always be a half-game made by a half-effort.

Welcome to my review of The Bureau: XCOM Declassified!
In A Nutshell:
Pros:
-Fairly Interesting Plot: Very Film Noir meets Retro Sci-Fi Convention
-Decent Graphics and Audio
-Good Eye for Detail with the Retro Elements (Like dated phones and propaganda posters)
-Micromanagement with Teammates (Could be a Con?)
Cons:
-Wonky Controls (No Crouch button? Really?)
-Team Management is Mandatory (Mine died if left to their own devices all the time. Whoops.)
-Too Many Gimmicks (Is this a Shooter? Sci-Fi RPG? Tactical Combat Film Noir? What?)
Full Review:

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified feels like a video game that has tried to be too many things at once. Part Strategy title, part Shooter, with RPG elements, team management, Noir vs. Sci-Fi themes, tactical combat, and more. It’s all over the place, but unfortunately it doesn’t do any of these things exceptionally well – or even moderately well, at times. It’s a game I was extremely excited to try, but ultimately was left feeling disappointed; the team management system isn’t my forte, but I struggled more with the clunky controls than anything else. I couldn’t toggle a key binding for a crouch, so if I approached a barricade the wrong way I’d just stand there getting shot in the face – that’s poor tactics, man. The very definition!
The storyline is fairly interesting, and it’s an odd mix of old Hollywood Noir with the Sci-Fi aspect so many modern games utilize. I really enjoyed the blend, and the subtle details in the landscape; not to mention the cinematic events, which tied in the story nicely, even if their frequency felt a bit tedious at times. All in all, I think other games blend Strategy, management, RPG elements, and the shooter genre better, but if you can nab this one on sale – at least if you love the idea of using wonky controls to yell at AI characters to get shot at – it might be worth adding to your library. Because of my neutral stance I'm going with a YES recommendation here, but with reservations.
In Conclusion: 5/10

This is a game that's clearly had a ton of work put into it, but suffers badly at the hand of poor design decisions. Most significantly, the controls are really really bad, owing mainly to the mouse-aim/keyboard move idea paired with complex key-combinations for executing some techniques that the game chooses to make necessary in so many different places. Having bad controls and then choosing to make the game primarily centered around performing ridiculous mid-air maneuvers every 2 seconds is not really conducive to a good gameplay experience. It just feels cheap and unrewarding. Adding the control pad support should have fixed this, but unfortunately it didn't. You have to use both thumbs to move and shoot, but a lot of the primary functions, like jumping, are on the thumb buttons, so you have to stop shooting to jump or use a special. Additionally, instead of letting the dash direction be controlled by the movement stick, they split it between the L/R bumpers, which is completely unintuitive and, again, just plain bad. It really is a deal-breaker.
The upgrade system seems like a decent idea until you realize that you not only have to find the upgrade item in the game, but you also have to spend currency on it. The currency is pretty ubiquitous, to the point that it sometimes literally rains from the sky (wtf), but you also spend it to activate your special moves, which is kind of stupid.
The graphics are very high-quality. They're at or above the level of AAA games of this kind. There is some noisiness, though, that gets in the way of gameplay, such as foreground girders concealing the fact that the ceiling is suddenly lower, and you find out by trying to jump over an enemy attack only to find that you have no clearance.
The audio is also excellent, with an appropriate high-quality soundtrack accompanied by decent SFX.
In short, it's a game that's worth playing, but it's not worth spending $10 on. Not even by a long shot.

I'm not going to say this game is the best multiplayer game out there right off the bat, because everyone is entitiled to their opinion. As "Endeblez" said in his review, its not for everyone. But I believe that the reason for that is because its gameplay is incredibly different from any other shooter. Here's why:
It focuses on tactical teamwork & objectives instead of little or no teamwork & kill to death ratios. You gain experience not only from kills, but gradually from completing or defending objectives, or from claiming command posts from your opponents. There are 4 different classes that you can spawn as and switch between in-game. Rankings at the end of a match are calculated by how much experience you received in the match. They even list mvp's for each class & overall at the end of a match.
The only game I can truely compare to BRINK is Enemy Territory: Quake Wars, both of which are made by Splash Damage & on the id tech 4 engine. Basically, the only 2 features that separate these 2 games is BRINK's fluid movement controls & ETQW's "MegaTexture" Planet sized maps. Other than that, they are basically the same game.
Overall: "My" opinion gives this game a 10/10 for gameplay, 8/10 for story, 10/10 for multiplayer (and yes, there are still people who play this game, and if theres no one in a server, there are always bots to fall back on.), and 9/10 for graphics (Mainly because its built on the id tech 4 game engine and they did an excellent job of modifying it to make it look modern.)
BUT that is my opinion, not your's. You need to form your own. This game is not for everyone, but it is a game you should at least try.
PS: This review can also count as a review on Enemy Territory: Quake Wars. I urge you to try both. However, If you don't like one, its likely you won't like the other, or vice versa.

Lords of Xulima is a true indie gem. It doesn't at all play like an indie game (perhaps thanks to the generously overfunded kickstarter campaign), even though it's the first game released by the developers.
In a nutshell, LoX is a classic console RPG re-imagined for the modern gaming age.
What really makes this game unique is the rich combat system. It takes already-established systems and greatly expands upon them to build a brilliant tactical system. For example, while most Final Fantasy games have a front-row/back-row system, the impact of it is minimal, and it's so automatic that some players won't even know it's there. However, it's front and center in LoX, and has a massive impact. Enemy melee attacks can only target your front row, and your melee attacks can only target their front row, usually only from
front row. Furthermore, neither you nor the enemy can have a unit in the back row without another unit in the front row to hide behind; kill that front unit and the one behind it moves up.
The game uses a turn-time system whereby faster units get to take more turns. I'm really baffled as to why more games don't use this. (It's quite similar to Final Fantasy 10)
There's also the rich debuff system; each weapon type inflicts one of three debuffs, each of which can stack to no limit. There's Bleed, which is a permanent damge-over-time effect which can easily do the majority of damage to a big character, Stun, which delays the unit's next turn and prevents attacks against it from missing for the duration, and Wound, which decreases the unit's stats. Some enemies partially resist some debuffs, and some flat-out immune one or two, but I've yet to find an enemy immune to all three, not even bosses. This is especially nice; your typical classic boss is immune to everything except raw damage, so bosses in LoX are more than just simple slugfests.
A word of warning: LoX is hard. Min/maxing, intelligent tactics, and some amount of save scumming will be vital to success.

I believe I either got this game in a humble bundle or steam sale. Either way, I expected nothing more than a dumb, silly, lighthearted bird-dating sim. Oh jeez, this game was more than that.
Following the routes of each bird is pretty short and nothing too special. The dialogue gets silly, and it appears to be exactly what I expected, aside from two very entertaining dating paths (Oko-San's and Anghel's).
However, wooing enough of the birds unlocks the "BBL ending" which provides an entertaining story that has nothing to do with flirting, and everything to do with character development - and with content that is dark, twisted, and answers some of the questions left by playing through the dating paths. I finished this plot somewhere between two / two and a half hours, and it was worth it. Unlike the individual dating paths, which tend to gloss over the characters and sometimes leave unsatisfying endings, the BBL plot throws a ton of additional background story into each character, a bunch of twists, and is written well enough to make you want to finish playing through it. The BBL plot plays more as an interactive story than a sim, but for a few bucks I'd say it's worth it.
Overall, the 'preliminary game' is alright but nothing too special, and each path is quite short. The BBL plotline is great and makes it worth playing through to unlock.

What makes it a bad game for me:
1) Dumb AI - The AI does stupid things like:
* pulls all its troops from a frontline thereby allowing you to march right in (especially the Meganoit line);
* 'reenforces' your line by dumping loads of troops on it then does nothing, and this causes your own troops to take lots of attrition;
* it cannot use paratroopers and often naval invades you but then does nothing except sit there and wait to be destroyed; * it cannot protect its coasts from player naval invasions, e.g. invading Britian as Germany is very easy - you can dump loads of paratoopers over it or naval invade them, when all they (the AI) need to do is put a few troops on their coasts and build some forts;
* they often send tiny fleets (but very good ships like battleships and carriers) unprotected which then get easily destroyed by the player;
* it doesn't protect its convoys - you'd think it would send some destroyers to hunt out those subs that you sent on convoy raiding;
* it doesn't deal with production management very well - I see many thousands of troops with no equipment;
2) The UI and player given commands
* giving orders to your troops in a sequence is a little difficult i.e. you cannot tell your armies "do this, then this, then this". The only way to give your army a sequence of commands is initiate each command seperately and at the correct time. This can be annoying when you have multiple combats around the globe. It is not uncommon to give your army a command then leave it thinking its doing its thing just to find that it got itself pocketed (surrounded by enemy troops) and didn't move into neighbouring provinces even though there were no enemy troops in them (again because of the dumb AI).
* splitting your navies is tedious.
* no way to see current conflicts - put it in a tab like EU4?
3) The nukes and rockets are pretty much useless.
* nukes and rockets are devastating - in HOI4 they are pathetic. There is no concept of damage to population, troops (dropping a nuke on enemy troops lowers their organisation a little - hahahahaha!) or radiation. Apparently Paradox are living in a paradoxical world where wars don't harm the civilian population, and nukes don't lower your manpower. C'mon!
4) Oversimplified economy and trade
* The current system is not bad but it is just too simple. I'd like to see more economics and economic impacts from peace and war, war and trade, etc. I think currency, taxes, national income, expenditure etc. should be in the game. What are your 5 million troops being paid with? What do your citizens think of the war taxes and rations? Questions like these should be addressed in a game like this, but they aren't.
5) Unrest is a joke - no really, it's funny
* You sue for peace and then suddenly, magically, unrest is gone and the Orthodox Russians, Catholic Polish, Hindu Indians, Satanic African homosexual, Jewish migrant, Islamic Turk etc. are totally happy to go work together in your factories making bombs to drop on their cousin's grandma... come on Paradox!!
6) Paradox's DLC policy and missing content
* The DLCs 'Together for Victory' and 'Death or Dishonor' are shameful. They add so little content that should already be in the base game. I want to be able to control my puppets. What is the damned point in puppeting a state in this game? If you do, you don't get their resources, you can't integrate them (unless you have the above DLC) etc. Why is this so? Lend lease and tech sharing should be part of the base game. Lending equipment etc. was a big feature in WW2, but not according to Paradox - unless you shell out (no pun intended) extortionate amounts of money, of course.
In essence the game is too simple and with the added problems it becomes boring pretty fast. You may say to give the AI bonuses, but I don't want to compensate an AI that can't think with bonuses and cheats. It's a shame because this game could've been really good, but it just feels too simple and at times stupid beyond reason.

Honestly, i can understand people who just give the game five minutes then go "nope, not even worth my coupon" but there are some exellent points to this game as long as you can stand minor bugs.
+ Fully customisable crew, from hiring to leveling
I love how you can literally to to any tavern in the game and hire up to 6-14 different crew members, all randomly gererated and with their own pros and cons, meaning any particular person could have a rare weapon you've never seen before, or have absolutely terrible stats, or be a complete genius.
Not to mention each person can have their stats micromanaged and changed over time to suit your crew; need a bezerker to hide behind? No problem.
+ Making your own ship
Ripping parts off of enemy ships and diplaying them in your own ship is personally one of the most satifying parts of the game, especially when a new type of ship is found and you can just ditch your old creation and entirely replace it. Eventually making your ship a titan so big you have to scroll to see it in it's full glory can by the end of the game.
+ Progression
The game doesnt go soft on people who run head-first into high level zones, and if you dont have cannons ASAP, the enemy can get a thirty second head-start whilst you get into boarding range to decimate you, your precious ship, and all the crew you have micromanaged to perfection. But people who slowly take out zones over time can have it the opposite, anniliating puny pirates who dared to stand in your way before you even cross blades.
+ Management
Carefully messing around with food supplies and repairing the ship is enjoyable, your crew can get scurvy if all you feed them pot noodles all the time, even if it is the cheapest on the market; plus food can rot if left too long, so proper storage or supply management is needed.
On the other hand, the game is still in developmet, and there are some bugs and flaws.
- Controls
There is no clear tutorial, and you will have trouble the first few times you try to survive and trying to pick out the opponents captain or any other person in particular in the middle of battle is impossible; the selector can have a mind of it's own, picking pots, chickens, and other random objects, leaving you fustrated, even if your crew takes him down anyway.
- Lag
when your ship become four times bigger than your screen, trying to place a single block is a good minute wait, so trying to make the Enterprise in boat form isn't happening any time soon.
- Endgame gameplay
Bluntly, there is no gameplay once you have finished the entirety this game for the first time, and doing everything all over again isn't very fun as the encounters get repetative really fast after the first playthough from start to finish.
In summary, i would give Pixel Piracy 8/10.

A Bird Story is a new story done by Kan Gao, creator of the previous hit To the Moon.  It's not a full sequel, but rather a short, minimally interactive story about a boy and a bird he fosters after rescuing it from a predator (said boy seems to be part of the real sequel, coming later).  If you're looking for something with the full depth and emotional level of To the Moon, then you won't find it here.  What you will find is, however, still good - a heartwarming tale of the empathetic connection between human and beast, told entirely through visuals rather than dialogue.  It's a short playthrough, with just over an hour needed to get through, but it's still true to Kan Gao's trend of a sweet story set to a beautiful soundtrack.
Pros: Great story, amazing soundtrack
Cons: Very short for the price
Verdict: Buy this for sure, but do it when it's on sale. And get the soundtrack version!
Opponents of the idea of games as an art form are refuted by Kan Gao yet again.

A fantastic isometric action game. The core combat consist of three moves - attack with your weapon, dash, and block. Do anything too much and you run out of stamina and can't act. Dash into an enemy when they are low on stamina to stun them. Using these basic rules, you can dispatch any enemy in the game. Once you play with the additional items and spells, you can come up with strategies and tactics that work for you.
Challenging, slow (in the best way), and mysterious, Immortal Planet is a real gem.

There are a lot of things I really like about this game - enough that I'm sorely disappointed that my enjoyment is crippled by two factors: the game is terrible at giving the player information, and arbitrary and frustrating design decisions have been made with the idea of making the game hard, not making the game better.
The first problem is mostly an irritation - the game explains itself poorly, providing you the absolute dirt basics in an opening tutorial, then the rest is just there, without even being mentioned.  Entire systems are present without so much as a clue about how they're supposed to work, you're handed a sheet of stats with no explanations, things like that - but fundamentally, that's academic, you can work everything out with enough experimentation.  The real issue here is the lack of good feedback.  It's sometimes difficult to tell when you've been hit, particularly if you just landed a flurry of blows, but even worse is that it's hard to read the enemies.  Each one only has a handful of frames of animation, meaning they make the same motion before and after every attack, making it impossible to tell if they're about to hack at you, say, three times, or just once; this turns attacking into a dangerous guessing game, but it's compounded by the second major issue.
This game is hard - and not in the way the Soulsborne games are.  There's no 'I understand what went wrong and I can work to improve myself with what I just learned', which is the beating heart of what makes those games compelling.  Enemies strike for a quarter to half your health per hit.  My 'immortal blood vial' (read: estus flask) still only has a single charge in the prison, the game's second area, and while you can find additional charges by opening containers, they're temporary, lasting only that life and vanishing when used - even worse, every time you open a container, there's a random chance that an enemy will spawn inside it, already halfway through their windup, punishing you for seeking out healing in a healing-starved system.  Dashing into an enemy with too much stamina will stun you, but given the game's top-down perspective and 2D art, it's unclear when your character is actually colliding with something, so an attempt to dodge around a boss to evade a slash can stun you for a painfully long time... come to think of it, a surprising number of things stun you for a painfully long time.  Numerous attacks from the first boss, dashing 'into' an enemy with too much stamina, an aoe attack from a common enemy in the second area with a very short windup, and I'm sure a great deal that I haven't seen.
These two issues combined mean that, for me, the game is not fun.  It might be fun for the 'dark souls is too easy' masochists that it was clearly designed to appease, but for me, a veteran gamer with solid reflexes and hundreds of hours logged across both console and PC versions of all three Dark Souls titles, it feels like an unrelenting wall of punishment.  Massive damage, constant stuns, chests dealing death at a roll of the dice, obtuse systems, and poor feedback turn this from a challenging and rewarding experience into a frustrating one - it invested too much into the 'difficulty' aspect of soulsborne design, and not enough into the 'carefully refined design' aspect.  Hell, if the game was a little less stun-eager, got rid of the nonsense rng-mimics, and dialed back the damage a little, I'd be willing to power through the rest of my issues; I love the premise and the setting from what I've seen, which makes it all the more painful that it seems like it just doesn't want me to play it.
I'm sure people like this game, reviews looked pretty positive when I bought it, but I can't in good conscience recommend a game that provides me frustration instead of enjoyment.

While this game had interesting gameplay and FAR more interesting lore, the game's developers intentionally lied about a "good ending" to the game that has never existed.
I can't support people who would trick players into sinking more hours into a game to give a false sense of more popularity -- and purely because players were honestly curious about such a unique and interesting narrative that they clearly never had the time or resources to finish.
The game has its other flaws, as well -- all weapons function almost exactly the same with the exact speeds and damages, extremely repetitive gameplay, minor yet persistent bugs with the game's all-important hitboxes -- but these flaws would have been forgivable had the makers of this game simply admitted that they weren't able to finish their very interesting story. The game has only one, single "bad" ending, confirmed by the developers: this ending is "bad" not due to any choices made by the player, but more because it is forced on you due to the fact that the game feels like it's missing one last dungoen that would tie all of its story together. Instead, where that final location may have been, there is simply a big button that might as well say "RAN OUT OF TIME: END THE GAME, WHOOPS."
The developers decided to give you the sense that, if you finished the game a second time, you might find that closure to the story they already told you. There is no different ending, though. Don't give these people money.

Immortal Planet is based on slow-paced melee combat. It's borderline tactical / action gameplay. You’re not going to rush in whirling your sword around your head and hope for the best. You have to dodge and block enemy attacks and manage your rapidly-depleting stamina bar, as well as strike when enemies are tired.
I like the aesthetic. Each level has a single checkpoint, so you drop in and start exploring. If you die, you go back to the start and lose experience, but you can pick that experience back up at the spot you died.
Patience and focus are much more important than reflexes. A slow but fun game.

I remember when I first came across Ronin, the developer's previous (and as far as I know, first) ever developed game. Ronin was a game I absolutely adored, and when I heard that "teedoubleuGAMES" was making another title, Immortal Planet, I was extremely excited. Fast forward about a year or so, and the game is released. And boy, is it a massive improvement.
While Ronin and Immortal Planet are two entirely different games, I feel that Immortal Planet is a great improvement in that it is far more enjoyable, and the mechanics, while some are borrowed from games like Dark Souls, are well thought out and executed to perfection.
Pros:

Just finished up, it took a little while to warm up to this game but Immortal Planet really succeeds on every level. It's a shame it hasn't found more recognition, and I get the frustration of the whole "Bad Ending" achievement being misleading wording and the developers not helping by being vague and sarcastic, but I don't think it's such a damning thing that it lessens the quality of the rest of the game. The ending fit the universe and the lore within so I don't think it really needs multiple endings in the first place. I don't think being coy about it looks great on the devs though.
The game looks and sounds wonderful, some of the boss fights had really pumping, exciting tracks, visual design was bold and interesting, I love the worldbuilding and what few glimpses you get into the history and background of characters via NPCs and the enemy compendium are nicely written and add a lot.
Gameplay is where Immortal Planet shines most, hands-down. If you enjoy Bloodborne, you'll feel right at home with an equivalent to the rally system that makes staying in and being proactive with your combat plan get you through some dire situations and keep your survivability up even when enduring hits from your enemies. Another Bloodborne carry-over is weapon awakening, by holding the attack button you transform your weapon, most of these extend range and power at the cost of speed, and I found most of the time there was little reason to use the normal forms of the weapons, but that may just be my playstyle preference. Otherwise, a focus on stamina management, some interesting tactics including a shoulder bash dodge into low-stamina enemies to stun them for a hefty period, and just generally slick combat flow makes this game a big winner in terms of drawing positive mechanics from its contenders, there's a lot of Bloodborne, a little Nioh, and the game infuses its own unique setting and abilities into the mix.
There's a plethora of weapons, though I went through my whole playthrough before even finding one, pro-tip: Keep talking to the frozen archivist until a shop screen comes up, it's easy to miss. He'll sell a key to an optional area in the tutorial zone that has another merchant and the other starting weapons after a boss fight. Some weapons have special distance covering transform attacks but on the whole they tend to run pretty similar to one another aside from a couple really cool stand-outs like a firesword or a shockspear that sacrifices a small amount of health to transform into a heavy damage-dealing trident mode, shocking nearby enemies with a bolt of lightning and remaining active until you get hit. The look and feel of beating down enemies is super satisfying. When anyone is defeated in the game they crystallize into an icy statue then shatter, blood stains also quickly freeze on the ground and dissipate, it's a really nice style and implements the lore into the visual gameplay feedback, really cool stuff there.
You also have plenty of spells and support items to find, from simple freezing ice projectiles to more strategically functional stuff like HP-sapping or position-swapping teleportation spells that disorient the enemy. A simple level up system bars some of the more powerful stuff but by the end of the game I had enough points to allocate to use everything bar one spell that required something like 25 intelligence. As the support items go, you have a selection of grenades that poison or stun enemies to healing injections that let you step back and restore yourself for another round of battle, or one that restores your stamina immediately as well as recharging an extra spell use or two for a little extra magical ammunition.
I could go on but really the game just rocks, it really deserves more credit than it got. If there's a few small complaints I have it's that the level design can get a little on the dry side, some paths to boss fights run a tad long, and more on the lack of community-side I'm not sure whether there's spells, weapons or key items I missed (a lot of your equipment screens won't be filled out by endgame) but these are really nitpicks in a really rock-solid experience. It's among my favorite games to take from the Souls-like formula and I know that's a very loosely thrown around term but this is a game that actually really deserves its most positive implications.
So go on, Awakewalker, restore the Cycles... Awakewalker isn't a word.

This game honestly falls right down the middle of the mediocrity line.
In terms of story and atmosphere it does what it aims to do seamlessly with perfection; Jim Raynor..... I mean; Jim Peyton is your main character; with his mannerisms and look you'll be reminded of your average cowboy hero. Which the inclusion of the soundtrack in your rig helps even more to solidify that.
However; it goes without saying this game has some major issues, when you play Gears of Lost Planet 3; you'll notice that things like button prompts are faulty; even for the default button settings. Which is sad.
Another major issue is that near the end of the game; you stop doing the you vs. weird plant creatures. Instead it becomes a shooting gallery.
All in all; the game does some things well; atmosphere, story, the way it fleshes out characters. All very well done.
The actual game aspect of the game is a bit of a tragedy however; it treats you like an idiot, gives you the wrong prompts, and the mech battles themselves felt anything but satisfactory.

(Be sure to install the free HD cutscene videos "DLC" before you start! The cutscenes in the game are really grainy if you're playing at 1080p or above, so the HD videos will make a big difference.)
After about 2 hours of playing Lost Planet 3, I was ready to uninstall it and move onto the next game. For some reason, I ended up putting in another 2 hours and I'm really glad I did! (I'm at 58 hours now, over two back-to-back playthroughs of the game.)
If you've played any of the previous Lost Planet games, the setting will be familiar. EDN III. Frozen wasteland filled with nasty bug-creatures called Akrid. You run around and shoot them, or occasionally crush them with your full-sized mech (not the mech-mini of the original game). The shooting and mech combat are both decent. They're not great, but they won't annoy you too much. (The mech battles might, until you get the hang of the controls.)
But don't worry about those details. The reason you should really play the game is for the story. The writing and voice acting are both superb, which makes for an amazing combination. You'll really start to care for all of the characters in the game, including some of the ones you never get to meet in person but only come to know from reading through the text and audio logs they left behind around the planet.
If you're a completionist, it's possible to collect everything and get all of the single-player achievements in your first playthrough (if you play on HARD), but I'd recommend playing through the game on normal first, and then doing a second run through on HARD. The pacing for a new player is really kind of rough, so it took me quite a while to really get into the game the first time through. But when you play through it agian (on HARD), you'll get to appreciate the game for how I believe the developers MEANT for you to experience it, which makes for a really great experience.
This game is not without its flaws. However, it is well worth a play-through. I hope that they make another one, to finish the story that they started.

You basicaly have to wait until World War 2 starts before you can do anything belligerent, and even then, that often means you're either already at war with someone tougher than you, or declaring war on someone means you'll have to fight everyone in the allies.
That being said, the game is a lot of fun, if super complicated, but it feels less like a sandbox game then other paradox titles, and more like a  "let's just replay history" game.

Funny and touching, surreal and dreamlike, and just a tiny bit sad.  A Bird Story is a masterpiece of pixel art design and endeavors to show rather than to tell.  The game has no written text anywhere in the game.  Everything is told through analogy, metaphor, pantomime, and thought bubbles.  It's interesting, all the small touches that are put into the game to emphasis emotion and idea.
The sprite work here is just amazing.  You can see so much in each expression and position of the sprites.
Why is this a game though?  It's a wonderful visual feast for the eyes and the soul, but control is largely...unnecessary.
Should you buy it?  Well, it's about an hour long, but it is an emotional experience.  That one hour makes you feel more than many games do in 20.  It's hard to justify the price though.
Nevertheless, this developer is one I highly respect and I want to see more of their work.  A Bird Story is actually a prequel to their future work...so, to make sure we get it, please support this game.  It's not an experience you will forget anytime soon.

~~WARNING, THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS, IF YOU DONT WANT THE GREATEST DATING SIM OF ALL TIME SPOILED, DON'T READ THIS~~
I first played this game a while ago, on its first English release. I believe that was over 3 years ago now? When I originally heard of this game, I of course reacted like everyone else. "Wow, absurd crazy Japanese dating sim about... birds??? This is so ridiculous that I have to play it."
A big thing that completely goes over peoples' heads, a conclusion they never seem to come to when they see this game in the Steam store, or when they saw it online wherever for the first time is... could this possibly be tongue-in-cheek? You know, a parody of generic Dating Sim/Visual Novel tropes? Which is kind of crazy to be honest, considering that's what immediately should be coming to their mind - that yes, this game parodies a lot of silly Visual Novels that take themselves far too seriously.
The first portion of this game, the "normal high school life" routes, a lot of them use very cliché anime/RPG/Dating Sim tropes, particularly Okosan's slice-of-life, non-serious route, Shuu's sort of yandere true ending, and Anghel's downright crazy and completely non-canon route (is it technically non-canon, considering the effect Anghel causes upon those around him?), but they're written in such a self-aware way, a lot of these storylines know fully well how ridiculous they are and they're not ashamed to be so.
A lot of the routes do give a bit of insight into each of the characters and you can start to piece things together, but the bulk of the actual plot comes in final route, the Bad Boys Love ending. Hatoful Boyfriend is not a dating sim. The Dating Sim section, in my opinion, was simply a very clever selling point of the game. It is essentially used as such because the devlopers KNEW people would buy something so out there, and for shock value. When you start to realise truly how dark this game is, it's genuinely shocking.
If this game was depicted as a serious visual novel about a political faction with extreme racist views, and their goal to rid Earth of the opposing race through means of biological weaponry, even if that requires unethical treatment of their own kind, this game would have been critically acclaimed. Which is funny, because that's EXACTLY what this game is about. There's a lot more to it than that, but that's the basic plot.
Albeit the writing is a bit goofy at times, even in serious parts, and there's a lot of unnecessary gore, this game is extremely cleverly written. Despite disguising itself as a dating sim at first glance, and being a mockery to those who haven't played it, this game has pretty interesting politIcal undertones and social commentary, and honestly? I'm awfully more attached to talking birds than I was to any of the characters in westerm, artsy, "plot heavy" (but not really) indie games on Steam such as Thomas Was Alone.
But yeah, I'd love to give Hatoful Boyfriend a 10/10 for how well marketed and well put together this game is, along with its amazingly witty writing, but I have to give it a 9.5 for being unnecessarily, I guess, "edgy" and fanfiction-esque at times.
P.S. I've very tempted to figure out a way of rewriting the entire script of this game to be... well, not about birds, and sending it to my friends not telling them what it is. And I can guarantee they'd never be able to guess

quake is pretty much perfect even 21 years after release. Everything that can be said about this game has been said and I would say if you want to know the details of the gameplay/history to watch Ahoy's and Gggmanlives's videos on youtube, so I will just give you some of my thoughts. *the hours is inaccurate as I have run the game mostly outside of steam with quakespasm*
pros:
-excellent visual design and castle/lovecraft atmosphere
-superb sound design, aside from shotgun
-very well laid out levels
-distinctive and strategic enemy types
-very smooth movement and controls
-distinct and fun weapons
-rocketjumping
-bunnyhopping
-it's quake
cons:
-single barrel shotgun sounds muffled and sad + too high firing rate
-strafe jumping isn't nearly as effective or easy as in quake 2+
-not enough ammo for nailgun/lightning gun in my opinion
-could use more enemy types
-no level select feature, but that can't be expected of a game from this time period
-the multiplayer, in my opinion, which appears to be in the minority, is not as strong as the singleplayer. The weapons are horribly unbalanced; the rocket launcher and lightning gun are very overpowered. Compared to quake ii/iii, there is just a very high chance that you will die within 1-3 seconds. It is also very difficult to find servers nowadays for obvious reasons, and it is a hassle to actually get to the servers, as quakeworld is not functional in the vanilla steam version.
compared to other games/quakes:
-I would say that Quake is equally as good if not better than Doom/Doom 2, as the full 3D environment allows for a greater depth to the shooting experience, although the decrease of size of the levels and the reduced enemy counts does make for a slightly slower experience
-Quake 1 is vastly superior to Quake 2 in terms of the visual design and layout. It has much more variety in terms of the visuals and the horror atmosphere is more memorable than Quake 2's repeated sci-fi environments. I feel that the dynamic between the different weapons is better because of the faster switching time, and the reduced ammo count requires you to be more thoughtful in your choices. However, I have not finished Quake 2 so I cannot really compare them accurately. And don't think that Quake 2 isn't also a very good game, because it is.
-Quake 3 is multiplayer only, so you can't really compare the singleplayer aspect of Quake 1 to Quake 3, but the multiplayer in Quake 3 is just simply vastly superior because the weapons are actually balanced, and it is just overall a more refined experience.
-I would say that overall of the first 3 quakes Quake 1 has the best singleplayer and Quake 3 has the best multiplayer, with Quake 2 sitting in the middle, although it is still a very good game and you should play it as well.
other stuff

-As others have stated, the steam version does not come with music, but you can very easily download it from the internet and load it from quakespasm
-if you want to play multiplayer, you should get nQuake

It is basically Quake 3 but with better graphics as well as the addition of Champions, different character classes that change the health, armor, and speed values of the player and add a special abilities such as teleportation or invisibility that changes the dynamic between players. I have not played it but it is generally considered to be very good, although there are some network issues at the moment, and if you want to play quake multiplayer today I would say check it out.

After 20 years, Quake is still a blast to play. Most of my playtime has been via the QuakeSpasm and DarkPlaces source ports,  so my Steam stats hardly reflect my experience with Quake.
PROS:
+ Fast and very fluid action.
+ Incredible level design that has aged like a fine wine.
+ Creepy Lovecraftian aesthetic and atmosphere.
+ Killer NIN contributed soundtrack.*
+ Among the very best single player experiences in gaming, ever.
+ Online multiplayer is STILL supported over twenty years later thanks to fan run servers.
+ Very LOW hardware requirements: netbooks, cloudbooks, streambooks...runs on anything.
+ Linux and Mac compatiblity via source ports like QuakeSpasm and DarkPlaces.*
+ A steal at only $5.
CONS:
- Steam (includes GLQuake) version lacks the versatility of popular source ports.
- Steam version has no Mac or Linux support.
- Steam version has no 'toggle' option for mouse look.
*Soundtrack can be ripped from the old CD ROM version and copied to id1/music, but must be renumbered to begin with track02.
*Simply copy the files from the id1 folder in Quake to the id1 folder in QuakeSpasm or DarkPlaces. Same with hipnotic (Scourge of Armagon) and rogue (Dissolution of Eternity).

Quake improved on every aspect on ID's previous title Doom. It introduced a generation of gamers to fully 3D environments, balanced and fair monstrousities, a great selection of memorable weapons, and dark lovecraftian atmosphere.
Quake has a unique asthetic that is missing from modern games. The feeling of dread and evil that is unlike the colorful demons of Doom or Painkiller. It feels fresh in 2017.
The gameplay is polished. The arsenal of weapons is polished. For example the super nailgun is great for Shamblers. The super shotty is great for going 1v1 with Fiends. The best weapons are the granade and rocket launchers though. Enemies stagger when hit hard enough. Something that some games just fogot about entirely. A reaction to being shot.
There is no hand holding, but the game is not hard. I've finished it on Hard difficulty and could probably go back and play though on Nightmare.
The only issue is its presentation on Steam. It is missing the iconic Nine Inch Nails soundtrack and you may have trouble playing the game on modern systems. The steam version could use some love.
Lets hope that this classic gets a remake like Doom did.

Immortal Planet is a top down dark souls like game. You walk around killing enemies to gain xp that you use at your rest location. When you rest, you can level up stats and change equipment; enemies will respawn as well. Combat is a bit slow and sluggish, but it feels rewarding once you get the basics down. Spells and weapons have a fun variety to them to help break things up. However, this is a soulslike so you have to enjoy the slow grind that is this kind of game.

Great combat and gameplay, without any of the overwhelming min max crap and abundantly useless items you encounter in other RPGs and games similar to Dark Souls.
For people who don't have time to waste on frills, this game is a perfect 3-8 hour playthrough on normal. Every enemy is someone to learn from. Strategies for dealing with enemies are naturally formed as they obey the same rules and use largely the same moves the player does.
Nightmare mode tests the skills you learned on normal, and gives the player additional lore that those engrossed in the story and setting will appreciate (the story is ignorable, but for those who enjoy it, the good ending is discoverable with sufficient gumption).
You can build physical and/or magic damage characters. For players who are less mechanically skilled, grinding up a build that can stomp the hardest of bosses will only take a few hours - but defeating the final boss with zero upgrades is a plausible, albiet difficult task.
All in all, the gameplay is compact and concise - the experience does not require tens or hundreds of hours to fully appreciate, which is a positive for players like me. The combat system manages to maintain simplicity throughout the game while simultaneously leaving multiple styles of combat open for the player - players can tackle a majority of the enemies through any mix of dodging, blocking, and dash stunning (bosses may require more than one, naturally). Magic damage can be used to supplement physical combat, or downright replace it with sufficient levels (no mechanical skill necessary to beat any boss and enemy if you just nuke it to death).
To those who find frustration or boredom out of a need to build up their character, this is likely your own fault. Beating the game in a timely manner does not require mechanical skill - the least mechanically inclined players can beat it in less than 10 hours by being careful with spending their experience at safe intervals - the only thing this game punishes is recklessness and thoughtless actions. If physical combat is too difficult, magic can make the game a breeze by removing much (but not all) of the need to read and anticipate your enemies actions.
tl;dr: get gud, or nut up - this game is fun.

Lords of Xulima is an old-school isometric party-based RPG with turn-based party combat in the classic RPG style. You control a party of six looking to end a war on your homeland and end up getting caught up in a war between gods in far off lands.
While Lords of Xulima is a good game, it's not necessarily a great game. The combat system is a nice and fresh take on a 25+ year old system. The world is large and well detailed. The game definitely doesn't hold your hand, requiring some decent wandering to figure out sometimes where to go next. (hint: make use of the in-game world maps, shows you at  a high level where a lot of things are). The exploration and plant mechanics are interesting and there's a lot to discover about the world.
Unfortunately, the story isn't particularly interesting. While the ending is good, the lead up is really just a series of "defeat X bosses. Ok, you did that, now defeat their Y bosses. Ok, you did that. Now defeat their Z bosses". With only one set character and 5 generated/built characters, only your one main character speaks to NPCs or has any personality. There's a ton of artificial gating in the world to keep you out of areas you shouldn't be yet. You sometimes don't realize that a path that was gated is now open because you progressed in the story.
Thankfully, the game does have a good amount of fast travel between most regions having a gate you can warp around to and each town having "hearthstone"-like crystals to allow you to quickly return to the town.
Look to spend about 40 hours on a playthrough. A lot of that will be grinding levels. The levels come somewhat quickly, but progression in the game is slow. The story is linear, though there are side-quests you can do in pretty much any order. The replay value is very low, except to try on harder difficulties. I recommend the "Old-School Veteran" mode. It was a decent challenge, particularly at the beginning.
6/10. I'm glad I played through it, but it's not a game I'll remember much of a year from now.

I liked the game.  It was well-done in that old-school Phantasie style I grew up enjoying on my Amiga.  But for the curious, I'll go over a few specifics which I think will provide for a better understanding of the game.
Storyline -- Well thought-out and engaging enough to keep me attentive.   It wasn't enough to pull me in and make me feel like I had a personal stake in the outcome -- but I didn't feel utterly detached from the tale either.
Game-play -- You can tell the game has been play-tested.  I got the impression that tweaks had occurred throughout the game in specific instances where you could sense something was approaching mind-numbingly repetitive or flatly unreasonable.
Money -- One of the major flaws in almost every rpg game is that at some point, money becomes completely irrelevant.  This wasn't the case here.  Again, I could tell the programmers intentionally designed it to always be important.   Some of tweaks were insightful (like buying skill points), while others were hamfisted (2600 gold for 6 days of food?!?)
Quests -- Most of them were pretty easy, but enjoyable.  There was one MAJOR exception.  The Hall of Heroes Quest was a complete and utter waste of time and resources.  When I finally completed it, I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  I didn't feel an ounce of accomplishment -- only a strong disbelief that anyone thought that pile of stink would improve the game.  It irritated me enough that almost stopped playing the game entirely.  Yes, I went from "Can't wait to play every night" to "I'm OK if I stop playing this game for a long time."  As you can tell, I'm still irritated about and I completed the game at this point.  To anyone who buys this game, don't bother trying to figure it out for yourself -- there's nothing clever or original about it.  It's just an unfortunate blemish.
Leveling -- The skill system was pretty straight-forward.  Perhaps it's in the documentation, but I rather wish I knew what skills I could've learned at later levels -- it certainly would've caused me to spend my points differently early on.  Which brings us to ...
Exploration -- Look, you're going to die.  A lot.  Save after every single battle.  I come from a school of thought where I tend to view this approach as cheating -- but honestly, it's not in this case.  If you wander into an area that you shouldn't be in, you'll die.  If you happen to meet a tough wandering monster, you'll die.  If you're in battle and you get an unfortunate roll, you'll die.  Exploration is basically a Lemming Mine Detector method.  You go there, die, and then you pick a different direction to go when you re-load it.  It's pretty much the only way you learn where not to go.   I've never been sure if this type of programming is intentional or not, but there you have it.
Leveling -- At the lower levels, you'll die.  A lot.  <see exploration>.  It's a common problem you see with rpg games -- you just don't have any strategic options at lower levels.  You walk into battle, attack in the only way you can, and hope the rolls go your way.   Becaue if they don't, you'll die in 1 or 2 hits.  Tough stuff, really.  At the higher levels, you have quite a bit more leeway when it comes to strategy and recovering from bad rolls.  Someone, some day will figure out a way to address this issue.
Favorite part of the game:  Probably the Herb gathering.  I'd walk into a meadow without any monsters and get excited.  That's pretty cool.
Least favorite part of the game:  Hall of Heroes Quest.  Whoever designed it should be shamed.  So much shame ...

Small review just to highlight some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t in this game.
Whenever the game shows a percentage for you, like 60-70% chance to hit, don't trust it. It probably means 40-50%. Every action has a critical failure chance (like 10%) where you hurt yourself and the rest of the time you're going to miss for whatever reasons.
So you think 70-80% is pretty good? Think again it means you'll either miss or hurt yourself half of the time. And you'll roll low on damage the other time.
And no, this is not "normal" or "typical for a RPG" or "oldschool". I have played plenty of RPGs before, Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Wasteland 2, Fallout series ... I know what 60-70% chance to hit is like. And this game's RNG is clearly not accurate. I can just spin up the game any time and get my parties to miss 3-6 times in a row despite the odds should be in my favor (and there are no character with "wounded" status either, in case anyone is wondering).
Expect your entire party to go on miss streaks at least one round every single fight. Yeah and that's really the entire game's difficulty - suddenly everyone goes on a missing streak, casters fizzle their spells and then you die.
If you still think that's fun or acceptable, go read other reviews, they'll do this game more justice.

It's a leveling playing field.
The reason I like RPGs over all other gaming genre's is the sense of character progression as you get further and further into the game. When this type of game is properly done,  you start of so wimpy, itty bitty little cave rats can take you down but by games end you should have a character stong enough to take down the game's god. Lords of Xulima understands this concept and gives you plenty of options to level up your character.
You can level up,  of course with the normal way by accumulating points from winning battle.
You can level up stats by solving the games dozens of quests
You can level up stats by gathering  and using herbs
You can level up stats by drinking from wells
You can level up stats by drinking from fountains
You can level up stats by items left over from your victims battle drops
You can level up stats by praying at statues (one way permanent and one way temporary)
You can level up stats by solving puzzles.
Some of the leveling up of stats is automatic, and some you get to pick. And there is so much to level up. You can level up stats, attributes, mind, body, prayers, spells, songs (yes the Bard characater is the most fully realized yet), weapons, armor, attacks, thieveries,  field knowledge etc. I would quess there are probably over a hundred things that can be leveled up. However some charaacters (spell casters) have more then others (soldiers).
Gameplay wise, its your old school turn based combat and it is well done. But that may be the one qualm I have with this game. There is a lot of combat and by late mid game it becomes tiresome. By the last quarter of the game the high stat/hit point monsters are taking a long time to take out. And while the game has a great story and great lore, it does tend to get lost with the continious battling. And speaking of story I was able to tell the story ending early on in this game but the story rail did not allow me to change my destiny.
Still, I had a lot of fun with this game. I loved the color palate. It was bright and fanciful like a Might and Magic or early NES game. And the music is spectacular. The composer, Nicholar De Ferrar, is on the same level as Soule (Skyrim) and Rosenkranz (Gothic). And with some limited voice over work, that was also of superiour quality, the music had to carry you over and it delivered. Qualms aside the game deserves an A rating.

So I am going to both be very critical of this game and Paradox in general, and praise it and the studio.
First the required pros/cons:
Pros:
* depth of Tech and Equipment trees
* overall design for units and the experience setup for upgrading
* mostly well scripted events
* overall art for a Strategy game and Music
+ This is the first game I have played in a LONG time that I don't need to either turn off the music
or add to the music list.  I find the music to be replayable
* I happen to like the map for the most part and how you can use it for a battle plan flow
* Navy seems to be a bit more useful than in past Paradox HOI titles
* Air Warfare is much more involved than before tho it now requires a bit too much micromanaging
+ This might be fixable with a few more tweaks from both Paradox and Modders
* Highly moddable (which is its saving grace, more on this in the Cons portion)
* First time in memory that an HOI title is stable to play from first sale date.
* MASSIVE choices in which nations to play and how to play them
* multiplayer, both that it is there, and that it is actually stable.
ESSENTIALLY everything not related to the AI is either A+ or at the very least a solid B in design, at
least in what is exposed to the player.
CONS:
*
oh did I mention the AI?
* There are still some bugs, which causes some really funky things to happen
+ the need to actually save and restart the game periodically (full restart, not just reload save)
+  This is actually a hidden plus since it forces me to leave the game and come up for air periodically.
My recommendation is save around every 6 months and restart game.
* Some micromanaging that I think is a bit too much, there should at least be an easy way to let
some of this be done by the computer.
* AI.
* oh and the AI.  arghhhh
Which brings me to the last CON:
* The need to use a mod to fix the broken AI!!!  there are a couple of good AI mods out there.
+ try out "Expert AI" and see how it works for you. but there are others, it is just the one I prefer.
I will also like to comment on something, while the game does get a little laggy midway through, I find that on my laptop (laptop!!!! with i5 6th gen, 2.4 ghz turbo, 8 gb's of RAM, and a 940m) I can run the game without any real between day slowdown (at the begging it is almost not noticeable, mid-game and late game, it is barely half a second between days and maybe one second for the autosaves).
Also with the mod AI, the game actually plays with some intelligence.  Tho I still find that Germany dies early on most games if I am playing the USA or any other late war entrance nation.  Tho if I play switzerland....
Then germany does a near historical seesaw with Russia...  Not sure what diplomatic options I am doing with the USA that changes the game enough to do these changes but, I am happy that there are differences between each game I play.
ARGH.  forgot this....
Paradox has gotten into a bad habit of releasing games with terrible AI.
While in general they have mostly fixed the AI in other of their games, in HOI4, it was the modders that made the "fixes".   Overall I am happy with HOI4, unlike HOI3.  Now that I finally started to play with an AI mod, I can feel like it is a sane game.  Before you could have 200 to 300 GERMAN Div's dying of thirst in the saharan desert while the russian front had maybe 30 div's facing the russian 500 divisions.  AND then the AI would declare war on the USA... and sweden and... brazil and... basically it probably thought that since it was about to get steamrolled by the USSR, then it should at least let the rest of the world get a piece of the german stomping action.
the current AI mods, all seem to address the worst of these issues, but they shouldn't have had to do so.  Also this is a scripted AI, which considering that only recently have we learned to do good quality deep learning AI, isn't in anyway surprising, but you would think they would have realized how broken the scripts were before selling it as full price, basically the AI felt like it was in Alpha, not even Beta stage.  Paradox products shouldn't have to depend on a highly motivated mod community to fix its major transgressions.  Modders should be concentrating on flavor and other alternative histories or stories for the game.  Because of the state of the vanilla AI, the mods that would use the mod AI's have to take into consideration not just paradox but also the specifics of the AI mod.  it is insane.
I HOPE that given the way the game was designed, that an actual real soft AI can be designed for the game and INCORPORATED into the vanilla game.  Then the modders can do specific scripts for changing the flavor of the game.  In many ways I still prefer the old "Darkest Hour" game based on the HOI2 vanilla game.  But this is also a case of modders doing the work that Paradox should have done.  The fact that a game now nearly 13 yrs old, can still feel at par or better in some instances to this new game, is why I am upset with Paradox.  Admittedly  "Darkest Hour" was a redone version released in 2011, of HOI2.  BUT that in itself should say a lot about the need to not only provide the right table top feel mixed with computer graphics of a strategy game, it should also include a solid (even if not brilliant) AI from the get go!
Anyway, those are my two cents.  or 22 cents as the case maybe.  )))
