I absolutely loved the hell out of To The Moon, so I was very much looking forward to this game, expecting I might get an experience of similar quality, but A Bird Story is... odd.
I can't give this game a definite thumbs up or thumbs down but am giving it a thumbs down mostly because steam forces you to pick one, but also it was just not personally to my taste, but that doesn't mean I would say it's BAD exactly.
The positive that it has going for it is that Kan Gao is still an incredible director when it comes to getting complexity out of simple 2D pixel characters. My favorite example from A Bird Story are the two silent interactions between the protagonist and the stranger on the elevator. It's such a small subtle thing, but little things like that give a game world huge character. Very few other games writers/directors have such great writer's perception to be able think of and effectively portray those types of subtle little human moments, but Kan Gao is an excellent director in that regard.
At the same time, though, I was also disappointed. While To The Moon was an extremely complex story with many characters, layers, and themes, A Bird Story is so simple it feels dull. To The Moon also had a certain degree of gameplay, what with hunting for memory links, solving puzzles, exploration, and some occasional mini-games. But sadly, in A Bird Story, it's pretty much just like watching a 2 hour cutscene where sometimes you press ENTER or hold down an arrow key for the movie to continue. (On more than one occasion, you can literally hold down any of the four arrow keys, and the protagonist just walks in any direction he wants. It literally doesn't matter where you want to go. It's just a movie that plays.)
The almost completely absent interactivity/gameplay might have been fine if the story was complex and compelling enough to keep you wanting to know more. To The Moon excelled at this by making you hungry for more information about Johnny and his life, what the rabbits meant, what the hackey sack meant, who Anya is, what the significance of the moon is, etc etc etc. There are so many mysteries, curiosities, and unresolved threads that you just have to keep going. But in A Bird Story you kind of know exactly what is going to happen, and it doesn't really defy your expectations or surprise you at all.
So my verdict is that A Bird Story is like watching a film that is the product of a pedestrian writer but an incredible director. It's hard to completely like it or dislike it.
To The Moon is as emotional and wonderful and beautiful as Eternal Sunshine of The Spotless Mind or Annabel Lee.
The writing in A Bird Story is unfortunately about as complex and interesting as its title. Still great direction, though.
TLDR: Do not expect to get To The Moon out of this, but you might still enjoy it depending on whatever idiosyncratic tastes you might have.

A strange take on XCom that I can't decide whether to regard as canon or not...
Realtime squad based tactical combat is not my bag, I'll admit, so this game was a bit painful for me. I really only got it because I love the X-Com series. And that's the only thing that kept me going.
It's pretty much X-com in the cold war era. Cobbled together technologies mixed with traditional weaponry (and no combat armor???) make a story that seems like it's a giant under reaction to an alien invasion while at the same time being weirdly preprepared for it all.
The enemies will seem partially familiar to X-Com Enemy Unknown players, but the story won't really make sense. The technologies seem very different than Enemy Unknown and the style of warfare entirely alien to that storyline.
Since it's the game franchise that sucked me in, it was only curiosity that kept me going.
A weak story that doesn't seem canon and clunky combat put this on my not recommended list.

It has its momements, but there aren't enough of them to justify $10. Some of the main endings are funny, but you have to trudge through the same year 7 times to see them all, with *many* events repeating each time and a skip function that doesn't stop for unread text. They take 15-30 minutes each depending on your use of said skip button, and several are obnoxiously set up so that you have to go back and do everything again (but only veeeery slightly differently) in order to get a second version of the ending that's exactly the same except that it cuts to the credits earlier.
And doing that is actually necessary to see everything - the final ending doesn't unlock until you've seen the other 13. That ending has the most to offer in terms of storytelling, but it drags on for far, far, longer than it ever needed to because of an obsession with repeatedly retelling the same events from perspectives that are minimally different. I started out thinking it was the highlight of the game and really should've been there from the start, but by the end I was just mashing space to make it end. There weren't any repurcussions to that approach, because this part of the game is also completely impossible to lose and provides zero choices with any impact over the course of two hours. That branch desperately needed an editor, and not just because of length - there's one part that has a sentence so badly mistranslated that it's completely meaningless.
I really wish I could recommend this - I normally love dumb things that wear their stupidity as a badge of honor - but HB ruins itself by simultaneously being too short to feel meaningful and too long for the joke to stay funny. On sale, it's probably worthwhile to see an ending or two, (again, a few of the main ones are legitimately funny) but there's just not enough here for $10. It isn't bad, but I was much more entertained by reading about the original version years ago than I was actually playing the remake. Oh well.

Hatoful -
- is a word pun between the Japanese word
- which means either dove, or pigeon - and the English adjectives of either
or
. On these terms, the title of the game is self-explanatory.
is a humorous otome/visual novel in which you get to date birds. Aside the humorous, or even strikingly unconventional nature of the game, this joke veils a deeper truth.
The story is set in the fictional future of 2188. A century ago starting with rock pigeons, birds all over the world started to take the next step in evolution and challenged the omnipotence of mankind. After a long period of conflict and even open war, the mankind survived only as a minority. Now, the majority of the world's conscient population consists of birds. In this particular dystopia, we take the role of the only human student invited to attend St. Pigeonation, the most prestigious high school for birds of the world.
At first, the display of the story keeps us oblivious to the grim face of our setting. Nothing indicates that
would be more than an unimaginably crazy joke. We keep playing the game in this meaningless context, as a silly joke, flirting with different kinds of birds and all. We laugh our hearts out for the absurdity of given situations, the reactions and portrayals of characters, and logical flaws of the setting are unbearably funny. It is like watching one of the most absurd anime series, like ever!
But as the stories progress, and we accomplish different kinds of romances, we learn a bit more about different characters each time. As we play, they become more than silly depictions of birds. We learn their stories, their backgrounds, their aspirations and their wounds... just like real people. I tell you, the narrative of this game, and the narrative's ability to conceal the most shocking fictional events in silly jokes are totally scary. As we play, bits and pieces roll up to their proper places to paint an incredibly political and ethical discussion with suspense and immense tragedy!
Gameplay wise, nothing is extraordinary. There are some pretty background pictures, and an incredible amount of bird photos flying around. Each character has their own separate background music. You start reading, and make some dialogue or event choices now and then. Finally, it wraps up to become a romance path for a bird of your choice. When you complete all endings, and start a new game; you face with the question whether you'd like to keep a long forgotten promise. If you say yes, things take an incredible turn, to reveal all past mysteries. Annoying or peculiar occurrences that you've been witnessing in your prior games now form a painful meaning. This final storyline reveals a darker side to our fictional setting, and brings question to concepts such as war, peace, misinformation, discrimination, racial and ethnic differences, and even biological war! Now, that was certainly unexpected, wasn't it?
starts as an absurd joke for you to kill some meaningless time, yet if you bear with its lame display and take a moment to look deeper, it rewards you with a most thrilling and disturbingly realistic story. Take your time, get bored by the joke. You'll end up picking a glass of water to wash the bitter feeling in your throat towards the end.

Really good level design. Many rooms end up having paths that wrap back around towards this game's equivilent of bonfires from Dark Souls. Enemies are pretty varied, but have simple movesets. Combat is pretty basic, but using your weapon's range and magic spells in tandem is necessary.
The mechanic where you can see your enemies stamina is honestly of little consequence. Many of the tougher enemies tend to have very high stamina regeneration, so you can't take advantage of their fatigue.
My only gripe is about the gameplay. In order to stun an enemy, you must perform a dash into them when their stamina is 1/4 full. When this occurs, they're stunned for a good while and can usually be killed. However, if you dash into them while their stamina is greater than 1/4, YOU will be stunned and probably die. This is a fine mechanic IMO, but many times I've dashed into an enemy while meaning to roll to their side, got stunned, and died.
All in all, this game is totally worth 15 dollars. Very challenging. Very creative. Kind of like HyperLight Drifter and Dark Souls had a baby.

To start with the positives the aesthetic and lore are all really interesting and unique. It reminds me of hyper light drifter and the way that much better game (in the mechanical sense) presented itself. The level design itself is also really good and has taken the right ideas from the likes of Dark Souls.
However it seems along with a lot of other games attempting to be soulsborne-like (what a mouthful) have all left me with mixed feelings only one I really liked with no reservations was hyper light drifter and that game was not trying its hardest to be JUST like dark souls in every way and had its own ideas for once. Many fail to understand the reason why FromSofts games are so good.
One of my first issues is just that, the game doesnt feel very unique. It borrows a lot of systems from dark souls and I cant personally place anything really new or diffirent. Not every game has to innovate but it would be nice to have a bit of variation here and there.
Secondly everything about it feels really sluggish. From the movement to the combat. Even more so than games within this new genre. This coupled with the janky "dash" ability. Sometimes you will plumit to your death when you SHOULD of made the jump. It should be also noted that often times attacks that shouldnt of hit you will because of the bad hit detection. Immortal Planet is a new isometric action RPG from indie developers, teedoubleuGAMES.
In Immortal Planet you take the role of the last immortal to wake from your timeless slumber. Before you, the other immortals have woken and become degraded somehow, fulfilling their roles in a corrupted manner. You must venture through the strange, platform-like levels that make up the world in order to discover what has happened.
When you wake you have no memory of your past. As you encounter other immortals -- all of them hostile -- you begin to piece together the planet's history and the role that each of the immortals plays in it. As you do so, you become more powerful and able to overcome the mindless automata that the immortals around you have become.
Immortal Planet's graphics have clean lines and a sort-of dark cartoonish feel to them. Textures and colours are mostly very simple and plain, but the overall effect is quite striking at times. The game is played from a fixed isometric view and though you can move freely about in any direction, characters only face in one the four basic directions.
Animations look reasonably fluid, though restricted to the four facings, and are mostly very slow. Weapon effects, dust from footfalls, and various other little touches bring a bit more life to the otherwise fairly sterile environment.
Levels are sparsely decorated, but interesting, with individual areas mostly made up of a small number of interconnected rooms and having certain themes to them. After you've seen each area a handful of times, though, they start to seem a bit bland and repetitive. After you've seen some areas 20 or more times, you might be wishing for a bit more variation.
Graphics options are limited to vsync and full-screen / windowed mode selection. I haven't experienced any graphical slowdown, but the game does play very slowly regardless.
Music is excellent. The title theme reminds me of Excalibur, with a low, rumbling bass and powerful, orchestral melody. In-game music is sparse and quiet -- like the levels themselves -- and elicits a feeling of loneliness and dilapidation, which matches the setting to a tee. Boss battle music is louder and more frantic, again suiting the action very well.
Sound effects fulfil their role respectably. Sword swipes, blocks, and various other effects are well normalised and appropriate, and footsteps are nice and quiet, but loud enough to be heard. Some sort of reaction from the various immortals, including the player character, when they're getting hacked to pieces would have been a nice addition.
There are no voices.
While Immortal Planet's story sounds grand, the basic gameplay has been seen before in other "souls-like" games. To mix it up a bit, Immortal Planet does it all from an isometric action RPG perspective, which is reasonably well done, and adds some frustrating platforming elements, which are definitely not. Like the original Dark Souls PC release, keyboard controls are pretty terrible, too, but the developers admit this at the beginning: "this game should be played with a controller." Listen to them!
The game begins with you choosing a weapon and a relic, from a choice of three each. These are quite different and each has a different play style to gain the most benefit from it, but beyond these selections, there is no character customisation at all.
You then spawn into a starting area that's relatively easy and provides you with a basic movement and action tutorial through in-game signs that pop up. It's quite well done and gives you just enough information to get started. The controls are basic: one button each for attack, block, dash/dodge, and interact, and four buttons for your inventory items. You can hold the attack button to 'awaken' your weapon, but other than some rather abstract in-game text in the inventory and compendium (available from the start button menu), the game effects of this are unexplained.
Each enemy you encounter will attack you when they see you, with various patterns available to them. Combat is all about learning the patterns and responding with your own patterns. See that guy? Swing three times, then dodge backwards, move out of the way of his ranged attack, walk around his grenade, then swing three times, dodge backwards, ... . If you don't know the patterns, you'll get hit. Get hit enough and you die, respawning back at your cryopod. Bosses only differ in that they have four health levels, with each level increasing the available patterns. They also do a lot of damage and take a lot to kill.
When you defeat an enemy you gain experiences, which you can spend to level up your five basic attributes: Strength, Agility, Endurance, Willpower, and Intelligence. These affect secondary attributes such as health, number of uses of items, and damage. Each time you level up an attribute, the cost for your next level up increases, reducing the effectiveness of grinding the same enemies. If you die while in possession of experiences, they will be dropped. If you manage to return to your place of death before dying again you can collect these experiences in full, as well as heal yourself. Whenever you return to your cryopod you are also fully healed, but all of the level's enemies respawn. This does not reset switches or other level state.
After some time you'll find a sort of shop where you can spend experiences on other items, too, and you'll occasionally pick up some different items and abilities. But this is not a loot-based game, so don't expect rogue-like loot drops. The game is rather small in size, with its longevity produced through repetition, grinding out enemies and areas until you're powerful enough to proceed.
There are a few niggling issues, but overall the game is quite stable. So far I've seen some rather glaring grammatical errors, though most of the text is surprisingly good, and I found that F12 doesn't work for taking in-game screenshots using Steam. The only definite bug I've encountered so far is related to achievements, which seem to only drop some of the time; you should expect to have to play through multiple times to unlock them all.
More important are some questionable design decisions. Instant death from dodging off a ledge is a big one, which makes combat in tight spaces very frustrating, and the platforming elements downright annoying. The combat is very heavily stamina based, but enemies don't seem to suffer quite the same effects as you do. The difficulty curve is quite strange, too: more like a seismograph readout than a curve.
Pros:
+ Interesting setting
+ Eerie music
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Instant death makes platforming elements not fun
- No character customisation
- Limited character progression
- Combat gets boring quickly
- Relatively short: longevity through repetition

I'm a friend of one of the writers for the game, so I got to play during beta as well as getting my copy for free. I also played the game for about six hours before I got an official steam key, so my displayed hours aren't accurate. It took me about eight hours to finish the game.
The game in general I found to be enjoyable, the main thing I found laudable was its actual build diversity and giving you reasons to try different things and play through the game multiple times. The Shieldaxe is garbage but the Spearsword and Assaultblade are very cool to toy around with and all of the starting gifts basically change how you play the game. The weapons themselves also don't have stats, meaning each weapon is viable and the only determining factor is how you want to play the game (plus the rate at which you unlock new weapons.) There are also a lot of consumables and spells you can use which change things up significantly, and they can synergize with your build instead of just being emergency exits. There are also a few builds which are actually kinda overpowered when you figure out what to do with them, but that's kinda the fun of having a varied build system like this.
That said, there were a lot of problems with the game, and thankfully the devs did fix some of them. The main one they have yet to fix however is that some bosses just aren't enjoyable to fight. There are two bosses in particular that are frustrating, both because of their ability to knock you off a ledge for an OHKO. One is more manageable than the other, and there are valid strategies there, but most of my boss deaths were due to falling. The other bosses were very enjoyable and creative, and in a broad sense I think this game has good bosses. Some might just feel cheap and unfair until you figure out how to stunlock bosses.
On the whole I'd understand if you'd feel cautious about paying $15 for this game, and the main campaign was a little short, but it has an interesting New Game Plus and if you play the game more than once you'll definitely get value for your purchase.

This is purely a hidden object game, similar to something like "Where's Waldo?" except that finding some of the people/objects involves multiple actions on your part before they become visible.
To be honest, I was a little disappointed with this game, at first. The Forest levels weren't my favorite. However, I really got into the swing of things as the searchable areas increased in size and complexity. The Factory levels were downright devious, in some cases requiring your to figure out what various buttons and levers did in order to activate things in the correct order to reveal the object or person you needed to find. I tried to avoid looking at walkthroughs (and felt super proud of myself for getting through the City levels without once looking up solutions), but the second-to-last Factory level had four items that defeated me. I could have sworn I'd gone over the entire picture inch by inch, pressing everything, but I somehow still managed to miss stuff.
The game doesn't really have anything that could be called a story, but if you pay close attention you'll notice that various people and items from previous levels appear in later levels. In one level, you have to find the kayaker who just got back from a long trip. In an earlier level, I noticed that there was a car with a kayak on it - probably the kayaker heading home. Then there are the monkeys. At least one shows up on most (all?) levels. I also spotted people in one level with party balloons, who were probably the same people attending the birthday party in a later level.
I got this slightly on sale and, in the end, was happy with my purchase. It was challenging and enjoyable.
Pros:
+ Has a good difficulty range. It's not necessary to find all the people/objects in order to unlock the next level, and finding just enough of the items on your list to do that isn't too hard. The game becomes fiendishly difficult if you want to complete the entire level.
+ Each person/object you have to find comes with a little description that gives you a clue as to where you might find them.
+ It's fun to click on things just to see what they'll do.
Cons:
- A little hard on the eyes if you play too long. There are three display settings: black lines on a white background, white lines on a black background, and sepia background. Those might help some folks, but I generally stuck with black lines on a white background. One thing that took me an embarrassingly long time to figure out was that I could zoom in using my mouse wheel. That helped tremendously on the larger levels.
- Some of the "hidden folks" you have to look for look an awful lot like a dozen other folks on the screen (*ahem* Shopper Walid). Their clues won't always help you narrow your search down much. Be prepared to do some slow, careful, and possibly frustrating hunting if you plan on finding everything on the list for each level.
- The graphics were a little messed up in one of the City levels. Some of the people were only partially visible. This didn't inferfere with finding any of the people and objects on the list, though.

If you enjoyed searching for Waldo, you're going to enjoy this game. However, there is no easily identifiable character like Waldo; instead, each area has a list of people or things to find.  At first some are daunting, both due to the size of the areas and due to the size of the items (golf ball, for example).  However, each item to find comes with a clue and the clue points to a bigger thing to search for.  For example, one item to find is a mushroom and the clue is that a pig is about to sniff it out.  So instead of looking for a little mushroom, you can look for a much bigger hog.  In fact, I was never stuck on an area due to the smallest items, and the couple times I did get stuck a little, I just wasn't seeing what was right in front of me.  In fact, in addition to the verbal clues, there are auditory clues.  I didn't discover this until the last few areas when I heard someone crying out in distress and looked for the source of the sound, but it's a nice feature.
There are two really unique aspects to the game that add oodles of charm.  First, the game sounds are all done with the human mouth.  Some are definitely more effective than others.  I think the birds flying away sound is pretty weak, but I'll never get tired of the alligators or vultures or garage doors.  That's the second unique aspect - you can manipulate the environment and, in fact, you need to in order to find things.  For example, opening doors or flipping switches or moving clouds out of the way or cutting bushes. It's so much fun!
Each area feels unique even when it has the same unifying theme - like the factory.  There is a nice variety - some areas are small, some are huge, some are puzzles.  My personal favorite is the desert, because this game also has a great sense of humor.  For example, in the city there is a boss lady at the top of a skyscraper surrounded by bags with dollar signs on them. That made me laugh. I thought the factory was going to be boring, but it wasn't at all.  Best of all, once you complete the game, you get a message that the devs are going to continue to add more areas.  They added the factory areas about 4 months after they released the game.   I'm definitely looking forward to more.
I have only two little criticisms.  Not everything you can click on makes a unique sound.  Lots of things do, but I'd love it if EVERYTHING did.  Secondly, at one point you're supposed to look for a sunbathing turtle that only vaguely resembles a turtle.  Small price to pay, in my opinion, for the quirky hand drawn art style, and that's the only instance I came across.
As for replay value, you can reset your progress.  You also don't have to find everything in an area before being able to move on - just a certain number.  However, it is like Waldo in the sense that once you know where something is, you know where it is.  But so much time and care was put into making each area a cohesive whole with objects to find spread throughout in a way that encourages the player to scan and enjoy the entire area, that I wouldn't trade that for any sort of randomization. Even if you only play through this game once, I think it's well worth the full price.  Personally, I love it so much, I'm sure I'll be back and I will instabuy anything else put out by this dev.  With so many slapped-together-to-make-a-quick-buck games on Steam, I definitely appreciate ones like this that are full of detail and heart.  I find myself smiling about parts of the game much later - like the ghost mail or those silly monkeys.  That's a rare find.
UPDATE - As promised, devs just added new snow areas.  Thank you!

Even though this isn't really review material, here are a few key things I have learned after just a short time playing. This may give you an idea of the design of the game.
1. EXPLORE! Early exploration is key, and can land you some early resources.
2. Always leave enough space between buildings so your soldiers can get through. Otherwise they take the long way which can lose a match or send them through a horde of infected.
3. Leave enough room around your main housing area to build a bank and a market, as both give great bonuses to houses.
4. When an attack comes, you can mass almost everything in that direction. Your other walls will usually survive with just one or two soldiers guarding them.
5. Executors are good for medium sized waves, but just don't kill fast enough to handle the large hordes (unless you have more than one).

A Bird Story is a sweet little game or rather story for that matter. If you
like a small emotional story, than you can definitely pick this game up, if
you're looking for a small interactive game (or any form of game for that
matter) than this is not for you.
Everyone considering buying this game be warned that this is more like a story
than a game, because the interaction possibilities are very limited for that
matter, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. Unfortunately the interactions
provided were simply so linear (you could not do any other thing except that
single interaction at a given time) that they seemed more forced than anything.
The story itself was actually extremely cliché, but it was executed perfectly
and did not leave any questions open.
The level design is the best thing about this game. It's not that the level
design was something special or breath taking but how well it was designed to
reflect the boys everyday life, especially the tunnel vision. Going from home
to school and going home back again, after some time you don't even completely
realize how you got to your destination.
The soundtrack also fitted perfectly into the game, not much to add there.
What I found to be extremely annoying though are those long pauses, moments
where your screen goes blank and stays that way for a moment. If it would have
happened once for every chapter it would have been ok, but there were moments
where it happened quite often in series which was simply put quite irritating.
All in all, I enjoyed this short little story and can recommend A Bird Story if
you're aware of its shortcomings and what this game is not.

After I bought this game a few days ago and just played it all the way through, I can say that this game is fantastic.
Being able to choose different paths to achieve goals is an excellent mechanic, and affects your mission score in the end.
Dishonored can suit many playstyles, whether you want to sneak around and get to the goal without being detected, or want to shoot everybody in a room guns blazing. You can do either, and you can get to the end without any troubles whatever your playstyle. The game doesn't punish you for being Rambo.
The atmosphere is quite gloomy at times, which really reflects the tone of the game.
The music fits perfectly in this type of setting, but the songs don't seem very varied, from what I've heard.
Difficulty spikes aren't noticable, so you can go throughout the game without encountering a strangely difficult enemy or area.
The story was enough to soothe my appetite, but definitely wasn't the
story I've ever heard.
The gameplay is fantastic, and can definitely pull in any stealth junkie. While the stealth isn't really tactical, Powers can shake up how you would kill an enemy. powers are different abilities that Corvo can use to his advantage in eney-filled areas or just for exploration. To name a few,
can get you away from a sticky situation, or be used to find different pathways to your goal.
shows enemies behind walls, and their field of vision, which can be very helpful at times.This power is ranged, however, so you won't be able to see every enemy in a building.
Overall, this game is terrific, and I would recommend this to anyone who's a stealth junkie, and wants a fun, mechanic-based game.

I wanted to like this, and it scratches a few itches, but overall I think I'm going to abandon it.

Writing is poor at best, I don't enjoy the "challenge" of the combat enough to consider playing hardcore, and the game breaks all sorts of guidelines that I look for in RPG design - with a point-based irrevocable class AND skill system there are lots of skill traps and poor party mixes. Now that I suspect 2 of my 6 party members are never going to be up-to-par, I don't enjoy the game or the story nearly enough to start over with a new party. There are things you *can* do early but you get literally 5x the benefit if you wait until the late game (and yes, that 5x boost is probably more significant in the late game than the 1x boost would have been in the early game, except perhaps at the highest difficulty setting).

5 Stars...2 thumbs up...However you want to say it.  This game is fantastic.  There have been very few truly great RPGs over the years, and lots of almost-but-not-quite ones.  The greats for me - Pool of Radiance(and nearly all of the SSI gold box games), World of Xeen, Baldur's Gate(1 & 2), Plansecape:Torment, and now Lords of Xulima.
The pacing is solid.  I basically have been leveling up just about the time I start to feel like I need to.  Too many games either level you constantly or make you grind it out.
The game runs smoothly and the interface is fantastic.  One example:  Whatever way you want to choose the next baddie to attack, it is there for you - Want to kill off the guy on the right that is threatening your cleric with oblivion; just click on him there in the field of battle - Want to focus your firepower on the next monster idue to try to put a stomping on you; just click on his representation in the attack queue.  It is a little thing, but it is right.
The mission feels meaningful, even if it is the old "chosen hero saving the world" overall storyline.  It doesn't feel like a generic group of pixels clicking attack buttons.  The classes are unique and each has a flavor (my favorite is the divine summoner - mostly because you've never seen a class quite like that before.
The biggest compliment I can give this game - it was obviously NOT written for the console jockey.  Don't get me wrong, I think the game would work very well ported to a tablet, or even a console.  I just does not feel like a console game ported to PC as an afterthought, which is what we have been getting way to much of for the last few years.
I'm sure people could find things to nitpick, and if I had one improvement to suggest it would be the way the story is expressed feels a little jarring.  Conversations don't feel natural...the more I think about it, I am not sure this is a negative - The game conversations remind me of listening to a DM in the pen and paper days of my youth - They tend to feel like they are coming from the same guy, just in different voices.  lol.
I recommend this game.

This could have been a brilliant game. The politics, industry, resources and research are all handed really well, although some of the larger minor states should really be more developed than pre-first world war. Yes, it has a steep learning curve, and for some of the major countries, the politics can be a little restrictive, but that doesn't stop it being a bad game. The problem really starts with the number of units that seem to miraculously appear when war starts and how army sizes are disproportionate in size to both the historical reality and as to whether it you as the player controlling that country or the AI. As an example, after the fall of France the Free French Army was created, This initially consisted of one light division based in North Africa and by 1944 had increased to four divisons spread across the West European and Italian fronts. In the game, within days of France falling, the Free French have a larger army in North Africa than either the British or the Italians and within months are invading Italy with armies totalling 30-40 divisions. The same can be true of both the United States and the UK, unless you are playing as one of those nationalities and then it is much harder to recruit. This isn't a gripe about the strength of th allies as I played as the UK very successfully but with a much smaller  but more realistically sized army than the AI gets, although I had to micro manage every battle, which brings me to my next gripe the AI during combat. Why don't the armies ever do what you've asked them to do unless you micro manage? Why if you are allowed to move troops through a neighbouring country under a troop movement treaty, are you then unable to attack from those countries? Napoleon used to do it even if he didn't have a treaty. Instead when you try to move your troops into enemy territory to enable a flank or encirclement, they don't take the direct route but instead march back to your country and the then try and move through the front line, where you are successfully pinning your enemies forces ready for the manouevre that is never going to happen, by which time the enemy forces have miraculously tripled in number. I have been playing wargames with miniatures and  board games and then on computers for almost 50 years, and I have to say that the AI and unit spawning breaks this game more than nearly every other game I have played. I haven't even mentioned the disappearing armies - I played as a facist Holland, joined the axis, kept my army in reserve and only commited my airforce during the attack on Belgium and France. After the fall of France, I was given all the territory in Belgium and France but my army had disappeared so I had no troops to defend my coast from the immediate invasion by 30+ divisions from the UK. Just one of a number of bugs I have come across. Disappointed to have spent so much time learning to play a game that is broken and doesn't look like being fixed.

Edit: I added a few things now that i've beaten regular mode.
Out of all the indie Soulslike games, this is probably one of my favorite.
Since i like the patient way of fighting, I really like the Dark souls series, especially 3, but I don't like Bloodboure all that much. If you are looking for Dark Souls mechanics in a different way, this is probably a good choice, if you like the isometric view of the camera and controls.
The gameplay is very solid, everything you do is meaningful in terms of fighting. Do you attack? Should you dodge as soon as you see the attack? Should you block? Is it safe to heal? This game rewards patience and reflexes. However mechanics wise, i have issues with the dodge/block mechanic. When you are blocking and try to dodge, it does nothing. Which is fine, but the thing is that it buffers the dodge. So when you hold block, press dodge, then let go of block within a few frames of pressing dodge; you will dodge in the direction you were blocking at, meaning most of the time you will probably be dashing into the enemy. Which can turn the fight sour since on how the dodge mechanic works in this game. This has been at least 70% percent of my deaths, where i dashed into a half stamina enemy when i didn't even want to.
Also, there is a lack of personal customization. You can't change the controls. To me that is a big minus, since I honestly do not like the button setup on both the controller or the keyboard and mouse, but I've delt with it for now. Can't really do much on the visual and audio, I mean I like playing my own music while playing the sound effects of the game, can't do that either. All sound and music is a combined volume.
When it comes to equipment, the idea is ok. The way how items work is fair. No qualms with it. BUT, I'm hoping down the line in, can an option be there if i just want equip all spells or gadgets. As well as the healing item should be it's own slot
Now when it comes to weapons, each weapon may have different versions that changes how the weapon works and usage. Usually it's like a weaker version and then a stronger version that consumes more stamina compared to the weaker version. There are a few exceptions, but not the norm. Usually the difference comes when you "awaken" the weapon, or transforming the weapon. All weapons seems to have to their own unique mechanic when they "awaken" which is neat. Some may have passives, i just don't feel like it's really explained very well if they do or not.
Which comes to my next topic, information. Specifically detailed gameplay information. I mean sure, it paints the lore really well, but doesn't really explain game mechanics that well. When you're leveling up, you don't know what your points do and you have to keep shuffling points to see what the points do. When you're shopping, some items need a requirement to equip it, and when you're buying the items, you don't know if there is a requirement or not. you don't know if you're buying an item you can't even use yet. Those are just a few.
Even though with those flaws in my opinion, this is a great game for anybody who like soulslike games. 4/5.

2.  For gamers looking for a strategic shooter, prepare to be disappointed.  The AI is useless and the squad/order/bullet-time mode may as well not exist.  Your squadmates offer nothing of value other than the occasional revive and they're so damn squishy the only orders you'll make are to tell them to get out of your way.  The only time this game is difficult is when it spawns so many waves of aliens that you run out of ammo.
3.  For gamers looking for a well balanced shoot 'em up, prepare to be even more disappointed.  The guns are completely unbalanced and unchallenging; human weapons are useless and alien weapons are a range of boring lasers with no recoil that are virtually indistinguisahble from each other.
4.  For gamers after an exciting first-person story in the XCom Universe, start crying now.  Stilted dialogue, an unintelligble plotline and terrible characters await.  The game tries hard to throw up a few 'dilemmas' but fails miserably.  You form no attachment to the stupid two dimensional main characters/plot devices.  This is in large part because any interaction with NPCs has no bearing on the game at all (it just sinks hours of your time in pointless dialogue and loading screens).
So, what does The Bureau: XCOM Declassified do right?
+ It is a mindless point/click shooter (which can be rewarding if you want to disengage your brain)
+ You *do* get to shoot at some of your favourite XCom baddies
+ There is a brief novelty of M14'ing an alien in the head
What does The Bureau: XCOM Declassified do wrong?
- They took my money before I realised how bad and rushed this game was
- Three years later it is still an unplayable bugs nest
- Story was written by a five year old
- Characters are less plausable than D-Grade anime
- Gameplay is so dull you'll need to be waterboarded awake
- Graphics are rubbish
In summary, this is a bad console port with basically no redeeming qualities.  If you're silly enough to blow $50 on this game, come back after 5 hours and all I'll have to say is... told ya so!

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified isn't everything it could have been, but it's not as bad as many have made it out to be.
Taking the events in the game as standalone rather than a precursor to any of the other games helps.
Where the game does shine is the freedom of choice you get compared to many other storyline/campaign rail shooters. It is however only towards the end of the game where gameplay choices start to open up. To get to that stage you have to deal with some repetitive gunplay and some mediocre controls. For example, the sprint/cover key is the same key, and cover seems to "stick" so you can't simply walk away from it. What ends up happening is when you intend to sprint past an obstacle you instead slam right into cover behind it, and then spend several seconds trying to get away from it. Many other games have done this a lot better.
Your squadmates also have some serious dependency issues. They stick to your tail like glue, so when you try to flank an enemy while your squad has their attention, they instead give up their cover positions to chase you around. If you don't give them any direct orders for a few moments they tend to complain about it by saying "We need orders!". They do at least return fire without being told to.
There is no research, new weapons are simply given to you as you progress. Given that at the start you're told that alien weapons self-destruct when their owner dies I was expecting a situation where you had to incapacitate an enemy and "capture" their weapon in order to get access to it and research it. This may have been the plan at some stage but it's been shelved. Now new weapons are strategically placed in certain spots in missions, and afterwards normal enemies drop them as well. The hardest choice you'll have to make is what weapons you want to start a mission with but there are so many around in a stage that you can easily switch to something else if you find ammo is short for the type you're carrying.
There are two-ish skill trees for each of four classes. It's not really a tree as such but really just two lanes you can switch between whenever you want. Agents under your command tend to be rather generic so you never really form any kind of attachment to them.
Overall I'm going to give it a thumbs up. Not worth full price but definitely worth a look on sale or if you were able to get it from the recent Humble 2k bundle.
Happy gaming.

Here's the thing about The Bureau: it's not XCOM. It is based in the same world, and sure there are some similiarties in that you control a group of people, but this is an FPS so comparing it to a turn based strategy is just not fair to anyone. Especially since XCOM is one of the best ever in the genre, with an incredible...well, everything.
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified (hereafter TBXD) is a good game if taken on it's own merits. Not a great game, but certainly not a game I have any regrets about purchasing. There are a few niggling issues, that mostly have to do with how colossaly stupid your AI teamates are, but then they are AI teamates so that's pretty much par for the course.
The guns in this game feel pretty good, and the controls work well enough to allow the sort of control necessary to get through the missions intact. I really have no complaints, so if you see TBXD on sale, I'd say it's worth the purchase.
It's really not that bad, tbh.

It's a mediocre FPS. The idea is that you're running a squad and are supposed to flank enemies but the maps are too narrow to do that effectively. Your squadmates are awful - you either need to micromanage them or do everything yourself.
I didn't play that long, but from what I saw strategies are limited. As I said before, the maps are narrow, usually a road with wrecked vehicles or the equivalent, and the enemies are pretty close to you when they appear, so it's not like you've got a lot of choices about where to move. I can't see a sniper being any use at all.
It's not the worst game I've ever played by a long shot. They did a good job of recreating the atmosphere of 1962, and I enjoyed that vibe they created. But this game is just not very good. I got this as part of a bundle and wouldn't recommend you buy this alone.

Most of the negative reviews are from the dev team trying new things, or implimenting things that dont work as well as people would like. Which is to be understanded, as it's still "Early Access".
TL;DR version? Is the game perfect? hell no. Is the game enjoyable and getting better? Yes. Is the development process Smooth? Ha, it NEVER is, but the game is getting better I think.
Now for the extended words!
The atmosphere of the game is -amazing-. Its very much like Subnautica in that its a survival construction game with rather subtle and at times not so subtle horror elements to it. The asthetics are very nice and believable in terms of how it looks and how it is designed. I especially liked the ice planet when it first came out as my friends and I got lost and had to rush back to the safety of our emergency hut to wait out the night as we nearly froze to death. Things lik that were what we loved about the game!
So if you are looking at this game for a minecraft / Space Engineer fix? dont, its not those games, but it isnt trying to be.
If you are looking to support (in my opinion) a rather decent dev team that seems to honestly care about their game, and dont mind getting a bag of bugs and glitches and incomplete content at the moment? I say buy it.
For reference, I obtained it when it only had 1 class, and constant crash issues, with space ships getting stuck in the sky. and I -still- enjoyed the hell out of this game. Play with friends if you can! running from bugs at night and trying to hide while your other friend is frantically firing with a rifle, while another is jetbooting with a hammer chasing after the bugs shouting "Get Off My Klandathu!", or when the meteors started falling on us and we all shouted "Sky Gods! why have you foresaken us!?" are memories I could not of had without this game, and I thank the devs for giving me many sensable chuckles!

This review may sound negative so let me start iwth saying that without a doubtt his game is worth the $20 price tag.  It is a lot of fun with a decent story and interesting combat.
PRO's:
-Good variety of enemies that can require changing combat tactics.
-Random encounters can be avoided 2 ways if you want to avoid it and you can also "clear" any area.  After xx encounters in an area the area becomes clear and you get an xp bonus.
-Plenty of exploration and a pretty big world.
-Puzzles, secret doors, traps and such
- In theory a good variety of spells/weapons/abilities
CON's:
-Some classes just seem completely useless compared to others.
-For all the opportunity to explore, solve puzzles, and treasure hunt the loot in this game is extremely dull.  It is so bad that multiple chests in one dungeon with give you an identical trash item.  Depending on who you are it can really take away the motivation to solve a puzzle knowing you will get complete garbage.  The only items I have used are sold from towns.
-Every boss fight has been a joke in difficulty and the challenging fights seem to be from random encounters.  Some can argue that if you play at max difficulty, dont use certain classes/weapons/spells its more of a challenge, well I could also play blindfolded to create a challenge.
Some petty complaints:
-Your main hero is a pre defined character by name/portait/class.  I think they should have let us customize him in some way and the game can still reference him as the explorer as they do now.  This guy just looks like such a goober.
-I have had this game for a month and from what I can tell the dev's have been completely silent.  Personally that is potentially a red flag that support has ended.
All in all this game is a lot of fun and a good buy.  There are some simple improvements that could be made that would go a long way.  Also if this game ever gets opened up for modding I would say it is worth double the price.

A Bird Story feels like it's been crafted by the steady hand of legendary director Hayao Miyazaki himself, with its deliberately-paced narrative structure, disarmingly beautiful soundtrack, and imaginitive storytelling. The game is undeniably short, but its length isn't a detriment to its quality or value thanks to its low price tag and excellent pacing throughout. There's not much in terms of interaction, with most of the story being told through numerous cutscenes, but when the player is allowed to take control, it's usually to partake in a significant or meaningful event that drives the story forward. There's no branching paths or alternate routes to take, but there didn't really need to be for such a tightly focused and well-crafted narrative experience.
For the price of a movie rental on iTunes, you can get this brilliantly-executed interactive adventure game. It might even surprise you with just how meaningful and poignant it manages to be in spite of its low budget and short length.

NOTE: This is a shortened review without screenshots. For my full review, please visit
2011’s
was regarded by many as having one of the best narratives in video game history. It was a gripping, heartfelt and original story that captured the attention and hearts of myself and many other gamers. Despite the sub-par gameplay,
remains one of my favourite games of all time. Needless to say, I was expecting a lot from
, the spiritual successor to one of the most emotion-driven games of this era. Did it deliver? I'd say
.
Like its predecessor, A Bird Story is very much an emotion-driven game. So much so, that it carefully flirts with the definition of what a “game” is. The developer Kan “Reives” Gao himself referred to this title as a “light interact animation”, and he’s certainly not being modest here. To put it lightly, the gameplay for
. On first glance, it may look like the long-lost cousin of a SNES-era Squaresoft RPG, but instead plays far more similarly to a point-and-click title. You’ll find no battles here. You’ll also struggle to find any puzzles to solve. The game is a very on-rails endeavour that takes you by the hand and leads you through the experience. It’s impossible to get lost or stuck, and there’s no way to fail during any segment in the game. It's a very bare-bones shell of a game, but It allows you to soak in everything that’s going on, sparing you from unnecessary or tedious gameplay elements.
This begs the question though – Why have any gameplay to begin with? There are other games such as
which are similarly narrative or emotion-driven titles that also, for the most part, lack meaningful gameplay elements, but allowing a player to control the central character in Gone Home added plenty to the atmosphere of the game, something that was paramount to the experience. In contrast to this, the gameplay elements in
add absolutely nothing to the experience and serve as a somewhat tedious guise for a game that really shouldn’t have had any gameplay elements to begin with. I spent the majority of the game sitting back on my chair, drink in hand, happily enjoying myself and watching the story elements unfold. Every time that the game gave me control of the character again, I
.
You might say that
had similarly awful gameplay, which was arguably more tedious and unnecessary (in particular, the meaningless puzzle segment in between the “stages”). However, what that title lacked in gameplay was more than made up for by its incredible storyline and the emotional journey the player underwent throughout the experience. So how does the story in
compare?
places you in the shoes of a young, lonely school boy, who befriends a wild bird that he rescues. Sadly, the narrative isn’t nearly as fleshed out or original as its predecessor – A lonely child befriending an animal is hardly anything to write home about. It’s been done before, and undoubtedly will be done again. In its defence however, the game lacks any dialogue at all. There’s no voice acting or text that appears anywhere on the screen to help illustrate what’s happening. Whilst this is adequate for the relatively simple story it’s trying to tell, constructing an overly-complicated and imaginative storyline in this manner would be understandably difficult.
What this game does do just as well as its predecessor relates to its ability to convey the emotions and thoughts of the young boy, as well as his connection to his wild avian friend – a feat made all the more impressive by the lack of dialogue. You
the character is lonely because throughout the game, no other human being in the game has anything more than a blacked-out face. It’s the developer’s way of telling you that the silent protagonist is socially isolated, and whilst other people exist in the world that he lives in, he and these other members of society have a mutual disinterest in each other. One segment of the game has you walking around a park full of other people, with a speech bubble occurring when you run your mouse over them. When you walk towards the people however, they disappear. It’s a powerful image that I’ve butchered with my limited vocabulary and inability to write English with any real flair, but hopefully you’ll experience it and understand it for yourself.
Visually, the game maintains the 16-bit SNES-era aesthetic found in its predecessor. Whilst there’s nothing particularly breath-taking about a graphics engine that we left 20 years ago, it’s an aesthetic that’s held up well and is pleasant to the eyes. On the other hand, the piano-heavy soundtrack for the game is phenomenal and adds a lot to the mood set by the game. It’s appropriately relaxing and serene when it should be, but becomes more high-tempo when the action picks up, and eerily silent when something ominous is afoot. My only complaint is that the music is often disproportionately loud compared to the sound effects of the game, with no option to balance the sound output.
Whilst overall not quite as impressive as its predecessor, A Bird Story does tell a decent, emotion-driven story about a young boy and his new pet that’s easy understand and relate to. With that said, the gameplay itself is both uninspired and, in my opinion, completely unnecessary. As much as I enjoyed myself “playing” this game, I’m more inclined to tell you to watch a Youtube video of the game being played rather than paying money to play through yourself. Regardless of whether you buy it or watch it, it’s definitely worth at least a run through. More importantly, I’m excited to see what Kan Gao has in store for us with future releases.

In short, I enjoyed playing this game, it was more enjoyable than I originally thought it would be. Before I go on though I would point out that, I am very much the targeted demographic being a huge fan of this style of gameplay, having finished the souls series multiple times. Also note that I played the entire game using an Xbox 360 controller so I cannot confirm how well the keyboard handles.
Pros:
•	Level design is well done, and encourages short cuts
•	The combat is immediately familiar and holds up to other titles in the genre
•	The weapon and item selection is quite varied allowing for replayability
•	Every single boss is good, some even great (Alpha Twin = Prince Lothric?)
•	The artefact choice at the beginning is great (needs to be a way to swap them)
•	From first glance, the builds that are possible seem varied and extensive
•	Dash into enemy to stun is a great mechanic whilst not perfect
•	The story whilst not perfect is surprisingly interesting, and a great take on the whole hero keeps resurrecting idea that the souls games are known for
•	Not to spoil anything but the challenges to get more healing is something I personally really like.
Cons:
•	Dash is not the most accurate of movements which causes some issues in both traversing the level and during combat
•	Resting resets the state of your weapon
•	Door mechanics can occasionally force an area reset
•	Some enemy attacks can be hyper specific at any distance (Prisoner One Laser Beam)
•	There is the occasional attack which does not give any time to react leading to some unfair deaths (Toxic grenade, Psycher Rifle)
•	Parrying seems a bit too easy (maybe just me?)
•	There needs to be some obvious rest point after a boss which isn’t always the case
•	Blocking does not seem to stagger enemy chain attacks
•	The mimic enemies are too random and I was mostly annoyed by them
Bugs:
•	Small thing where going up an elevator into the hub section, before the elevator even arrives you can move the camera like you are walking normally before you are even in the level.
•	There were two points where I had to reset the level as a door closed as an enemy on the other side of it had seen me
•	The biggest issue by far is that the final boss in the ship got stuck on walls a whole bunch, which ended the fight prematurely for me
Summary
I beat the game in 8 hours, and I did not feel I was rushing, the time whilst not huge is fine for a game like this as the levels don’t vary significantly and the game does not want to waste your time. Because of the 2D plane the combat whilst enjoyable is not as nuanced as something like dark souls, and the shorter time means that it does not get exhausting like a 20-hour game would. In summary, I don’t think the game is for everyone but souls/ soulsborne fans will enjoy it, I personally would pay full price for this but getting it during a sale would be even better especially if people see value for time put into a game as it is not the longest of experiences. I would love to see more of this, especially some kind of local/ online vs mode.

(Edit) After spending some more time with the game and having far less salt, I am going to rework my review. Granted my complaints are still there but hopefully this time I can word them properly instead of letting the salt take hold of me.
First Problem:Keyboard controls.
I'm just going to gloss over this since the game tells you upfront that its meant for a gamepad, and it shows. Now the controls for keyboard aren't bad but you can really see what they were going for when you use a gamepad. SO yeah, this is a game where a gamepad is a must if you want to be as good as you can be.
Second:Immortal Blood
Thanks to the developer actually telling me in his response to the review mixed in with me reading items, I now know the name of this game's Estus Flask. My complaints are basically the same as my last review. Lets say I have 5 immortal blood and I die, when I respawn I am dropped down to 1, which not gonna lie, is kind of annoying. Granted you can reloot the chests which had them before but it is still tedious to go back and get them. However thanks to the developer's response you can actually go out and buy them from certain npcs. I would have prefered having the same amount when I die but at least its something.
Third:Combat (kind of)
Now I still stand by my previous review that the game is meant for one on one combat, with fighting more than one enemy seeming to be an after thought. However, it's not nearly as hard I previously made it out to be. I was simply being an idiot and panicking when facing more than one enemy. With that being said it can be difficult facing one oppent when others use moves that you can't block. Granted you can dash buuuuuuuuuuuuut I'll just save that for my next point.
Fourth:Dashing
Now I am fairly sure this is a problem with me specifically but I want to point it out in case anyone has a similar one. Dashing is honestly hard for me to do properly, though this is mostly when I am in a bind more so than anything else. Though from what I have seen with keyboard controls you generally just aim the mouse where you want to dash. Sounds simple enough but the mouse is kind of insane with how precise you need to be. Being slightly off can often result in you just passing enemies with low stamina or even falling to your own death. But like I said, this is me sucking at the controls. I just wanted to point this out as a nitpick more so than anything else.
Fifth:Looting Surprises
I recently discovered this and am now puttign it in this review. Sometimes when you loot a chest you can face the possibility of an enemy sort of popping above the loot and attacking you. However this seems to just be a percent chance of happening with specific chests. Unlike the first Dark Souls games they don' t seem to have a specific feature showing that they contain enemies. Unless I am just an idiot and miss the clear warning signs.
Sixth:Unblockable attacks (kind of)
This is mostly about the bosses you face later on and is mixed in with dashing, but I'll get to the point. Bosses will have three stages of attacks shown by bars around their health. Each stage with show new attacks and pattens. Some of these include a dash which stuns you and gives your enemy a free hit, or more annoyingly, a beam of light which can set the ground on fire along with causing decent damage. The main problem I have is that the move itself seems to have some obscure tracking to a degree. Plus mix this move with orbs that will lauch themselves at you at different times and you have an annoying obstacle to overcome. Now this could just be me sucking with the dash, but more often than not my attempts to dodge just leave me getting hit.
Seventh:Blocking
Super small nitpick but sometimes enemies can get a free hit dependent on where they are standing, since they might slightly be at an angle that I can't block. You see your character faces in four ways, and has a bit of aoe when they block, sometimes enemies can be just outside of this aoe but you can't really tell since its so small.
(Edit 6):Red Highlighted Enemies
Sometimes if an enemy is highlighted in red you can block the attack, and others you can't. I'm ♥♥♥♥ing sorry, what? Who would make such a stupid design choice? Sure you can learn from playing which ones you can dodge and can't but that is such a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, leading me to believe that I can block specific attacks when the enemy becomes red, and then being punished for it since the game lied to me. Honest to god I'm not sure if this is an over sight or just a♥♥♥♥♥♥move on the dev's part.
And that's about it, just a bunch of small nitpicks which might not even exist if you use a gamepad like the game tells you. Even with all of these problems I have a love-hate relationship with this game likely the hate coming from a mixture of me sucking and not using gamepad controls.  Though with that aside the game has pretty nice art, interesting NPCs similar to the first Dark Souls game, along with lore and concepts seemingly from dark souls but with a nice sci fi element to them. However, I am still not 100% if I can recommend this game with confidence without using the game pad more. BUT, if you have a gamepad I would highly recommend this game, if not, you might want to wait a bit.
Ultimately this game is a lot like souls, with bosses being difficult, individual enemies having the ability to kill you on their own, along with a lot of interesting story and character concepts wrapped up in a neat package.

After playing this game for a while I really can't recommend. There are a lot of things about that I like ,the aesthetic, setting, even the combat, but there a lot of little things that when brought together drag this game down.
1. Slow combat
This isn't actually a bad thing, and the combat is enjoyable. My only gripe is that the best method is often just to knock enemies off the edge since it can be much quicker than killing them straight up.
2. Slow movement speed
Walk speed being slow doesn't really matter, but the sprint speed is barely faster, and this just makes the game annoying to play.
3. Collecting heals
Like dark souls you spawn with a healing item. However, in immortal blood you can only ever spawn with one, and if you want more you must collect them. On its own not a problem.
4. Doors
Doors won't let you pass if there is an aggro'd enemy nearby. Not usually a problem, except one time I tried to bait an enemy who was waiting for me at the end of a hallway. I aggro'd him from outside of the hallway, but the door just closed blocking us from reaching each other. Leaving the area and returning did not reset the door, and as it was the only path fowards I had to jump off an edge.
5. Random spawns
enemies will randomly spawn from chests which contain heals. On its own no big deal, and makes the game more interesting.
All of these things on their own are fine, but when they are all present in the game they slow it down so much that it just becomes a slog. This is epecially the case when you are trying to go fight a boss. You have to try to dodge all the enemies (so you can get through the doors) while also collecting some heals, which could also randomly produce an enemey. Its slow, but fighting enemies is even slower, and it just becomes annoying to have get through each time you want to fight a boss.
TL;DR
Aesthetic, lore, setting are good.
Combat is slow, movement is sloor, doors are funny, only 1 innnate heal must collect others, random enemy spawns from chests. On their own all these things are fine, but together they just make the game really slow and suck the enjoyment out of it.

Hearts Of Iron 4 is a world war two grand strategy game where you take on the role as the head of state of a country. Choose any country you like and see how well you lead it through the turbulent thirties and fourties.
You are given a decent amount of control over your armed forces. Divisions are put into armies, which on their turn are put in theaters. When you have amassed your forces you are able to draw up battle plans, which will let you order your forces in huge numbers. You set up the front lines, offensive lines, fallback lines and much more. Once you activate your plan, all of your attached units will automatically spring into action and will only stop once you say them to stop. If you don't like this much automation, you can still manually take control of you units and armies.
In contrast to previous Hearts Of Iron games there is no real hierarchy system. Lavish order of battle are a thing of the past and in my opinion that is a shame. As a result there is less emphasis on battlefield strategy. Victory on the battlefield is not won by swift moves and cunning tricks but with gaining the upper hand in terms of troop concentration and having a good mixture of units on the right time. In short, it is more a simulation of a country at war rather than a true war simulation
Hearts Of Iron 4 does do a lot of thing right though. It streamlines a lot of the archaic gaming notions into a more understandable system. This makes controling your nation a lot easier while not oversimplifying the simulation side of it. It almost plays like a big, utterly complex, boardgame.

For fans of the series, or for someone who enjoys a TPS with a first person, melee oriented mech to switch up from being a squishy human to a crunchy mech. A prequel to Lost Planet, and Lost Planet 2 (odd I know), the game ditches its arcade like moments, for the most part, in favor for a deliciously awesome narrative (and some generic third person shooting with a lot of dodge rolling and less grappling hookin' your way out of trouble).
So while the shooting mechanics are pretty simplistic, when compared to most other games out, the game does allow you to select your loadout, customize your weapons, and worry about ammo when you come across bullet sponge bosses. Unlike the previous games that had heavily armed VS', this game has a mech, called a Rig, which is basically a minning mech that serves as your horse. The lack of 'weapons' on the rig give it a nice twist, reminding me of Pacific Rim in that you'll be slugging it out mono eh akrid quite often as you explore the surface of E.D.N. III...oh yeah that's right, the game is somewhat open world.
Somewhat of an open world in that you can go back and visit the areas you've already been to, usually to fight the same enemies that were there the first time, and usually just drain a T-Post of it's precious T-Energy, only to return back to base, go back onto the main path for the next story mission, or to go after your next side mission, because yes you can have side missions (though there isn't all that many of them that you can get at once). After completing your side missions, main mission, or killing spree on Akrid, you can return to base to spend that money on character upgrades, new guns, upgrades for your guns, speciality ammo, or to buy specialized components to upgrade your rig, probably because you passed up most of the ones scattered across the game. So there's that.
Finally there is the main campaign, which I think is the best of the three, though before you play you might want to go and catch up on the plot of Lost Planet: Extreme Conditions, since this game is the prequel to, as well as other things that I don't want to spoil. With a solid narrative, though somewhat repetitive at times, with atypical missions, predictable boss fights, and mechanics that aren't really all that and a bag of chips.
That being said, I liked the game, a lot, since I loved the first two, it offers a really solid campaign that sets up the scene for the first two, with some good characters, some new mechanic twists, and a lovely setting that makes me feel like a pioneering colonist, or badass frontier mechanic, fighting waves of Akrid that really serves to fulfill my Starship Trooper fantasy while trying to colonize a new world. I'd recommend this game to any fan of the series, or enjoys this type of genre, or even for someone looking for something 'new' since the game is relatively cheap now, and has more pro's than con's.

I can only think to describe Lost Planet 3 as such: A triumph of mediocrity.
It's one of those games that is frustrating in how pedestrian it is. The acting isn't offensively bad, but it's not good by any means; even by VAs I respect like Laura Bailey who pretty much phones it in. The story is as boring, uninteresting, and yet cliche as it can be. It has a feeling of designed by commitee. So many elements survive very limited purpose, especially when it comes to the RIG upgrades like the Shock-Jumper and Torch, being used pretty much once and never again. Countless mechanics are taught to you like planting and rechecking T-Drops, but most can't be planted until you have X tool and will never refill before the game ends anyway as they are triggered by story, not real time. The planet of EDN 3 has promise to be interesting to explore, and fails to ever be so. The Akrid enemies rarely pose any sort of threat other than the ranged enemies that hide, spam fire, and then charge you if you get near; and the bosses always boil down to idiotic QTE fights.
And then there is the last hour or two. Holy cow it's like they were going for the gold medal in stupidity. In the final mission the game has a serious identity crisis, quickly becoming a bad third person cover shooter (cover has existed whole game but due to Akrid AI you almost never use it, now you HAVE TO or you die), then it turns into a round of rock'em-sock'em robots, followed by some forced stealth nonsense, and culminates in an amazingly boring final boss that isn't explained for♥♥♥♥♥♥and yet is shockingly easy once you realize what you're meant to do. And in these final two hours the game keeps trying to pull stunts like "gasp, did Peyton die?" but you already know he won't because the story is told as a goddam flashback by Peyton, so there is no tension and trying to create any is pointless.
Oh, and it ends on a sort of cliffhanger because someone actually believed they'd be allowed to make a fourth abomination in this series.

First of all, the LOST PLANET doesn't seem lost at all. What if certainly feels like is: extremely boring. In my five hours of playing, all I've experienced was: get an assignment, enter your rig, go somewhere, get attacked 2-3 times by the same half-dozen types of creatures, push some levers/retrieve some item, get attacked some more, go back, have coffee, etc.
Combat in this game is mainly dodge and shoot, dodge and shoot, repeat ad nauseum until all creature are dead. As I said, I've played this game for five hours, which is about four more than I mildly enjoyed it. I continued hoping that something would happen that broke the endless continuum I was stuck in, but nothing ever did. And don't even get me started about the rig and the bizarre catch-and-drill combat mechanics involved with it and the fact that it can't even take a few blows from a significantly smaller creature but will auto-repair in a minute under the condition that you exit it.
To sum it up: I've had significantly more fun at playing ALIENS:COLONIAL MARINES than at this game. It's a pity because the graphics are nice and the main character is quite likeable; not your run-of-the-mill supersoldier dude. But the game has no sense of exploration or alienation and at no moment did I feel lost. What the game certainly transmits is the feeling of being a blue collar at work, listening to a simple man's country songs on the radio of your truck... uh... rig and getting his job done so he can go home.

I wish steam had a neutral rating.  While I did give this a thumbs up, it is barely a thunbs up. I am also writting this review after giving this game a break for a few weeks.  I didn't finish it because I got bored of it.  I wanted to give it time to see if I could get back into it because I wanted to see how the story turned out.   As of this writting, I do not plan on playing this game again to finish it.
The good:
It has an interesting story (which is sorely lacking from so many games these days) and an intresting world to explore.   It does a good job at drawing you in.
The Bad:
The game-mechanics are opaque.  You have no idea what skills / powers will do before you purchase them.  The descriptions can give you an idea, but you really do not know.  I am convinced that there is some kind of level mechanic in combat calculations because some encounter will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ and then you level up a few times and suddenly it is easy when nothing else much changed about your party.
The loot is also fairly uninteresting.  Its mainly +stats on most gear and some +damage on weapons.  It is just very dull loot.
The Ugly:
The game is gated such that there is really only one path to go at any given time.  However this path is not clear.  Basically the gates are monster stacks which will destroy you.  As you "open up" the world, you get a much larger area in which to test these monster packs to find the one pack that you can beat.  It gets quite frustrating at times.
The combat itself, which you do oh-so-much of, is terribly dull.  At some point many encounters will become trivial to you, yet you fight the same kinds of monster packs over and over and over.  It gets tedious quite fast.  This is the reason I put the game down.  There were a few more "gates" of uber monst packs around, and while I was trying to find the one I could beat, I was plagued with endless random encounters that were trivial to beat.  I just cound't deal with anymore and put the game down.  As it turns out, it will be for good.  Still though, I got a tremendous amount of play time considering the money spent.  This is why I gave it a yes vote instead of a no vote.

Quake is awesome. I'll admit I wasn't a fan of it the first 10 minutes, but the game definitely grew on me. The atmosphere is fantastic, as most people say. The music is amazing, and definitely adds to the atmosphere. The level design is very good. The progression feels very natural, and I like that the levels teach you things in a controlled environment, and then provides more twists as the levels get harder. I also love the art style. As is with the music, it amplifies the atmosphere. The gameplay is some of my favourite ever. Also, get a source port, because the base game has a maximum resolution of around 600p (it's probably more than that, I'm just guessing.) With source ports you can play Quake at an HD resolution.
Yeah, the game is good. It's the game that ushered in the FPS genre. Before Quake, FPS games were Doom Clones. It's innovative, fun as hell, and it has a great atmosphere. Quake's one of the best of the best, in my opinion. Buy the game, it's only 6.50 CAD.
EDIT: I'm also going to mention a part of the game that stood out to me. In Quake, enemies take more hits to kill, with even the most basic enemy requiring 2 shotgun blasts before it's downed. This is in complete contrast to Doom, where the shotgun can obliterate hordes of enemies. Quake's weapons are far less satisfying to use. However, the enemies are far more rewarding to kill, because each enemy takes quite a few hits.
