I'm just gonna go ahead now and gush about this game like a teenage girl gushes about books about vampires and questionable morals.
My first experience with Quake was back in the 90's when I found it on the Nintendo 64, safe to say, although still fun, it wasn't the best introduction to the series. I didn't really think about Quake again until a family member stabbed me and then used my computer to play Quake III. I remember watching while I was bleeding out and thinking “Oh hey, this looks neat.”
I managed to get myself a copy of Quake 1 from a second hand store and my life was changed forever.
The Steam release of Quake comes with both WinQuake and Gl Quake. WinQuake being the official source port for Windows, and GL Quake being designed for OpenGL and for things like hardware acceleration. WinQuake fought with me for a bit until I downloaded another Sourceport called Quakespasm and playing the Steam version through that instead of WinQuake.
Everything about Quake just feels like a step up from Id's last few games. The graphics are better, the controls feel smoother, the enemies are 3d instead of 2d sprites. And the levels are clearly designed to take mouse support into account.
The sound and impact of the weapons mix together with the animations of the suckers you're shooting at. Now enemies can be stunned for a short period of time as well as turned into meaty gibs from explosions are sometimes close range shots from your double barrel.
The map design, in my opinion, is also a step up from Doom. Now less of a maze, they're much more straight forward and easy to navigate while not being a linear mess of corridors and checkpoints. Everything is expected to be handled by the player, as you're given the ability to save anywhere, basically making your own checkpoints. It was a main stay feature of shooters back in the day, but now it's actually a breath of fresh air compared to riddling the map with checkpoints like they do in newer games.
Speaking of competent design, at the beginning of the game you're put into a kind of “Welcome to Quake” room. From here you're given three portals that work as your difficulty options, with the portals being marked as easy, normal, and hard. You can actually die choosing the Hard difficulty, considering they put a big pit of lava you have to jump over to get to it. It's really cool just how much attitude they use to put in games, you even have to hunt for the hardest difficulty since they hid Nightmare away somewhere in the episode select room. This game is just friggin cool.
There are multiple ways to experience Quake, but the only console alternative is vastly inferior to it's PC counter part. The N64 version looks and plays like mud, and doesn't even have the cool difficulty select room. Source ports like GL Quake are vastly superior to the original MS-DOS version in terms of graphics and performance, and you can also find other source ports that modify the game in some way.
I would recommend Quakespasm, but you really can't go wrong with a bunch of them.
Other than that, there's also Quakeworld, which is the official multiplayer source port for the game. There are also other mods such as the now legendary Team Fortress. You can still find a few people still playing either of these, and if you cant you can always just ask around, someone somewhere is always down for a bit of Quake.
And if you absolutely just cant get enough Quake like I can't get enough expired prescription medication, then there are two official mission packs for Quake: The Scourge of Armagon, and the Dissolution of Eternity.
Then when you're done with those, you can start hunting down mods for the game like the already mentioned Team Fortress. There's also Soul of Evil and it's sequel, as well as the newer Arcane Dimension.
Do I have any gripes with the game?
Well for some reason, the Steam release of Quake doesn't have Trent Reznor's amazing soundtrack, and you have to mess with the game a bit to get it working.
If by some chance you have never played Quake, then you should get around to doing so. You have absolutely nothing to lose and there are a ludicrous amount of ways to get your hands on it.
Play Quake.

'A Bird Story' is a very sweet interactive story about a lonely boy who befriends a little bird with a broken wing. I guess it's not really a "game" in the traditional sense of the word, as there is very little actual gameplay. However, that doesn't really detract from the story, rather it makes it more immersive and meaningful. Simple controls and a beautiful soundtrack round out the game.
As for achievements, well, there is only one, which you get for completing the game, making for an easy 100%.
I think you'll get the most enjoyment out of this game if you don't go into it expecting the best graphics, the most innovative controls or the most incredible story ever imagined. And don't expect it to be just like 'To the Moon', because it's not. If you expect all that, you won't enjoy the game for what it is.

Remember your first time playing Dark Souls, how you treked through the Undead Asylum, struggling through these underlings that were no more than wasted flesh and broken swords? Do you remember feeling like something bigger was lurking behind the walls, and that feeling when you finally came face-to-face with the Asylum Demon? Do you remember the story slowly unraveling before you, with the feeling that you were a player in an undertaking unfathomably larger than yourself?
Immortal Planet captures that feeling perfectly. The combat in this game is extremely polished; Once it clicks, it clicks *hard*. Soon, you'll be dashing, slashing, dodging, and participating in fast-paced combat that feels natural and intense. Every death feels justified, and the game really demands that you improve.
I can't recommend this enough. I've played several hours in what felt like minutes. If you liked Dark Souls, if you liked Monster Hunter, or if you like games that force you to grow as a player as you improve stats and your skills, get this game.

Haven't played much of this game yet, but here's an early opinion from the 20 or so minutes that I've spent on it so far:
It's not bad...but it could be better.
I'm not trying to be coy here, as there's genuinely a lot I like about this game. Even from the early previews (e.g. video and screenshots on Steam), I absolutely loved the art style that they were gunning for, and that hasn't changed in the beta release. The aesthetic of the game is absolutely brilliant, truly immersing you in its twisted sci-fi roguelite world, and some of the weapons are pretty fun to use for the most part, a great example being the gun (firing it feels so satisfying and you really feel the IMPACT of its power).
With that said, the game's kinda clunky. The biggest example would be the melee combat, which, while not overbearing, isn't the most fun thing in the world. Oftentimes you'll think that you've parried an enemy's attack successfully but then see your health bar go down, and realise that it happened because your timing was just-ever-so-slightly off. Yup, the melee combat in this game is NOT. LENIENT. AT. ALL. Now, that may seem like a good thing to the thrillseekers that live off the challenge that is Dark Souls combat, but it's slightly different here. Dark Souls combat isn't clunky by any means; hell, it's some of the smoothest to have ever existed in a game. Don't get me wrong, the game itself is difficult as all hell, but the combat mechanics certainly aren't. Immortal Planet is on the other, wrong side of the same spectrum; it's a challenge, but not in a good way. It's just clunky, unresponsive, and somewhat inherently annoying.
All things considered, though, I'd still recommend this game, especially if updates continue to come its way. There's a great idea at work here, and it's clear that the developers are genuinely passionate about making this game a good one. There's just a bit more work to be done here before this goes from a "decent, I'll buy it on a good sale" to "Must buy, Game of the Year" status.
Innate problems like devs not giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥about their own game can't be fixed (*cough* Age of Survival *cough*). Surface issues like minor clunkiness most definitely CAN. Immortal Planet clearly falls into the second category, as its devs appear to love the game that they've created -- the brilliant art and attention to detail will most certainly attest to that.
TL;DR: There's a GREAT game hiding somewhere in here; it just needs to be nurtured before it will bloom.

I hate that question. Approximately 8 to 12 Hours. I have beaten DemonSouls and DarkSouls but I don't rush through games. It was a respectably long experience for the price.
After beating the game you can play Nightmare mode which changes some things like dialogue. The game is fun enough to play around with different builds and weapons. Unfortunately, no achievements to encourage that.
There are 4 main areas and they all have different enemies, backgrounds with lots of detail and unique challenges.

If you ever played DarkSouls it is heavily mimicked after it. Just about everything you do requires stamina like attack, dash, run, block and even shooting. Reliance on stamina is what creates back and forth combat that many Souls fans enjoy. Whenever you kill an enemy you gain currency that you can spend to increase stats. If you die the currency stays on the ground for you to pick up on next try. The level layout is very user-friendly and even incorporates limited platforming. You can't really jump but you can dash across platforms and die if you misjudge the distance. That plays a bigger part in gameplay when platforms start moving or when enemies use gaps to their advantage.
This game sort of has a Bleach(anime) treatment for weapons. Each weapon has 2 forms that have different range, damage, and sometimes special ability. Balancing between weapon forms can be questionable and some of them feel very similar to other weapons. It is a very fun feature but I would have preferred more abilities between fewer weapons . Around the game, you will find all kinds of consumable items like flying discs, mines, pistols and even several different spells. It adds a lot of depth to combat and fun factor in general. Spells and some items scale in damage depending on stats. At higher stat numbers the maximum item/spell capacity also increases.
The difficulty is fair. Don't get me wrong the game can be frustrating but I never felt like it was BS. Even if you find the game too hard you will eventually overcome it with flat stats like spell damage if you want to make it easy. I don't like some of the balancing in the game and in that regard, the developer should have added achievements for using less ideal tactics. (like beat the game with no spells)
Levels are very easy to memorize and the lack of a map is not a huge problem. Each time you beat an area you will usually get a short cut to travel faster. If I am not mistaken main areas are Temple, Archives, Prison and Fortress. They take 1 to 3 hours to complete based on difficulty. In a true spirit of Souls, you can do a harder area first . I really enjoyed the artwork and unique set pieces around the levels ( they are not just color swaps )
I found the game to be very Atmospheric. It really reminded me of Harbinger which is one of my favorite immersive games. The ambient music is not very noticeable but it really fits the tone of the game. The story is told through next but it was well written. The subject of immortals who are stuck in an eternal struggle for the purpose is very intriguing. I got to say that the regular ending was extremely disappointing. You will probably get a very sour taste by the end ( considering that game was so good up to that point )
Immortal Planet has a very specific target audience that likes a good challenge and mothedicly slow combat. If you want to progress fast you will pay for it with sweat and tears. I am sure not everyone will like it, especially if this is your first Souls game. However, I have to rate this game based on what it tries to accomplish and it is great Souls-Like game. Few things that bother me are very nitpicky and overall they did not ruin my experience.

I had the opportunity to play the beta of Immortal Planet a few weeks prior to it launching and spend some time in the game.  Keep in mind the version I played was incomplete and subject to change at release.
Immortal Planet is very true to the soulslike genre of games today.  Many games boast "soulslike" combat or gameplay but Immortal Planet definitely hits the mark.  If you are a fan of Dark Souls, you are going to like this game I'm sure.
Pros
- Thoughtful combat - You cannot just run in swinging or you will die quickly.  It is slower paced and more strategic since you need to manage your stamina to attack and defend.  Every enemy can pose a threat to you if you are not careful.
- Beautiful 2d Graphics - Immortal Planet is a very pretty isometric 2d game.  Everything down to the particles of your dodges and the explosion of ice when an enemy dies.
- Challenging - This game is no walk in the park.  If you enjoy a good challenge that gives you a ver rewarding feeling after completing the next stage then you are in for a treat.
Cons
- Vague Story Initially - The story starts off vague and mysterious.  You slowly get more tidbits of information as you go along so if you are not interested in a game that's story doesn't hook you in right away, you will have to push through the game to learn more
- Challenging - Yeah I know I put this as a pro but this game is pretty punishing.  Just like in Dark Souls, when you die you lose all of your experience.  If you die before you make it back to your last spot of death to recollect your exp then it is lost forever.  Some people might be put off by the difficulty instead of enjoy it.
- Main Weapons Lack Variety - You can choose between one of three main weapons to start and they each have two forms but only a couple of different attacks in each form.  I found some secondary items early on but no other mainhand weapons.  I think more variety would be nice.
- I Died A Lot - Not really a con but I want to ♥♥♥♥♥ about it anyways.  I need to "git gud" more :)
Conclusion: If you like the Dark Souls series, you are going to feel very at home.  I really enjoyed Immortal Planet and will continue pushing through it to find out more of the mystery going on with your character.  It has beautiful 2d graphics and combat that keeps you on your toes.  If you are not a fan of a challenging game then this one is probably not for you.  If you are ready to learn enemies and bosses attack patterns and master the art of dodging, blocking, and attacking while managing your stamina correctly, then you are in for a real treat.

So before I go into this, I should mention that I am a huge sucker for anything soulslike, so I have a special place in my heart for games like this. Immortal Planet is, as advertised, an isometric souls-like game. It uses the same familiar stamina system. There is no rolling, but you do dash, so in that regard it's more like Bloodborne.
The story is captivating, the controls are tight, all enemies require study to defeat. So all is good in that department.
The bosses are also very interesting and complex. The two I've faced so far have 3 phases which are outlined by some UI bars above their heads. The boss hits deal HUGE damage, but they are very well telegraphed, so it works out.
The character leveling system and customization is also reasonably robust. So far I've discovered 3 spells that all have interesting and situation dependent properties. A lot of strategy here.
I think anyone who's a fan of the souls series would not be disappointed with this indie title.

The game's industry sure loves to have its titles go through development hell sometimes. Aliens: Colonial Marines suffered this fate when Gearbox decided to use resources for Aliens on Borderlands 2 after seeing how successful the first one was. The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a similar story. This is a game which has exchanged hands within many internal 2K teams for half a decade while being put off to instead focus on Bioshock 2 after 2K saw how well the original Bioshock sold.
However, unlike Sega’s sci-fi catastrophe, 2K’s sci-fi title is actually not horrible trash. In fact, it is very much playable. That being said, sometimes it is better to be trash quickly forgotten. It pains me to say that, after getting into the story and very much enjoying my time with the game, I cannot deny that The Bureau is still the very definition of mediocrity and deserves its 60% mixed Steam rating which I see as a “6/10”. For each moment I was enjoying this game, I was noticing a ton of wasted opportunity.
The story is pretty straight forward. Aliens from XCOM: Enemy Unknown have invaded in the 1960s instead of in present day. It is up to the player to lead a small squad of soldiers with unique abilities into heavily outnumbered situations and save humanity. The game’s cast is diverse enough to be interesting though they do very easily fall into overdone archetypes such as “hot-headed partner that shoots before he thinks”, and “commander that treats the mission with utmost importance”. Voice acting is good. The story of this game actually expands upon the lives and troubles of everyday people more than the other XCOM games do. The player will actively find notes and dialogue from people during various stages of the invasion and see how the aliens have ruined the lives of actual distinct people with their own small backstories which the player can choose to investigate, rather than generic NPC’s with no voice in the main strategy turn based games of the franchise that just get shot at the same way every time.
However, those moments end up being merely window dressing or side show attractions for the otherwise extremely linear and generic (destroyed town, stereotypical high tech alien buildings, etc) levels in this 3rd person shooter. There really isn’t any interaction at all with everyday people you meet despite you seeing into their lives and one of the big themes of the game being about keeping the alien invasion a secret so that everyone on Earth doesn’t panic. In all the trailers and even the game’s cut scenes, the game emphasizes keeping the whole alien invasion under wraps while tricking the populace that it is in fact the communists which are attacking. Neat idea, horribly executed. Aside from people in the XCOM base mentioning efforts of spreading propaganda which you never see, and a few notes referencing it while on a mission, the idea is never expanded upon. So when the player sees whole towns destroyed by what are obviously extraterrestrials, the whole idea that XCOM is keeping everyone from finding out is ludicrous to say the least.
Also speaking of protecting the entire Earth, aside from one potential Soviet (which doesn’t even end up mattering), literally every other character and member of your squad is American. One of the coolest parts of XCOM for me is the forming and growing of this elite global task force comprised of men and women from every country in the world. It made the conflict truly feel like I was fighting for the survival of the whole world and helped me differentiate between my various soldiers who all eventually became important characters in their own right in my XCOM Enemy Unknown/XCOM 2 playthroughs despite really just being randomly generated characters. For me heroes like specialist “Vapor” with her bandana and ranger “Athena” with her baseball cap from my XCOM2 playthrough will always be remembered.
In this game on the other hand, everyone is a generic American. After going through the entire game with mostly the same soldiers, I can’t remember a single one’s name or even what they look like.
The original gameplay demo showed off in 2010 of this game showed off a first person shooter with investigation elements. The player was shown taking pictures and analyzing scenes of alien attacks. Sadly, there is no such gameplay element in this version of The Bureau. All you do is walk from point A to B killing all aliens in your path while the lab back in home base magically finds out how to use alien tech without any input from you at all. This kills off a lot of the progression in the other XCOM games which made the acquisition of new gear so rewarding. In this game you just find it on the field lying there for you to pick up without any prior knowledge or training on how to use the weapon.
Now gunplay is just like your generic 3rd person shooter. The weaponry on offer honestly starts off very weak with just basic American guns of the 60s at your disposal. They don’t feel satisfying to shoot and don’t do that much damage. 50% of Steam players failed to beat the first level. That should be telling of how boring the gunplay is at first. However, if you stick at it, eventually you will gain access to alien weaponry, and those guns do feel much more powerful and rewarding to use (Even if they are just “alieny” laser versions of Earth weapons).
The main meat of the gameplay is instead in the tactical mode where you can issue various commands to your squad mates such as moving to a specific location or using an ability at a target location such as putting a shield dome or a turret down. Some people find this to be gimmicky but I found that for the most part it works alright. For some reason the command marker moved like a regular unit so would be blocked by walls and stuff but that’s a minor annoyance. It was actually fun to micromanage all my units during heated battles, especially the later ones where a few mistakes can easily wipe your whole squad out.
Now onto the main complaint of most people and why this game deserved to be “mixed” on Steam. Squad AI is not good. When playing on lower difficulties where you and your squad mates can still die very very easily, but will be ready to fight again after a simple co-op game style “push e for a few seconds to revive”, the bad AI isn’t too much of an annoyance. But on harder difficulties where a revive only stabilizes squad mates I honestly think the game is borderline impossible. With the AI constantly making your squad mates being open to enemy fire and there not being any option to let your squad mates auto their abilities, aka you must babysit them all the time, while enemies charge you in real time I don’t see anyone having fun playing the higher difficulties. In fact, I salute the 1.5% of players who were able to stomach the cancer such an experience would entail and beat the whole game.
So then what is wrong with playing it on a lower difficulty? Simply that it ceases to be an XCOM game at that point and becomes more of a very very poor man’s Mass Effect. In fact, that is basically what I am trying to get at. The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is an above average generic 3rd person shooter about aliens invading America, not all of Earth, in the 1960s. It is not a true XCOM game. I recommend it only during a sale for anyone looking for a fun 3rd person shooter that isn’t expecting too much. Die hard XCOM fans will probably enjoy the added lore (which doesn’t really make sense since wouldn’t the modern XCOM know of aliens if they invaded in the 60s) and hate everything else this game represents. Now that I look back at it. Yes, I did have fun. But I also recognize this game is just 2K milking the XCOM franchise.

Starting with Splinter Cell on the PS2 at my cousins house, I have been introduced to the "Stealth Action" genre. Got my XBOX in 2004 and later Splinter Cell 3. Then I played THIEF (4). And then there was a drought of games like this. My cousin asks "Why don't you play Dishonored". Me: "Nah, it looks strange". 2 years later, I eventually tried it and - wow, such a good game!
~PERFORMANCE~
My system is an ACER PREDATOR built in 2012. It has a i7-3770, 16 GByte of RAM and a GTX970 working together.
Since the game came out in 2012 and the CPU as well the amount of RAM was good for that time as well as the GTX970 yet to come, I could play the game on MAX settings at 1080p with stable 60fps. Loading (off a HDD) takes several seconds, loading a savegame or entering a new part of the same map roughly 2 seconds.
~STORY~
The story starts out as a plot that reminds me of some Harrisson Ford movie: You are accussed of murdering the Empress and kidnapping of her daugther Emily - and getting jailed, tortured and are about to get executed. A mysterious organization frees you and set up a list of people that need to get killed in order to restore justice. And you are the one that has to eliminate these ladies and gentlemen. But the times are rough and of course, the whole thing spins a bit out of control...
I personally liked the story and I often felt like "Payback time". The writing makes you really feel you are doing the right thing for you, the town and Emily. I was also actually surprised how the story turned and did not quite expect that, so it's not a game that boringly goes on and on but made me really play every day to see what♥♥♥♥♥♥will happen next.
~GAMEPLAY~

There is a safe zone in the abandoned part of the city and there is your bed and a way to restore your supplies with gold found in the game. The actual missions are started by talking to boat driver Samuel.
The game has some sort of "open world" city of Dunwall going on, a plague-riddled, rat infested place with a now-paranoid government. You, as escaped inmate, are of course immediately attacked when being seen, so try to be undercover...
...which I failed at. I found myself shooting the first pair of guards and expected GAME OVER as I know from other stealth games. But no, the game kept going. And this is what I really like about this game: There is no restriction on how you play: You can make your way trough the levels silently, you can take out enemies by knocking them out - or by using your pistol, blade, crossbow, grenades and mines. The difference is the so-called "Chaos factor". The more you kill, the more changes the world. E.g. more guards. But that's it. In fact, I liked my high chaos run (I killed almost everyone hostile) and the way the city turns into a even more dark, paranoid version is a nice idea.
The whole idea however is not gamebreaking in any way. When I read that it'd cause the game to become "darker", "more violent" etc. I thought the developers want to be the moralist voice on "killing ain't good, man". But in the end, the "high chaos" ending was reasonable, e.g. Samuel, the boat driver, basically telling that I turned into a monster and behaved like a♥♥♥♥♥♥in the last mission. There are several changes that I just read off, but I am fine with my High Chaos ending.
Killing your victims always is a joy, they all have this "You deserved it!" feel. Also, the way the wanted posters and the ambient chatter start to change (about people fearing the guy in a mask that killed person X last night) adds to the immersion. There are many civilians out there that can also be killed, but usually just panic and hide.
You are also free at your mission when it comes to movement: You can steal a key off a guard (that has been either knocked out or by sneaking up him and taking the key off of his belt) and walk trough the side door, you can try the roof, a ventilation shaft, the sewer, an open window from an adjacent building. You see, it's pretty neat. Or you just can shoot down 25 guards with blazing gun and wade trough a pile of bodies. It's up to you! :-)
The levels and the city are very, very well designed! Especially the fancy dress party of Lady Boyle were beautiful visually and audio-wise. Nice lighting effects, too!
~COMBAT~
The first person combat was a bit weird at the first moment, because I found it a bit strange because I wield 2 weapons at once: In the left hand there is a selectable weapon or item (grenades, crossbow, mines etc.) and the right hand is always your blade/sword/dagger. So you basically fight with two weapons at once by pressing the corresponding trigger. Later in the game I grew to this idea and it works out very well, even though a bit unrealistic (reloading one-handed while having a blade fight...?). But it plays very well to block a guards sword attack, swing at him and while he is tumbling I turn a bit to the right and fire my pistol at another guy that charges towards me. Meanwhile, I finish off the other guard and take care of his buddy as well.
The amount of guards walking around (and attacking) can be overwhelming, and you know what? That's good! You are not invincible, and thinking you are Arnold Schwarzenegger will lead to a fast game over screen. The combat never feels unfair, even when I fought like 8 guys at once of which 2 were shooting at me from a balcony. What I really enjoy is the fact that what happens to the enemy can also happen to you: E.g. when you blast a foe with your pistol, he is stunned for a second and recovers. This is the time when you can finish him off. However, this can happen to you as well: Getting blasted turns your screen red and you can not fire or move for the next second. Or that the enemies also throw grenades at you in the first mission already, the same you can do after picking them up. This way, it feels like a good 1vs1 and not a "I kill you anyways" situation like in other games. You are not superman, right?
Well, not quite, because you also get super powers that consume mana. These powers include teleporting, bullet time modes and such. I actually just used the teleport ability. In general the combat is very fun and you are free to place traps and knock out guys or just bomb your way trough the levels.
~CHARACTERS~
The main character, Corvo Attano, well... I never really could get into this guy. He never talks, the only time you hear him is when in pain, but that's all. I don't know how I look like, I don't know anything, there is no mirror. The only way I know he/I loook/s like is the artwork. That could be done better...The mirrors are also blind you never see yourself. Eh. id Software used that for DooM in 1993 and said "We don't give the Doomguy a story because he is supposed to be YOU", well, I think this is the same. Since Corvo can be pacifist or spree killer, I think it was understandable design-wise, but still, I feel like Corvo is nothing more than a pair of floating hands on my screen. I can not even see my feet - I know, it sounds strange, but I don't like games that do that. It's like a floating camera with two hands on a stick in front of it hovering trough the levels. More "head movement" or hand animations would've helped a lot!!
~SOUND~
There is nothing special around. Actually, I hear too many stock sounds (footsteps on sand and grass are the HOGS OF WAR footstep sounds....) But the ambient dialogue is always combined by a bunch of random words. Guard A says something, and guard B replies. Both is picked by a pool of lines and combined result in new "dialogues". The way the announcements on the speakers make you feel like you have an impact: News on your recently assassinated victim are heard on the streets and such are nice.
I always turn off music and just play with ambient sounds, and it works very well in this game!

Whether you like creeping in the shadows, running across the rooftops or decapitating guards, Dishonored is a game that demands your attention.

What a wonderful start to a new game!
Initially, the premise of Osiris New Dawn will sound very sci-fi survival to you and there are certainly elements of that. But at its heart, this is a space-based RPG sandbox. If you enjoy world-building games like Medieval/Space Engineers or Factorio, you'll love it right off. But there are so many neat influences and clever twists, including specific callouts to The Martian, Starship Troopers, and REDACTED (I don't want to spoil; you'll know it when you see it).
Initially, the game is about survival, yes, but soon enough you'll build yourself a habitat and at that point, Osiris will start slowly but deliberately drawing you further into its world, putting goals in front of you to meet and justly rewarding you when you meet them. But those goals are ones you set for yourself. Want to play the game as an explorer? Go for it! Want a Halo-style combat experience? There's the start of one here. Want to be an engineer and build a sprawling base? Do it! At each step, Osiris will give you choices of what to do next and encourage you to chase whatever part of the game appeals to you. And you can do all of it eventually if you want. That's what sandboxes are about.
The graphics, sound, and "feel" of the game are spot on, particularly if you enjoyed The Martian. You will really feel as if you've been abandoned on a whole planet and have to fend for yourself, survive, and succeed. There are so many wonderfully well thought-out elements. Just to call out my favorite two: first, about half the wildlife you'll encounter are NOT interested in eating you and will ignore you if you don't provoke them. The feeling of a surviving, sustained ecosystem with its own food chain happening around you is really well-done and well thought-out. Second, the game is incredibly intuitive. As you discover you need things, as long as you're thinking Osiris will subtly point you in the direction you need to go to fulfill that need.
Osiris is surprisingly bug-free (I encountered only two major bugs as of 10 Nov 2017) and completely crash-free. Playing casually bit in a goal-oriented way, I finished the major "content" in about 20 hours but there was still a huge amount to do and explore that I hadn't touched at that point. If any of the above appeals to you, give it a whirl! You won't be disappointed.

Graphics:  This game is supremely well optimized for an Alpha...even a few months ago, when it was more bare bones than it is now it looked awesome and ran incredibly smoothly.  Jaw dropping visuals, especially with some...particularly large creatures.
Crafting:  A bit different than most survival games out there, but pretty easy to pick up and learn.
Building:  I LOVE the way building is done in this game.  Most games have you building individual wall segments, maybe flattening/removing terrain...and while I think this game could benefit from being able to dig down into the ground, the way building works is awesome.  Get the resources you need, select the object/structure you want to build...place it, then hold down the build button.  Easy, quick, and so very sleek.  So far hasn't been boring.
Vehicles:  I haven't gotten this far yet, not enough time to really play, but I've seen vehicles around and they look pretty impressive.
Combat:  Basic and intuitive...takes some of the more tried and true formulas and doesn't mess with them.
Sound:  Sound effects in this game are really nicely done and feel very sci-fi.  Not much more to say on them, really...they add to the experience!
Music:  Very reminicent of ME1, very good sci-fi sound.  Pro:  Great audio queue when you come under attack, in case you can't see what's sneaking up on you.  Great help when you're exploring.  Con:  The main exploration music, when it plays, tends to be a bit boring and repetative.  A little more variety would be good!
Starting off: This has progressed quite a bit since the last time I played...you break out of your escape pod, now, and follow a decent starting tutorial.
Look to the future:  The game has a mission system and instances, which were not present when I first played, so it looks like they're planning on -really- expanding gameplay options...and it looks like there's going to be a story to follow as well.  This will set it apart from a lot of pure surival games and add to the fun factor and longevity immensely.  I'm hoping the developer keeps going with this product, because as it stands it's the beginning of something grand.
You could wait, but I think watching what's added and adjusted as time goes on will be interesting, so you may not want to miss out.  Also, supporting the developer by picking up the early access and showing them there's interest in their product will make it more likely they'll continue to build it up.
Overall:  Beautful game with a near-future sci-fi feel, and tons of future potential!

You mostly just get in the way a lot because two people can't access the menu for a building at once, but you can't tell when someone else is using the building until you try to access it (so you also can't tell when they're done).
I'd sooner play almost any other crafting-based game. This has promise but right now it's no fun, and they need to fix the fundamental problems before adding new game mechanics.

When I heard about a new version of ARES I figured what I'd get to play improved on the game I knew and had a like/hate relationship with, it was 60% off and since i owned the original I figured what the heck.
Gameplay: They've moved to 1 currency, essentially everything is now 1, so you have 1 higher cost instead of trying to farm a particular resource for your upgrades. Thats a positive... you now have to find unlocks to unlock your upgrades, thats a second plus... You get a new character thats like a heavy class/tank compared to the original character, and he plays... kinda meh. His special is a shield that uses up energy vs health...
Other changes is that you have infinite bombs/electrical blasts and they are on a CD. Repair kits are also on cooldown and have a 100 resource cost. All can be upgraded.
Graphics: Uh, I don't like what they did with the supporting cast, the characters and bosses look just as great, but what did they do to the women... its like they changed how they wanted them to look and they look awful. The gameplay is still as crisp and looks similar if not better than the original.
Controls: Yup, did you hate Ares, you'll hate this... love it... you'll love this... its not changed, and its still as wonky as when I played it the first time, jumping off the ends of ledges... good luck and do it early.
So that I've writen this game, if you haven't played the original, you may like what you see, if you have... I'd avoid this for awhile, its in a kinda crashy state in which you have to launch the game again nearly every level I think the changes they put forth are positive for the game, but the new levels aren't really impressive, and the new character while plays slightly different, continues to be similar to what you've done before.
Verdict: Pass, and if you want to get a version get the original for now... I might review once they patch all the crashy bugs... but I cannot honestly reccommend as of 10/4/14

Well, this game has feels. I dont think it is fair to compare it to To The Moon, since it is its own entity, so looking at this game on its own, I think it's easy to recommend it. It isnt fast paced, and takes about half the game to develop, which may be a turn off for some people, as that first half was kind of boring. However, once everything really starts to come together, the set up was revealed as pretty necessary for developing the conneciton between the boy and the bird. The second half...well...I think it is pretty gripping. Not as an adult♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but as seen through the eyes of a child, or simply through the act of remembering your own childhood, this game scores in spades for waht it was trying to accomplish.
the controls themselves are as basic as can be. Directional moving and clicking on the occasional item. You will run into things and get stuck occcasionally, which can be a minor annoyance, but really, the gamepolay is secondary, and just the avenue towards the telling of the tale.
The music was pretty spot on for the game. Very nice piano work.
There was a moment of humor and many moments of levity, and the game will carry you through many emotions...sadness, happiness, pride, etc...
In the end, I think this game deserves your attention. It doesnt leave you in as introspective a state as TTM, but that isnt its goal really. I think if you see it through to the end, you will find it to have been a satisfying experience, and this development team has the potential for even more greatness in the future  (in fact, at the very end, they let you know what their next project is/will be). A perfect use for the RPG Maker programs as well.
8/10
btw...my total play time was around an hour and fifteen minutes. When I get done farming the rest of the cards, it will be more, but that was the actual length of the game.

It's made in RPG Maker, so it's using very pixelated graphics and it can even look like some jRPG from screens, but that's not the case, don't worry. I have to say the art of this game is absolutely magnificent. I was thinking a little while playing this game and you know what? I don't think any other art style could tell story such as this one. Creator of the art is the Artist (with big A). Another thing is animation. It's extremely clever and smooth, sometimes I couldn't even believe how well the animations were used, really. You are walking in the forest and suddenly, you are in your living room and it even makes sense! Graphic side of this game is top notch. What else does the story need? Oh right! The music. The music is absolutely amazing and fits very well with the story. Most of it is piano music, but don't worry, it's not pretentious and you won't cry. A lot.
About the gameplay - keep in mind that this is very linear game with a lot of cutscenes and it's not the longest, the playtime is around 1 hour, so keep that in mind, please. Story itself is great, I didn't except it to be that great, especially after To The Moon, because that was masterpiece, but I was very pleasantly surprised. I mean, it's not as good as To The Moon, it didn't bring me to tears, but it still made me feel. I was very satisfied with the ending. So I absolutely recommend it. Go buy it, it's cheap!

I bought a bird story 66 minutes ago. They have been some of the most beautiful minutes of my life. A Bird Story is not a game, in that it doesn't provide you with an aim, or an enemy to overcome. It invites you to share in the dreams of a boy, and his only friend: a wounded bird. This is the first game (for want of a better word) I have ever played that has successfully conveyed both a story, and a truly touching character. There is no glorified murderer here, running around a small enclosure butchering those with slower reactions, nor is there a spurned plumber fighting his way to his royal girlfriend. There is simply a boy, a bird and all those that reject him. Many won't like it, but I hope those that do love it enough to overcome preconceived prejudices as to what a gaming experience should be like and can simply bask in the magic of the dream world, and its exquisite music, for single glorious hour. I have never before regretted buying something on sale, why oh why can't I pay more for this game?

Let me start by saying, that I personally am a huge fan of "To the Moon" also made by this developer.  "A Bird Story" however falls far short of my expectations, and is frankly more of a short low graphic film than an actual game.
To be completely honest, this game has few redeeming qualities other than the soundtrack, and to some extent a better control system than what I experienced in "To the Moon".  The story line itself however, is much shorter, very confusing, and does not draw any sort of emotional connection, as I thought I would get after reading other reviews of this title.
I frankly am majorly disappointed by this title, and I hope that the developer can closer replicate the layers and intricacy of the story as seen in "To the Moon" before their next release.  My honest advice, would be to wait until they finish the sequal, as this is a pointless stepping stone that is both a waste of time and money.
Pros - Soundtrack, perfected control system of series
Cons - No emotional depth, Almost no player interaction, Short and dry
Overall - 2.5/10

This is not only a literal fact about the absense of written or spoken language, but also very much true of the emotional experience that it creates. In putting aside conventional story telling technique, A Bird Story takes a massive risk, but pulls it off amazingly
There's no manual to get a backstory from, and the interactive elements are extremely minimalist. Yet despite all that, those brief pieces of interactivity and choice are enough to make you feel emotionally invested in the story.
Kan Gao's musical score is superb, reminisent of those found in the SNES games of Squaresoft & Enix. More than that, though, the entire emotional pacing of the game is driven by expertly used audio cues and sountrack changes. It may not be one that you would listen to outside of the game, but you will want to own it none the less, so I strongly recommend picking it up too.
The lack of written word was hard at first, but it actually worked better than any prose could have. The player is put in the position of the child, with the world being confusing and scary, yet full of promise.
Much like Dys4ia and other works of interactive fiction, there will be debate as to if A Bird Story really counts as a game or not. But even if it doesn't, game developers could learn a lot by looking at what Freebird Games are doing

This game was advertised as a short story without any dialogue and barely any gameplay, and that is exactly what you will get.  It gets that fdone very well. Its easy to get immersed in the story specifically because there isnt any dialogue, you start to notice all the nuances of the main characters life. Because its a story with no dialogue, the creator of the game made it so that you wont get bored. This is done by putting omages to other games like Zelda and Mario in throughout and making the whole thing feel like a dream. You never know what will happen next because literally anything can happen. Thats what makes this adventure feel so great.
As far as the story itself, you start feeling a bond to the boy and the bird. Despite the dream-like feel of the game, these two characters feel very real and their problems are also real. This is an hour long tale of a lonely boy and a hurt bird which will leave you happy in the end.

Quake is one of those FPS games that got my blood flowing and my heart beating. There's a twinge of fear throughout the game, especially if you don't know what's ahead. At first the game feels like Doom with the way you can literally blast your way straight through enemies such as Grunts and Ogres (okay ogres take a little more ammo to kill), but then you meet a Fiend and it lunges and eviserates your armored *** the first time you meet it. Okay, you have to be more agile and careful than in Doom. When you can kill one of those things effectively, you'll find that was only the start of your combative worries.
The feel of the game's design is like Hell, a Catholic Cathedral, and a poorly maintained sewer system (swimming is a big part of the game) having a threesome and a subsequent love child. Now that you have the image of that child in your mind, teach it Lovecraftian lore and give it literally hundreds of vicious monsters as toys. Watch it give most of those monsters weapons that seem a bit out of place now that I think about it, and scatter the remaining weapons and ammunition it had around the floor, and hide away some of that remainder in camoflaged closets for safe storage. That is in essence is what Quake is all about.

Pretty fun horde survival RTS, a bit like the Zerg infested holdout missions from Starcraft but a hell of a lot more fleshed out.
You're thrown in a random generated map and have to survive a set amount of time, every few days you get attacked and each attack is stronger which means you have to expand, research and build more powerful units to survive, just like a standard rts game. There are different difficulties as well as maps of varying difficulty and you can also edit the amount of time you have to survive to win, so it's got difficulty progression in that sense.
A part of the game I really enjoy right now is that there is no savescumming at all, if you die you can't reload a save and try again, you're thrown right back into a new game with no chance to correct the mistake. This really forces you to learn to build a real defence, learn how to manage resources and thin out hordes because there's no option to just go back and fortify the point where you know the next horde will hit. However some more 'casual' players might not enjoy this too much.

One of my favorite games of 2014.  The game is not incredibly complex, but harkens back to games of old like the Wizardry and Might and Magic series (which the developers are admitted fans of).  The combat is fun and many fights require strategy to defeat without the fights being getting very repetitive.
Combat is a mix of random encounters and static encounters (which you can see on the map).  You can fight enough of the random encounters that they stop spawning (which gives you extra experience) - so they don't bother you forever.
The game is not flawless.  There are some points which are obvious road blocks which you aren't meant to pass without proceeding elsewhere (or levelling up) first.  That's fine - but there's not always an indication or hit of where to go next.  Some areas are intentionally meant to be time consuming to get through, such as the deserts and tundras which require tons of food to get through.
Regardless, a great fun game - especially for those who enjoyed the classic RPGs of the late 80s and early 90s.
One tip: Level your speed skill heavily on all characters (every level up, or close to every level up).
Great RPG.  Would recommend to RPG fans who are not afraid of a bit of a challenge.

I won't go into the general pros and cons of this game because everyone has covered them pretty exhaustively here and there's really no need for me to cover them again. However, I want to go over my own particular gripes with the game, not because I think my opinion will be of use to anyone, but because I want to express some small act of defiance for a purchase I regret.
I'll admit I didn't give the game much time, but it didn't take me long to figure out why I wouldn't like it. I create my characters, drop into the game, and find that my entire party is represented by some boring schmuck who proceeds to speak for everyone in the conversation that shortly ensues. What kind of roleplaying game lets you create a party and then sidelines them to focus on the blandest man in fantasyland? It appears to me that your characters have no presence in the story whatsoever, their only purpose being to back up the bog-standard chosen one in the combat sequences. Some may find this to be of little significance, but it really upset me. Polished, entertaining game.  Played through it straight twice, and I can see myself playing through it again in the future.
I could list some pro's and con's or repeat what others have already said, but instead I will highlight a few points which may clarify some of the mixed points you will see in other reviews.  The purpose, I hope, is to help potential buyers in figuring out the perspective from which other reviewers are coming from.
1.  The game is "linear" in that you are expected to go a certain path on the game world, but the path is not in a straight line.  This will throw off some players who are used to the typical themepark RPG set-up where the game holds your hand on how to get to the next area.
For a slightly spoiler-ish example:  Early on you will get a quest to kill a high level enemy blocking the road, a road which also leads to another part of the game map.  You are not supposed to kill said enemy at that point, as your party will get slaughtered.  A note tells there is a back way around, which is the intended path.  Thus, some players get "frustrated" by trying to brute-force their way through an encounter which is designed to be avoided until later.
The game has several of these set-ups (and honestly, get a bit predictable by the end).  If you are the type which prefers the modern take with quest compasses and the game telling you exactly where to go next, this will be a con.  If, however, you enjoy seeing the game map as a "puzzle" and discovering how to proceed to the next area, then don't mind this "con" you may see in other reviews.
It should also be noted that the game does drop clues on how to proceed, so it doesn't feel "cheap" as long as you are paying attention.  With the above example, there are 3 or 4 hints that try and tell you to take this back route.
2.  Difficulty.  The combat in this game is turn-based whack each other in the face.  Thus, like other games of this type, combat boils down to which side has the bigger numbers.  The discrepancy you will see in regards to difficulty comes from the game starting you out with "smaller numbers" than even the beginning fights, which may feel like it is overly difficult.
For better or worse, the way around this isn't necessarily advertised.  There are priests in each city which can apply a 24 hour (in-game time) blessing.  These blessings are very powerful early on, because they take your "small stack of numbers" and boost it up to the point where early fights are no longer overly challenging.
Thus, the best way to get through the early game, to get some early levels and gear on your characters to make fights manageable, is to quest in "bouts".  Apply a few blessings, then do a quest or clear an area.  Head back to town, heal up, re-apply blessings and head back out.  You won't need to keep doing this the whole game (in fact it would get extremely expensive and tedious), as later on they are not as needed, but they are the best, efficient way to start out.
So don't be fooled by reviews claiming the game is overly difficult or challenging.  The game does offer the tools needed, but the "flaw" is that the tools aren't exactly advertised well to the new player.  If you dive straight into the game without blessings, you will find the early game to be extremely unforgiving.  If you get past the early game, you will find the difficulty pacing more comfortable.  Perhaps even too easy.

Lords of Xulima (shoe-la-muh) is a 2D isometric post-modernist turn based fantasy RPG created by Numantian Games. The lands of Xulima are beautifully presented throughout impressive hand drawn backgrounds all covered in blood. I have not felt so satisfied since Ultima VII.
The core mechanics and combat are strikingly well implemented. Without respawning enemies of meaty experience, planning ahead is critical. The only way to progress is by becoming an armored armadillo rolling under / over / through every obstacle. This world is huge, but an unobservant party will miss a sprawling jungle behind one violently lonely rose.
Beatings received in Xulima scale well between game settings. I have found the most entertaining difficulty to be Hardcore mode with Ironman enabled. Characters in a party receive a fraction of leveling rewards while demonic cursed hounds might as well render themselves as earth moving ironclad tanks pounding out bolts of electric death.
Unfortunately, my Hardcore party hit an unstoppable spike in brutality after a solid thirty hours. I accepted their wonderful and savage defeat by transmigrationing them into a world filled with far less grim synergy. Veteran difficulty is the Goldilocks zone of Xulima and remains severely enjoyable. The difference being one is a world infested with flesh eating bears, while the other is merely plagued.

What a great game!
Starting with Splinter Cell on the PS2 at my cousins house, I have been introduced to the "Stealth Action" genre. Got my XBOX in 2004 and later Splinter Cell 3. Then I played THIEF (4). And then there was a drought of games like this. My cousin asks "Why don't you play Dishonored". Me: "Nah, it looks strange". 2 years later, I eventually tried it and - wow, such a good game!
~PERFORMANCE~
My system is an ACER PREDATOR built in 2012. It has a i7-3770, 16 GByte of RAM and a GTX970 working together.
Since the game came out in 2012 and the CPU as well the amount of RAM was good for that time as well as the GTX970 yet to come, I could play the game on MAX settings at 1080p with stable 60fps. Loading (off a HDD) takes several seconds, loading a savegame or entering a new part of the same map roughly 2 seconds.
~STORY~
The story starts out as a plot that reminds me of some Harrisson Ford movie: You are accussed of murdering the Empress and kidnapping of her daugther Emily - and getting jailed, tortured and are about to get executed. A mysterious organization frees you and set up a list of people that need to get killed in order to restore justice. And you are the one that has to eliminate these ladies and gentlemen. But the times are rough and of course, the whole thing spins a bit out of control...
I personally liked the story and I often felt like "Payback time". The writing makes you really feel you are doing the right thing for you, the town and Emily. I was also actually surprised how the story turned and did not quite expect that, so it's not a game that boringly goes on and on but made me really play every day to see what♥♥♥♥♥♥will happen next.
~GAMEPLAY~
The game is being played in first person view and this works pretty well (also a reason why I bought it in the first place). There is a safe zone in the abandoned part of the city and there is your bed and a way to restore your supplies with gold found in the game. The actual missions are started by talking to boat driver Samuel.
The game has some sort of "open world" city of Dunwall going on, a plague-riddled, rat infested place with a now-paranoid government. You, as escaped inmate, are of course immediately attacked when being seen, so try to be undercover...
...which I failed at. I found myself shooting the first pair of guards and expected GAME OVER as I know from other stealth games. But no, the game kept going. And this is what I really like about this game: There is no restriction on how you play: You can make your way trough the levels silently, you can take out enemies by knocking them out - or by using your pistol, blade, crossbow, grenades and mines. The difference is the so-called "Chaos factor". The more you kill, the more changes the world. E.g. more guards. But that's it. In fact, I liked my high chaos run (I killed almost everyone hostile) and the way the city turns into a even more dark, paranoid version is a nice idea.
The whole idea however is not gamebreaking in any way. When I read that it'd cause the game to become "darker", "more violent" etc. I thought the developers want to be the moralist voice on "killing ain't good, man". But in the end, the "high chaos" ending was reasonable, e.g. Samuel, the boat driver, basically telling that I turned into a monster and behaved like a♥♥♥♥♥♥in the last mission. There are several changes that I just read off, but I am fine with my High Chaos ending.
Killing your victims always is a joy, they all have this "You deserved it!" feel. Also, the way the wanted posters and the ambient chatter start to change (about people fearing the guy in a mask that killed person X last night) adds to the immersion. There are many civilians out there that can also be killed, but usually just panic and hide.
You are also free at your mission when it comes to movement: You can steal a key off a guard (that has been either knocked out or by sneaking up him and taking the key off of his belt) and walk trough the side door, you can try the roof, a ventilation shaft, the sewer, an open window from an adjacent building. You see, it's pretty neat. Or you just can shoot down 25 guards with blazing gun and wade trough a pile of bodies. It's up to you! :-)
The levels and the city are very, very well designed! Especially the fancy dress party of Lady Boyle were beautiful visually and audio-wise. Nice lighting effects, too!
~COMBAT~
The first person combat was a bit weird at the first moment, because I found it a bit strange because I wield 2 weapons at once: In the left hand there is a selectable weapon or item (grenades, crossbow, mines etc.) and the right hand is always your blade/sword/dagger. So you basically fight with two weapons at once by pressing the corresponding trigger. Later in the game I grew to this idea and it works out very well, even though a bit unrealistic (reloading one-handed while having a blade fight...?). But it plays very well to block a guards sword attack, swing at him and while he is tumbling I turn a bit to the right and fire my pistol at another guy that charges towards me. Meanwhile, I finish off the other guard and take care of his buddy as well.
The amount of guards walking around (and attacking) can be overwhelming, and you know what? That's good! You are not invincible, and thinking you are Arnold Schwarzenegger will lead to a fast game over screen. The combat never feels unfair, even when I fought like 8 guys at once of which 2 were shooting at me from a balcony. What I really enjoy is the fact that what happens to the enemy can also happen to you: E.g. when you blast a foe with your pistol, he is stunned for a second and recovers. This is the time when you can finish him off. However, this can happen to you as well: Getting blasted turns your screen red and you can not fire or move for the next second. Or that the enemies also throw grenades at you in the first mission already, the same you can do after picking them up. This way, it feels like a good 1vs1 and not a "I kill you anyways" situation like in other games. You are not superman, right?
Well, not quite, because you also get super powers that consume mana. These powers include teleporting, bullet time modes and such. I actually just used the teleport ability. In general the combat is very fun and you are free to place traps and knock out guys or just bomb your way trough the levels.
~CHARACTERS~
The main character, Corvo Attano, well... I never really could get into this guy. He never talks, the only time you hear him is when in pain, but that's all. I don't know how I look like, I don't know anything, there is no mirror. The only way I know he/I loook/s like is the artwork. That could be done better...The mirrors are also blind you never see yourself. Eh. id Software used that for DooM in 1993 and said "We don't give the Doomguy a story because he is supposed to be YOU", well, I think this is the same. Since Corvo can be pacifist or spree killer, I think it was understandable design-wise, but still, I feel like Corvo is nothing more than a pair of floating hands on my screen. I can not even see my feet - I know, it sounds strange, but I don't like games that do that. It's like a floating camera with two hands on a stick in front of it hovering trough the levels. More "head movement" or hand animations would've helped a lot!!
~SOUND~
There is nothing special around. Actually, I hear too many stock sounds (footsteps on sand and grass are the HOGS OF WAR footstep sounds....) But the ambient dialogue is always combined by a bunch of random words. Guard A says something, and guard B replies. Both is picked by a pool of lines and combined result in new "dialogues". The way the announcements on the speakers make you feel like you have an impact: News on your recently assassinated victim are heard on the streets and such are nice.
I always turn off music and just play with ambient sounds, and it works very well in this game!

Hearts Of Iron 4 is a world war two grand strategy game where you take on the role as the head of state of a country. Choose any country you like and see how well you lead it through the turbulent thirties and fourties.
You are given a decent amount of control over your armed forces. Divisions are put into armies, which on their turn are put in theaters. When you have amassed your forces you are able to draw up battle plans, which will let you order your forces in huge numbers. You set up the front lines, offensive lines, fallback lines and much more. Once you activate your plan, all of your attached units will automatically spring into action and will only stop once you say them to stop. If you don't like this much automation, you can still manually take control of you units and armies.
In contrast to previous Hearts Of Iron games there is no real hierarchy system. Lavish order of battle are a thing of the past and in my opinion that is a shame. As a result there is less emphasis on battlefield strategy. Victory on the battlefield is not won by swift moves and cunning tricks but with gaining the upper hand in terms of troop concentration and having a good mixture of units on the right time. In short, it is more a simulation of a country at war rather than a true war simulation
Hearts Of Iron 4 does do a lot of thing right though. It streamlines a lot of the archaic gaming notions into a more understandable system. This makes controling your nation a lot easier while not oversimplifying the simulation side of it. It almost plays like a big, utterly complex, boardgame.

Just like Civilization, Hearts of Iron IV is much more fun with a friend than it is in the random online lobbies you'll come across, but the single player is still enjoyable on its own. First things first:
This is an Early Access Review.  Meaning, I had a foolish moment of weakness where I pressed the "Purchase" button, while knowing perfectly well what a dissapointing and/or frustrating experience these have historically been for me.
That said, I am reviewing this through the lens of "Early Access".
Let's get the suspense over with right away.  This game is incredible, all things considered.
I wouldn't even be entirely unhappy with it, if this was it's retail-release version.  I've spent a few hours a night for the last couple weeks playing it, and I still have loads more to do.  I havn't even started with the multiplayer yet, which I expect will renew the experience all over.
There have been AAA games out there with less content and entertainment value at launch than this game in it's current state.
And for all those Devil's Advocate people:  Yes, there are bugs. (besides the ones that you can crush with your conduit bender)
Invisible walls in space, if you park too close your ship can attach itself to an asteroid, custom structures can't be pressurized, robot assistants vibrating and dropping through the ground, and some minor issues with object placement and camera behaviour.
There are a number of features that do not work yet as intended, but are in the works.
Bottom line, none of these are "game breaking" and most have been acknowledged and been given a work-around.
FYI: 35 hours in, and the game has not crashed once, or even bogged down.  It runs amazingly well even for long sessions.
I don't know much about Fenix Fire (the Developers), beyond that of their "about us" page, but if thier small team is capable of this kind of work, at the same time as maintaining great quality control and community interaction, the final product of Osiris: New Dawn, will undoubtedly be a Must-Have for everyone who enjoys this genre (and likely convert a few who typically don't!)
What initially was an impulse purchase during a Steam-sale, has turned into a Genuine desire for this game to become an overwhelming success and achieve everything they outlined in their vision.
Keep up the great work! I'm looking forward to every update.

Nutshell: 9/10 - Really nice classic game, graphics may be dated, but it sure is a fun game, just make sure to read through some of my fixes to common bugs.
Setup - 10/10 - Pretty simple, took, like, 2 seconds to install (50MB isn't exactly a big game, trust me 50MB was like 50GB back in the day, a lot of the simple stuff in this game were a huge deal back when it was released)
Will it Run on My Computer? - 10/10 - As long as you use a windows computer, it should run, in terms of how hard it is to run, well, if your computer can run steam and view this review I'm writing, your computer probably can handle Quake.
Bugs - 8/10 - Easily fixable bugs, first thing, close out ALL windows and the steam program before playing (double click the desktop shortcut, don't click the "play" button in the steam program), it won't crash the game, but once you exit the game, you will find that you can't view any tabs that you left open, if this happens, just restart your computer and problem solved, it's an easily preventable bug so I'm not complaining too much.
Optimization - 9/10 - Only thing I think is truly lack of optimization is the maximum resolution this game supports (1024x768p, cheap laptop users rejoice because it'll look just fine on a 768p screen), it's not a problem, but it'll just look a little pixelated, this isn't a problem, it's just resolutions this low don't look great on 1080p monitors, or even worse, 4K monitors, if you got a cheap laptop with an only 768p monitor, I actually recommend you play it on that computer due to 768p looking better on a 768p monitor. another thing people might complain about optimization-wise is that you use arrow keys, esc, and enter to navigate the menu screen, and also that you cannot look up or down with the mouse (only side-to-side), but I won't count that as lack of optimization because back in the day this was completely normal and it would probably be buggy if you modded the game to use modern control schemes.
Graphics - 7/10 - Yeah, graphics don't look great, but this was from 1997, back in the day, graphics like this were almost unheard of on PC, this game truly was an early pc-master-race game.
Gameplay - 8/10 - On singleplayer, this game is just great, best 6-7 hours of gameplay I've had in a while. only thing I think you should realize, is the online community is DEAD, there is no real multiplayer anymore, to play online, you will need to have your friend come to your house, log their computer on to your wifi, then play a local server, essentially, the odds of finding someone else to play with are slim, and you should accept that.
Test of Time - 8/10 - So far, this game is exactly 20 years old, though it's graphics are REALLY dated, the game is still fun to play, so it scores well on the test of time.
Overall - 9/10 - Really good, you know a game is good if 20 years after release it's still fun to play.

Did a lot of digging into the game systems and now I finally finished the release version.
My final conclusion is: LoX is a very combat centric game similar to Might and Magic X – if you like that, you will probably like LoX. If you expect a deep story with choices you will not like LoX.
A summary of Pros and Cons:
Pros:
-Character system is well designed, gives you a lot of choice. Distinctive and relatively well balanced classes.
-Combat System which is easy to get into, while offering a good amount of tactical options
-Big game world with different areas, explation is fun.
Cons:
-The Stoy is badly written. You do not have any choices and your main character's conversations tend to be very silly.
-Overview of Skills is not existant in the game. You have to use external information, which is cruicial on higher difficulty levels.
-The game slightly pushes to into "grinding" enemies.
-Food mechanic: You can save a lot of money by spending 5 minutes per hour for gathering food. This is not adding anything to the game but a time sink.
-In the last third of the game you have a couple of "hard fights" which block your path, after which you have to kill a lot of trash which is not challenging you at all.
-Difficulty Curve within the game isn't optimal: It's hard in the beginning and gets easier.

WOW....where do I even begin...After 124 hours of playing Dishonored I am done. Completly done.
I started of playing the game in 2015, and I think I must have finished alot of the story, until I just quit one day. The icon laid on my desktop for almost 2 years, until I wanted to try it again, and boy it's been a long ride!
Now when I started I didn't know so much, so I just kept playing. Even deleted my old saves to start over again. As I am a big fan of achievements, I started looking at some of them, but didn't really care that much until I was done with my first playthrough. The good thing with Dishonored is that you litterary never get tired of playing it, no matter how many times you replay most of the game.
MAIN GAME:
Follow Corvo through his story about the rise and fall in the empire. Fight guards, weepers, rats and meet some very interesting people. You decide the outcome of the game by who you kill or not, and the amount of it. Some people like to just slash their way through the game, but I loved the clean hands and sneaking. Many cool levels and ways of getting to your goal. Gaining new magic skills makes the gameplay even cooler...and you will probably go "how did I get away with that?" Playing stealthy makes it absolutly awesome, and your heart beats a little bit faster when you wonder if they will see you in the next second or not. The game will be alot shorter for those who just fight their way through the game.
I'm not gonna say much more about the 2 DLCs that it involves a hired killer Daud, and it's a continuation of the game from his point of view, up to the level where he meets Corvo. Many cool levels and ways of playing the game.
NOW! The final DLC....Dunwall City Trials. I'm not sure how much time I have spent on getting to finish the rest of the achievements in the game, but it took quite some time. Many hundred tries, sweat and screaming to the monitor, and frustration over things not working as they should. It was fun, in it's own way...I gotta admit it, but when I now just recently before writing this review finished the last one, I am very sure that now it's time to end it, and play something else. For the achievement hunters this is the one. Gain these achievements, and you have actually done something really really hard. Practicing alot and tons of patience is required to finish these, unless you are very lucky or a natural.
ALL IN ALL! I've had tons of fun. I've killed tons of people, but also let them live. I made alot of decisions, loaded the game ALOTS of times to make it go my way. There has been frustrations with alot of things I am not gonna mention here. Might be bugs, or bad coding, but overall...there isn't much to say about Dishonored that is wrong. Being an assassin with superpowers is awesome, and there is so many ways to do it too. Bethesda always makes games that makes me spend over 100 hours on a single game, simply because I don't get tired. Achievements are involved too, and I think they made the game better.
Not everyone is so thorough, as I have been in most games I play, and it's entirely up to you how much time you wanna invest in this game! So if you haven't already got this game, go get it and play it! I highly recommend it!

This game has some potential, but it needs major gameplay tuning.
2 friends and I played the game together for about 4 hours.
In the beginning, the game tells you to hike ~2000m to the first Osiris base mission. On the way, you innevitably lose the robot when it runs out of power.
None of the enemies on the surface are particularly scary, you can always just evade them and mine somewhere else. The worm scares you at first, but it only dives at you once, then that's it.
It doesn't feel like a survival game, an occassional alien will wander into your base, but there are no organized attacks that we noticed. There's no reason to build the shody space debris stuff in your crafting tab. The game needs to make night much scarier to give the players a reason to shelter at night.
We built the initial stuff, Habitat, Furnace, Forge, Printer, Chem Statiton. Our goal was to build a vehicle so we could do an expedition to look for Lithium, which we weren't finding. But when we realized how much Gold we needed and how low the drop rate was from Precious Metal nodes, we decided the game was becoming too much of a grind.
I had hopes based on one guide that robots could do mining for us; maybe even target certain resources. I found my robot control panel, saw my robot was out of power, and ran back to my robot's coordinates. For some reason, these coordinates were for a Forge in Osiris, not my robot. I'm not sure if this was a bug with waypoints or my robot was inside the Forge. Nothing in the skill tree indicates you can build robots. Maybe the Laboratory lets you, but at this point we were unimpressed and frustrated and didn't want to grind to build the Lab.
Suggestions:
* Make nodes drop a single resource identifable with mouse-over. Get rid of the random drop mechanic when hitting a node. Cluster nodes of a type together more. Allow the scanner to filter on certain resource types.
* Reduce the material requirements for most things by at least half. Or provide a tutorial/mission for how to build and organize robots to gather and refine materials for you.
* Make the aliens more interesting. Hunting behavior, group behavior, different behavior at night.

It has a nice aesthetic. The Space Age is primed for this type of alien invasion story, flying saucers and all. It's also a functional third-person cover shooter.
Too bad it was made by people who apparently don't know how games work. Outside of the poor optimization of the PC version, the game offers repetitive gameplay, generic mechanics and an ambitious "commander" system. In said system, the player can give orders on the battlefield to his two squad-mates, which range from basic "kill that" to some nifty tricks and alien tech. Unfortunately, in order to use this system efficiently, you need someone to design good maps and whoever designed this game's maps was high on that day.
Bad enemy placements, terrible cover positions and an idiotic AI. For the most part, one can ignore the many faults if they choose to just immerse themselves in the 1960s setting; but then, the final mission comes. The final mission, which involves a large map, where cover is useless, where the stronger enemies can cover distance you can't via super-jumps and in which both shooting and planning are thrown out the window. It's a mayhem that throws the player off, a sensory overload that makes the experience anything from tedious, to absolutely, physically painful.
There is hard and then there is unbalanced; this is what this game is. It's painfully clear that, in order to increase difficulty, the designers thought they'd just throw everything in, including the kitchen sink. It's telling that the stage plays practically the same regardless of Difficulty Level. Doesn't matter if you play on Easy or Hard; what hinders your progress is that you need to employ stiff controls to be constantly on the move while everything's shooting at you. It's a cover-based shooter that suddenly decides to undo its core mechanic. It's like playing Super Mario Bros and the devs suddenly deciding that you need to sneak up on Bowser and snuff his life out with a dagger, because it's a stealth game now. No planning, no strategizing, just sheer laziness.
I guess you can still get the game on a sale; it's the type of title that's good enough for 2-5 bucks. I still wouldn't recommend it, though. It'sa game which, after the experience is over, you feel like you have wasted way too much time for little-to-no reward.
