I got into this thinking it was going to be another turn-based tactical game, but I was pleasantly surprised. It turns out it's a TPS where you can slow time and issue commands to your three-man squad while moving around and shooting the faces off of aliens. Much like the other XCOM games, you and your comrades can activate skills which you acquire by levelling through a skill tree based on your class. Also like the other XCOM games, there's a cover system.
Overall, the game was fun, and the mechanics felt fresh. It's like experiencing XCOM through the eyes of a field agent, and that's awesome. With all that said, the game had two main drawbacks. The biggest one is that your followers are clinically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They're highly inaccurate with weapons, they have a tendency to run straight into enemy fire or out of advantageous positions, and they often do stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥like dive away from a grenade and then run straight back into its blast radius. As a result, you have to micromanage them just to keep them alive, using them mainly for their abilities or to draw fire. That isn't to say they don't do damage; you just can't trust them to take down any enemy on their own, so your strategy generally ends up revolving around you personally taking out key targets. The second issue is more minor: movement is clunky, at least on the PC. Part of it has to do with it being a TPS, but there are other problems as well. As far as I know, in order to jump over a wall, you need to take cover behind it first. Also, when you're sprinting, you automatically take cover behind any wall or obstacle you run into, which is frustrating when that either causes you to get killed or fail to revive an ally before he bleeds out. I feel like this could have been avoided this if the button for taking cover wasn't the same as the button for sprinting.
I feel like the game would have been a lot better if you could at least tell a follower to hold a position, take cover without firing, or provide cover fire (along with an improvement in follower accuracy). Too often, an ally gets killed because you can't tell him not to move or not to shoot. And without using any abilities, you have to personally provide cover fire for your allies in order to have them move safely to another location.
Overall though, I had fun so I'm giving this a thumbs up. The only thing is that since it's so short, I recommend that you try to get it at a cheaper price than $20.

I am actually on the borderline of not recommending it. I preordered this game way back, played it for 3 hours (most of it was me tryiong to fix many technial issue I had), and hated it. But upon trying it again... It's actually okay.
Here's the deal. Have you played Mass Effect? Saw the tactical squad combat and thought "wow, I wish I could use this system more rather than blasting everything"? That is what this game is. Set in the 1960's with XCOM enemies. Basically your team's survival depends on you using the slow-down time tactical cover shooting.
The problem is, I often find my squadmates immediately running from cover, in order to stay close to me. Which means they get shot. They also like to keep peaking over cover to shoot at the enemy, even has they are almost dead. Making them get shot.
However, I also found this was only much an issue in the first few hours before your squadmates level up and you start getting better equipment. At that point, along with you being able to decrease the charge time on your group heal, it becomes much easier to manage. That is when the game starts to become enjoyable.
Another problem is the controls. They can be wonky occasionally. There's also a problem with the audio that I cad to fix. Basically the game tried to play 5.1 audio when I have headphones, making all the sounds sound either really quiet and tinny, or completely deafen me dispite my audio settings. I had to go into my audio devices and disable everything that wasn't my headphones, and that fixed it.
TL;DR It's okay, doesn't desearve a lot of the hate it gets, but it's not great. Just forget that it has 'XCOM' in the subtitle and force yourself though the first couple hours and you're good. Buy it on sale.

So, thanks to a friend of mine and Humble Bundle, I got my first game in this series that I had always thought of playing but never had the monies to buy this, as this wasn't really something I had a really big interest in to put it in top priority in my low amount of purchases.
So I decided to install it and give it a try. Here's what I got:
Simple menu, few options, few graphical options (I have a really low-end gaming machine. How low is that? A first-gen i5 and a GeForce 9500GT, so the first thing I do when I start up a new game is set everything to low), and could even rebind every single control in the game.
Time to dive in.
Game starts, some interest sparks in me and I decide to even let the cinematics kick in and introduce me into the game. Not anything big happens, some strange stuff, old guy telling a story. Yeah, that sounds okay. Cinematics end, first mission. Run around the icy field, through aliens called "Akrid", to try to find a piece to repair the vehicle I'm in. Clichéd enough, a guy with a terrible french accent saves me in his giant mech. Woo. I do some more stuff and go to the base where the expedition is located.
First thing I decide to do is wonder around the base. I find it to be quite big, but unnecessary to have three floors and to access each of them I had to take an elevator ride that puts me in a loading screen. And yeah, I saw an unnecessary amount of those during my 25 hours of gameplay. I do my stuff and get my first real mission, to get my "rig", which is basically a giant mech without any real weapons, and go outside the base to find out where the heck the guy that saved me in the start was, since he wasn't answering his radio. Of course he was having troubles. Of course I was going to be the hero since the first mission in the game, but actually, who cares? It's an AAA game anyways, so I was expecting that. That's how I get introduced in the gameplay. Walking around the snowy world in my rig (in first person!) felt really good for the couple of hours. I felt protected, I felt like nothing could stop me. Then I help the guy and shoot some aliens around. This leads to my first encounter with real animations, models and textures.
Everything looks really great. Animations aren't all f*cked up or just plain bad, they're acceptable and I have nothing to complain about it. The models are quite detailed, each enemy type is quite well-detailed and has a unique feel to them, not like they were copy-pasted from eachother and just a few things added/removed. Textures? They look quite good too.
Some hours in and I could already talk about the gameplay itself. I was thrown in an open-world, quite big levels with transitions from one to the other. Everything looks majestic and you feel like you're but an ant in there. What do I see? A lot of snow. It got me tired at some point but I couldn't complain about it because it really adds something to the atmosphere. And of course not everything was cold. But the landscapes... Wow. I was truly amazed by some of the stuff I saw and it really kept me going, so a point to level design.
What about quests? Yeah, there are some. Just A VERY few to be honest. And they most of the time require traveling around (thank god they put some half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quick travel) and seeing loads of loading screens. Yes, I will ♥♥♥♥♥ about loading screens throughout the review because really, there are just so many of them. From my total time, I bet you that AT VERY LEAST 2-3 hours were wasted summing up the loading screens. But some of them add up to the atmosphere and to the story. And they encourage two different things, exploration and hunting an specific type of enemy. At least a way of farming some money fast.
About the action... Well, there are two types of action in this game: The third person one, which is always with your main character; and the First Person one, which is with your rig. Yeah, your rig doesn't have weapons but it has it's tools which you'll use to crush some aliens. The third person fights are quite okay. Not much different from other third person shooters, so there is cover-based shooting, enemies have armor and weakspots (most of them need to be hit in the weakspot to take damage), you feel progression and new ways of fighting with new weapons that are gradually introduced to the game, and the AI is quite good, REALLY good. The first person fights are... bad. They could have been MUCH better. You're in a friggin' mech and the only way of doing harm to most enemies you'll face in it is through quicktime events that are triggered by countering their attacks (basically press a key when the enemy is about to hit you to trigger it) and then doing something that you are supposed to find out by yourself. It took me more than 20 minutes of trying to kill one kind of enemy before figuring out I was supposed to press forward after grabbing him. How the heck was I supposed to know that? I needed to seriously button-mash to find out what I was supposed to do after countering him, which was a really big let down.
The story itself goes uphill as the game goes on. It starts off really slow, and then with every main quest it starts going up and then something kinda predictable happens in a very unpredictable moment, so yeah, the story starts taking off from there and it starts to get interesting. Then, later into the game there's another moment kinda like this that I really enjoyed. I was actually really surprised, but nothing much happens after that. If you want to know if I liked it, well, actually I did. It was fun(ny), just don't expect anything out of it and you might actually enjoy as much as I did.
What did I not like about the game? I'm a b*tch for sounds. The Akrid have a lot of similar sounds to eachother, so you will not get that interested about them. The music is okay, there's even a small playlist for you to listen inside the rig, but I turned the music volume off after the first hours of gameplay and just put in some post-rock and shoegaze to feel better. Then we have the voice acting. The protagonist's voice is quite good, but the rest is total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Basically all of the other guys have really stupid accents thrown in their voices, like that french accent I said earlier, a mix of "COD-like" russian and "generic german" in quite a few characters, some "asian" guy with bad lines. Most of the lines were quite bad and the game itself made fun of them in quite a few ways.
So, summing it all up:
PROS:
CONS
TL;DR: I can surely recommend this game if you like normal games and if you feel that you won't be getting an amazing experience. Just think of this game as it had another name, like "Cold Space World" and you can even forget it's not a Lost Planet game and have some fun if you're a fanboy.

Rather than writing a standard review i'd like to focus on how the game lost my interest by noting it's many flaws in a quick easy to read format.
-Ultra compressed and ugly pre-rendered cinematics often interrupt game and should have been in-engine.
-Poor enemy AI that's worse than prior games. Roller akrids will stop aiming at you if you side dodge no matter how far away.
-No jump button so you often have to take the long away around knee high rubble.
-No crouch button, it happens automatically and takes away your ability to shoot to be "cinematic"
-Can't use grapple hook whenever you want, only when prompted by QTE.
-Can't fall off ledges or fall to your death, invisible walls everywhere.
-Stupid random QTE sequences with generic enemies and environment that aren't fun.
-Spaghetti space western atmosphere in how people talk and in the music. I hate that crap personally.
-No "VS" to pilot, only the "rig" which is for QTE boss fights, environmental QTE and slooooow mandatory transportation.
-Unnecessary hub at base and "open world" that's really not very open but just waste your time.
-Screen jelly HP regen, T-Eng no longer keeps you alive, it's just a form of currency to buy stuff.
-Characters are generic and unattractive. Lack of Japanese design philosophy shows and no one is iconic looking.
-Akrids all look worse than previous games, once again, lack of Japanese design philosophy.
-Story was giving off some Dead Space vibe but not sure if it elaborates on it or not since I quit playing.
-No cool boss fights. I left the best for last because Lost Planet has always been known for awesome bosses.
In conclusion, I much prefer the Japanese developed LP1/LP2 which are quirky, imperfect but FUN and replayable. If you like Japanese game design more then you'll probably despise Lost Planet 3 with every fibre of your being. It abandons the arcade shooter roots, the cool boss fights, the over the top action and the cool mechs. This game is definitely aimed more toward the crowd who loves "narrative driven cinematic experiences" and doesn't mind having their hand held with mediocre gameplay. If you come into this game only caring about the story you'll probably have a good time judging by some of the positive reviews.

In this game there are four hunters that fight against a monster. In the main game mode, which is called "hunt" the purpose of the hunters is to prevent the monster from destroying a "relay" in a specified amount of time; the monster wins if it manages to have all players incapacitated at the same time, or if it destroys this "relay" after it evolves to stage 3. The monster, is controlled by a human player in a 3rd person perspective, starts at stage 1 and it needs to eat wildlife to evolve. With each stage the monster is more powerful and you get to improve some of its potential abilities. The 4 hunters, which have a 1st person perspective, are from 4 distinctive classes: "assault" is a tank and damage dealer, "medic" is a healer, "support" helps in different ways, and "trapper" is specialized in tracking the monster. When in rage, the hunters can "dome" the monster to force a fight; the "dome" is like a huge temporary cage.
I love the concept and the adrenaline of playing monster. They made the game more dynamic with a lot more action but sneaking also has a role. The diversity in characters, including monsters, is decent. The number of maps is really small and contributes to the making the game seem repetitive after a while. Also it kind of lacks an end goal for the player, except maybe getting all characters. If you stumble on a founders key (these are no longer sold by the developers), then you'll get a ton of characters and a lot of other rewards. The game had a huge problem with the cheaters but they are still present to some degree and it's very difficult to report them.
Before starting a game, you need to choose some perks for you character. There are three tiers of perks and you can pick one from each tier. Also each perk has three levels which makes them better. This is great because it enhances the diversity of the characters even more. But I think it's a very bad thing that they are unlockable (by character leveling or buying them with in game credits) because some people can get in a game with better perks than some other people that didn't unlocked them, but at least they are not purchasable with "gold" credits (that can be bought with real money).
Rating: Here comes the tickle monster!
Recommendation: Very interesting "free to play" game, well worth a (free) shot.

Im very reluctant to give this game a negative review. Very reluctant. I love the gameplay to death. Its one of the few that keeps my interest for long. The grind is not as bad as people are saying. They give a lot of free content including characters and perks ETC. The key cost of stuff is only the tip of the iceberg and the truth is you get pile of them for the various accolades, character progression, account progression and even just logging in.
Where this game fails for me tho is the division of the community and the toxicity and terrible balance thats caused. The devs were too quick to throw out massive nerfs for monsters and large buffs for hunter. Everything from queueing solo to their perks. I can list tons of them and most hunters quick excuses will be that hunters were nerfed too and thats true.... sorta.. just their nerfs were considerably smaller and theyve been given enormous generic buffs in other areas. My theory is that since the hunters are the majority of the playerbase they get the most attention and TRS is very hesistant to do any nerfs at all. Even the new monster perks have drawbacks mostly where hunter perks almost never do.
Monster players have been screaming to do something about Sunny for months and absolutely nothing is done. The way it is now theres pretty much two types of battles you will get. Battles against noobs or mid tier players with odd ball mixed comps. Sad to say these are the most interesting, not because they are noobs (often they aren't) but because you at least have a chance and the battle is probably going to be a fun, close and intense match where even if you lose you walk away satisfied.
The other much less pleasant kind of battle are with veteran players who will only run the absolute best chase comp they can and the entire match will be spent with them on your♥♥♥♥♥knowing you will never get away to feed or evolve.
- You get knocked off food with minimal damage
- You know that even if you sprint across the map to try and evolve they will be on you in seconds
- Depending on the monster you are playing you might not have hope at all
- They have solo queue buffs that give them more speed and health and jetpack
- Maps are far too small to really escape
- There is no stealth. Now and then you might get a lucky juke but against skilled players they pretty much know where you are
What is the point of having a bunch of characters if hunters only ever use like... 6? They will do everything to defend their precious comp all the while trolling the monster players they stomp on. It was enjoyable shortly after they released stage 2. Now... not so much.
Its free tho so give it a try and see for yourself. The early play is not indicative of the total experience though. Monsters are only really strong against new players. Beyond that... it can be hell. Im not a terrible player and i don't mind losing but being harrassed and crapped on is no fun. The way you lose has an impact on the experience you have.

Wow what a gem of a game. I buyed it because i liked the cool Steam-Punk setting and i am also a huge Fan of RTS games and the idea to be constant the defender of always stronger hordes of enemys is something i have also not seen in any RTS games so far,  so i thought i give it a try. Because honestly i really dislike anything that has to do with zombies, let it be movies or games, so i thought at first that this szenario will kill my interest immediatly.
Boy was i wrong.
This game is very addicting. But not because you have to grind something, but really just, because its a lot of fun. But its not a game for everyone, so i try to explain for which kind of persons it is...and for who it isnt.
The game is very VERY hard. Especially at the first 10 tries, while you still figure out how everything works. One huge reason for that is that there is currently no tutorial, so you have to figure out everything by yourself, or you have to search for youtube tutorials for yourself. But honestly i highly advise against it...because it will destroy much of the fun that you get (more to this topic later)
Also the game is very punishing: One zombie who infected a single tent is often enough to kill your whole base, so that you loose. Why? Because once a zombie infect a building, every worker in it is becoming infected and start to attack other buildings. And since the infection spreads VERY quickly and the buildings are very clumpt, this means that just in a couple of secounds you dont have to fight one slow zombie but a hord of 1000 former worker zombies...and you will most likely not have the firepower to kill them all before they kill your headquarter which leads to a defeat.
Also this game is a roguelike: While a game least depending on your difficulty (the more time you have before the final wave attacks, the easier is the game) from 2-5 hours (in which you can of course end the game and continue sometimes else...you dont have to play it for 5 hours straight) a single mistake will force you to start all over again....and especially at the beginning where you figure out how the Zombie AI works and how to expand your base, you will make mistakes. So if you are getting quickly frustrated by loosing, i really dont recommand the game for you, since as long as you dont just copy a perfect build from a Youtube-Pro, you will loose...over and over again.
What you shouldnt worry about though is the RTS aspect (in the case that you are unfamiliar with RTS or you werent very good in RTS games before) because while it is a RTS game and enemys can and will attack you from different directions at once while you are still forced to continue to expand...you still dont need any high APM (ActionsPerMinute) like a Star Craft professional to play it. Because you can pause the game at every secound and give all your units commands without  having to fear that you will be owerwhelmet while you thing of the perfect solution how to defend the attacks.
In general i wouldnt really call the game a RTS. But rather an survival base-building game, because in my oppinion it has way more similarities to an Anno, or an Sim Cites, than to a Age of Empires, because while you still can micro your units, and play different strategies, the focus is still way more on the side of "how do i build up my economy most efficient" than a "with which strategie do i overwhelm the enemy" Because you need a very good economy to survive the final wave, which means that you have to expand. You cant just zerg-rush the enemy like in a "real" RTS. Also the strategie part is very thin: to fight back the enemy zombies, you have only 6 different units to choose from, and also 3 different towers to kill the zombies and also a few traps and walls to slow the enemy down. So you dont really have much strategical choice of how to defend: you always have to tech up, build walls, build the same units every game, and the differences of the games develop out of the maplayout, since its always random regenerated, so you always have to think anew, where to place the walls, where to expand first, where to send patroling my guards etc.
On the other hand, the economycal part is really complex, you have 7 different resources to manage (food, money, energy, wood, stone, iron, oil) buildings that increase the production of certain other buildings that you have to place smart to make the most output, research buildings, storage builings, you have to tech up to survive the later and bigger waves, but then you also want to increase your money, and its situations like this who makes the most part of the game.
So you really learn with each game how to build your base more and more efficient, always trying to improve the future builds more and more. And this is also the reason why i highly recommend you, to NOT watching any tutorial videos on youtube, because once you have figured the perfect build for every situation out (or copyt it from an already experienced player) the game can be quite repetitive, since it is exactly the task, to find a better solution and to improve your base more and more, what makes the most fun. Also it is very satisfying to see, how you improve from every single game ending mistake that you made, to hopefully be wiser in the future. But until you figure the basebuilding aspect out well enough to figure out how to survive/win the game on the easiest difficulty, you will have countless numbers of defeats, so you really have to bring the will to improve from your mistakes to really enjoy the game.
Also the game is still in EA, a campain and hopefully a tutorial that explains you already how every unit works is still in developing, so that the frustration for new players, to loose over and over again even on the easiest difficulty should become less if you wait a little bit with buying. But i highly doubt that it will become an easy game, the game is very hard, and very punishing and it is ment to be so.
So if you enjoy the idea, of improving your base more and more to survive a little bit longer on every try, to finally beat the game (it took me about 24 hours to win the game once...and i dont know how many tries) while planning your defences and expansion to hold the horde of enemys back that are becoming stronger with every minute. But if you are getting frustrating with defeats, and are looking for an instantly rewarding experience, i would recommend to search somewhere else, because in this case you will get very frustrated by the high difficulty (even on the easiest settings) of this game.

The game doesn't hold your hand and I love it. There are times were I had no clue what to do or where to go (sometimes due to my own fault, not properly reading what was in front of my eyes!), so I'd visit a zone 2/3 times eventually giving up and reading the forums (most of the time I figured it out tho).
So if you are a person that gets annoyed easily with trying to figure out where to go, or things not being overly clear I would say: don't get this.
I've heard comments on it being repetitive and a grind, I can understand why people feel like that. It's not an overly complex combat system. I didn't mind it as much because I was having a blast with exploring the map, picking flowers and getting distracted with the side quests/activities. There's plenty of stuff to bring in some variation.
Only 'downsides' for me was: sometimes the story can be a bit silly and the cheap version of Russel Crowe' as a voice actor. The tone didn't fit for me (otherwise a well done job)... So not real downsides, more personal preference.
I fully recommend this if you are into the genre, if you don't have love for the genre (Boo! :p) there might be other games that suit you better for an introduction.
Would love to see more games from this developer.

Test Drive Unlimited 2 is like no other racing game from it's time. In 2011 the idea of a racing game where you can control the character outside of of the vehicle (in buildings such as dealerships, player owned houses, and the community racing center). This game takes place on the islands of Oahu, Hawaii, USA and Ibiza, Spain with both islands being in a 1:1 ratio (meaning that the roads are exactly as they are in real life and that driving from one point to another on the island would take the same amount of time as it would in real life).
The selection of cars is a bit dull but is easily spiced up with mods (more on that later.) Cars are organized in classes ranging from A1 to A7 (A1 being the highest of the Asphalt Class Cars) B1 to B4 (Off-road Class) and C1-C4 (Classic Car Class). There is a large emphasis on asphalt class vehicles in this game since the car list for both Off-road and Classic Cars are small compared to Asphalt Class Cars. With 101+ cars there is bound to be something that you will like.
TDU2 has a huge social aspect; which if ignored won't completely take all of the content out but WILL make it so that you cannot 100% the game. In TDU2 you can buy houses to store your vehicles and also customize your interior of said houses by changing the flooring, wallpaper, and furniture all to make the houses look and feel personalized. You can also paint vehicles in a very rudimentary painting/stickering shop but truly great designs are held back by it's horrible paint shop controls and even with a Photoshop painted car (using Texmod) the paint skins are still limited to a low resolution paint job. That is why even the best paintjobs often get ruined when you look up close. Racing clubs were possibly the worst idea Eden games has put into the game. The reason for that being is that the clubs are dead and no one actually does club races against other clubs. But since that's the case you cannot legitimately unlock any club of the 3 club cars. This game is 100% best experienced when playing with at least one other friend or even a group of friends. But playing with friends can often be a challenge in it of itself; which leads me to my next point.
Online gameplay. This being a Massively Online Open Racing Game is a real bummer when servers don't work. More often than not the servers are shoddy as hell and sometimes go down all together. Trying to get into a lobby with your friends is a real hit and miss. It's been getting worse over the years and I suspect that it won't hold up much longer and the servers will be shut down all together soon or at least until TDU3 comes out.
Modding. The single best thing to happen to this game. Without it, it would be dead. The modding scene for this game is or at least once was rich and plentiful and you could download entire unofficial patches for the game that add hundreds of cars and fix lots of bugs that the game has. Some things like teleport anywhere can be achieved through modding and since this game has no official support anymore you cannot risk getting banned at all. I have made a few texture and sound mods myself too!
Final note. This game is honestly a love it or hate it game. I personally love it for all that it is and I will forever cherish the memories I have of playing this game with friends. If you like open world racing games with lots of content (with mods that is...) then this is most definitely the right game for you!

WOW....where do I even begin...After 124 hours of playing Dishonored I am done. Completly done.
I started of playing the game in 2015, and I think I must have finished alot of the story, until I just quit one day. The icon laid on my desktop for almost 2 years, until I wanted to try it again, and boy it's been a long ride!
Now when I started I didn't know so much, so I just kept playing. Even deleted my old saves to start over again. As I am a big fan of achievements, I started looking at some of them, but didn't really care that much until I was done with my first playthrough. The good thing with Dishonored is that you litterary never get tired of playing it, no matter how many times you replay most of the game.
MAIN GAME:
Follow Corvo through his story about the rise and fall in the empire. Fight guards, weepers, rats and meet some very interesting people. You decide the outcome of the game by who you kill or not, and the amount of it. Some people like to just slash their way through the game, but I loved the clean hands and sneaking. Many cool levels and ways of getting to your goal. Gaining new magic skills makes the gameplay even cooler...and you will probably go "how did I get away with that?" Playing stealthy makes it absolutly awesome, and your heart beats a little bit faster when you wonder if they will see you in the next second or not. The game will be alot shorter for those who just fight their way through the game.
I'm not gonna say much more about the 2 DLCs that it involves a hired killer Daud, and it's a continuation of the game from his point of view, up to the level where he meets Corvo. Many cool levels and ways of playing the game.
NOW! The final DLC....Dunwall City Trials. I'm not sure how much time I have spent on getting to finish the rest of the achievements in the game, but it took quite some time. Many hundred tries, sweat and screaming to the monitor, and frustration over things not working as they should. It was fun, in it's own way...I gotta admit it, but when I now just recently before writing this review finished the last one, I am very sure that now it's time to end it, and play something else. For the achievement hunters this is the one. Gain these achievements, and you have actually done something really really hard. Practicing alot and tons of patience is required to finish these, unless you are very lucky or a natural.
ALL IN ALL! I've had tons of fun. I've killed tons of people, but also let them live. I made alot of decisions, loaded the game ALOTS of times to make it go my way. There has been frustrations with alot of things I am not gonna mention here. Might be bugs, or bad coding, but overall...there isn't much to say about Dishonored that is wrong. Being an assassin with superpowers is awesome, and there is so many ways to do it too. Bethesda always makes games that makes me spend over 100 hours on a single game, simply because I don't get tired. Achievements are involved too, and I think they made the game better.
Not everyone is so thorough, as I have been in most games I play, and it's entirely up to you how much time you wanna invest in this game! So if you haven't already got this game, go get it and play it! I highly recommend it!

Hatoful Boyfriend takes a fun one-note gag of dating birds and executes it flawlessly, then executes half a dozen other things flawlessly while it's at it. It constantly mixes up its approach, and the result is a story that manages to be hilarious, goofy as all hell, but also legitimately touching.
Ultimately, playing Hatoful is something of a question of sincerity. Yes, the world and story are totally bananas. But the game's willingness to change tone on a dime and play things completely straight leads to no small number of poignant moments. The world of St. Pigeonation's is absurd, but is it really any more absurd than the latest tale of heroic space marines, robo-Nazis, or godlike gangsters? Not really, and at some point, after dealing with characters that act, talk, hope, and fear just like people, you're going to stop caring that their portrait is a ridiculous looking bird. And then, just when you start to get a little emotional, it's going to hit you in the face with another pie.
If there's a downside, it's that the actual gameplay can get a little tedious. A huge chunk of the game doesn't open up until you've romanced all of the birds, and a few of the birds have "normal" vs. "perfect" endings that make for two near-identical playthroughs. So after a few times through, you'll want to pull up a guide (and thankfully there are some good ones) and make judicious use of the fast-forward button to breeze through repeat content. I promise it's worth it, though.

If you enjoy team gameplay like Team Fortress 2, I suggest buying Brink. Brink is a FPS game with team-oriented gameplay mechanics with medics, soldiers, engineers, and assassins. Medics can revive team members, give accelerated healing abilities to other team members, and has specified special skills and abilities. Soldiers can give ammo and can unlock grenades. Engineers are like the engineers in TF2 where they can set up sentry guns. Not only that, they can give upgraded ammo or armor to teammates and they can also drop mines. To add to that, the members all have different tasks to do such as planting C4 to blow up bridges or walls preventing escape, hacking into systems to complete tasks, and more. The "new" Call of Duty Ghosts fuction of running and then sliding was already utilized in this game where you can slide by pressing the hotkey. Sliding can also knock down enemies so you can kill them without them shooting back. Weapons are customizable and you can unlock some other weapons through mini-games. Depending on the size of the character you chose, you can parkour through maps, jumping off the walls and whatnot.
The only unfortunate aspect of this game is that the multiplayer is dead. I hope that my review will cause a few of you to buy this game or to take another look at this game in your library and revitalize this great game.

I got a good ten hours out of the game before I stopped playing, raising multiple pirate crews in the mean time. The last crew I played I decided that I would reset every time one of my crew members died so I'd finally get to challenge a legendary pirate. All in all, I had a lot of fun when I was playing it, and I was glad that I never had to look up a wiki thanks to an in game help section, which really wiled away the time spent sailing. I definitely recommend it to anyone who likes pirates, just don't expect too much out of it.

Perhaps one of the most boring, and unprofessional games I have ever played.  If you're having trouble falling asleep at night and don't own Unepic, buy this game and play some pixel piracy.  It sure puts me to sleep.
Edit: 2015, July 20th.   I've tried once again to get into the game and see what's what in it, and I've encountered numerous bugs; all of which have been reported and have had devs reply to; most of which back in 2014.  The devs seemed to have a tendency of replying once saying something along the lines of: "It is working", then never getting back to the poster when they say it's not working.  And now they're releasing a sequel to the game with the same concept except in space, someone earlier called the game a scam; and I am starting to agree with that sentiment.
There is no animating done, at all in the game.  I'm not an animation expert myself but I can at least make a walk, talk, and attack animations in only a few hours; the extent of noticable animation you'll get in Pixel piracy is your character moving slightly.
Then there's the voice system; all the voices feel like the devs asked some random kids "Hey; say something piratey"; and it really gets annoying after a while of them just saying the same things over and over again.  The character traits and professions seem to be completely pointless and serve as just eyecandy; the type of world seems to have no real effect on things, the interface doesn't work very properly and you'll occasionally get a blank screen forcing you to restart the game.
Overall I'd say this game is probably worth a dollar on the android market; but does not belong on any sort of Windows store, let alone for the price they're asking for.  And I still agree with my original thought all that time back;  this is perhaps one of the most boring, unprofessional games I've ever seen.  The formula is simply: Go to random square, either land on island, shop, or combat.  If you land on island, reopen map and go to another square, if you land on shop, see about getting new units, or upgrading them, if you land on combat, left and right click enemy ship, wait, then left/right click your ship, wait, and click plunder button; and repeat.  Oh, i also forgot to mention all the waiting between each block while your ship is "sailing".
It's funny, I bought this game on April 1st from a bundle for a dollar; it sort of feels like a joke of them to even have it.  I rate this game a 2/10; it is a waste of time, it's not good, it's not awefull, it's just a black whole sucking in all the potential entertainment you could have watching paint dry instead.

Ever since I played Shambler's Castle for Doom 3 I've been thinking I could go for more of that. I have not been playing Quake in steam so ignore my hours.
The original game and the old engine? Revolutionary at the time, whew, pretty dated now. And it is lacking easy customization and some out-of-the-box options. Got questions? There are great guides on steam by Johnny Law. I went with this (which uses the Darkplaces engine):
I pulled the reshade and id 1 files not in epsilon from the hd pack and stuck it with epsilon, worked great. Possible I made some conflicts but I haven't noticed any problems. All I did besides that was tweak the reshade to my taste. There are more vanilla engines/looks if that's what you want, and they look and run nicely from what I've seen. HD Quake is nice and easy to set up thanks to these mod packs.
Music is easy enough to find, different solutions are around the web. With darkplaces at least, you can just have ANY ten .ogg files in a folder named music inside id1 as long as you rename them track02 to track11.
Quake really is a classic. Loaded with atmosphere and great levels, lots of custom maps. Its a great deal for the regular five bucks but goes on sale semi-regularly. The premise: you're an android sent to this desert planet to serve a team of researchers. For most of the game you perform tasks for them, eavesdrop on them, and in general observe their little dramas. What's cool is that you can meddle in them - make choices that influence life and death, how they feel about you, and so on. Because oh, the planet wants them dead, and there's at least one sociopath in the cast. As the game procedes you see everything come to a head, and it leads to a finale that - of course - influences the fate of the galaxy.
Thanks, aliens.
For the price of this, it's well worth it if you like sci-fi stories that ask what it means to be sapient. I mean, assuming you don't mind fetch quests.

A Bird Story is a 1 hour story told with the simple but effective format of old JRPGS (japanese roll playing games) like Final Fantasy 6, Chrono Trigger, Secret of Mana etc. What makes this special is that it's not told in dialogue in written text but in body language, gestures and facial expressions. Combined with some well written music it's simply super effective.
The interactive elements is simple but is implemented in a way to strengthen the involvment on a emotional level so don't expect what would otherwise be called "gameplay".
A Bird Story should be enganged when you don't have a craving for active gameplay but rather want to be told a touching story.
In perspective of what A Bird Story sets out to do (tell a story, draw upon the strenght of interactive elements to make you engaged in the story rather than a passive observer) there is nothing which I can complain about.
And yes, I cried my self silly when playing this.

The loot.  This has been mentioned many times before, opening the treasure chest in the third sisters house to find an AMAZINGLY POWERFUL... dagger, and a necklace made of the best possible material is rather... blah. I want to start off by thanking Numantian Games for making a game with such an old school feel and a huge world and play time to back it up. I feel bad buying this game for 19.99, it is definitely worth a higher asking price. Lords of Xulima was an awesome experience.
Here are my thoughts on the game, both good and bad:
POSITIVE:
+ The graphics are gorgeous. They are the perfect balance between old school and modern without being overly flashy. I loved the aesthetics of the enviornments.
+ The animations while in combat were much more than I expected. The models of some of the more epic fights are extremely well done.
+ For the most part, there are a ton of different enemy visuals. Some games tend to just rehash skins for certain enemies over and over with different colors to "differeniate." Lords does this a few times, but for the most part, there are a ton of different visuals and it adds to the flavor and keeps the game fresh.
+ Open world gameplay. Lords is not completely linear, and it gives you the freedom to roam around and just kind of do your thing. Tons of sidequests/areas to explore. Do what you please!
+ As far as gameplay length versus asking price, this game is unbeatable as far as indie games are concerned. 70+ hours of gamplay for 20 bucks? On an INDIE title? That is unheard of. Wow.
+ Challenging. I have seen a lot of people on the forums complain about the difficulty of the game (too hard!), but I felt it was near perfect. There are three difficulties and different levels of challenges for all types of players, from casual to hardcore.
+ The Lore. Numantian created a beautiful world filled with all types of creatures and Gods and they all have their personalities and roles.
+Combat and strategy is well done. You have things to consider like positioning, resource management, different weapon types, debuff strats (should i stack bleeds/wounds/stuns?), skill allocation, among much more. There is a pretty good amount of depth here.
The MEDIOCRE:
+ The story. I understand this game is not completely story focused and development was probably emphasized on other aspects. I actually liked the story, it wasn't bad by any means, it just wasn't amazing. For the books though, I really enjoyed the ending. A lot. Props on the ending!
+ Slightly grindy with the aspect of food. I understand the food system is necessary for this type of game and it adds a lot of strategy and decision making, but it can get repetitive to just grind out food resources in order to conserve precious gold.
+ Itemization is a bit boring. Because of the way the stats on gear are designed, they aren't overly interesting or force you to make deliberate choices/tradeofffs. A few stats are just a bit too overpowered and could use some balancing (I won't mention any names).
The BAD:
+ This is my only big complaint about the game. The way that you obtain loot.. For the most part, much of your gear will come from the vendor. Basically end game is just constantly checking all the vendors over and over again hoping a good item spawns. You will occasionally find a good item naturally from a chest, but it is very rare. Having vendors being the strongest source of loot in the game seems like a poor design. Finding a really strong item on a vendor does not have the same rewarding effect as if the item was obtained after overcoming a difficult encounter.
Suggestions:
+ Crafting. I really wanted to see a crafting system in Lords. I don't see why a regular base item plus some unique crafting currencies couldn't yield some new items.
+ I feel like some really cool items could have been created that would have fit the themes of the lore. Something creative like "Life's Spark - Febret's Touch," a unique staff which can only be equipped by certain classes and has unique effects/stats. Explore the design space!
Overall Lords of Xulima is an amazing title. If you are a fan of Baldur's Gate style games, definitely give Lords a try. It is the best game of this style I have played in years.

That's when I got sucked into the game for hours. The world is very beautiful with huge open spaces to explore, gather resources and battle alien life. There are many structures available for base building, everything you will need for survival, shelter, defense and exploration. Similar how Matt does his things in Martian, you can also grow your own food, have different vehicles to drive or fly around the planet. There's even kitchen where you can cook alien beasts, and build excrement collector to make fertilizer for them potatoes.
This is a survival game so you will have to keep your eye on hunger and thirst, as well as oxygen and condition of your suit, but there's nothing a good old duct tape can't fix. ;)
There are many different creatures roaming the land, most of them are hostile but some aren't so be careful what you shoot. Plant life is also rich with different kinds of edible fruits and ingredients that you can use not only for eating but crafting into different things.
You can make basic melee weapons and firearms, ammunition, medicine, different types of stimulants, tools and useful devices for marking areas, illumination, etc. Remember that friendly robot, you can upgrade that screwball as well, it can help you fight, gather resource and repair your base if need be.
Base building itself is a pleasant experience, with a lot of different modules you can mix and match together to build your perfect Martian outpost. You can even surround your base with walls, mount some turrets and watch towers because at night monsters come to visit.
Animation on creatures is nice, haven't seen any lagging or teleporting issues. Injured creatures start to limp and often take defensive stances. And with jetpack the combat can be very enjoyable with a lot of mobility.
So far I'm having a blast, and I'm barely into the game. Only built couple modules, still no vehicle, so a lot ahead of me. For a 13 Euro game this has very good content in it, and I hope there will be more in future. You can play it with friends too thought I'm not sure how many can play at once as I'm playing solo.
Anyways, get this game if you're a sci-fi survival fan.

- You can't save the game yourself. Autosave is a nice feature, but if it is the only possibility it s*cks! You can only choose between the last checkpoint, the checkpoint before that and a new game.

- Interaction of badly placed checkpoints and cutscenes: some checkpoints are choosen very poorly! For example there was one in a cave, before a bossfight. Everytime a failed to kill the crab I had to walk trough a cavern, then enter the area where I had to place something, then I had to watch the cutscene and after I died I had to do this over and over again. Loading the checkpoint before that (in the attempt to switch my weapons) didn't work either, because it was only 30 seconds away.
- Bugs! There are severall bugs in this version. Starting with wrong instructions (press WASD to rotate, though you have to hit F), akrid spawning out of nowhere, akrid standing around without doing anywith, problems with taking cover and so on.
- Difficulty: except for some bossfights and very few situations the game is too easy, even on hard settings.
- Multiplayer: there is one, but nobody is playing it.

Quake is, obviously, a good game; a downgrade from the unfettered design genius of Doom 1 and 2, practically the Super Mario Bros 1 & 3 of old-school first person shooters, but what it lacks in perfectly timeless enemy & level design it makes up for in sheer atmosphere; whereas the atmosphere of Doom was an over-the-top heavy metal song, Quake is a dark, atmospheric and moody Nine Inch Nails album... quite literally; the soundtrack was, after all, made by Nine Inch Nails. These kinds of unique artistic statements are what indie devs behind such obnoxious "retro-style" FPS games as Strafe and "GUN GODZ" (all-caps, for extra zaniness!); games which replicate only the dated blockiness of the graphics for vapid "such a geek" ironic appeal.
So why am I downvoting this? Well, putting it simply, this version offers far less content than the fan-made QuakeSpasm engine; the latter makes the enemy animations more fluid, offers more control options and, above all else, actually allows you to hear the iconic NIN soundtrack assuming you have the audio files on your computer. Not only does it offer less options overall, the Steam version failed to include one of the most important and memorable aspects of the game - because iD Software/Bethesda are just really, really poor and can't afford to license the soundtrack again, I guess? Regardless, I'm not paying for what is clearly an inferior product compared to what I can get with an ancient copy of the game run through a fan-made program, so I'll return this as soon as this review is posted.
The only issue I could personally find with QuakeSpasm was that, by default, the engine smudged up the textures into a disgusting mess; you can fix this by simply typing GL_NEAREST_MIPMAP_LINEAR into the console (`/~ key, or creating an autoexec.cfg file containing that exact command and placing it in the iD1 folder (or the main game folder, not sure)).

By the creator of To The Moon, A Bird Story is a short prequel to the next game, Finding Paradise. While the soundtrack is well done and the story is well thought out, the lack of dialogue has a negative impact on the game. Dialogue would not fit the story fantastically, but without any clear ideas or progress I found myself distracted from the story. To The Moon had plenty of serious dialogue and would still be great without the comedic portion of it. Sadly, A Bird Story failed to draw me into the plot as well as To The Moon did. This does not mean that A Bird Story lacks other merits, I was just dissapointed that it was missing the emotion that drew me into the previous game. A Bird Story has great backdrops and sets, and in my opinion a lot of them are better than those in To The Moon. I still enjoyed the game quite a bit and I recommend it especially to anyone who has played To The Moon.

If you're looking at this game because you played To the Moon, be warned: you won't get the same level of experience, in all likelihood. This is not to speak ill of A Bird Story--it's a fantastic experience.  The story is wonderful, though it can feel a bit slow and rocky until the last ten or fifteen minutes, where it all wraps up with some amazing scenes.
The story itself is very fanciful at times, and it can be difficult to separate reality from whimsy and imagination, as they blend together at many points.  Further, the story is told completely without words, which is an interesting choice that I think pays off.  Everything is told through interactions and setting, and you get to peice together whatever sort of stories you want about some parts.
My only complaint about this game is that the transitions from gameplay to "cutscene" are not always clear.  Conrol is given and taken away from the player in such a way that is ocasionally annoying or odd, but it never bothered me enough to take me out of the story.
Definitely buy this (and the soundtrack, which is, as usual for Kan Gao, absolutely wonderful) if you liked To the Moon, or if you just want an interesting and at times touching story.  I highly recommend this game to everyone.

Flashy graphics, a world where YOU are the hero, open to your every whim. Opulent graphics, action-based combat and you can get even a nude cheat.
That is all what this game is NOT about.
Lords of Xulima is a game which is old-fashioned. In a very good way. You lead a party. It has turn-based combat. And in this combat positions, skills, side-effects like bleeding, poisoning and so on are really meaningful and at the same time not annoying. The food system is something I was very critical about in the beginning but now I see how it adds to the tension (in this game you have food reserves and deplete them slowly by wandering about and quickly while resting to heal up again). I admire this game especially for the economy. It is tight but not too tight. There are games out there where gold has no meaning: you have always enough and buying potions and such is more of a hassle than a decision. Not so here. Money is scarce, potions are expensive and you need them.
The graphics are not Skyrim but they are beautiful. The back story is not a high point but it does its job, that is giving you a goal and mile stones to achieve it. There are secrets and lots of puzzly stuff. You know these old rpgs where you get a hint, then a seemingly unsolvable situation appears but then you remember the hint and you can progress? Xulima has that in spades.
You can save whenever you want. You need to save often. Because you can lose fights. Yes, it is one of these games. No mercy for the weak. Ok, there is a kind of mercy: you can always lower the difficulty. But on the normal difficulty setting ("Old Veteran") the game is challenging - but just in the right way.
I always searched for a game which triggers the same feelings like Might Of Magic and Bard's Tale of old. Here it is. With just the right adjustments for modern times, with an automap where you can make your own notes and a comfortable journal. If you are grown up with Bard's Tale, Might of Magic, Wasteland 1 or Dungeonmaster: buy it. Now. If not, buy it anyway. And take some weeks off. You'll need them.

Definitely a 'old' style RPG, where you're given the choice to start a new game, make a party of your own choosing (minus one character, who is the protagonist of the game) and then you're left to figure things out for yourself. It took me a few times of starting a party, playing a bit, and then going back and making a whole new group. There is no right or wrong approach to party creation, although the game will punish you if you decide to, say, make five casters and the protagonist.
You're required to think and actually read the dialogue, the game nips grinding in the bud quite well with scaled areas that have a preset number of hidden and visible encounters. Clear an area, and you obtain an EXP bonus. It is quite possible to put yourself in an impossible situation where it appears that a restart is the only answer, however this typically means that you are missing the next area that you are supposed to go to. A bit of intuitive thinking (as a lot of the game are puzzles) and you can get right back on track.
Gameplay wise, the artwork is amazing for an indie RPG. There is the ability to both run and walk on the map, and more often than not I find myself walking, if only to look at the visuals. The world, characters, even combat animations are all gorgeous for the caliber of this game, and every area has its own unique look. The feeling of "I've been here before" is not present, unlike some other games I've encountered.
Combat is all time and turn based. Pretty nifty system in my opinion, and one that's quite fun. You have your straight up damage, but then there are effects that, depending on the weapon type being wielded, can also come into play. Bleeds, which cause damage per combat turn (and every 10 'seconds' of combat time), stuns, wounds (stackable debuffs affecting ability to hit and evade incoming attacks). Then, you have poison, freezing, setting things on fire... the combat system is a well tuned machine in my opinion.
Characters are a bit tricky, I'll admit that I had to go and read one of the guides to get a better understanding... after all, you have 9 classes, and can only create 5 members. You are slightly railroaded here, in that if you don't have a healer of some type, you WILL encounter untold difficulties to the point that you will most likely end up dumping that save file. Core stats and skills run the game, you have 5 primary attributes which in turn affect various stats. The Skill System is also pretty filled out, making you carefully weigh and decide what you want your character to specialize at... The points are limited, and there's always going to be something else you want to put them in that you can't.
The only potentially annoying aspect that I've found thus far is that there is a food system in place, which decays based on the land you are traversing at the time. It caps out at 8 'game days' so that there is no extreme stockpiling, but even then, it hasn't been too large of a pain.
Definitely recommend this game for anyone looking for an RPG more in the vein of the classics. Simple yet complex, makes you stop and think, and is rather rewarding in my opinion. Would probably put it around an 8.5 or 9.0 out of 10 myself. Already nearly 40 hours in, on my 5th party, this one I'm keeping, and I'm already thinking about my next playthrough, even though I've barely scratched the surface on this one.

All right, I'll start with the positive stuff, having just completed the game.
-- it's cheap
-- it offers many hours of gameplay
-- it's polished, has no bugs at all
-- has nice ideas that don't exist in other RPGs, the single person representing the party is nice
-- the leveling system is interesting and gives freedom
-- the "face to face" turn based combat is quite interesting and fun
-- it's not "easy" like a walk in the park if you play it on the level it's meant to be played (old school veteran)
-- the class and weapon system is clean and fun
Now for the bad stuff
-- it's incredibly repetitive, (I won't go into details so as not to provide spoilers)
-- it's a grind fest
-- they say that it's a none linear game and that you can go anywhere you want, that's wrong, you can only go where you "can" go according to your level
-- the story isn't deep at all
-- there are no choices and no consequences to any actions, all the "talking" is pre determined
All in all, you'll be spending most of the time killing monsters and/or walking around, the story is totally predictable after some time I was only playing the game because I wanted to finish it out of principle. Even though it's polished and has some nice touches, the grind and repetitiveness of it all just got to me.
My advice, good value for money game but don't expect anything special.

Sentience is a RPGmaker scifi adventure game that explores transhumanism, AI rights, epistemology,  as well as more familiar concerns of faith, fear and prejudice. As a game, it's passable. You are placed in the robotic shoes of an android who has been dispatched to a small work site on an otherwise uninhabited planet. You move around, speak to people, and interact with things. What you normally expect from an adventure game. I thought the visuals were superior to what I've come to expect from RPGmaker, and even gave me a classic Fallout feeling. Sound effects and music were sparse, and I would have loved a little more audio. Feel free to play your own music while you play. Your android avatar is very special, and demonstrates free will. Of course this comes through in your actions, but also in your dialogue. When presented with speech options, one options is highlighted, and represents what your programming dictates you should say. You can make whichever choice you desire, but it's interesting to see just how often your natural responses feel pre-programmed. On the subject of choices, there are many of them throughout the game. Some have little impact other than slightly different dialogue, other choices can have results that completely change a characters actions, attitudes, and even if they live or die. Sometimes these consequences are more obvious than others. The colonists you interact with are all believable, and it's an interesting perspective to an automaton. Some humans treat you as a friend, some as an alien or monster, and some see you simply as a tool. Sadly, for a game about humanity, this game lacks much of it. Except for hidden video cutscenes, you are rarely treated to spontaneous situations or colonist interactions that don't directly involve you or your current tasks. Without these, the pacing and development felt a little stilted and robotic. Although I completed the story, I didn't develop particular interests in the characters until halfway through the game. Sentience is elementary as a game, but it's a game that enables a science fiction story. I"m not a literary critic, but I found it worthwhile, especially considering the cost of the game is that of a small paperback.

You either like the idea of "visual novel where girl dates sapient anime-trope pigeons" or you don't, so it should be easy to decide if this game is for you. But here's the thing: if you like the idea, you're going to like the game more than that. While all the characters are recognizable tropes, they're executed in engaging ways. The main character herself is weird and enthusiastic and charming. The writing (and translation) is light and humorous until the moments where suddenly it's *not*, and the transitions there are nimble. came for the lols, stayed for the surprising quality.
And then there's the BBL route, the one you unlock after you've gotten an ending with each major character. Do yourself a favor and clear all the other endings first, both so you'll have as much character background as possible and so you can unlock the epilogue right away. Then clear a few hours to play through the whole thing -- it probably took almost half my total play time -- make the "fulfill a promise from long ago" choice at the start of a new game, and let your hunter-gatherer instincts lead the way.

At its best Evolve is filled with tense moments of narrowly dodged boulders, bullet and skill flinging hunters and the pressure to take on or become a growing threat. But the best does not come often in this game. Every single monster ability has such a huge AoE and quick timers that most abilities are impossible to dodge if the monster has a decent internet connection. While you can burn your jetpack to run away from the monster for a bit, prepare to get focused and constantly battered if you are playing support or medic. Most hunters are either strictly better than other hunters in their class in all circumstances, or are so awful you should never even consider them if you want to win. Weapon variety is minimal and the weapons themselves are unsatisfying, as is running around a half an hour as a monster eating wildlife. To boot they increased the prices of all store items, can you guess what they added in a recent update? A P2W currency. Lost Planet 1 and 2 were decent, if completely forgettable shooters.
Lost Planet 3 is one of the worst games I have made the mistake of playing in recent memory.
In no particular order:
--The devs were so lazy that many of the in game prompts are wrong. I don't mean the game give controller prompts when you're using a keyboard and mouse. I mean that the on screen prompt actually tells you to press they completely wrong key.
--I have never seen such a bad autosave system in my life. Several times I loded my last save, only to discover four powerful enemies within five feet of me. Loading the save before, I was in the same situation. Luckily, you can load one of your manual saves. Just kidding! There are no manual saves, because this is an incredibly lazy console port.
--The lighting is all over the place. Buildings and caves are so dark that I frequently had to adjust my gamma up to see. Upon leaving the area, I had to adjust the gamma back down because the world was blindingly bright.
--Enemies are either so weak that using the handgun on them feels like overkill, or fast moving bullet sponges with powerful melee attacks. There is no middle ground.
--The game has a completely useless cover system. There is only one enemy I encountered that taking cover would have helped against. That enemy can just race around your cover and slash you, or simply lean over it and strangle you.
--Actually, I take it back. The cover is worse than useless. Half the time you just jump over it instead of sticking to it, leaving you out in the open in middle of a bunch of Akrid. If you do manage to stick to cover, rolling away from it to avoid melee attacks doesn't work half the time.
--The Utility Rig, which should be one of the highlights of the game, is a joke. Most of the time you only use it to slowly trudge from one place to the next. Sometimes it functions as a glorified fetch quest, demanding that you run around pushing buttons to open the path for it.
--When you finally do get to fight a giant monster with your rig, don't expect much. Giant Akrid fights are simply disguised QTEs. Tap a button to block, then tap another button to grab with your claw arm, then hold a third button to attack with your drill. Wait until the enemy attacks, then repeat. Giant robot combat has never been so boring.
--You do a lot of pointless running around. Run to the TEng post to harvest it. Run to the lab to turn in a quest. Run up a mountain hitting buttons for your rig. Seriously, if you were looking for a winter hike simulator, you found it.
--The characters. Oh, god, the characters. You play as "Mr. Gruff Space Enginner Who Left His Wife And Child Behind So He Could Go Into Space To Support Them". Because, you know, that's original. Along the way you meet several interesting and unique characters. There's "Base Commander Who Totally Isn't Hiding Anything", "Young, Socially Inept Genius Technician", "Arrogant But Brilliant Science Man" and "Frenchman". I'd love to tell you more about Frenchman, but his entire character seems to be that he's French. Oh, and there's also a few extras that seem like they got lost on their way to shooting a mildly racist Pocahontas film.
--I won't "spoil" the "story" for you, but suffice to say that it is an incredibly generic, cliche riddled lump of turd. It's like someone had a copy of the scifi cliche handbook. And they didn't even paraphrase. They just tore pages out of the book, stapled them to a blank sheet of paper and called it a day. Phoning it in doesn't even cover it. The writers left a sticky note on the door that said, "Just watch SyFy for a couple hours and figure it out yourself." and never bothered to show up for work again. They probably didn't even spring for the name brand Post-Its. If you've seen more than two science fiction films, there are absolutely no surprises to be had here.
I got this incredibly cheap in a Humble Capcom Bundle, and I still feel like I got ripped off. Also, that's probably the only time you're ever going to see the words "Humble" and "Capcom" in the same sentence.

This is the only Lost Planet I've played, but LP3 is apparently a prequel to LP2.
In Lost Planet 3, you're on a distant planet working as a contractor mining energy due to an energy crisis on Earth. Your primary obstacles are arthropods that inhabit the planet. You are able to purchase and upgrade firearms and you travel around in a large, upgradeable robot suit that you will use to do battle with. The game consists of a typical primary and side-quest system that allows you to stray and then progress the story at your own pace.
I felt that the story was fairly good and I say that because I actually wanted to play through it to find out what happened next. The gameplay isn't particularly difficult, I played through on 'normal' difficulty, but there are maybe a couple moments where you might get frustrated; there may be some tricks to defeating certain bosses.
I thought that the graphics and audio were good considering that it's a last-gen console game. I ran it at 2560×1440 @ 144Hz and it sat at 144FPS the entire time with the exception of some small hitches in one area. I had no bad technical issues with the game but there were a couple issues: 1) the 'turn the claw' button is displayed wrong and 2) it seems that if Steam goes offline that the game boots you to the title screen; fortunately it auto saves often.
I enjoyed it and I might even re-play just a bit but it's not a game I'll probably entirely replace since most things are achievable in the first playthough.
SLIGHT SPOILERS:
1) You're run out of ammo on one boss and will have to use the handgun to pick away at it.
2) One of the later bosses seems to be immune to grenade damage.

The game begins with a crash landing on an ice plan several years in the future. You, a lone mercenary, are equipped with a basic weapon, survival suit, & bad controls. The opening to the game is extremely reminiscent of Dead Space 3, in fact, several parts of the game are pretty close. That said, there are some key differences between the two. In Dead Space, you get to make your own guns & upgrade them freely, in lost planet, theres a store where you buy weapons & a few upgrades for them such as scopes & extened magazines. In Dead Space, everything was compact, linear, & required little back tracking, in Lost world, you have a base of operation where you will return to after every sortie & which you can wander out of freely to do side mission. This gives it a sort of open world feel, but instead of it feeling like you can wander freely around, it feels like you have to go out for hours at a time since it takes so long to march back to base in either your boots or your giant mech that moves at about 3 mph. Combat is rigid at best, you are constantly swarmed by either waves upon waves of small weak enemies, or huge boss monsters that have very repettative patterns. Another huge difference between Dead space & this game is that Dead Space is a survival horror. You have a set health bar which you have to scavence to replenish, ammunition can be scarce depending what dificulty you play. In Lost Planet, you have regenerating health  & ammo is avaliable around every corner, or you can rely on your pistol which pulls infinite ammo from space & time. In other words, this game is extremley easy, even though I played through it on normal diffiulty. All in all, you have better uses for your money, but if you're just bored, this can be a c+ game
Was it a good game? No. Is it worth $10? Again, the answer is no. But was it fun? Meh not really, it moderately enjoyable for a few hours, so buy it on sale if you really care that much.

The first few times I played this game, I really had no clue what I was doing.
then it slowly started to click, now I'm having a great time playing this little game.
First off, this game should be *needs to be* played with a Controller, be it Steam or Xbox, it's just easier. (I had problems with it not responding to my keystrokes on my laptop, controller use is near flawless (you'll occasionally charge an arrow and have it drop as if it didn't register the charge.)
The idea is you've been killed, but your soul escapes the underworld are you come back to life. you choose a "challenge" to keep your life, be it killing your killer, making money, or killing monsters, amongst other things... additional challenges unlock with subsequent playthroughs, you can only start with "Killing your killer" or "exchange your soul for another"
When you start, go to a town ASAP, talk to people, add one to your team, you can have up to 6, with 4 active, this is based on your influence or level (+1 to party to every 5 levels gained, max team size by lv. 30) and whether or not you fill their requirements, (stat levels, skill levels, number of kills, amount of wealth, etc.)
Moving, searching for treasure, and clearing mines takes food. if you don't have enough food, you'll be forced to gather more. you can hunt/fish/gather it from any tile but towns, make sure you cook it before you leave the area. it's super easy, point and shoot, then pick it up, push a button to cook it, simple as simple gets.
Characters can learn each others skills by setting them as  one anothers mentors, this makes for skill raising to be an easy task (I'm dealing 3k-5k damage with my strongest attacks), the stronger the skill, the longer the combo, and the longer to learn it (I've seen as high as 8 hit combos). different weapons and classes make for different skills, some can be learned regardless, (my whole team knows Lunge and Triple Strike)
Each tile has a level, if your lowest team member's level is lower than the tile, the number is increasingly red. If your lowest level is higher than the tile, it's increasingly dark grey. a white number is equal to you. I DO NOT RECOMMEND going more than 1 or 2 levels above your own, you're gonna have a hard time.
The controls are simple enough, choose your attack, your target, and hit the A button when the two moving squares line up. if they're not overlapping, you miss/break your combo, the closer they are, the critical hit chance goes up. all in the reflexes.
The isometric graphics are meh, and the camera has ADHD during the battles, and there's a terrible blur in a couple areas... Redaval Town is almost unviewable, but I discovered its that way for a reason, FYI...
-expect it to move slow in the beginning, expect to die in the beginning. it's just the way of the game.
-check EVERY MOUNTAIN for mines, the monsters are great for grinding (you'll have to sooner or later) and the resources are necessary for decent progression.
-always go for the investigate events, it's a valuable farming resource.
-Craft often, you'll need the skill 100% Maxed asap.
-you'll run out of leather more than anything.
-sell everything you don't use, there's no reason to keep it unless you're one of those 100% sive file completionists.
-you WILL grind. and grind, and grind, and grind, and grind, and grind, and grind, and grind, and grind....
all in all, I'd give it 8/10 certainly replayable, but quite repetitive.

I am a huge fan of To The Moon, and therefore I was very excited for this game. I bought it on release, but interestingly found myself not playing it for a couple of months after. I cannot say why this is, other than I knew I wanted to wait for a completely free day so I could sit down, relax and immerse myself in what I expected would be a game as beautiful and fun as To The Moon.
How wrong I was. A Bird Story is, simply put, tedious. I found myself looking around the room or to my tablet every few minutes about fifteen minutes into the game. There is simply not enough going on. It plays as though it should be a short film; any interaction the game lets you have is short, repetitive and wrested away from you at a moment's notice. It hardly even feels like interaction at all, because the game is so linear and I feel actually punishes exploration. The protagonist will have a little picture of what he needs to do before letting you continue the story, meaning that he refuses to leave an area before you 'accomplish' his goal, which usually equates to going to an item and pressing enter. This means that the world created feels incredibly small and confined; it consists of the protagonist's house, one classroom, a vet's, a forest path and some skyline.
I could have let the tedious gameplay go, if only the story was interesting. However, sadly it was not. It was predictable, cliché and vague, to the point where when what I suppose is the story's climax happened, I found myself not caring. To The Moon was an extremely emotional, complex story that had many layers of hurt and tragedy hidden beneath artificial happiness. A Bird Story felt pretentious, trying so desperately to be packed full of meaning and substance that it simply became meaningless and empty.
It is unfair, of course, to compare the two games, but I left To The Moon feeling as though I had just played a masterpiece, one that I went to bed with the night after playing it without playing a different game or reading a book as I needed to sort out its meaning and beauty in my head. I left A Bird Story feeling as though I was ready to play a different game straight afterwards.
It's more a cinematic than a game, but it's a great little guy to add to your collection.

One of the first fully 3D FPS games, which set the standard and pioneered both singleplayer and multiplayer games and mods for years to come. The gameplay is composed of straightforward progression in unique and atmospheric environments with a set of fairly balanced weapons and enemies. The levels contain various secrets and puzzles, and tons of closet monsters, but despite its age Quake is still very enjoyable and playable with a modern client. If you are into first person shooters, Quake is a must playthrough at least once. There are also about a billion user made maps and mods for Quake, not to mention the multiplayer side of things which is still active. Highly recommended game! However the Steam version really needs to be fixed as you will need to do some messing around to get things sorted and working properly.
Steam version of Quake/Mission Packs do not include the soundtracks, for best single player experience you will need a more up to date singleplayer client like Quakespasm and to download the soundtracks elsewhere in OGG format. For multiplayer Quake use ezQuake client.
