XCOM: Enemy Unknown is quite possibly the best PC game I have ever played - turn-based shooters never really appealed to me, but the strategic planning of attempting to keep your whole team alive simply made for addictive gameplay. The Bureau: XCOM Declassified was released one year after this game (some might even say, unnecessarily).
The Bureau is a 3rd person tactical shooter set in the 1960s and tries to emulate the strategic gameplay that made Enemy Unknown so brilliant, and mostly succeeds as a result of its Battle Vision - which allows players to order their comrades into cover, use their abilities or direct their fire to a specific target - this is a system that actually works and make it feel like playing a proper XCOM game.
However the gameplay is generic to say the least - most of the time is spent ducking for cover, clearing the area of enemies and then repeating until the end of the mission; essentially basic cover shooter mechanics employed in the XCOM universe.
That's not to say that it's a bad game, sure the controls are a bit clunky when trying to aim and the AI companions can be annoying at times (but this is a "strategy" game so its best to use Battle Vision since it actually has a purpose and negates this apparent criticism), but it feels like a generic action game with the XCOM label attached. Still, this is a fine game that will be played through multiple times.

I loved this game. No idea why it's getting such a low average rating.

I am going to give it a recommended rating even though I think the game has some flaws that may frustrate people.
But overall I do not regret the purchase so far it has given my quite a few fun hours. The game does many things right. Combat is pretty fun and a radically different experience can be had when playing with different classes. I love that the game is fairly simple but still offers plenty of challenge. The maps are nicely drawn and engaging.
My problems stem from the obscure puzzle like approach to questing - this confuses the heck out of me. Time and again I find myself not knowing what to do next. How do I get into this tower? How do I get to the next zone? How do I get into the castle? How do I cross the woods? Each time I have to tab out of the game and scour the internet for advice.
I would love it if this game just kept the hack/slash attitude and toned down the puzzles greatly. I don't need puzzles in my hack and slash and I don't think others do either.  Another problem is that the food mechanics feels very punishing for exploration - makes one regret exploring the map. I think the food should be reserved to restoring health only and not used when just walking around.
I am still playing the game even after the above - that means that there is a good game to be had here. My main regret is that the game could be so incredibly better if they only made a little more accessible. I don't recall ever having to tab out from Baldur's Gate for example to finish a quest...

I normally don't write reviews on steam but I felt I had to for this game.
If you like oldschool RPG epic journeys similar to Might and Magic you will love this game.  There is a slight learning curve, the start could be a bit smoother and but overall the game is amazing for RPG fans.
I'm now about 20% into the game and enjoying every bit.  Lore is great, graphics are good for indie game.  Some things you may want to know before starting are there is no hand holding in this game, the enemies are finite.  If you can't deal with an area come back when your stronger.  There is a food mechanic to prevent you from resting and healing up unlimited times.
For the down points I'd have to say I dont like how spells inflate in mana cost so rapidly, I suppose this forces you to manage food properly.  Not too fond of the minigames for disarming traps and chests but that's a personal taste.  The skill point system doesn't let you lvl up multiple times to "catch up" on old skills.
Check out a let's play on youtube and decide if its for you.  Overall the good out weighs the bad by a far margin.

I watched Lords of Xulima for a few months before deciding to get in on the early access. In fact it was only 3-4 weeks before the v1.0 release. It was incredible how interested the dev was in user feedback and how quickly they worked in even major additions like the character quick-bar we now have or how they implemented weight info for shop items you intent to buy. All on user feedback and I have to say it again: amazingly fast.
Now on to the game itself:
The game consists of an overland map where you move your group of 6 chars (5 of which you can design yourself out of 9 classes) and of a turn-based fighting screen which is best compared to Wizardry 8. Chars get turn depending on their speed. This means you can get more turns than other group members or enemies, if say... your thief is very quick on her feet. You have many tactical options in the form of spells, skills, moving chars around and using items.
On the map you have to look out for your food consumption and remember to restock in time. This mechanic shouldn't be a big problem in the easy and medium difficulty, if you are not too much into such things. Different terrains have different food consumption rates (think desert, meadow, forest, road, snow). There are also skills which influence this.
This game is oriented on old-school RPGs like Wizardry and Ultima. This means that there is little hand-holding and you have to use your brain and pick your fights. The dungeons have hidden doors and other environmental puzzles. Some of which are hard nuts. This may turn off some people who have never played older RPGs. I recommend to give this game a try nevertheless since it is a real gem. If you want to have a little bit more help you can always get the add-on "The Talisman of Golot" which has (among others) the option show you the right direction of your quest.
The world is full of little secrets and just wandering off and go exploring is great fun.  The art of the game is very pleasing and more than sufficient for the game to work. You can even use custom portraits now. Just like back in the Baldur's Gate days.
Depending on how you play you can get 60 to 120h of game time out of one walkthrough. I have over 100h on the clock now and enjoyed every minute of it. For what you get this game is almost criminally cheap and the devs really deserve it. I can't wait to get more tales of the world of Xulima.
If you are interested in RPGs and liked the revived old-school gems that came out this year, you owe it to yourself to give this title a chance. I'm pretty sure you won't regret it! And there are always nice people on the steam forum to help you out with tips and clues if you are stuck ;-)

Short Review:
+Nice graphics, acceptable options, acceptable UHD support.
+Native controller compatibility.
+Good characters, good voice acting, good story with some genuine intrigue, immersive.
+Gameplay is average but polished.
+Good enemy variety and bosses.
-Vague QTEs that are easy to fail and sometimes don't display correctly.
-Jim moves too slowly to achieve a lot of dodges and rolls.
-Game often fails to adequately describe mission objectives.
-Some discrepancy when aiming in close quarters.
-Very large deviation in style and gameplay from previous titles.
-Thermal energy is now just a currency and is not necessary for survival.
Long Review:
Does "Eurotruck Simulator meets Dead Space 3" sound good to you? Probably not, it doesn't seem to have appealed to many people, but if you're like me and it does, then you'll find something to enjoy in this game.
The first problem is of course, that LP3 is very different from previous installments, it abandons the arcade score attack feel and takes a notably more "Western" approach to the gameplay and story. The third person shooting is very off-the-shelf, but it works well enough, character animations and models are especially nice, and a lot of attention has been given to the story and characters this time.
I often felt lost in LP2, I didn't know who was trying to accomplish what or why, it was very confusing and disjointed, but the stellar gameplay and action held it up.
LP3 kind of has the opposite problem, while the gameplay is good, it's nothing to write home about and would be at home in any third person shooter since Gears of War, but I feel that such special attention has been paid to the characters and story that these elements make LP3 noteworthy and elevate it above bargain bin cover shooters.
Jim is just so damn relatable, we all know someone like Jim, we identify with his goals and his attitude.
Where other games might make their protagonist a heroic space marine slaying aliens, Jim is just a contractor, and he sees his work as mostly routine and mundane.
This simple fact grounds the whole game and makes it so much more immersive and believable. Jim has keepsakes in the cab of his mech, he has favorite music tracks he likes to listen to, he sends video messages to his family, he's helpful but sarcastic bordering on passive-aggressive, and he just feels like a real fleshed out person who has a reason to exist beyond driving the plot.
We identify with Jim, we like Jim and we want Jim to succeed.
The story is well written and well acted, and it will keep you playing because you want to uncover the mystery, and I'll leave it at that so as to avoid spoilers.
The game borrows many design and gameplay elements from Dead Space 3, infact at times the inspiration borders on plagiarism, but LP3 never quite manages to reach the same technical and graphical competency. Not that the game looks bad, the graphics and animations are pretty nice, but it invites the comparisons to DS3 and just can't live up to them.
In short if you like Dead Space 3 you'll find a lot to like here too.
The game is just comfy, it's immersive, the thin layer of ice you see coating the windows of the mech contrasted with the steaming mug of coffee Jim is sipping, the way Jim's facial expressions will change during gameplay to reflect the tone, the attention to detail in the way your heavy machinery and equipment is operated, just all these small touches that come together to make you feel like you're really on EDN 3.
In conclusion, the gameplay is a downgrade to LP2, but if you give it a chance to immerse you, you'll find a very underappreciated story.

QUAKE is certianly brimming with balls to the wall run gun fun, and it was on the absolute cutting edge of technology at the time, but it is noticeably unrefined. Compared with DOOM, which was also a huge technical achievement at the time, QUAKE feels simply unpolished and possibly unfinished. While the core gameplay is engaging and all the weapons feel good to use, the enemy designs lean more toward annoying than interesting and the later levels start to rely way too heavily on springing massive ambushes on you. However, the actual layouts of the levels stay intricate and aesthetically pleasing throughout, although the the pervasive brownness does eventually become fatiguing. All that said, in the end what seals the deal on this game's inferiority to DOOM, in my mind, is its lack of interesting boss fights. There are two boss fights in the game; at the end of Episode 1, you fight Chthon, who is beaten by pushing 3 buttons to electrocute him 3 times. At the end of the game overall, you fight Shub Niggurath, who is beaten by teleporting into her for what may be the first recorded instance of a telefrag. Historic though this may be, I can't help but notice that neither of these bosses are defeated by engaging them with the actual core mechanics of the game; and Episodes 2 and 3 don't even have proper boss fights, with Episode 2 opting to introduce a new regular enemy as a "boss" of sorts, and Episode 3 simply choosing to corner you between two fiends, forcing you to drop to an earlier part of the level in order to survive the ordeal and make your way back. Neither feels particularly climactic. It's these sorts of things that can make the difference between a truly satisfying and engaging first person shooter, and a pretty fun diversion to drop a couple hours on while listening to podcasts. I do recommend QUAKE on this basis, it's a very fun way to while away the time and keep your motor skills engaged while your mind is on other things, but don't go expecting a true successor to DOOM's legacy.

Hearts of Iron IV:
I really enjoy this game. The tactical decision making and preparation is very clever, it's the ultimate Armchair General's strategy title for World War II.
+ Hearts of Iron IV has meticulous attention to detail, the strategy element closely reflects real life war planning and logistics. To succeed you'll need access to resources (oil, rubber, steel etc) to build aircraft, tanks and weapons. You'll also be required to construct military factories which can produce all the equipment for soldiers in the field. In order to get important resources, you might need to conquer specific regions which were historically rich in minerals. Furthermore, you must plan every action you make, just like a real war. For example, in order to launch amphibious assaults you'll need transport convoys, naval supremacy in ocean areas covering the travel destination and a range of other prerequisites. There is considerable realism, for instance, unit movement and supply will drop rapidly when there is a lack of infrastructure, hilly/mountainous terrain or no nearby ports to deliver rations and reinforcements.
+ There are quite a few major factions to play as, each with a unique national focus tree which allows you to repeat history or take a completely new route. There's France, the U.K, Germany, the Soviet Union, the United States, Poland, Italy and more. There's also a research tree which gives the player many choices on how to approach the early game, before 1939. Build up your civilian industrial power, or if you're a smaller nation expecting invasions, fortifications and radar.
+ There are a multitude of positive and negative combat modifiers which determine whether you will win or lose a battle. If you manage to encircle the enemy and cut off supply, they will fight far less effectively. If you have air supremacy and ground support, your air force will inflict heavy organisational damage to the enemy. Naval bombardments from capital ships also contribute to coastal battles. Researching decryption results in an intelligence bonus, directly impacting troop performance. Moreover, the unit template you designed can have a great effect on engagements (adding engineering support, recon and so forth yields bonuses to a unit's entrenchment, defence, hard and soft attack statistics + more).
- As someone who was brand new to the series, I can tell you this game is EXTREMELY confusing. Be prepared to ask a lot of questions on the Steam forums, google extensively and watch youtube videos to understand how to play. However hard it may seem initially, it is learnable and SUPER fun once you comprehend everything. It took me about 50 hours to master the theory behind this game, but it was totally worth it.
Overall Score: 9/10

I've owned this game since shortly after having first started using Steam. Yet just months ago I decided to actually play the 'campaign' to its end. If I didn't like the original TDU so much on XB360 I likely would've not been interested in this one.  As it stands I did enjoy my experience playing through the story/campaign, but the flaws are too many and too great to warrant a recommendation.
TDU2 plays host to open-world racing on two islands starting with Ibiza and within about 15-20 hours of getting to level 10 opens up to Hawaii. For those who have played the original TDU; the version of Hawaii ported into TDU2 is the same with some minor touch-ups. All the cars look nice and within the context of the game's driving physics do behave mostly how you would expect comparatively. However those afore mentioned driving physics leave a lot to be desired. Throttle traction breaks loose to spin cars around WAY too easily as if they are near weightless. Presuming you don't like using arcade-style driving aids that is; I prefer to play as near simulation as I can. AWD cars are your best go-to in TDU2 if you prefer the same.
Event variety is rather good. There's your standard lap and point-to-point races both street and off-road, time attack, speed, speed trap, and elimination. No drifting based events for obvious physics-related reasons, but they do try to shunt drifting into some arbitrary mechanics.
Car variety is rather lack-luster and the notion of having to slowly walk around a dealer lot to look at and buy cars (you can skip the majority of this by interacting with the always a 'hot chick' sales woman) is a massive time-sink. I can tell why they did it; they want to maintain the immersion... while jump-cutting you in and out of your car at every interactable location including car dealers. Speaking of the afore mentioned, you can go clothes shopping and get plastic surgery done to modify the look of your character. YAY!!!~... /sarcasm The real thorn in the side here if you are a completionist and/or collector in games like this is there are "DLC" vehicles you CANNOT buy. Not normally... You could jump through the hoops needed on Atari's website to buy some premium currency and then unlock the vehicles there for you to buy with in-game money. Or for all but the motorcycles you could use the sales woman and highlight the car directly above a DLC car and immediately after pressing "A" to select it; press down once and it'll switch to the DLC car with no unlock needed. The only reason this doesn't work on the motorcycles is because there's no non-DLC vehicle to start from. Pretty sure this violates Steams terms of use forcing us to buy something external to the Steam client. I'll be reporting the game for that when I'm done with this review if I'm right about that.
Lastly the online play and functionality is extremely limited. The launcher will check your NAT type and constantly complain that it's restricted even with UPnP enabled. You can disable online play entirely which will prevent meeting other players in the game world. I can't speak to how active the online community is as I played it purely offline.
Ultimately there are much better racing games available now. You can get the majority of a better experience imagining or RPing a similar series of racing tournament events in GTAV; not to mention the plethora of other racing games that - while most aren't open-world - offer vastly superior driving physics. Burnout Paradise! There's a GREAT open-world racing game vastly superior to this. Not a Sim racer, but if you wanted a sim you're looking at the wrong game anyway.
This was such a good game. It's a shame it's turned into abandonware now. Expensive abandonware at that.

Gave the game a good go. Really tried to enjoy it but ultimately it's a complete disappointment. An amalgamation of multitudes of other RTS games compounded into a Frankenstein's Monster of a game, but with all the odd bits hanging out. In short the game is about as enjoyable as sliding down a razor blade using your balls as breaks.
Most hotkeys don't function, or are not responsive. You can't rebind any keys at all. No option for legacy keybinding either. Tooltips are misleading. Music is generic, and soundbytes are re-used MS-DOS soundbytes. Unit AI is buggy at higher populations, they don't follow commands and will randomly run right into a bunch of zombies for no reason. Building placement is unclear and inconsistent. Sometimes a formation of buildings will work, and then the next time you try the exact same layout they won't sit near each other. The maps are randomly generated leaving a large portion of them in a state where you just cannot win, or get past day 25. There are even those that spawn no resources in your initial energy range leaving you extremely gimped and it's better to just exit and restart. There is no restart option, you have to save and exit, then start a new campaign and overwrite your old saves name. No loading option to back up and try a different strategy to see if that would work. Because of the whole RNG map system infected harpy's can spawn just outside of the FoW and end your game immediately. Understandably the voicelines are meant to pay homage to older RTS classics, but the line delivery is terrible.
Probably a good $10 game. The artificial difficulty of Random Map Generation instead of an actually challenging experience is cookie cutter game making at best.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Hours of compelling and addictive oldschool tactical turn-based rpg goodness, with a lot of attention to detail in crafting the world, its lore, and its gameplay mechanics. It's one of those games that demands that you keep playing it, even when you're knackered and should have gone to bed 4 hours ago. More polished and non-buggy than I've seen a lot of games at release lately (including AAA games), provides more content than many modern RPGs (including AAA games), and has a combat system that on the middle difficulty and above absolutely insists that the player thinks about tactical decisions carefully and rewards gamers for playing cautiously and thoughtfully and picking their targets well. It doesn't pull punches on difficulty, which is great, and the maps are nicely made for a decent amount of exploration (and with lots of hidden secrets and fun stuff to do when you wander off the roads).
And I'm so glad that the devs didn't water down and effectively sacrifice any prospect of robust and tactical gameplay by insisting that players co-ordinate their party of multiple characters in combat in real time so it can 'look more action-packed' and frenetic on video footage (dear Bioware: stop doing that, most rpg fans do actually like to think and are capable of doing so).
If you like crpgs with tactical turn-based combat like the classic crpgs had, I'm fairly sure you will enjoy LoX and find it staggeringly good value for money. If it were full price I would still consider it good value for money based on the amount of content, detail, and hours of engrossing gameplay.

The first thing to note about 3dRPG is that this game’s music is awesome. 3DRPG is a randomly generated simple game with cute little voxel style graphics. What I mean by a simple game is that so far from what I have seen the game involves simplistic rpg elements. This isn’t a problem because who doesn’t love to sit down and play a simple game? However the simplicity might mean that children will enjoy this game a lot more then adults. Not to say it isn’t enjoyable because it is.
As for the story behind the game you are a deceased soul in the armies of the dead whom suddenly and randomly remember who you are. Curious by the strange soul the boss in charge offers you freedom if you succeed in a quest of his choice. Although it’s really more your choice. The first quest choice you get is to seek revenge on the person who killed you and thus you are released to the land of the living to begin your quest.
After customizing your character and chosen your specialty you will first find yourself in a town. The town has 3 major buildings, general supplies, armors and weapons. If there is more I didn’t see any. Populating the towns are a whole bunch of ‘npcs’ I say npcs like that because one of the jokes the npcs make is that they are not really npcs because you can convince each and every one of them to join your party and help you on your quest. So if you ever need items or new party members don’t hesitate to head to the nearest town. Oh and the civilians tell you which direction you need to head in for your quest objective.
On the world map you will notice food meter at the top right corner. It seems that every action you perform on the world map requires food, the only action that doesn’t require food is collecting food. Just go over any old random spot on the map and you will get to choose your action. From what I have seen there are only two options and that is collecting food or finding treasure. When collecting food you just run around the map picking up random plants, murdering innocent wildlife or going fishing, not too many options there. Still if you enjoy murdering adorabubble deer then food collecting is for you.
The second option ‘treasure’ allows you to enter the map in a similar function to food collection however this time the map is populated by treasure chests and slime monsters. If you keep collecting treasure chest you don’t need to hunt for food because the chests are filled with food and other nice little goodies. However if you choose to say hello to the slimes you get to pick a fight with them.
Combat is a very simple matter. When you command your character to attack you have a little moving target mechanism thingy similar to say guitar hero maybe?? I don’t know what the mechanic is called however so long as you get your time right you attack. The only real complexity to combat is that monsters have certain colours next to their names on a little shield symbol. Using an attack that has the same colour allows you to deal more damage, like an elemental weakness. You have a certain amount of energy and every action uses that energy. If you run out of energy then you need to rest a turn to recharge your energy.
Now when traveling around the map there is also random encounters. So far every random encounter I have found has been glitched because the monsters just stand there and ignore me like I don’t exist. However from what I can tell you get unique monsters attack you, you defeat them then you take their treasure.
Finaly the leveling in this game isn’t anything complex. Every action you perform seems to have it’s own xp and the more you use the action the more you level up. Same said for defeating enemies. Zones in the map are all level based so if you travel too far without fighting and leveling up you could end up in a level 10 zone with only a level two character. Towns also have levels as a means to gate stronger items so if you want stronger equipment, find a higher level town. Just don’t go too far out of you depths otherwise you might be killed by a stronger level enemy encounter.
I suppose that’s all there is to say about this game that I have managed to discover. This game is a very beautiful and simple game with some absolutely lovely music that I go gaga over and I hope you all have enjoyed this review.

3DRPG
Doomster Entertainment
Doomster Entertainment
Role Playing Game
Aside from its deceptively simple title, 3DRPG is a very fun game. The voxel graphic-style used isn’t anything new in gaming but even after so many iterations, I still find it amusing and befitting the indie game scene. Another big plus from me is awarded to any title which successfully mixes random generation of as many assets as possible with a coherent set of objectives. And 3DRPG is as open-ended as they come. You might actually say that it falls within the other extreme of linearity and open worlds: sacrificing the chance for a proper story. And yet the sheer number of activities, characters and locations, should keep players busy for quite some time. The combat system is functional (though it takes some practice, getting used to it) but the necessity for grinding, quickly bored me. This is purely subjective of course, since many RPG fans don’t really consider that a con at all. And the game offers plenty of value, given its price point. The NPC dialogues provide comic relief and the soundtrack was surprisingly good. You can’t go wrong with 3DRPG if you like voxel graphics in general and particularly if you prefer an unpredictable gaming experience as well.

CAPOM in their infinite wisdom decided to push development of the much beloved cult classic Lost Planet IP on to Spark Unlimited.  Both Spark Unlimited and Lost Planet 3 can go straight to hell.

I have never played a Lost Planet® game before this one other than maybe a demo level for the first game on someone else's PC so I’m pretty new to the franchise.
TL:DR - If you have never played a Lost Planet® you should get / try this one, it will make you want to play the other ones.
Intro:
Keeping that in mind this is the perfect game to start out on. Supposedly this one has worse game play than the other two (probably because the game is more focused on telling its beautiful story) but it’s not terrible or unplayable or anything. This game is a prequel to Lost Planet 1 and sets up the game. It really gave me a feeling of wanting more when I finished the game.
Story:

The game's story is really polished. It does feel a bit rushed at the finale as everything gets really crazy and I do question the motives of characters. I think if the game had been longer and had more time it wouldn’t have been as harsh a transition but then a longer game would have made the story seem too drawn out. It’s a compromise and sadly it makes the ending feel rushed and not nearly as polished as the rest of the game.
Characters are good though sometimes they come off being a little robotic with animations and such. The game has a lot of colorful NPCs you can wander around and talk to or overhear throughout the game. Cut scenes are well done except for the moments where you have difficulty and die repeatedly having to watch one over and over again.
Game play:
The guns all feel same-y. The only real different one is the grenade launcher and that’s just because it shoots grenades. There are like 3 rifle / SMG weapons, 2 sniper rifles and a shotgun. The pistol is like a mix between the rifle and the sniper as it has slower fire but more accuracy. The game will recommend you use a certain type of weapon to beat certain types of enemies but it really doesn’t matter. Each gun roughly operates the same so its just a matter of finding which ones you like.
Each enemy is different but there are only like 12 types and that’s including bosses. You got swarmers, flyers, rollers, cat-like panthers, face-huggers and grenade like lobbing ones. They all kind of just swarm you. The game is like "why make harder enemies when we can just make more?" and I get it, it’s supposed to be an alien swarm attacking you but basically you just mow em all down. The panthers are the most strategy oriented.
The only enemy I didn’t list is these centipede crawlers that shoot bolts at you while others flank you. So you are forced to take cover but you can't because if you do another one comes and wrecks you.
Bosses are mostly lame. It’s basically a game of find out how to hit the glow-y spot enough. Most the time a new boss is fun but it’s when you fight it the 2nd or 3rd time that it gets old. Bosses are usually based on crabs and so it’s usually, dodge the pincer and shoot the arms and then the underbelly / back area.
The construction rig you get in the game is fun but it’s too slow. I’m pretty sure you can get out of it and run just as fast. It feels really tedious to walk from area to area in the game in this slow giant mech. The cool thing though is fighting bosses in the rig / giant construction mech. It makes a boss you have fought previously on the ground a whole lot more fun because you now get to fight a fair game size wise. Those pincers you had to shoot off before, now you can grab and just rip off like it was a real crab. It’s awesome.
Finally, the entire game you fight Akrid (the lost planet alien bug/plant life things) but in the endgame of Lost Planet 3 you finally get to shoot other humans. Sadly they often times do not shoot back. I found most weapons take them down in 1-3 hits which for machine guns is really easy. The snipers in the game make even faster work of human enemies as 90% of the time a sniper rifle can kill them before they even notice you. Often time’s enemies would spawn and I'd wipe them out before the elevator / drop ship even left.
Overall:
This game is good, I enjoyed it. It has some game play issues and some pacing issues with its tedious intro and the slow giant mech you have to pilot for the majority of the game. The combat is good, but way too easy and not varied enough sadly. The environments in the game are amazing and the story is fantastic. I would recommend getting it on those two points alone. If you have never played a Lost Planet® you should get / try this one, it will make you want to play the other ones.

Lost Planet 3 is certainly not an "incredible" or "mind-blowing" game. It wont win any awards and it certainly has some issues. That being said, it is FAR better than I was expecting and probably the best LP game. Certainly leaps and bounds beyond 2 at least.
The good:
- Good world building and a decent-enough story. Sure it is a bit cliche at times and I cant even tell you any of the characters names, but it serves its purpose.
- Pretty good level design / open world.
- Fun gunplay / exploration.
- Upgrades / sense of progression.
- It can be quite pretty. Except for some (not all) faces.  Something about the main characters face bugs me.
The bad:
- Bugs. (Ironically). I ran into 3 so far. One minor, the others more annoying.
----1. Dialogue from past conversations randomly playing when I am in a mission doing other stuff.

Don't get me wrong. Quake is a fantastic game, but I recommend buying the GOG version which you can buy
. I find this quite useful to install quake on older machines because a client is not required at all.

Id's previous shooter may be much more legendary, and rightfully so, but it was Quake here that put the final nail in the coffin to so called "Doom Clones" and truly defined the FPS genre. Being one of the first, if not the very first, FPS to use fully 3D polygonal graphics, Quake took the storm Doom made and turned it into a hurricane. Valve's own GoldSrc engine being a modified version of the Quake engine, the game branched out to create more classics such as Half Life, Team Fortress, and then branched out of Half Life to create Counter-Strike, the creation of the Source engine, and Steam as we know it today.
Yes the version here on Steam doesn't have the original soundtrack, but all you really need is this patch here
Just run the exe and it should automatically detect the Quake directory in your steam files. It's just that easy. The Patch also helps re enable the Steam overlay and help adjust the resolution to your liking, so the game doesn't look like Notch ate Minecraft and vomited it all over your computer screen.
Quake is hard for newcomers,  and even as a seasoned Doom veteran I found myself shamefully walking down the Easy difficulty corridor before starting Episode 3. You will die. A LOT. Enemies aren't pushovers here, a tradeoff as the time Quake was released, fully 3D enemies in the same numbers as Doom's sprite based would've slowed the game to a crawl, if not outright crash it. Ogres will chuck grenades at you, Vores fire homing purple projectiles, and zombies will keep throwing an endless amount of damaging innards at you until you blow the undead buggers away with either a grenade or rocket launcher, or a point blank shotgun blast while under the effects of quad damage. Not to mention the Shamblers, which will make you retreat halfway across the map in an attempt to find cover if your health is seriously low. You will be forced to learn what weapon works best against enemies, lest you be stuck dying endlessly by the claws of a Fiend or the barb of a Scrab.
Quake is, and can be frustrating, but it is always rewarding.
Like Doom, even if you're not a FPS fan, Quake is still a game that anyone who considers themselves a gamer should play before they die.
Without the patch I linked above, the game is barely playable. Once you run it though and open up the game, it's back to it's old playable self, and a 10/10 experience you won't forget
In short, buy this game.

Like many children, I was afraid of the mythical monster under the bed, but in time, this nightmare fodder gained a face and a name. It was the Sasquatch, a creature I came to fear when watching a cheap television film late at night which demonized the fictitious (or is it?!) beast. I refused to go into the woods by myself for years afterwards, for fear a giant hairy fiend might grab me and abscond with my limp body, for Lord knows what reasons. By avoiding the woods, I could avoid the monster lurking there.
Evolve doesn’t let you hide. This unusual and entertaining team-focused shooter forces you to face a grotesque monster in each and every match, and should you find it, you cannot always flee. Here’s the setup: a four-person team of hunters, each touting very specific talents, is on the prowl. The quarry is a single creature with an appetite for flesh. Not just the flesh of the hunters, but indeed, for the flesh of anything that moves. By attacking the wildlife and chomping down on its meat, the monster evolves through three stages of being, each more powerful than the last. Clearly, the hunters would rather tear the monster down with the least resistance possible, and thus finding the creature quickly, and efficiently destroying it, is a good team’s opening goal.
Hurry it UP Parnell. Maybe you should have taken that "faster reloading" perk.
Would that it were so easy. Should you join a team of hunters, you rely on a particular squadmate to lead you to the beast. That would be the trapper, and while you eventually unlock two other trappers to chose from, Evolve smartly taps Maggie as the initial leader. Maggie makes for a good guide through the ins and outs of pursuit, for she is not a lone ranger. Instead, she relies on her best friend Daisy, an animal called a trapjaw that you might think of as an ugly beagle, or perhaps the result of a hyena and a shark’s unholy coupling. In any case, Daisy is truly woman’s best friend: she follows the monster’s tracks, and leads you to its current location, should all the proper pieces fit in place.
I describe the trapper first because she is the de facto team leader. Trappers Abe and Griffin have their own tracking tools--a pistol that shoots tracking darts, in Abe’s case, and sonic spikes that alert you to the monster’s whereabouts for Griffin. Yet Maggie and Daisy are crucial in those early learning hours, and if they join your team frequently, your first match without Daisy feels rather lonely, as if you’ve lost a buddy and have been forced to fend for yourself under duress. With or without her, this phase captures the essence of a true hunt: it’s tense, simmering with the possibility of a sighting at any moment, and, like a real-life hunting trip (or Sasquatch search, depending on your predilections), there might be stretches of boredom. A sneaky monster crouches to hide its tracks, or doubles back on its own path, thus leaving a befuddling set of paw prints. Even with a veteran crew, Evolve is occasionally the Blair Witch Project of online shooters, replete with creepy noises, signs of a deadly presence, and a whole lot of running around, hoping for something to happen, at least in its central Hunt mode. How long it takes Evolve as a whole to become stale is difficult to gauge, but after close to three dozen hours, I'm not yet ready to leave it behind. If anything, I'm eager to discover more ways to use the landscape as part of my strategy, though I find this world a fascinating enough place that time outside of battle still engages me. If you prefer to run your engine hot, the hunt may not satisfy you.

Lords of Xulima (LoX) is an old school CRPG influenced by the classics like Might and Magic, Wizardry and Ultima.
While ToX does contain a good amount of story and dialog, its focus is clearly on combat, exploration, and progression, similar to how Might and Magic and Wizardry games are.  And I'm happy to say that it really shines in these areas.
Progression-wise, the game lets you build a party of 6, including a premade main character with a unique class.  You can pick from 9 classes when making your other 5 characters, and each class offers unique abilities, strengths and weaknesses.  You can definitely agonize over what the optimum party config is for hours if you are prone to that madness :).
As your characters level-up, you gain skill points that you can spend as you choose.  In LoX, weapons, spells and skills like "lockpick" are all treated as "skills."  The majority of skills have "levels," with different skills having different max levels.  What this means is that you will probably want to focus on maxing out a few skills so that you don't gimp your characters with a bunch of weak skills as opposed to a few strong ones.
All in all, the progression system is nice because you have a lot of wiggle room in how you customize your party and each character within your party.  You also unlock new skills as your characters level up, so this makes leveling pretty fun.  You won't find the absolute crap-ton of skills in LoX that games like Wizardry had, but the fact that you can level up skills independently and that each skill feels pretty unique makes up for this.
As for combat, LoX has turn-based combat with the turn order displayed on the side of the screen so you can see who's going next and strategize.  I was really pleasantly surprised by the combat.  It is VERY challenging, and you feel like you really need to consider every action, especially early on.   It's really imperative that you think about how your party is going to work together effectively if you want to succeed in combat.  You absolutely need defensive characters in the front row to soak up damage, or you will find your poor fragile mage getting his or her face kicked in repeatedly.
The combat interface feels slick and snappy, and the combat graphics are very impressive for a $20 indie game.  I was really impressed with the combat overall, stellar job here.
Next, the exploration aspect of the game,  Exploring in LoX seems pretty good so far, the zones all seem to have interesting things to find, like puzzles, riddles and lots of loot to gather.  The exploration also has an element of danger, because you never know when you're going to wander into a trap, or get ambushed by a monster that will absolutely destroy you.  Make sure to save often!
If I have any gripe about exploration, it's that sometimes there are secret doors and the switches can be insanely frustrating to find, requiring you  to combat over wall after wall with your mouse.
In conclusion, I would highly recommend this game to any fan old school CRPGs, or new-old-school CRPGs like Divinity:OS.  It's a really quality indie-RPG that seems to be a cut above most indies.  However, if you're looking for a very story-heavy experience, or you don't want a challenging game, you may want to look elsewhere.

A Bird Story is an absolutely beautiful tale, one that really leaves you wondering how a game with no dialogue can make you feel like someone spoke to you something so heartwrenching.  It's a great prelude to the next game and the music is so gorgeous.  I definitely recommend checking this game out!

Let's get this clear, this is not a game in the traditional sense. A game is defined generally by winning or losing at something, this is not one of these games, I'd dare to call it more of an interactive linear story. This is a game about values, artistic and emotional values, although simplistic in it's format it conveys well its message and does it with a superb music composition.
If you enjoy a game for the story and emotional appealing, this is an interactive story for you. If you do not, skip out.
Not much of a game, A Bird Story is more of an experience. It feeds on sentimentality and nostalgia, producing another emotional masterpiece from Freebird Games.

To the Moon was a work of art. This is not. I hate to give this a bad review; I was really trying to like it.
I think the idea was to try to be like Wall-E and tell a story more through no-dialogue, gesture-based characterization. Problem is...this is RPG Maker, not Pixar. The goal is just not possible given the technology.
Sorry Gao, but please stick to the extremely well-written and good pacing momentum you built from To the Moon. This game is beneath your talent.

A Bird Story is a short adventure game, more interactive fiction than anything, with minimal interaction - some moving around, and occasional prompts.

I'm recommending on the basis that it does what it sets out to do quite well, but many - possibly even most - people will not enjoy this game simply because the style is not what they are looking for. Go in expecting a nice narrative, and little if anything else.

i had already written a review of this game at one point i thought but it seems to be missing.... so here goes:
i bought this game AWHILE back now... because of some really kind of over-unnecessarily negative reviews, and the fact that the game intrigued me.
this game is... not very well polished, a bit repetetive, and overall may not be for everyone... BUT!
this game has some really cool points to it, and is actually kind of fun to do a playthrough every here and there. it'll only take you 2-5 hours more than likely to complete most 'storylines'.
if you've played other simple RPGs you may like this one. i used to play a lot of games that other people would scoff at, like final fantasy mystic quest and some of the old dragon warriors and the like on the old snes/nes and i have to say it's nice to have a game whose sole purpose is to just make a character and go on a journey casually at my own leisure.
the game has some cool mixtures of elements, like a survival element with food, and hunting/gathering... it's kind of interesting to have in a game like this, especially since that sort of brings the feel of a survival-crafter into it (which it isn't, at all, but still kind of cool to have elements of).
there's a lot that this game sort of leaves for want but... i can see a really cool sequel to this coming out at some point and rocking the socks off of this one, but in the process getting more people to buy this one too.
i would recommend it if you have the cash and dont mind casual exploration and random battles with very little focus for story. it's clunky and odd but charming nonetheless.

15 minutes was enough to see this game wasn't for me.
I do enjoy the art style, but the game just completely failed to keep my attention past a few minutes. Everything in the world seemed bland and pointless. You start off on a world map and select one of four tiles around you. You can look for food, look for treasure (find the 4 or so treasure chests and open them), look for a mine, or select another 4 tiles to travel to and repeat. That's not fun to me and it sure as heck didn't make me go "Ooh, I wonder what comes next!" or "Ooh, I want to better my character by <blank>!".
The second thing that put me off about this game were the controls. Why lock a 3d game to four fixed viewing directions (north, south, east, west) when the game was designed for a modern controller with two analog sticks? To anyone who believes the hyped "tower defence" and "rogue-like" aspects to this game, this has neither.
-No maze, the enemies just attack whatever is close to them, so forget any strategies...
-Horrible UI, so forget any RTS Micro-management, units move too slowly for this to be effective anyway...
-Map dictates difficulty, which is the only "rogue-like" aspect that there is, you have no control of where you spawn.
More then likely your experience will be this:
Spawn, find no resources, or not sufficient recources. Looking around for the resources you will find anywhere from 6-10 entrances into your base.
There is no solution to this, except to construct a solid wall which takes a massive quantity of lumber (that you may not have access to because of the map) and then constructing anywhere from one to multiple guard towers to defend them.
These guard towers must be manned in order to fire. You will not have enough units to man the towers that you have, so you will end up running single units around from one tower to another more or less constantly, for at least an hour untill you have some units coming in.
If there is a breach, that is more then likely your game over, and you will spend hours doing it all over again...
The only other difficulty comes artificially in the form of resource starvation, and trying to manage space within your walls. You will find that your base becomes a maze for your own units, you have no control of this becasue you cannot cut down trees or remove ore/stone to increase useable space.

Trion is a company fighting a losing battle... their revenue is slowly drying up, things Trion has done during my time in Rift to try and keep going:
- Gate gear slots behind a paywall, 2 earring slots were locked and made unlockable by paying credits, decision reversed some time later after uproar(and probably loss of players).
- $39.99USD to $59.99USD charged for the last expansion, keeping in mind this game is touted as a F2P game where many players still pay a monthly fee for patron which gives anti-penalties/bonuses(same charge as a subscription) and many players purchase various items from the extensive cashshop for real $$$(expansion is now free to newer players)
- $99USD mount lockbox added to cashshop, removed shortly after after uproar.
- $249USD pack added to cashshop that gives some fluff items but mainly: a large amount of endgame currency called Intel for buying high-grade gear, and a large amount of loyalty points which unlocks fancy items that many players have been working toward unlocking for years.
- every few months they add a new RNG Lockbox for $$$, something I like to call a gamblebox...contains mostly trash but lures you in with the faint hope of getting a new rare desirable item. Some people call this 'predatory monetization' taking advantage of players who are particularly prone to addiction.
- at this point expect any new content additions(big or small) to cost you real $$$ to experience.
*A few people may argue that a lot of stuff in the cashshop can be obtained by buying a REX with ingame currency, that may have been true in the past, at time of writing this review the cost of REX is around 3500platinum and slowly but steadily pushing up to 4000platinum(about 1.5 years ago it cost 2000platinum), a lot of time there wont be any REX on the AH due to demand. You can certainly farm enough platinum to buy REX at these prices... if you're willing to turn Rift into your 2nd job.
So you reached level 70(and read this far), you're now at end-game, what is there to do? The latest paid expansion has been out for over a year now.

- get stomped in PvP warfronts until you are wearing good gear, you can always buy the $249USD pack ;)
- upgrade your eternal weapon through extremely repetitive tasks, btw Trion's eternal weapon idea is a cheap knock-off of

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a 3rd person tactical shooter developed by 2K Marina and published by 2K Games. In The Bureau it seems as if 2K really tried to expand the XCOM name and branch off with the hopes of making XCOM more than just a turn-based strategy series. Most AAA game developers these days are scared to try new things and branch out into different areas so I give 2K props for at least trying to do something different. I have no problem with 2K trying something new but the fact that they seem to have used the XCOM name as little more than a cash-in is deplorable as this game has very little in common with the rest of the XCOM series. The only aspects The Bureau takes from its predecessors are a couple of the same enemies and a general setting outline. The game seems like it wanted to be an XCOM version of Mass Effect but The Bureau is neither particularly good at being an XCOM game or a third-person shooter.
The Bureau's story is essentially that the world has been hit with a series of alien attacks and you, Agent Carter, have to go on a variety of missions for the XCOM program, essentially humanities last line of defense, in order to stop the threat and save the world. There's obviously a bit more to it than that but overall the story is just your basic alien invasion story and has pretty much nothing unique about it to deserve the XCOM name. The setting is interesting as instead of modern weapons you engage the aliens with 70's era weaponry which means that early on in the game you'll be at a severe disadvantage when fighting aliens wielding plasma cannon and laser rifles. The environments that The Bureau has you trekking through are extraordinarily bland and offer very little in terms of uniqueness since the game is as linear as linear gets. The Bureau wants you to explore to find new weapons and backpacks, the only real customizable gear the game has to offer, but what it means by "exploring" is to just walk down another hallway or look behind you. I found all the characters to be absolutely repulsive save, ironically, the alien prisoner you acquire early on in the game. Every character has heaps of voice lines overusing phrases like "we're going to make the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s pay" and as the aggravating dialogue piles up you end up skipping through it all and not caring at all about the characters or what they have to say. The Bureau also features one or two moments where you have to choices and these moments make you feel as if The Bureau wanted to try and be an RPG in the vein of Mass Effect but instead just couldn't perform. In the end, after listening to nothing but the same old faux-patriotic quips from the whole character lineup you end the game begging for the aliens to hurry up and get on with it.
The combat is really where you begin to see peeks of how The Bureau could have been something great but instead really defaces the XCOM name. The Bureau prides itself on tactical combat where you have to use a bit of tricky maneuvering and strategy in order to save the day and truly this is where most of the enjoyment is at. The gun progression is pretty bad since about halfway through the game you have all the weapons that you'll need and The Bureau doesn't give you good reason to use any of the rest. Some of the guns feel decent but other are like peashooters and even that seems like it may be an exaggeration. The gameplay itself though is very interesting as you really do have to use traditional XCOM tactics like positioning your men in cover or flaking your foes to do extra damage. Every one of the squadmates has a class and these classes each come with unique abilities that progressively unlock as you level each character up. These abilities allow not only for very satisfying visual shows but also for a suprising degree of synergy with the squad as a whole. For example, you could have one man throw down a turret, have another shield it, and then have the final man lift it up so it ignores cover. These abilities and how they synergize with each other is really what makes The Bureau unique and worth a purchase. However, the AI is quite possibly the worst I have ever seen in a game and certainly shouldn't be in a game with such a renowned name as XCOM. You spend most of your time babysitting the AI to make sure they don't run into enemy fire or charge a minefield and in some points it feels almost like artificial difficulty. The AI seriously impacts combat on the higher difficulties but even still there's enough here that I can say it's worth a try.
A third person tactical shooter with a mediocre plot and cliched characters that is only brought to light by the unique combat system.

Quake is nothing short of a PC gaming landmark. There's a lot going on in Quake- it's the spiritual evolution of DOOM, a technological revolution on many fronts (including a game-changing 3D engine and online multiplayer system), a completely realized vision with industrial-gothic graphics and incredibly immersive sound design by Trent Reznor of NIN fame. Quake is an all-encompassing masterpiece.
My tastes run more towards JRPGS and quirky adventure games, and I'm not a big fan of gore, but there's something about Quake's purity of vision and excellence in execution that has grabbed me since 1996 and refuses let go. Without hyperbole, this is one of the greatest video games of all time and its impact and influence continues to be felt to this day. If you're at all interested in game design or history, I encourage you to visit (or revisit) Quake. It is inspiring.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is the second of the third-person shooter style game within the history of the series, which primarily takes on a top-down strategy style approach. The first title that took on a third-person shooter perspective was 2001's XCOM: Enforcer, which received mix reviews from fans and critics alike. Like all XCOM games before it, Declassified was published by 2K Games, but developed by 2K Marin instead of MicroProse Software, Inc., or any of the companies that worked on the Enemy Within release.
I'm not going to pretend to be some sort of XCOM enthusiast or expert, as I'm neither of those things; in fact, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is the first title in the series that I've ever played. With that out of the way, you can guarantee this review will not be pining over the fact that this release isn't of the same gameplay style of say, UFO Defense or Enemy Unknown. Even though this is the second of the third-person shooter XCOM titles, it's a great refresher of the franchise in general, and it has the potential to reel gamers into the XCOM universe who may not be so crazy over top-down strategy games. As I was playing, I never once felt like I was out of the loop when it came to plot, in all reality it actually felt like I was starting at the beginning of the story.
It's 1962, and you're Agent William Carter; a man who has some deep demons to face from his past, but who is also an excellent operative. You've been assigned to XCOM, a top-secret government organization that by all official accounts does not exist. It's your job to take out the alien scum, or "Outsiders", that are invading the United States, and possibly the world; their reach is unknown, as all communications outside of the immediate area have been blacked out. There are some survivors that have been infected by the Outsiders, known as Sleepwalkers, and it's your hope that a cure will be found for them. You and your crew must find a way to ensure that humanity prevails, and depending on your decisions it may cost a lot to do so. Be prepared to take on some of the most dangerous alien elites.
Without a doubt, this game is a definite merger of Mass Effect and Gears of War. Its primary combat system relies heavily on cover-based shooting, and even on the easiest difficulty if you do not make use of cover... you will die. Despite the third-person shooter aspect of XCOM Declassified, there is still a tactical influence that will make your gameplay experience a whole lot easier if you utilize it. You are able to bring two other agents on missions with you, and you can fully command them on the battle field; you can tell them where to move to, which foe to shoot at, and also make them use their unique skills which will come in very helpful at times. There are four types of agents that you can choose between, all of which have their own benefits and skills that will come in handy during the numerous Outsider onslaughts. New skills are unlocked as the agents, and yourself, rank up by earning kills in combat. However, it's an unfortunate downside that the agent AI in this game is mediocre at best, and if you do not keep your commands on them at all times, their helpfulness is extremely low.
The Mass Effect influence comes in to play via dialogue choices, and even the dialogue system itself. Once you complete a major or minor mission, you will return to the central XCOM hub where you are able to interact with certain characters. Generally, you will also have three dialogue options to talk about to any given person. Talking to them will reveal much more of the storyline and backgrounds, and many of the choices that you make will have an affect on the ending that you will receive; in total, there are seven different endings. There are also letters, photographs, and recordings that you can pick up throughout the game; while they aren't required for any advancement or achievements, they do add further depth to the story that helps bring everything together.
While the story is extremely well written and exceptionally executed, so long as you take the time to talk to people and review letters and recordings, XCOM Declassified really shines when it comes to overall atmosphere. The environments are lavishly detailed, and no two mission areas are alike. Hands down, even though the game is dated by three years now, this is one of the best looking titles that I've ever had the pleasure of laying my eyes on. Between the fog effects, dynamic lighting, the clashing range of soft pastel colors and cold metallic alien structures, and spectacular recreation of a 1960's environment, there's absolutely no denying that this release is a visual stunner. All of it is wrapped together with an equally amazing soundtrack that will keep you engaged from beginning to end.
There is an unfortunate downside to XCOM Declassified that has resulted in the largest amount of its negative reviews. The controls are fairly unpolished and convoluted, while they could've followed the formula of so many other titles of the same vein. The worst of all is how hard it is to aim, even if you set the controller and/or mouse sensitivity very low, if you nudge in the same direction for even a fraction of a second too long, you overshoot your target and end up missing your mark entirely. This happens more often than not, and causes a lot of ammo to be wasted; which is unacceptable in an environment that requires some moderate resource management.
However, given the utterly brilliant storyline, jaw dropping landscapes, immersive atmosphere, superb optimization (60+ FPS at all times), and the huge bang you'll get for your buck (13-15 hours of play time), it's easy to forgive the control flaws as you will become so engrossed in everything that's going on around you that you'll just... what's the famous XCOM term?... Adapt. Survive. Win. If you're looking for a long lasting, totally immersive third-person shooter experience that has a story and visuals that you won't soon forget, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a must have for your Steam library. It'll leave you wanting more, and luckily there's some DLC for that.

I grew up in the 80s. I remember oldschool games. I was a teenager in the 90s, and remember the RPG gems of the era, a lost age as far as I'm concerned. Games where the story and sense of exploration, strategy in combat was more important than flashy cutting edge graphics. Games where literacy was important and they came with huge manuals, with a fleshed out backstory and bestiaries of all the monsters.
Lords of Xulima hearkens back to that era, the late 90s isometric RPGs, but with the traditional turn based first person "enemy in front of you where your chars portraits are on the bottom of the screen" RPG format. Its fun. Its awesome. Ive wanted an RPG like this for ages.

I know it's almost 3 years late, but I really did want to write a review about Lost Planet 3.
If you have played the first two, then you should already be familair with the setting and a bit of the story for LP3. A planet covered in ice and snow but pumped full of a liquid thermal energy that is humanity's "last hope" for a renewable power. the reason I put the quotes is because, well, for a last hope energy source, nobody really seems to be in a rush to to get it, but I digress.
In Lost Planet 3, you play as Jim Peyton. An Adrien-Brody-looking "Rigger" who takes a job on the planet E.D.N. III mineing and harvesting the thermal energy in the planet to support his wife and child back on Earth. The catch there being that the planet is infected with insectoid-like aliens know as Akrid who seem to also have the T-Energy in there own body as well.
The game features both a story mode and multiplayer mode. The story it's self is strong, way better then the first game, with a lot more focus on the main character and less of an arcade feeling. It works well with the third-person set up. It also offers upgrades for both the weapons you purchase and your rig, which is also your main way of traveling on E.D.N. III. The NPC's are also fun, but really cliched. You have the foreigner who is your main rival at the base, the young, cocky mechanic, the scientist that wants to go to far in his experiments, and lastly, the doctor that is the only real voice of reason whom everyone ingnores.
The Multiplayer, well . . . Have you ever been sitting in a movie, and you think there is going to be something post-credits so you wait and wait and the credits are completely over and there is you and like, two other people left sitting down and you get that awkward feeling in the pit of your stomach becasue the ushers are ready to clean up the floors but you and those two guys are holding them up, and it's just. . . dead? Yeah, kinda like that.
I do need to say, before I wrap this up, that I did not complete the story mode. Aprently the PC port of the game was riddles with bigs that caused a few things to not work in the main story and a few of the side quests. Locked in a location, enemies not spawning, and even one boss that will not die. Capcom promised for months after the release that they were working on a large patch to fix the story (along with a deleveling bug in the MP) up to 6 months after the game launched, but arounf the 1-year mark, there was silence, and Capcom mvoed on from LP3.
Should you paly the game? Eh. . . uuhh. . . yeah?
I mean, the game is by no means perfect, and the bugs seem to be game by game and not that consistant. I was danceing on a fine line between yes and no, but I really enjoyed what I played and even if I knew ahead of time that I would not be able to finish the game, I still would have played it.
So Yes, play it, wait for a crazy sale before you buy it though, that what I recommend.

A buggy mess, filled with bad and strange gameplay decisions. Dead Space 1-3 are FAR better games, and feel incredibly similar. The Dead Space games actually feature some genuinely creepy and horrific moments, and the atmosphere is top-notch. In comparison, everything here just falls flat.
75% of Lost Planet 3 consists of walking around in a very slow, defenseless Mech / Rig. When you get to where you need to be, you spend 15 minutes turning a valve, and then when that's finished, walk a few more steps and spend another 15 minutes turning another valve. Every single button \ computer you interact with breaks down, leading you to find 'another route' / far away button \ computer. It's just dull, uninspired, tedious game design.
You also have to backtrack for a lot of objectives, and enemies spawn in exactly the same locations; there is no variation, in both the environments or the enemies. When enemies spawn, you can also see them literally appear in front of you most of the time.
The checkpoint system is inconsistent; especially before some of the bosses and harder encounters. After dying, you have to sit through 5-minute unskippable cutscenes again and again. Very annoying on harder difficulties.
I made it about 5 hours in and encountered a game-breaking bug that prevented me from continuing. I'd encountered the bug several times in the game, but they were overcome (eventually). When using the Mech, you have to turn a valve (again) and the controls simply stop working. I tried it on both M+KB and a 360 controller and it just wouldn't let me pass. This is a fairly common bug apparently.
At this point, I'd seen enough of the game and wasn't enjoying it much, so it was the last straw.
The PC controls often don't work, and when the button prompts appear on-screen, they're very often wrong, even using the default control scheme. The game clearly wasn't bug-tested or had much, if any, quality-assurance. Even playing on a 360 controller has some issues with wrong button-prompts and slow interactions.
When very similiar and much better games like Dead Space exist, I find it impossible to recommend this game.
Play Lost Planet 2 with a friend instead. Waste of time.

Let's start by saying I like what Kan Gao is trying to accomplish.  I just don't think it was accomplished here.  Kan Gao would like to tell beautiful (or cute), and meaningful stories with beautiful art and music, with pixel graphics for the 'mundane' bits.  Some of that is there...  Yes, there is a pixel graphics for the engine, the music is quite nice, and there are some nice static background art.
What there isnt is a particularly interesting story this time, and the gameplay, while secondary for this kind of VN/game hybrid is simply leading you around by the nose doing things rarely relevant to the story.  I wanted to like this game, and for perhaps $1 or less (say, in a bundle), I would feel like I got my money's worth.  Unfortunately, I bought it 50% off, at US$2.50, and feel like I did not get very much for my money.  I use a $1/hour baseline, and then adjust if the game is short but amazing, or the long time is boring time.
I was bored at least half the time, honestly.  Sorry.  There it is.
I wish Kan Gao and the team success and look forward to the next game, which had a little teaser and reminded me and many others of To The Moon... I won't do it here, because I don't want to spoil it for anyone who may want to play.

Xbox One Controller walking left issue fix
On Windows 10, go to device manager, right click Xbox Controller, update driver software, browse, pick from list and select Microsoft Xbox One Controller, let it install. Now you should be able to play the game without walking left and be able to go left and right on the over world.
If PS3/PS4 controllers still piggyback off the xbox drivers on PC then this should work for it too.
Hopefully this will help everyone else who is having this issue.

Sooooo this is my first ever review on steam!
I watched the Youtube vidoes, heard all the comments about how this is what no mans sky should have been etc etc etc and decided to jump in to decide for myself.
I was not dissapointed.  Heres my main point that I have taken from the game in my 23hours of play so far.
The good bits:
The game looks fantastic - I find my self at times just staring up at the sky or across the horizan taking in the gorgeous graphics and fantastic representation of an alien world.  The look of this game is perfect for the stranded on an alien world feel.
Nice Tutorial - Its a survival game, you gather and craft like all the others however I feel the current tutorial is good enough to show you the basics of how to survive before it lets you off on your own building, surviving and dieing adventures.
Building and customization - Building is simple and easy to get into and looks really cool whilst having a decent amount of depth, once I had found the space I wanted to call home it didnt take me long to build my base, a little trial and error to get positioning right but nothing that spoiled the fun.  The customization options are something I feel is missing in many survival games, you want your base bright pink..... you go it.... you want your vehicle as red as the sand...... no worries.
Vehicles - The vehicles are sooo cool and varied, I've only built two so far but from what I've seen they are all unique and serve a purpose and not just there for the sake of it, its also realy fun driving around in your 6 wheeled armoured vehicle.
Multiplayer - This game rocks solo, but is taken to another world (see what I did there) with a mate or two tagging along. Teaming up to take on giant crabs, exploring a dark mine whilst your both scared and worried about the life in your flashlight or just wandering the surface toether marvelling at the view.
The not so good bits:
Controls - Personally I felt the controls felt a little clunky to begin with it quickly passes and starts to feel normal in first person, however the third person mode just doesnt feel quite right to me.
Planet Surface - I feel that the amount of area to explore is fairly limited at least at this stage of EA, I understand that there is another moon/planet you can get too but the size of map on Proteus seemed a little small.  This is a minor negative as it is in EA so is likey to change and evolve going forward.
Bugs - I have encountered a few minor bugs one where the tutorial wouldnt let me continue and had to start a fresh world but nothing thats surprising in an EA title and nothing that made me want to turn it off.
The verdit:
Do I recommend it..... HELL YEAH! One of the best EA titles I have ever played, a decent amount of content right now with soooo much potential moving forward. If you enjoy playing EA games and supporting devs while watching a game develop this is a must have in my opinion.

My first review on Steam.
This is a game with great turn based depth. It has similar combat mechanics with the Disciples 1&2 series(the good ones), with M&M series, with M&M Legacy, but it seems way better, cleaner and more fun.
It also has interesting puzzles, very neat and crisp 2D graphics and exploration mechanics. But make no mistake, this game is all about combat. And combat it does very very well. If you like a challenge and a game where you must think hard before you just push buttons, then Lords of Xulima is the right game for you.
The game is recommended for the Veteran level, because at this level the challenges imposed by the enemy parties require you to use everything at your disposal to win. Be it potion, spell scrolls, buffs, debuffs, usable items, there are many fights in which you must use tactics and think ahead more than a few moves to be able to move forward. Also it is one of the first games where threat assesment is spot on. When you right-click an enemy and it says Troublesome, it will be TROUBLESOME.
The rpg mechanics are well-thought, being a progression based game. The higher you level up, the stronger your heroes get, but at the same time the enemies begind to vary in their attacks, properties and sizes. Each class brings something to the table; there are no useless clases in this game. As there are tons of varied enemy combinations, the game encourages you to make a diverse party, not try to cheese it with 6 archers(that does not work, you need dps tanks in front). you will need heals, thief skill,etc.
This game is also very long (50 hours in, almost at half) and, to be honest, it can take a seat near Wasteland 2 and Divinity OS as inovation, feeling and attention to detail. Like those games, it combines the game elements in a way that entices the player to keep playing, ignoring sleep and food to just finally defeat that last monster.
The only negative part in my opinion is the mediocre story, but as you play the game, the design is so good that you never notice it during gameplay.
I really recommend it, as it offers huge and complex content for a low price.
