Let me start this out by saying I REALLY WANT to love this game.
I played the original on PS4 and enjoyed it to a certain degree and
when my friend told me it was F2P on PC I was stoked.
Playing on PC is so much less clunky and clumsy than using a controller and I
really enjoy that part.
I also want to say that my poor review has very little to do with the store prices that everyone is complaining about. I understand that it is really difficult to get additional characters because of the price hike (For scale I have about 13 hours now and am just being able to afford my first 14k hunter, and that 14k I have saved was boosted by the extra cash you get from starting the game and doing the tutorials), however it is not my main fault with this game.
I serious fault I have the game in its present condition is the balancing.  When I played on PS4, the balancing seemed pretty good and I would win/lose games and either hunter or monster. It didn't seem all that slanted to me. Playing Stage 2 is completely different.  The game FEELS extremely slanted towards the  monster now. I have played in all four roles on the hunter team (My best being Medic and Assault) and no matter what I try I cannot beat another player using the monster (Co-op vs. AI is a little better, where I can sometimes beat the monster)
Here are some of my MAIN observations and differences between the original and S2:
In the original, a Stage One monster who gets trapped was in SERIOUS trouble.  It is even said in the game that at Stage 1, the hunters have an advantage. In this version of the game, not only
will the monster survive being caught at stage one, but he KILLS 1-2 of my team members and suffers very little damage. Even if I am playing assault and trying my hardest I can only ever get through the monster's armor before the shield goes down and he gets away, only to eat like 4 things and get all his armor back again.
In the original, keeping up with the monster was not that hard if you were good at managing your Jet Pack and using high ground to keep an eye on him.  I feel that the hunters base movement speed has been nerfed to the point where most games my team can't even get a location on the monster before he is already Stage 2.
Even if I DO take all the perks related to Jet Pack/Movement speed.
Finally, in the original the Trapper actually felt like he could be the make or break of a team.
Your Trapper being on his toes, fast, and after the monster was vital to scoring those Stage 1 and 2 wins as the hunters. Now that the TRAP that the hunters use to TRAP the monster has just been given to everyone, the Trapper just feels like a waste of space terrible extra damage dealer with no point. Seriously if the TRAPPER doesnt have any actual TRAPS to TRAP the monster, its like he doesn't matter. I hate playing trapper now because all you do is shoot when you see the monster and set up harpoons to slow him down a bit. Your damage is nominal and you
only really offer a moment of directional insight to your team (Most of us already knew which way to go) with the Satellite thing.
Overall, fix the balancing, and this idea is still ABSOLUTELY GOLDEN. I love the 4v1 aspect and I love the thrill of the hunt. The Trapper feels useless and hunters feel like they're running through mud. Fix it and I will enjoy it so much!

I am legitimately surprised to say that Hatoful Boyfriend is one of the most emotionally engaging games I have had the joy of playing. When I saw other people talking about how drastically it shifted from its lighthearted wrapper, I was under the impression that it was some running joke from within the community.
"A dating simulator about pigeons?" I said, "There's no possible way that this could be anything but jokes."
I was wrong. And the people at Mediatonic made you realized exactly how wrong you were while you stare at the ridiculous pictures of birds whose expressions never change. The same, unblinking gaze they had when they were being goofy cornballs but a few bittersweet playthroughs ago haunts you as they proceed to rip out your still beating heart and dash it across the pavement of the busy intersection joining grief and suffering.
If you want a game that seriously lives up to the idea of refraining from judging a book from its cover, this is the one you're looking for. Sit down, go through the motions of playing a fanciful dating sim, and unearth the wealth of melancholy that exists just under its chipper surface.
It unfortunately suffers from a pretty obnoxious grind and, though it offers a fast-forward button to quickly pass through repeated scenarios on subsequent playthoughs, every arc offers new scenes with no warning whatsoever. It's possible to miss a huge chunk of a storyline because of it.
Still, I would say it's worth the frustration. If you like being sad.

Fan of the first game? This game is for you! Fan of the second game but not the first game? This game is not for you (and please stop saying that it's worse than LP2... You are a fan of a game, not a series). This game is immersive and deep, not an arcade shooter.
TL;DR - Dead Space and Lost Planet had a beautiful love-child. Minor things make the game UI/engine feel unpolished when exploring, but overall experience is excellent and unique if players allow themselves to be immersed.
Cons first. Personal game experience is entirely controller based. Multiplayer not reviewed.
- UI occasionally doesn't work properly, only minorly though (map displays player position slightly wrong or something similar)
- Repair minigame's UI doesn't correspond correctly with joystick direction (still playable, just disorienting)
- When opening a lock with rig, "press A" is displayed. "A" does nothing, rotate joystick instead.
- Rig is slow
- Collisions occasionally odd (punch NPC for giggles, particle and "clunk" emanate from random box several feet away)
- DX9 only. Graphics could be fresher but alien vistas still make jaws drop.
- Cutscenes are inexplicably low-res. 8 gig free "DLC' fixes that.
Pros.
+ Story is phenomenal. (SciFi at its best. Character development is spectacular. Voice acting, animation, and environment make all characters supremely believable, if not lovable).
+ Environments are incredible (The planet is portrayed as hellish and inhospitable, and by god does the level design deliver. Environments often change as the game progresses. As an example, imagine a blinding, otherworldly snowstorm. Massive, house-sized chunks of ice ripped from the earth and tossed about in the storm, crashing into your rig and slamming into the ground. This game delivers.)
++ Ambiance is supreme (as someone who has always prized ambiance in a game, this game makes me giddily happy. Iced over wreckage from a long lost expedition echoes and creaks as ancient ice shifts and cracks. Crew quarters at the home base glow from the warmth of wall heaters and sing with the music of a guitar wielding crew member, who gets better as time goes by. Inhospitable alien caves pulse and crackle with forbidden energy and echo with the feral screams of frenzied akrid. Frigid wastelands howl with freezing gales of wind, as you, the pilot, huddle securely in your rig's cockpit. A good set of headphones and a decent computer will transport you to this unforgettable experience.)
+ Gameplay is polished (Guns handle well. The rig feels every bit to be the one-of custom machine that it is claimed to be. The player gets stronger and more skilled as the game progresses, but the volatile, aggressive enemy never becomes any less of a threat.)
Overall, the story and immersion are unparalleled. Anyone who played the first two games can attest to the minimal, often confusing story that the games presented (frequent faction switches and cut-scenes certainly portrayed EDN III well, but the players still generally had no idea as to what was going on beyond "Those enemies have T-ENG. Shoot 'em!"). This game more than reconciles that, giving context and clarity to the first two installments, as well as carving a beautifully crafted story for itself. Many of the game tweaks that nay-sayers complain of are actually meticulous details that improve immersion.
To address some:
-Rig is slow? It's a utility rig, not a fast attack vehicle. I feel like a pilot in a lumbering machine, not like a speedy player in a twitch run-and-gun.
-Guns suck? Guns are actually great! Upgrades make a noticeable difference, and every gun has a purpose, rather than some guns becoming washed out by later acquisitions. All this just makes the giant, armored akrid in front of you that much more intimidating when it doesn't go down easy.
-FPS drops? I have a 5 year old rig, am running everything on max, and have never dropped below 60 fps.
-Controls suck? Keyboard controls do suck, yes, but this game was always intended for use with a game-pad. Use one.
-Repetitive and boring? Yeah... Tell me more about how you came to that conclusion with only 3 hours in-game... Go back to your run-and-gun.
Overall, highly recommended to anyone that digs a good story and fans of Lost Planet/Dead Space. Just don't expect CoD action pacing. You aren't a 'roided-out super soldier (Hi, Marcus!). You aren't the Hero of Time. You are a married man, looking to make a living for his family on an inhospitable rock. If you have a good set of headphones and want to be transported to a savagely beautiful, icy world where untimely death is a daily consideration, this is the game for you!

a slightly-above-mediocre TPS game that has a lot of excellent ideas and mechanics that with more polish could come together brilliantly(and in parts should be integrated into other games). Most importantly having your HUD tied to your mobile but massive mech works, removing minor quality of life stuff when "going into the wild." The writing and performances are above par, though story itself is generic at best. Game looks great and there are a few really enjoyable weapons, but only a few of the enemies are properly enjoyable to fight against.
Most impressively Lost Planet 3 is extremely close in succesfully having you "do a job" amongst the rest of the game without it being a chore. Lumbering around in your mech is great as is, and a lot of the writing really enhances the feel of you being there doing work along a long period of time, though most of what you do is actually story stuff. And yeah that doesn´t sound exciting, but Lost planet 3 is very close to pulling it off 100% and as is it´s still absolutely enjoyable to play through.
It´s a shame how close this games gets to greatness, seemingly without being given another chance.

Okay, so I'm gonna start out by saying I don't typically write actual reviews for these recommendations - check my history - but I felt like I needed to say a thing or two about this, even if only a couple people read it.
As someone in a creative field, myself, I can see what's happening in the reviews for this and it's starting to make me sick.  The last thing a creative person needs is for the world to say "I liked that last thing you did better", and that's all that the big review sites are doing right now.  For someone to really push themselves and find new aspects of their art and their creation process, they have to stretch their legs and try new things - in my case I try drawing different art styles, I try different media, just to see what I can learn about it and whether I like the way I do it.
This is a pretty bold step in game creation for these guys, Mr. Gao in particular, and it might not seem like such a big deal but to try and tell a story through just actions and visuals (and fantastic music) is a lot more challenging than you might think.  I think they did a great job, considering the length, and considering how little we got to know the characters within the frame of the story.
I understand if you have your preferences between games from Freebird, and that's fine, I have preferences with my own work as well, but at the end of the day you can't vilify people for trying new things.  Personally, after playing this, I can see how much their talents have grown and I'm really excited to see what they do with what they've learned in future games.  You have me on board for life, guys, please keep going, keep expanding and exploring new places!

3DRPG is a game that sells itself with its voxel art style, but in terms of fun its flat, basic and empty. It's ready to live and die by that voxel art style so much that its encompassed as generic name as it could. 3DRPG what's it about? Its about 3D and RPG! It may look like another game with the same art style, but rather than playing like an adventure with real time combat and puzzles,  3DRPG is a traditional role playing game played out on a flat surface with turn based battles. If you are expecting a game where you build things with mini cubes or fight against enemies in real time, avoid this game. Everything that may look like a real time battle is just a different camera angle during combat.
When the game begins, its revealed that you're a lost soul, an imp on its way to damnation until you remember your name and who you are. By this I mean make your character. Give yourself hair, an eye color, shirt color, gender and so on. Then you pick a class, a weapon and assign your stats. Once you make your character, you're given the choice of a plot in order to stay out of the infernal pits. From the start there are two plots unlocked which are kill someone or get someone to take your place. The game seems to play out the same with either selection.
From there, the game is devoid of story, plot or quests. You're just plopped down in a generated town in a random generated world. Townspeople give you hints on how to play and if asked for directions, they tell you where your destination is such as a town to the northeast, but never reference names or quests. You can also ask any towns person to join your party with a starting limit of two. In town you can buy weapons, armor and items. If you leave town and return, a new town map is generated for you.
Your player can move in 360 degrees, but the camera is limited to four directions: north, south, east and west. You can go into a first person aim mode that lets you look any which way, but takes away your ability to walk.
Outside of town, is a world map where you move square to square in a cumbersome fashion. Normal games would let you move left and right, just keep moving. This game is a square by square basis. First you chose right, then move, then a selection pops up if you'd like to hunt for food, go treasure hunting or mining depending what type of terrain you're on. Each move on the map costs food depending on the terrain. Treasure hunting and mining cost food as well.
Hunting for food, costs no food. Here you're just dumped into a random map and given a bow and a fishing pole. You can either go fishing in a river or hunt down animals with a cumbersome control scheme where you take on a first person view and then rotate your way around to shoot bunnies, chickens and other things. When you're in first person view with a bow, you can only turn and aim. There's no way to walk forward. Other than killing things for food, you can find random plants to eat that are hovering above the surface.
Searching for treasure is awful because its this giant, empty flat surface of a three dimensional map that has you looking for three small boxes. So its a three dimensional game with flat maps that have a rock formation here or there. It becomes quite an unenviable chore to scour an uninteresting flat surface for more than five minutes. Where are the real dungeons and environments? The towns manage to have buildings and trees, but the random generation just lacks something that was designed to be fun.
I managed a few times to get stuck after walking over water, beyond town fences and getting wedged between a rock and a tree. The game lets you exit a map at any time and back to the world map.
Scavenging the land, killing things and so on will reward you with leather, gold, wood and food. With these items you can craft them into weapons, armor and potions. You can cook raw food into edible food. All crafting recopies are laid out easy. There's no guess work, just a system of menus. Select the type of thing you want to create between weapon, armor and item, select what you want to make and then what you want to make it out of. You see everything, there is no guesswork. The menu itself could be smoother.
Unlike hunting, when you're searching for treasure you'll see slimes on the map. Touching a slime sends you into combat! However, battles can occur at random, but they are rare. You can also be ambushed with a battle on the world map as well.
Combat is turn based like most other role playing games. There is a twist though, because your attacks are timing based. One square pops up on screen while another square moves toward the first. When they meet up you need to push a button to determine if you hit or miss. I managed to glitch the game where after a few battles, the prompt would never show up. When the squares were about to touch, it would just register as a miss with no opportunity to allow me to attack.
Each attack used costs action points. So attacking is an action. Once you run low, you'll need to defend or standby which replenishes your action points. The game only allows you to flee one battle per day, but once I fled one battle the game never let me flee again. That's an issue that can be sorted out.
The combat is just dull and shallow reliant on tedium of a mini game that makes you push a button. This makes every battle tiresome because there are other timing mini games that are more engaging than 3DRPG, but from a role playing game. I want combat to be a deeper game of chess.
You get to see the enemy health and skill points along with who is ready to attack. Its a good system that shows you everything, but the big issue is how awkward the fight menu is and that sums up the game as a whole. To select an attack, its up or down on the directional pad. To cycle through attack, flee and item its the bumpers on the controller. Once you've selected an attack, chose who to use it on by using the left and right arrows. It feels so alien. Controlling the camera with the bumpers also feels so alien too. Maybe this game was designed for a Super Nintendo controller with modern technology.
I should also point out this game's minimum requirements are above Skyrim's requirements. That seems crazy for a game that's under 500 MB. I'm also curious what this game would get for an age rating considering there's a lot of blood when enemies die.
After the pummeling I've given to this game, I'd like to see something better with the art style. It just feels so hollow. You need to want to play it, but it does nothing to make me want to play it. There's no story, no quests, you just keep finding your own entertainment and when a game makes me find my own entertainment, that opens me up to the idea that other games are more entertaining than this.

Wow - I overlooked this one on release, due to the bad press it received. So far, I'm impressed and the earlier reviews don't do it any justice.
In a way I'm glad I did overlook it before because now I get the whole package for under £7!
Had to retune the colours on my monitor for this one.
It's not quite an XCOM/UFO game, but it is definitely part of the series - the atmosphere is good, with sense of time and place established throughout, although the dialogue and story are "DC comic-level". This is less than I was expecting.
However - the story and dialogue improve a lot as the game progresses - it actually becomes pretty good and I am enjoying discovering the twists and turns of the plot as it unfolds.
The gameplay has become easier (on veteran) and the missions "shorter". The only time I had to reload (2x) was for a "mid-mission" where the team were about level 3. That was the only frustrating challenge in the whole game. All the others have been legit "hard" battles and I've felt accomplished at scraping through, or that, "ok I deserved to lose that one" or whatever.
The game feels as if Mafia II, Bioshock and XCOM were put into a gene splicer and shaken up a bit. Garnished with Alpha Protocol (although the "dialogue decisions" all lead to the same place).
That's a good thing, IMO.
It is one of the few games I've played lately where the cutscenes are of a lower quality than the game itself. They're not bad, but they're not good - the dialogue parts... I think they could've been a lot better. There doesn't appear to be any reason to give me a choice in many of the exchanges other than to hold my attention in an otherwise motionless and flat conversation - it means I get to push a button - and this distracts me from the disappearing-reappearing pistol and the fact my guy's arm is clipping through his body and the shotgun he's waving around looks glued onto the back of his hand...
I can glitch some parts - through walls, escape the area, fall off things, have the "troops" appear in random places / teleport, and I keep wanting to cover against things in places I can't. It's possible to exploit a few things in order to gain an unfair advantage over the game.
For some reason, my character occasionally is using weapons or waving a shotgun around like its a pistol - but that's only the cutscenes, as I've mentioned. The weapons themselves fell very "cartoony" and that's cool. This isn't Red Orchestra. I don't feel that I am doing anything other than playing a fun game with tense moments - it's not an immersive world like Portal 2, Dark Mod, RO, Long Dark or Deus Ex, etc... It's more along the lines of LA Noire or GTA kind of immersion. Easily broken and fallen back into, between chores or whatever.
The voice acting - well... it's that one guy again. The guy from every Bethesda game among others... He must be the most worked-voice actor in the industry and I'm sick of his voice!!! He even voices two characters in a conversation in this game. Kinda sucks, but is forgivable. You'll recognise the voice when you hear it, I'm sure. He really annoys me now, because he's become a gaming cliché.
Sound is otherwise excellent. Music is very good for the moment.
I've found the pace to be pretty good. It matches the linear progression / corridor play of the game.
During "combat" I've barely had to make any kills myself, and the "planning" phases generally have been 3-4x as long as the "action" phases.
I've felt like a real badass when quickly devising a simple plan, having the team execute it exactly as I intended and the whole fight being over before I've even had a chance to aim my own weapon. That's a good team-tactics game, right there. There have been a few moments where I've just decided to speed things up by walking down the range with a shotgun, and that's also been very satisfying and much fun.
I'm playing on Veteran, and I've only had to reload once, due to a control malfunction (wat is buttons i is noob?).
Thinking of controls - the vibration in this game does not feel tied to what is going on at all. It's a little disconnected and I'm feeling that I want to turn it off as it separates me from the gameplay.
The game follows the simple FFF tactics of games such as Brothers-in-Arms and Rainbow 6, etc... and the firefights feel like they have impact in the same way that Bioshock did. Much of the level and area design is a series of inter-woven corridors that zig-zag between areas with easy to reach flanks. The enemy is aggressive, reactive and are unrelenting in an "army of two" / "gears of war" way. That is, if they are alive long enough...
I was wondering how the "tactical" side of the 3rd person shooter would manifest and I think they've done a great job with this "focus" system - it is easy to use and there's little room for error.
Items are liberally scattered throughout - there's no need to conserve bullets or grenades so far, but exploration is very limited - there are not many things to investigate, but what there is... it's in-line with events and the characters have good banter.
I'm finding it very enjoyable after the first few chapters and playing this game is making me want to quit my Deus Ex replay in order to play some of the old UFO/XCOM games again (esp. the new version of Enemy Unknown). I'll probably be playing this the whole weekend, might even get to finish it.
Not sure about replayability, as it's like Mafia II in this way - not many different ways to tackle situations - however I think that I will replay this at least once or twice, as there are challenges and achievements to complete - plus some DLC missions to get into.
There's definitely scope to "meta-game" - the liberal ammo and weapons everywhere mean that I forget to use grenades and I'm considering a run whereby I change weapons every time I see a new one. I'm at the end of the game now, and the last 50% has been the easiest part - I've veyr much enjoyed the "progress" through levels. Not lost a single agent, had to "retry" a mission on 2x when I got stuck without ammo in a particularly tough farmyard battle on a side-mission.
Regardless - The Bureau is much better than I thought it was at release, going from the reviews and criticism it received - I'm enjoying it very much and it cost less than a gram of weed - definitely better than buying drugs.
I like the fact that - when I take a smoke break - my character does too :)
30 hours for an initial playthru is fairly decent. I think I've done and explored everything. The DLC I expect to add another hour or so. Plus a replay - that leads to anything up to 50 hours solid entertainment for less than £10, which is 50 pence per hour - that's very good value for money on any game, I think.

This game 90% about resource gathering and base building.  There's some combat too, but it's secondary.  If that's appealing to you it's worth a look.  The world looks good and I didn't think the early access bugs were bad.
But if "survival" is what you care about - don't bother.  I honestly think it's a bit deceptive to call this a survival game at this point in it's development.   On the _hardest_ setting, a single piece of meat from the easiest pushover critter will keep you fed for... 8 DAYS!  Food and drink, even life support (shelter, heat and beathable air), rarely have any impact on your gameplay decisions.  You can literally travel to another moon, gather resources and travel back without any consideration for survival.  In a couple extreme harvesting scenarios you might plan for heat or oxygen, but even then it's not too hard to just wing it and come out ok.
Different strokes, I know.  But for me this game falls short because I like survival games where a gamble or my failure to plan ahead could kill me.  The lack of risks and tradeoffs means there's no sense of accomplishment here for me, which kills the desire to replay.
UPDATE -- changing my recommendation to Nope, because of the new direction the game has taken.  I'm a science fan, not a fan of mysticism and the supernatural.  And certainly not a fan of ditching all the unique possibilities of contact with alien life for a tired old Ghostbuster theme.  If you want to see a game that gets contact with a complex alien econsystem right, see Subnautica.
This is not the first early access title I've bought where the direction of the game took a sharp turn into something different than advertized.  Very sorry to see this happen to O:ND; they lost me as a fan.

First off, do I recommend this game? It's hard to say. I want to give the game a good review for the effort put in, so this is the best I can do.
I'll try to keep the review as quick and concise as possible, so read on :)
While the game has a good concept, the actual result needs some work. I like how it is open world, and it has what I wish a lot of open world car games would include - a first person mode, where you can walk around, explore, and hop into other cars you see.
I know GTA allows you to do this, but I don't like the extreme violence in that series, and therefore don't play em.
Physics wise, the cars behave fine at low speeds but once they are moving, I feel that they are not loose enough on the rear wheels, and thus feel a bit weird (i.e, they don't slide out at the back if cornering hard).
The game uses the Unreal engine, so the graphical effects are quite nice. However, the quality of the car modles, and overall world detail could use some work. I understand that only a few people made the game, so it's not always possible to go into heavy detail like AAA games have, but still, they could have delayed its release and worked on the models a bit more.
I noticed some graphical shadow bugs when running fullscreen - not sure what was causing that. My computer definitely isn't underpowered, so it's most likely some bug.
Content-wise, what you get is appropriate for the price (I think there are around 10 cars). For the most part, I noticed a dfferent suspension setup values for each car. For example, the Camaro looks and feels different to the Mini.
The world, in my opinion, needs some more stuff to do though. After half an hour of driving, I found myself wanting to either challenge someone or upgrade my car. I know there is a race mode, but in any game, I much rather race real people than AI.
All up, I appreciate the work put into the game, but I honestly have to say that I won't play the game much, because there is nothing to bring me back to it later - which, in my case, is multiplayer.
It doesn't matter what game I'm playing - if it's single player (especially in the racing genre), sooner or later I'm going to get bored of it. Good example: the very first GRID game in Codemaster's series had multiplayer support pulled - and I haven't played that game in a good 5 (or how many years since the servers were shut down, I can't remember) years since driving against AI is so... boring.
Final Conclusion:
If you have a few bucks to spend, and some time to kill, then maybe you will like it. Like they say, it's the price of a cup of coffee (although I never drink the stuff :P). If you're looking for a multiplayer game with a huge world, high quality models, and lots of content, then no.
As a side note, young kids will probably enjoy the violence-free open world and ability to walk to and drive different cars.
The game certainly needs more work to be a polished and fun experience.

A Bird Story is a short narrative about a boy who saves a bird from being attacked. However, the bird does take an injury and so the child takes care of the bird and builds a lasting friendship with it. Your take on the game is to follow this narrative with minimal interaction. The stroy is rich in detail, and if you place enough attention to detail you can get caught up in story. A very emotional journey of growth as we see this boy go from no purpose in life to enjoying imaginative adventure with his friend.
This is a very simplistic artstyle, but one that stays with you if your paying attention. The most powerful part of the game is the music which really carries both a whimsical fantasy and a tone of everlasting change. And each scene is very powerful with both mediums working together and blending well.
A Bird Story is a great narrative, and one that I would recommend to anyone who follows Freebird Games as they make powerfully moving games, but the question that is asked when making this review is, "Do you recommend this game?" And in all honesty, as much as I loved the story and was able to connect with that child...it wasn't a game. Very simple. Those who have played To The Moon will really enjoy this, and those who appreciate art and music will as well, but there is no interaction, no reward, and no real input from the player that affects the game. Like I said a great narrative, but a very boring game.

This game is... problematic, to say the least.
First off, it is NOT a terrible game; Gameplay functions as it should, bugs are rare, sound and music are solid as are the graphics for the most part.
But the problems are that the story, aside from the few twists towards the end, is a generic alien invasion story that we have seen over and over. While other games with alien invasion stories try to put their own kind of spin or add flavor into execution that makes them worthwhile, this one follows a formula without any real intention of adding anything of its own.
Characters are also a downside, they are just not interesting. Except one alien invader character who is, in the end, just not used in any interesting way. The final boss has a pretty cool voice, but that's about it.
But my biggest axe to grind with this title, is in fact the title; why does it need to carry the X-Com franchise name? Considering it has zero elements from the source material; No base management, no real global defence, no strategy elements and the permanent death system is easily exploited and nullified because of its checkpoint save system.
It could just as easily be its own game and not be measured and compared against its counterpart(s). Especially since before this one was released we got a genuine strategy X-com game, so this one is just... redundant. Yes, it was in production hell and we knew it would be released one day, but with all the delays and push backs, it is just disappointing that THIS is all they could come up with.
It just has no real reason to exist.
Shooting aliens in this game is fun, i will not deny that and in the beginning it does set up a very bleak, desperate setting to fight back an overwhelming invasion.
Yet as the base becomes operational, that premise just does not live up to the pace that was set up at the beginning.
The base itself too feels like its just there for window dressing.
All in all, on basic mechanics and gameplay it does its job but on everything else it just falls flat.
As an X-com fan, i would not recommend it.
As a gamer, if you can get it cheap or as a rental, i would say check it out, who knows? you might find more things to like about it than i do.

I love voxel art, but I do not like Minecraft or any other survival/crafting style genre.  I am hard pressed to find games with this particular art style that don't lend to it's own tropes that seem to follow it around.  However, I did really enjoy 3D Dot Game Heroes on the PS3 (albeit I found frustratingly hard at times).  I'm also a huge fan of active/timed combat in a turn based environment ala JRPG.
This game hits all of those marks.
Pros:
- tight, responsive and tactile controls
- sharp, clean voxel graphics with that tilt-shift style lens filter
- smart and active response turn based combat (at first, it's not, but the more you play, the more it evolves)
- fun music with a little bit of a J-pop sound
- exploration exploration exploration (go out, do things, discover what you'll do next)
- randomly generated everything
- the grind? (I love grinding)
Cons:
- lack of story depth or quest options; I would like to see side quests available (fetch? kill count?)
- mild tutorial without much introduction (I found it easy to find my way through the game, but without anyone to tell me things were going to get better...I assumed the worst)
- not all controller keys/axis are configurable (can't adjust rotation to thumbstick, etc)
- the grind?  (some people don't like grinding)
I appreciate the subtle humor in the game, the art, and even the homage to all the games that came before it to make it what it is.  As the developer noted the game was inspired by 3DDGH, Breath of Fire, Legend of Dragoon, etc...and it really shows in all the good ways.

What starts of as an endearing cute styled RPG turns into a nightmare exercise in frustration due to poor design, poor controls, and a boring repetitive world.
This game feels like Early Access and should have been released as Early Access.   Right from the start you get a feel for the poor controls, the boring unresponsive combat and repetitive gameplay.
I won't go into details about the bugs, but this video will show a few.   But the bugs don't bother me, it's the core design of the game that does.
For a start, forget using a Keyboard.  Just forget it.  Although the controls are simple, they are poorly thought out and frustrating.    You use WASD keys to look around in Bow (hunting) mode, while to look left and right at 90 degree angles you press the Q and E key.   Why these aren't bound to mouse movement I don't know.
Using a controller isn't much better.   While walking around the square slab of the current flat boring map you use the left and right shoulder buttons to look left and right.   Again, why you can't use the controller's right stick I don't know.
While walking around on a map in treasure mode you can initiate combat with a generic looking enemy which represents any enemy, and will become a random amount of actual enemies once combat has started.   We've all seen this before in older RPGs, but not everyone was a fan of it.
This is where the frustration really starts.   Every single attack is a simple
where you have to push the button at the right time to make the attack make contact.  Every single attack, every time, a damned QTE.   What makes this really frustrating is that it rarely works properly, which results in a complete miss.  It seemed to miss more often with a controller.  Being turned based, every QTE attack (which is the standard attack), uses stamina.   Run out of stamina, and you need to manually select a "Defend" ability to pass your turn.
Every battle was the same thing.   Missed attack, Missed attack, run out of stamina, have one enemy kill your companion (who also missed attacks even though you SWEAR you got every one right) killed in two turns.   An escape or "Flee" option is available, but even that doesn't work correctly.   When I select it, it says "Already used today" even though I have never used it one single time in the entire game.
There's also crafting, cooking, fishing and mining, but none of it is ever explained to you.   The game basically just starts, plonks you into a town, and you'll find yourself just rubbing up against everything to see if you can interact with it. Is there a gate here?   How do I get out of here?   It took me a while to figure out that to even leave the town I had to press the EXIT button.  I saw it there but thought it would exit the game, not simply leave the "Dungeon" (town?)  Again, nothing is explained.
It's purely a game of experimentation to try and figure out what you can and should be doing while getting annoyed while doing it.   Same goes for the crafting, map modes (Treasure hunting/hunting for food), it's kind of just there, and assumes you already know everything.

This would be fine for an early access title, but this is not Early Access.   This is supposed to be the final product.
If you want to make the claim "Of course there's bugs, customers please help to fix the bugs so the bugs can be fixed", then release it as an EA title so people know what they are in for.    This doesn't feel finished at all.

I bought this game specifically because of
, and I am glad that I did so. While lacking polish, this game is surprisingly fun.
Control of this game is intended for controller, and controller is active by default. If you plan to use a keyboard, make sure to set controls in the pre-game setup menu, and go over them so  that you may become familiar. Once in game, navigate to "options" and set the control type to "keyboard" so that you have proper control of the game. Beyond this, still expect some odd control choices, such as a second confirm button when crafting.
Be warned: There is no tutorial in this game. You will have to learn everything yourself.
Gameplay is broken in to two distinct modes: map and exploration. In map mode, you travel the overworld square by square, consuming food to move or perform actions such as adventuring or mining; exploring the map can also trigger events, which can lead to treasure, events, or combat.
Exploration encompasses hunting and gathering food, adventuring for treasure, and exploring towns. When entering an explorable, the zone is randomly generated, giving constant play even in a single playthrough. Monster kills and treasure finds generate resources that can be used to craft equipment, while hunting/gathering/fishing provides food necessary to perform exploration actions.
As noted in the game description, all NPCs in towns are recruitable - simply talk to an NPC and, if you meet their requirement, you can add them to your party to be used in combat and crafting actions.
Character development follows two systems: level and skill. As you kill enemies, you gain experience, rising in level and gaining HP ans SP, as well as progressing "killer" tracks for enemy types. By using skills, everything from your attack skill to crafting skills, they rise in effectiveness over time, much in the way of adaptive level games such as the original Dungeon Siege.
Combat follows the semi-standard "line formation" style. Your party and the enemy are on opposite sides of the field and take turns, based on stats, performing actions. Attacking an enemy in combat uses a quicktime event, requiring input when a target passes in a reticle to perform a successful hit. All attacks take SP, which are regenerated in combat using the "rest" command, artificially slowing combat both on your side and on the enemy's side. After a successful battle, experience and loot is awarded, monster log entries are updated, HP/SP are restored, and the game continues.
A playthrough consists of selecting your appearance, class, stats, and main task, with "find someone to take the place of your soul" and "get revenge on your killer" being the initial unlocked tasks, then running the game. The goal of a playthrough is to complete your main task to win the game, but gameplay is otherwise freeform.
Overall, gameplay is fun, if a grind, but the quicktime events and artificial stretching of combat requiring rest produce a dull, "do I have to go through this again?" break from the game.
Let me clear the air in light of Rusinylancer's review.
Voxel graphics are exactly as you see in this game: objects in game are comprised of "3D pixels" - filled cubes - rather than shaped polygons. The misconception that voxel games are solely sandbox or destructible builders can be attributed to the fact that the style is used in an abundance of such games, most notoriously Minecraft (though this itself is a misconception) or Steam-distributed games such as Trove or 7 Days to Die, while it's use in terrain and objects can be dated back to Amok on Sega Saturn in 1996 but likely goes back even further.
By using small voxels to render objects, in much the same way as PlayStation 3 game 3D Dot Game Heroes, with which this game shares MANY similarities, the game produces a "neo-retro" feel, being both 3D yet pixelated at the same time. While the voxel usage produces uncommon, pleasing visuals, this is weakened by a pervasive blur effect on even close objects, a camera locked to 90 degree angle turns at a non-adjustable plane, and opaque zone walls that obstruct the camera when too close to the screen-side wall of a given zone.
To an extent, the game feels a little "cranked out". Text bleeds over some menu boundaries, graphics could use a second opinion on some design choices, mouse cursor follows keyboard/controller choices in many cases leaving it hanging on the screen when not in use, menu cursor that remains on the same "row" when flowing through cascading menus, combat is artificially lengthened, and no tutorial explaining any mechanics in the game whatsoever. Needs a lot of polish.

I was quite sceptical, expecting a wild hodgepodge of ideas thrown together from all kinds of sources as is usually the case when people take on science fiction in our time. But it grew on me and at some point I was completely intoxicated by the athmosphere of being on a different planet, which this game recreates better than anything I have seen or played before.
Reviews give a rather confusing picture. Some praising the game others complain endlessly about bugs. Which is strange, I have not seen any bugs whatsoever. In fact in the first 25h I noticed a game of extreme stability. The game crashed exactly ZERO times.
The graphics, sound and resulting athmosphere in this game is simply stunning. I am sucked in completely and hope the world would never end. I know it does end somewhere behind the horizon, but is is still a rather big map that provides many hours of exploration. A lot of similar games have the problem that they dont look like they take place on another planet, but are just a rehash of 3d objects created for Earth. Osiris New Dawn really feels like being on an alien planet that in climate is halfway between Mars and Earth. I can literally smell the regolith when wind blows over the red volcanic rock-
The engine is well optimized, with excellent visibility ranges and no popping in of objects like in other Unity games (eg Subnautica). The one really negative thing is that on public servers framerates go down below 20, which is unacceptable. It is in development and I cannot rate that part. But you can play on private server or single player and it is smooth as butter (I get 60 fps all the time on maximum settings) so the problem must be with the multiplayer side, and will hopefully be optimized with time.
Gameplay wise, it is a mixed bag with a positive overall impression. As of this date, there is not enough challenge. Monsters are everwhere, their animation, behavior and aggression is very realistic. But still, they don't challenge the player. What's the problem?  I think that combat with space weapons against crab monsters simply has no inherent gameplay potential. It's either too hard or too easy, and the developer for the time of the EA phase chose the latter.
The only thing that can kill the player is a sandworm (from Dune) but it can be avoided too. I found the whole sandworm thing unoriginal and tacked on to a hard scifi game, a sort of deus ex machina that I could live without. While the sandworm looks amazing, I would prefer it to be optional. The are some other corny features of the map: the gigantic, sky scraper like skeleton, the floating rocks. The trees could also use some redesign, they look more like exhibits of modern art. But otherwise the world is rather realistic - though not NASA realistic - it makes a lot of sense to me.
The building part is logical, modular and looks spectacular. It is also the most strategic part of the game right now, with many new ideas like collecting gas from geysers, or water from trees and lakes, which are located only in some places on the map. Wonderful, I have never seen such features in a game before, and can already see myself building an entire warehouse of various gases and liquids.
A word for singleplayer users. The game can be fully played and enjoyed in singleplayer (until you realize that you are craving to playing with friends). You can start private servers easily from within the game, invite only your friends to PvE and set a wide range of gameplay paramters (most difficulty and character progression options are there) so most reservations against PvP multiplayer games don't apply.
It is however important to know that the game does not work like eg Skyrim where every item is persistent. This game stores only important things like your build structures or the content of chests. Objects on the ground get erased, which is frustrating at first. Resources replenish. It is a bit weird if the metal you just harvested reappears upon reloading the game, and it may explain many bug reports. While I was a bit critical of this from the singleplayer side, I understand it's necessary due to its multiplayer nature and the game would not work otherwise. The players would roam like a nomad around the map looking for new resources, and the performance would at some point become unoptimizable mess.
To sum up, I find this game fantastic even in its barely half finished state. And with the developers stated intention of creating other planets, it could turn into something truly outstanding. They still have a lot of work to do like: increasing the difficulty - eg through natural effects, diseases, technical malfunctions or monsters working more unevenly over the map, and in some places in packs - optimizing the multiplayer - creating more content, and the usual things that have to be done before a game can be called complete.

Osiris New Dawn is a fun building / exploration game with some 1st / 3rd person shooting elements depending on which view you want to play as. Graphically the game looks really good it does a nice job of making you feel immersed in the world with these strange plants and creatures running around. There werent any graphic glitch's to speak of the game ran perfect. The frame rate was constant and I never noticed any dips. (running on a 4770k and 980) Which for a game in early access was a pleasant surprise.
Mechanics and Gameplay
There wasnt a time in the game were I felt overwhelmed by the mechanics in the game. The gameplay features were very straight foward and easy to use. The movement and aiming with the guns felt a bit clunky but thats something Im sure they can improve on but it didnt take away from the overall experience of the game. I particularly like the use of the talent trees splitting up points between engineering, science and combat. It made for some interesting during the gameplay session and changed my focus during my gameplay session to make sure I was gaining points for that particular skill tree to unlock certain items. The crafting system was easy to grasp and it was pretty rewarding I found myself wanting to unlock the next item and search for more resources to build that next thing. It didnt feel grindy or like a chore unlike other games I've played.
Balance
One thing I think the devs need to work on. At this point in time there is no reason to play any other class but the Marine class which max's out your combat points at the start. During my play session it is extremely easy to get engineering points you'll find yourself maxing out that tree before anything else. Science is pretty easy to gain points for as well, combat however is relatively hard to get points for unless you are a fan of picking up rocks which for some reason give you 5 combat points for each rock picked up or fighting every random alien you encounter.  I think the devs could balance this out a little better but I was in a single player campaign and not in multiplayer so this could have drastically changed my experience.

Lords of Xulima is a good, old-school style RPG. (Very similar to Wizardry). The Art-Style is charming and the music is very good! The best part of Lords of Xulima is the battle system, which is very in-depth. The game is fairly non-linear, usually there is more than just 1 thing to do, outside of story specific things such as temples, often the only thing that is blocking a path to another area is a monster, so if you are able to defeat it you can advance into new areas without doing them in the intended order. The map opens up a lot once you have defeated the second prince in the game.
Story: The Story unfortunately doesn't make a good impression to begin with, It is Pokemon style, you are tasked with purifing 8 temples, killing 4 princes, 4 witches etc. There are a few good pieces of dialogue that give you a back-story into Gaulen's (The main Characters) past, and some nice dialogue between the Bosses and Gaulen which I found interesting, there aren't too many NPCs around in the towns to really give much of a history on the setting of map. It is workable though and the other aspects that Lords of Xulima more than make up for it.
Gameplay: Lords of Xulima has you create a Party involving Gaulen (The main character which you must take) and 5 other characters of your choice from 9 different classes. There is enough variation in the classes, and in the skills you select as you're leveling the classes up, to warrant 2-3 playthroughs of the game. The battle system is what really sets Lords of Xulima apart. It is very good, very in-depth, if you are a fan of old turn-based RPGs you will love the LoX battle-system. You control Gaulen through-out the world and fight your way through forests, deserts, snow, demon-infested ruins, dungeons, temples and castles to achieve your objectives, there is a nice variety of enemy types (although some are palette swaps, there is plenty of original enemies to keep you interested) and settings. There are a lot of tough puzzles and riddles in LoX which are very good and make you think, again, like classic old-school RPGs. Everything you do in LoX is limited by your supplies, which you will need to use to rest (to heal) and to move around the map, you can regain supplies by picking them from the terrain, using Gaulens hunting skill after killing monsters, and buying them from towns or looting them, there are plenty of secrets hidden in the maps to have you searching for. The game is hard as you might expect for an old-school RPG, seeing an Ironman mode is very refreshing :)
Music: Very good, there are plenty of times where you'll find yourself humming away to the music, especially in the snowy town :) . Good variety of battle music, dungeons sound creepy etc. It is very cool
Art: I found the art style very cool and classic looking, but modern enough to be charming. Keep in mind that this game is working on a very tight budget, I think they've done a great job with the music and art.
The devs are releasing 1-2 updates per day (Even on weekends) and bugs are getting fixed very quickly. Even though it's an Early Access Game I have never had any problems with crashes. The only bugs I have encountered are localization issues, the developer is a spanish developer so there is 1-2 weird translations here and there, but they get fixed quickly if you post them in the forum.
If you are a fan of classic RPGs, get this game, it's great value. I've already gotten 50 hours of it. For £12 that's a bargain.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified feels like a frustratingly incomplete mixture of Bioshock and Gears of War. This could have been a great game. Here are my specific gripes with the game:
Some abilities are over-powered, others are underwhelming. Aiming doesn't seem to matter too much aside from headshots. Guns take a back seat to the abilities and you will spend much of combat waiting for cooldowns. Upgrades and items don't include important percentages so that you can determine which gear is best for your characters (this is fixed in the DLC). Levels are sprawling but often feel too sterile or empty. Many of the NPC interactions and other world building elements feel hollow and pointless.
You know that point where you are halfway through a bag of potato chips, no longer hungry and filled with self-loathing, but you eat the rest anyway? I had a similar moment halfway through XCOM: The Bureau.

Personally I love the noir feeling of the game and how it takes place in the past rather than nowadays, or in the future. It isn't like the other XCOM games, which is a welcome change. I like the leveling up system, and that you can customize Carter and your squadmates, though more customization options would have been nice.
The combat feels like Mass Effect, and has its own charm to it. I like the action mixed with having to use tactics. Battle focus is a neat thing as well if you want to know more about your enemies. Though sometimes the AI behavior can make combat a bit frustrating. It's pretty silly when I want to flank an enemy and I see my squadmate running towards me through the middle of the battlefield.
The characters and missions are, to my mind, interesting. The information you get through the dialogues and documents adds lore to the XCOM universe. And I actually really enjoyed the main story. It had a neat twist. I liked the occasional choices you could make, even though they were quite insignificant, it did make some difference in a few aspects.
I'd recommend this to anyone who is a fan of XCOM and doesn't mind the different approach!

A fun little indy roguelike by a 1 man team.  While 3D, it's actually more like a 2D game presented in 3D -- 3D Dot Heroes style, sorta.
The game's claim to fame is a significant amount of procedural generation -- like Dragon Quest Monsters 2 on the original Gameboy's key world system, the game generates a randomly generated world map, complete with randomly generated plains, mountains, caves, towns, et cetera.
Every character in the game is statted and can all be recruited to your party.  The game also has a decently implemented crafting and harvesting system, with gathering and crafting being a valid strategy.
Combat is a turn based JRPG-like affair, with an interesting mechanic where everything you do requires stamina, which you regain by defending.  In this way it's not dissimilar to Bravely Default's system, although there does not appear to be any automatic regeneration of these stamina points.
Long term, the game has you pick out a goal at the start of the game -- only a few are unlocked during the first playthrough, although some of the later ones get more and more outlandish.
The game does work much better with a controller, I use a wired 360 pad.
Looking forward to future updates, perhaps a tutorial and the ability to see treasure on the minimap or somesuch, as currently finding "interesting things" on the map (like chests) can be a bit of a pain.

I don't review games very often, but I have played a quite a few, and I feel as if the current reviewers are not giving the game enough of a chance, so lets begin shall we? Lets talk about the controls.
Control Scheme:
From the moment you start up the game, it is configured to be used by controllers, this is an easy fix, just use the arrow keys to navigate down to options, and set it to keyboard and mouse.
Something to note is that you don't have to really use the mouse at all, and it tends to be a bit awkward if you do.
When you first load into the game itself, after the intro cinematic and character creation screen, you start out above a town, and if you look at the bottom of your screen you will see the default controls.
(It's important to note that these controls can be rebound as by default they may be awkward for some)
By default, Space is set to confirm, with B bound to Cancel, Esc to Escape, C to menu, X to submenu and so on.
I've played about thirty minutes so far, and I have had no issues with the menus or interfaces minus a bit of awkwardness before rebinding.
Gameplay:
As said in the paragraph before, you load into the game, a cutscene plays, and you design your character. After chosing a main objective, (The thing you'll be working towards throughout the game) the game puts you above a village in a sort of top down view which lets you plan your moves. I'm going to call this for simplicities sake the Map. On the map you can do a few things, the first of which is moving. You're able to move up, down, left, or right, each time consuming two food, (You start off with 10 if I remember correctly) At first, you start above a village, which you can choose to enter. Upon entering said village it puts you in a third person view, and you're able to move around the village freely. (Unfortunatly you can't use the mouse to reposition the camera and instead have to use Q and E to move it left and right, and while this is a bit awkward, and the animation for moving the camera is sometimes jerky, you get used to it pretty fast)
In villages you can either choose to buy things like armor, weapons, or potions, or you can choose to recruit someone to your party. At the start you are limited to having two people (including yourself) in a party at one time. (I think this number increases as you level) Other than that, there is nothing much else to do in villages.
Combat:
The combat system is a pretty standard JRPG setup other than one thing, which is a quicktime event upon attacking, if you time it perfectly, you score a critical hit, if you hit it a bit off time you get a standard/weak attack. While it is a bit unforgiving and difficult to score criticals, I think it should be.
Crafting:
There is also crafting, in which you can create weapons, armor, and potions from things that you collect around varying instances. Pretty run of the mill.
Food and Treasure hunting:
When you get too low on food you'll find yourself in a situation where you have to go out and scavenge for it. When you select the option to hunt for food you get put into an instance that has things such as chickens, rabbits, berries, and tomoatoes around. You can switch between a bow, a fishing rod, and a third option that simply lets you observe things around you in first person. This is something I dislike, as hunting for food can get tedious, but that is just out of my lazyness as it is easy to get a lot of food in a relatively short amount of time. Treasure hunting puts you in another instance that puts you in whatever biome you are over, like Food hunting, but instead of spawning chickens and berries, its spawns monsters, and treasure chests. The treasure chests are thrown randomly through the map and can be hard to find, and the monsters tend to chase you which makes it all the more difficult.
Overall I think that this game has some work that needs to be done on it, but it isnt outright broken, and will give you at least a few hours of fun if you're willing to get over/rebind the controls. As I play more, and time progresses, I will update this review as it is not complete, nor have I played enough to fully review it.

I remember cruising around Hawaii in my 1984 Ferrari 308 GTS Quattrovalvole. God the nostalgia is killer, take me back!
It featured 2 huge beautiful maps that you could cruise around in and explore alone or with your friends.
You could challenge other players along the way you while driving just like in NFS or simultaneously switch to join a race no matter what you were doing. The driving mechanics, car models, engine sounds and graphics were pretty solid.
Not to mention it had an amazing soundtrack that still has me kicking today.
You had a player avatar which you were able to customize. Visit town to buy new Clothing, Hair styles, Vehicles and even Real Estate where you could store your cars. You were also able to customize your cars and even the interior of your homes to some extent.
When visiting any shop or personal house, you would switch to first person which hasn't really been done in a racing game. You could see real players while shopping around and you could even invite friends to visit your virtual home.
It had many and more customization elements that even Grand Theft Auto 5 has now.
Atari doesn't seem like they are doing all that much to keep their servers up and running these days so unfortunately the online aspect seems to be slowly dying away. You can still play Singleplayer mode which is pretty fun but I found that Multiplayer was more enjoyable.
So, should you buy it then?
Definitely pick it up on a sale if you enjoy racing games. It has a good amount of customizability that you rarely find in racing games nowadays.
It has a special something that no other racing game has really given me before, and no thats not just the nostalgia talking.
It really has earned its title of being a true legend.

As of v0.13.3:
Lords of Xulima is a turn-based RPG with some interesting mechanics and pretty hardcore old-school gameplay.
It's quite unusual to see a project like this being developed at year 2014. It's hard, it's old school, it's not exactly the most forgiving game, and it does not holds your hand at all. And frankly, I love it :)
And once again, we have a kickstarter to thank for this.
Storyline of the game is pretty well write but somewhat typical for a fantasy RPG. Although the fact that game features riddles where you have to enter answer yourself, does motivates you to read and remember all the dialogues thoroughly.
The core of the game though is it's overworld and combat - since that's what you're gonna be doing most of the time.
Turn-based (or rather time-based) overworld features stationary enemies as well as some random encounters.
Combat has a very simple set of rules to follow, but can be extremely hard (especially on higher difficulty). And it's definitely damn enjoyable if you like the idea of turn-based tactical combat in general.
More detailed look in the video:

If you enjoyed old school rpgs such as the Final Fantasy series, Chrono Trigger etc then you will want to pick up this game. Have only played a little more than 20 hours and not even a quarter of the way through but I am thoroughly enjoying it myself. The learning curve is a little steep but not so bad once you learn to make use of the tooltip system (hint: Right-click to show the tool tip straightaway without having to hover over for a sec). Remember to save often and keep more than one save file as this game only quicksaves upon changing an area.
Pros
- Very polished visually and acoustically
- Fleshed out immersive gameplay with plenty of optional side quests and challenges.
- Engaging and highly strategic combat system
- Great character building system
- Plenty of hours of gameplay and lots of replay value for the price
- Classic RPG feel
- Fairly open world (strong enemies are used to keep on the path of the games normal progression but if you are able to defeat them you can go wherever).
Cons
- Takes a bit of time to get the hang of if you haven't played similar games before
- It is possible to lose a lot of progress if you don't save regularily (hasn't happened to me but I can see it being a possibility)
- Some players may not like the games scaling economy where prices slightly increase as you level up
This game belongs in the libraries of classic rpg fans or people looking to play a classic rpg.

Asked by a few people my opinion on this game. I'll try keep it short and sweet.
Looking for an 'oldschool' rpg to scratch the itch? This is probably the game for you.
You play a party of 6 characters choosing either the default setup or custom classes. Decent mix of classic and hybrids are available from Bards through to Arcane Soldiers. Choice of class effects base stats, starting skills and weapons but can be developed into modified variants depending on how you choose to play. 3 difficulty levels are available and while the game has been criticized for being a bit brutal, playing on normal or easy with the default party should be more then managable and enjoyable for most.
Combat is Turn Based and feels very similar to Legends of Grimrock or the Might&Magic Series. Position of units on the battlefield plays an important role with two blank spaces available for you to move units around as you see fit. Traveling on the worldmap acts in pseudo realtime consuming up time and rations as you move. Which is what you will be spending your gold on earlygame, stockpiling food before traveling is a must.
Depending on party skills as you travel you will find extra rations, detect traps and just discover curiosities in general. Which leads me to my next point, this game has a strong focus on natural exploration along the same lines of the early divinity games and the eschalon series. Far from being linear you are often moving around trying to find the next 'questline' thats achieveable by your current level, which works extremely well. That's not to say you don't have quests handed out from towns either. Content wise I have been told there is around 50-60% unlocked and 100% already ingame which is just getting some refinements.
Graphically the game supports 1440p+ setups and I assume being handdrawn art it really is a joy to play. Small nitpick would be the fact you can't seem to enter inside many(any?) buildings early on, but you do go inside dungeons and other locales. Doesn't take away from the game too much. Voice acting is of a bare minimum but the text and colours used is well written with good readbility. The soundtrack is mostly instrumental and not only relaxing but fitting for each environment and I would love the ability to purchase the soundtrack on steam. :)
TL:DR
Enjoyed any of the games I referenced? Should at the very least be keeping LoX on your shortlist.

A small game with a lot of soul.
The game talks a lot about childhood perception and memory.  It doesn't take long before you realize that this isn't a typical game; this is a game with a lot to say.  This game is brief and simple but there are moments that gave me pause.
To those who complain about the game's length let me ask you this: would you rather pay $5 for a one hour game that you will always remember or $5 for a longer game that you won't?  I usually don't care for game critics very much but there is a quote from Kevin VanOrd that I think articulates the viewpoint really well:
"A game's length, on its own, is such a meaningless indicator of a game's value or worth."
Personally, I would gladly pay for a brief game that leaves an impact on me.
I'll end with some pros and cons:
PROS:
+Heartwarming Narrative with Memorable Moments
+Clever usage of childhood perception in both the story and the landscape itself.
+Has a clever way of demonstrating nostalgia, I won't spoil it.
+Sprinkles of humor help maintain narrative balance.  The humor often references other things like old TV shows and other games.
CONS:
-The player is often left watching rather than playing.
-Slow start.  This is surprising because of how short the game is, luckily things speed up relatively quickly.
-The player is often asked to retrieve certain items or perform specific actions via visual cues.  In some cases it feels like it adds to the narrative in a meaningful way but there were a few times which felt unnecessary.
CONCLUSION:  If you like memorable artistic games with 'feels' I would highly suggest playing this game.

Not only is the story heart warming, but the visual art is striking and appealing, worthy of being it's own art piece. The soundtrack played a nice role in making it emotional, since there is no dialog so I would grab it with the soundtrack just to have that great musical piece. You can decide if $4.99-6.99 is too much for a twoish hour long game, but I think when it goes on sale it's definitely worth the price.

I liked To The Moon, for the record, but this is just boring and uninspired pixel movie where you ocasionally hold right and press space bar. Pixel Piracy is the only game I know of where the results of your time investment can just randomly be taken away from you, leaving you in a state where its almost impossible to progress with the game.
You take the role of the captain of a ship, build yourself a crew, buy them food and pay their wages to keep them happy, kit them out with the finest of weaponry... Oh and fight other pirates in navel warfare... Sounds cool right?
Except when you tell your crew to go board the enemy ship and, with their captain mercilessly slaughtering enemies in front of them and the expansive blue, shark infested sea behind them... They choose the latter.
And that's it, they're gone from the game.
Taking with them the initial hiring cost, however much food they've helped themselves to, items you've used on them to cultivate them into the perfect ship mate you've always wanted...
All because the game makes them walk left instead of right.
And this was a consistent issue, which meant I couldn't progress that far into the game because I was constantly spending all my gold replenishing my ranks.
I bought it cheap in a sale, so maybe I shouldn't complain too much. But as bad as other games I've played are, they at least haven't decided to just randomly remove the results of my labours because the AI can't work out what to do.
But there's a lot of other little issues that as a collective really just suck all the fun out of playing.
Quite often after issuing an order to a "group", some will decide that obeying their captain isn't in their best interests. Then I didn't mind them drowning so much.
When you select somewhere to go on the map, you're treated to a "traveling" transition... Where you just watch the ship sail while a percentage counter slowly increases. Sometimes your crew sing a shanty. I have no idea at all why this is in the game other than to pad it out.
Rewards from chests were usually around 10g... After returning to the ship I was blowing up the enemy ship for 100g. The rewards are just garbage.
From what I've seen of it the actual gameplay loop gets old pretty quick; go fight pirate ships, go explore tiny islands, go back to town for supplies, repeat. The game gives very little incentive (at least short term, as I've said I've not really been *able* to play long term) to actually play.
The menus are unpleasant to look at, I'm fine with the pixel art aesthetic, but the menus are just really unintuitive and take way longer to navigate than they need to. I couldn't even find my items for the longest time.
I have no idea how they managed it, but the framerate would regularly slow to a crawl in towns.
I like the idea, but I hate playing the game.
This is even playing the "enhanced" edition.

I still don't know do i like the world of this game or not. It's raw, the levels look all the same. A human military base at the beginning of each episode which houses a portal that takes us to medieval-themed levels. Castles and temples filled with secrets and monsters that kill you in matter of seconds. All my "problems" with this game are just in the overall look of the game, and they're just preferences. This world just isn't my thing, everything else is spot-on, though the lore is a bit too similar to Doom. Instead of hell, this time we're facing a mysterious hostile creature codenamed "Quake", and his army.
Levels are again like mazes with their complex layouts, filled with secrets. 4 episodes featuring 7-8 levels consisting of clever level design, arena-like open areas and tight, twisty corridors, underwater areas, jumping traps and various enviromental traps. If you have played the original Dooms, you have an idea about the levels. It's just taken a bit further here. Every episode has a secret level, accessed through a certain secret from the normal levels. Secret levels also have some distinct gameplay mechanics, like low gravity.
One fun thing about choosing the difficulty that i have to mention: Instead of choosing it from the menu while starting a game, we begin the game by facing three portals labelled easy-medium-hard. But there's a fourth one, the hardest difficulty is actually hidden. I always found it a fun remark, you're already facing a puzzle even trying to find how to play game in the hardest possible difficulty. Whoever came up with that, my hat is off to you, sir.
Gameplay itself is fantastic! Especially on the harder difficulties the enemies put up a good fight (but not enough, since they're all dead now!). Controls respond tightly and weapons offer a lot of variety. Every weapon is needed, you won't survive with just running around with the machine gun, err, the nail gun i mean.
Like in Doom(s), the ammo is scarce, that alone forces you to use different weapons all the time. No regenerative health, no covers, only skill. Remember watch out with your grenade launcher, they really do bounce off from walls. Easy to clear corners with and even easier to commit a suicide, especially in hectic moments.
Overall the weapons feel brutal and powerful, making the action feel fun and enjoyable to play.  The aforementioned nail gun for example. It's a completely different thing to fire a submachine gun compared to an high powered nail gun spitting out big sharp nails. As a melee weapon we have an axe and the lightning gun is amazing. Mowing down the hordes as the BFG does, if not even faster. Blast from the shotgun sound and feel heavy, nails hurt and grenades devastate everything around them.
Bosses are also a bit different, there's usually a certain mechanic involved rather than purely shooting them to death. There isn't those epic fights with a boss in this game, they're over quick and usually they're just standing still. Another thing that i'm having mixed feelings about. It's very anti-climax when you finally reach the boss after slaying hordes of demons, but on the other hand, it's a nice twist and something else than the usual shootout.

I guess there isn't much of a story or emotional depth to be had about a kid and a wounded bird and while I love Kan Gao's To The Moon, I must say that this one is terrible. Kan Gao's game is about the story the emotional journey it brought us through but a bird isn't human, or it isn't River, and it doesn't have anthropomorphic quality for us to feel anything about it at all. A story about a dog would've been more interesting because dogs can actually look like they have emotion whereas birds don't. Also what made To The Moon a feast despite its graphic and its weird mouse control was the conversation, because it was funny (not because it was deep and everyone has some sort of deeper understanding about life or whatever). There were important issues being talked about, but far more than that, the delivery were top notch. You laugh, you can't wait to know more. A Bird Story has no conversation at all, it's funny moments aren't funny. Musis is not so good. Let me put it this way, To The Moon can be and hour and a half movie and it can work, A Bird Story at best would be the short movie Disney or Pixar put in their movies before Toy Story 3 or Big Hero 6 plays. You'll pay for Big Hero 6 and you get a dog-human relationship short movie at the start, before the movie begins, and that short is free, bonus package. If it's good, nice, if it's bad, well okay, this isn't what I came here for. In this case, A Bird Story is the bad short movie (not that Pixar had ever produced a bad short movie before their main feature screened). There sn't much story to tell, there isn't much depth, yet they make the short movie a one and a half hour movie. That's what it feels like playing A Bird Story, it's can be as a side story, it's not good as the main event. All throughout the game, I can only think of "quick, hurry, continue, go on, get on to it already, get through with it, please be over!!"
It's not a bad story, but a whole game shouldn't have revolved around it. It's a bad game, yes. If we're talking gameplay To The Moon was also a bad game. But what it lacks in gameplay, it pays up with a hell of a damn good story that we can feel about. I used to have 4 bird as a pet. I wasn't a very good pet owner. One of them died to a cat and I cried. Two of them died because I forgot to put the cage in when it rains, I cried. The last one flew away while I was feeding it, I left too much opening for it to jump out, I CRIED. I was heartbroken a few times but I couldn't even feel anything about this.
It's not worth buying, it's not worth playing. This is the kind of story you'd like to share around when you feel sentimental, but not the kind of story people should pay you to hear.
