I think many of those who bought, are willing to buy or are interested in A Bird Story loved To The Moon, Kan Gao's first, acclaimed game. I am one of those. I bought that game on
(that's why it's not on my Steam library) and i consider it one of my most important games of all. A Bird Story is barely a game, but that's not necessarily negative. It is the surreal story of a boy and his friendship with a bird with a hurt wing. It is a rather vague, short story with some obscure metaphore in it and the peculiar choice to be told without one single word being spoken/written on-screen. I liked this choice, it's rather brave and remembered me the first part of a movie i loved (it was Wall-E, basically the demonstration that cartoons are not only for children). Anyway, even if i liked the setting and some of the narrative, i have to say that the rythm is very, very slow (i have finished the game in 71 minutes, half of which was boring roaming from one place to another) and it really feels like the few "interaction" moments could have been avoided, because they just felt needless to me. The story is nice as it is, though kinda cliché. Globally, i don't think i can recommend this prequel-to-the-sequel of To The Moon. It's overly short, and doesn't transmit anything particular. I think the most heartfelt moment for me was the reveal of the next game's name, which is really commoting. The art in this game is beautiful, but it felt like a super unnecessarily long trailer to the next one, and the constant surreal aura that's in it is very confusing. I think you can play Finding Paradise, when it's out, even without playing A Bird Story. It's not bad, and unlike someone else i didn't think that it automatically had to reach TTM standards, but i think this game is, simply, rather boring and irrelevant. I suggest to skip or, even better, watch a gameplay, since it doesn't change much.
DISCLAIMER
I'm not criticizing the lack of interactivity in any way. I don't think a work of videogame art obligatorily has to be interactive. Actually i'm criticizing that they INSERTED those random, boring interactivity moments inside the game. It felt complete without them.

Background: I'm a FPS fan, I enjoy some similar game play types such as Unreal Tournaments Assault.  This particular game didn't click with me.
I played this game in early 2013 as part of a personal challenge to play some games on my backlog.  Naturally I had to play SP with bots as the MP community had mainly moved onto other things years ago.  Also as your have to "level up" I didn't want to start as a noob with rude people who would be telling me I was doing it wrong.
The levels are quite fun at first, you can pick what type of  character to play, follow the other bots to an objective and either earn it, or death zerg until success.  Be prepared to hear about capturing or losing command points a hell of a lot.  You could be about to win the level, then the enemy AI take one of your command points and the AI on your team decide to go get their revenge.
The movement to the game is kinda fun, but really its just a gimmick.  In battle you'll either kill the guy or get killed, its not about fancy movement and gunplay at the same time.
The game has 2 sides, each map lets you play the story from either side, but really, does anyone care what the story is about, why the are getting wound up?  The third time you have heard the bots talking about "WE HAVE TAKEN THEIR COMMAND POST" you have forgotten what or why you were doing.  You just know you have to get closer and press and action key to win the objective.
Overall the game wasn't fun enough.  Apart from going back to get some more achievements I won't be going back to this.
Things that annoy me:
I don't want a choice of voice actors
One of the maps was impossible to win at the normal difficulty.  Partly as the bots never teamed up with me. I dropped the difficulty and got through the map flawlessly.
Lots of focus on things that I'm just not interested in.
The bots dialogue
The bots, both friendly and enemy are the main reason you'll want to quit.

Lords of Xulima is a very interesting game. You would never guess from looking at the screenshots, but it's a very original and well-thought game, that takes lessons from old-school RPGs and adds some unique flavour.
For once, it has a very challenging combat and a nice mix of a Wizardry-like first person combat with isometric exploration, featuring traps, mazes and hidden passages. It also has one of the best resource management system I ever saw in a RPG.
Clearly the developers played hundreds of RPGs, and tried to fix issues that old games had. For example, Xulima has random encounters, but only on certain areas. And they are actually limited fights, that scale up in difficulty as you beat them. Defeat all enemies in one area, and it becomes a safe zone, and you even get some bonus XP. And the game is full of other "twists" like this.
So in short, if you like old-school RPGs try this game. It isn't revolutionary, but it's very well designed and clearly made with passion. If you want more details, I wrote a longer preview at the RPG Codex:

Consiglio vivamente Lords of Xulima a tutti quelli che amano i giochi di ruolo vecchia scuola (Eye of the Beholder) ma con nuove idee e meccaniche.
La grafica è gradevole e pulita, le classi tipiche dei gdr ci sono tutte, impostando il giusto livello la difficoltà è appropriata e gli sviluppatori lo aggiornano costantemente (è in Early Access) per eliminare bugs e apportare migliorie.
Fatevi un favore senza pensarci su due volte, acquistatelo e non ve ne pentirete.
I highly recommend Lords of Xulima to all those who love the old-school role-playing games (Eye of the Beholder), but with new ideas and mechanics.
The graphics are nice and clean, the typical classes of RPGs are all there, setting the right level of difficulty is appropriate and developers constantly update it (it is in Early Access) to eliminate bugs and make improvements.
Do yourself a favor without thinking twice about it, buy it and you will not regret.

Brink is what happens when you try to make a multiplayer FPS game that promotes movement and fast-paced action but feel constrained by the modern trends of "tactical" play and cover mechanics. Simply put, it falls flat in every way imagineable.
It's disappointing because I was really excited for this game when I first heard about it. I thought it might actually be the next best thing since Unreal Tournament 2004. "Finally, a new competitive shooter that encourages movement." But nope. In fact, most of the time, you get more points for being near an objective and just standing there. That's already a bad sign for a game that supposedly encourages you to run around, climb, and jump off walls whenever possible, but if the guns didn't all feel like pea shooters it'd at least be tolerable.
One thing I'll give this game credit for is that it doesn't keep track of your kill/death ratio. It's all about the objective here. All about the teamwork. But even then, as mentioned earlier, you'll find that the easiest way to play this game is sitting still and shooting at people running by. It's not inherently a bad thing if a shooter isn't pure run and gun, but when a game puts a lot of emphasis on its parkour system, I certainly expect some faster-paced action.
Even if you somehow find a way to enjoy this kind of gameplay, the horrible optimization will completely kill off any desire to keep playing it. If you use an ATI graphics card, you better pray to the gaming gods that your game won't run at less than 10 fps for no reason at all. And THEN if you happen to enjoy it and can run it well, you'll be disappointed to see that the game is pretty much empty online. It died off that quickly.
Short version: Don't get this game. You won't find anything worthwhile here.

Pixel Piracy Enhanced
Intro: Hello and welcome to my Pixel Piracy Enhanced edition review where I’ll be doing a slightly longer than average review to help you decide if this game is worth your time and money* It’s not*. So this game was made by Quadro Delta and published by Re-Logic the same people who made Terraria. That raises the expectation that the game should be good it was made by some of the people who made Terraria which is universally praised as being a good game. Does the game met that expectation? Let’s talk about the gameplay, graphics, story, and sound to find out.
Gameplay:
On the games website the game is marketed as a strategy/sandbox/simulation. Is that true? Only partially the game’s only “strategy” comes from the fact you can control your captain and pirates and point them at the thing you’d like dead. The “simulation” comes from your pirates needing food and pooping on your ship since they’re too stupid to realize that they should be doing that on the island and not the thing they live on. Why would they poop on the ship? Because it’s on the poop deck (hur hur hurrr) the game has a very immature sense of humor more on that later. The only true thing that the advertise the game as is a sandbox the game’s map is kind like FTL’s where there are these “beacons” that you can sail to that have things to do on them unlike FTL you actually land on the islands you may pass. Every island you go to will feel the same though more on that later. So how do you control the game? Left clicking for controlling the captain and right clicking for the crew group you have selected. How about combat? It’s the same control scheme left click to tell the captain you’d like that thing dead and right click to tell the crew you’d like that thing dead. The combat must be pretty cool sword fighting on a ship sounds like it’d be awesome, not here you click the target and hope your pirate hit’s harder and more often since it’s pretty RNG dependent one of the biggest variables is knock back where falling off the ship/island means death by very lazy looking shark sprites (no they don’t even have a eating animation). You can increase your odds of hitting by the RPG style leveling system they have where you just slap some points into a stat like strength to hit harder or dexterity to dodge better or put the points into a skill like cleaning this goes for crew members as well. Speaking of the crew you have to hire them at a tavern where they’ll charge you x amount for their services and they’ll have a blurb with what they did before becoming a pirate does that mean anything? Of course not. There’s a moral system in where being on a ship covering in their waste makes them grumpy to mitigate this you could pay them their wages, go fight another pirate, or clean that stuff up. You can also capture and tame animals to be crew members though they’re effectively the exact same thing only dumber (can’t learn skills). There’s a hunger system as well where the pirates get grumpy when their hungry and eventually starve to death this was a big problem with larger crews since they were too stupid to eat when they were hungry I hear that isn’t an issue in the “Enhanced edition. There’s a travel time system that seems to serve no purpose aside from free EXP and loading in the next area. The AI for the game seems pretty terrible where they don’t avoid hazards and don’t position themselves to avoid environmental kills like getting knocked off the ship.
Graphics:
The game is retro sprite based which maybe a turn off for some since so many games do that since it’s cheaper. Normally they make sure they actually have animations in before shipping out the game though. The animation quality in this game is terrible it tries to do the South Park thing by having the sprite shuffle from left to right and sword swings are just the sword sprite moving from and upward position to a downward position. The games UI is pretty ugly there’s way to much unused space with the color scheme they chose and way too much clicking to get where the player wants. The game’s style is pretty ugly to the point where the game’s cards from steam poke fun at them such as the one for the cat where it says it looks more like a sausage weasel than a cat, that’s all over the place in this game. The water looks decent at least. The things that live in the water don’t though the sharks look pretty stupid as do the fish who just kinda slide around in the water without any semblance of an animation to be found here. The areas the player visits are randomly generated to my knowledge that doesn’t stop them from looking all exactly the same. Every island has the exact same back drop EVERY SINGLE ONE at least have like 3 different looking ones that the game picks out at random for the islands. Making a sprite is a relatively easy thing to do animating one is difficult but that’s no excuse for a game that’s selling for $10. For that can get you all sorts of good games on steam like Terraria all of which will have animations.
Story:
The isn’t much of one it’s just go kill the 4 big name pirates and you can choose what kind of back story you want for the captain, was their dad a brave pirate, was he a drunk pirate, was he a coward. You get to name the world and decide it’s story by that I mean do you want more pirate encounters, do you want people you hire to be more likely to get sick, or are you a night owl and want night to last longer? Do you want it to be mysterious, do you want it to be a drama filled, or do you want it to be dangerous? That’s all you get. I’m not sure what age group this game is aimed at I’m going to assume kids since the game’s jokes and writing are normally just poop related or pointing out lazy item descriptions you know the highbrow stuff that everyone thinks is funny.
Sound:
The sound in this are pretty hit and miss the swords sound like hulks of metal clanging against each other the open sea sounds like the open sea but then there’s the voice acting it sounds awful. When you make your captain you pick a voice for them all of them sound like unprofessional, some of them sound like the dev’s child, and some of them only have a line that they spam. There’s singing in the taverns that sounded terrible to me but that might be your thing though. The games music is nothing special it just serves the ambiance although you’ll probably never find yourself humming anything from it.
Overall Verdict:

Quake is one of the best FPS games I have ever played. The levels are A M A Z I N G (beside for some in episode 4, imo.) and the weapons are pretty cool, although they have some flaws. (DISCLAIMER: I played through Quake using a source port called Quakespasm. I highly recommend it, as it adds higher resolutions and better control options. It also has compatibility with almost all custom levels. If you want to get Quakespasm, go here (
) if you want to fine-tune Quakespasm to get a more vanilla-esque experience, go here (
)) With that out of the way, let's begin the review. The textures in Quake are bland. They kinda forshadowed the brown shooters we'd have in the 21st century, but don't let that turn you off of the game! Despite the bland textures, the levels themselves have very distinct and high quality atmospheres. You know you're in a hellish, Lovecraftian medieval world with knights and gargoyle-like demons chasing you. The enemies are pretty great, except for the Fiend, which is pretty annoying. The weapons look cool... but they don't feel great. Enemies just bounce back a little when they're shot, and the weapons sound a little... soft. Nonetheless, the weapons are awesome. The super nailgun is great, the rocket launcher is legendary, and the arc gun is absurdly powerful.
PROS:
-You get to choose what episode you want to play, in a single playthrough!
-The weapons are great
-The atmosphere is unique and great
-The enemies look cool
-Each episode is unique
-The levels are so much fun to play
-The "music" is good
CONS:
-The weapons FEEL lame
-Enemies just kinda bounce back when you shoot them

tl;dr: A game with many flaws and to some, bad quality. But I've had a lot of fun with this game, it just comes down to what you're actually looking for. Want a serious racing sim? Look further. Are you searching for some (although buggy) old-fashioned fun? You might want to stick around. My recommendation however: buy it in the sales, you'll probably be better off that way.
(WARNING: long review ahead, proceed with caution)
General thoughts
I've followed this game since it's early days on IndieDB, I've been looking forward to it's release on Steam. Now one small, quick (but important) note: the game description is too positive. "Features the biggest, most detailed and alive open world city". This is
true. Yes, it's a decently sized city, but nothing more. Let's compare the size of the map with the size of the map of GTA V. You know that airport at the bottom of LS? Yeah, it's about that big. It's a bit more spreaded, but surface-wise, about the size of the airport. Probably even smaller, since a big portion of the map is occupied by buildings and inaccessible parking lots. Yes, it has an Underground Tube station... Sort of... It's about 50-70 metres long, and you can't go on the traintracks or on the train. Yeah, kind of dissapointing. Furthermore, the cars differ in quality, some are plain old models that are, if I'm not mistaken. taken straight from UDK. Others seem like rather crappy, low-poly models that have a bunch of modelling and texture bugs. What about the livelyness of the city? Well, maybe as lively as a town full of zombies. There are about 5 models for pedestrians, all wearing meme-shirts. You can drive straight through them, no interaction at all. They don't fall over, jump out of the way, you can't even push them around. Then what about traffic? The traffic consists of a bunch of cars (with even lower resolution!) that seem to be on Scalextric tracks. You can push 'em around all you want, but the front wheels will always point to the direction they're going, That doesn't mean they're completely inanemate, you can cause massive pileups, send them flying and make them go all sixes and sevens.
Now let's talk about gameplay, shall we?
The handling, let's just get on with it straight away. Ehmm, boring and obvious is the only way I can describe it. It certainly doesn't have ground-breaking physics that would put
to shame. It's rather bland, unoriginal, almost as if the developer had just taken a default code for the driving physics. Which is probably what actually happened. Is that a particularly bad thing? No, most definitely not. As a manner of fact, I'd rather have someone just take a premade string of code, rather than creating their own code from scratch and messing up.
Races
This game comes with a few racemodes. Time-trial and checkpoint races. It's pretty straight forward, timetrial, you drive on your own, through one of the few courses. Finish before the timer runs out, you win. When the timer runs out and you haven't yet finished, you lose. Checkpoint races: you drive around a course with other opponents. Finish first and you'll win, and you know the rest.
Bugs
This game is riddled with bugs, so many in fact, it's somtimes a guilty pleasure to just play a game of 'How to break a game in as many ways as possible'. Just take this example: When you go over the bridge away from the city, you'll arrive at a teeny tiny, almost roundabout-sized island. in the middle: a bunch of rocks. Hit those rocks at high speeds, you'll jump, do massive flips with an incredible amount of air-time, and with a bit of luck, you might just land on the next bridge. It is however, way more likely you'll miss the bridge, and land in the water. Big problem? Not really. Underneath the surface of the water, or I could just say texture of a surface, there is a bonedry, hard floor. And now you can endlessly drive around in the water. But watch out, if you manage to find the edge of the map, you'll fall down into oblivion. And don't expect the reset-button to help there. When your car resets back onto the road you are closest to, the car will just freeze. You're able to bump into it with other cars, and it'll move, but you can't drive it. And once you're out of it, you can't get back in.
Just a small example of a bug.
Final verdict:
Alright, that was a long, long review. Buy my final verdict is... 6/10.
Surprised? I bet you are. This game is horribly made, I completely agree, but for the fun-factor, I'll give it a 9/10, probably. Yes, there are bugs, yes it's a short game, small map, done playing in probably two hours. But for me, it was a fun experience. It's still a fun game. But do beware: buy it when it's in the sales, when it costs next to nothing, because I sitll do not think it is worth that much money.
And if you enjoy bug-hunting, this is fun as well.
All jokes aside, buy it at your own risk, read the reviews, look at the trailers, maybe look up some gameplay footage on YouTube, whatever you do, take a deep thought. I had a lot of fun, but if you're after a serious racing game, look further.

Hidden Folks is a relaxing, and at times challenging, hidden object game with a unique art style and cute details.
The hand-drawn art style is visually appealing, and I found the detailed interactions fascinating, along with the sound effects. For example you can click on holes in the ground several times to "dig up" things, or click on crops to water them and grow different plants. These interactions, sometimes puzzle-like, kept the game fresh in each new section.
I am not a big hidden object game player, but it is straight forward: there is a list of objects you have to find to progress to following levels. The detail in the levels is simply stunning and apart from finding your objective items it was entertaining to look around and interact with the environment.
My favourite thing to do in the later levels is opening the many window blinds and doors and looking into the Hidden Folks' lives - some are counting money, some are working the cubicle life, or jamming out to music... I forgot about the objective items at times and just explored!
Some objective items are very, very tiny, or difficult to see due to the black and white colour scheme, and I had to look up a guide at times. Owing to the unique art style I don't have gripes with that, but it could frustrate some players.
Some of the hidden object games I've played had story, and after finding all the necessary items you could progress the story. Hidden Folks doesn't quite have a cohesive story, but each item you find has a short blurb and some entertaining backstory. This brings the world to life as the Hidden Folk you're asked to find isn't just the "person with the hat", it could be a flower vendor whose business is slowing down today due to a traffic jam. (With animated cars stopping in front of his flower stand and you have to wait for a gap in traffic to click on him!)
Hidden Folks' art style is a pleasure to look at, and its levels are entertaining to interact with. Once again I have to mention its attention to detail - each character and item you find has an interesting blurb.
However, I only recommend this at full price ($8.99 CAD) to people that want a hidden object game first and foremost. For players like me who just wanted to relax and enjoy the art, get it on a discount.

When this game came out after the topdown isometric strategy XCOM game by Firaxis, I remember a lot of people talking MAD sh*t about it, claiming "THIS IS NOT XCOM!" and things like that. I myself was underwhelmed when I saw gameplay footage of it. It looked like a boring third person shooter to me, and I was really dissapointed to see that this was what had become of the first-person XCOM game we all saw trailers for.
However, after buying and playing it myself, I'm glad to say I was pleasantly surprised. The combat is pretty standard fair for third-person shooters; it's the squad-based tactical element that really makes this game shine. Deeper than I thought it would be, ordering my squad to flank enemies and throw out turrets and mines while ordering my sniper to higher ground under the veil of his cloaking ability was quite unexpectedly satisfying. And the squad tactics are VERY necessary; the enemy AI in this game is intelligent enough to put up a really tough fight sometimes, with one enemy flanking you while another tries to keep your attention by chucking a grenade with the intent of mearly flushing you and your squadmates from cover instead of endlessly spamming them. Mutons and Walkers charge your position while drop pods bring in reinforcements to support them, and drones floating high in the sky successfully flank you while healing the Mutons and Walkers just when you think you have them beat. Every arrangement of enemy forces, whether it's comprised of frontline fighters like Sectoids and Outsiders, long-range support like Outsider Elites and Rocket Snipers, heavy hitters like Titans and Walkers, or a combination of them all; every possible arrangement of enemy combatants forces you to incorporate different strategies, and change them in the blink of an eye if an enemy you forgot about suddenly downs a teammate, forcing you to decide whether you should risk reviving them or let them die and start from the beginning with a brand new recruit. There are no clearly superior weapons in this game either; you'll find yourself going back and forth between alien and human weapons very often, with neither being particularly stronger than the other, but merely different enough to suit certain situations better. All these factors add up to a game that is surprisingly deep, and very satisfying to play through.
Ultimately, this game is one of those games where the advertising campaign did it no justice. Since it is currently $20 as of the time of this writing, I'm confident in saying that is a PERFECT price for a very engaging, occasionally janky game. Don't believe the naysayers. Pick this game up and enjoy the tactical, conspiracy-filled universe of The Bureau: XCOM Declassified.

Disclosure:  I received this title for free, as I already own it in physical form on Nintendo NES cartridge.
First and foremost, this is a game programmed for, and completely able to be run on, the Nintendo NES.  It isn't styled after 8-bit classics, with modern amenities and fancy new programming tools to make crafting it a relative cinch.  It is built from the ground up by one guy with a passion for keeping the system alive and relevant, even today.
This port to PC/Steam maintains all of the charm and challenge of working with this old hardware, while making look as good as it possibly can within these limitations.  It also adds in a few small, but appreciated features, like savestates and minor option tweaks.  Beyond these small changes, however, lies a truly retro and unique experience which draws some parallels to classic NES games such as the original Zelda, Star Tropics, and Crystalis.
The game is fun, challenging, and feels as though it could have easilly been in the original NES library.  If you are a fan of true classic NES gameplay, I fully recommend you give this title a try... and let's be honest; that owl is friggen adorable!

This is game reminds me of when I was first playing Legend of Zelda and other NES games that I've cherished over the years. It has a good storyline, which is Adlanniel, a student of falconry, and her owl companion, Tyto, are asked by Great Owl King, Silmaran, to save five of the Great Owls from Mermon, the Merman King, who is bent on taking over the land of Owlia. It has a wide variety of floating sea creatures you can defeats and different dungeons with a lot of puzzles. If you want a preview of the game, here's a link:

Disclosure Up Front:  I received the digital product "for free" since I already own the ACTUAL NES cartridge and would otherwise be unable to supply a Steam Review.
--------------------------------
A Background Regarding Style:
--------------------------------
Before digging into a review of the game, itself, I think it is important to clarify that:
THIS IS AN ACTUAL GAME FOR THE NINTENDO ENTERTAINMENT SYSTEM, THAT REALLY WORKS ON REAL CONSOLES!
It is not "retro style".
It is not "LIKE an NES game"...
It IS an ACTUAL NES game (with an actual cartridge available for play on NES consoles).
The clever guy behind GradualGames wrote and released his own emulator (GGVM) in order to port his NES game to PCs.
As a result, there are going to be some design limitations related to NES hardware that anybody with an enthusiasm for that system (and that era of gaming) should have no problem with.
This stands in stark contrast to mountains of indie games over the last few years that LOOK LIKE classic games, but ARE NOT (and face none of the subsequent design challenges that GradualGames conquered to put this game on genuine hardware).
----------------------------
Gameplay
----------------------------
The developer states that he was inspired by games like Legend of Zelda, Star Tropics, and Crystalis, during his design process, and I think it shows (in a good way).
The "Star Tropics" inspiration comes in the form of distinct "Chapters", where you are limited in your ability to retrace your steps to earlier dungeons and areas.  It also shows in the unique and charming implementation of your character's owl companion (which has a range of abilities like retreiving items and long-range attacks -- and is INTEGRAL to the puzzle solutions of the game).
The "Legend of Zelda" inspiration shows very clearly in the dungeon room styles, some of the in-room block patterns, as well as the character life meter.
The sword-based combat (when not attacking with the owl) has a decent feel like either Legend of Zelda or Crystalis.
Recognizing that this game is a real game for the NES, the quality of how well these elements were implemented in a homebrew game really contends for top marks on the system.
Released in NES period, this game would have received top marks, as while it won't rival many of our loves for Legend of Zelda, itself -- simply due to deep nostalgia -- it is easily as good as any Zelda-clones of the early era -- i.e. Neutopia, Golden Axe Warrior, etc)
The dungeon puzzles and exploration in this game are varied and satisfying, and the game gives a good level of challenge that a lot of us classic gamers just don't feel when playing "retro style" indie games.
------------------------
Graphics and Sound
------------------------
Can't say it enough -- this is an actual NES game.
If you fully understand what that means, you'll see that this game looks and sounds great, compared to most of what that system has to offer.
Don't fool yourself with comparisons to any "retro-style" indie games, because they face no underlying limitations of any practical sort, and are an imitation where THIS GAME is the genuine article.
-----------------------
Controller Use
-----------------------
GGVM has X-input controller support, so most modern controllers should work.
Personally, I've taken to using a Steam Controller, and I have published a mapping to Steam that uses the keyboard map for GGVM.    So if you have a Steam Controller, please take a look for the "Owlia Optimized" configuration.
------------------------
The Final Word
------------------------
If you enjoy NES games like Legend of Zelda and Star Tropics, this game is well worth the price, and you won't be disappointed.
This is a good game, that is well worth playing, even viewed in the modern context (as opposed to the NES context).

How fun! The game itself is fun and inventive, balanced yet still challenging. It's quite an amazing programming achievement when you think about the limitations of the NES palette and music chip. This (steam release) is a great option if you missed the NES cart release! For those of you who don't indulge in physcial retro game media, pick this up if you enjoy retro gaming!
also, when's the sequel?!?
This game looks and feels like an NES game because, well, it is! This game delivers the fun of the classic adventure games with a fun story and excellent game play.

Faithful adherence to a retro aesthetic isn't an excuse for poor design. This would have been a middling title back in the day, and it's a middling title now.  It's not a Crystalis nor a Startropics.
That said, compared to prior 8-bit era titles it's only below average, not outright bad.  While I feel there are better titles for getting one's retro what-could-have-been fix (which is ultimately my reason for not recommending the game), it does provide what it claims to, and sneaks in a few amenities despite appearances (for example, there's a password system, though if you die your end password is also auto-entered in the Continue menu, and you aren't actually penalized for dying).
EDIT TO ADD: This is a near miss for me, and re-reading my review makes it sound more harsh than that. If you want a faithful NES game, it absolutely is one, and I'd recommend it for that. Otherwise, I would have trouble recommending for reasons discussed in the comments.

Owlia is a game that hits the nostalgia just right in terms of graphics, sound, music, and boss battles...but that's a small portion of the game. Too bad most of the game is excruciatingly cryptic. Many puzzles require bombs and whatnot that require a lot of grinding if you're not lucky enough to figure out the solution to the puzzle before running out of bombs.
In Owlia, every treasure chest contains gold pieces. Strange, being you don't purchase anything in Owlia. Gold is used to enter every dungeon.... Yep, you have to grind hundreds or thousands of gold pieces just to enter a dungeon.  Too much tedious grinding. If the grinding was removed, the game would be fairly decent. If the puzzles weren't terrible, the game would be good, even. But in its current state it is not good, imo.
In the game's three to four hour duration (the game would be maybe 1-2 hours if the puzzles and grinding were removed), there are a few good boss battles and nostalgia inducing sounds and imagery. But if you want a FUN game, you're going to be a bit let down.

I ONLY RECOMMEND THIS GAME IN THE SENSE THAT I WILL BE KEEPING AN EYE ON ITS PROGRESS AND I THINK YOU SHOULD TOO!  Heres why.
Bought this on a whim, and it is extremely well put together, but the problems it has makes it a miserable experience to play in its current state.  The balance is very poorly done.  I only played it for a couple hours, but the entire time was just me running around trying to find an enemy I can actually defeat, and trying to save up enough money to actually purchase some equipment.  The problem is, when I finally leveled up, prices for everything also went up....Not to mention the fact that the guards charge you an entry fee the first time you enter town, and will do so over and over after a certain amount of time passes. Also, running in this game isn't actually "running" so much as it is just speeding up time making you appear faster...but everything else happens faster too.
The combat itself needs an overhaul.  I found that even during fights with some of the weaker enemies, only 1 out of every 3 or so attacks would actually land without a miss...a problem the enemies rarely have, making spells my only guaranteed damage..  Most of my combat experience has been me quicksaving before a fight, and trying over and over again until luck went my way and I landed enough hits to kill them.  I also found that when leveling up, it seemed almost counterproductive to level some spells.  The absurdly small increase to the spells power in a some cases isn't even close to being worth the extra mana cost considering the super low mana pools.
Another thing, I found the system for purchasing food supplies which are gradually depeleted as you play/rest (camp)/etc to be bugged...maybe?  It seems like purchased food doesn't stack with the food you're carrying.  Say I currently have 16 hours of food left, and I go to the vendor to buy some and I pay 60 gold to buy 1 days worth of food.  That fills me up to 1 day on the dot.  Basically only giving me 8 hours of food.  Which sucks, because it is more expensive to buy in bulk.  1 day supply of food - 60G  2 days supply - 150G starting out.  Those prices also increase as you progress.
All in all, this game has a TON  of potential.  And if they could get all the numbers lined out, It'd be a hell of a game.  Again, all of these issues were experienced in just a couple hours of gameplay, so maybe something changes later on...but combat based entirely on chance kills the experience right out of the gate.  Don't drop your money on this expecting anything but an extremely unbalanced early access title.  Again, my recommendation is to keep your eyes on this one, because it could be something awesome.

Lords of Xulima
Concept:
An isometric, turn-based, single-player, 2D role-playing game that is heavily influenced by Old School Classics such as Ultima, Baldur’s Gate, Might & Magic and Wizardry Games. It is set on a mythical lost continent called Xulima, where the world makers lived in ancient times. The game features a vast, challenging world where you will lead Gaulen the Explorer and five of his companions on an epic journey filled with the struggles of Gods and Humans. Create your party with up to six characters, choosing between 9 classes and more than 100 unique skills.
Graphics: ★★★☆☆
Attractive hand-drawn 2D graphics and 3D Pre-rendered models. Overall it looks pleasing.
Sound: ★★★☆☆
The music is reminiscent of some of the classic older titles and the sound effects and ambient sounds are nicely done.
Playability: ★★★½☆
Easy controls and interface with an easy to follow Tutorial.
Entertainment: ★★★★☆
If your familiar with games of the past like the Ultima series or the Might & Magic games, you will love this title as it takes you down memory lane. Those who are new to these type of games will get to experience the games that revolutionized the gaming industry.
Replay Value: ★★★½☆
I feel the game has a Good replay value since you party consists of 6 members and there are a total of 9 possible Classes to mix and match with 100 different skills to choose.
Overall Rating: ★★★½☆
MY PERSONAL REVIEW
***This is Based off the Beta and Early version of the Game***
The Game is a throwback to some of the great classics of the past all mixed into one Game.  It has a Top-down view like the Ultima games and hand drawn backgrounds like the Baldurs Gate series. Combat switches to a turn-based combat system with a first-person view like Wizardry and the Might & Magic series. You start the game with six party members five of which you can create manually or you can simply click quick start to have the game create them for you. You have 9 classes to choose from each with there own skills. The game offers a lockpicking mini-game which I felt kept me entertained. Playing the early released version of the game is quite fun and I definitely recommend it to both those familiar and unfamiliar with these type of games.

I've only played about a little over an hour (I really want to save it for the final release), but so far I'm finding the game very enjoyable!   Nice mix of Might and Magic style 1st person turn-based combat, and Ultima or Balders Gate style 3rd person exploration.   The game is pretty well polished for being early access, so that bodes well for the final release.   Definitely recommended for fans of old-school turn-based RPGs.

This is a review of the beta; I was a Kickstarter backer, and have substantially more hours in than Steam will show.
I backed LoX on Kickstarter because I liked the idea and direction.  An old-school style RPG, with everything that entails, seemed an investment of interest to me.  Alas, that is not what we get in this version of LoX.  Let me start with the good.
THE GOOD
The art.  Character portraits are well-done, the world is very detailed, and every single thing I've encountered is easy to recognize.  All too many independent studios are going for a eye-bleedingly ugly 8-bit pixel art, but this game has an art style much more like Eschalon.  It's quite pleasant.
The customization.  You can select a pre-made party, if you aren't really into chargen, and it's a good group.  But you can do much better with a little experience, you can make a party that really supports one another and is strong against what the game will throw at you.
The sound.  Though quite loud, the quality of the music, speech, and sound effects is solid.
The lockpicking and trap disarming minigames.  Seriously.  Numantian hit that sweet spot; easy to grasp, quick enough not to be a bother, requiring player input to keep some interest, and no long animations to waste your time.
THE BAD
Basically everything implied in "old-school RPG."
There is no manual (though of course this will be fixed on full release).
There is no in-game explanation of the game mechanics.  The old-school RPGs that we remember, we remember because the rules made sense, were easy to learn and reasonable to master, and did not get in the way of the gameplay.  LoX cannot claim this, alas.  How does the game decide if you resist a sleep effect?  You'll need to go to the forums for that.  How much does a point of armor reduce incoming physical damage?  No explanation in-game, and the implication that it's a flat reduction doesn't hold true.
Movement speed is arduously slow.  It feels like you're actually fighting the game to get from one place to another.  With a speed increase, moving about will be much less painful.
The game economy scales to your level.  Old-school RPGs did not do this.  In the first town you meet, you will find that each time you level, essential items become more expensive.  Food, resting, even things like lockpicks and torches.  The economy in fact punishes you for levelling up, for completing quests, for exploring beyond the critical path.
Enemy spells are not yet well-balanced, especially with respect to status effects and spell cost.  For example, one of the earlier enemies you will face in game is a caster who will deal powerful damage, with a high combat speed, and also provide solid healing to the front-line fighters, and a massive AoE stun that is difficult to resist.  While it is possible that they will eventually run out of spell points (called Power Points in LoX), during a typical-length battle, they will be able to cast a spell every round; not a feat you will be able to replicate even with a dedicated caster character.
Randomized item stats.  If you liked that in Diablo (and every other appearance since then) then you wouldn't consider this a negative, but games that leave you at the mercy of the RNG reward luck as much as player skill, and that's not really what old-school RPGs were about.
I hope that Numantian will take this opportunity to fix a few of the more painful problems with this game.  I would really like to be able to recommend it, because at its core, there's some real potential.  But as it is, right now, I would strongly suggest to anyone, no matter how much they like the top-down RPG, that they not buy this game.  It's just not worth your time and money.

This is great old school game. It feels challenging, polished and well designed, and combines some of the best aspects of the isometric Ultima games + Wizardry style battles. It's in better shape as "beta" then many games are when they release. Kudos to the devs.

Lords Of Xulima is an isometric party-based RPG mixed with a few casual elements. For those looking for a game similar to the recently released Might & Magic X or last year’s Legend Of Grimrock don’t necessarily need to look further, because the combat is, as mentioned, turn-based and shown in the same way as those games (although not entirely) and even the difficulty can be hard for the unexperienced or unwary. Furthermore, the game plays like a mix of Hero Of The Kingdom (where you also have to collect herbs by casually clicking around) and classic RPGs, with your central hubs and huge amounts of quests to be completed.
As far as the gameplay is concerned: you walk around by clicking on the ground, or by using the WASD keys. By default your party moves at a low (read: walking) speed but by pressing and holding the Shift button you can let them run. You engage enemies by moving into their territory and if you’re walking into an area that originally belongs to the enemies random encounters will also appear. Here you can choose to fight, evade/avoid combat or to use a skill to hide. Obviously, the last two choices don’t always work and require on luck and in-game skills.
Besides fighting enemies you’ll find treasure chests and other loot. Some of these chests will be locked and can be lockpicked with your thief and or anyone who has this skill and enough lockpicks on hand. A small Minesweeper-like minigame will trigger.
You also have to take into account the food supplies.  Collecting edible plants allows you to add a small amount of food to your supplies. This is shown in a circle in the bottom right corner of the screen. Fill it up and you can walk an entire day around without having to worry that you’re going to run out. Food is used for activities like resting and traveling and when it’s empty you won’t be able to use these as efficiently, or they may not even work altogether. So it is advisable that you fill it up for at least a few days because who knows where you might end up and when you might see the next town where you can eventually stock up again.
The graphics have a casual look. Some of the portraits could use a little work, but the world itself looks splendid and detailed. The combat seemingly uses 2D animations converted from 3D models (not sure, though) and they look a tiny bit wooden to be honest. Even if they are technically okay. Other than that I have no issues.
Navigation can be a bit hard but that’s mainly because you can get stuck or walk into objects that you shouldn’t get stuck into to begin with, like trees or stones. It doesn’t happen very often but it’s definitely noticeable when it does happen and sometimes you have to backtrack a bit in order to get past the obstacle.

The user interface isn’t always entirely clear or user friendly and therefore not as intuitive to use as it should be and some tooltips that definitely would’ve come in handy seem to be missing. It would’ve been nice if there was a checkbox for this in the Options menu or something.  I understand they don’t want to hold your hand, but at least explain some of the buttons or mechanics for the less experienced gamers out there, or for those who have no idea what they’re looking at (trust me, once you’ve clicked a weird looking button you exactly know what to look for next time). I don’t think the interface should be part of the difficulty level (as you can see in the comments below you can right-click on most of the important things to get more information, but this doesn't work for everything you see unfortunately).
And why can’t I close ‘Level up’ window without having to select my skills and stats first ? Sometimes I just want to compare things before I choose. This should absolutely be optional, and not forced.
I’m also missing things like pop-ups when you level up and/or sound alerts. I know that this information is displayed in the upper right corner, but showing these events on-screen, in the center, in full detail gives a sense of progression and fulfillment. This is just a personal preference, of course.
The music is subtle and is well done. I think it fits the game well because half of the time I hardly even notice it. And yes, that’s a compliment. It all feels very natural and well integrated. The sounds used for the creatures and in battle are decent so far, and the narrator is doing a good job at telling the story sequences.
Finishing the story should take you quite a while. I’ve taken a look at the map and it’s pretty big. The game isn’t finished at the moment of writing this so we can’t experience the entire thing just yet. But I think it could easily take you anywhere between 25-50 hours. It’s hard to exactly pinpoint at this moment, and it also depends on what sort of gamer you are (do you want to complete all of the sidequests and explore every nook and cranny, for example). I’m somewhere between 8-15 hours into the game and I’m still hanging around near the beginning I think. So there’s plenty to do in this game.

As a fan of the Lost Planet series, I was really looking forward to playing this game, so once I received it from a friend, I gladly jumped into it. I had high expectations for the game due to my previous experiences with the series, experiences that were hugely enjoyable and memorable. Jumping around the place and letting it rip from mech miniguns was definitely a fun and enjoyable memory that made me return to Lost Planet 2 every once in a while.
I knew that Lost Planet 3 is different from the previous entries because it's a prequel, due to which many mechanics of the game such as the harmonizers simply weren't created in the game universe at this point. T-Energy was necessary to survive in the previous games, both in terms of generating heat and healing damage done to the player. Those two purposes made it necessary to collect the energy from fallen foes and advance quickly through areas. Lost Planet 3 is very different in that aspect, T-Energy is now used as a currency and is no longer necessary to survive in the game world. Unfortunately, the gameplay aspect is nowhere near as fun and sophisticated as it was in the previous games. The nimble mechs have been replaced by huge and almost unmovable rigs, the grappling hook is fairly unusable and the environment doesn't allow the player to do much more than rinse and repeat your typical "dodge the attack and shoot" tactic. The combat feels nowhere near as dynamic as it did in the previous entries, and often it feels almost monotonous and boring.
The story isn’t particularly exciting either, it explores the events prior to LS1/LS2 which is interesting to see from the point of view of a fan. Considering the story was never such a huge part of Lost Planet series, it is somewhat acceptable to adopt a rip through enemies view and just play for the gameplay, however, since the gameplay in this game isn’t particularly amazing either, it is hard to see what exactly this game should be picked up for. One high point of this game in my opinion, was the atmosphere of solitude and isolation that exists on EDN III. The player really feels the loneliness of the main character Jim Peyton, who is working on this giant ice cube somewhere in space, away from his family and home.
Overall, Lost Planet 3 is by no means a bad game, however neither is it a memorable experience. It’s playable and I think it’s a nice addition to the series, but it simply doesn’t live up to the gameplay that was offered by the previous entries to the series.

After playing this for a while can say it's my fave Lost Planet title. Feel guilty that it was largely overlooked when it came out and that developers Spark didn't survive as a team, I only got it when it was like $8 on Steam. If you prefer the wackier Japenese style of the first two games you may not like this one, as it's more of a traditional Western third person cover shooter. To me that's a good thing, as are the nice visuals, mix of on foot and mech gameplay, and superb voice acting/facial animation. Despite a rather cliched and predictable rundown future story with mega corps, LP3 manages to have an excellent sense of place with a somewhat open world environment that you come to like, and cool references to Aliens, Blade Runner, and of course Dead Space 3 - which it very much resembles. Places include your cozy home base as well as several other locations. Characters are quite interesting and compelling, especially main protag James Peyton, who is very relatable.
There's a few cool upgrades, several very nice weapons, and a mix of fighting and grappling. On normal this is a very easy game, including the boss encounters. I'm fine with that, but if you want a challenge maybe look elsewhere.
An example of an overlooked title where it's obvious people put a lot of work into it for naught. Can only blame myself as I also didn't buy it new. To sum up, this does the Lost Planet series more justice than the first two games, but that's my take on it, i know many disagree.

Holy crap batman, this game is a lot of fun. I really do enjoy this game on a level I haven't enjoyed an RTS on in forever. Between the challenge of making a strong enough fortress to resist the "billions" that assault you, particularly in the final wave, to the amazing art-style, to just the plain old fun of killing zombies this game has got a lot going for it.
BUT, there are considerable drawbacks that make this current version of the game borderline impossible to win on anything but the easiest setting.
1- RNG. ♥♥♥♥ing RNG. The map is totally random, and because of that it makes your potential to win totally random. The map is created with plenty of choke points to set up defenses, but depending on how many choke points you have to hold down, this alone could kill you. Not enough iron/wood/stone in an easily defendable area? You'll probably die. Not enough room to build all the buildings AND have enough for housing? You'll probably die. Have a super small choke point that you can't set up enough defenses in to reliably hold off the hords of thousands at the end? You'll probably die. The game takes hours for just one match and the chance of you dieing is pretty good if the map Gods don't like you.
2- The freakin' difficulty is a little unreasonable. You can get through 80% of the game before you really start getting into the meat of the difficulty curve, but once it hits you have to be on your game every second. Doesn't matter if you have double thick stone walls set up with 4 guard towers, a compliment of extra soldiers to help, and maybe even a giant gatling gun tower, the last 3 to 5 waves, not including the final wave, will mess up all those pretty defenses. And at the end of it all, that last damn wave just kills almost every freakin' time. I set up 3 layers of walls and guard towers and gatling towers and units, and still died because they hit 2 spots much harder thand the rest, and it was enough to overrun my entire base. Oh, which reminds me, if even a small handful of zed get behind your defenses and manage to "infect" almost any building, you're dead, because the "workers" in that building will then be infected and within seconds you've got hundreds if not thousands of zed running around and no amount of soldiers can hold back that wave. It's crazy hard, and you can't unlock the other maps unless you play on harder difficulties. So basically unless you get real good at it you're stuck to just one map.
3- The resources feel like they need some tweaking. Every single building needs workers to operate, along with gold and depending on the builing sometimes wood or stone or oil. Fine, fair, but the yields for stone, oil, and iron are pretty low unless you own the vast majority of the map (good luck defending that) and even then getting gold enough gold to keep up with everything AND keep expanding your defenses and army AND research new tech. Because the only way to get gold is to build house for more people. But those require energy and food.  And energy requires people....and food requires energy...and both require gold...and none of it seems to be properly balanced yet. Especially late game where there are advanced farms and windmills that produce double the yield, for more than double the gold maintenance and energy requirement. And it all takes up room so then you need to expand to try and fit it all in. By the end of the game your are desperately trying to fit in just one more house or windmill or farm to try and push out a few more soldiers or another tower. It's about 2 to 4 hours of just trying to find room for things so you have the resources for something else. All to watch it get destoryed in about 5 minutes.
I love this game. I really do. I don't regret buying it and I will play much more of it, but it's too difficult even on the lower settings and RNG plays way too big of a roll in whether or not you win. I recommend it, but it needs work.

A Bird Story is a quirky little "interactive movie" about an overimaginative boy and his bird.  It's about an hour long, there's barely anything that could be considered gameplay (even less so than To The Moon), and a lot of it is surreal and purposely ambiguous, so with that, you probably already know whether or not this game is for you.  But for anyone like me that enjoys the artsy-fartsy stuff, you'll be coming out of it with a smile.

Kan Gao is the genius behind 2011’s To The Moon, an RPGMaker game that tells a science-fantasy story of wish fulfillment wrapped around a powerful love story. It’s a singular achievement and a work that has moved even the manliest of gamers I know in certain internet circles to find there’s something in their eyes (including the rather less-manly me). When he released his latest work, I didn’t hesitate to spend some of my Steam credit picking it up. A Bird Story is exactly what the title indicates, a brief narrative about a boy and a bird, and it’s not necessarily for everyone. I say this not because it’s bad but simply because it’s nowhere near as impressive and heart-wrenching as his previous work.
Freebird Games’s bird story is that of a lonely boy who rescues a wounded bird from a badger attack and, in nursing the creature back to health, develops a relationship that gives meaning to his otherwise largely-friendless existence. The nameless boy is what we used to call a “latchkey kid”–his parents are an unseen presence known only through the notes they leave him on the door. The boy (literally) dreams of flying and plays with paper airplanes. One day, he finds the bird with the broken wing and his imagination soars. Naturally the journey of bird and boy has an inevitable ending, one which the player will reach in about an hour. Gao uses no dialogue in this story, and as a consequence, the other humans are both figuratively and literally shadows; while this de-emphasis on any but the main characters has a narrative purpose, it does weaken the connection one can make with this world. Another flaw, in my view, is how fantastical the story can become at times. While the boy’s imagination clearly plays a strong part in A Bird Story, it’s a little hard to take much of what you see at face value, and this also serves to hamper immersion.
As with the earlier game, this RPGMaker-based title sports a very limited keyboard interface, and once again Freebird has made the unusual decision to disable most common forms of screen-captures. The keyboard controls you can get used to readily enough, but I’m at a loss to understand why Gao seemingly wants to make it harder for people to review his games.
Part of what made To The Moon so powerful was its haunting and evocative soundtrack. A Bird Story has a similarly well-done soundtrack and I highly recommend it. As for the game itself, as Gao freely admits, it’s different. What I like about it is that he’s stripped out many of the gamey elements that frankly just didn’t work very well in To The Moon. Unfortunately, in its brevity it tends to sacrifice the strong characterizations and narrative complexity of its older brother–thus it suffers by the inevitable comparison. However, if you approach the title with an open mind and don’t set your expectations too high, you’ll find that it’s a gem that’s well worth your $5 investment. (Frankly, even if it isn’t your cup of tea, there’s little risk involved on your part, because Gao is offering a no-questions-asked, money-back guarantee, which I think is extraordinarily generous.)

Dishonored... What can I say about this game... It is simply TOO GOOD of a game that I am at a loss of words.
Okay, I will try to spit everything out now. So Dishonored is a game that follows Corvo, an assassin, who gets framed for the queen's murder and is sentenced to death. Quite obviously you don't die from that, lest there be no game. Pretty much for the whole story you are trying to rescue Emily, who is the princess, now turned heiress to the throne, that everyone is trying to exploit. But during that endevor, you embark on a journey of justice, betrayal, and vengeance (if I say anything more, it would be highly spoiling).
So basic story aside, the best part of the game is hands down the gameplay. As an assassin, you have your basic assassination tool: your knife. Additionally, you can use weapons such as pistols, crossbows, grenades, etc. That all good and stuff, but you also have special abilities. Some of the abilities include a short range semi-teleport, night vision, slowing/stopping time, and possessing something. These synergize together to give you a wealth of ways to fight. Now, that isn't the good part, as Dishonored is also a stealth game if you want to play it like that (which you should do at least once). You can stealth kill almost any single enemy, whether that be through your knife assasination or some other means. If you choose not to kill, you can grab and essentially set enemies to sleep, then drag their bodies away. In my first playthrough, I chose simply to stealth murder every single possible person/thing that I could murder >:D hehehe... Your choices actually do affect both the story and the game itself. Killing a lot will give you a higher chaos, which leads to some other things.
The gameplay itself is already very fun, but what makes it even greater is the amazing level design. Every level has multiple paths, multiple options, multiple routes, and some even have multiple endings. For example, do you want to take over a rat and go through a small sewer enterance? Or perhaps you want to teleport yourself around the top of the buildings avoiding everybody? Or maybe you even want to waltz in through the front door not caring about stealth at all. Any way you want to play it, Dishonored has a way pretty much. That is just such an amazing thing. Because of this versatility, Dishonored provides a bountiful and excellent replay experience, because you can find a different path, use a different method, and try a different ability when going through the game.
Overall, I really cannot find many flaws with Dishonored, and it is simply one of the best games I have played.

Clever and concise puzzler with just enough humor, heft, and gravitas to become something special.
With your trusty portal gun and little else, you'll navigate through a set of 'tests' organized by GLaDOS; the sentient AI that appears to have imprisoned you within a vast laboratory...and may have dubious plans for your future.
At least there's cake to look forward to...right?
Each room builds on your previous experiences, and manages to guide you towards the solution without spelling it out. You'll likely be stumped on occasion, but never for long enough to become frustrated.
Even better, many of the puzzles are deliciously open-ended, allowing for multiple solutions. Case in point: On replaying one of the larger stages, I suddenly realized that I could bypass the entire challenge and get straight to the exit with a single sets of portals and a running jump...ha!
By the way: I've seen some complaints about the length of this game -- because, after all, any game worth its salt should contain dozens -- nay, hundreds! --  of hours of gameplay.
Personally, I couldn't disagree more, and wish we could see more games like this -- short, focused experiences without feature creep or filler.
Highly recommended (and don't miss the sequel -- from what I've played, it's even better than the first).

I got Lost Planet 3 with low expectations because of the reviews, and honestly this is probably the best way to approach it. There are a number of things to turn you away from the game. The multiplayer is empty (I mean it), the controls feel like unrefined Gears of War rather than lost planet, the rig fights become monotonous fast, and - I cannot stress this enough - this game is entirely unlike LP1 & 2. Different tone, themes, pacing, and enemies. Bigger environment but narrow linear paths. Grapple points are limited and pre-selected, and the VS play I loved is practically non-existent.
That's a lot of quirks. Which means that when I say I enjoyed the hell out of this game anyway, you know there has to be something good under all that ice. If you can get used to the controls, settle back into your rig and open up to the world, then there's a lot in this game for you to love. The characters are far more human (though still a bit contrived), the story is vastly improved over previous LP's, and the environments are absolutely enchantingly alien. It's enough to make you fall in love with EDN III, if you can't love the game itself.
In a nutshell - you've gotta deal with a big, rough drop to get to EDN III, but damn if this world doesn't have charm once you get here.

If you're a fan of atmospheric sci-fi action/adventure games (or films) this is a good game.  Good, not great.  Lost Planet 1 is one of my favorite shooters of all time, mostly due to the unusual story, characters and the setting/atmosphere.  This game acts as a prequel (by a longshot) of that original title.
The story grabbed me out of the gate, and the setting and atmosphere are just right for Lost Planet.  The planet feels even harsher and more alien than it did in the first outing, which is great.  There's a certain "Alien" quality to it.  (In case you're wondering, I hated the characerization-free, multiplayer-ish, terraformed Lost Planet 2).  The characers, acting and emotive faces really reel you in, especially the very human-interest bits.  It's an unusual, almost Disney animation-ish art style (but more realistic)... it's hard to describe, but it works.
Yes, this game plays more like a "western" 3rd person game (read: Gears of War) and has quicktime events.  And backtracking.  And some repetitive bits.  And a few minor glitches.  But hey, so it isn't perfect.  It's still good if this whole endeavor sounds appealing to you.

The idea is simple - build an efficient colony that is able to muster enough defenses to survive waves of zombies. What makes the game so awesome:
- Great gameplay, a mix between a tower defense game and Warcraft 3-like RTS, all that in steampunk setting;
- Beautiful graphics, lovely art style and epic soundtrack;
- Lots of love and attention to details - every map looks different, feels different and plays different;
- Tough learning curve that makes a rare well-deserved victory feel very rewarding.
You should get the game and play it just for the sake of "They are billions! They are coming from all sides!".
However, there is also a possibility the game might be frustrating to you, because:
- It has zero tolerance for mistakes policy. If a zombie reaches your building, he infects it in a couple of hits, meaning it spawns several more zombies. This triggers a chain reaction which destroys your colony in a matter of seconds. Even if you lost only half of your colony, repairing and rebuilding is expensive, so you effectively lost once any major mistake is made.
- RNG plays too important role in this game. While you can set stuff amount of days you have for preparing for the final wave as well as the total amount of zombies on the map, you have no power over the map and your surroundings. If you didn't get a spot with a lot of wood, you will lag behind in terms of economy and lose. If you didn't get enough place for housing, you will lag behind and lose. If you got the map with too many approaches that you're unable to cover effectively early game - you lose. If you didn't get good mayor choices for your colony - you'll probably eventually lose, too. I have over 80 hours played at the time of the review and I've only won twice. Both times RNG gave me a ridiculously good spot with 1-2 (as opposed to 4-5) approaches to defend as well as lots of resources nearby.
- Since there's currently no campaign, learning the game has to be done on your own and is pretty tough. What to research first? How to expand? What units to build? There is no tutorial that would guide you through all that, so it's either lots of trial&error exercises or watching youtube videos.
All in all, it's this kind of game that isn't perfect and you know it, and some things you even hate, but it is too addictive and exciting experience overall to dwell on that. Furthermore, it's still Early Access and the game gets better with every update, so get on the hype train.

I think I just finally figured out how to play. I'm not joking. There is a huge learning curve and no tutorial. This REALLY needs a tutorial but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥was it fun to get blasted by my first zombie rush. Please note its still early access and I have a hunch their campaign will act as the tutorial. So I thought I'd share some of my experience.
1. Population/Workers are very important prioritize the house buildings. Guard these buildings carefully! 1 rouge zombie will turn these buildings into your worst nightmare.
2. You'll need food to do number 1. Before farms you can litter grasslands with hunter shacks.  It's usually better to place them at sub optimal positions if it will result in you being able to place more.
3. Lumber\Stone you want to restart if lumber is not near you when you start. You can get lucky and pick up stone from ruins if you scout around. This helps by not needing a stone quarry right away. Later on you get Iron and Oil. Quarries can gather from multiple things if they're in range.
4. Research buldings are important. Don't lose them! Keep them tucked away safly in your base or heavily guarded.
5. Troops are how you expand. Try to micro troops to get veterancy in the begining. Don't use soldiers unless you mass them in force as they create noise which can be troublesome.
6. Telling troops/defense structures how to target has many uses. Snipers are amazing when set to focus on highest level targets. Also use the patrol action to set a patrol route. Very usefull in the begining when trying to ensure no sneaky zombies get your tents.
7. Expand to useful terrain and use the terran to your advantage. Use mountains as choke points so you don't have to build as many walls.
I haven't unlocked any of the other maps or even beat the first one. So I'm by no means an expert.

In Lords of Xulima you control a hero called Gaulen the Explorer and his five friends (these five can be completely created by yourself, with 9 classes at your disposal). Guided by a dream sent by the gods of this world, he sails to a forgotten continent. During exploration, the game is very similar to classics like Baldur´s Gate, but once combat begins, it will look like a mixture of Dragon Quest, Final Fantasy 10 and the newer Etrian Odyssey series.
Major Features:
- A charming atmosphere, travel through a mystical world and explore secret graves, forsaken temples and more.
- Challenging and strategic combat. Very original due to the elaborate debuff system.
- Character skills and equipment management are rich and rewarding.
- Extremely polished for a beta: bugs are rare, less than in many recently relesed games.
Possible weakpoints (depending on your taste):
- Story plays only a secondary role. Exploration, combat and character management take the main spotlight.
- Hard to get going. You have to manage the party, food reserves and find your way in a huge non-linear world. (If you have troubles, try the easiest difficulty. There you can learn the basic game mechanics without getting your head chopped off for every mistake.)
Minor addittion: You CAN run in this game, the trailer shows only the walking speed.

It's not too basic of an MMO. No in this game, it will allow you to play multiple roles when playing a single class. Example, play a rouge, and that rouge depending on soul build can ether melee or range damage, even tank, support with buffs, and even heal ether single or group. Each class can do any role based on how you build your character's soul. And you can also switch preset builds during gameplay in raids PVP PVE and whatever. But of course some of these roles in each class is behind a pay wall. Like the Mage's Arbiter or the Warrior's Liberator soul. But some of those from experience is well worth it like the Rouge's tactician where you get to use technology like flamethrowers. I did pay some money in this game time to time, and so far not disappointed. My only buyer's grief here is for the mage's stuff. Most of that save for the latest I haven't bought is mostly melee fighting. I like my mage traditionally ranged.
Also it does have a mentoring/sidkicking system. What this does is give the player the ability to control their physical level. So if you want to play in a low level area but don't want to be so overpowered, just adjust your level to the area from your portrait menu. Or if you want to team up with a high level player for a high level quest, you could sidrkick with them at their level. It is a good system, but too bad not everyone uses this. Example an event in a low level area can end too quickly if a high level player kills the boss in seconds. But you know damn well they can mentor down and play fairly for everyone else not at that level yet. For the sake of argument, that's the point of the mentoring system there.
Everything else is pretty basic. Go out, do quests, grind, get stuff, and ether show off or have a more easier time playing. It's not for everybody, but it is what it is there.
Now I would be carefull buying things from this game admittingly. It's mostly fair business enough, but example allot of the cosmetic clothing in their cash store can be earned in game and permanently too. Learned this the hard DOH way. Also, this game is still all free to play today. Yes some were correct that they did charge for the new expansion at first. Then they made it optional to buy it with points granted from subscribing. Then they decided to give it out for free for a weekend. And finally a week or so after this, they made that content free for all. So yes their business ethics is chaotic, and again be careful doing business here because of this. But today it is all still free to play. Just next time they have an expansion and charge for it, ether buy it or just wait until they make it all free anyway.
The social aspect is okay. Most are ether quiet or friendly enough. I'm usually pretty quiet too but will talk if invited and in the mood. No different from other MMOs there. There are the occasional trolls and bullies of course. Had one harass me about my character's looks, another bringing up some vauge argument about porn, and another annoyed me with raid marks who I think just got angry when I got lagging problems as the group's healer. Okay I'm sorry, but this is not appropriate behavior for something out of my control. And there's the goofballs and nuff said there. But the antisocial behavior is not vary high. I been to MMOs and other games where this can get a bit high like in Star Trek Online, Gears of War 2, or Halo Reach, and do I got stories from those like the awkward little boy singing about oral and a degenerate player with the word "wolf" in his gamertag with daddy issues and who I witness sexually harassing a woman. All this over Xbox Live. That was disgusting behavior, but it happened. But Rift is not this bad. It may sometimes happen, but not this bad.

The Guardians is a faction that embrases a group of gods known as the "Vigil", and your character aligned to them would be resurrected by them as an "Ascended". In a way, they are suppose to be the good guys although sometimes I don't know. And there's the Defiants. A faction run by a spoiled brat of a scientist who would rather use technology to solve problems than religion. But he's not at all a good guy. He helped create the problem the game is based on, rifts, and he does engage in experimentations that purposefully harms people pacifically Ascendeds. This is just fantasy, but reality would be more complicated. Not all religious people are good natured, and not all scientists are amoral borderline psychopaths who torture or kill people to advance science. Some religious people are dangerously aggressive, and plenty of real athiest scientists can be more moraly good than certain religious crowds. But I can see the message in the lore. Religion good. Science bad. But as said, the game isn't too bad at all when the lore is ignored. I don't take my moral standings seriously all the time.
In all, I can still recommend this game. Just be careful with the business, ignore the lore as even I agree it is a bit questionable, and ignore the occassional troll or bully that comes along. Like any MMO out there. And I do try to keep my reviews as objective and bias free as possible.

The most in depth gameplay you'll find in this game is searching for supplies about half an hour in and that's about as deep as it gets. You have just discovered the daddy of all true 3D shooters.  It's primitive compared to today's games.  The graphics are from a simpler time - a time when game play ruled and stories were for children.  It's not pretty.  No... It's dark, brutal, and unapologetic.  It will rip out your gaming spine, chew it up, and spit it back in your face.  There's no hand-holding here - no tutorials, no hiding behind things to heal - just an "easy" mode for those who don't know what a real FPS game is, and "Nightmare" for those that accept no compromise.  Out of ammo?  Look for some, or see how useless your axe really is.  You get hurt?  Find your own friggin' health box.  They're all gone?  Well too bad.
This is QUAKE.
Forget your 360 no-scopes.  Forget your controllers.  Forget your sissy regenerating health.  Forget your backup.  There is no backup.  It's just you against evil unleashed.  You will clench your mouse in fear.  Your knuckes will turn white scrambling for your strafe keys.  You will watch with utter horror as you find there is no substitute for skill, no mercy from your enemies, and nobody to hear your screams except your own twisted mind.
You think you know gaming?  You think you're hardcore?  Are you ready for four complete episodes of nightmare-fuel visions of Lovecraftian horror that will pummel your pride and assault your senses?  Are you ready to face Quake's fearsome hordes with nothing but your wits and your weapons to save you?  If you want to know how true gamers were forged, this is the anvil upon which they were beaten.  This is the crucible of champions.  It is waiting for you.
If you dare.
