Okay, I see these reviews and I wanted to write one for myself.
Disclaimers, I bought this game when it was 3 dollars. I've played through the prologue and first mission on xbox and wanted to try it out on my new pc.
Gameplay:
Holy crap this game is fun to play. I've played through the game both high chaos, and killing one (god damn weeper ruining my achievement chances) and both ways in every attempt I had at the game, I found new and exciting ways to complete my objective. The maps are designed extremely well and allows for the player to traverse the environments complete at their will. I loved hopping from rooftop to rooftop once I understood my abilities better, or bypassing entire guard squads and light walls by taking over a rat. I enjoyed dropping and killing, blinking behind people to perform assassinations, I even enjoyed running, as the level design allows for you to fight, and easily get away, allowing you to use this for tactical advantage. My only problem with the power features is that the blink particles, IMO, are not always accurate, nor does upgrading it, at times, help it.
The AI is probably the most frustrating part of the game. The guards took turns being the most oblivious people ever hired to do their job, and also being ultra-elite sniping units, able to pick you out from a bush, a half mile away, and then proceeding to hit a flintlock pistol shot. I understand that no AI will ever be perfect, and these problems can also easily by attributed to when the game was released, its just a frustrating aspect that we now have to deal with. I also wish there was more variety in the enemies faced. The thugs were reskinned guards that threw flaming bottles instead of grenades. The only introduction to new enemies is an almost invincible (without explosives) man on stilts, and an assassin enemy who miraculously has the same powers as you do. The repetition of the guards vocal lines is also kind of frustrating, after hearing "you think you'll get a squad after whats happened last night" makes you want to quit the game sometimes. I'm nitpicking of course, as the AI in the game no where near the worst i've experienced, and the games fluidity in its killing, should you go high chaos, makes killing every guard a unique experience.
Story:
I thought the story was well put together, with not terrible voice acting and a decent plot. Most of the outside world is only known through excerpts from books and literature you acquire. Unless you're a savvy map explorer, you won't find out a lot about the outside world. Conversely, if you ARE an explorer the lore goes very deep in these texts and the sheer amount of them is a testament to the game.
It did a great job of bringing me into the character of Corvo, and the responsibilities of being an assassin, to an extent. I found that most of my choices in game didn't actually affect the game. An info screen pops up telling you the actions you take will affect the city and what you encounter as far as enemies, however, in both of my playthroughs, I ran into the same amount of guards up until the finale, and the only noticible effect was an increase of weepers during my chaos play.
Conclusion:
I sound super pessimistic about the game but all in all this game is definitely worth any money its selling for. The story is alright but the sheer variety in level design is what will keep me coming back to play.

I love Burnout games.  They're some of the best car racing games in my opinion, very arcadey, but when you mess up it turns into beautiful beautiful destruction porn.
Dangerous Golf looks to be the same game, in fact I've been tracking this game for awhile, ever since the first beautiful destruction video came out.  The entire world getting destroyed in beautiful slow mo, and I was in love.  I wanted this game.  I bought the humble bundle with this game in to finally get this game, and ... well the love affair is over.   The destruction porn idea is still here in some extent, the problem is it's trying to be burnout without the game behind it.
In dangerous golf you hit your ball into an object filled room to try to destroy as much as you can.  This sounds good.  The downside is the golf game is awful.  I'm a fan of Mario Golf and hot shots golf.  Arcadey golf is acceptable. So that's not the problem
The issue is when you start playing the game, you don't get to see where the ball might go.  Where you aim the ball with the camera does matter, but there's no guideline and you just hit up on the joystick to hit the ball.  Disappointing.
Once you do enough damage (counted in objects, not money) you can go into "Smashbreaker" mode where you bounce around and can do more damage.  There's a set amount of time (or movement), and no bonus time awarded, but you can go around smashing things to your heart's content.     Then you land the ball (you can decide when to stop or when ever you run out of time/momentum).  And you can use a smash shockwave (I forget the name).  Then after all of that, you put the ball into the hole.
Again it seems like it works, but the first time you get to a putting challenge the whole experience falls apart for me.   You realize that putting is a rather shallow point and click experience, point at the whole and put it in.  The puts are so strong, that you can pretty much put anywhere in the general direction and it seems to go in.    The same is true for the tee off.  You basically don't know where the ball will go, because there's no arrow, instead you give it a vague direction and hope it'll smash into enough stuff.  The entire problem of the game is that the player agency is heavily lacking.  The player gets to see amazing destruction, but barely causes the destruction.  There's not even a golf club to hit the ball, the game just fires the ball forward as if out of a cannon.
Granted there's some agency in how the player bounces around the room in a smashbreaker, but overall the experience isn't an orgy of destruction as you'd hope, but the only part of the game that's really interesting.  It's violence and destruction, but rather than being a reward for a particularly good shot, it's the only thing in the game, if you don't get a smashbreaker, you might as well just restart.
"But stuff gets blown up, right?"  Well yeah, that IS what happens.  But the images above are not representative of the game as most of the time, you're so focused on the ball and moving it, the destruction is only there to distract you instead of let you revel in it.   Where every piece of destruction of your car in Burnout Paradise is glorious because you can't do anything but watch, in this game, if you watch you are losing valuable time, and the fact is you camera is so close to the ball you barely can watch anything.
The game is built off a scoring system where you can destroy certain objects for a bonus, usually having to destroy between 3-6 at least early on.  And there's a little sparks of interest there.  There's very little strategy to the destruction.  You might hit bucket 1 first instead of bucket 3 but you're still going to hit a ball in a random direction and hope for the best.
The thing is everything in this game is trying to be "To the max" this is "EXTREME!" and "Totally awesome".  Everything seems to be trying to be an 11 (the graphics the sound the UI) But this game doesn't earn that. When everything is an 11, everything really is a 5.
If you had three strokes to do a lot of damage and maximize the destruction and if you hit a level THEN you get smashbreaker, they would be a hell of a lot more strategy to this game.  Instead what you get is a single stroke, and then a smashbreaker, and a single putt.  It's a shame because there's a good destruction engine in this game, but that's about all this game is.  There's not an amazing game wrapped around the destruction engine, and from past experience programming games, I have a feeling the destruction engine limited the room size, which is why the game doesn't allow multiple strokes and so on.
It's a shame because I LOVED looking at this game and dived in lustfully, but then I hit my head on the bottom of the shallow pool, and chipped a tooth.  Some of the images from the game are glorious, but overall the game doesn't live up to those hopes and dreams of the best parts of Burnout, the destruction.  I might be able to recommend it as part of the humble bundle, but there's no way I could recommend it for even 10 dollars.  A fun diversion, but not much else.

When it comes to reviews, I favour those that get to the relevant points as quickly and briefly as is reasonable, I will therefore attempt to do so myself.
Visually, I think the game's exteriors are wonderful, it really does convey an extremely cold, foreboding landscape. The interiors are also very good but not quite as convincing.
I find driving around in the rig/mech cumbersome and therefore tiresome, with the relatively late introduction of a quick travel mechanism not helping to ameliorate this.
The controls felt a little unpolished, two examples: an on-screen prompt to use the 'WASD' keys to turn a valve with the mech's claw was inaccurate, you needed to press 'F'; when using the mech's grappling hook to access ledges occasionally you had to be very carefully positioned, other times the positioning was less critical.
The overall plot line was good, not too complicated but gave the game meaning, though there were a few minor oddities which I will not go in to for fear or spoiling it.
Perhaps it is just me but I find the classic boss battle rather tiresome in an “oh look, this area looks just like the sort of place we could have a boss battle, oh what a surprise it is a boss battle, I guess I'll have to spend the next half an hour working out exactly how to defeat it,” kind of way, and this pretty much that tiresome old formula which added little to the game.
Overall, I liked it, but the slow game movement mechanic and control issues detracted from this, making some parts of the game a chore rather than a pleasure.

Despite all the negative reviews, I found Lost Planet 3 to be a fairly enjoyable game. I tried playing it on hard to start, but the battles against armored Akrid got to be too trudging, so I lowered it to easy and really got into the story.
Like most Capcom games, it is lacking as a PC port, since it keeps the sorry autosave of consoles instead of a save-when-you-want and quicksave feature like a real PC game. The keyboard and mouse controls were serviceable (though the incorrect prompt for turning the claw took some research to overcome - Press F, not WASD). There were a few too many quick-time-events, like in the Resident Evil games, which made my forearms ache (I can only press F so fast, people!).
The game looks great, and plays pretty good. It was a bit different than Lost Planet: Extreme Condition, but I didn't think that game was the best ever, so a little change was fine by me.  The boss battles were challenging and maybe a bit too picky about how, exactly, you did what the game wanted. The overall experience was positive, though, and a fine addition to the Lost Planet story. It makes me even more interested in playing Lost Planet 2, which I've been waiting for a super cheap sale on.

HIGHLY RECOMMEND

Oh boy. I just keep finding ways to get impressed. At a retail price of $3, Ocean City Racing (well, OCEAN CITY RACING, but I think you'll forgive me if drop the caps) is a pretty cheap buy, but as a lover of racing games I'll give almost anything a try. It doesn't always go well, like
or
, and Ocean City Racing is stacking up to be another mistake languishing in my library.
The game already fails on a technical level with a barebones options menu, offering an extremely limited resolution choice—not even offering my native resolution of 1600x900, the third most common resolution by Steam's hardware survey—no graphics options, no volume sliders, no rebindable controls...it's just a mess. And the game runs terribly and looks worse, with a massively overdone motion blur to boot that makes it more or less impossible to see what you're doing. Of course, as mentioned, there is no way to turn this off. Additionally, all the button prompts given are for keyboard controls, so anyone who wants to play with a controller will find themselves randomly pressing buttons to try to figure things out if they didn't memorize the controls from the options menu.
The car handling is utter garbage. You have very little control and will find yourself bumping off walls left and right. Conveniently there's a reset car button that doesn't seem to have much penalty, so I think this was expected. The handbrake button has been replaced by a spin out button, leading to further resets. The boost fails to give any real feeling of speed, but nonetheless makes the car all the more likely to go out of control in corners, adding yet more usefulness to the reset button unless you save it for straights. And of course there's the random physics bugs where a tap against a wall can send you flying into the air. And despite all this bumping around and lost time, the computers have it even worse; I watched them crash on their own all over the place. They don't know how to play this game any better than I do! I had an atrocious time but still somehow came in second in my first race.
So, after the disaster of a race, I decided I would try free roam mode. You walk around in a first-person camera and can't interact with anything but the cars. You drive around a little more freely which leads to a little bit less bumping around, but the driving still feels terrible, the game still looks like someone dumped Vaseline on it, you still randomly get launched into the air, and there doesn't seem to really be any point to doing any of this.
It was at this point I realized I had about all I could take of this game and decided to try collecting my thoughts together into words. That really is all there is to it: nothing in this game inspires me to play it, and on both technical and design fronts it actively discourages me from playing. There was not one moment when playing this game that I thought to myself "I had fun," and for that I cannot recommend this game for any reason.

Historical Roots
The year is 1996. The games industry had already been presented to games like DOOM and Wolfenstein 3D but Quake take the experience of first person shooters to another level. The Game inserts you into an environment full of darkness and fallen demonic beings – all of them willing to kill you, off course. You walk – or run –  by yourself through dark and scary corridors solving puzzles, pressing buttons, dodging bullets and escaping from traps. Each new area guards a new surprise and, most of the time, you going to fell relieve when you find the last portal and complete the stage.
Why play Quake nowadays? It’s simple, no one could truly respect the FPS genre without knowing his history and his historical development process. To play Quake is a prior condition for anyone who wants to set himself up as a gamer. 21 years after his debut the game remains fun and challenging – try the nightmare difficult – the sounds are iconic and, of course, the gameplay is remarkable. There’s no present without history and there’s no history without the present. Just play.

Quake is a FPS game made by id software and released in 1996. it stood put among the FPS or "Doom Clones" at the time for a few notable reasons. It was fully 3D, had smooth animations and complex (for its time) level design. But how does it hold up? How does it play for a first time player? The awnser to both is amazingly well.
Game:
The game is set across 4 different dimensions. This causes each of the four episodes to have its own unique location. The weapons are plentifull and fun to use. The line-up includes grenade launchers, nail guns and a lightning gun. The only problem I had with the game was the two bossfights. They didn't require shooting, but pressing buttons. You may have to shoot you way to the buttons, but the bosses themselves doesn't require one bullet to kill, which really sucks. The games difficulty is on the heavy side. I played on normal and found the difficulty what I would expect on hard with other games. Respect to the people finding nightmare enjoyable and finishable..
Technical:
The game works out of the box with the steam version, but there are a few issues. The controls are not as smooth as modern FPS games. The soundtrack ran off a cd, that means no soundtrack for the steam version. the resolution is really low (Doesn't bother me but can bother you). To fix all three issues mentiones above (The only technical complaints I had) I used the Ultimate quake patch. It uses the DarkPlaces engine developed by LordHavoc, the plasmagun fix by OoPpEe, the music patch originally hosted on
and the NSIS install system by Nullsoft. The Ultimate Quake Patch was compiled by (as I understand it) MenaceInc.
I would highly recommend this game to ANYONE!!
P.S.
Don't forget to download episode 5. Its calles DOPA and was developed by Machine Games (Who did a amazing job with Wolfenstein the New Order and Wolfenstein the Old Blood) for quakes 20th birthday. It has te same old school design and if it was included with the original game, I wouldnt have know that it wasn't id that made this episode.I can't think of higher praise for DOPA. Get it if you get Quake. It was released for free. To install it you just have to create a dopa folder where quake is instelled, extract the zipfile in the folder and double click the batch file.

There were a lot of problems during the deveploment of Quake, which eventually led to John Romero (main level designer) being fired and several other members leaving the company. id Software died (well, a part of it anyways) and the repercussions showed up in 1997... But that's a story for another day.
Despite the chaos during deveploment, the game turned out to be pretty good, and in my opinion is the best game from the old id Software.
Even for today's standards.
Seriously, this game has freaked me the f*ck out more times than what I would like to admit. The darkness of the environments and the deadly speed of some of the enemies (specially in Nightmare) really make this a pretty tense game.
And the soundtrack. God, the soundtrack. It makes you wonder in what horrible corner of existance you got yourself into. Unfortunately it isn't included in the Steam release (copyright or something I think) but this can be solved by installing the Ultimate Quake Patch or by downloading the .ogg files and using a source port. Don't you dare to play this without the music. IT'S A CRIME.

-The "hostile" and "uninhabitable" world poses no threat at all (you can walk around in major storms to your heart's content)
-Controls are lazy and stupid (P is to pick up ammo! Why not the "use" button??)
-The cover system is the epitome of crappily-made. They don't even tell you it's there, which makes sense, since it DOES. NOT. WORK.
-The strategy for killing the akrids (including the bosses) is always the exact same (dodge as they charge, shoot when they're stunned)
-Fighting in the rig is beyond pointless (it's ALWAYS better to get out and fight in-person)
-The boss fights are ridiculously stupid (the one in the rig is mind-bendingly atrocious)
-Bosses are recycled all over the place (you kill the giant crab thing in 3 different boss fights alone)
-The game straight-up lies about button prompts ("W/A/S/D to turn wheel" really means "tap f repeatedly")
-The audio logs are filled with SO MANY juicy, lip-smacky, mouth-poppy sounds that it sounds like the mic is being eaten
-The base only has a few people you can actually interact with, so it feels lifeless
-It is completely arbitrary where/when you can grapple/repel
-There is no visual indicator of health (other than when you're near-death), and your ammo count vanishes and reappears whenever it feels like it (EDIT: I've been informed that your ammo count and the rest of your HUD disappear when you get too far from the mech)
-And so many other little tiny annoyances
If you're a more patient person than I am, you could probably put up with this game, and might even enjoy it. I, however, found it joyless, tedious, and boring. It is a paint-by-numbers, designed-by-committee, heartless blob of checklists, man-hours, and coding. Life is too short to slog through uninteresting crap, and this game didn't make the cut (for me). You may enjoy it, but please don't spend more than $5 on it.

Nicholas (Cage)*(Tom) Hanks is the protagonist.
You cannot unsee this.
While I don't think it should at all be called a sequel of the series, since it's so wildly different, it does share some similarities in name and in lore. It's an OK game, but it's a shootoff, not what one should consider an official installment.
I can appreciate the work that the team put into developing it, and the boss-fights were at least well-thought-out. I had very low expectations going into it, but have since been pleasantly surprised.
Do not go in expecting any similarities, other than superficial similarities to Lost Planet.
The gunplay is mostly decent, the enemy design is decent, but the weapons are somewhat bland, and it has lost any sense of outlandish caricatures of robotic weaponry that the previous games had. It is a cover shooter and a robot beat-em-up with some additional collection features.
The game does have its good points, though.
-Attention to detail
-Characters (other than the main character)
-A sense of... coldness
-Boss fights are engaging and well-designed for the team's level of development experience
-Enemy design means you have to engage each one differently
-RIG Combat is actually pretty fun (when you do fight against large Akrid)
The bad parts, however, plunge the game into mediocrity
-Pacing in combat sections isn't very-well thought out for some instances
-The game feels like a cover shooter that borrows many elements from other games without making them its own
-The upgrade system for the weapons is shallow and wasn't explored deeply enough by the development team
-It's not really Lost Planet other than names and lore
-Some of the weapons (esp. the Pulse Rifle) feel clunky.
-Some explorational/collection mechanics aren't explained very well
I cannot recommend this game, however, due to how much of an offshoot it is from its predecessors, quirky and zany as they may have been. It's a completely different game and doesn't really come into its own. Plus, a lack of co-operative play is a big no-no since MP was DOA.

The graphics in Osiris: New Dawn are gorgeous.  At first I was truly enjoying the game, but after playing for a little while I've changed my mind.
Suvival elements?  Basically none after you learn that you can harvest tree sap to drink.
Character development is kind of a joke as it's way to easy to level up your skills.  I would only pick Ranger or Marine class for the extra gun.
Base building? There doesn't seem to be much in the way of base building, not in any meaningful way.  It's a pretty big snoozefest putting your base together.  If you are playing as part of a colony, you have to unlock every single storage box, workbench, etc...and make it public to the colony -- a major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Content?  There really doesn't seem to be much to do for a game that's been around for a year.  Vehicles sometimes sink into the ground and disappear.
There worst part of Osiris: New Dawn?  It's the servers...you can't seem to reliably connect and stay connected to the public servers.  I'm running a Ryzen 1600x, 32 gb RAM, Vega 56 GPU, and a fiber line using an ethernet connection from modem to the computer -- and I have a lot of trouble connecting.  I'll get connected (sometimes first try, sometimes I have to run an endless amount of attempts) and my friend who is a few miles away will have trouble connecting.  The game says two people logged into proteus2 and when my friend finally connects I will get booted from the game and have to go through the hit or miss process of reconnecting.
When I enter an instanced area (any of the mines, etc..) and I'm grouped with a colony mate, one or both of us will get disconnected when trying to load in and we'll have to go back to the whole hit or miss reconnect issue again.  The servers also seem to be completely unpopulated.  There were a couple of people playing the first few days I played, but honestly I don't know that's I've seen a soul log in other than my friend since that point.  When I first saw the server capacity at 18 players I was worried, but that never materialized as an issue.
There definitely is potential in Osiris: New Dawn, but there are way too many problems and not enough content to justify putting up with the issues.  I'm honestly not certain how the overall review score can be so high.  I wouldn't recommend the game at this point, but hopefully with some more work the game will live up to it's potential.

Pixel Piracy is a game that has never felt finished, and any enjoyment that may have been possible is doomed by its repetitive nature.  Every island looks similar, and feels identical.  Enemy ships suffer similarly, although they at least benefit from some more obvious variety in appearance.  The gameplay never changes.  Kill everything on an island, or kill every pirate/use canons upon the enemy ship.  In both of these circumstances this entails throwing your pirates at the enemy.  Little variation, and minimal required strategy from my experience: every battle that I fought was won by just ordering every crew member to head in the direction of the enemy and then sitting back and wataching inevitable victory, no matter that difficulty level.  It all results in an experience that feels exactly as repetitive as it is.
True, one can say with relative certainty that there will be an element of repetition in any game; but the best games hide this well.  Pixel Piracy not only fails to hide it, it never seems to make an effort to do so.  And that, perhaps, is the biggest failing.  In spite of what the developers may or may not have to say on the subject, it never felt to me as though very much effort was put into the game.  What content there is (and, again, it never feels like very much) feels slapped together and unfinished, or poorly thought out from the start; and while I could overlook a feature or two that felt that way, EVERY feature elicited the same sort of response from me.
I cannot recommend the game.  Its execution is far too poor, and it seems unlikely that any more effort will be put into any sort of improvement or addition.

I bought Rift years ago on launch day. It was full price with a subscription, and I played for about 6 months. I cleared all of the available content at the time, and cancelled my sub. Came back a few years ago, put in some time, was disappointed with the cash shop. Now, the game is a pretty great time up until level cap.
Most MMORPGs have you grinding tokens or reputation at endgame. Rift has you grinding both, but also a third dimension: grinding gold to buy paid currency, or buying paid currency with money. You need the cash shop currency to unlock classes and additional content. If it was only cosmetics, well, that would be a different story. As evidenced by other reviews, having to grind or buy your way into new content (the cash shop content, not tokens or rep) makes players lose interest, because it simply is not fun or intuitive. Particularly not when you're already grinding reputation and tokens.
It's not the cash shop itself causing players to leave, it's just a side effect of how the whole system plays out. Even at release when there wasn't much content available, Rift felt authentic in a way that it likely never will again.

The game isn't a great golf game, and it isn't the old Burnout crash mode experience I was hoping for.  Dangerous Golf is closer to that ruined Burnout Paradise version of crash mode (the one that isn't very fun).
I do actually like that the tee off is simplified (no hassle power meters or spin or anything).  But my problem is that everything else in the game is simplified too.  You have so much ball control when bouncing around that the strategy and finesse of the Burnout crash mode can't happen (like using your explosion to baarrrely nudge your car right where ya need it).  And the golf side of the game isn't very satisfying either because there is a strong auto aim when the ball bounces.
The game also has minor annoyances like . . .
-Menu buttons that are finicky w/ mouse
-An unskippable, overlong, and unneeded tutorial video
-A ton of animation when levels end so the flow is really bad
If I was the dev and looking to improve Dangerous Golf, I would personally:
-Streamline all of the stuff at the end of levels
-Add a "hardcore mode" with a more interesting rule set.  For example: Little to no ball control while moving, allow pause/slo-mo on bounces and let the player spend smash meter to change the bounce angle, reduced auto aim
I don't think Dangerous Golf is a terrible game, I just don't recommend it unless it's on sale.  The most fun I had was watching nice CG rooms blow up.  That enjoyment only lasts so long.

2011 was a game of big releases, we can all agree on that...Skyrim, Arkham City, Fallout New Vegas DLC's, Portal 2, MW3, Battlefield 3, Gears of War 3, Serious Sam 3, FEAR 3, something that ends with a 3, etc.
But no other game, NO OTHER! Got my attention as much as BRINK, BRINK had my highest expectations of 2011, more than skyrim, Arkham City, Portal 2 or any other game.
Did it meet the hype? Sadly, no...maybe I hyped it too much, but many people have the same feeling as me.
Starting with the graphics, they are not groundbreaking, but not bad either, ok-ish I would say, however it has pretty slow texture pop-ins...
The game also feels to be poorly optimized and console ported (you can't lower teh shadows more than normal, and besides that there aren't all that many options besides texture quality and V-Sync. So, if you have a crappy computer, you're screwed!).
Moving to the gameplay, it's what somewhat saves the game, your character flows really nicely thanks to SMART (Smooth Movement Across Round Terrain, I think it stands for...) and teamwork is a very important aspect focused in this game, so there wont be any Lone Wolf crap here (I mean there can be if a noob enters, but he will get totally owned...). Sadly, the guns lack punch, only some assault rifles and shotguns and pistols, SMG's feel terrible and they have like a F2P-like handling (watermelon seed shooter).
A good thing about the game is the customization: It's enormous, absolutely HUGE! It's impossible for 2 people to have 2 characters look the same. It's very deep! Both the character and weapon customization.
The game also features a class based system, assault, medic, etc. There is even the secret ops guy or whatever the name is (which is like the spy from TF2, can sap and hack stuff and disguise as an enemy. Except BRINK, unlike TF2, requires skill...). It's varied and VERY interesting.
Audio quality is pretty good, surprisingly (not the guns, btw), your movement, jumping, the effect sounds, etc. All are really well done.
Map layout and level design is absolutely phenomenal! It has many twists and encourages tactics, like ascend to higher places or flanking, as it's very team and objective focused!
The word of the day for BRINK is definately: Potential! Potential! Potential!
Sadly it's just the potential. If Bethesda gets their thumbs off their asses and stop supporting Skyrim and start growing balls and investing in BRINK, I would be very pleased, but more careful, after all, I paid 50 euros for this game to get 80 minutes out of it. -.-
But before BRINK 2 or something along those lines, I'm still waiting for FALLOUT 4! HUH?! Oh sorry Bethesda, I forgot it's your money-bath time...
Anyways, I wont give a score. get under 9,99€ anything equal or under that is worth it! Beware, this game isn't bad! It's a colossal disappointment, it's different. If the expectation were much lower, this game would be GOOD! But all that hype not met...it's disappointing and it saddens me. A lot...

Quite honestly the best dating simulator I have ever seen. I walked into it thinking the same thing as I'm sure anyone else does; thinking "Oh, a game about dating birds? This should be good for a laugh or two."
After clearing two routes I had already made up my mind that this silly little game that should only have been good for a couple of laughs was genuinely better than most dating sims I've come across.
The true ending of the game, known as Bad Boys Love, made me cry. I am not ashamed in any way to say this. This game is hands-down the best dating sim that I've ever played.
Come for the silly bird dating premise, stay for the unironically good stories and memorable characters.

Hatoful Boyfriend is easily one of the best games I've ever played, and the "gimmick" that is a "dating sim with birds" quickly reveals some of the most interesting (and surprisingly dark) backstory I've seen in a game. The positives of this game cannot be over-stated, and though it may start a little rough, it will quickly fly its way into your heart.
Positives
+Engaging and distinctive characters with branching story paths that encourage multiple playthroughs.
+Tremendous writing that gradually sets up the strange, comedic, and dark world that you (the protagonist) is residing in.
+Multiple endings and characters, including some secret ones!
+Puns... So many puns...
+Great music selection that excellently promotes the tense, calm, and (most importantly) romantic moments that you'll be experiencing with the birds.
Negatives
-During the "courting" section of the game, you'll be asked to pick from a variety of seeds to give to your feathered lover. While you'll eventually learn the different preferences, the game offers no clear explanation of which bird likes what, and it often will turn into a guessing game.
-A similar complaint appears with the "skill raising" portions that occur during regular parts of the game. It's not really made clear (except in obvious cases) what skills will help most with a specific bird. As with the first negative, this turns the game into "trial and error", something I don't enjoy in any game.
Taken as a complete package, Hatoful Boyfriend is an amazing game, even if you're not a fan of the typical "Japanese dating sim" genre. A memorable and diverse cast of characters, deep storylines filled with comedy, tragedy, and romance, and the environment that the game creates are good enough reasons to overlook the "trial and error" portions that initially slow it down. All in all, Hatoful Boyfriend is a tremendous game, and deserves to be given a chance, if only for its sheer creativity and the opportunity to drown the world in pudding.

I never thought I'd be reviewing a bird dating simulator, let alone this positively, but here I am, so if that doesn't say enough already...
I bought this game a few months back on a whim while it was 40% off. I started off not expecting too much, since visual novels aren't my thing and I figured it was pretty much a just dating sim parody filled with bird puns. It is a dating sim parody filled with bird puns, but it's also much more.
See, visual novels aren't my type because I'd rather have storyline mixed with more effort on my part than just clicking, but I think this was done really well. Your choices throughout the game are quite obvious as to whatever bird the decision would earn you favor with. However, the storyline is fleshed out. Like, really fleshed out. I don't have experience with dating sims but I can tell this one has a lot more going on than usual, despite the obvious fact that they're birds.
So the storyline seems pretty out there at first. You're an unquestioned human girl at a school for birds, in a city of birds. You can date the birds. Or, if you don't court a bird properly, you'll
. Anyway, as you date these birds, you get a story out of each of them. Your sickly best friend, the stand-offish french transfer student, the eccentric track captain, the narcoleptic teacher, the quiet freshman, the flirty upperclassman, the bone-chilling school doctor, and the bizarre fallen angel are all choices where you can find love. However, once you've gone through the game a few times, the start screen informs you that instead of playing the regular game, you can choose to fulfill a promise from long ago... which pulls you into the ending that ties all their stories together
. If you want to know more than that, seriously, just buy it. It should be noted that I started the endgame expecting it to be 15 minutes long then found myself finishing it at 3 AM that night.
The mechanics are simple, gameplay surprisingly isn't too slow for my tastes, and even though parts can feel slow after you've played dating a few birds, you can fast forward through parts.
If you have the time and the patience for something slow going but interesting, please do yourself a favor and buy this game. Do it for the birds.

Ocean City Racing is an indie racing game, made in the UT3 engine.
The game feels and plays like an old arcade race game made by SEGA. Whenever you crash into other cars or buildings you car stays intact. There are 3 game modes: Time-Trial, Race Mode and Free Roam. Obviously, Time-Trial is to beat your own times, Race-Mode is just racing opponents and Free-roam is driving around an 'open world' city.
The graphics are not that special these days but they are not that bad. The city looks OK but I doubt anyone plays this game for sight-seeing.
Although not my taste, the music is pretty good however, totally not suited for a race game, in my opinion.

First, this game isn't nearly as bad as the critics would have you believe. The shooting is very competent and the structure of the game, while not unique, is pretty cool. It basically feels structure-wise at least, like the first Arkham game. An open world that opens up more as you gain new equipment and upgrades, more or less Metroid style. I love the aspect of being a miner essentially in a giant mech, setting forth into undiscovered and dangerous territory on a frozen desolate planet. This scenario lends itself to a great atmosphere.
Secondly, This game is literally nothing like the previous 2 entries, unfortunately. Lost Planet 2 is probably the most unappreciated game of all time, and is easily one of the best co-op experiences ever. So, obviously fans of the series will be turned off by Lost Planet 3 at least initially.
While not much of a Lost Planet game mechanically, LP3 stands on its own as worthwhile experience in my opinion. The music from Jack Wall (Mass Effect 3) is outstanding and haunting. The core gameplay is good enough to not get repetive or frustrating in the some odd- 15 hour playtime. Taking out big monsters on an ice planet will always be rad, so its got that going for it. The story is actually really good, which is a first for the series, and it basically tells the story of how EDN III came to be the way we find it in Lost Planet and Lost Planet 2.
All that said, Lost Planet has gotten a bum wrap by critics in its last two entries. There is plenty here to enjoy, and if you like scifi or third person shooters, you will be suprised by how much you enjoy this game. I know I was. 7.5/10

I'm a fan of MMORPGs and I tried RIft since open beta when it was monthly subscription based.
Really enjoyed a lot of its features and built-in macro-generation and video recording are very good and shows consideration for the users.
After I quit due to repetitive boredom of dailies and rifts at end game (the same reason I quit many other MMORPGs for), I found Rift again on Steam. Now it's Free with microtransactions.
I personally don't mind microtransactions, but even with or without the in-game-market, Rift still deserves a try.

Up until max level the game has plenty to offer.  After max level, if you're not a raiding type there's not a whole lot remaining.  Same as all the other games out there so, really, for F2P (not Pay to Play), it's worth playing through to max level on at least one character, if not more.
Crafting can be a grind and I found nothing useful past level 60 and levelling slows significantly.
Events are well done.  There are plenty of grindy quests, but also some that are just fun.
Story lines are entertaining and I find myself reading rather than clicking through most of them.
Solo is easy.  Duo is fun.  Group I don't really know about - I prefer solo or duo.
Gear is kind of blah.  There's not a lot of variety, though it can be changed up with dyes.
Mentoring is a good system.  You're not boxed in to playing within your level.  At level 70 you can mentor down to level 12 to play with a pal, if you so wish.  This is a boon during the aforementioned events that often require the completed objective net a player experience.  It can be a crux, too, because players tend to overwhelm lower level areas to get through events quickly.  Either way, it's a somewhat unique system that opens the playing field.
Artifacts.  I'm addicted.  I can play the game for hours searching for these little gems.  I once got myself into a seemingly impossible situation in EverQuest (yes, I'm showing my gaming age) because I just Had to see what was way Up There.  Thankfully a kindly higher level ranger came along to rescue me.  He died four times doing so, but still . . . chivalry exists.  I digress . . . artifacts Reward the curious souls for wiggling their way into nooks and crannies and figuring out apparent insurmountable jumps.  I've often had to /stuck but the rewards are greater than the punishment.
Dimensions.  When you have nothing else to do, or if you're the creative sort, dimensions offer a distraction.  There are some über creative players out there.  Every time I think I've figured out something nifty to do in my dimension, I visit someone else's and wander around in awe at their out-of-the-box thinking abilities.  The sky is Literally the limit.  Don't have enough room to build out?  Build Up.  And up.  And up and up and up up up.   Okay, the sky isn't literally the limit, because there is a cap on the number of items a player can place; however, that can be expanded several times to allow for more building genius to occur.
I play for the artifacts.  I'll be honest.  :D

Evolve is a unique take on the FPS genre pitting 1 player as a monster versus 4 players as hunters, where both sides rely on both wits and their unique strengths to win the game.
The gameplay itself is an interesting idea, where instead of balanced teams one player is a monster while the other 4 are hunters tracking said monster. In a single round the main goal for the monster is to get stronger by eating the wildlife, while trying to evade the hunters until the monster is ready to fight, at which point he must either kill all of the hunters or a power relay that every map has. As for the hunters they must track and kill the monster, or should they fail to do so at least survive for long enough. This creates a dynamic that the hunters work to try and find and capture, then kill the monster so he can't get too strong, but the monster can use a variety of tricks to avoid this, or should he choose attempt a classic brute force method. This leads to 2 main parts of the round: The hunt and the fights. While hunting the monster must use his surroundings to elude the hunters while the hunters must use the environment to prevent the monster from escaping, and it ends up being a battle of wits. Fights on the other hand involve the monster trying to use his superior strength take down players as effectively as possible while the players rely on their teamwork and versatility to survive. Whichever side you are one you end up making full use of your kits, and this leads to engaging gameplay through the entire round.
Hunters get an enjoyable thrill of tracking and hunting strong prey while the monster gets a statisfying feeling of being an unstoppable... well... monster.
The atmosphere is well suited to this idea as well. While a little on the gray side, the maps are designed around a certain theme that inspires a wild chase feel. Through the varying weather patterns (that do reduce visibility, something players can make use of), to varying terrain such as caves and forests, there is a beautiful amount of eye candy that doesn't detract from the gameplay all the same.
Characters are also bursting with personality. You get a nice taste of who they are through their combat interactions to their pre-game banter (Hunters need to wait about 30 seconds for the monster to lead, so instead of leaving it on a screen the characters will have a bit of a talk). Even the animations help bring each character (and monster) completely to life. I never really felt that a character seemed out of place, or that a monster moved in a way I wouldn't expect.
In addition, the variety of characters lead to a lot of different concepts on how to play without leaving their desired role. Best excample is Lazarus, a medic who's main gimmick is to let his team die then just revive them, as opposed to the standard idea of "just heal". Meanwhile a medic such as Val is what you would expect from a medic, and Slim focuses on dealing damage and being in the thick of the fight to do his job best. It's the only game I've seen people fight over supportive roles.
With the perk system you can even refine your character to your play style. Like more damage? Here! Wanna focus on staying light on your feet? Here! A little flawed, granted, but it helps boost your chosen gameplay style.
In terms of main issues one I can think of is it is NOT new player friendly. New players get less selection, but still get paired up with other people who are higher level. This means that while you may have no perks unlocked yet, you may be facing a monster (or hunters) with these, and as such you are thrown into a distinct advantage beyond your possible skill level. In addition the game itself has a high difficulty floor, and you will likely find yourself losing round after round at first. This is mostly due to the matchmaker being flawed, and pairing people up with vary different skill levels.
This can also lead to weird issues where you'll be facing players much better or worse than you forcing a one-sided fight that was doomed from the start.
TRS also seems to have a bit of a bad issue with not testing/announcing things before rolling out the patches. One example was a recent update that raised the price on things in the shop. Myself, I don't mind, since I had nothing saved up so I didn't lose much, and you can still earn a fair amount of Keys (the in-game currency you earn from playing. If you play for even a couple hours a day you can earn around 3-4k, and most unlocks are around 10k now) but for players who were holding onto some for when a new character came out it did hurt them since they lost their value. Forewarning on things like this would be nice, since it isn't the first time they've done it either.
However if you can tolerate those couple issues then the game is a beautiful twist on the FPS genre that I would definitely recommend. It's free so you have almost nothing to lose, and if you can get some friends (either to lay the smack-down as a monster or to join up in a hunt with), I would say give it a shot!

If H.P Lovecraft, the heavy metal of the nineties, and the intense atmosphere of Doom was smashed, reconstructed, smashed again and reconstructed again into a glorious product, it would be Quake.
Unlike Doom, where it pitches at you various demons from hell, Quake throws in horrific eldritch beings in their place. We still have the loveable zombies from the last game, but instead of Cacodemons we have Scrags. Instead of Revenants, we have Vores. Instead of Cyberdemons, we have Shamblers.
The weapons have changed as well. Instead of fists, you get a bloody axe that is more useless than trying to cut down a tree with a herring. The Pistol has been ditched for a Shotgun, which is unfortunatly not as fun to use as Doom's shotgun. The Super Shotgun returns as well, and it somewhat becomes a mainstay later on ingame. Instead of a chaingun, we get the Nailgun and Super Nailgun, which are FUN AS HELL TO USE. One new addition is the Grenade Launcher (Which bizarrely shares the Rocket Launchers ammo pool), which can take out groups of bad guys in no time. Theres not much to talk about the Rocket Launcher, aside from its amazing "Rocket Jump" capability. Finally, we have the Thunderbolt. Think of this tool as the games version to a Plasma Gun/BFG 9000 combo. It does not have much ammo, so use it in the most lethal of situations.
The game has such a forboding atmosphere, at times I felt as though something would actually sneak up on me and rip me to shreds. Combine it with the soundtrack made by Nine Inch Nails, and this game will make you feel more nihilistic than the ending of the first F.E.A.R.

I've been watching this game for awhile and was pretty hesitant to get on board with all the issues coming up in reviews. Last week I bought this game on sale and Im really glad I did. Overall considering early access I'd give it a 7/10 being worth the purchase on sale, maybe not at full price. That said, the potential for this game is huge, see the full review below. Note: I've only played single player. Havent tried multi.
Gameplay:
There are a few awkward things about gameplay that simply take getting used to. For one, the game uses F as the interaction key. After years of using E for interactions, F feels odd. Not a huge deal, just takes getting used to. Another thing is running. Running is interrupted by stepping off a rock that is slightly too tall while
Again not a huge deal but it feels clunky. Once you get used to it you'll be running around no problem only running into the issue when going downhill mostly. Other than that gameplay wise the game feels pretty good. Survival feels good and could be made a little more difficult (maybe it is on harder difficulties, only played on normal) but there is enough there that you have to think about it without it bogging you down much. In all 8/10 gameplay. Imo only minor tweaks needed.
Skill Tree/Leveling/Experience:
The system works though could use some minor tweaks. One thing is that getting combat and science experience is tedious compared to engineering. For science you can just farm gas, empty tanks, rinse repeat. Crafting mostly provides engineering xp but some items provide science. It would be nice for a tooltip to tell you what kind of xp you get from crafting an item. Combat experience is easy to get but enemies are so easy to avoid for the most part that it feels like you could just avoid that whole portion of the game. More on combat ahead. I havent had any of the issues with skills being unlearned after rejoining. 6/10. The system is there but needs more work for sure so that the grind is still there with a little variety in how you gain xp to round out science and combat.
Combat: When you do decide to engage in combat, each enemy type engages in different ways. At first it was fun to analyse the pattern to kill each mob but after 5 or so enemies you get it and its the same dance. Guns are underpowered and leave you using melee in most instances to save resources/time. On top of that the best melee weapon I have is made from the engineering skill tree, not the combat skill tree. Now to be fair I havent researched all the melee weapons in the combat tree but, I feel no need to. Oh, the Gun vehicle dual laser turret does less damage than my engineering melee weapon. Definitely needs some balancing and attention to this area of the game. Lastly, enemies are so easy to disengage or dodge and you can largely avoid combat all together if you so choose. 4/10.
Building:
This seems the most polished aspect of the game and my main draw. At first you'll flounder around figuring out certain aspects of building like the multi-tool and why you cant build a fabricator. Once you figure it out you just have to play your base accordingly. Really the parts are all here and the system works well. All it needs is some sort of tutorial to tell you what is going on. 9/10
Crafting:
Honestly, crafting itself feels right and balanced. I give it a 8/10. Now for my wish. Machines should be able to be placed inside or have a building dedicated to their use. Maybe a laboratory? Wait thats for making cars only. Eh, its kind of petty and you can get around this by designing your base properly but you'll still need to go through the airlock sequence each time you want to use the fabricator. Just let me put them all in one room or at least don't make me do the airlock every time.
Graphics:

Hidden Folks is a cute and playful game about finding tiny objects in gigantic maps full of things you can interact with. It's like Where's Waldo, but everything is moving, everything has to be searched, everything is chaotic and the maps can get really, REALLY huge and so finding that one tiny garden fork can take a whole lot of time.
I think I would've sold my soul to play something like this when I was younger. I loved looking for small details and so point and click was my favourite genre, but this game takes small details to a level so high that it can only be compared to finding a needle in a haystack - a really fun haystack, that is. You're given the map, you're given the targets, and each one has a small clue for their whereabouts. This is usually some sort of riddle or hint. And then all that remains is a whole bunch of opening windows, searching the crowds, looking in tents, pressing the buttons and even solving cool puzzles all to find a target that's just one of many. The 4 worlds with multiple maps in each will offer a whole ton of fun for a few hours, and even if that seems short for you, they're still adding more!
The minimalistic graphics are pretty charming and actually a great design choice as it adds more challenge to finding the targets. The full gorgeousness of this game can only be appreciated if you zoom out far enough, and then you stop noticing the hand-drawn sprites and start noticing the great level design. Every level seems like organized chaos if you look from far enough - it's sort of divided in sections, but they're spread out and overlapping in a way that it doesn't seem to systemized. If there'd be a whole lot of tents in a huge square and a square forest next to it, that'd be bland, but the game puts a few tents outside of their dedicated area, adds in different things between those tents, clearings in the forest, and a whole bunch of more chaos that makes finding targets that much more interesting. And also, there's an incredible amount of sprites and small details everywhere, making it far less boring. Adding to that, it seems that they've thought of everything - for example, I've seen games that depict suburbs as boring rows of houses. This game had a suburb and sure, some houses were kind of bland, but there was a pool party, a haunted house, a house where somebody was moving in, a yard sale, a house where people were playing golf, a supermarket and much, much more. This helped them make levels that were unbelievably large, but at the same time, they never felt boring and they never seemed like the same thing repeating over and over again.
If you couldn't tell from the trailer, the sound design consists solely of sound effects done with voice acting only, which adds a very playful and childlike feel to the game. The sound was also used cleverly as a tool that can sometimes be used to find targets. For example, if you have to find a monkey in a lab, you can move around until you hear monkey sounds, which indicate that it's not far away. I understand why some people would find the sound effects annoying, but I personally thought they managed to fit in with the atmosphere just fine.
For fellow completionists - this game gives you achievements for finding all targets. It doesn't take too long and it's extremely fun to do.
Overall, I think the game's rating speaks for itself, and, even though it's very short, it definitely is very good, and even if a few (but very fun) hours of gameplay seem like not enough, you should at least get this on sale - you won't regret it.

I've enjoyed being a part of the development of this game via early access. While it still has a few kinks to work out - the building system can be maddeningly difficult to get pieces and buildings to "click" properly, space travel is still a bit glitchy and there's only a single, frozen moon to explore -  and its story is still in the embryonic stage, there is the beating heart of a good game here. The developers seem to interact with the player base, and respond in-game to the community, which is always to be applauded.
If I had to describe it in a short phrase, I'd say, "Survival strategy." You make decisions about prioritizing different resources, skills and structures that will shape your game throughout. There is some "grinding," but not a great deal of it, and there is some combat, but it isn't the major focus of the game.
The graphics are very good, and the sound design works well. The controls make sense, and the menus function efficiently.
As the game develops and more areas are open to exploration, and more fauna and story elements are added, this could be the richest and deepest of the "stranded sci-fi" genre.

This is a hard one to be objective. It gets praise from pretty much everyone. And this game deserves all of it. The ideas of not only making a gun that's unique and fun to use, but to use it to make mindblowing puzzles that tests your creativity, is amazing.
The graphics still hold up and has nice details, the sound is spot on and the characters all have great lines that make you crack a smile. There isn't too many sound tracks, but I enjoyed the ones that it had. The controls are pretty much half-life 2, and that's a good thing(but no ladders so you won't fall, ZING!). The story while minimal at first, picks up fast in the last 30 mins and becomes one of the stronger points of the game.
The main draw is, of course, the portals, and for good reason. You create one, then another and what goes in comes out the other side no matter the distance between them. This also includes objects and enemy turrents. You also gain momentum the more you fall and using different angles can help you achieve insane distance from jumping and falling. It's fun just to use this gun, but add some great puzzles and using everything the gun can do to the fullest and you have a game that's incredibly satisfiying to play.
If there's a weakness, it's the length. It's very short, and while this helps the pacing of the game, there's no way around the fact you could do everything the game has to offer in about 7-8 hours (this includes the challenge's and advanced maps you unlock).
But I don't feel my money was wasted. It was a very memorable experince. And I couldn't recommend it enough.
overall  9.5/10

I did not enjoy them anywhere near as much as other people did, and lost interest with them quickly. That being said, there are a few fundamental, concept based, canons from the series that have carried over here. Aside from that this is a drastic departure, and an incredibly good one so far.
The game takes it's time developing the characters and plot, which (so far) are incredibly good. The game play is solid. There is the occassional odd camera angle that can be a pain in the butt, nothing worth getting frustrated over. All-in-all this is an amazingly solid and fun game.  As other people have mentioned you can listen to your own music in your RIG which makes mech-smashing akrids all the more enjoyable. I've found the easiest way to do this to be creating platlists in Windows Media Player. They will automatically show up in your RIG's menu. They need to be mp3, so if the music you want to listen to isn't in that format use a free tool like Freemake Audio Converter.
As a gamer who thoroughly enjoys plot, character development and doesn't mind a bit of grind if it fits the theme and tone of the story I recommend this.
If you are a fan of a company rehashing the same game again and again, but making it shinier with a few new features you'll probably want to pass.
On a side note, there are times when the keyboard layout is not great. A decent gaming mouse and remapping some of the keys easily rectified this. For instance, picking up items is [P], switched it to mouse5.

Well what can I say,
The enjoyment I got out of Lost Planet 3 came out of nowhere. I played the first two when they were released and the experiences I had with them led me to not bother with the 3rd for the longest time, boy was I wrong.
One of things I look for in a game is a great story wrapped in a solid campaign mode, also being huge science fiction dork, this game had everything I needed. It's an absolutely solid story through and through, plenty of twists and plenty of exposition throughout. So many things that bug me about most science fiction stories where outright done away with within the first hour or so, Jim Payton is perhaps the most grounded and realistic protagonist i've ever seen in a game. He asked every question I would have asked and done everything I would have done in the same (albeit totally ludicrous) situation. The voice acting and dialogue where outstanding, full of really great writing and genuinely likeable characters. The story never dragged, it never slogged and there was just enough to keep it going at a great pace, highly enjoyable right up to the credits.
The gameplay is doled out through perfectly serviceable a solid 3rd person cover based shooting and giant mech sections. Running around on foot can be a little slow outdoors, but you'll be busy soon enough fighting off hordes of giant bugs and loving every minute of it. The combat on foot feels tight, all the weapons maybe your standard game fare but they all pack a hell of a punch, they handle great and upgrades keep things nice and dynamic. The mech sections are fun for whole other reasons, it just feels so cool to wander round the frozen tundra smashing and drilling your way to success. The game is almost half exterminator half space drilling simulator and I loved all of it. The world itself is a mash up between Hoth (some of those corridors look awfully familiar) and the Ishimura from dead space, each sections bring their own challenges to combat and traversal, exploring was a blast.
Lastly the graphics, boy is this a pretty looking game. Maybe not the most technically advanced but the animation was top notch, lip syncing and cut scene work superb and the whole thing just had a real science fiction feel to it. Seeing that stark orange color against the cold blue background just made me happy.  Framerate was flawless, never dropped and never stuttered, audio mix was great. Really have nothing to bad to say about it. Game time clocked in at about 11 hours with a few side quests still left to do. Unfortunately I haven't gotten round to the multiplayer yet, I remember the other two being a blast so I'll be interested to see what happens with it.
So at current, for a few quid you can have one of the most grounded and entertaining  science fiction stories in years, and I highly recommend anyone who likes a good space age drama to give it a go!

This is one of my favorite games I have played over the last few years. It strays away from the magic that made LP1 and 2 so unique and instead goes for the more standard American-ized third person action style. But really what most people don't realize is that a large part of what made 1 and 2 so independent from other third person action shooters was simply their unique presentation style. They had a distinct Japanese action game presentation style. I think that this is still undoubtedly a LP game, and the only real thing I miss is that in this game it is just you and in the other games you could work with a squad. Not that that is a big loss or anything considering how ♥♥♥♥ing totally stupid your squad was in those games, especially LP2, but nonetheless it still makes this game feel more lonely. But that is the point with this one. You are supposed to feel lonely. You are one of the few people on the planet that you are on who are there to extract resources and study bugs. You work alone and you go out on missions alone with only your mech, some cockpit music, and occasional video messages you receive from your wife back home. Those are a nice touch because they are very well acted and voiced and you get the feeling that your guy is really homesick and that they miss each other dearly and he can't wait to get back to her. I would be homesick too if I was on another planet and a hot piece of tail like that was waiting for me back on earth. I would constantly need to be detained from trying to sneak into the escape pod room and blast back to earth d-ck first.
The game's biggest problem for me was how short it is. It took me about 10 hours or less to beat it and it feels like less than that. I have more hours than that in it because over time I had to reinstall my OS a couple of times and the game only saves locally, meaning you might want to back up your save files with a program like Game Save Manager if you don't plan on playing through it quickly.
The game engine performs flawlessly and the combat is some of the most satisfying AAA grade that I have seen in a long time. The game runs flawlessly smooth at 60fps which I am thankful for because most developers are too stupid to figure out how to program games to run smoothly and most games that come out nowadays run horribly or are just flat out horrible ports.
The graphics are great. Everything looks good from enemies to character models, to effects and level/area design. The sounds are great, the weapons pretty standard but fun and satisfying to use and really pack a punch. I do really want another LP2 styled game, but I have to say that this one is my fav in the series because it is just so much more technically smooth than both of the first two games combined. I gave MP a try also and it was pretty cool, but nowadays it is dead and you will never find a match online.
8/10 Gameplay
9/10 Sounds/Music
5/10 Length
8/10 Overall. Blastin' back to earth d1ck first!

Wasted Potential.
This is the main thing that comes to mind when thinking about The Bureau. It's really hard to recommend this game because of all the mistakes made in its design. It still however can be enjoyable so I would say it's worth getting on a sale but at least 50%.
Some highlits:
- The game clearly tries to be like Mass Effect but fails in its main aspect - meaningful choices, or really just choices at all. Most of the time you really don't think like you're choosing anything at all, the game just plays itself out and you're taken along for a ride.
- The story isn't bad but feels like it's been written by an absolute xenofobe or is intentionally making all '60s Americans look like ones. Some characters are actually borderline fascist. There is not one likeable human here.
- Oh so many issues with combat. The AI is horrible, you will often find your squadmates setting themselves up for crossfire or staing way behind to get overrun and constant micromanaging is neither very helpful nor pleasant. The ammo placement is odd, you will always have plenty when you don't need it but you will feel a lack of it quite a few times, especially in the final mission. Ability aiming 'thingy' tends to get blocked on terrain even though most of them are executed by throwing something in a curve and the weirdest part is that you sometimes have to virtually walk a flight of stairs with it. There are some viewing angle issues at times, one is that you can't look straight up and it can get frustrating when fighting flying enemies.
You can get used to all of this and in general the game is rather ok, it's just you can clearly see why there won't be another one like it in the X-Com series.

A long, long time ago, before XCOM: Enemy Unknown, there was talk of a First Person Shooter set in the XCOM universe, with the XCOM name. This talk, however, was mostly mixed. Fans of the series were angered that ANOTHER classic strategy game was going to be turned into a First Person Shooter, while others thought it looked interesting. Since I had never played an XCOM game up to that point, I fell in with the latter, and was interested in what a Tactical FPS could offer if it had more strategy elements in it. Then came the day where all the XCOM fans rejoyced as 2K revealed XCOM: Enemy Unknown, and there was no word on the promised FPS. Then, out of the sudden, they revealed the old XCOM FPS again, under a new name, and style. This intrigued me, even after having played a demo for the excellent Enemy Unknown, and I was curious about their changes, though, I never bought into it until a friend gifted me a bundle with Enemy Unknown and The Bureau... and, even then, it was still in my Library for a long, long time without being played.
This all changed the other day, when I installed it, booted it up, and began playing, having heard nothing about it, other than it's mixed reception.
The way the game began was interesting. The very first thing I noticed was the admireable art style and graphics, which, despite me having to lower later due to me having a quite low-end gaming PC, look pretty good. Then, I started playing. The first thing to note about The Bureau is that it's not a FPS, but, rather a TPS (third-person shooter), that controls quite well on PC with K+M. As for story, I was surprised that this had a story at all, though, not a very original one. The game also surprised me with a dialogue system similar to that of Mass Effect, though this has almost no reason for having this system, as the only real dialogue options are the typical questions that no real human being would actually ask, that lead to typical expostion, though, gracefully, there is an option to skip all these.
As for the supposed strategy... there isn't much, other than hitting a button, clicking a few times, then finally, hit another button. If you haven't already guessed, the strategy here is as shallow as it can get. However, not only is the strategy shallow, but the gunplay is, too. Hitting enemies starts out feeling well, but 10 minutes in, it gets very tiresome, and, since really not much happens in this game to begin with, you fight ALLOT of enemies.
Playing The Bureau makes me feel sad. I know at one point, this game had great promise, and, despite having a nice setup, decent graphics, and acceptable K+M controls for a TPS, I can't help but feel the shallowness of the strategy, the weak gunplay, unneeded dialouge trees, and overabundance of enemies really weaken any sort of promise not even an hour into playing. Whether I will finish this game to do a proper review is beyond me, because, as it stands, I don't even want to do that.

This is the best of all walking simulators. It only allows you to walk up, down, left and right, but the setting is so wonderful that this flaw in a otherwise completely realistic walking simulator is quickly forgotten.
A Bird Story, is a story about a bird, and a boy, and it is deeply emotional, it succeeded in making me go from laughing to crying and back to laughing in a few minutes. It has some amazing references to game and popular culture that are used in a way that fits Kan Gao's style perfectly.
There is a trend going on in games journalism claiming that "games should aspire to fulfill their artistic potential" (never mind that the main purpose of games is entertainment, regardless of whether it is seen as art). Yet these same journalists fail to give games like To The Moon and A Bird Story the attention (and ratings) they deserve ... while giving Gone Home perfect 10's ... something seems wrong.
The game is not as good as To The Moon, and it does not claim to be. It is a very different game, but it is still beautiful, and certainly worth the 4£ I paid.

Quake can probably be best describe as the peculiar case of taking Lovecraft, Heavy metal, and guns galore and mixing it with its own touch of Nine Inch Nail ambiance. I'm no Nine Inch Nail fan but even I can appeciate a good mind♥♥♥♥ that is the soundtrack to this game. However, perhaps that’s what stands out most about Quake… is The Lovecraft worship. No, were not talking about the sorry excuse of a Elric Rip-off style worship imbedded into the Witcher franchise, were talking about a disturbing reimaging of the idea of twisted. A twisted that crawls up your spine and pulls it out while at last laughing in your face spitting your own blood back into your eyes. Yeah a cruel sight, but I would be damned if it didn’t hit the mark and make me ask for seconds. Quake is no different. It doesn’t apologize, it doesn’t hold your hand, and it sure as hell doesn’t slow down so you can duck behind cover and whimper like a little♥♥♥♥♥♥as you wait for the guillotine to chop your sorry♥♥♥♥♥in two. You shouldn't be ducking to save your life you should be blowing your enemies into pieces to save your life. In a time where Iron sights where but a distant idea, and quick action events were nothing more than a way of describing your sex life Quake stood the test of time as a master of its craft. It’s FPS at its best, with no compromises and no Bull$*&#. You want filler, well take that crap back to anime and give it a resounding middle finger while your at it because that doesn’t exist here. This is pure mayhem and death like never before all in its own twisted world to boot. It's not here to pour out the horrors of war or to make you feel for someone its here to blast you away like a good Bolt Thrower riff. I didn't ask for a melodrama I asked for a damn game, and Quake gave that and more.
To say that this is a doom clone would be a little bit of wrong misrepresentation of what is otherwise a ground breaking game in not just the FPS genre but in 3D gaming at large. I’m not here to give a history lesson but to be frank with you, this game deserves more than just praise. Quake expanded the graph from being purely horizontal to being horizontal, vertical and misdirectional (if ever that was a word) without taking a second to stop and say “well my works done here lets hit the can…”. Yeah, enjoyed the most recent entry in the Doom series (Doom 4) then you can thank Quake (and Id software who HELPED make the recent DOOM) for making what is practically an identical experience. Let’s be honest, Doom needed a little Quake to take it out of its primordial roots. No shame in what Doom started as but a facelift didn’t hurt this Hollywood failure from getting a deserving reboot.
In short, Quake is to FPS what Judas Priest is to metal. It’s the ♥♥♥♥ing embodiment of FPS at its best. I couldn’t recommend this game more. Between the twisted creatures, the atmospheric environment, and a soundtrack that even Penderecki would smile in glee and lube up for... this game was FPS heaven, before cliché after anime level cliché took over the industry and Metal Gear Solid was praised as the second coming of gamer christ we had Quake. Praise the high fathers of whatever mad studio (Id studio) had the balls to do what most couldn't, make a great FPS!
Sadly, we have yet to get a proper sequel to this game, and it doesn’t look promising in the future. But hell, it doesn’t stop you from going and getting this damn game. If I have any criticism of the steam version it would be simple… “Where the hell is the soundtrack?” I mean I understand copyrights a ♥♥♥♥♥, but how hard is it really to get such a thing done, I shouldn’t feel the need to make it an addition to the game but such is life. If it isn’t already obvious get this game… Better yet, get the real version of this game and enjoy you what FPS could, and should be.

Quake was id Software's follow-up to DOOM, so right off the bat it had a lot to live up to. At the same time, Duke Nukem 3D had come out just a few months earlier, and had raised the shooter bar by quite a lot (according to people at the time). With these external circumstances, Quake under a lot of pressure to perform; luckily, at the time it was seen as amazing and technically astounding (although divisive). Having completed it, I'd say it's pretty damn good, better than Duke Nukem 3D but not as good as DOOM.
Quake is, tonally and aesthetically, very different from DOOM in some ways and very similar in others. Like DOOM, it's about fighting horrible nightmare creatures in their strange realm; however, while DOOM is basically the tonal equivalent of someone covered in tattoos and piercings screaming in your ear for five hours, Quake is more grim, gloomy, and gothic. It works very hard to be haunting and unsettling, and pulls it off pretty well, with an off-kilter, disjointed soundtrack of wailing guitars and ambient noise (that you have to install a patch to have on the Steam version, which is a bit of a pisser), a grimy, subdued color palette (it's all brown and gray), plenty of shadows, and lots of Lovecraftian elements. It's all very surreal, and I like it a lot.
This was the first fully 3D FPS (thanks to those wizards at id), and it does a very good job of introducing this new mechanic. There's a lot of verticality in the level design that could only have happened with 3D, and the models are all pretty well-done. Unfortunately, a few things are pretty simplistic because of the limitations of 3D (you can't have DOOM's spectacular gore, basically), but it works out well enough nonetheless.
The shooting is excellent. There are 5 weapons, three of which have upgraded versions that you can also collect (and then never use the basic ones again) and each has its niche in gameplay. More importantly, they all feel great to use, which is mostly a function of the sound design, which is fantastic. The monsters are more varied, and they're all pretty fun to fight (except for the Ogres, because Jesus ♥♥♥♥in' Christ). The game also showers you with ammo, because most of the monsters take plenty of hits (I think I ran out of shotgun shells only twice). It's all very fast-paced and flow-y and everything I want out of a 90s FPS, gameplay-wise.
The level design is not as great. It's got the aforementioned verticality, but it's also about as screwy and hard to figure out as 90s FPS level design gets, which is not helped by the bizarre absence of a map (I guess they couldn't figure out how to generate one in 3D, where levels can overlap each other). The episode structure also returns, which is dumb, especially considering they realized that they could drop it back in DOOM 2. I'm guessing the levels are designed as such to pad out the game time, which is otherwise not that long. There're only 27 of them, each completable in about 5 minutes if you know what you're doing.
There's no use button for some reason. You just stand next to things you want activated, although you occasionally shoot them instead.
The bosses are pretty easy. They're both puzzles, not shootouts, and one of the puzzles is incredibly easy do while the other is easy to accomplish but ridiculously unintuitive to figure out.
All the text is really tiny.
Overall, Quake's a pretty damn good game. It hasn't aged perfectly (anti-aliasing the textures would be a good start), but it's still very well-designed and a barrel of fun. Also, it's been astonishingly influential; pretty much every FPS from the past 20 years owes something to Quake, more so than even DOOM. For all of these reasons, I recommend it.
