I noticed this game in my backlog and figured I'd give it a go. I love driving aimlessly in an open world! So I start it up and it sorta chugs through the loading screen, on this rather powerful gaming PC. So I check the graphics options and... there's really just resolution. Now, I've used the Unreal Engine before, there are PLENTY of options built in that could be easily listed there, but okay, I turn down the resolution and try the free roaming.
I start on-foot, walking to the nearest car. Quite slowly, but a neat touch, at least, and I can jump slightly. Get in, start driving around. Hit a pedestrian, and... they stand stock-still while my car thuds to a stop like it hit a brick wall. Okay, then. Drive away, go to head to the bridge in the distance. Try to drift, brakes make steering no longer a thing. Okay, then. Try to drift with the e-brake, practically instant stop. Okay, then. Bump into the car in front of me and it cartoonishly soars over my hood. That's pretty neat, actually! Probably not right, but very entertaining. Hit the next car, thud to a stop. A Bird Story, is a story about a bird, and a boy, and it is deeply emotional, it succeeded in making me go from laughing to crying and back to laughing in a few minutes. It has some amazing references to game and popular culture that are used in a way that fits Kan Gao's style perfectly.
There is a trend going on in games journalism claiming that "games should aspire to fulfill their artistic potential" (never mind that the main purpose of games is entertainment, regardless of whether it is seen as art). Yet these same journalists fail to give games like To The Moon and A Bird Story the attention (and ratings) they deserve ... while giving Gone Home perfect 10's ... something seems wrong.
The game is not as good as To The Moon, and it does not claim to be. It is a very different game, but it is still beautiful, and certainly worth the 4£ I paid.

A Bird Story is really at the fringe of what constitutes a video game, as, here, interactions are neither providing you with any kind of choice or even the illusion of freedom, nor ask of you some sort of performance, they are only there to reinforce the identification, to make you enact the story of the character. This approach is not without merit, but it might have been better served by a slightly shorter or better paced game.
That said, A Bird Story is without a doubt a pure product of video game love, in all its 16-bit pixel art glory, its narration through digital puppetry, and its skewing of video game codes.
Sanding out: the originality (at least for a game) and the confident delivery of its wordless story, the fascinating use of space as a dreamscape and the beauty of some of the painted backgrounds.

I have searched high and low for an easy to use game making app that doesn't require scripting knowledge.  I have found a few but none is as much fun as Platfinity.
Platformers is not a genre I have much experience of either as a player or a developer. However, once I started making games with this app I started to appreciate the appeal. Within minutes I produced a very simple level and I was surprised at how much fun it was to play - I felt my adrenaline pumping and thought "Wow! I created that!".
Making a game is super easy. Everything is drag-and-drop. You make the environment by placing tiles and objects. There are Normal Tiles (which the player walks on or jumps over) and Special Tiles (which have diferent properties allowing for a range of different functions). For nice visuals, there are forground and background tiles. There are also platforms (of course) which can be set to move vertically, horizontally (speed customisable), diagonally or motionless.  You can also set them to be either sticky, icy, bouncy, fallaway, disappearing, or conveyor.  Objects are basically the enemy. They can be set to move in either direction or rotate and you can set the speed.  If the player collides with them he goes back to the previous checkpoint.
There is a nice built-in painting tool (very reminiscent of an older version of MS Paint) which you can use to edit objects and tiles. You can also import your own just by clicking a button. Tiles and objects are arranged in standard sizes. At first this might seem restrictive but you can make your tile or object effectively any size up to 260X260 because transparent areas won't cause a collision.  There are plenty of stock graphics to get you started and ample slots to import your own.
You can export your games as standalone.  They can be multi level but this involves a bit of manual copying of files. This procedure is well documented and fairly easy but I hope the app will be updated to automatically export your multi level games with all necessary files and no fiddling around. If you're planning a huge game with 100 levels beware: there's no facility for the player to save progress. Games are exported for PC only (shame it doesn't support mobile platforms).
You can customise controls and other game settings such as gravity, climb speed, etc. You can also import your own audio (including music).
All that adds to up to enough customisation to make a unique game. However, there are obvious limits. There is no combat, no power ups, no collectables... The player just gets from point A to point B, using platforms and without colliding with hazardous objects. It is gameplay at its most basic.
Overall: A great app, very easy, fun and stable. What it does it does extremely well but it needs more features.

After the pleasure and joy of the first Test Drive Unlimited, and other great open-world racing games, this game, TDU2, just falls completely flat in SO many ways!  Decided to pick it back up off the shelf, after getting bored with Forza Horizon 3's end-game grind, and at least there you can reasonably reach end-game!
First of all, even though the world is open-world and even a bit pretty in its own right, the gameplay is EXTREMELY linear and layered.  You need to acquire specific licenses before you can get the cars requiring those licenses in order to win races to make money which then is used to purchase properties and clothes which are only unlocked once you reach a certain level of exploration, etc.
So, here's where the problem begins, which gets even more complicated given how unstable and buggy this game is (especially if attempting to use something like ENB to try and make the graphics look a bit more reasonable and not quite so dated).  The licenses are the biggest bottleneck... they remind me so much of the Stuntman games and why I completely abhored that entire series and am glad it faded away into the lost and forgotten games of the past as a learning experience on the mistake that it was.
The license tests are so abysmal in the fact that after the initial license tests, they give JUST ENOUGH time to get all the way through from start to finish... meaning you can't over-skid, you can't bump anything, you have to do each test 100% perfect more or less with only perhaps a 1% spacing for even slight error.  Which then each test couples in their own challenges, from a timer, to having to dodge and/or not hit other cars, along with having to navigate barrels/barricades.  Some will have time-penalties for going off the road too much, but others are instant fail... if another car hits you, or you just BARELY graze a barricade/barrel, it's instant failure and having to start back over from scratch.  The instant failure and restart might not be so bad on smaller tests, but when you're in a test with 49+ checkpoints, and you happen to barely graze a barel or a barricade (even when it doesn't look like you do on your screen) due to even a slight hiccup for any reason... you have to start back over from the first checkpoint.  (Also worth noting that each of about 9-18  [the categories with different tiers to each] licenses have 8 test or so each!)
Another huge issue is completely borked physics and handling.  Even with a mod that's supposed to make the handling like TDU1, there's still so much constant fussing with the sliders to try and get the perfect handling for your experience, and it never quite hits the mark.  From vehicle to vehicle it changes... so for one vehicle where you might need steering dampening all the way to the right, for others you might need it in the center, or all the way to the left... then the same applies to the other 5 or so sliders to fine-tune your control... ultimately to deliver one of the biggest cluster-!@#!s in a racing-game to date.
Furthermore another huge issue is the fact the world seems SO empty compared to TDU1... perhaps I'm recalling TDU1 incorrectly, but the world felt more alive with more to do.  There's something like 4 or 5 clothing stores, several car dealerships, Casino, real-estate agencies, safehouses, and other bits... but the fact they seperate them into different categories so only so much shows on the map at a time, along with the fact the maps are huge with having them so far spread out... it sadly has a Just Cause "empty lifeless village" feeling pretty much everywhere.  Becomes even more painful when you hit lvl10 and start going to Hawaii from the airport... you drive through the hugest city area of Hawaii and actually have to drive aimlessly for quite sometime before you find even one point of interest, which is a massive shame!
Was also rather disappointing that they had finally added motorcycles to the game, but was more just for vanity, as (unless I'm completely missing something) there doesn't seem to be anything single-player/offline to do with them... haven't found any way to paint/sticker a motorcycle, no way to improve motorcycle license, no motorcycle races, no motorcycle tuner upgrades... the motorcycles just seem to be there, and for anybody that's a massive enthusiast of motorcycles like I am, it's VERY disappointing!
Then there's the issue that there are SEVERAL cars (as well as the motorcycles) that are locked behind cash-shop purchases (DLC) that require tokens.  Not sure if the website still sells tokens, but luckily I was able to buy the Harley Davidson before the official shutdown.  In game, I seem to have the option to purchase the other motorcycles if I wish, but come across several cars that say they're a DLC purchase and download, yet the source/download appears not to be available... so you get to stare at a car model that you'll never be able to access!  For the DLC content that is availabe, that you have to spend tokens to unlock (which I still have 440 tokens left but am hesitant to use them in fear of there being an error with no support to help with such error), even after you've unlocked them, you still have to have the in-game currency to buy them... which refer to the second paragraph and the massive headache involved in making money.
Then the issue with making in-game currency... there are some collectible challenges that will earn you chump-change, but the only real reasonable way to make money is winning races, which again, there's a gigantic headache/nightmare involved in evolving on that front.
Even the time-sync and patience required might be doable if I was still younger and had a lot more time to invest... problem is, when you work all the time, want to hop in, have a decent chance to make money and buy cars, to find it's a giant cluster-!@#!, it kills off most any real casual gameplay, which is sad coming from me who's usually a die-hard player at most games!
Overall, in an attempt by Atari to upgrade beyond TDU1 and evolve to something better in TDU2, it's sadly just the opposite, much worse.  Which is an even bigger shame considering they completely shutdown TDU1 in order to keep TDU2 up and remaining functional (term used very lightly here!), and even more disappointing when so many fans of Test Drive want to feel like between TDU1 and TDU2, Atari could have had a chance to really learn from mistakes, and make the perfect game in a TDU3, but now that the developers/publishers behind this are no more, that will sadly never happen.
Disclaimer: I'm hard-pressed to have to say all this, especially considering I'm a massive old-school gamer, and the first major racing/driving game I ever played, beyond Turbo for ColecoVision or Pole Position for Atari, was the original Test Drive in all its splendid CGA greatness back in 1987! :(
PS - After having unshelved this game for a total of about 3-5 days, modding it up, and giving it an honest college-try go, I'm already ready to shelf it again, as well as uninstall it to free up the drive-space, while quickly realizing why I've shelved it so many times in the past. -_-
PPS - Other games, like Burnout Paradise, manage to pull off a license-mechanic rather well... whereas in this, licenses are just beating your head against a brick-wall that's covering a titanium-door, only to find the key for that door is locked behind 20 other things you have to tackle first. xD
EDIT: I even tried getting a trainer to freeze timer during license-tests & still found them unbelievably stressful and frustrating just driving through them at a casual pace, not to mention mind-numbingly boring!  Coupled with constant off and on crashes every 10+ minutes (that were there even before the use of a trainer, FYI)!

Its pretty neat for what it is. And what it is IS a very simple, easy to use platform game creation engine.
I think it appeals well to the following people:
1. Retro game enthusiasts
2. Kids
3. Non-programmers who want to make a simple game
4. Indie game hobbyists
Pros:
===
- Fairly priced, $9.99.
- Very easy to use and learn how to use.
- You can import your own sprites and sounds, although sounds are much more limited.
- The standard assets are available within the directory so you can edit or inspect them to determine what file formats are acceptible as well as the pixel sizes for sprites.
- Developer actively seeks feedback, uploads tutorial videos to youtube, and shows interest in updating the software further.
Cons:
====
- As of now, if you touch an enemy or environmental hazard, you go straight back to a checkpoint. So you can't "fight" or "jump and squash" enemies, to my knowledge. I'll edit this if that changes or I'm mistaken.
Conclusion:
========
Whether you're a kid or an adult, you could make a playable level within a couple of hours and easily export and share the executable with others. I think kids would really be into this, but so would adults who are reminiscent of old 8 or 16 bit platformers and want to make a simple recreation of their favorite classic games. I could imagine people who like those brutal platformers such as "I wanna be the guy/boshy" would find this fun to play with. For what it is, its cool.
I've spent under an hour and have figured out how to import my own assets and use the platform editor to the fullest. You really don't need to watch tutorials, but the developer has them if you need them. Its simplicity is its charm.
Edit: I think the negative reviews were probably written by either little kids who shouldn't be reviewing anything on Steam anyways, or people interested in more advanced game development that expected this simple game engine to have the same community support and script compatibilities that more expensive game engines have.

This is basically Mass Effect gameplay with an XCOM story. In summary, it's good but not outstanding.
The premise is that aliens are invading mid-20th century earth, and only a secret (American) government agency can save the day. It's not as well polished or as deep as the Mass Effect games, and there's less emphasis on story and dialog choices. However, the basic gameplay elements are there:
- During missions, you control the leader of a 3-person squad.
- You can enter "Focus Time" to make tactical decisions and issue commands (time isn't totally frozen, but it goes much slower than normal).
- There are various weapon and ability upgrades available for all squad characters.
- Between missions, you can explore the base, talk to people, and do side missions.
The story is surprisingly good and the voice acting is superb. Also, a big plus in my view is the fact that "Easy" mode is actually easy, but still fun at the same time. I know a lot of gamers hate easy games, but it's nice for the less trigger-happy among us who play games to relax. :)
There are quite a number of minor issues in the game, such as glitchy animations and AI. Most of them didn't have a serious gameplay impact for me though, but might be more of a problem if you're playing on higher difficulty modes. The only major problem I had was that the control scheme was fiddly (primarily related to the way you enter/exit cover during a fight).
In conclusion, it's a good game and I would recommend it to any moderate gamer who likes tactical and/or story-driven shooters. More hardcore gamers might be frustrated by it though.

So, I was told across the board
to play this game. I heard it was just plain bad and not worth the time of day. After perusing some of the reviews, it seems like the community agreed with that sentiment.
But, after playing it through from start to finish, it's really not that bad. The gameplay is wanting. The music, art, and graphics are pretty fantastic and although it came out 3 years ago now, it's still pretty buggy. But if you're a fan of the Xcom franchise and really enjoy the care and detail that 2K puts into their games, this title is no exception.
The Good:
+Graphics: For an older title, it looks fantastic! Turn up the settings and enjoy killing sectoids in first-person HD.
+The Story: It really is engaging. Talking to everyone, hearing their story, seeing the damage up close and the twist at the end were all really well done.
+Art/Design: The maps, the weapons and the enemies are very colorful, interesting and well designed. When you're inches away from a Muton you can see the attention to detail on their scuffed armor to their veiny faces.
The Bad:
-Glitchy, glitchy, glitch: I had to do a physxcore.dll fix right out of the gate. The game kept crashing and, after a short read of the forums, I found out that they had an older copy of the .dll instead of the most recent. The result was a keyboard bashing 15 min of trying to figure out why the hell a fresh install was constantly crashing.
-Gameplay: It's not that revolutionary and not that exciting. After a while, you get the drill. Walk in, proceed to the encounter area, set up cover, deploy all of your stuff, focus fire the important targets, and finish the rest. Rinse, repeat.
-Mechanics: If I want to throw a grenade over let’s say, a knee high wall, sometimes the game won't allow you. You'll have to navigate down the steps, around the wall, in order to get a clear path for your grenade. Things like that should have been cleared up in QA/ play testing.
-"Choices": I hate games that give the illusion of choice. You make a lot of "tough" calls, but if they actually effect gameplay is a different story.
Overall:
This game isn't revolutionary. It's not going to make you sit on the edge of your seat and mutter, "Woah..." But, it's not a
game. If you're a fan of Xcom and are looking for a pretty easy game to kill a couple days while you're in-between titles, give this one a play through. The story is interesting, it's really not that difficult, it's has a LOT of Easter egg throwbacks to Xcom: Enemy Unknown and Xcom2 (and the earlier games), the design is phenomenal and unlike other titles the glitches it exhibits are easy to fix.

I would put a neutral rating considering it's a small project made for an academic thesis, but as it's not possible the game gets a negative rating. It's just too rough to be recommendable. With a bit more work the game could be better but at least it's dirt cheap.
Graphics are not too bad, even though quite disappointing for an Unreal Engine 3 game. The models are very low quality, texture work is from the 90s, shaders are very simple and there are many, many bugs (such as the shadows being projected "upwards" on some locations). But some areas are not too bad looking and the lightning can look really good (notably at night).
Sounds are pretty bad. The engine sound curve seems tied to the speed of the car, which causes sound glitches when cornering: the engine alternates between two "gears" and sounds really bad.
Complete lack of actual video settings, and absolutely no audio settings.
Race mode and Time trial mode can be done in a couple of hours, if you manage to never miss checkpoints. As the game doesn't show you anything to tell you the checkpoint is validated, you may end up losing 10 minutes of racing because a checkpoint wasn't validated. It's a bit frustrating but something that, I reckon, could be fixed in minutes if the developer decided to go a bit further with the game. The AI is incredibly basic and slow and won't hesitate to run into you or another opponent. It's not uncommon to lap one or more AI cars on some of the longer races. Free roaming is empty and a bit boring (also, 60 FOV is quite tight). Not a very challenging game.
Driving physics are acceptable for an arcade game, though a bit understeery, but the gameplay is let down by the way the collisions are handled. Overall quite pleasant as long as you keep away from touching anything.
Needs more work to be good.

VERY IN SHORT : Conditional Recommend! Ambitious game which disappoints with shallow mechanics, yet can still entertain! Buy on sale if you like its pirate concept!
-----
Pixel Piracy is a unique little game with many interesting ideas on board, but overall fails to deliver on most of them with sadly shallow game mechanics and a very clunky UI. However if the concept they are pitching appeals to you, it is not hard to sail through quite a few hours messing around building different ships and acquiring and training a crew into full blown battle-hardened pirates.
There really is no other game that I know of which offers exactly what Vitali Kirpu and Alexander Poysky have dreamed up here. Indeed other pirate games exist on the market which do a lot of what Pixel Piracy does, and in most cases they do it better. However the ability to create your own ship from scratch, and hire individual crew members to man it into ship to ship battle, or an island raid alongside you certainly adds a certain charm to this game which sets it apart from the rest in the pirate genre. Unforunately the most endearing part of the game is marred by exactly what should enhance it. Exploration can be tedious as all islands look essentially the same, and contain little to nothing to do outside of fighting enemies. (Though there are towns, they aren't much better.)
All in all I feel that this is a game that, had the developers put in a little more love and the necessary time to flesh out the existing mechanics and add a few new ones, could have been the next big indie game. Though as it stands it feels more like an Android or iOs game, I can only recommend one to pick it up while its on sail (yahar!), but only if you are a fan of the genre or the concepts on offer appeal to you.
-----
Note: I understand that although the game is technically 'released', they have hired someone who is currently working on Pixel Piracy updating and adding new content to the game. If my opinion changes based upon this, I will update this review.

Did it in 4.0 hours on normal difficulty, I think I completely explored the game and killed every single enemie, too.
CLASSES:
I started with the "Knight" class. "Mage" and "Hunter" are the other 2 available classes.
MELEE WEAPONS & COMBAT:
Weapons which apply burn or have life steal are just OP and get you through the game even easier than regularly.
It's very easy to stunlock enemies by using a "Zweihänder" sword, I guess even a one handed would do, but I played with the two-handed fire sword most of the time and that's where i noticed it the most.
SPELLS & COMBAT:
You only need the lighning spell, which deals damage and paralizes every enemy, except the boss, for a long enough time to get close and kill them. It also doesn't cost much mana, which you'll regen very fast anyways and it can't be charged, so you can just spam it.
You don't even need to aim exactly at the enemie because it has a relatively big hitbox, so if you'd fire it a bit to the left or right of an enemy, it will still hit.
I don't know about the other spells but I think they won't be as useful.
RANGED WEAPONS & COMBAT:
I didn't use crossbows but normal bows are okay, not too good, though, because the hitbox for "headshots" seems off and aiming is a pain.
Sometimes a hit in an enemie's head will deal as much damage as a shot anywhere else in their body, and sometimes it deals like 300 extra damage.
MERCHANTS:
Merchants are pretty useless and the 3 merchants in the game just pop up at certain spots during the story, all three of them almost standing in each other. That makes it seem like they've just been dropped there without a second thought.
Buying stuff isn't necessary at all, you'll find anything you need in chests, which aren't even well hidden, and you can craft good gear, if needed and if you found the recipes in chests (which again is hardly a challenge).
EXPLORATION?!:
There isn't very much to explore, though. It's a linear setting and you can see caves on the mini-map so you don't even need to search for those.
What I hated the most was, that you only can sprint with an ability ("8" on default), which has a painfully long cooldown. It took so long to walk around that it took my joy in exploring away after 5 minutes.
OTHERS (Graphics,AI etc.):
For a stand alone it feels kind of unfinished and empty at many parts. For example the water "animation" which glitches, the environmental shadows are jumping around, the background looks plain and loveless, enemy AI has it's problems at times (enemies just standing around for 2 sec after I approached them, for excample). But besides all that it has fairly good graphics.
Charachter models and Enemies are well designed.
The mobs won't respawn, so after a while you just cleared the few enemies and turtles in the areas and go on.
RESULT:
I got the game as part of the Gothic Pack on a Steam sale and therefor the price wasn't too high. I won't recommend buying it any other way, because it sadly is not worth it.

I have slightly mixed opinions on this game. Although the pros outweigh the cons (and because, when buying the Portal Bundle on sale, the game costs maybe 40 cents), there are some things that make me want to slap the developers across the face.
But let's start this off with typical [Attribute] [Score] system.
Sound and Music: 7/10 - Sounds are completely uninteresting. Music, although rather scarce and definitely not something I could listen to out of context, creates a rather claustrophobic, unsettling atmosphere. Where the music's present it fits and sounds well, however for the most part there's barely any music playing. Still Alive remains one of my favourite songs in games to this day.
Visuals: 7/10 - I wouldn't call this game pretty, but I wouldn't call it ugly, either. Just like with sounds, it's implemented well, but the game's design doesn't create any places where I could say "Ooh, pretty" or "Ugh, ugly".
Gameplay - 9.5/10 - This game is made in Source engine, just like almost all Valve games (this includes titles like Half-Life 2, Team Fortress 2, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive and Portal 2), so if you've played any of them, the controls will be familiar to you. The main gameplay component of the game, Portals, is incorporated well, with pretty much the whole game being the tutorial, constantly presenting you with new gameplay mechanics and letting you get accustomed with them, all the while presenting you with more complex and difficult puzzles.
Keep in mind that the game is quite short. Playing through the game once will take no more than 2 hours, while getting every achievement will take about 10 hours (or a lot more, if you decide to not look up guides for the challenges), and, unlike Portal 2, it doesn't have access to fanmade content, so the replay ability is nearly non-existent. The main game is entertaining from start to finish, and the advanced chambers (of which there are six) provide an extra challenge and finishing them feels rewarding. There is another addition to the game, though, which consists of 6 test chambers with 3 different challenges; Least Portals, Least Steps and Least Time, all of which have three different medals (and 3 achievements associated with those medals), depending on how well you accomplish them. This part of the game made me want to post a "Not Recommended" review. Am I just too bad to complete these? I consider myself "in the middle" when it comes to skill in this game, meaning I'm not good, but not bad, either. The problem isn't that some of these are hard puzzles - the problem is that many of these require either glitches, or solutions so elaborate, that you'd need an IQ of 150 or higher to come up with them without help from online videos and guides. For example, the Least Time challenge for Chamber 16 requires you to use a glitch (not a trick, a glitch) that makes you go through walls and skip 70% of the puzzle. How do I know that it
you to do that? Because when you do it, you're not left with a lot of extra time - you can actually fail quite often, if you're just a second or two too slow. The challenges for Least Footsteps and Least Time in Chamber 18 require you to... use a computer case available in a semi-hidden room to jam the exit door, so that you don't have to retreive the box, skipping about 50% of the puzzle. Not all challenges are like that, some of them just require elaborate moves and clever thinking, but some of them just take it too far and require you to exploit glitches or use mechanics not even touched upon in the original game to have any chance of getting a silver or gold medal.
Overall, if you're a casual gamer who won't try to complete the game in 100%, then buy this game and enjoy it. However, if you like getting every achievement, then this game will test your patience and resourcefullness to its limits.

In short: Buy it.
In long: Do you like Age of Empires II? Do you like Rise of Nations? Do you like zombies? Of course you do. Take AoE II, RoN and mix it into the zombie survival genre and They Are Billions is the result (throw in an "Attack on Titan" atmosphere for good measure).
Gameplay: This game doesn't look too deep on paper but it has the depth to keep me coming back for more games (even though I have beaten it on max difficulty). You don't just build and defend, to expand you need to cleanse the area of zombies. Zombies are not just simple NPCs either, there is an in depth noise generation feature which I find very interesting. Different troops create more noise (marines with guns vs rangers with bows who are silent) and more troops together create even more noise. This means you have to be smart in purging areas for expansion. Make too much noise and you might get overrun by a makeshift swarm. Zombies get progressively harder as you explore to the edges of the map and the game does a good job of giving you incentive to explore. On the final wave every zombie in the map will come rushing at you at once, it makes the final pretty much impossible to beat if you haven’t cleared the map of map zombies by then. Also your troops level up with kills so exploring/levelling up troops is paramount to victory.
The base building itself is also a ton of fun. The walls work like AoE II if AoE II had a viable gate system which makes them super intuitive to use. There is a fair amount of option as to how you want to progress. You can focus on defensive towers, troops, traps, walls and any combination thereof. One really neat feature of your base is that when zombies take down a building the colonists in that building will become zombies. This means if you aren't careful and even let one zombie in you could be facing a horde of your own colonists that grows exponentially as they destroy more of your colony. Then after killing your former friends and family you have to send troops to reclaim the infected zone of your city, wiping out remaining zombies, repairing buildings and plugging the walls.
There is never nothing to do in this game. There is a pause feature for a reason. You need to be expanding your base, building up defences and exploring/clearing the map all at the same time. If you fall behind in any of these things it can really hurt your chances of winning.
Graphics: Very nicely done graphics, looks 2d when zoomed out but it's actually cell shaded 3d models. Zombies look really good with excellent animations that really help with immersion. The game can handle 20 000 sprites at once which is kind of insane. You have to defend against oceans of zombies that move very much like liquid waves smashing against the shoreline.
Music/Sounds: Great soundtrack that reacts to what's going on in the game (ie: different music for attacks, supensful buildups, regular base building/exploring. Sounds are basic, nothing spectacular but nothing that detracts from the game other than some of the voice lines are...unique.
Content: This is an early access game. Right now there are just 4 maps. Still, I was impressed with the amount of buildings, troops and zombie types that already exist. Seems like this game has very active developers, updates drop faster than I can keep up. Right now there is a just a survival mode but the devs are working on adding a campaign (personally I’d like to see an endless mode but that’s neither here or there.)
Overall: This is one of the best strategy games I've played in awhile. It's truly a breath of fresh air. I can't remember the last time I've enjoyed a single player rts experience so much. They've solved the issue of boring bot matches by using the same weaknesses of most RTS bots (being predictable and...well robotic) but instead turning them into strengths by making the enemy a predictable robotic foe (zombies). Whatever they are doing it really works, I highly recommend this one.

This game has an extremely wide range of cars and a good amount of licensing. There is no Porsche licensing (which is hard to obtain anyway) But there's a few RUF cars around, which is Porsche's tuning brand. The map is huge with loads of things to discover, such as clothes shops, car dealerships, tuning shops etc. It takes a good amount of time to get from one side to the other (like a really good amount of time), the map is just huge.
The graphics are a tad lackluster but still kind of hold up for 2017, but the scenery looks great, with good lighting effects. Everywhere looks different and there's a lot of variety between asphalt and offroad locations.
There's a decent amount of things to customise, such as your cars, your clothes, hairstyles etc. You can put stickers on your cars and do a whole load of different things to it. You can make your cars feel like your own.
The support for this game is basically completely out the window, it's hard to make an online account, so much so that I've skipped it completely and stuck to single player. Also there's a ton of DLC cars in the game but nowhere to buy the DLC? So these cars that I can't even acquire have been advertised to me, but are nowhere to be found.
Probably the worst DRM I've seen since GFWL, 4 machine activation limit is stupid and the DRM just gets in the way. DRM that's this extreme just makes people want to pirate your game even more, just don't bother.
: The game starts off incredibly slow, and it's hilariously easy to the point where I could literally crash into a wall 5 times and probably still win at the end of it. Also it's waaay too easy to acquire good cars in early game. I had an Audi R8 V10 after about 2 hours of playing, because you get pretty excessive amounts of money at the start.
It's still one of the best racing games, which is why I recommend it, but the DRM, the lack of support and DLC bogs it down from what it once was. You'll see by other reviews, that people feel the same. If you stick to single player, this game is still pretty easily an 8/10 or so, it's just the multiplayer that you might struggle with.

Would love to eventually see this thing fleshed out with powerups, double jumps, wall jumps, platform trigger switches, guns etc to add a bit more variety to the game styles, But for now it is what it is, a fun little beginner tool to dip your 2d platform making toes into without breaking the bank or requiring a huge time investment to learn.
Don't think I'd invest many hours into this right now as I'm currently invested in Stencyl, but I'm very keen to see where this ends up as Stencyl can be difficult in places.

This game plays and feels different from the other Lost Planet entries. That much you can get from any other review, and that by itself puts some people off - but not me, and I think you should give this game a chance. That said, I'm not much one for multiplayer, so my comments are about the campaign.
The sound and graphics are good, especially the sound design for the weather. Very atmospheric, it really gets your attention when a howling, thundering blizzard rolls in and whites everything out. The music is not bad, and comes in two flavors: moody science fiction-style instrumentals, like what you'd hear in Aliens or Homeworld, and some surprisingly classy western-style guitar and fiddle tunes the main character likes to listen to. They're both understated, but nice touches.
The art design and graphics fit the mood as well, giving E.D.N. III a stark beauty you don't find very often. The character animations are a little stiff in-game, but not anything that really breaks immersion - and the mech animations feel nice and stompy, like they have real weight to them. It's a nice effect that I appreciate.
The storytelling style is well done, particularly given it's a Capcom game. I don't think they'll ever really live down Resident Evil's infamously cheesy dialogue, but this game feels like it was written by Joss Whedon. Some commenters have mentioned the game feeling similar to the movie Aliens, and I can see that, but I think the main character has more in common with the frontier pragmatism of Jim Raynor or Malcolm Reynolds.
So, that's scene-building and mood-setting, and it's done well. But this is a shooter, right? So, how is the action?
It's a solid third-person shooter. You have different loadouts you can switch between, upgradeable weapons, and a basic cover system. Getting new weapons can be kind of slow, especially if you focus on side-quests, but every weapon always has some utility: there aren't many trash guns in this game.
The pacing can be a bit spastic, and is my only real issue with the game. One of the first QTE's - sorry, I didn't mention those, did I? Yeah, there are some QTE's in this game. They're pretty forgiving, though, and they don't show up enough to be obnoxious.
Where was I? Oh, right, pacing. One of the first QTE's is in the middle of a "help us, player character! Fix this problem RIGHT NOW!" situation that blows in out of nowhere. The urgency of that errand is a pretty sharp break from the smoother pace the game had had before that, and afterward, it goes immediately back to that "take your time if you want" approach. It's a bit jarring sometimes.
So overall, if you're a fan of shooters and gritty science fiction, you like mood-building and atmosphere, and you don't mind some pacing shifts, I would definitely recommend this game.

I originally gave this game a negative review due to a gamebreaking bug. Having come back months later this bug seemed to have been fixed so I decided to edit my review.
Unlike a lot of space shootman games, LP3 takes its time introducing its characters and giving you the opportunity to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about them, it also focuses on civilians like scientists and engineers instead of your usual "HOORAH SPESH MAHREENS!". Biggest example is the protagonist, Jim Peyton. Jim is no Master Chief or Commander Shepard, he’s just a contractor out to get a paycheck to support his family. He’s a relative everyman and the game does a quality job actually showing you his relationship with his family, mainly through videos he exchanges with his wife, Grace, back on Earth. The game takes it time establishing Jim’s day to day life and I think it works. All the approaches the writers make to establish the characters really help give some real heart to what otherwise could have been a generic TPS game. Though there is also the atmosphere which is really freaking good, EDN 3 looks like an utterly hostile planet filled with freezing blizzards and massive lava pools. The country music Grace gives you also adds to this “space trucker” vibe that the game gives off and it really adds to the atmosphere, though you can just play your own music if you want. Overall, it was clear the writers (One of them wrote Anachronox!) wanted something more than flimsy cardboard excuses for story and characters most actions games have. They do well for a while but disappointingly it craps itself at the end with a transparently evil villain that ruins the whole theme of not having any real villains. This really brings the game down from being great but the writing is still solid.
When it comes to the combat it is essentially Dead Space and its serviceable but way too many enemies tend to spawn and there’s not much enemy variety. Fighting in your mech can be cool but sometimes it can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥due to some obtuse mechanics. It’s not a game you really play for the combat, just stick to Easy.
Overall LP3 has a really strong start with a more unique character driven take on an action game but this peters out as it goes on. It’s still a solid game and worth picking up on sale now

They came up with the brilliant idea of not warning anyone of the 300% increase in character price that basically screwed over anyone who was saving up their hard earned keys (coins). Then they have the cheek to throw around the new currency in the faces of those who've just been robbed of their money, telling them how easy it is to buy characters and perks by purchasing this new in-game currency. New updates came in making Monsters somewhat viable again, which I'm guessing helped since I mainly play as a Hunter and noticed I wasn't winning every game. This is how JoWooD ends. Not with a bang, but with a $15 expansion for a game nobody bought or liked very much that re-uses a lot of the same assets from the main game. Originally supposed to come out a few months after ArcaniA shipped, the expansion seemed to be destined never to come out until Nordic Games (now THQ Nordic) picked up a lot of JoWooD IP, along with ArcaniA, and put this out.
FOS is basically the ending to ArcaniA, locked up behind $15. It takes place immeditely after the main story concludes with the Shepard being sent to assist forces in Setarrif. Remember the cool looking  white and gold Persian-esque city with the miniarets that was under siege and could not be accessed? That's Setarrif. However, a volcano has errupted and has cut off the city from the rest of the island, as well as seriously affected the city and the surrounding wildlife. The expansion is pretty linear and there are exactly two side quests outside of the critical path. It's worth noting that you can start FOS with an end-game character from ArcaniA along with all your equipment and inventory, although it will all get quickly replaced with better gear.
The engine performs slightly better, with none of the *many* glitches and bugs that hounded ArcaniA present, and there are some interesting sequences where you take control of Lester and Gorn for story-related purposes, but overall, FOS is pretty bare-bones. I paid $3 for this and I still feel like maybe I could have spent it on something better. Also, the voice acting is weirdly delivered in FOS with lots of unnatural pauses and volume levels versus how it was in ArcaniA (although that had it's fair share of audio problems too) which can probably be explained away by its traumatic development process.
Your money is better spent elsewhere.

I didn't know what I was getting into when I first purchased this game. I had heard good things about it, but I didn't know for absolute certain if I would like it. Don't get me wrong, I love visual novels, and I like birds, but a visual novel about romancing birds? That was something different.
I went into the game not knowing what to expect. I came out of it completely in love with everything it had to offer.
The storyline seems simple: you play as a girl who is entering an all-birds school as the only human. Your life as a high school student is determined by the choices you make, as well as who you choose to romance.
The more I played the game and unlocked endings, the more I fell in love with the characters and their stories. Everyone in the game is more than what meets the eye, and are actually deep and well-developed (sans Okosan; he's just comic relief).
The story, as simple as it seems, is actually really dark and heartbreaking, especially the "BBL Route". I won't spoil anything, but it caught me off-guard. Throughout the character routes, I actually found myself tearing up a bit. Nageki and Ryouta's routes come to mind when it comes to emotional storytelling.
Overall, Hatoful Boyfriend is a game I can't recommend enough. It's funny, cute, and still manages to have a story you can take seriously even thought the cast is made up of birds. This game is worth the $10, but if you want to wait for the price to drop, go ahead. This isn't a game you want to miss out on.
Pros-
+ Funny and charming atmosphere in the beginning.
+ Still manages to be taken seriously when things take a dark turn.
+ A lovable cast of characters.
+ It's one of the most unique visual novels I've played/read.
Cons-
- The looks on your confused friends' faces when they see this game in your library.
- Having to explain to them why you bought the game in the first place.
Recommended for:
Bird fans, romance anime fans, and those looking for something different and refreshing.

This is a game that's not only aged well, but arguably gotten better with age. It's stylish, it's simple, it's a hell of a lot of fun. In what other game do you get a wild juxtaposition of sci-fi themes, anachronistic medieval environments, and demonic enemies all in the same package? If you like first person shooters, chances are your favorite fps uses a distant branch of the Quake engine and those of you who play TF2 frequently might find a comforting familiarity with the controls and weapons.
The game still has an active modding community to this day, and while not as prolific as Doom, I find this game more enjoyable and a visual treat especially as the "low poly pixel aesthetic" is becoming popular again and has a much tighter art direction.
Just be sure to get a modern engine like Darkplaces or Quakespasm. The steam release doesn't include the music so you'll have to download that. I /highly/ recommend playing with the music on as it gives a unique and chilling atmosphere to the game like nothing else.
If you finish up Quake and are looking for more action, there are plenty of maps and mods to download that continue the Quake experience. One I highly recommend is Arcane Dimensions if you're looking for new weapons, new enemies, and newer, bigger worlds to explore.

Brink is your standard establishment versus rebels (government v terrorists) FPS story arc. The game itself has a relatively weak story, told mostly by a 1-2 minute cutscene before each mission, first narrated by your commander giving objectives, then from the perspective of the soldiers. This game definitely didn't invest heavily in the campaign as it is basically a series of objective missions with AI, which means having a friend is definitely a plus as the missions become much more enjoyable when playing with friends. Even with this, the game takes less than 7 hours to clear 100% meaning low return on your funds. The gameplay offers combat most similar to Killzone 2, there is a class system and there are weapons useable across classes but they have their trade offs, and there is a unique feature of this game which is the parkour system (freerunning). The classes follow the Killzone style, with the soldier, sabateur, engineer, and medic which offer some class abilities which differentiate them from one another. Furthermore there is weapon customization like call of duty where you can modify your weapons with attachments, the good news is most of the attachments are easy to get, thus most people are on a level playing field. The leveling of characters unlocks more abilities and makes the character's more diverse, the classes are relatively balanced although personally the medic seems to be one of the stronger classes minus his inability to perform objectives (which is what all gamemodes are around). The parkour/freerunning mechanic is the main draw of this game, you can essentially climb any wall within reason, jump ledges, slide under obstacles or behind cover. It is a feature which worked well and gave the game a good "feel" to it, as your mobility was greatly increased. The graphics are relatively good despite the style leaving some things to be desired, some regions have low res textures (even on max), the character models look extremely similar even with the customization options (although the contrast of the slums and the ark is well done in level design/graphical appearance). The problem with this game at the time of writting this review is the online is effectively dead, either being too laggy or being nobody playing ever, which is kind of depressing because I did enjoy the game despite its flaws, and the game is obviously orientated towards multiplayer. As a result I cannot recommend this game unless you can purchase it for very cheap and are looking for a gaming experience which takes between 5-10hours for everything.

It's a "third person tactical shooter experience with strategy video game elements" -Wikipedia.  One has to wonder if the developers were playing Mass Effect during its creation considering development began in 2006 and finally released in 2013.
To complete missions, you recruit agents from a list of different available classes, each with their own background training, and then take any two agents from your roster into the field with you.  As they gain field experience, agents unlock their special abilities known as perks.  At certain perk levels, you decide between specialisations.
Being a huge Mass Effect fan, this game brought a smile to my face.   It was a lot of fun and I couldn't stop playing it.  I finished the campaign in a week.
Questions you should ask yourself if you are considering buying this game are:
Do you like alien technology?  Do you like special augmented abilities?  Do you like plasma, laser and lightning weaponry?  How about combo kills that are announced when successful?   Did you enjoy the Mass Effect series?  Do you like the genre of science-fiction?  Then you should play this game.
I decided to buy The Bureau on a steam sale because I received my copy of XCOM 2 in the mail upon release from...an online store...and I like to play games in chronological story order.  I also bought XCOM: EW and EU from Steam as well and I'm looking forward to playing them next.  All of this, of course, is building up to play XCOM 2.
Additional thoughts and criticisms:
Graphics wise, the game is par for the course for a game released in 2013, which is to say they're good even by today's standards.
The XCOM base of operations is highly detailed, roomy and there are plenty of NPCs to converse with between missions.  Scattered throughout, are also files to read, pictures to view and audio tapes to listen too; all of which adds depth to the story.
The voice acting is good, but I found the voice of Agent Carter, the main character you play as, reminding me a little too much of Batman's voice.  It made me laugh at times and took me out of the story momentarily.  Of course, it could be due to the fact that agents seem to be smoking non-stop throughout the game.
The other criticism I have is that there isn’t much of any ‘new game plus’ upon completion of the campaign, save for playing it over with different classes of agents.  Also, and unlike in Mass Effect, there aren’t choices you make that have consequences in the story line other than if you play on the hardest difficulty and one of your field agents die, they are dead permanently and you have to rely on your other agents to fill in and begin leveling up a new agent.
Final thoughts:
I finished the game wanting more missions to play.  I think that’s a good thing.  It was fun to play and I recommend it, especially on a Steam sale.

Platfinity™ is an easy-to-use Game Making software that makes it easy to create and share (of course) your own games.
Having been in development for a while, Ian Martin had a lot of time to make Platfinity™ the best it can be. What he gave us is a great program for anyone to use. I would recommend this software for anyone trying to begin their game developing career to test their skills, or someone who just wants to make a game. Either way, Platfinity™ will no doubt be fun to use.

Easy to use as the store video suggests - and has plenty of basic retro looking stock assets,  these  might not be to everybody's taste but you can easily import your own graphics, sprites and artwork, so don't let that put you off at all.
Easy to import or create custom assets as shown in the video below. You can make a level like this in literally minutes or sink some time into your artwork and level design and make something pretty impressive if you have a bit of talent.
The developer has put a lot of thought into making it user-friendly as well, this stands out.
There is a built in pixel/sprite editor, and it is very simple to import sprites and images (png) to use as platforms, rotating/moving hazards, normal/background/foreground tiles, and you can set tile properties as well as their graphics (sticky, slippery, bouncy, normal etc). Movement speeds and directions of platforms is done on the fly, you can edit a game as you play. Or play it as you edit.
Updated now to run in a window as well as full screen.
The player-character's physics can be customised, and global properties like gravity etc can be customised too.  You can also set areas of "space" or "water" physics using background tiles and setting these properties for individual tiled areas.
The engine cleverly uses transparencies to automatically make what seems like pixel-perfect collision. If it's transparent it effectively doesn't affect anything in the gameplay.
If you are a sucker for these "easy game makers" and you want to make a 2-D platformer with a minimum of fuss or bother this gets you there without any scripting or programming. Just bring your ideas. If you want to sell them and avoid the wrath of the likes of Jim Sterling, bring some original artwork as well.
If you are gifted with any skills as an artist you really could showcase your talents very nicely in Platfinity.  All the mechanics for a good 2-D platformer (without guns) are in there at the click of a mouse button.
It has useful features which are expected by users in your finished games, but which a lot of these game-makers leave out, or force you to code/script yourself:  - screen zoom, user key mapping, controller support etc. So it hasn't just been written for the budding game developer, it has the player in mind as well.  Your finished games should run on the most modest spec PC as well. (Windows, but not IOS or Android)
You can drag and drop static or moving platforms, ladders, traps background tiles and foreground tiles around, change their properties, movements etc, you really can make a multi level game in no time at all if you have the ideas.
There is a good manual, in plain english, but you won't need it for long because most of the functions are very intuitive and there are also comprehensive help files in game, and playing through the demo games provided with the software will give you a good taste of what you can be doing in no time at all.
Ultra low PC requirements, and it's a small download. Generous licensing terms, you can install on two computers for one user, and if you sell your games all the revenue is yours to keep, and the developers have released it at a very low price.
You will be able to have a lot of fun with this, and there is nothing to stop you making some quote polished entertaining games for friends and family, or something more ambitious if you have the the creativity and ideas.  Well worth it just for prototyping a platformer concept, because it is so quick to work with. You don't even need to restart a level to play-test (almost a process of adding stuff as you play)
It has a built in paint app to create or edit tiles and sprites
It really is a joy to use, totally stable, reliable and solid. The store page details and video don't do it justice.

The manual available in the steam store page link is written in plain english, so it should be easy to understand even if english isn't your first language. Less is more seems to be the ethos with both the manual and the steam store page description.
Trading cards and steam achievements included.

Got this game for free by one of the devs as a gift, back in xmas when copies of the game were being thrown arround. I have spend 0€'s on this, and because of that, I feel bad for the people who actually bought it. I'll go with the bad stuff first:
The biggest dissapointment is that the game is unfinished. This is something that I just can't tolerate. You don't sell someone a house without roof, so you should
sell an unfinished game. Does the game have the features that the devs promised? No weather system, no sea-monster battles, no hideouts, no bases,you don't get much with a 10€ purchase. You have islands where most of the NPC's (or all of them) are hostile, peaceful islands where you can buy stuff, and ship battles that are bland and repetitive. And that's another thing...
Sea battles. They're horse-sh#t. Maybe at the start, they're somewhat okay, you just tell your guys to aboard a little ship, or they board yours... But then later on, they have cannons, you have cannons, and all the fun explodes. Crew members are expensive and take forever to train so they're useful (and training also takes money), but they die easily by the cannons. AND THAT'S ANOTHER THING TOO!
You only have two commands to give: Either move the captain arround, or move everyone else. That's it. I'm not kidding. Mouse 1 selects a place where your captain can move, and Mouse 2 moves everyone else to that point. You can't, for example, tell someone to stay ready at the cannons, or to stay cooking for everyone else. Your pirates, captain included, will do whatever they feel like. This isn't Sims 2, this is a Pirate Simulator, and let me tell you, PIRATES WERE COORDINATED. If they weren't, THEY WOULDN'T HAVE A CAPTAIN!
I've also managed to find bugs. I mean, it's no surprise, I'm able to find bugs even on my house (the lightning works like sh#t, and the windows barely work, everyone smokes weed, 4/20), but I'm talking about bugs that force you to restart the game (being stuck on the enemy ship, even though you blew it up and can't go back), and even bugs that will force you to restart the game again! (crew members, captain included, suddenly refuse to eat, I managed to find out that boarding another ship and taking it for your own fixes it temporally) And I refuse to think that they haven't found any of these bugs yet. I found them in less than an hour of playing the game.
That being said, does the game have good stuff? Yeah, there's a lot of potential for a great game, but sadly the Devs left the boat (ironic) to make other games. I remember that in December of 2013, they promised those features to be added. We're in 2015. It's been more than a whole year, and the only thing that was added have been Steam cards and achievements. Oh, and some XMas items. The characters look okay, the voices and soundtrack are decent, the gameplay can be dull at times, but it's fun for a few hours, the graphics are beautiful but lazy (you see the same stuff WAAAAAY too much), the character and world creating is creative, even though it doesn't seem to matter much in the end, there are some good references to other games and movies hidden arround there, though I expected more... And it goes on to infinity.
I can't bring myself to recommend the game. I really want to, because I had fun for a while... But I can't even bring myself to finish it. Why? Because I know it's going to be the same, over again. I defeated one of the 4 "Legendary Captains" without much effort, and the other 3 will surely be the same. There's no story either, so why would I expect an ending? It's probably a screen with text, and maybe some credits. If they EVER finish the game, then I'll play it again, redo the review, and update it, maybe even recommend it. But for now? Spending 10€ on this is a ripoff. Maybe just wait for a sale that drops it arround 1-3€ if you're interested in helping the devs, that's it.

A strong narrative experience wrapped around solid and enjoyable action gameplay. Plausible, relatable characters with some genuine depth to them, along with a wide variety of enemies that challenge you to improve and adapt as you play. A smallish but well-chosen selection of weapons, larger if you consider the offensive potential of your giant mining robot... which you should, because not every game that lets you pilot a giant robot really makes you feel like you're in one -but this one does. It doesn't zip along on jet feet, sure, but that just makes it feel more real, more massive.
Controls are quite functional, one issue exists where an incorrect on-screen instruction says "Rotate W/S/A/D" when it means "rapidly tap F", but a quick googling could have told you that much. To make it up to you, if you have an Xbox Controller for Windows, you can literally plug it in as you play, use it to do perform the gamepad versions of various tool interactions, then unplug it again to return to mouse aiming. Or you can use it all the time if you like, just saying.
Graphics are perfectly fine, bordering on gorgeous. Depends how picky you are, I suppose, but I find it hard to imagine the type of person who would actually complain. This game has a lot to offer and should not be missed by anyone who enjoys mechs, shooting, narrative or combinations thereof. At its current price of €40, I would wait for a sale, but if you can catch it at a price that works for you, I say don't hesitate. The sound of your rig's soundtrack, echoing across a snow-swept canyon and up to your perch on a recently-grappled cliff, is waiting.

Are you a 75-IQ brainlet that fancies themself a 'grand strategy gamer'? Do you enjoy clicking a few boxes, dragging a few sliders, and sitting down for 5 minutes doing literally nothing? Does incredibly unintuitive, mindless gameplay focused on "war" that is exclusively made up of selecting all of your units and letting the AI do everything else appeal to you? Then get HOI4. You'll get to jack your ego off a bit and pretend what you're doing requires any mental effort. If not, steer clear. EU4, CK2, and VIC2 all work much better in all metrics of what makes a grand strategy game 'good'. Hell, even earlier entries in the series are of far higher quality. HOI2 and HOI3 are far more balanced, entertaining, and interesting. I've played this game quite a bit, in social, online, and single-player situations, and in nearly none did I actualyl enjoy the run. It's not really any more easy or difficult than other GS games, but doesn't require much skill to win or lose. Just click, drag, and wait. The outcome isn't really influenced by your actions once you reach a certain point, which isn't really too far on. It fails as a HOI game, a grand strategy game, and, considering it's lack of intuitivity, as a game itself.

This is a very good hidden object game.
It ought to be worth several hours of poking around.  Some scenes are easy, and some are very large with some items taking a good bit of effort to find.  I wouldn't have thought that all the sound effects being vocal noise would be good, but it's quite well done.  And those scenes can be quite interactive, mostly in obvious ways, and there's plenty of things to come across that aren't on the list of objects to find.  Plants to grow or chop down, holes to poke at, Xs to dig up, most things to open, many things to move around.
I particularly like that each object has its own hint, and they're the creative sort rather than just pointing you to where it is.  I found it can still be tough to figure out some of them.  I cleared the first two areas in three hours, of the four areas, but each area is getting more scenes and more large scenes.  No time pressure or other gimicks either, just searching around the map at your leisure.
If you enjoy the hidden object puzzles, I strongly recommend this one.  There should be several hours worth of poking around.

Note: It should be known that toribash hasn't been on steam it's whole lifetime, so my hours are more around the 3k mark, moving on :]. I'll add on-to the review over time. I don't care to polish it mostly.
You rip other players bodies to shreds, what more is there to do you say?
Toribash is a turn-based fighting game, and don't let this discourage you because NO OTHER game can do it better. It truly isn't a one-mode game with inconsistent gameplay. Their's thousands of mods to choose from with its own boundaries and mod settings which bring an entirely new experience, even if you play thousands of hours, you'll truly never be able to experience the whole game as it's meant to be.
It's hard, and it takes time. But anyone can do it, an hour a day, and after a month, you'll finally understand what to do. From there, you can explore mods no holds barred. Some range from parkour, sparring(realism), martial arts such as taikwondo, ninjutsu, aikido or swords, boxing and so on.
Your in-game account is also automatically connected to its forums, As such, you can buy yourself joint-specific colors and variations, attend in-game events for a chance of rewards and general community affairs for texturing, modding, scripting or marketing.
Clans are also a huge part of toribash, although the games died down a lot, clans can still be seen everywhere. Usually being based around aikido, but many, including myself, also have clans for mods they whole-heartedly enjoy, for me, that's boxing.
Bettings servers come every now and then, they used to be very popular back in the day. If you want to test your luck on the better fighter to earn some quick cash, you can go for it.
All in all, toribash is a fresh experience away from the repetitive bullcrap seen from other games this age. It's a dying breed of gameplay, and soon enough toribash will die. However, hampa just released news that he's working on the next version, [Toribash Next]. Hopefully the community comes together again to revive a great nostalgic game for what it is.

This is a fun little game that I think is well worth the money I paid for it.  The devs are responsive and the community is active.  Lots to recommend it.  I don't see myself going back to playing it again any time soon, however.  I like the current crop of rogue-likes quite a lot, permadeath and ridiculous difficulties are great with me.  My problem, though, is that I've run into three game-breaking bugs in the dozen or so hours that I've played it and at least one of them went away when I provided my save file to the devs.  They loaded it up, couldn't see the bug, gave me back the save and when I loaded up the one they gave me back I didn't see the bug either.
These are the three I've hit:
- my captain got 'stuck' trying to climb back aboard my ship when leaving an island.  I couldn't make him move back or foward, so I quit.  When I restarted the game I would get one second of activity before "Game Over" because my captain had fallen in the water and drowned.
- my captain got 'stuck' on the far side of an island and couldn't move back through the various shops to the ship.  Even after reloading the game.
- during a combat three of my crew fell off the island into the water and drowned.  As the game clearly states it does not save during combat, I reloaded the last save.  Which seemed to have happened immediately after the three crew members had drowned, a second before.
The game is fun.  Make no mistake.  And usually your game will end the way any rogue-like ends, you'll die because some fight went against you because you under-estimated your opponent.  Occasionally, though, be prepared for the game itself to just smash your tower and make you start building over again.

I really wanted to like this game.  I watched a few Let's Plays from when it was in Early Access and thought it looked like a lot of fun, which it can be at times.  I mean, you get to enlist your own pirate crew!  You can travel around, searching for treasure, fishing, getting scurvy and watching your pirate crew poop all over your boat!  What could be better?!
However, I soon discovered that the finished product is just as unfinished as that Early Access alpha footage was.  Gamebreaking glitches and a poor UI plague you at every turn.  Sometimes, your pirate just decides to fall into the water and die.   You can give your pirates a bunch of different skills, but only the most recent one actually has any effect, leaving many players to wonder "why doesn't my fisherman actually fish?"
The developer is promising a new "enhanced edition" free update, however all of the official word on this update indicate that bug fixes aren't even on their radar.  They are treating the game as though it is basically finished but just needs some balance tweaks, when the truth of the matter is this game should still be on the Early Access list.   The phrase "buyer beware" has never been more applicable.
If you don't mind paying for unfinished products, don't mind when a developer lists their product as finished when it is still very much in alpha stages and ridden with glitches, then you might still want to try this game.
If you are of the opinion that a little bit of faith in indie devs is warranted, then you will probably be willing to buy this.
But take my advice, wait for this game to go on sale.  It absolutely is not worth the full price, unless you have really low standards for games.  Even then, it's not really a good idea to throw money at devs who display no indications of understanding what their game's problems actually are.  The industry has enough of that already.
UPDATE:  A few months back, the lead developer of Pixel Piracy posted a public apology for the state of the game.  In this apology, he admitted that Pixel Piracy was not in a finished state, that they weren't happy with it, and they would be addressing the numerous legitimate complaints that had been expressed.
However, there is no record of this public apology on Steam anymore.  They have also appointed a new moderator to their subforum, and this moderator is insisting that the game is a finished product and that the developers are working on a new title.

Ковчег являлся частью современной экологической концепции, примером самодостаточного местообитания. Огромный плавучий город, созданный людьми, стал прибежищем учёных и мыслителей, которые хотели реализовать эту экологическую концепцию, а богатые руководители города предоставили им для этого поистине курортные условия.
Но угроза глобальной экологической катастрофы вскоре стала реальнее некуда: таяли ледники, поднимался уровень моря, и выживание самого человечества оказалось под вопросом. Многие тысячи людей со всего земного шара бросились на Ковчег в поисках спасения. Беженцы всеми силами старались выжить, а отцы-основатели города и их потомки пытались во что бы то ни стало сохранить над ним контроль.
Теперь Ковчег утратил все связи с тем, что осталось от суши, и находится в полной изоляции. Предположительно возобновляемые ресурсы Ковчега истощаются, и есть риск того, что власть сменится, и противостоящие социальные группы вступят в кровопролитный конфликт.
Напряжение растёт, а Охрана и Сопротивление ведут бой за власть над Ковчегом. Чью сторону примете вы?

I LOVED To The Moon and defended it against the "not a game" type of people. It had, at times, awful gameplay and a lot f times I just felt like throwing away my controller and close the game but it always pulled me back in with it's story.
This however I feel has all the bad things from To The Moon and almost none of the good things.
PROS:
- the soundtrack is very nice, it may not have a For River in it but none the less is very nice
- the visuals are nice, I especially like the transitions, and there is one place when you go from home to the school in a "corridor" kinda way, which I liked. It meant to symbolize that you do not want to go, you cannot wander around in the places you previously could, you HAD to go to school. Or at least that's what I got from that scene :) and I really liked it.
CONS:
- What disappointed me the most was the story. It was just meh. I was very hyped when I found out it was going to be a story told without any words, but it just didn't grab me. It was touching at times but very predictable and it didn't leave with anything. Months after I finished To The Moon I catch my self thinking about it but this is just a story about a lonely boy who saved a bird and remained as lonely as before.
- And finally the gameplay who managed to be even worse that To The Moon. You can only move a tile at a time and I constantly went to far before turning right or left. I know it was probably meant to be played with the keyboard and not with a controller but as long as it has controller support I think it should be  more optimized for it. Given that the only "gameplay" it has it's movement I expected to be more...OK. You push the left stick up and it plays an animation until it reaches the next tile, the problem is the tiles are quite large and if you want to move left or right you have to wait for the up animation to finish and then it moves you so you always end up on the tile above the one you wanted and more often than not I was kinda running in circles which is really frustrating and immersion breaking. I didn't try it with the keyboard and I don't intend to because I feel it's lazy from the part of the developer to not test and optimize it's game.
I know that it's a small indie team but movement on a grid has been around for more than 20 years and it's not rocket science.
So in conclusion I cannot recommend this game even though I was looking forward to it ever since I played To The Moon and I bought it in the first day it appeared on Steam. I feel the developer was just lazy at what makes a game be a game. I'm all for story oriented games, I love To The Moon, Gone Home, Dear Esther but those being "walking simulators" they did a very good job at the walking mechanics, this is just rubbish at it. Maybe if it was 1h long animated film I would have appreciated more, but it's not.

The result is a story that both engages and captivates, an object lesson to other games on how to tell a tale with subtlety and grace.

Really annoyed with myself that I got this. For some reason, the devs have decided to have a 1 save system, like FTL or other rogue like games. This means that you spend the first 10-20 minutes slowly building your base, and sitting around wait for ages, then if you mess up, you have to do it all over again... from scratch.
What's with developers making games that assume people have time to waste like this?
In my last game, I had a really good map, with what appeared to be a really good layout, and was progressing well. While I was waiting for my base to build a few things, I was looking around the level, only to suddenly notice a flash of red on my map. I scrolled back up to look at it only to see 15 zombies infecting all my tents (spawning new enemies) and instantly wiping out my base.
This was so early on that I had no walls, defences or turrets. The only thing I could have done is had people stood there defending that area, but they would have been overrun instantly with the sheer number that attacked.
You can allocate a group of soldiers a number, so Team 1, Team 2, etc... but if you ever put them in a tower, they lose that number, and you have to click on the tower to get them to come back out. Also, in the later game, you'd better hope you'd allocated your soliders with numbers, because if you haven't, good luck ever finding them again. Due to the bad AI, they can get stuck anywhere, and the inability to rotate the camera means if they're hidden behind a building, you'll likely never find them.
Yes, yes, it's early access... but I'm really struggling to find the fun. The game looks like it was designed in the 90's, with awful voice actors and dumb AI. Once, I told my people to return to my base, but instead of running through my claimed area, they found a shorter route... through a hoard of Zombies, and lead them all into my base. Why on Earth the developers allow the AI to plot a route through uncharted space is beyond me.
The ONLY impressive thing about this game is the number of on-screen sprites, but I guess that's their biggest selling point.
For me, everything else is just unbalanced gameplay mixed in with over the top micro-management.

Do you know Ocean City? Are you down with Ocean City? Are you for real? Really real? Really really...really....really real REAL? Then maybe you should play this game.
It's illegal street racing at its finest as you get behind the wheel of the sexiest imports. We're talking borsches, hamborghinis, ataris, and go-karts. Each of the 10 races features chills, spills, and speeds that'll leave you wearing adult diapers.
You wanna know how extreme it can get? Some of these courses are designed so that racers will get in head-on collisions! Can you believe that? I certainly can't, and I just experienced it firsthand. The races are twisted because everyone, is you, and you, are everybody. Is that deep or what? It's like you've just had this psychotic breakdown and now you're racing cars with your selves. I mean I'm just a generic guy with a goatee and cold dead eyes, but at least I don't look like Odo from Deep Space 9. Either that, or everyone was too focusing on delivering the ultimate racing experience. I'm guessing it was the latter.
....
....Alright I've had enough fun.

I had fun with it though, more fun than I've had with numerous polished videogames. I'm a big fan of open-world driving games like Burnout Paradise, Test Drive Unlimited, and the Crash Time games. Simply being able to goof off and get stupid with expensive-looking automobiles is perpetual entertainment to me.
I'm actually worried that eventually the developers of this game will fix it. It'll be complete, well-designed, and yet, something will be lost. I like making all the weird discoveries, such as finding the burger king ads, pedestrians more disturbing and with creepier animations than the last, and new ways to flip my car. Eventually all that might get taken away, and I'll be sad.
