Western devs taking over a mediocre japanese franchise and running it into the ground.
Let’s start with the positives. They fixed the stiff and slow controls from the first Lost Planet.
Now to the bad stuff. They added tons of unnecessary things that only hurt the game, such as the base where you start every mission. Running around the base only wastes your time and doesn’t add anything to the game. The need to return back to the base after a finished mission is similarly unnecessary and only adds frustration.
The fights against the monsters are in some ways better compared to the first Lost Planet. Monsters are more aggressive and can get in your face very quickly. But since the roll, a pretty useless move in LP1, is now extremely powerful, you can easily dodge most attacks. Overall the fights still aren’t very exciting. The added QTEs are annoying as well.
They also managed to completely ruin the mech aspect, which was, while still lacking, definitely one of the better things of LP1. Now your mech can’t even shoot anymore, all he can do is attack with his arms. You aren’t going to fight in the mech very often anyway. Most of the time you’re just walking around in it up to an arbitrary point, where the game forces you to leave it and continue on foot. The whole thing feels completely pointless and it seems that the only reason the devs added the mech was, because it was a part of LP1. Same story with the grappling hook, which can now only be used exactly at times the game tells you to use it.
The graphics are decent, though they certainly are a big step back in terms of style compared to LP1. The human faces and the mech as well as the armour of the main character look especially inferior to their japanese counterparts.
What made me quit this game very quickly, aside from everything mentioned so far, are the annoying characters, mainly the main character and his wife. Who in the world would want to play as this unfunny ugly familyman? The stupid cutscenes, where they send each other video messages, that interrupt the boring marchings with your mech during the snow storms, are the low point of the game.

TL;DR Overall a fairly solid puzzle game. 200 puzzles total, 100 of each type. Both feature multiple colors, although the colors only are a mechanic in the Fill-A-Pix type. In my opinion there's enough value here for the price (I got at least $0.50/hr). The game is not without its issues, though.
One of the first things you'll notice is the "give us your email" popup. This made me very angry, given the price of the game, since it seemed like you couldn't turn it off, only "not right now". The third popup, however, does give you that option. 3 annoying popups, meh, it could be worse.
The puzzle difficulty was pleasing to me, rarely being too easy (only the first 10-20 are 'very easy') and rarely being frustrating. That doesn't mean I didn't make a large number of mistakes causing me to restart puzzles, which brings me to my one major complaint:
As a Red/Green color blind person, I struggled quite a bit with the Pic-A-Pix puzzles. The colors used for completed numbers in the clues were sometimes so hard to see that it caused mistakes. Also, squares marked as empty are faded into a colored translucent square, which also was hard to distinguish at times from other colored parts of the puzzles. Crossed out clues and the use of 'X's for empty squares (perhaps as an optional color blind mode) would be VERY appreciated.
Other issues: Despite the appearance of a story, it is basically 10 locations on a map, each with a slight blurb about that location before the first puzzle. Don't expect anything in regards to story. Also, these random locations are not in any way marked with the exception of a name. If you quit the game and come back, it can be frustrating trying to remember which location you were working on. Click a location, see all the puzzles are complete, back out to the map. Click another... rinse and repeat until you find the right one. A simple checkmark or "path" or even a basic story you'd remember enough to know where you are would be great here.
Fill-a-Pix. Good price for 100 puzzles.

Ok, we all know the Amaze series.
We all know we all reviewed this series quite positively - it features lots of mazes, which get larger and different in shape, and you may spend hours to complete every single game 'cos the biggest levels are quite challenging.
Nothing spectacular or impossible, of course.. you just have to reach the center of the maze or the exit. It can actually become quite boring.
But this instalment is timed, and has two parts: you have to collect a key, and then reach the center of the maze.
Of course it's a tweak, so that the games aren't exactly the same, but actually the key thing adds nothing. I mean, it's no more go from A to B, it's go from A to B and then to C. And this makes every level at least twice as lengthy, which REALLY becomes annoying.. not to say that the key is a simple "tile" of the same color of the borders (and often similar to the background) so it can be frustrating when it's super small to even locate it.
And then on to the "time attack mode": it's really too challenging. I mean, it's "easy" if you first get the path to the key, die, repeat the path, die while you seek a way to get to the C point, but the timer is so ♥♥♥♥ing low that you still die and then on your fifth try you manage to rush to the exit.
And this makes the whole game unplayable and unenjoyable.
And then comes the surprise: you somehow learn that you can turn the timer off. I mean, you start timed, keep on playing timed, and then you go back to the menu and see that you can actually turn it off.
'Cos of course the developers saw that no one was capable to play this forcibly timed, and then turned it off.
So, why a negative review then?
'Cos this is actually Amaze 4 - it's the fourth game, the other three were already out for months. And you're making a time attack mode which is unplayable - it would be challenging, but the timing is so ridiculous that it makes you die ten times per level. So you turn it off.
Then you have the key. And so you have to spend twice or thrice the time on the same level.

All that can be said about how bizarre the premise is has already been brought up in other reviews, so I'm just going to skip right to the real question; is this game worth buying?
Pros:
-The story is surprisingly deep.  Once you get over how strange it is, it's a fascinating world, and even though you only see part of it, it feels like there's a lot more going on out there.
-The characters all have their own unique personalities; it's difficult to find yourself bored by them.  My least favorite route was still interesting enough for me to enjoy.
-Lots of replay value.  Each route that you take reveals a little more about the world, which, as I mentioned above, is quite fascinating.  Be sure to play again after getting all the endings.  It's definitely worth it.
-This story has both a great sense of humor, and a surprisingly good sense of drama.  Stick with it to the end, and I can almost guarantee that you will have shed at least a single tear over these characters.
-This is the only game of its kind, so I can say in no uncertain terms that this is the best pigeon dating simulation on the market.
Cons:
-The save feature is totally broken.  You're going to want to play through an entire route in one sitting, because loading a game won't actually work about half the time.  The game itself doesn't take THAT long, so it isn't a total deal-breaker, but it's probably one of the most frustrating things about the game.
-Despite the replay value, you're going to find yourself sitting through the same dialogue over and over again.  Each route has its own unique dialogue, too, but there are scenes that happen in every single playthrough regardless of your choices.  Mitigated somewhat by the fast forward button, but then you might end up missing some new dialogue by mistake.  That, and the fast forward still isn't that fast when you're sitting through the intro for the umpteenth time.
-If I remember correctly, three characters have both a normal and a true ending, and - unless by some incredibly stroke of luck, the save feature is actually working correctly for you - you're going to have to play through the exact same route making only slight alterations to your stat choices to get both.  I ended up getting the true ending for two out of the three the first time I played, so I ended up spending two entire, tedious games fast-forwarding through dialogue I'd already seen.  It would be a little forgivable if the endings were actually different, but the "true" ending is just the same exact ending with a single short, extra scene tacked on.  This is unnecessary padding; I wish they'd just count it as both endings if you got the true ending the first time.
Conclusion: This game has a fantastic story told through bits and pieces in various playthroughs, and a great sense of humor.  Endings range from predictable to totally out of left field.  You'll probably have a favorite pigeon by the end of it all.  Mine is Shuu.  :D  Still, fun as it is, it isn't without its flaws.  There IS content you can only unlock by getting all of the endings, and as I said, that can be a tedious process.  This content is well, WELL worth the effort, though; I can promise you that much.  Just make sure to use all the save slots in your final playthrough, since it's rather long, and if you have to quit in the middle of it, you don't want to put all your eggs in one basket.  In my experience, a save is more likely to work if a bird portrait isn't on screen behind it at the time, but that could just be a fluke.  Good luck with that.  ^^'  Anyway, I have to recommend this game, but do keep those issues in mind.  If you can, get the normal endings before the perfect ones so you'll at least have some new content to look forward to at the end of the second run.

If I reviewed this as a historical simulation and compared it to previous grand strategy games, it would almost definitely be a negative review. Instead, I will review this not as a historical simulation or a strategy game but as a creative outlet. I don't play Hearts of Iron IV for its historical accuracy or its strategic depth, because honestly it falls short in both departments when compared to its predecessors.
However, that doesn't mean I don't enjoy every minute I spend playing this title. I just mute the in-game music, turn on The Thieving Magpie Overture, and use the world map as a canvas for whatever historically ludicrous WWII-era fantasy world I can dream up. When I experienced the rush of seeing how the game responds to all of the 'what if' scenarios in my mind, coupled with some of the most intriguing mods I've ever seen including alternate history, WWI, WWII, and Cold War mods, I quickly realized just how wildly entertaining this game can be. And for that, I can only give a thumbs up.
Now on the other hand, I do despise this publishers current business practices. I am reluctant to ever to buy any of their DLC and I avoid paying full price for any of their games. I only paid sixteen dollars for this game and I refuse to buy any DLC unless it is on sale, so I certainly feel like I got my moneys worth.

Lost Planet has been a gaming franchise that I have loved for years. When I heard news about Lost Planet 3, I was completely looking forward to it. Though when it came out, it got mixed reviews, so I decided to wait for the price to drop before actually playing it, due to skepticism.
Lost Planet 3, puts you in the shoes of Jim Peyton, as man who gets a job on EDN III to harvest T-Energy so he can support his family. Jim is a likable protagonist, and I actually really enjoyed the storyline of Lost Planet 3 a bit more than past entries in the game. They also did a pretty good job on the cutscenes and it is a step in the right direction for the series. While the acting wasn't perfect, it was still pretty good.
The graphics in Lost Planet 3 are great, and it is what a Lost Planet game should look like. While they aren't the best out there, they are an improvement over it's predicessors.
Now the important part of this review, is the gameplay. It's good, but different. It definately does not feel like a Lost Planet game, for better and for worse. The gunplay felt a bit smoother than past entries, but the aiming isn't great as it could be, and overall it kind of loses that signature Lost Planet feel. Some of the animations like rolling and reloading also seem a bit clunky, and with a few minor tweaks they could have been far better than what they are. The mech combat is also somewhat shallow, but isn't bad. The enemies are very simmilar to past Lost Planet enemies, and if you enjoyed fighting them in past entries you'll find that these guys will be what you are expecting from a Lost Planet game.
Overall, I would have to say this entry is one step forward and one step back for the series. While the cinematics and graphics are great, the combat could use some work, but yet it does add some things that improved it. It's fun, but you should wait for it to come on sale, as it's difficult to reccomend at full price. If you are looking for an experience simmilar to past entries in the series, you won't find it here. Instead you'll find a fun Third Person Action Shooter game set in the Lost Planet universe. Hopefully, they'll take what they learned from branching out too far and use it to help make Lost Planet 4 better, and hopefully, more like Lost Planet 1 and 2.

I kind of wish there was more of a rating system in place in the review system, as it is, all I can do is state that I don't recommend this game, and the big red thumbs-down that comes with it seems a bit harsh for a game like this. It isn't bad, but overall, there's really only a small group of people I would recommend this game to, and for that, I'll go through a series of questions:
1. Did you play and enjoy "To The Moon"?
If your answer to this is "no", then you're already in the group I wouldn't recommend the game to. If you haven't played it, I'd recommend playing it, it's about 10 times the game A Bird Story is for only about twice the price. If you played it and didn't enjoy it, then there's really no hope for you to enjoy A Bird Story whatsoever. It's a somewhat similar style game, but there's much less to it, and it's a much less memorable experience overall. I played A Bird Story today and I can't even remember for sure if there was more than one song in the soundtrack, there must have been, because there's a soundtrack for sale in this game, but all the music sounded the same to me.
2. Does the idea of a story told with no dialogue, or even any text whatsoever, appeal to you?
This is the thing that nearly turned me away from the game altogether, it's an extremely unappealing concept to me. The story had to be kept extremely simple because of it, and even then, there are some parts that can be a bit confusing with no text of any kind explaining it, nothing major to the story, just a few little things. I can't really understand why the decision was made to make the game without text though, the only possible benefit to it I can see is that it would make localizing the game in countries that don't speak English extremely easy, you wouldn't even need to hire a translator.
3. Are you interested in the background of the patient in To The Moon's sequel?
I was, and that was the biggest influence in my decision to buy the game and play through it, but I'd say it's not worth being the big influence that it was to me. Really, after playing through the whole game, I still feel like I know next to nothing about the main character, there are a few character traits, but they would be so apparent that I'm sure they would have to be obvious in the next game, so you wouldn't miss out on anything by skipping this. At least, I don't think you would, I can't say for sure until the next game is released, so I can come back and update this review then.
4. Do you like really simple short stories?
I'm kind of on the fence for this question, I don't mind a simple story in general, but it feels like in a story-driven game, the story should have at least some depth to it. I didn't find this story to have any, really. Basically, read the description for this game, and try to predict exactly how the story plays out based on that short description. I'd be willing to bet more than 90% of people's guesses would be right in line with how the story goes. I mean, the description of the game does specifically state that it's a "simple story", even with that in mind, I didn't expect it to be as simple as it was.
---
Basically, if you answered yes to all those questions, I would definitely recommend this game to you.
If you answered yes to most of them, you might want to think twice about it. The developer does have a refund policy if you're completely unsatisfied. I won't be asking for a refund as I was okay with the game as a whole, I just found it underwhelming.
If you answered mostly no to these questions, I wouldn't even consider buying it. Even if you play through it and go get a full refund, it wouldn't even be enjoyable enough to you to be worth the time spent playing it.

A wonderful visual story that is told entirely without words, using only motion, gestures, signs, and daydreams. Daydreams are the central theme of this story. I have rarely seen such an intelligent use of imagery, and I suspect many people won't get all of its meanings.
For example: In class, the blackboard shows the square root of some number, and it equals the drawing of a cat. It is only a little tidbid in the background, but shows that our character is not interested in school, does not pay attention and perhaps only remembers what he draws in his sketchbook - a cat in this case. We only experience what he remembers, and so his daydreams and reality turn into a mixture that we see on the screen.
To our character, school life is a cage that he wishes he could break out of and fly away. As we walk him through his daily routine, we also walk through his daydreams, often not remembering the real way through town that he took. One day, he discovers an injured bird in a clearing. It is a symbol of his wish for freedom, and as he takes care of the animal, we see them bond and become the best of friends, exploring the dreams of flying away together.
A Bird Story is not a game, it is a story that you participate in through simple actions. It is a touching and amusing prelude to the future sequel of "To The Moon", for our character is going to be the patient in the next installment of the series.
Anyone who loves nature or spends their days dreaming will bond with this story and its characters.

I didn't really know what to expect when trying The Bureau - I'm a big fan of the XCOM series, but I had my doubts about how it would translate into the TPS genre. The game was a surprise for me, and a pleasant one at that. If you're into tactical shooters and like the XCOM theme, I recommend giving a shot to this title!
Pros:
+ Exciting tactical combat (not unlike Mass Effect 3's combat system)
+ Well executed tactical mechanics and UI
+ The atmospheric setting of a 1960s secret service
+ Challenging enough
+ The XCOM base provides a nice transition between missions
+ Some pretty nice and brave twists at the ending
+ Environmental storytelling really shined every now and then
Cons:
- In the early period of my walkthrough my squad mates fell way too easy (on Veteran difficulty), so much that in many cases I had to order them to stay the hell behind so that they don't die on me (which isn't exactly how I imagine tactical combat). However, once the team (and I) got a bit more effective, this wasn't an issue any more, and the AI became slick and knew what it was doing
- Though this genre can be used prety well for bonding with squad mates, it felt to me that The Bureau didn't really try making me care for my soldiers, even though that is a crucial part of the original XCOM
- Lore-wise this prequel pretty much felt like an afterthought, as I just can't see how could this incident not be mentioned during an invasion a mere 50 years later... They couldn't have classified it that well!

In my first few days playing Toribash, I had no idea how to play it, what everything did, and ended up losing even in free play. What I have to say though, is that the gameplay is very smooth, and the physics behind it are edited to the perfect point. Even if the collisions and dismemberment can differ greatly to real-world physics, the game does a splendid job incorporating that into the gameplay. The controls aren't hard to learn, and after a while you can even start trying to create your own mods or levels. True, this game is hard to pick up, but the speed it takes for you to learn it is about the same as any other game, such as League.
I would recommend new players to spend some time on YouTube as well, to see some possible strategies or how the controls work out. Not just the move tutorials, but also the tournaments and competitions.
Some general tips I have for new players:
Play both free play and multiplayer, and don't be afraid to experiment with some of the mods. You can even try playing against yourself in free play.
Try different playstyles, such as grappling or striking, holding or relaxing.
And finally, don't bother challenging Uke. You probably can't beat him when you start, and by the time you can beat him you don't even need to try to beat him.
By the way... Toribash should add multiplayer, not like multiplayer 1v1, but multiple people in the same match.

Games like Fall of Setarrif really bring me to think that some guys in the development team didn't know what they were doing. The flaws of this game are so obvious that they scream in your face. The AI is dead stupid. When the enemies go into attack mode, you can dodge on the side and continue attacking while they aim where you last stood. At times enemies fail to attack you at all and just stand there while you're finishing them off.
Another thing that bugs me is the loot, or rather the lack of it. The environment is rich in detail but you can only interact with a fraction of it. I also noticed that when you loot clothes, amulets and rings, the game sometimes replaces them with items you've already equipped. The stats of the equipment seemed higher in a way so I'm thinking if the game was programmed to do you a favor. I sometimes discovered that my character was wearing some amulet with very good mana stats and the amulet with decent health and armor stats was placed in the inventory.
Then there were those little logical flaws that were ok 10-15 years ago, but start to appear as amateurish when you still see them now. Example: a guy is locked up in a bamboo cage, you have to help him out. What does your character do? He asks where they keep the key. I mean, c'mon, I'm sending archdemons to the abyss here, if you need a key for a bamboo cage then I've got this magic ore battleaxe here, just take one step back. Or on other occasions you're fighting off 30 feet tall trolls and sending exploding fireballs towards a swarm of enemies, yet can't climb a wooden fence. I wish games were past such nonsense and come up with something better.
On top of everything they also didn't fix the moon gravity. The nameless hero keeps floating through the air. I guess they thought it looks cool. So cool that you don't get tired of it till the end of the game.

Someone in the development team did they're job.
I decided to lable it as a negative review only for one reason. Throughout the game I kept thinking about the flaws and bugs and what they might have done better. Portal is an instant classic and paved the way for a new approach to first person puzzle games. It's a game worth digging up every few years, replaying the levels and enjoying the narration.
The puzzles are wonderfully logical, yet require a pinch of dexterity and timing. With every level, the complexity increases incrementally so that finding and executing the solutions holds a good balance between challenge and success. After completing certain levels of the main game, advanced versions of those levels with revised conditions or levels with goal-based challenges can be played.
Subject to its setting, Portal builds a visually and aurally dense atmosphere. Besides the fitting ambient sound, the voice acting is superbly done. Thanks to the witty dialogue written for her, the narrator and antagonist GLaDOS is hilarious. Also, the catchy credit song “Still Alive” still gets to me on a monthly basis ...
The only nitpicky nuisance in the game is the typical Source engine carrying technique. Accidentally letting go of picked up items because of jumps or weird collision detection can be mildly frustrating. Apart from that though, Portal is perfect.
Portal should be in everyone's library, as it's nothing short of a timeless epitome of PC gaming.

Hearts of Iron IV a great strategy game. You can play as any country basically in the WW2 era and the differences between countries is tremendous. Every country has a unique tech tree (although most have the same type of setup). It's interesting how there's 3 main factions battling each other most of the time (Allies, Axis, Comintern) and you can choose to be any one of the 3 political stances, Democratic, Fascist, Communist or then neutral if you want to avoid getting attacked by huge alliances.
Co-Op/multiplayer I found to be super fun and I'd say the game is way better if you have someone else to play with (at least for a few playthroughs), you can forge very powerful alliances or get a big friend group to play against each other.
The game basically revolves around war though and it's not really possible to play peacefully or defensively, it's just not fun whatsoever. The combat system might be underwhelming for some since it's just a bubble showing whether your troops are winning or the enemy. Your combat effectiveness is decided by logistics, terrain, support from air forces and of course how advanced your troops and weaponry are.
You can play the game from 1936 where the game will not follow history mostly and there can be some very interesting alliances and events, or you can start from 1939 if you want a more historically accurate game.  If you play with Germany vs playing with a small South-American country you're going to have vast differences in gameplay, so you can choose how you want to play the game. Some want to start with huge amounts of factories and manpower and be able to take over countries instantly and some want to fight against all odds with a less influential country.
You have to take into account land, air and often sea to gain an upper hand on your opponents. You need to have fighters/anti-air to counter your opponent's airforce, bombers to help your infantry gain an upper hand, infantry obviously to capture areas and cause the heavy casualties, and ships to block off the enemy's supply convoys, foreign aid, destroy carriers and whatnot.
In the late game though the game becomes almost unplayable. The lag becomes so bad that it doesn't matter whether you're playing on the fastest time setting or the slowest because they both go at the same speed. Peace is in my opinion done very poorly. You'd think that the 2 major things in the game are war and peace but even starting a peace negotiation is impossible 90% of the time. The AI is definitely not as smart as you'd hope in a game all about strategy and how intelligently you play your country.
Most of the tech tree is the same with all countries but even the ones that have differences like the models of your tanks, the vehicles still have largely the same stats as other countries (eg. Russian tanks having the same stats as US ones).
Overall if you can get the game on a discount I think it's worth it but the game has a lot of things it could improve on. (Hopefully things that are going to get improved later on and not with 20€+ DLCs.)

Great game, except it is a bug-ridden horse***t. Heard a lot of good things about this game. I'm guessing it got worse as time went on?
The game feels more like early access or beta test version, and only couple hours into playing I encountered a "two captains" bug which forced me to kill my best crew member. Aside from crew randomly failing to get on board the ship correctly and plunging into their deaths - which apparently is part of the game design -, I encountered random mutiny bug late game when I got about 18 crew members, and had to resort to constantly loading/saving the game which was extremely frustrating that I finally gave up.
More about the bugs:
Two captains bug - it happens when you load/restart the day in the midst of battle; your "first mate" becomes the new capptain, while the old captain is still alive. You effectively have two guys with [C] on top of their heads, and the bottomleft side health/hunger/morale HUD constantly flickers between the old and the new captains. I tried looking into editing the xml savefile to no avail. The only way out was to kill one of them.
Random mutily bug - Someone in the crew keep mutinying randomly even though morale/hunger gage are full and I constantly pay their salaries every two minutes. It started happening after I hired bunch of new guys to train as♥♥♥♥♥♥removers while I train my older crew to man the guns, and it's extremely frustrating because the one who mutiny is chosen completely at random including my old crew whom I've invested in significantly. It happens while sailing, while onboard enemy ship, while on land/town/tavern you name it. Again I tried virtually everything including teaching everyone to clean and poop less, increasing the ship size to almost twice the screen width, installing sword stations to keep them busy and separated, etc.. - oh and of course paying them every two minutes and stocking♥♥♥♥♥♥load of rum and food. At first I suspected a sudden and synchronized pooping of 20 pirates caused flash crash in morale, so I taught every one of them to clean and poop properly; no not it. I installed 5 pictures and 3 plants and separated them into groups of 6~7 across the ship; no not that either. I even went into xml file and changed crew traits that are potentially negative such as 'liar', 'greedy', etc., and increased friendship points; still happens. We take down Lv.8 pirate ship and the captain is busy running around enemy ship looting chests and urns, and one of my oldest and best guy (lv 40) decides to "go bad" in the middle of 18 other guys and kills himself instantly.
Few other bugs/quirks that are worth mentioning:
- Ransom kills do not increase "renown" points. It says it does in the game, but in the savefile it is stuck at 0.
- Stations that increase pirate stats, such as swords, books(?), and grinding wheels are almost unusable because they are like pirate magnets; all my fishermen guys are busy sweating with swordplay and end up starving the crew.
- Cannot place cannonballs at sea and must dock to place them. why?? also since when cannonballs are called "bombs"? Never would've figured that out on my own.
- When you try to move few pirates at once, one or two always ends up not getting the order and stay behind.
- Teaching swimming is a must since when you move a large group of guys(~10+), one or two will always end up slipping and falling into the sea; and this is without "careless" trait, mind you.
- Other minor interface glitches: After selling the same items a few time (such as wooden block) sound is gone. You feel like something is broken but it's not. When you close shipbuilding interface while placing a block, block info HUD remains on the screen. Come on guys, these are pretty basic stuff.
All in all it was pretty interesting game; with great potential. I really enjoyed the game otherwise I wouldn't have played it over ten hours and tried so hard to "fix" it somehow. However the game has some very serious shortcomings, such as unfriendly and glitchy user interface, broken game mechanics, and some serious bugs that could completely ruin your experience. For that I'd give it 4 out of 10. I personally believe this cannot be a production version, v1.0+. If it were early access/dev beta I would've understood, but this isnt. Lastly, from now on I'll ignore any "official" reviews that gave this buggy software 10/10 and go straight to reading customer reviews first. "Mostly positive".. Wow.

Quake, twenty years on, is still an amazing game that has endured the test of time. I played it for the first time only last year and I enjoyed it immensely. The gameplay is incredibly fast and smooth--it differs itself from Dooms methodical room-clearing by being all about movement. The only way to play this game is on the hardest difficulties, when rooms filled with obsticales are littered with dozens of enemies and you're utilizing the game's fast paced movements and gravitational physics to bounce around at high speeds, doging projectiles and spraying bullets everywhere. Quake is a punishing game that rewards constant vigilance with your movement, and it's what makes the game shine. Every level is intense on an emotional and logical level, so no encounter is ever dull or boring. It's immensely rich, gameplay-wise.
Aesthetically, the vistuals are naturally dated, but I think this works in the game's favor. If Doom was that excitable 80s metal head who's presence demands attention, Quake is that mid-90s industrial loner in the corner, brooding quietly. The levels are a mishmash of industrial gothic castles and cathedrals, but the atmosphere itself is a perpetual sense of nihilism and dread. The choppy and rusty graphics just work in favor of the game's visuals.
This is aided immensely by Trent Reznor's work on the sound design. The sound effects are meaty, the guns sound piercing and LOUD, as they should, and grabbing an ammo box gives such a satisfying CHH-CHH sound that I can still hear it now. It's not just the sound effects either--the music is also equally amazing. It's one of the best ambient-droning-industrial soundtracks out there for video games, and the fact that it's not somehow packaged in the Steam release is an absolute shame, since I can't imagine ever playing this game without music. If you are going to buy it on here, get a CD of the game and keep it in your harddrive, or use the music pack mods. I cannot stress that enough. Playing this game without the gloomy, screeching soundtrack takes away so much to what this game already has to offer.
Playing Quake is like seeing all the rings on the inside of a tree-stump for late 90s, early 2000s PC FPS games. Absolutely play it.

I picked this game up for 2.99 so I am taking that into account in this review, and I think it is probably even worth full price.
The game is, in a nut-shell a poor man's Mass Effect set in the Xcom universe's version of the 60's. The atmosphere is good, and the game itself is 'ok' in so far that it is almost good at a lot of things. It doesn't quite manage to pull off what it wants to though, but still falls into the 'ok' category.
Most of what I am about to say is negative, because the game is so close to being good that I am disappointed in how it turned out, but I would still say buy the game - especially if you are a fan of xcom or mass effect, or perhaps only if you fall into those camps.
Combat is tough, at least early on which is where I am, because you are vastly outgunned and frequently find enemies that you can hardly hurt. You are also forced (Pretty close to forced anyway) into an Alien shotgun if you want to kill those enamies, and personally I hate shotguns. I expect when you unlock more guns the game will improve, but I haven't made it through that far yet.
The big issue with combat for me is that when you bring up the orders menu the camera isn't the most responsive, and since time isn't fully paused it can lead to you giving messed up orders (Such as sending one man left and the other right when you want them both down the same flank).
AI is also pretty poor too, especially for your own team who have a bad habit of getting their heads blown off when they should be in cover.
Character development is a miss since you only have one progression tree to go down. Why you go down that tree makes sense, but I like more options in my games.
The other miss is the research element from the base xcom series, here you just find the odd gun lying around. They make an explanation for why you can pick up some but not other, but it is a bit half hearted.
So overall there is a good game trying to get out from under a not quite there exterior, worth playing, worth the £10-15 they are asking, but probably not much more, Go in knowing what you are getting, and you will come out with hope for The Bureau 2 (If they ever make it) rather than disappointment at this one.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a vapid tactical TPP shooter.
Unless you are a die hard XCOM fan, keep out.
And even if you are, it'll most likely leave you dissatisfied.
PROS:
+ the setting
+ little details(squaddies going on a smoke break if standing idle for a while, the protagonist's hat falling off his head when suffering major damage)
+ the story has some cool twists
CONS:
- the gameplay
- imbalanced difficulty(once you get the hold of alien weaponry- the odds skyrocket in your favour)
- very limited soldier customization
- zero mission diversity
I've completed the game for the sole reason of feeding my inner XCOM fanboy while waiting for the release of XCOM 2.
The game starts slow and makes a horrible first impression.
I couldn't resist the feeling that Declassified is suffering from a disturbing case of schizophrenia;
not knowing whether it wants to be an action TPP title or a tactical cover-based shooter.
It fails at both.
Gotta admit- after pushing myself through the first 2 or 3 missions it started growing on me, mainly because of the awesome setting.
However, it isn't enough to make The Bureau a good game.
So much locked potential remaining.
Would love to play a solid TPP XCOM shooter one day.

text: It's nearly impossible to live up to such a gem like To The Moon so Kan Gao obviously tried to take a step in another direction with A Bird Story. I liked the game for having no dialogue and also for being shorter than To The Moon. But the overall story is by no means as rich as the latter's.

Don't buy this if you are expecting some sort of a game with puzzles and interesting game mechanics. As the developer puts it, this is an interactive pixel-animated story and that's exactly what it is. The interactions are very minimal and if you're going to spend your money on this product, you have to do so knowing what to expect. This is a very simple and sweet short story about a boy and a bird. There's no complex twists or lines of dialogue. The art and music are great and provide contextual tone and emotion to the story.
(Resolution is 640x480, limited by the RPG Maker engine. Again, know what to expect and you'll probably enjoy it for what it is.)

Each item to seek comes with a single clever hint to suggest its location. The game is better played by meticulously observing the environment and following this tip than by poking at any random thing.
Deciphering the hints and exploring the map is quite congenial since the world is filled with small surprises and amusing details, so even clicking on the wrong reactive target can be rewarding.
I expected more sequential puzzles, such as series of events to trigger in a specific order. For the most part, items are obtained with a single click, or never more than a handful (with a few exceptions). Making future areas more deeply interactive in upcoming updates would strengthen the game's solid but basic formula.
Maps range from incredibly tiny to overwhelmingly large. On the latter type, a few rare items can be barbarously difficult to find.
There is no pressure to complete challenges or timers to ruin the relaxing mood, making this the perfect game to play in small doses to wind down at the end of a day.

Loved this game when Storm Legion came out and vanilla, bought Nightmare Tide but never tried it!  Though, I did love the idea to take the fight to the planes, but I couldn't help feel like they could have expanded Telara and not have killed off Regulos so quick.
PROS:
-Enjoy the art style on a lot of things, some armor is just bad
-Costume system is great
-Dimensions/Housing is great
-Rift "public events" are nice
-Adventures are great way to level up if you already have done quests in the past and wanna skip

-Potential lore and new content
-Fortresses look like a potentially great content if worked on
CONS:
-Lack of multiple Dungeon finder/Raid finder roulettes like you would see in FFXIV that would make people WANT to participate regardless of what level that dungeon is
-Missed opportunities with Telara, could be expanded on and make us actually care why we are trying to save this world
-Missed opportunities with Port Scion
-Missed opportunities with Time Travel
-Missed opportunities with the Eth Empire
-Missed opportunities with Storm Legion's Empire that was destroyed
-Vanilla zones could use a make over and better flushed out

-Sound Effects with combat, especially melee attacks not sounding pretty weak

-Dungeons can be rather boring last I played, nothing like FFXIV's dungeons

-Wished the combat was slower like FFXIV
Despite a lot of con's I have listed, most are my personal wish list, it is still a great game to play!

I've been playing a lot of Choice of Games products lately and feel like this falls squarely in the middle of the pack. Reading through the other reviews, some seemed a little harsh.  I do think this is a game suited for people who like shows like "Smallville" and are happy to stick in the straight middle between silly/hillarious and dark/edgy.   My biggest criticism would be that I felt most of the side characters were a little hollow and didn't feel as attached to them as I have in other CoG games like Choice of Robots, Tin Star, and Ratings War.

In a way it made me think of "Buffy the vampire slayer" : a group of teenager led by a powerful main character and some more or less useful support characters fighting an evil plot lurking under highschool all the while living the drama of teen years. It's funny and really teen-like, believable. The characters and the story do lack a little depth here and it's still far from matching the epicness of something like "Buffy" but still it is nicely written.

This game is, how would I say, "unpolished." The AI is horrendously inconsistent, pathfinding is absolutely awful, and the game sports the most unfriendly UI I have ever has the displeasure of using.
As an example, let me walk you through the string of actions necessary for one of your pirates to say, read a book on how to better crap on the deck of your ship.
STEP 1: Hit 'esc' to bring up the main menu
STEP 2: In the left menu bar, click on the 'crew' option.
STEP 3: Click on the crewman in question
STEP 4: On the middle left of the crewmember stat page, find and click on the 'passive equip' slot of his inventory
STEP 5: On the left had side under the menu bar, scroll through your entire inventory (as the game glops every single inventory item, useable, equipabble, or not, into one big list) to find the specific skill book and click on it.
The way to even USE items I had to google, as the game provides no instruction and no intuitive path to find any of this information.
Crew behavior also seems to follow a very linear order of operations that neither makes sense or is controllable in any way, save for limiting resources such as grindstones or training swords. Spending half an hour configuring what seems to you as a effeciently laid out ship with easy access to cannons turns out to waste half of your shooting phase as your gunners scramble up and down ladders in some feeble attempt to imitate 'Donkey Kong.' Skills sometimes have to be dropped just to force certain crewmembers into certain behaviors.
At $5 dollars during the steam sale, this game did at least provide some entertainment, but I can't help thinking that my money would have been better spent on four chocolate bars or three bunches of bananas.

There is something I feel needs to be said about these, given the nature of some of the negative reviews. They are books. They are not games in the sense of playing with graphics and sound and such. CoG got its start on kindle, which is where I first found them, and since then, they have made quite the impressive library of chose your own adventure books in the style of old: Pure, immersive, branching narrative. If you like to read, and love a story that feels like you control it, then you will like Choice of Games in general (though some individual stories are duds.) but please understand that it takes a lot of work and effort to get a story that does allow this level of interactivity, and given the nature of the games, I think they generally do a tremendous job of it.
In addition, they tend to release a demo of the first few chapters, and sell each individual book at a very low price. I think that these games are a good buy, and enjoy them quite a bit. They have multiple authors, and each has their own unique style, so even if one of the game books does not catch your interest, download one of the other free demos, and don't let one of them being bad push you away from the company in general.

A short, simple story about a boy who meets a bird, and goes on a whimsicle journey together.
A fan of Freebird's previous work, To the Moon, I came to the understanding that this isn't supposed to be anything like a sequel or a full game.
But to me, there is a fine and skewed line to what can be called an 'interactive story' and a 'game', and it doesn't really impress me to cover it up with the words 'interactive pixel animation'.
Now, before you jump to conclusions - yes, I did enjoy the general feel of this game. The artwork was smooth, the controls felt acceptable, the soundtrack and sound effects were beautiful. It impressed me up until the point where the words 'interactive' were introduced.
The story follows a boy, seemingly walking a blurred line between his imagination and reality, finding a bird, and going on a whimsicle journey together. I have to qualms with the story, although it didn't really strike me much, but the interactions of the adventure felt limited to one or two directions - the game often popped up a little box showing you which direction keys, or enter/space, to press, at what time. Sure enough, you can walk up, down, left and right if you want, but you're still forced to take a certain direction to progress the story. I know it is required if you're an 'interactive pixel animation' to keep the story going, but it felt more like you were being ordered to do soemthing rather than properly interact with the pixel animation. Go left. Press space. Go right. Keep going right. Although the music gives the player some emotion whilst going through it, I was left just keeping my finger on one of the directional buttons, only to be distracted if I bumped into a tree or something. I'm not going to lie, the 'waiting period' I experienced whilst keeping my finger depressed on a directional button was met by some anticipation to get it over with. Maybe I just didn't have the patience, but a lot of it was just going back and forth, and I felt it didn't really add much to the story.
And that's another area I think the game fell short on as well - the story. It's slightly interesting, but at the same time I don't think it conveys the ideas Kao had in mind. One minute you're in your apartment, and the next you're in school, and then you're in a mixture of both - yes, the symbolism and 'blurred line between imaginary and reality' does play a part in this, but I don't think it really has a purpose. Why is this boy blurring his lines? What do the treetops coming out of the lockers mean? What is it actually meant to symbolize? With these burning questions in my mind, I became less and less intrigued with the story. It was good for the start, but I think it didn't need to keep 'blurring the lines' so constantly - so much that it was a blur altogether.
A Bird Story does have some good ideas in mind, but at this price I don't think it adds up. It isn't bad at its core, but the amalgamation of all its shortfalls makes it an 'experience' that tests your patience rather than immerse you in story. It has great art and music, and I can tell a lot of effort went into the sound effects and background art, but the linearity of the story doesn't quite do it justice. That being said, Freebird is at least offering a refunds policy to people that feel genuinely ripped off, so that's nice of him.
From this game, I can only partially see what to expect in To The Moon's sequel, but unfortunately it was hampered by what could have been a great preview of it. I wish all the people at Freebird all the best, and I'm having high hopes for To The Moon's sequel despite me feeling underwhelmed by this game.

The only real way to talk about this game is to wax poetic about the story. Suffice it to say, if you have an hour to kill, enough spending cash to buy lunch, and at least a single empathetic cell in your body, you should give A Bird Story a shot.
Spoilers below:
Overall, I feel the story works. In To The Moon, Ken Gao stripped almost all 'gamey' elements in order to tell a relatively uninterrupted story. A Bird Story feels like the logical extension of that trend by stripping away all dialogue, opting to tell the story through pantomime and the distortion of reality. What I mean by this is the main character, an estranged little boy, is somewhat of an unreliable narrator. We perceive the game world through the filter of his imagination. Environments blend, objects shift, and minor characters are faceless almost as if we're experiencing his dream.
This works... mostly. It's certainly a unique way to present the story but sometimes confuses what is actually happening in the real world. Perhaps that was the point. Another issue I have is the comedy bit. It just didn't work for me. To The Moon had some wonderful moments of levity because they were based around characters we got to know. Here, it felt like an overly long homage to the Benny Hills/Scooby Doo chase scene that came out of nowhere and broke the mood Ken spent 40 minutes building.
Anything I say about the ending will become immediately irrelevant once the full sequel puts it into full context. Taken on its own, I thought it was alright. I got misty eyed but by no means did I go full tears like THAT SCENE from To The Moon.
Just play it. It's $4.25 right now. That's like- a urine sample sized drink from Starbucks.

The concept of this - creating an FPS out of a different genre whilst retaining a number of elements from the original - reminded me of Command & Conquer: Renegade (anybody else remember that?). I recall the fun of walking around and in a Hand of Nod and being pretty excited about it. Decent game, that, though a bug meant I never did finish it.

Anyway, this takes some of the things we know and love about X:Com (a base, an Avenger, Sectoids, laser and plasma weapons etc) and turns it into a Mass Effect-lite squad-based shooter. You have companion agents, some rudimentary squad management and abilities and (limited) command in the field. I say limited because, whilst you can move your teammates to exploit flanking opportunities, as soon as you move, they move with you, thus negating any positioning you set-up - the AI for them isn't great.

It's far from perfect - it's not exactly a looker, there isn't a great deal going on with the environments (it's small-town America, a farm or an alien base pretty much), there's not anything to actually anything to do in the base and it's never anything more than walk forward, shoot, walk some more on missions.

Still, I found this to be quite fun. The story was decent, though completely silly, there is variety in the skills you and your teammates get, numerous weapons (though you'll probably stick to 2 or 3 favourites) and the various systems all work.

Given that game had a rather torturous development it turned out ok; at least, for the £3 or so I got it for, I certainly got value for money.

This game is headed for the grave. Maybe this time it won't get revived for a cash-in.
Some backstory: I'm one of the people who bought the original Evolve (on PS4, since I didn't have a good PC at the time, just add ~40 hours to my playtime). I bought the game for $60, and also bought the Hunting Season Pass for (I believe, it's been a long time) $25. The game had balancing issues and a f*ck ton of cosmetics, but I could look past this since it was new, different, and the devs had promised that new game modes and maps would be free. The balancing got worse, the gameplay got repetitive, the only new game mode they added was complete sh*t, but I was able to look past all that. Until I discovered that the "Season Pass" I had bought (which, again was $25- $5 less than the Fallout 4 season pass I would later buy that gave 2 dlcs with entirely new areas and stories + a bunch of workshop dlcs that were varying degrees of fun) only unlocked 1 TIER OF HUNTERS- the rest, I would have to pay more for later. It was then that I came to and realised that Evolve was a giant scam designed by the publisher to milk consumers for as much money as possible and poorly handled by developers who acted like they had no idea what game design even was. I immediately stopped playing Evolve, and didn't even think of returning until Stage 2.
So, fast forward to Evolve Stage 2, what has changed? The new microtransaction update proves that nothing has changed- it's still a scam, but now it's a "free" scam. An update or two ago, the devs made everything in the store 3x more expensive; now the most recent update added microtransactions which, according to my math, prices a single hunter at $10 (the hunters vary in pricing, so I used the price that looked like the average (1050 keys). So now, it's near impossible to get new hunters without spending a stupid amount of money to do so. -Please note this review is for an older version of the game-
I was unsure about this game when I purchased it. I got it on sale for about $3, so I didn't spend too much. I went through three phases whilst playing this game:
-1) When I first started playing this game, I thought it wasn't too bad but it also wasn't too good.
-2) I got a little more into the game and thought it was pretty fun (this was about 2 hours in).
-3) I played for long enough to get pretty powerful and realized there was little content to this game (about 8 or 9 hours in).
-Note: This review talks mostly about easy mode for the game.
The main point of the campaign is to kill the 4 main "pirate lords." Basically, you are supposed to build a large ship, gather a massive crew, and then sail to the locations of these pirate lords and either take or destroy their ship. Pretty simple right?
Yeah, it is simple. Just like the rest of the game. Getting there isn't too hard, it's just time consuming.
There are 3 different types of map encounters:
-1) Islands
-2) Pirate ships
-3) Pirate lord ships
Every map encounter has a difficulty rating. The further you are from the island you start out from, the higher the rating. Every Pirate lord has a rating of 10. If you know the difficulty rating of something, what is the point to playing? If I know I can only take on a rating of 7, then I know how and when not to die. If I know what I'm getting into, there is no challenge and it has no fun factor. I just know I need to stay around the ratings of 7 until I get powerful enough to take on an 8. Hence, this game isn't hard; rather, it is just a huge waste of time.
You have to travel between these different map encounters. The game does NOT deposit you from one destination to another. Rather, it makes you sit through a "sailing" screen where you wait for your crew and ship to drive to the distination you designated. The game MAKES you wait seconds to minutes (depending on how far you are traveling) to even get to your destination. This is not the fast-paced action-packed swashbuckling game I believed I was getting.
Let's start off talking about islands. There are three main types you are going to encounter:
-1) Town islands
-2) Regular islands
-3) Small islands
Town islands are the same size regardless of the town. Town islands and regular islands are also the same. These towns have randomized buildings on them. These buildings range from an armory, a library, to taverns. Each shop buys and sells certain things. You can hire men from the taverns and get skills at the library (more on that later). Every town island follows this pattern.
Regular islands are the same size as town islands as I stated above. These islands usually have some sort of enemies on it (i.e. pirates, tribal men, spiders, etc). They also usually have some wild animals. Lastly, they always have a "point of interest." These points of interests could be palm trees, tribal poles, chicken farms, etc. When you inspect these points of interest, something happens. This could be some enemies jumping out to kill you, animals being freed, fruits being dropped, etc. Every island of this type follows this exact pattern.
Small islands are MUCH smaller than the regular islands; seriously, they are like the size of small ships. They usually have some sort of castaway or hobo that will instantly attack you on sight. They also usually have a palm, banana, etc tree that drops fruit when you inspect it (this is like the point of interest on the big islands). Every small island follows this pattern.
Lack of content? I think so since it lacks different island sides and different patterns.
Let's move on to pirate encounters. There aren't too many different types of pirate ships. The difficulty rating of the encounter generally dictates how many pirates are on the ship, how much hp they have. and what type of ship it is. These ratings don't always hold true, however. For example, I had an encounter that was probably level 2 or 3. The pirates were easy, but they were driving this MASSIVE ship.
When you defeat pirates, you can do 1 of 2 things to their ship:
-1) Plunder it
-2) Steal it
If you plunder a ship, you automatically get 90(+). Sometimes you get more gold the stronger the pirates were. You also get some ship parts to improve your ship (more on this later).
If you steal the ship, you take the valuables off your ship and leave your old ship behind. You don't get the gold, but you do get the ship.
Now let's talk about the crew. Your captain and crew know basically nothing when they start out; they don't even know how to poop properly or clean up after themselves. The skills they learn need to be bought from a library. So you are telling me I need to travel to the local library to know I shouldn't poop in my living/eating space? This game believes so! It takes 1 out of the 2 level up points you get to learn a new skill. Some skills are pretty important (i.e. cooking) while others are stupid or not needed (i.e. pooping correctly).
Leveling up isn't too bad in this game. You get 2 level up points to dump into stats. These stats change your crew; they become more powerful and better. Yet, it just seems so generic.
The crew also has a morale rating. The lower their morale, the higher chance of a mutainy. OH! Did I mention that their poop, if not cleaned up, will drop their moral. Something you can't control at the start of the game will ruin your crew's moral. However, you can restore their moral by paying their wages or giving them nice things like booze or tobacco. If you don't keep killing things and pludering, you will have no money to pay the wages, let alone get more men and things for them.
The crew also likes to eat A LOT. Be prepared to use a lot of your funds to stock up on food.
These different aspects of the crew make them the most unique part of this game. They all have a backstory and a personality, even if it doesn't change the gameplay. Their stats are random but generally fair.
Let's continue to the ship customization. Every time you plunder a ship, you get ship parts. You can also buy ship parts from stores in towns. You can make your ship however you like. This is about the only real variety in the game that I saw. I could make a really cool ship from the parts of the ships that I killed. Pretty nifty. But after awhile, I realized that there aren't that many parts for the ship. There are cannons, sure. Masts are cool. Wheels to guide the ship are nice. But so what? If you only have a few things to really customize your ship with, it doesn't make it all that customizable. This part of the game is fun and all, but it still lacks content.
Now I want to talk about the graphics. I LOVE pixel graphics. This game has some pretty fun graphics to it. Yet, it is TOTALLY ruined by a fog-like blur. There are ways to less this blur, but it still remains rather blurry. I prefer a crisp line over a blury one. This game doesn't have that. It forces you to look through a fog to play this game.
The sounds for this game can be fun. But listening to them say their catchphrases over and over in their tiny voices will drive you mad. The soundtrack can be epic at times while not living up to expectations at other times.
P.S. This game did not have tutorials for most of the game. It basically just told you how to move.
So what happens when you win? I don't know. I wasn't about to sit here playing this game any longer and grind my way up to another couple of difficulty ratings just to kill a legendary pirate. I'd prefer to play something I actually enjoy.
Tl;dr:
This game lacks content and is a major grind fest. It isn't hard at all and give no challenge to players if the player knows how to play.
4/10 It wants to be good, but it falls short.

I will rate this game based on the following things:
Art/Graphics
Music/Sound
Content
Mechanics
Updates
Art/Graphics - 4/10
What you're looking at onscreen isn't always clear as the pixelated art is very blurry. The style of art doesn't fit the feel of the game as it feels very weird. You cannot zoom in either to see what's going on more clearly.
Music/Sound - 3/10
There isn't much many sound effects and if there are, they are drowned out by the music. The music is pirate themed, but there's only one track and it gets very annoying very quickly. The music is not very good, either, in my opinion.
Content - 1/10
There are only 3 types of places to go and that's it. It may be open world, but every place you go to is pretty much identical to some other place you've visited. A lot of the time you're playing the game, you're waiting for 2 minutes to go to the next location.
Mechanics - 2/10
The mechanics never change from the beginning of the game. Fighting other ships is boring and land combat is exactly the same. Nothing new happens as you progress except that you get more materials to build your ship and more crew members. But with those things, you're still doing everything you did when you started out, but on a larger scale.
Updates - 2/10
The Steam page says that there is constant updates, but the updates aren't constant and they mostly consist of a few bug fixes. However, there is a couple of tiny content additions every so often.
Total - 24/100
The developers have given up on this and it was released was to early. It is extremely unpolished.

What was the point of getting a job if it was barely acknowledged?
(spoiler) It also all just seemed so convenient to take down the villains, like how the protagonist just *happened* to find confidential tax information by doing some internet research, of all ways. Thing is, taxes aren't public unless the protagonist was some kind of elite hacker, but the game didn't make any mention of that. Also, students would not be normally suspicious about a teacher's salary and a nice house unless they had real reason to care or had it out for them. As for the villains, they barely had any chemistry at all. Their partnership was barely just a thread. People who commit tax fraud and brainwash people together would have a more familiar relationship, no?
Anyway this story has potential, but my impression is that it gave the bare minimum and it's still not complete. Even the endings could've been a bit more expanded upon to at least instill some satisfaction on the choices I've made, but it didn't.

Would I reccommend Psy High? Only to certain people. It's a well written storyline but it was also very short. I was very excited to play but came away from it very disappointed. Personally I look for a game that's going to take the time to make me care about characters, or a game that's long enough for me to get into it. I'm sure that for someone who doesn't want to be locked in their bedroom for two weeks while they finish a game, this would be a great investment. Don't buy this game if you want a game that you can commit to.

1996.  One of the very first full 3d first person shooters.   combine the fast-paced action from Doom and throw in some hellish-outerworldly evil with a faint scent of medieval vibe to it while Ogre's with chainsaws and grenade launchers, undead knights and even those raptor things that spring out of the dark and rip you to shreds.
You also got weapons that that makes today's military firearms in modern fps shooters look like kindergarden playsets that you find in toys r us, such as nailguns, shotguns..even the supershotgun loads it's shells in automatically in a second, grenade launchers, thunderbolt guns (don't shoot that in the water for the love of god) and even iconic Rocket Launcher that♥♥♥♥♥♥rockets which gave great results, and also gave birth to a risky technique called "rocket jumping"...and... that weapon made an unfortunate dumbed down return on Team Fortress 2 for the Soldier class with only 4 shots in the chamber before you have to reload.  bummer.  you don't ever reload the QUAKE rocket launcher.  EVER.
The Story of QUAKE has you going through slipgate dimensions to stop this thing from sending their armies of unspeakable evil to earth.  Yea it's got that Doom vibe to it.  each set of 8 or 10 levels are all broken up into episodes and you just walk to the area whichever episode you want to play.  I'd start with episode 1 if I were you.   You just clear out each section that's crawling with hostiles, so you just shoot to kill, find any keys, and move on to the next level.  Find better weapons as you go, and kill each boss at the end of the episode and at the final boss in the game, you have to telefrag it.  You figure it out how to do that.  It's not that hard.
While Doom pioneered the term deathmatch for multiplayer, Quake Perfected it and brought a new name to first person shooters involving a competition based on weapon/item/powerup pickups, player movement, map knowledge, weapon skill: Arena FPS.
Unfortuntatly, there's not much people online but you can check out Quake World and other communities that are still around keeping this game somewhat live.
The other thing is that the visuals are very, very outdated.  again, this is an almost 3 decade old game, but in my opinion it has stood the test of time.
before you play the game, be aware the programs that come with the game are outdated and may not fuction properly on a modern OS.  You should download Darkplaces, which is a modern engine for Quake.  unzip the files into the directory of this game and just run Darkplaces.   Better yet, there is an ultimate Quake Patch you can download as well.

Update: I have absolutely no clue what all of these negative reviews talking about $100 loot boxes are referring to. There are no $100 loot boxes in this game.
tl;dr;tl;dr: Rift offers more than any other F2P game I've encountered. The negative reviews here are based on individual hangups that shouldn't damn such a hugely diverse world.
tl;dr:  Rift has some of the best customizability in the genre. Cosmetics are account-wide and can be changed at will regardless of level. The class system (soul/role system) is a stroke of genius that no other game has come close to emulating. There are even Dimensions which allow you to build a completely personalized "home" from building blocks all over the game world. Rift isn't perfect, but in spite of all the people whining about P2W, it really is a free game, I think all the negativity is based on misplaced expectations
First, almost all of the negative reviews are from people who seem surprised the game has had the audacity to change over the past 6 years. The other negative reviews are mostly from people who claim the game is P2W. This is patently false. You can literally obtain everything including premium cosmetics and a monthly "patron" subscription just by accumulating in-game currency (plat). And it isn't particularly hard to get plat. Sure, things move much faster if you're willing to pay $$, but if that's surprising to you, then you must be new to this whole industry.
Other's claim the game is dead. Rift is *not* dead. I played vanilla, but I only started playing regularly in the past year. I've seen the population steadily increase in this time, and as an officer of a guild on the RP server, I have noticed our recruitment significantly increase as well. Sure, it's not as populated as it once was, PVP only happens at higher levels, and it's very much end-game focused, but the devs do still release new content and do try to listen to community concerns. There is a community forum where players can air their concerns. People act surprised when a loud minority gets changes when there was no effort to argue against the unpopular idea. Only after implementation everyone starts crying in gen chat "Trion only listens to people who whine on the forums!" Anyone can whine on the forums. Put your damn input in then instead of complaining after the fact.
You used to have to buy an expansion to get to max level, but that is no longer the case. You can pay $0 and have a toon that is just as viable as someone who has paid $1000. Perhaps they will have prettier colors than you, but cosmetics are always a cash cow.
I haven't seen anyone claim this, but I want to add that the community isn't toxic. On a 1-10 scale where Club Penguin is a 1 and League of Legends of an 11, Rift is probably around a 4. There are trolls, but they are easily ignored. It's incredibly easy to get help in gen chat. Multiple people are usually willing to help a single person. A lot of people will actually give you free money and bags if you're a new player and you ask nicely enough.
The class/role/soul system is remarkably flexible. You can use a pre-made if you want, but discovering how roles synergize with each other is part of the charm. Macros are easy to use if you have half a brain, but they aren't entirely necessary if you're willing to creatively use keybinds.
I just think all the negativity is based on misplaced expectations. Rift isn't perfect, but it's a free game, with some of the best customizability in the genre. I've grown to really love this game, and I worry a lot of people will miss out because of negative reviews from people who have individual hangups.

I bought Hatoful Boyfriend as a joke at first; 1 hour into it I was surprised and hooked by how far it stretches its branching storylines. It is NOT some crappy Youtube indie jailbaits; however do realise it is a visual novel and gameplay is NOT its forte. Be warned one gameplay is relatively short; its replayability, however, compensates it.
If you are into scrutinizing avian's personal life, expecting some endings with 'weight', or simply just a fan of Japanese visual novel (with no/minim fan-service [I presume]), Hatoful Boyfriend is a game for you, and yes never judge a book by its cover.

Hatoful Boyfriend is a fantastic dating sim. You might think the whole concept of a dating sim with birds as the characters a bit silly, but it has a story and characters that really pull you in. Plus, the extra storyline, Bad Boys Love AKA Hurtful Boyfriend, could be a short game of it's own.
Buy if you're interested in this kind of game, or if you want to try the genre out. If you're unsure, wait for a sale, you just might love it.
The characters are extremely well designed, in general. In the beggining you'll be introduced to a relatively small number of characters, which may be hard to remember, due to their names, which are Japanese names like Sakuya or Yuuya, but after your first playthrough you should become confortable with remembering some of their names.
For me, most characters are interesting, with the exception of Ryouta, who isn't as interesting, due to being the more normal out of the group, and because
The story is absolutely amazing. With various ending, you'll be entertained for various hours. The story largely depends on what route you take. For example, San's story is mostly comical, but Nageki's is mysterious and a bit saddening. I haven't played through all of Bad Boys Love, but from the great part I've seen until now, it's extremely mysterious and depressing, and, as stated before, could be a game on it's own.
The graphics are good for a game of this kind, the human counterparts are beautifully designed, and the backgrounds are generally well drawn. All I'd say bad about them is that the birds might not always be as high quality as the backgrounds, but don't come with expectations of AAA quality graphics.
The game has music that almost alwyas fits the situation, and can vary from the depressing tunes played all over the game, to San's cheerful theme, to Hurtful Boyfriend's frightening songs.
I think it's a must have for visual novel/dating sim fans. If you're unsure whether you'll like it or not, wait for it to go on sale, and pick it up then. Or offer it to a friend as a joke, and maybe he'll love it (like what hapenned to me!).

Battle Academy 2 is an accessible tactical wargame.
The turn-based combat system is solid and rewards the player for thinking. Scenarios can be either be large and take an hour to complete, or very small and take 15 minutes.
The campaign scenarios are well crafted and offer hundreds of hours of gameplay. The in-game skirmish generator is also well-done and offers much more replayability. This game great for PBEM multiplayer and it's easy to find matches, even in 2017.
I dislike how the numerical values of the three main stats, AT, AP, and armor, are only displayed in the detailed info menus. There is a meter in the main UI that shows AT and AP and range effectiveness, but seeing the other values would be helpful. It seems the first Battle Academy had this and I wish they didn't remove it.
The resolution stretch is also a bit odd. You can tell the game was made for devices that were less wide. It's a bit jarring at first, but you get used to it.
Overall this is a solid turn-based tactics wargame.

I was thinking about writing a serious review for this, but I have no clue how to actually do it, with
game...
What we have here is basically a cheap phone app in which you click (tap) the screen to make your character, the ninja, jump. The ninja moves on its own and the challenge comes from how the stages are set up.  Sometimes, you change gravity instead of jumping, sometimes you switch positions from the top of the platform to the bottom, sometimes the stage is rotating, affecting your jumps. There aren't a lot of stages either (36 in total).
But then you notice something. There are
in this game!
Yeah, there are a total of 36 achievements for each of the levels, and two for the two kinds of ways you can die. The rest are all emojis, flags and whatever else there was that you unlock when you start the game. After the 14 minutes of actual gameplay (that is, beating all the stages) are over, all you have to do is leave the game running and you get all the achievements. There is also a mute music button in the main menu, clearly indicating that this was never intended to be a game, but just a joke.
Now, if the game was actually fun, I could forgive both the joke and the length. But such a simple, crudely made excuse of a game cannot receive such blessings.
Buy it if you find enjoyment in the amount of achievements it has, but if you want a good Ninja game, look elsewhere!

It blows my mind how this went under the radar. Brink is an extremely unique and impressive FPS. There is absolutely *exceptional* character AND weapon personalization, three different character classes each having different positives and negatives, and around a hundred unique character abilities. The campaign, regardless of which of the two factions you decide to fight for, really does an impressive job at making you care about your side. Will you be a freedom fighter trying to resist Ark suppression, or Ark Security trying to put down the terrorist group? The campaign maps are the same but starting points and objectives different, making each faction's campaign different yet tied together quite well. To top it off, the AI, which is terrible in most games, actually *isn't* in Brink. In fact, playing with the AI is usually better, as they actually go after the objectives and help you out with things.

I highly recommend this amazing game, that Brian McRae and his crew have been creating.
It is still under development, and here and there expect issues - up to having to start your character over, although that is rare.
I was driven to update my computer, just to improve my play experience. I'm so glad I did.
Visually rich, the game at times rewards you with beautiful landsapes, or space vistas while you explore and hunt for basics.
The crew continuously puts out updates that make the game better and better, based on their own designs, but incorporating a LOT of user feedback and suggestions.
Originally the game was geared toward survival and battling aliens, but has incorporated so much more, with the ability to build amazing base structures with an easily understood menu of choices, and to explore and find other cool things. Bases, and some elements are customizable with a color palate.
They have opened not one, but two worlds to explore, with an entire solar system yet to come, and space stations planned.
Although I have not joined servers yet, the game has a multi-player mode allowing you to join colonies and fight other groups. The new character creation mode allows you to choose your specialty, strengths, skills, and has both 'male' and 'female' avatars, accomodating anyone.
This game is still in Beta, which I almost hope they never finish. For their hard work they should probably stop somewhere and offer "map-packs" to get a little more income and keep going like other well-known franchises.
At posting, I've played over 220 hours, and have enjoyed it thoroughly.
Fenix Fire, keep up the great work.
