The game and it's mechanics are rather dull and very plain. In a sense this game feels like a huge downgrade when I'm looking at Hearts of Iron III and Darkest Hour:  A Hearts of Iron Game. Many mods in the Steam Workshop actually fix the game like: Increased Resources, Player Led Peaceconferences and No Guarantees.
A couple of notes:
- Minor nations are useless unless they have some good resources (Guangxi Clique = Troll)
- Untited Kingdom guarantees every nation once world tension is above 20-25%
- Game begins to lag after 3-4 years because the AI keeps pumping out units which the game engine cannot handle that well
- Nationalism focus is OP for manpower
Apart from these negatives the game is simple yet fun to play. Drawing fontlines is easy and can be managed good enough soy uo don't get confused. The multiplayer is fun too once you get a good match without the host being an utter edgelord and enforcing rules upon everyone. Then again the Hearts of Iron franchise isn't known for it's multiplayer but for it's singleplayer.
All the majors nations have their own focus tree of decisions, the regional powers lack these in the vanilla game. The minor Axis powers do get their own focus tree but only if you buy the DLC. IT SHOULD BE INCLUDED IN THE BASEGAME PARADOX!
Unit production and management is also made easy so you can always keep track of what is being produced and how many. You can even select which units use what equipment. The managing of airforces and navy is somewhat simplified but it manages to hold up fairly well.
All in all it's doesn't even come close to compete with HoI 3 or Darkest Hour, but at the same time it's not trying to be those games. It's fun, somewhat addictive, intreging and there are loads of mods that improve the game and it's mechanics BECAUSE PARADOX CHARGES YOU €20 FOR SOME FOCUS TREES!
Mods that I used:
- The Victorian Era
- The Great War
- Kaiserreich
- All Nations Liberated
- Increased Resources
- No Guarantees
- Player Led Peace conferences

Not the best cover shooter but a decent one.
The game pretty much delivers what can be seen from the ads. Visuals, mood and gameplay are as I was expecting them. It's not a game that will easily win you over, but its a game that can provide a lot of fun if you are willing to commit to it.
Control over the main character is sometimes a bit annoying. Sticking to walls when you want to run, jumping over cover when you need to hide etc. (But with a bit of practice it only happens now and then)
The Bureau is a true cover shooter in the way that it cannot be pulled through like a classic fps. Sticking to a wall raises the defense even against enemies on the same side of the wall etc. Upgrades for the agents are fun and actually make a difference on the field.
The command system works fine. You are acting as the field commander and your primary concern is to organize the abilities of your squad. There are efficient and satisfying combos like lifting a strong enemy in the air, disrupting its shields and taking it out with a critical strike.
However The Bureau also has a few limitations. There is no Endgame or replaying certain parts. Savegames won't let you do that. There are some side missions parallel to the story of the campaign but thats it. The story is ok but not mind blowing. The delivery is fine. If you want to enjoy some "1960s USA fights against Aliens" there is enough in there for you.
The Bureau is pretty much a big chunk cut out of Mass Effect. Skipping the travel and talk and jump from one squad mission to the next.
NOTE: The framerate is an issue. If you want to play with all details, effects etc. you might want to check first if it will run fast enough.

Poorly designed, feels unpolished.
The game looks nice, and has a very good idea behind it. It is a puzzle-action-platformer. Your objective is to reach the end of each level, and you need to think how to navigate the environment and how to interact with it in order to complete the level.
However, it has several faults:
- No mouse support on the menus.
- Nonsensical button prompts ("A", "B") if you play with the keyboard.
- Poor default keyboard bindings: arrows and I/O/P keys. The hand position on the keyboard feels cramped and uncomfortable.
- Destructible brick walls look like the brick background.
- Incomplete/insufficient player training for the techniques required to complete the levels. For instance:
and
- I hate throwing the weapon because it never lands where I want it to. It feels unpredictable (even though I believe it isn't).
- It is easy to screw up and require either a suicide or a level restart.
- Since restarting a level is something so common, it should be easier to do (currently we need to press Esc, then use the arrows to select Restart, and then press the fire key).
- There are no checkpoints. Be prepared to restart the same level several times.
I can see the level design is nice, the puzzles are well thought. I wish I could enjoy this game. I wish I could feel challenged on how to complete the levels. But instead I ended up feeling bored (of redoing the same parts over and over) and frustrated (ragequit after failing a level and thinking I had to redo it again). Instead of forcing me to think on how to solve the puzzles, the game made me careless (doing this part yet again? let me do it as quickly as possible) and afraid of experimenting (why should I try something different if the cost is too high?).

I've been meaning to write this review earlier, but I know that no one in the world knows about this game.  Now with the achievements, I have an excuse to finally write this!
Quake is id Software's first foray into a true 3D game, a first person shooter in the vein of Doom.  During it's debut, it was groundbreaking for its technological advancements, and is now well known for being the basis of some of video game's biggest hits, where they originally branched out of a Quake mod.
Most remember it for its multiplayer, but few talk about how its single player campaign holds up.  Admittedly, the story is very anachronistic and shoehorned due to it being based off of an earlier build; Quake was slated to be an RPG in a dark fantasy world before id decided to turn it into an FPS, which is why you'll see a blend of futuristic weaponry mixed in with medieval backdrops and Lovecraftian-inspired monsters.  A lot of people will dismiss the graphics for running the "Real is Brown" trope to the ground, but I personally love it.  It adds to the atmosphere of the game along with the ambient music (wonderfully crafted by NiN) and truly lets you feel like you're alone in a desolate dimension.
The gameplay is where it truly shines.  While it was always marketed for its (at the time) amazing visuals, not a lot of people payed heed to its amazing gunplay and well-crafted difficulty.  While the original game suffers from lack of customization, source ports more than help to enhance the overall experience.  The controls really feel tight and responsive, with the gunplay rivalling modern-era games with how all the guns have a real sort of "punch" to them (the Super Nailgun in particular is absolutely cathartic).  The difficulty is also very tough, but fair.  While it still falls under the usual usage of "higher difficulty = enemies do more damage and you do less", it isn't exaggerated like in a lot of other games.  I, myself, found the highest difficulty to be a good challenge.
In all, I'd say this game has aged fairly well.  Whether it be my nostalgia goggles or not, I feel like the muddy graphics enhance the overall feel of the game's otherworldly tone.  The gameplay is as excellent as ever, and the sound design is truly phenomenal.
If you're a fan of FPS games and you're looking for another classic to play, I'd recommend this title to you, as well as the expansion packs with it.  While the multiplayer's pretty much dead (at least to my knowledge), it's worth it if only for the single player.
There will never be another first experience like this.

The Test Drive franchise has ever been an "also-ran" compared to more famous franchises like the Need For Speed or the Gran Turismo games, and Unlimited 2 did nothing to improve the series. Although it had a huge open world - still larger than those found in many competing series today - even at the time of its release in 2011, the game looked substantially worse than any other racer and it certainly hasn't improved with time. Worse, it was saddled with an uninteresting TV race show - with the requisite unlikable and shallow characters - as a framing device for level progression. But it's real sin was that it just wasn't fun to drive.
The driving mechanics are terrible, with every vehicle over-steering to such a degree that it is almost impossible to drive. Even at low speeds, the cars slip and slide all over the road as if the asphalt were coated with ice; racing is far more chore than adrenalin-fueled excitement. To be fair, driving around the vast open worlds is quite enjoyable - there's a lot to see and find - but this pleasure is hampered by the substandard graphics and the too-slow progression. There's just something wrong if a racer is more fun to drive at 50mph than at 150mph. The game also does its best to force you online - whether you want or not -  with numerous features locked away until you create an online account, but given how empty the online community is these days I wish the developers had put more effort into the single-player.

People oft complain about how the first-person shooter genre has grown stagnant, but then they overlook an experience like Brink. This game is a diamond in the rough: though the context of your battles aren't developed enough, the setting is refreshing, the voice acting is believable, and the brief cinematics give you a decent sense of purpose. More to the point, Brink's combat design is innovative. Teamwork is emphasized through a series of buffs and unique skills, with mission objectives requiring a certain class to be completed. The relatively low level cap (20) and limited ability points place priority on customization and strategic playstyle over grind. To top it off, the touted parkour system works well: movement is smooth and streamlined and grants you a degree of freedom rarely seen in other games. Brink is a wonderful take on why you should play FPSs; it's just a pity that the world at large didn't seem to notice.

It's hard to really describe how this game works. RTS, I guess, but with zombies. LOTS of zombies. They really aren't joking about them being billions. Even a small horde has about 2-300 zombies, vs a handful of whatever infantry you can scrounge up. Late game, your screen will fill up with undead eager to feast on your colonists. Needless to say, it doesn't always end well. With ironman mode always on, one screw-up can lead to a complete restart. Strangely, this only makes it more attractive.
At the moment, the learning curve is steep. With Campaign mode still in development, you're pushed right into the thick of it, and need to pick things up fast or die faster. You need to manage resources, build homes for workers, and as many defences as you can put between you and the hordes. The sometimes tight limitations on space force you to think strategically, and anyone who only has one single wall between their HQ (If that gets destroyed, game over) and the rest of the map is asking for an infestation to hit them. If zombies damage buildings enough, they spawn even MOAR ZOMBIES, to only add to your problems. So if even a single one makes it past your defences, you'll be in serious trouble, if not utterly destroyed. Add in the various special zombies (think the player infected from L4D), and you've got a game which constantly tests you, but you feel rewarded even in failing. There is no better teacher, after all.
Tl;dr - Yes, play this. It's hard even on low difficulties, but it's enjoyable even as your citizens get their faces eaten. Just watch out for Harpies.

You are Earth's only hope and last chance, using your time machine/ship you have to go back in time and save the Earth from it's inevitable destruction. How? Basically just kill the hell outta everything that doesn't look human. Rogue Continuum feels like a game that was built for a group of friends/players, all the features seem to lean towards this idea. From the distinct and unique four characters, upgrades, non-stop action this game is all about laughing manically as you blow crap up all around you with your friends. For the most part Rogue Continuum accomplishes this but the experience becomes different when playing alone. Some classes are best used in combination with others, leaving them feeling very under powered when the hordes of aliens come for your lonesome warrior. All the game really needs is some balance, which is what Early Access is all about. So I am sure this won't be an issue for long. Other features like Online play will solve this issue once it's in place as well. The graphics are sharp and have plenty of over the top explosions, and huge aliens. While Rogue Continuum brings it's roguelike elements to the table, one thing that I loved is that it really is simple to just pick up and play. This is a no fuss type of game, just shoot stuff and use your cool powers, collect loot, kill more stuff. It's just that simple.

It's exactly what it looks like; a sci-fi roguelite shooter with some RPG elements, upgrades, etc... - Does this game do anything revolutionary? No - does it manage to be some awesome fun? Absolutely! The game is early access and from what I can tell is lacking content, but that's to be expected from an early access game. It's actually very, very fun though and as long as development goes smoothly from here on out, should shape up to be the great game it looks like it's going to be. If you are ok with being an early bird in a game like this, I would highly recommend it.
I've tried every character, but I spent very little time with the melee guy. Every character felt genuinely unique. Each character has a "limiter" of sorts to stop them from putting out endless DPS. The generic shooter guy has to reload, and thus plays much like you'd expect a generic shooter guy to: small engagements, reloading inbetween, etc... He was very fun though, don't get me wrong. He is clearly meant to be the "basic" class of the game, but manages to do so with finesse.
The sniper girl also plays like you'd expect: She wants to engage as few enemies as possible at once and does extremely high single (or few) target damage. Some of the later levels have large enemy swarms and I haven't made it that far with her yet, but I imagine she is VERY difficult as the game goes on. She was very fun though. Her gimmick is that she needs to charge her shots up, and can "overcharge" to do extra damage. She ♥♥♥♥ing DESTROYS bosses.
The melee guy, as I said, I didn't mess with much. It was difficult to deal damage with him without taking damage in return. His gimmick is that his weapon can overheat and be rendered unusable if spammed for too long.
The robot is by far my favorite character. It has amazing stats all around and a shield to absorb damage before losing health, but to deal damage drains an energy bar that slowly fills up. You can switch between 3 modes that charge your shield bar faster, your weapon bar faster, or split charge power equally. You HAVE to switch to do well, trust me. It's a very fun character though.
The game has a fun unlock system for content, but as I said, there doesn't appear to be a ton of content as of yet. But early access is early access. If you like roguelites and sci-fi, this is a fantastic game.

Having spent just about 3 years on this games non-steam version I can safely say this is one of my all time favorite games I have ever played. Seeing as you have absolute full control over every movement for your character of course that means there will take ALOT of time to master the movement system.
While this game obviously isn't an RPG there's still lots paths to walk. The game is divided in 2 different main communities with several branches to follow. The 2 main groups are the competetive players and the replaymakers.
The competetive players are the ones to probably earn a bunch of ingame profit as they are the ones to spend the most time on the multiplayer section of the game which is where you earn ingame currency. This path goes up into a huge variety of different competetive mods. Some which you will very likely prefer more than the other.
Then there's the replaymaking community. These are the players that focus on making singleplayer or collaborative/online multiplayer replays that are aimed at looking as good as possible. This goes up to several game modes such as tricking which is where you make a replay aimed at acrobatics such as flips, twists and spins without an opponent involved. Then there is Madman replays which are aimed at completely destroying your opponent as stylishly as possible in a singleplayer match. Note that the opponent named Uke does not move and therefore there is pretty much an unlimited amount of opportunities of what to do to him. Some people chose to manipulate Uke in the air and spin him around to then finish up with a simple decapitation. Others chose to go a more extreme path any try to fully destroy Uke, not caring about the style as much as others may. These are only a few branches of the tree that is replaymaking.
Now let me tell you... This game would be NOTHING without the community it has. At least 70% of the enjoyment you get from this game is through the toribash forums
. This is where you interact with the community properly and parttake in everything from events, sharing your replays with others for criticism to purchasing items for your ingame money to make your character look amazing. Be sure to check the forums out if you are planning to play this game on a regular basis.
Here are a few pros and cons
Pros:
- Amazingly rewarding to master
- Active and friendly community
- Not pay 2 win in any way.
- Fully skill based, no hackers.
Cons:
- Very hard to master
- Will eat up alot of time in your life
- Minor micro-transactions for money used for customization. (You can still earn this ingame)
To sum up:
This game is super hard to master. It's gonna be months if not years until you can fully master the control you are given over your character. However, if you keep at it you will eventually get addicted to the game. You will feel proud over your accomplishments and you will improve with time in a way that motivates you to keep going. There's nothing more rewarding than finally landing your first backflip or successfully supplexing someone across the entire arena. If you've got time on your hands, this game is definetly for you.

Pros:
A wide variety of weapons, enemies, and places.
An interesting strategy component based on ship design.
A good resource and crew management system.
A well designed leveling system.
Cons:
It's boring. You spend a long time preparing for battles, and you do very little in the battle itself.
No skill. This is not like Terraria. It is not a platformer, it is not a game of skill or accuracy, you can't even move your guy. Everyone has an AI, even you, and though you can guide this AI to some extent, it doesn't give the satisfaction of you doing it yourself.
In the end, I simply didn't enjoy this game for as long as I would have liked to. I'm quite sure more strategy oriented people would be interested in Pixel Piracy for a greater period of time. Personally, I just got bored very quickly. I recommend Sid Meier's Pirates instead. It is based off a similar idea, however the execution is much better and there is a strategy AND skill element in it. It also has a larger variety of career paths available.

Summary: They are Billions is a good and fun game, which I recommend. The long list of criticism is there because I've seen people compare They are Billions to a strategy game, which it isn't. Strategy games involve strategy, tactical decisionmaking and weighing the risks and rewards of your decisions. These things are lacking completely in They are Billions once you're figured out your generic win strategy that works every time.
They Are Billions features:
+ Many many units onscreen
+ A charming graphic style and universe
+ Good difficulty
+ Tense action
- Long and tedious tech tree where it takes ages to upgrade your houses two times and get a bank and a market and oil and stone and wood and iron and electricity and food and workers and colonists and upgrades...
- Tedious base building where you have to place every building in the optimal spot
- Without exception annoying and cringy oneliners from your units
- You play versus an ai who does the same every game, and there is only one optimal strategy every game. There is never any real decisionmaking once you've figured out how to play. Just the execution of your generic strategy has to be perfect, because every mistake can turn into a disaster.
. There is no real attacking. There is no catching the enemy army off guard and crushing them while they're trying to run (like harpies can crush you when you try to run). There are no unexpected early attacks to catch your enemy off guard. Of course you clear land, but the risk/reward of attacking a player is missing. Instead, there is only reward if you play correct. Again, no meaningful decisionmaking.
- Subpar combat in which first you slowly and tediously clear land with rangers and soldiers, don't make too much noise! Later you attack move your snipers and defend the base with thanatos. This is the optimal endgame army, other units are only used in wacky challenge runs. There is no decisionmaking on what attack formation to use, what units to use and how to use them.

The infection mechanic,  where if a building is sufficiently damaged its inhabitants or workers become zombies, is a nice touch, but otherwise there's not much to this game.
I don't think it's worth 20 euro's.

Evolve Stage 2 is a perfect example of the budding future, and imminent failure, of microtransaction gaming. The quick breakdown I can give you, after having waited until after its original release, is a game lacking content, features, and replay value; redressed with expensive skins, expensive characters, and expensive monsters, geared at being the next big competitive FPS-with-a-twist.
The idea is fantastic, and for the most part, a solid execution: 4 Hunters and 1 Monster duke it out to the death. Each Hunter is specialised, one for Medic = Heals, one for Support = Self-explanatory, one for Trapper = Sniffer-dog, one for Assault = Big-Gunz. Depending on the synergy of the characters as Hunters, teams can crumble or come away with an easy victory; and depending on the skill of the type of Monster, Wraith =  "lightweight", Behemoth 'Bob = heavyweight, middleweight = (Meteor) Goliath, Goliath, Kraken, Elder Kraken, Gorgon = Shelob, victory can be as simple as evolving once (from Stage 1 Monster to Stage 2), or twice (Stage 2 to 3, whereupon the monster can destroy a shield and win the game by outfoxing the hunters).
The characters themselves, the voice-acting (without lipsync), the story (kill monsters = terraforming planets), is good enough. The gameplay is what you come for and stay for, and that... that is another beast entirely.
Stage 2 is the culmination of a steady realisation that developers can't half♥♥♥♥♥a triple-A title and expect people to 1) Pay for it, and 2) Play it. Stage 2 is the culmination of a steady realisation that without a playerbase, there is no multiplayer experience. Stage 2 is the culmination of a steady realisation that multiplayer games without meaty solo content to boot (*cough* DICE *cough* BATTLEFRONT) really don't deserve triple-A status. Stage 2 is the culmination of a steady realisation that some games developers aren't in it for the game, they're in it for the money, and gamers need to understand that the nature of gaming is, like all areas of life, becoming more about marketing and advertising than it is about the quality of the product (*cough* No Man's Sky)
So, when you get Stage 2, enjoy it for as long as it lasts. It's free and I recommend it in its free form. It's regularly patched, and while a lot of supposed 'bugs' are being fixed and characters are being tweaked; by and large, when it comes to getting Hunters and Monsters, as of recently, their price (in Keys) has skyrocketed. I can only anticipate the soon-to-be-included microtransaction future of Stage 2, and with it, again, the death of the game.
The simple way to fix Stage 2 is, in my opinion,
1) More Hunters. 30 or 40 more, if you want to be taken as seriously as something like League of Legends. Each Hunter as diverse as the last, with synergy to boot. Microtransactions on easier-to-play-easier-to-get Hunters; big-ticket in-game currency (Keys) for stronger, harder-to-play hunters.
2) More Monsters. Anywhere from 5 to 10.
3) About 50 new maps. Enough so each hunt feels unique.
4) Unlock all the colours. In the badges. Nuff said.
My recommendation comes so long as the game is free. As soon as you have to pay, and before any of the above changes are made, I'd either avoid it altogether, or get it when it's on special.

After finally going F2P the game still needs some MAJOR touch-ups before I can recommend it. For example...
- matchmaking is atrocious and flakey (it's not uncomon to pop into and out of lobbies several times when searching for a match)
- navigating menus to find a game is non-intuitive and lacks proper prompts for character/skill selection
- earning credit for new characters is brutally slow (as of most recent patch costs have risen 300% while daily login/challenge rewards remain unchanged - currently takes between 30 and 50 games to afford the cheapest characters)
- monsters are far from balanced (particularly the newly relaunched Behemoth)
- hunters have all been 'standardized' and share common abilities instead of having a full repertoire of unique skills that match their backstory (though I understand this may make the game easier to balance in its early F2P iterations)
I'm going to watch this game's progression because I love the idea behind it and still manage to enjoy many aspects of the experience but I just can't recommend it until at least some of the issues mentioned above are addressed.
Keep working on it guys, I know it'll be great eventually!

There are very few games that can tell a beautiful story without any words. Games such as Journey and Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons are some excellent examples, and now we have A Bird Story.
While short, about an hour or so in length, this is a fantastic story with beautiful visuals and music. While it may not have the same impact that To the Moon had on me, it felt as though it was trying to be something different; hence the complete lack of dialogue.
On the whole, this is a quite nice, if short experience, and it is certainly worth your time and the $5 asking price. The soundtrack is absolutely worth it, as well, so I recommend picking up the soundtrack along with it.

A Bird Story is yet another masterpiece in Kan's collection. To The Moon was, and still is, my favorite game of all time. After playing the shorter A Bird Story, I express similar thoughts. While the story takes roughly an hour to work through, the game attaches the player to each and every character with an emotional connection stronger than most every other game I have played. With a library currently filled with 224 games, A Bird Story easily makes the top three. Kan Gao's new transitions and seemless storyline worked well with this new piece. I am willing to bet that, no matter who is reading this, if you were to take $5 and one hour of your time to play A Bird Story, you would feel just the same as I do now. Don't get deterred by the slow-paced progression, because most of you will be sobbing by the end credits. In conclusion, I honestly believe A Bird Story has got a little of bit of everything for everyone. It was a true pleasure to play.

Ah, Quake...how much we, the gamers of the 21st century owe thee So much of the technology and so many of the conventions we now take for granted were developed for this game. So many great games were built within the Quake engine or its immediate derivatives. It is truly a landmark of gaming history. Some of the greatest geniusus of game development history invested their talents into this game and changed the industry forever.
But that's not why you should buy Quake. You should buy this game because it is still one of the best shooters ever made. It's stilll scary and exciting in equal measure. Its design is still darkly original, it's arsenal still finely balanced, and its gameplay still wickely slick.
Once you are done with the ~9 hour campaign, why not check out the multiplayer that remains active more than twenty years after the game's release (if that's not proof enough of Quake's superiority, then nothing is). Or perhaps you could head over to
and try any one of the 1200 user-made single player maps and map packs.
For two decades Quake has been an unexhaustable source of pleasure for gamers and I full expect to still be basking in its glory twenty years hence.
The grandaddy of all FPS. Still fresh, fluid and FAST today. QUAKE IS FOREVER. QUAKE IS GOOD FOR YOU.

Normally I don't write reviews, but the hate on this has gone WAY too far. As someone with a not so great back/neck, I tend to lean back and play games with a controller whenever possible, so it just so happens I have a controller. If you want a TLDR review: this is Mass Effect's combat system 1:1, in Mafia I-II world, with enemies from XCOM:EU. Nothing more, nothing less, and with a few spots that could have been better.
First of all, the story is close to non existent. Basicly everyone is functional as role that keeps an undercover agency working, instead of having any kind of personality. This isn't a negative thing, it's not why we ever liked any XCOM for, and this one isn't any different - until the very end. That where the devs decided to go for Mass Effect 3 storytelling, and not only they achieved a similar, but an even worse disaster of things that doesn't make sense anyhow, even on a single character's decision level or as game in a whole. Or just basic logic. But, this is mainly the last hour, and you'll have about 10-13 before that. How's that?
That part, is actually great. Just don't even think about touching a console controller or playing on normal difficulty. The combat is really challanging, smart and tactical, later on however can become slightly automatic and boring even on Veteran difficulty, just because you naturally reached better technology, levels and abilities. Other than that, it's like you have a dream Star Wars: Republic Commando, just not Star Wars, and there is more customization to it. Which leads me to my last point where I can throw anything bad on this game: customization. XCOM:EU could have been better on visual customization of our soldiers (and it's sequel is really good looking on this part!), but Declassified is another step back from that. You can change names, 3 or 4 colors on a suit, and that's it. When you recruit a new agent, you can also choose from ~8 premade faces, plus skin color. You cannot have women as agents, or customize visual looks, which is really a miss because you are not supposed to blend in to the crowd, you meet noone but aliens anyway.
Overall: Declassified is good, as an average good game can be. It has some unique touches here and there, the action depending on your chosen difficulty level can be really great, but it's one of those games that have absolutely great gameplay, but nothing else. The story is non existent, the customization in it's current form is really hurting that it's not deeper, the characters are throwaway faces. And that's totally fine for XCOM:EU that is a strategy game, but the whole reason Declassified exists as it is, is changing the perspective and bringing it down to a personal level of a group of agents, and it's a failure at that. If there is ever a sequel on this and they can improve on that, it's potentially GOTY material. For this, it's great, but you have to know why you buy it, to not have expectations the game cannot meet. My only problem is, that it still tries, and does it bad. But that's only the last hour, don't let me made you back off if you are thinking about buying it. That means you are looking for a good, really tactical TPS. Declassified, is really good at that.

I think this is an example of a game which has poor reviews for the wrong reasons. Like many, I'd just finished playing XCOM - Enemy Unknown and was hungry for a continuation of that. While still set in the XCOM 'universe', it's a very different style of game and many of the negative reviews will be because of that, which is unfair to what is actually a pretty good game. They've made a brave attempt at making a game which isn't a guaranteed money maker, and I think they've done a pretty good job. I love it when developers don't paint by numbers.
It's a third-person shooter not dissimilar in gameplay to Mass Effect, though set in the swinging 60's (with a very 50's feel), you have 2 squadmates who you give commands to during Battle Focus (slo-mo), as you work your way through linear mission levels. Personally I'm not fussed by linear levels - I'll take them over non-linear ones which just give the illusion of choice to fill out gameplay time.
The game itself is fairly short if you just go through the main missions, though if you're a completionist doing all the side missions and exploring the base properly, and going after achievements, you'll get roughly triple the game time to about 20-25 hours.
The graphics are good, and the scenery and level design excellent. They've clearly put alot of work into quality over quantity, and I actually feel bad about not standing around too long to just look at what's been put into it, especially mid to late game. However, if your computer's falling behind on the ol' hardware department, you might find your framerate dropping noticeably in areas.
Aliens are what you would expect from an xcom game, and I found the later game to get a bit easy due to a strong compliment of abilities. Still, I enjoyed all the combat, and if you're having trouble with your agents chasing after you when you try to flank the enemy, just manually move them to cover first so they aren't in follow mode.
This game's not for everyone. Some will find the pace a bit slow, especially in the base, but honestly the game is 80% off at the time of writing this review (£2.99 ..$4.43 at current rate), which is an absolute steal for the work that's gone into it. If people reviewed the game removing both their expectations, and personal preference for what games they like, and instead based it on the quality of the game itself for its genre (which is what reviews should be based on, not personal taste), then it would be somewhere in the positives for sure.

I started playing right before beta and after playing quite a few hours and dealing with bugs ect. I still really enjoyed the game. I opted for beta and wow, just wow, a much cleaner feel, more responsive and more polished. If you like Subnautica then I would really recommend this. It's like that feel but different mechanics and in space. So here are my pros and cons.
Pros.
It allows for single player. If you are itching for pvp combat then go for it but I like to relax with a fun game and not worry about coming back and finding my base looted and all my stuff gone. I want to play in peace and this allows it. PVP will give you the combat, single will give it more of the alone survival suspense feel.
I haven't found all the dungeons and caves but the ones I have found I like and the atmosphere , music and lighting aren't too far off from giving it that dead space feeling.
Highly customizable game play. Many games cater to one or the other and  regardless of the fact that you can like a game, if its just too hard your forced to sit through frustration after frustration. Eventually these games offer people jeering and yelling "git good" and the game is shelved. Or the game is just to plain easy. This has A LOT of controlls to manage all parts of the game difficulty. From "I want to sit back with a cup of coffee and chill on an alien planet to barely
clinging to existence.
Quite good on the combat and smoothness of it's delivery. Many survival games like this just don't seem to implement fighting well. Blocky guns that act like pop guns, blocky fighting or weapons that are wielded in such a way as to remind you that "this wasn't meant to be a fighting game".
(As a side note, I'm not comparing this to games with massive wallets that release for $60.00 Sadly a lot of those games
deliver in the combat and fall horribly flat in the game play)
$25.00 is not bad for the hours you can play this. I will end up playing this  and coming back to it far more often than say Deus Ex or Dishonored which I really like.
This game put confidence back in me for supporting pre release games. These guys are doing right and really putting the
effort in. You can really tell when a person likes what they are doing and these guys doing. Example, compare
Deadspace 2 with Deadspace 3. One game shows all the effort and the second game shows the money grab.
It's nice to have a survival game that deviates from the overwhelming genre of survivals these days. If it's survival you want then you normally have only two options. Wade through zombies or live in a post apocaliptic world that's all drab
in color mostly deserts and dismal overall. The views in this game are fantastic from the orbiting moons to the massive
ringed planet that dominates the night sky at times.
-------------------
Cons.
Other than the little tutorial at the start (in beta) that is all you have to go on. With all the crafting and menus and tools
used for crafting you'll be left scratching your head at times trying to find which item is crafted where. I need to craft a
solar panel, where do I do that? Oh there it is, wait, it says I need to craft a solar pannel kit first. Now where was that?
Do I craft it with the forge, the printer, the fabricator, the chem table the furnace or the chem station? Or sometimes you
find out you don't need any of those and can simply craft an item using the tabs next to the back pack.
Water is the a basic requirement and first priority of any survival situation. If your playing easy then this will be of little issue. If you are playing on even moderate then get ready for major difficulty. You can't just find water, if you do, its not
drinkable. You have to craft water and that takes ingredients you have to go far and wide for and requires crafted goods
that are surprisingly a bit of a ways into the engineering skill tree.
It's buggy at times or construction is a bit finicky. Careful with your multi tool. I finally had my whole base created and
wanted to wipe out a wall of the main habitat hub. Instead of destroy wall I destroyed the whole building. I couldn't
rebuild and re-attatch it so I ended up tearing everything down and starting over. Tearing down something only gives
back half the resources put into it. Sure I should have been more careful but at the same time, you'd better be REALLY
careful.
-----------------------
To sum up this essay - Any issues I've had are not enough to make me want to stop playing. It's five stars in my book
and belongs in my library next to Subnautica. Last little detail is this. If you ever played a game called The Dig then I think
you will like this game a lot. Very much the similar mood and the colors are vibrant.

How do you make something that looks so beautiful so boring? Yeah, I know, it's not like LP1 or 2. A sequel can take a series in new direction that's amazing like Max Payne 3. This is not the case with LP3. It's not the mundane, gritty, realistic story of Jim the offworld mecha heatminer that makes it boring. No, it's the on the rails "press E (and sometimes V,T,or P) to advance plot".
"JIm, go here."
"Jim, press mouse 1 here."
"Jim, run back and forth to pad out game time."
Nothing in this game feels like a game. It feels like an interactive movie. Events don't have to necessarily advance the plot, but they should be engrossing. You should want to learn more about EDNIII, but picking up random audio logs and the already snails-pace at which the story goes along makes you want to just get it over with.
The on foot combat is boring and tedious compared with the earlier games. Roll, shoot, roll, shoot, roll shoot. It's Dark Souls in Akrid land. And what's with the vast number of game mechanics they keep trying to throw in? There is even cover based shooting, but you'll never use it because the Akrid are always up in your grill. There's a knife for melee, but it's useless so you end up just shooting everything while rolling and shooting. You get plenty of T-units from "quests" so why bother killing Akrid and collecting their blood? It's all busy work. Somehow giving the player grappling hook is also boring and rail-like. Everything feels like this. Too many different mechanics that don't fit well together.
The only redeeming factors for me so far is the "rig" segments and the hollywood level of voice acting and animation. You feel weighty, you feel powerful (sometimes), and it's just plain fun to navigate this world in it. But even then, no real weaponry early on makes it boring as ♥♥♥♥. The characters feel real and believable, although sometimes to a fault. We get it Jim, you miss your family. Please stop interrupting the main storyline with the constant ramblings of your wife. It's meant to connect the player with the protagonist, but they overdo it.
tl;dr: You know what this feels like? Binary Domain, Dark Souls, and Dead Space mashed up in the Lost Planet universe, but without the gameplay that made those games fun and interesting.

Perhaps if I got this game when I was younger I would have been able to enjoy it; as it is, this experience has reminded me that just because so many others have enjoyed a game does not mean I would.

More an interactive story than a game, A Bird Story tells about a friendship between a lonely boy and a bird. Because it's only little over an hour long, I'll withold the rest of the plot for you to enjoy. However, I'll tell you this: it's a beautiful, a little bit sad story.
With an interactive story I mean there's not much real gameplay. You can only move around and interact with some objects. Instead of text dialogue, the story is told by the graphical events and occasional spoken or thought pictograms. I was initially sceptical how that would work out, so I was pleasantly surprised to see it's a splendid way to convey little tasks and small bits of story.
Graphics are nice, hand-drawn pictures and bitmaps. Especially the music is beautiful and atmospheric, well thought to fit the story. It will change smoothly when traveling through the surreal landscape of the boy's memory.
If you played To The Moon, their previous game, know that A Bird Story is shorter, less sad and there's (even) less "playing" or decisions. If you liked it or story-driven adventure games in general, you'll probably like this one. Games like this are more about feeling, observing and art than skill, action and doing. It's a single, whole experience: I don't see myself playing it more than once, but that was a happy experience.
Yes.

+ Beautiful music
+ Touching story, even if it is a little cliche
+/- Because it mixes reality with imagination/fantasy the story isn't always completely clear, but it allows you to have an own interpretation
- Gameplay is pretty much non-existent, and what's there is kind of boring
- Graphics are subpar (but it's an understandable choice for a game like this)

Even though improvements over HOI3 in terms of UI designs are highly visible and HOI4's relatively easy gamming mechanism makes this installation generally entertaining, the vast simplification of the overall system makes it look like a reductive and down-scaled version of its predecessor, despite its visual superiority. The complex mechanism in HOI3, even if it hindered many players from fully appreciating its content, serves as a distinguishing feature from other, arguably more simple, strategic games. The current state of HOI4 is well below one's erstwhile expectations of this series, as aspects including diplomacy, economics, technology and, above all, warfare require hardly any expertise for players to maneouvre. AIs at this stage are far from being competent enough either ad rivals or allies to be taken seriously. All these problems are indicative of a giant step backward from what Paradox had achived with the final version of HOI3 (Their Finest Hour). It really surprised me when I realised that many good features from HOI3 (command chains, warfare mechanism, etc.) are  almost completely ignored. It appears to me that developers are really not bothered taking advantages of their previous achievements. With regards to historical accuracy, this is when HOI4 is at its worst. Obviously HOI games allow players to deviate heavily from the historical version of WWII, but HoI3 can easily allow players to follow the orthodox path; in this game, however, anyone who has any knowledge of the events between 1939 and 1945 would wish to smash Paradox's face when Soviet divisions appear (despite them being volunteers) in Benelux in 1940 fighting ALONG WITH the Allies AGAINST the Wehrmacht. One wonders the fate of the Baltic states during the same period. This was an catastrophic failure for the game as, before reaching this stage, I had tried everything I could to ensure the accuracy of the 1939-40 Western front. Sadly this is just yet another flaw the developers do not care to fix. In any case massive updates are neccesary for HOI4 to be nearly as good as HOI3, although to get those updates players will inevitably be required to pay lots of extra money, which is what Paradox Interactive always does. The very release of the game at its current state is an egregious mistake on the part of Paradox Interactive.

Dishonored is easily one of Bethesda's best games and I would argue that it beats out The Elder Scrolls in raw fun. There are so many different ways to approach missions and although the world may not be as open as Skyrim or your character as customizable, that doesn't matter because Corvo Attano is a freakin' badass and nobody needs to change him. Enter the city of Dunwall; a corrupt, plague ridden metropolis being torn apart by Weepers, Guardsman, Gangs, Overseers, and Nobles. Everyone is vying for power at once, and NOBODY is worthy of holding it.
Corvo has been framed for murdering the Empress of Dunwall and must go on a long redemption journey to recover Lady Emily and restore peace to the kingdom. Or.. he could just slaughter everyone in his path, and destroy the city entirely. The missions play out in a linear-esq style, with branching pathways and multiple endings depending on your play style. Want to kill everyone? Go for it. Want to sneak around and only kill those that you need to? Go for it. Want to kill NOBODY? You can do that, too. Depending on how much slaughtering you do, you will recieve a "Chaos" rating; low meaning you're a good guy, high meaning you're an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This not only affects the ending of the game, but affects the gameplay. A low chaos playthrough will have the city coming back to life from the Rat Plague, and civilians around the game will look a lot better near the end than when they did in the beginning. A high chaos playthrough will cause the Rat Plague to just ravage everything, with high amounts of Weepers (or zombies, really) roaming the streets, and your dear friend Samuel slowly being ripped apart from the inside. People will react to your chaos level, and though it's not very unique to have a system like this, it is flawlessly put into the game and it works 100% of the time with no continuity errors.
The missions are very varied, surprisingly. On paper, they're all the same; infiltrate building x, eliminate target x, get out alive. But the way they play out through the surprisingly varied and expansive environments really adds a flavor to this game that hasn't been matched by any game to come out since (except for maybe Dishonored 2, but I haven't played through that just yet). From the opening mission until the final confrontation with the big bad guy (who shall remain nameless for this review), Corvo will sneak through some fantastically thought out level design to bring justice to Dunwall City.
The party is by far the best mission, and also one of the hardest. You have the option to run in murdering everyone, but that is just no fun. Instead, talk smoothly and coax the Boyle Ladies into some one on one time, and RUTHLESSLY MURDER THEM AHA. Nobody will even know you've done it, and the party will continue. Don't forget, on your way out, sign the guest book. Let them know who was there. ;) Corvo Attano, man.
Though the story only sticks out at points, and most of the story is picked up through little notes that drag on wayyy too long more often than not, the gameplay is just so ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic that this game is a legendary addition to any library and is a must buy.
Ten out of ten would get "Clean Hands" achievement again.
P.S: ♥♥♥♥ THE FLOODED DISTRICT, DUDE. Those assassins will one second be looking one way, and then BAM, they've teleported across the room and they're looking right at you, ♥♥♥♥ing up your perfect run.

So here's the thing. I've been seeing two main complaints, so far. The first being that the game offers no form of guide or tutorial, and only the briefest of explanations as to what the controls are. The other being that the game ONLY supports an xBox controller.
Here's the thing about all that: a lot of the problem there is that they couldn't be bothered to read up on what they were buying. They may have thought "Ooo, Burnout! But with Golf!" and just bought it outright. (Full disclosure: I was going to as well.) This is my solution: read. Do research. It took one (1) click once I got to the store page to find out that it needed a controler (if you don't count looking through the reviews, where it's plastered with negative comments about it). And as for the controls, it's in the options. A complete breakdown of how to play. It's conveniently listed under "How to Play". Now, some people want to be able to just jump right in and play with no delay, and I get that. But frankly, sometimes that just isn't the case.
Don't get me wrong, this game isn't perfect by any means. There's room for improvement all over the place. Better camera controls, more accurate movement, less resource intensive, there's definitely room to grow. As it stands right now, however, it's a good game that's fun to play, as long as you don't go into it already bitter (and have an xbox controller handy).

The only real critique/suggestion I would make:  keep speacialty skills as purchasable items, but turn them into professions(boarding party, gunners, shipwrights , etc.).  Things like swimming, cleaning, and other basic seamanship skills should be default progression when your sailors level up.

I reviewed this game a while ago before the Architect Update and gave it a negative review; and felt like I should give this game a new review considering the many improvements.
First things first: Why should anyone buy Osiris?
Buy Osiris if you are looking for a space survival adventure to play on your own or with a small group of friends. Don't buy this if you're looking for a deep and immersive challenge. The game's "story" is currently unfinished, and there are a number of bugs which make large player groups difficult to manage, if not even unplayable.
There is a lot of content, much of it very functional, but there isn't a whole lot of depth to it. My friend and I managed to get a maxed out base with vehicles in about 10 good hours of play. For some people that's great, but for those who expect a more challenging survival experience you're not going to find it here. The AI is pretty basic, the weapons lack variety, and the leveling system leaves much to be desired.
Ultimately this game is something of a love letter to the hard SciFi genre. Combat is fun, the controls and UI are easy to use, and playing with a small friend group on a private server is great. If a lot of the bugs are fixed and the remainder of the story finished, then Osiris is definitely going to end up as a very fun survival co-op game.

Low Points:
-There probably won't be a lot of replayability :/
-Yuuya's romance was hard to figure out; I got the Bad Ending just trying the first go around, and Ryouta fell in love with me the second time. There's a bit too many complaints about games being P2W... Sure in PvP it sucks..but if you're looking for PvP, I'd say majority of mmorpgs are not for you (granted of course I havn't played the majority of them). MMORPG at their core is a PvE grind. Which comes to a slight downside on rift, you just don't run into many players while leveling. The majority of players seem to all ready be at max level, or close to..Well welcome to a game thats been out for 6years.
When you look at a mmorpg don't look at whats paid for, instead look at what's there for free. For rift, while there's become quite a bit behind the pay wall, there is still plenty to access while playing without paying. You get 4 classes with 8 souls, and you get to combo 3 souls at once. Then you have your professions you can work on. Go artifact hunting, go fish, claim achievements, pet/mount collect. Then there's the rifts and invasions, I personally loved the foothold system. Upgrade a base and defend against incoming waves, but if not enough waves it does disappoint. This isn't all there is, but I don't want to make this much longer.
Give it a try, dislike it and leave, like it and play. Want extra content? Grind your heart out and buy REX (an item that grants "real money"), or decide if the game is worth droping some money on for that extra enjoyment. Don't look at the equipment section.
I've played on and off since release, mainly off of gylph instead of steam, and I do subscribe and buy their extra content.

Just finished Lost Planet 3. Finally.
I figure I ought to do a mini-review for this.
Gameplay: 3.5
Graphics: 9.
Musical Score: 6.
Animations: 4
Storyline: 9.5
The game in itself is what you'd expect from the LP franchise. At least, it goes back to the foundations set down by LP 1, thankfully the whole affair didn't follow the lead of LP 2, and have the whole dang "Single Player" campaign be focused upon the Co-Op aspects, and "Objectives" for points. It's all focused on the story, not making your character look shiny, thankfully.
The first thing you'd notice about this is the graphics. Even on the lowest settings, the landscape is breathtaking, the cutscenes are incredibly lifelike, and the effects around you are very exceptional. The small downside that took the graphics down from a 10 to a 9, is that for the most part, the maps are nothing but snow snow snow, and looking at the inside of your Rig. Alright. Might not be a graphical qualm as such, but the impact of having flawless graphics like that, and then generally restricting you to looking at machinery and snow...Well. It's not the full potential, but it's still pretty damn fine.
Coming on from Graphics, Animations. I'm quite the mixed bag when it comes to these, to be fair. The animations from the actual gameplay side of this is fairly smooth. In the intense Rig-Combat parts, things get a little shaky. Animations will occasionally merge together, like you'll be swinging your arm at something, and it'll try and hit you back. It generates awkward situations where you hit them, they go backwards, and their arm'll go flying off backwards, but it'll then still hit you. There's times where the enemy will just lock up if certain animations try to occur at once, giving you a fairly simply time of firing them down. Had this on the last boss, and the animations bug there provided me with a fairly easy win, which was quite the let down.
Alongside it, is the animations in the cutscenes. While some of the gestures the characters make in them seems perfectly fine and everything, there's quite a lot of gestures they do which seem to make no sense, and are incredibly robotic looking. They're nowhere near what I'd define as "Fluid", but more "Wooden". The Cinematics are a different story of course, but that's more in the region of CGI Graphics, than model animations.
Gameplay. Now...The gameplay has been rated so poorly, because 7/10ths of the game is tramping around the map, either in your rig or running around the "Hidden" offshoot areas of the maps. To begin with, this is perfectly fine. You're wandering around. You're stomping the indigenous wildlife (The Akrid). You're drilling down stalactites of ice to carry on your path. It's all good. But after a fair few hours of doing nothing but tramping from one place to the next, it gets incredibly tedious. There's points where you're told to go from your base, all the way to another area, only to have them send you tramping back the way you came, to go somewhere else. And as you dot his, you've gotta hop out your Rig, walk over to the place you're supposed to go, or the person you're meant to talk to, and then you've gotta turn around after a small cutscene and walk alllll the way back again. That gets old. Fast.
The on foot combat is the usual sort of thing you get from the LP series as well. Run about slowly, aim at the red "Weak" spots on the Akrid, rinse and repeat until all enemies are dead.
Fighting in your Rig is a different ballgame though. And not the good kind, really. To say you're in a giant robotic suit, kitted out with a crushing claw arm, and drill hand to start off with...You'd expect the combat to be good. Or at least the fast paced sort of thing you're used to in the LP series, with Vital Suits zipping about all over the place and whatnot. Nope. You tramp about, until some big Akrid shows up. Then it essentially comes down to a series of Quick Time Events (QTEs). Get close. Hit Q when prompted. Click your mouse to grab the Akrid. Click the right mouse button to drill away at it. Rinse and repeat until they're dead. It's as dull as it sounds.
The open world aspect of the game is a nice touch, when it comes to the diversity of the environments. But for the most part, the secondary objectives you receive feel utterly pointless, and really not worth their time suffering through the monotonous tramping, just for a few more points of T-Energy. This becomes quite excruciatingly clear towards the end of the game, where you get quite a large amount of side objectives to do...But all are completely unrewarding. They give you a few token things to do, like hunt rare albino akrid, to get "Buffs" to your character, like quicker reloading, HP regen, or an in-cover aiming reticule. But since you get them essentially two main storyline points before you get to the final stage, you're at that point where you just honestly can't be bothered spending an hour or even two, just tramping around to finish the objectives. Even the completionists out there might struggle to find the willpower to complete this to it's 100% state. What with the fast travelling system you get as well, you can just jump past those objectives without ever really feeling the pain of missing them.
Now. Storyline in itself. Thankfully, this is where LP3 really shines. You can look past the extremely dull and monotonous gameplay. The wooden movements of the cutscenes. And the fact that despite it all, you essentially know how it turns out for Jim, the protagonist, right from the word go. What you don't know, is how he gets there.
For fans of the LP1 storyline, you'll love the storyline in LP3. It provides all the lore you'd ever need about the origins of the Snow Pirates, and what NEVEC are after. It gives you a deeper understanding of the planet as well. All in all, it fills in quite a lot of those questions you might have had after playing LP1. But that's not what the story focuses on. It focuses on Jim. A contractor from Earth, looking to make some cash to keep his family running back home on Earth. He's a family man, and that's brilliantly brought to life through the messages his wife sends him from time to time, and the messages he sends back. The little banter, the humour thrown into it all. It generates a very real and deep character from Jim. (And the messages certainly do help relieve the monotony of tramping around the wastes.) The messages are heartwarming, and full of the sort of things you'd expect a message to contain to someone working a long way from home.
But even the characters around you all have deep characteristics. They all seem quite real as well, rather than just broken archetypes thrown in for filler.
And the story itself? There doesn't seem to be much of one when you begin the game. Heck, for the first half of the game, there's not a whole lot of "Story" going on. There's no goal. There's just Jim, working away to keep his wife and kid fed. The game does throw you a couple mysteries along the way, and it's evident there's something in the background. But everything still focuses on Jim carrying on with his life.
But then the story abruptly starts, and from there, it's got you hooked in. You want to push through the dull gameplay, just to find out what happens next. Again and again, it just keeps you going, like a book you daren't put down. "Just one more chapter. Just one more chapter." That's how it goes, more or less. All I can say about it is, if you loved the Storyline from LP1, then the Story from LP3 will make it worth the hefty price tag.
Overall, the game in itself, isn't worth the price of it. You'd have to invest a lot of time and energy into going through with all the terrible gameplay, to draw out the rewards of the story. I would recommend it, but only for those that are aware that the gameplay in itself is tedium encarnate.
Overall score: 4.5

LP3 is a fresh take on the existing LP franchise filled with breathtaking atmosphere and environments but not enough to keep you interested.
If you are new to the franchise then I'm hesitant to recommend this title, while it's a prequel to LP1 meaning you don't need to have prior knowledge of the universe, the game really doesn't excel well on any direction other than visually.
Level design is contrived and the constant mundane task of "go here, fetch this, kill this, oh wait plot filler trap, come back" repeat is predictable when you are going through the same maps over again over again. I'm not Link or Mario! Don't get me wrong, if this is the intended by the director for "character immersion" by all means go about your mundane task of being a miner but I bought this under the pretense of an action mecha game, not mining simulator.
Gameplay mechanics aren't anything to sing home about. At it's core LP3 felt sluggish and the constant QTE... just stop already. I didn't mind it at first, felt like it fit in but every fight will consist of QTEs really feels like a lack of creativity on their part. Weapons and your rig are presistantly upgradable but feel rather shallow with the lack of personalizable upgrades. Being on foot is rather underwhelming in general. The suggestive "duck and cover" mechanics is a mindless plug and useless 95% of the game; rarely do you have to hide from acrid and humanoid ranged attacks. Rolling for some reason is faster than running, wtf? However, the mech felt just right; yeah it's sluggish but it's a old utility mech and not a VS mech. Homely with constant reminders of why your on that planet to begin with.
And don't get me started about the gdamn PC port. The controls are utter sht, who the hell designed this? Why does every similar action have it's own key? It should all be mapped to the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ key! Who needs another key dedicated for planting a bomb or picking up ammo, it should all be E (USE)!
Ultimately, I can appreciate the story and narration because I've played LP1 and 2, the tie-in with LP1 is touching, I love the ice cold atmosphere and the detailed acrid environments, however, this isn't enough to want to play it: The game still sucks.
They took what I loved about Lost Planet 2, got rid of all of that, and gave us this pile of bile.

As a wordless, interactive short story, A Bird Story is just as amazing as Freebird Games' previous title, To The Moon. It merges fantasy with reality as it tells a tale of a child who struggles through his monotonous school life until he meets a friend who gives his life meaning.
The game contains far less exploration than To The Moon, and is focused on telling the story with minimal interaction. To The Moon has a lot of heavy themes in comparison, so if you were struggling through To The Moon, A Bird Story is a much lighter alternative.
A Bird Story is approximately one hour long, and bridges the gap between To The Moon and Freebird Games' next game, Finding Paradise, yet it works as its own standalone story.

Bying this game to me feels like literally being able to buy yourself some time of pure joy and relaxation, you know, being able to go carefree and forget about where you are at the moment. Firstly, you must understand: THIS GAME IS NOT XCOM 2. If you're looking for the same experience, look elsewhere.
Now then. The Bureau is a 3rd-person squad-based shooter. If you've ever played Star Wars: Republic Commando, it's a bit like that mixed with Gears of War. Only with more color and less mindless gore. The story is interesting, if not totally compelling, and while the protagonist's voice constantly reminds you of a hard-boiled detective from a black and white film that's smoked a pack a day since he was twelve, overall the voice acting is pretty good. My only real complaint about this game is the relative uselessness of your squadmates if left to their own devices; during battles, you must micromanage your team, giving them explicit orders constantly or they will literally stand around doing nothing, shooting blindly every once in a while. That said, the gameplay is entertaining and the squad control scheme is actually rather intuitive, so while at first it may seem like you're constantly babysitting your teammates, as battles grow more challenging and they get more equipment and better abilities, that babysitting becomes frantic strategizing and praying for cooldown timers to hurry up.
This game is not XCOM. This game is not Star Wars: Republic Commando. It's not even Gears of War, though constantly getting behind cover or reviving teammates who don't (or dying) will make you think it is a few times through the game. No, this game is an amalgamation of all these, a pot-luck of fun that, for the right people and the right price, can be well worth the buy.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is the prequel to the much loved and well received XCOM: Unknown and XCOM: Enemy Within.
It is set in 1960s America during a massive alien invasion that has swept through the planet annihilating any resistance with very advanced technology and sheer numbers. You play as Agent Carter, an anti-hero with a dark past as he recruited by a shadowy general - with more secrets than him - into the top secret XCOM programme. From there Carter and his squad launch a desperate guerilla war against the invaders.
XCOM Declassified utilises a third-person perspective with standard controls but differentiates when it allows you to lead a squad tactically and thoroughly - much like XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
But that, and the lore, are where the similarities end.
This game is demanding and requires tactical awareness at all times, it is
turn based and you must rely on checkpoints (which I personally don't like).
It gives you a massive degree of control over the battlefield and (with the ability to choose your character lines) parts of the - very engaging - storyline.
The commands are difficult to learn but once you've got it, it opens up a world of opportunities.
That method didn't work? Make him do that while he flanks and you provide cover.
As for graphics, they're typical and reminiscent of ye-olde times (okay, 50 years ago) but that's not a bad thing. The sound quality is good with an original dynamic soundtrack.
I've had no problems with my low-end rig so I expect it to be a good edition to your library.
I recommend this game for quick, tactical thinkers. Anyone expecting an average TPS will be sorely disappointed.

Even though improvements over HOI3 in terms of UI designs are highly visible and HOI4's relatively easy gamming mechanism makes this installation generally entertaining, the vast simplification of the overall system makes it look like a reductive and down-scaled version of its predecessor, despite its visual superiority. The complex mechanism in HOI3, even if it hindered many players from fully appreciating its content, serves as a distinguishing feature from other, arguably more simple, strategic games. The current state of HOI4 is well below one's erstwhile expectations of this series, as aspects including diplomacy, economics, technology and, above all, warfare require hardly any expertise for players to maneouvre. AIs at this stage are far from being competent enough either ad rivals or allies to be taken seriously. All these problems are indicative of a giant step backward from what Paradox had achived with the final version of HOI3 (Their Finest Hour). It really surprised me when I realised that many good features from HOI3 (command chains, warfare mechanism, etc.) are  almost completely ignored. It appears to me that developers are really not bothered taking advantages of their previous achievements. With regards to historical accuracy, this is when HOI4 is at its worst. Obviously HOI games allow players to deviate heavily from the historical version of WWII, but HoI3 can easily allow players to follow the orthodox path; in this game, however, anyone who has any knowledge of the events between 1939 and 1945 would wish to smash Paradox's face when Soviet divisions appear (despite them being volunteers) in Benelux in 1940 fighting ALONG WITH the Allies AGAINST the Wehrmacht. One wonders the fate of the Baltic states during the same period. This was an catastrophic failure for the game as, before reaching this stage, I had tried everything I could to ensure the accuracy of the 1939-40 Western front. Sadly this is just yet another flaw the developers do not care to fix. In any case massive updates are neccesary for HOI4 to be nearly as good as HOI3, although to get those updates players will inevitably be required to pay lots of extra money, which is what Paradox Interactive always does. The very release of the game at its current state is an egregious mistake on the part of Paradox Interactive.

As a non-Early Access title this game is a mess. I was OK with what seemed to be a limited amount of content (4 areas) but was pleased when I found there were multiple areas and holes within each area, each with it's own challenges. Apart from that, however, this feels much like an alpha Early Access release title.
1) You can only play this game with an Xbox controller. I'm not sure why they thought this was a good idea. I could see if there was an intricate control scheme much like maneuvering on your skateboard in the Skate franchise, but there isn't.
2) Speaking of the controls, the only time you can even see them is during the loading screen which (Although great) goes by so fast you can only make out 1 or 2 buttons before you're back in the game. On top of this, it seems most of the controls don't even work. The basic scheme is A) Press the left stick forward to hit the ball. B) Press the B button during the special "Smashbreaker" mode and somehow use the left or right analog stick to steer the ball. None of the other controls I read seemed to do anthing.
3) The game basically plays itself. Ready to go for the hole? Hit the stick and the ball magically flys in, ricocheting off of walls and objects as necessary to make a fancier end to the round. Granted, I only played 3 holes before I requested a refund, it seems there's no way to miss the hole. There is no aiming or planning or thinking required.
4) The menu system is very wierd, in case you're looking for the Options screen, you need to go to Clubhouse first, then you'll find the settings for the game.
Overall, I am very dissapointed with this game. I'm not really sure what the devs were going for here other than EXPLOSIONS, and, IT'S RUNNING ON THE UNREAL 4 ENGINE! Save your money for now and if they decide to drastically overhaul this game later down the line it may be worth it.

Pixel Piracy was not exactly a game that I was looking for, but after picking it up, it definitely surprised me in how fun the game actually was. Graphically, the game is quite charming. Gameplay itself is an interesting mix of hands on and hands off. And the sandbox-esque way of creating your ship is quite lovely. The audio is a bit more of a mixed front for me than others, but all in all, positive.
When it comes to how the game looks, Pixel Piracy is very much a retro throwback indy title. It's filled with lots of lovely blocky pixels, and really has that old school charm to it. If you are a fan of the low res, chunky looking games, the art alone just might sell Pixel Piracy to you. The only visuals that seem a bit mismatched and out of place are the sails and the sea itself. While every other bit of Pixel Piracy is nice and blocky, the sails and the water look more modern, and it can be a bit offputting.
The gameplay of Pixel Piracy is wonderful! It is an interesting merger between a god game, and a game with a bit finer tuned controls. With the exception of more absolute control over the captain of your ship, most of the sailors go about their business as they please. (Particularly if they are unhappy!) Unless you select the ship group the sailor is directly associated with, getting them to move where you want is impossible. It can be a bit frusturating at first, but it really spices up the gameplay when you're trying your best to keep newer shipmates alive during a wild brawl amid decks!
Pixel Piracy has the appeal that most sandbox games have. Do what you want, when you want, and the way you want. Moving up from a dinky little boat to a massive customized warship takes time, but finally getting there really feels rewarding! Building up a ship from scratch and using it to mow down lower tiered pirate ships is just a great feeling.
The audio in Pixel Piracy is the one area that may need a bit of work. The shanties are funny, but limited. The sound effects in general are quite fitting to the game, to be completely fair. The real issue is how sailors will begin to have a "conversation" onboard your ship, which basically just results in them filling your ears with "Yo ho!", "Dead men tell no tales", "Blow the man down", and "Shiver me timbers!" over and over and over again. It was funny at first, but as the game progresses it does begin to wear on you a bit.
Overall Pixel Piracy is a GREAT game! Sailing around the world, sinking the ships of your unworthy foes, and conquering islands gives the game a lot of replay value.  8.5/10

As a long time Lost Planet player and huge fan of the series since the beginning, I can say that this game is not for us.
The canon is broken from the first ten minutes of gameplay, and broken moreso at every single bend, turning the Akrdi threat into, well, not a real threat at all, VSs somehow sprouting from mechs three times their size, and the entire setting being....just ignored.
The game seems to set up it's own canon and it very much shows through gameplay, environments and design choices, that the development team either developed this as a standalone title because they wanted to show their own style, or that they completely have no clue about what the series is based upon, as the only design elements left from the original two titles, are the designs for some of the Akrid, and glowy bits on your armour. TE no longer works like it used to, grappling hooks went from fun to just a means of getting to exactly placed points and can't be used elsewhere. While the combat on foot is par for the previous games, the combat in the RIG is sluggish, slow, unreactive, and while the QTE-like moments while battling larger Akrid is sort of fun, the windows for counters are so tiny that you need to be quite good at the game to survive, and it is often better to simply combat the Akrid on foot.
The game does a good job at creating it's own world, however, and when viewed as its own title, rather than a sequel, it is honestly not bad. I could see myself really, really enjoying this game due to the beautiful, awe inspiring graphics, colour and environments, and while some of the designs are pants on head (Ie: not a single main character covers their face in the -50C weather), they often come off as their own product with it's own feel. The models are very much unlike game characters, and feel more like watching a live action series or movie.
The mechs, as a fan of the genre however, are garbage. The design team laxed back on huge, impossible to balance, utilitarian piles. The desperate attempt to seem believable and realistic is overshadowed by things like a giant, breakable cockpit window that constantly suffers damage, has complete ice overs, and serves as nothing more but face recognition that is impossible to see, as you're locked in first person view. VSs do exist, but the fact that these bloody things in no way resemble them but are somehow developed from them, and look not a thing like the original VSs, is a bit of a kick in the balls to fans of the mecha genre and fans of this series, the two of which often overlap. Instead of quick sliding and manouvering, we get CLANK CLANK CLANK. LP1 and 2 did the utilitarian mecha well, with it being reasonably sized, and with enough variety to suit anyone from the average anime fan to hardcore fans of old style mecha, and even to fans of western styles such as Battletech. However, this is mostly one bitter robot fans lament, and this is really up to personal opinion.
All in all, solid gameplay with a few problems and quirks. Beautiful graphics and design and a relatively believeable story, if not hindered by very poor dialogue at some points.
But, this all has to be ignored to some degree, as this is a title in an ongoing series, and indeed by that logic, must follow in the steps of its predecessors. The game fails on almost every level in this, and is something akin to an insult to long time fans of the series, and with Capcom's standard "It was your fault" schpiel to us for not demanding another game like Lost Planet 2, this game feels more like an insult than a new addition. This is a game for casual fans of the TPS genre, fans of sci-fi and sci-fi horror, but not a game for fans of Lost Planet.
