This was a fun game to play through Christmas break. The game is difficult for sure, but since each game only lasts for about four to five hours it's not too crushing to lose; so long as you have a few days to play its fun. In game economy flows really well and I've found myself needing every single resource at one point or another, and being able to sell each resource off at one point or another for extra income. Defenses are fun to manage since the undead will literally swarm from every single side. The AI is very difficult to read and makes for a very fun opponant.
It's basically a base building RTS with a pause element that fully utilizes macro and micro RTS styles. This game is much more focused on defending your base than Star Craft where you don't have walls. As the game progresses there are more and more zombies that start lumbering toward your village. Wave one will be a mild rush of a few handfuls of fresh zombies. The final wave will have so many zombies you feel like the game lives up to its name. Not to mention the zombies have varients so you'll encounter several types of zombies, and some have some scary abilities. As you upgrade your base you'll eventually get to some interesting Steam Punk stuff yourself to combat the scarier zombies. Basically you're prepping for a huge attack at the end. If you survive the final wave you win the game. While building up you're constantly on the defense from all sides.
Part of why I'm so forgiving for the difficulty and the inability to hardsave is because each time you start a new game the map is completely new since it auto generates every time you start a new game. The game can screw you with resources though I've noticed. If you can't produce the price to buy those resources in the market are so high you can forget being able to depend on it steadily. I've seen this game called the Dark Souls of strategy gaming and I can definitely second it's difficult nature, but it still manages to be more fun than frustrating.
I have had a lot of fun building tons of glorious defensive points and watching them hit with a gargantuan horde of zombies and somehow get overrun. In these moments I'm not angry, but rather impressed with just how much stuff the game sent at me. Just when I felt I had a rediculous amount of defenses the game makes me feel like an idiot for feeling so comfortable with only three layers of walls all guarded with Executer Towers.
I'm happy this game is an early release, and I hope the Dev is able to add in a lot more stuff to this title. It definitely feels like there are some missing things in the game, but overall it's already a fun experience, and for $25 I would say it's worth it for how many hours you'll probably end up putting into it as is.

It is with a very heavy heart that I write this review.  I first started playing Rift YEARS ago, and actually had left World of Warcraft for it because I felt it was a better game.  The world, story, soul trees (ability trees), and character customization is phenomenal and there was a great diversity on how to play/approach the game and it had lots to do.  Sadly, that game - the game I loved - is not what Rift is anymore.  It has nothing to do with the game, and everything to do with Trion and their team.  I have nothing good to say about them.
They ignore their fanbase, the are rude and will shut down anyone who even remotely criticizes them, they refuse to provide answers to their community, and I'm pretty sure they're drunk at work (literally - they're almost always drunk/drinking on their livestreams).  They are very unprofessional and frankly, they make decisions that leave all but their paid fanboys scratching their heads going "wtf?!"
Also, I have to say Rift needs to be removed from this and all "F2P" lists. Beyond how denigrating Trion has become to its customer base:
1. Almost everything can be bought with cash. Raid gear? Yup. Instant-Level boosts? Yup. Costumes? Yup. Etc, Etc.
2. Not all content is "free" but because you can grind in-game money to buy credits (or via sellers) to buy the content they consider it "free-to-play". Of course then they implement policy changes to make earning in game money harder and nerf in-game revenue streams if they get "too unbalanced" (their wording, not the players).
3. They have literally taken dyes, gear, etc that people have earned in game, or bought with cash away and will remake the same thing with a different name and lock it behind credits/real cash.
4. They constantly nerf quest, daily, kill, etc XP to try to keep people from reaching max level easy (because too many high level alts allows people to grind things easier instead of buying it from their store).
5. The newest, and all future, expansions must be bought with cash or you can grind in game cash (which they continually nerf) and hope to find a legitimate seller who isn't going to rip you off.
6. Many of their "world events" now have aspects locked away behind credits.
7. They constantly add craftable/sellable things such as dyes and wardrobes to their store with enhancements making the actual craftable ones crap - i.e. killing in game revenue. One of their last changes made Apothecary almost useless as a revenue stream, etc.
Sure, Rift is "technically" free, but for all intents and purposes they try to back players into a corner forcing them to spend cash on them which is pragmatically, to most, not "free-to-play".
In addition, the community resources suck, there are still glitches from YEARS ago, this last expansion which was delayed for months and then "released" last November is STILL unfinished, etc.
I'm really sad cuz this game deserves more love!

I adored the first TDU. Hooning about Hawaii.
When I got TDU2, I was quite happy. That changed when I started playing.
Granted, it's open world. Granted, the scenery and the vehicle renderings are good. However, I don't have a steering wheel. I play with a joypad. And it took me ages to actually set the damn thing up to work as near as possible correctly. Once I'd done that, then the game became pretty decent.
I enjoy the idea of passing the tests for various vehicle classes before you can proceed with various races to ultimately win the Solar Crown. Some of the races can prove challenging, so it's not all just a hoon about.
Mooching around Ibiza and the jaunt to Hawaii, gives ample opportunity to find various vehicle dealers, small side quests, outfitters, hair dressers, plastic surgeon, real estate agents, and vehicle upgrade sites, both cosmetic and mechanic.
The other racers in the game, that form the people you're pitted against are generally planks. Even though it's a game, there's a real sense of "I'm up here becuase I'm freakin fabulous, you're just a nothing", and it all seems to be about image. Hence the reason for the outfitters, hairdressers and plastic surgeon. Which I feel is ironic for a driving game.
Graphically, it's very pretty, and the rendering internally of vehicle is quite good, although I wish the dash binnacle worked properly, not just the speedo and tacho.
There's a good few MODs out there, and availability to add other, non stock vehicles to your garage is quite good. There's no Lamborghinis for example in the stock game.
Apart from the initial niggles, TDU2 is a decent driving game, with lots of exploration, a decent choice of motors and a good place to while away many hours.

Admittedly, I was hoping for a new and improved version of XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within, and this isn't that at all. Having said that...after a shaky start learning the new interface, I absolutely enjoyed this game. You still get a bit of the turn-based battle feeling (not frozen, but slowed time), while now being personally immersed in the fights (which can become very intense at times). No more viewing everything from above, with only a few kill shots and cut scenes up close! You run missions in squads of three, commanding their targets, special abilities, movements, etc. If given no commands your men will just stay near you, in cover when possible, and auto target with their equipped weapons.
The mission gameplay is fairly linear, and the story dialogue can be slow and admittedly boring at times. Though they do allow quite a few choices as you progress, which change your overall path (and how the game ends). The game doesn't have nearly as much potential for replay and endurance play as the EU/EW game, but it's fun nonetheless.
They also added some small side tasks for some reason, which must be completed. They have you (squad leader) do silly things like track pipe leaks, and send sick people to the infirmary... That was odd.

The Bureau is a solid squad based cover shooter with tactical and RPG elements.  You must fight off an alien invasion to 1960ies earth and unravel the mysterious forces at work.  You command a squad of agents with different specialties and you and your agents can be leveled up with different abilities and buffs as the game progress.  You can control your 2 allies on the field (very similar combat to Mass Effect 2 & 3) by placing them in different positions and assign powers to use.  The powers are fun and vary from bio and machine allies, bombs, turrets, mind control, levitation and more!  Combat is fluid and fun and the best part of the game.
The setting feels like 1960ies America, or at least what the movies describe as 60ies America, and I really enjoyed the ambiance from the visual appeal of a town, college or rural area.  There are lots of aesthetics thrown in like old TV screens, lab equipment, diners, cars,  etc that really capture the feel of 60ies living.  Unfortunately your squad and other characters you interact with are wooden and bland.   However you are able to make choices in conversation and there are a few interesting twists near the end that your choice will have some impact on the story.  For a sci-fi invasion angle, I enjoyed the story, it’s just that the wooden NPC’s drag it down and take away some of the immersion created by the set pieces and combat.
I hate to review a game in the context of another, but my advice is if you have played Mass Effect 2 & 3 and loved it, you need to play The Bureau as it’s the closest thing to more Mass Effect.  On its own the Bureau has enjoyable gameplay, solid atmosphere with a fun campy story that is brought down by bland characters but is still a worthwhile light RPG experience, plays great with a gamepad.
FYI – if you have an AMD graphics card turn the physics options off to have a high frame rate.  Otherwise X-com Declassified is a looker even on mid-level machines.

Background: Won a free copy over at Bloody Disgusting. Never played the first 2 despite really wanting to coz i like the look of the location and aliens.
Impressions:
This is a great game hampered by a load of minor irritations. While I think it's worth playing I found myself constantly reminded of how the better games this one is aping handled things better. In fact I'd just 100% completed Dead Space 3 on hardcore when I started LP3 and found it extremely similar in mechanics but with a less interesting story and weapons.
I hated the quest system right from the start. It pointed the way but not to what level of the base so you randomly pick a floor, wait for loading, wrong floor, try again. Maybe I missed something but it was beyond me.
I was excited to get into the Mech and do some damage but early on it seems you trudge for minutes, get out and kill a bit, get back in, swipe some ice, trudge, repair with Mech, uneventfully trudge home. Even when the Mech gets into a fight its sadly quicktime events which I know some find pretty boring and these aren't as forgiving as Dead Space.
What I found baffling was when on a repair mission the repair was done by holding down a key.. why wasn't the repair a mini-game? That could have been really fun and while the rest of the game feels a lot like Bioshock and Dead Space it seems a huge mistake not to have added this element as well.
The Good:
*Looks great, the snow planet and it's occupants are impressive.
*Weapons and aiming work well.
*The story is functional and your characters situation feels real.
*The tutorial is built seamlessly into early play.
*Good voice acting.
*Grapple hook works well but rarely tactically useful.
*Camera locking makes for some interesting switches in movement mechanics.
*Quests make sense and the main plot develops organically as you play.
*Feels a lot like Dead Space 3 in mechanics and locations (take that how you will).
*Reloads on death are quick enough and auto save gets you back into the action.
The Bad:
*Lots of wandering around for audio logs.. for an achievement.
*Walking Mech from location to location, at the start, is tedious
*Guns are boring standards: pistol, shotgun, machine gun, rifle.
*Mech Grapple line sometimes frustratingly picky about targeting.
*Lack of damage info means your not sure if your shots are actually damaging.
*Characters are mostly stereotypes with fetch/repair quests.
*Early on the HUDs limited info makes the map confusing.
*Some sections have no clear sub-objective and leave you stuck.
*Walking the Mech for 3 minutes without diversion gets boring.
*Repairing? Hold a key down... not even a mini game?
*Missions usually have a tedious return journey back the way you came.
*Aliens are confused by the Mech and get stuck on it while you kill em on foot.
*Mech battles are quicktime events.
*Seemingly random keybindings that could have been consolidated into one key.
Recommended for: Dead Space 3 fans looking for a very similar but lesser experience. Shooters who don't mind console cliches like QTE's.
Conclusion.
6.5/10. Both fun and frustrating and worth while if you can forgive console tropes and minor irritations.

If you're a fan of Kan Gao's work, I recommend trying this game. Like To the Moon, this is very much an interactive story with little actual gameplay. There is no dialogue, and the themes and motifs explored in the game lend themselves to the eventual sequal of To the Moon, called Finding Paradise.
That said, this game is definitely different from To the Moon. There are no plot twists, less intense emotions, and only an hour long. I would recommend trying Gao's other games, like The Mirror Lied, to gauge whether or not a game like this might interest you. This game isn't for everyone, and fortunately Gao understands that, so if for any reason you don't like this game, you can message him for a no-questions-asked refund. I don't know if it's quite worth $4-6 for the game (+soundtrack), but I think of it as a way of supporting the work of Freebird Games, so I certainly have no regrets.

A wonderful short story. Unique in it's ability to tell a heartwarming tale without saying a word, If you liked To the Moon, you'll like this one. I can't wait to see what they come up with next. Art and Music direction are incredible. If you want something different you can lose yourself in completely for about an hour, this is it.

It's strange how a story can be told without a single bit of dialogue and still create an emotional reaction, yet Kan Gao has managed it. Although it didn't cause as many tears as his previous game To The Moon did, it is still an emotional journey about a boy and an injured bird and their journey together.
The transitions used to shorten journeys and change scenes are very clever and still make it very clear what has happened even though you don't see every part of the journey, and they aren't just fades, they are seamless transitions.
It's only around an hour long, but making it any longer would detract from the experience. It also reveals the name of the next game, so make sure to stay until the end of the credits.

Music plays an important role in the game and every track suits the game really well.
It's a good game to enjoy between the two To the Moon titles but don't expect this to be as epic as To the Moon.

Initially, this game was very accessible to almost any fan of survival games. You'd find yourself in trouble, get yourself out of it and set about building a shelter and shoring-up resources. Osiris' twist on the theme was your ability to craft yourself a way out of the gravity well and onto another planet in the system.
It took a while to gather enough resources to build a foundry and advanced electronics enough build your vehicles, but it wasn't exactly hard. There were plenty of various metals, gasses and usable flora around to slowly craft an entire colony, complete with it's own shipwright and dry-dock, hydroponic garden and waste facilities.  This is where I took a break to play other games in my ridiculous backlog...
I've basically just restarted (7/28/27) and honestly....I feel like the devs completely lost the plot. Yes, there are sliders for most of the obvious settings...but even on "casual" alien settings, for example, the weakest type is going to kill you in twenty seconds.  You have ONE magazine/battery/wtfever for your gratis pistol - which used to be unlimited - and if one is attacked by multiple aliens, they will find it impossible to stay alive...because your jetpack - which also used to recharge over time - has fuel that is quickly depleted. Food is scarce, water requires the collection of gasses and being able to actually craft the station required to combine them...  Oh, and your skil points are limited, so good luck playing solo.
Honestly, the current iteration feels like the devs played Dark Souls and got so enamored with it tha they tried to integrate it's difficulty into a gem of a game that honeslty didn't need it. It DID need minor tweaks to make it more challenging., mind you, but not the full-on wtf-is-happening-fest that I just experienced. The game is GORGEOUS - seriously. The visuals are great. The gameplay, unfortunately, has moved from fun and exploratory into inexplicably far too hard in some aspects and simple in others. If it released today, I wouldn't play it at all, to be honest.
Given that this is alpha-state, I'll update this review as new content rolls out and adjustments are made.

Together with Wolfenstein 3D and Doom, Quake completes the unholy trifecta of classic FPS games, the ones who started it all. Truly an ageless game, few things come close to its frantic gunplay, awe-inspiring levels and horrific, if low-resolution, enemies. I can't say anything that hasn't been said already, but I do advise anyone who's ever been slightly interested in FPS games to buy it and play it, after eventually patching it with the DarkPlaces engine. It's worth your time and money and demands your respect.

Everything you are about to read is entirely my opinion, proceed with caution. Now, before an angry mob comes and chews me out. Just hear me out, alright?
I
(as some may agree) think that Doom was a much more enjoyble experience than this. But that doesn't take away anything from Quake itself, the game is great, fast paced, definitely set the standards for the FPS games we have today, as well as introducing tricks such as b-hopping, rocket jumping, etc. Without Quake, there would be no Half-Life, without Half-Life, there'd be no Counter-Strike and so on, you get the picture. Quake was also id Software's first full fledged 3D game, everything is fully modeled. From the maps, to weapon models, and to enemies. Definitely a step up in a technical standpoint compared to Doom, kudos to John Romero and John Carmack.
I appreciate what Quake is, and what id Software was going for. A kind of gothic sci-fi shooter that's episode based, much like the style of Wolfenstien and Doom. Only except you choose your skill level, and episodes in game by walking through portals, "slipgates" to be more precise. There are 8 regular maps in each episode, again like Doom. The soundtrack however...is meh to me, it's not bad. But it's nowhere near as memorable as Doom's, the only track I remember from Quake is the menu theme, all the other tracks are just ambience that only fit when listened in game. Surprisingly enough, the soundtrack was made noneother by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails. (Who happened to be a huge fan of Doom might I add), but it's just kinda strange to me how none of the other tracks really just stick to me, you know? Considering NIN puts out some really good music.
Wait what? You can't be serious, you're not playing id's games for the story, are you? Ok, well the plot is very minimal. You're a guy named Ranger, you kill stuff, you travel to different dimensions, and you kill stuff and collect runes at the end of each episode, where small plot is given through text,
like Wolfenstein and Doom.
In my experience, the enemies also seem to both lack, but at the same time have variety to them, you have the standard former humans you encounter in the beginning of each episode (a la the zombiemen and shotgun guys in Doom), then later you fight these demonic kind of enemies. Most common enemy you'll face mid to late game is the Ogre, which use a grenade launcher in one hand, and a chainsaw in the other, fairly easy to kill, just shoot at it until it's dead.
Though, the one enemy that stands out the most to me would have to be the Zombies, you think giving them the good old one-two with the super shotgun will kill them? Think again, they're a lot more resilient than you think. You'll have to launch a grenade at them, or maybe jam a rocket in their mouth to make 'em rest in pieces.
Now I know what you're thinking: "Oh, but Mr. Dude Man Guy, what about the Shambler?!" yes, yes. Calm down, I was just going to get to him, it, whatever. Basically this thing is the absolute most putrid offspring between the Arch-Vile, Cyberdemon, and maybe a bit of the Baron of Hell, it's very tanky (like the aforementioned Cyberdemon). It has an attack that is based on line of sight, as long as you break it, you should be fine. It also has a very strong melee attack, like the Baron's. Truly a challenge to take on.
Quake itself is a great game, pioneer of the FPS genre, I'd recommend this to about anyone who's willing to go back to the roots of FPS gaming (ofc Wolfenstein mainly popularized it due to its success if you want to go deeper). But seriously, it's worth the money, I'd pick it up, especially during a sale.

Created on the heels of the runaway success of the Doom series, Quake paved the way for the first-person shooter with its fast-paced action and graphical advancements. Fully realized 3D graphics resulted in some of the most intricate and well-designed maps in the genre's history. The feeling of running around the various honeycombed shortcuts is an unmatched satisfaction in FPS movement. Each map is made eye-catching and memorable by the game's distinct artstyle which draws from a fusion of medieval and metallic. The same can be said for the game's enemy roster, which range from laser rifle-lugging shock troopers to muscle-bound bundles of teeth and claws. Unfortunately the base game doesn't take full advantage of the diversity of its enemies, with later levels sinking into the tedium of firing shotgun shell after shotgun shell into ogres and death-knights. This is rectified somewhat by the higher difficulties, which see no problem in pitting unrealistic numbers against the player. Quake is an addicting and wonderful game at any price, and it's worth owning to understand what makes this game such a solid pillar of the genre. Now let's hope they don't give this an ill-fitting modern reboot as well...
If you want to improve your experience check out some of the community guides on how to implement things like different engines and the soundtrack. The base Steam release is unfortunately lacking in some areas, and the work getting in fixes can be well worth the effort.

Hidden Folks is one of the very few hidden object games I like. It’s not like the others that have a weird story or extremely nonsensical item layouts. It’s Where’s Waldo with a strange sense of charm due to all the mouth-based sound effects and abundant animations.
I’ll start off by saying the game has very few problems. I found the default color scheme much too hard on my eyes with the generous amount of white, but the developer included a sepia filter and an inverse color scheme if you wanted to see tons of black. Sepia was perfect for me, so I’m glad it’s there. The only other issue was the number of interactive objects on the big city map. I did not enjoy clicking and dragging open a bunch of blinds, only to have them close again shortly after. I tended to forget what was in there and I would have preferred they just stay open so I didn’t have to open them repeatedly.
Most of the little people and creatures have animations and sounds that play when you click on them. They also produce an ambient murmuring type of deal depending on the map and how zoomed in you are. It feels lively with all the movement and I appreciated the number of silly mouth sounds. I highly recommend clicking on things multiple times to hear all the voicework. You’ll not find a soundtrack, so having a podcast readily available wouldn’t be a bad idea.
The gameplay is what you’re probably thinking. You’ll have objects and people at the bottom of the screen that you must find. They all come with little hints which helps greatly for some of the very large maps. You’ll have small maps and large ones which will require zooming in and out and some screen movement. It all works without any bugs during my experience.
There are more levels incoming from what I saw in the game, but what’s there provides a pretty good time. It’s a wonderfully pure searching experience that I hope to have more of soon. I also wouldn’t mind a sequel that introduces some maps with colors.

I downloaded rift recently, while itching to play an mmo where I could sling spells from a distance and had some nice bredth of classes.
Playing as a 'Reaper,' on the both fronts I was not disappointed. Although the information on Rift's website is rather vague and the wiki isn't much better, there's a satisfying depth to each 'calling.' Callings are your basic fantasy classes of Mage, Rogue, Warrior and Cleric. Within these 'callings' there are a variety of skill trees, of which the player may choose three, although there are in-game guides to help the player with recommended combinations which synergise well. You may also change which three 'soul trees' you're using and redistribute points, when not in combat.
After your beginning instance, you're let out into the world to do you generic WoW-esque questing. Some small villages centre on teaching you about skills like fishing and survival or crafting professions. One introduces you to 'dimensions,' which are basically small home instances for you to decorate, although figuring out how to get there requires fumbling through various interfaces. W/r dimensions, the ability to rotate and adjust objects on xyz axes is nice and it's pretty smooth too.
The negative aspects are however, quite significant. The questing system, graphical style and f2p model feel very reminiscent of various Asian f2p mmorpgs, which are lagging behind in the genre somewhat. In this regard, the game feels very same-y, there's not much I can get from it that I couldn't get from ArchAge or Jade Dynasty, the prior of which has cool things like boats, trans-continental trade and pvp against pirates at sea, to make it stand out some more.
Like a f2p Asian mmo, Rift also suffers from the over-zealous use of premium currencies, boosts and other micro-transactions that we're all familiar with by now. As other reviews have pointed out, throwing money at the game gives you the ability to bypass a lot of the levelling(which makes up a lot of the content) and removes a lot of the grind. Not to mention that small cosmetic changes, like changing hair or character's gender costs thousands in this currency. Saving up for your first mount is instead chump change, if you choose to buy premium currency, something which I feel cheapens many aspects of the game. Rift is not shy about advertising patronship to the player either, including a button which is visible on-screen at all times, unless the player deliberately changes the ui layout to conceal it.
The dimension home-instances seem like another way to squeeze money out of the player, by encouraging them to purchase furniture using premium currency, as much of the items above-beginner level became substantially more expensive.
Lastly, although there's a sustantial effort made to explain how the 'soul tree' skill tree system works, there are other areas of the game which require more explanation. A number of quests required that I craft say a fishing lure, but gave no explanation as to how to do that. Instead, I had to read through the dialogue to find instructions clearly added in after much player confusion and frustration. Granted, I would have seen this had I read the dialogue the first time, but so much of the questing was so very boring and outdated that I had little motivation to really care about why I was collecting 10 Mutated Meat or killing 8 undead. Again, there's little information on either the website or the wiki, regarding this.
I don't have anything against the game, nigh pay-to-win features aside, but it's just not very good. If it wasn't f2p I wouldn't have played it at all and I have a hard time believing people once willingly paid a continual subscription to experience Rift. The good features of the game are unfortunately drowned out by the more generic or out-dated aspects and what enjoyment I did get out of it, quickly drew to a close.

Do you like/play videogames?
Do you like/play First Person Shooters?
If the answer to any of those questions is "Yes" then PLAY THIS GAME
QUAKE FREAKING RULES: It is simultaneously the most important PC videogame to ever be released aside from Unreal and Doom, and at the same time one of the most pulse pounding, erection throbbing, masculine pieces of hardcore videogaming to be ever devised.  If you haven't played this game, you can't call yourself a lover of videogames.
The story is.... Well WHO GIVES A HORSE?? But in case you want to know what's going on:
You are Ranger: A warrior of earth who is sent by the leaders of earth through these ancient portals (Called Slipgates) into other dimentions to retrieve 4 runes and stop the evil overlord Shub-Niggurath that is controlling all the monsters that you fight. The whole story is told through the level design, and from the text and the end of each episode, just to make sure you haven't ran away to burn down your school.
The art style is very reminisent of Gothic, Sci-fi, Hell, and the Occult. The whole art style feels like a love letter to the powerful H.P. Lovecraft (if you don't know him, get out and read Cthulu).  Playing Quake feels like being trapped in a metal band's nightmare of awesomness. It's dark, gritty, terrifying, and it just feels wrong. but plays so right. And it should feel like a metal band's nightmare, because Trent Reznor of the band Nine Inch Nails helped ID Software create this masterpiece. He did the amazing music, some of the iconic sound effects, and the voice of Ranger.
The level design is SECOND TO NONE: This is as criptic as Doom, and every single map is carefully constructed and planned so that you feel overwhelmed on where you need to go, yet they are simple enough to navigate so that you get the feeling of being a baddass, overcoming the criptic levels. The sheer amount of effort and detail that went into these levels puts every single fps level made today to shame. Even Doom 2016's levels, while criptic and challenging, are childs play compared to the epicness of Quake. The only other games I can think of that have better level design that this are Doom 1 & 2, Heretic/Hexen, Blood, Duke Nukem 3D, and Unreal 1. And even then, I would say that Quake is more complex and better than all of them: the levels are not as straightforward as Dooms, nor as brainkilling as Heretic/Hexens, nor as believable or iconic as Blood or Duke Nukem 3D's; Quake's levels feel like something out of a nightmare and there has been nothing like this ever been seen since.
The music in Quake is just simply amazing. It captures the whole mood of being in a nightmare, and is as iconic as Quake it'self. Just listen to this, and it sums up what playing quake is like:
The enemies are amazing and very original too: You have to learn and memorise all their attack patterns and behaviours to overcome them, and use the right weapon for the right enemy.
The weapons themselves are also metal as ♥♥♥♥: You start off with Ranger's iconic
Axe, and a fast firing shotgun. There is then the Double barrel shotgun, and the rocket launcher, all stuff you expect. Instead of a machine gun, you have NAILGUNS: a Double barrel nailgun, and a Gattling nail gun, and the nails are not hitscan attacks they are projectiles, so you have to lead your targets. You also get a grenade launcher and a rocket launcher to kill the undead zombies, as they can only be killed by Gibbing them. Finally you have the lightning gun, which requires you to have a line of sight on your enemies to use, so you can't simply use it and duck behind a pillar, meaning you have to THINK on how you will use it.
And did I mention this game is hard? FREAKING hard? Even on the easiest difficulty this game will test your skills to the bone. In fact the Nightmare difficulty is so hard that they hid it in the episode select hub. See if you can find it and takkle the ultimate challenge.
This is also one of the most important PC games ever made: It was one of the first games to use 3D polygons and run itself off a computers CPU, which was mindboggling for the year 1997. It was the first FPS game to implement the WASD+Mouse controls as standard for FPS, it cemented the fast paced arena deathmatch multiplayer, and it's mindblowing idTech graphics engine created a game engine for HUNDREDS of games to use. So many iconic games today have used this game's engine; Call of Duty, Half-Life, Counter-Strike, the original Team Fortress was a mod for this, and I could go on ALL DAY.
Quake is one of the greatest videogames of all time, and the aftershock of it's impact and legecy are STILL being felt to this day. Quake changed videgames forever.

Come to find out it is because of an update built into Windows 10 named KB3086255 which disables Securom and Safedisc or whatever it's called, which is something that a lot of older games and physical discs used. Stage 1: disadvantage
Stage 2: Equal
Stage 3: Advantage

I recommend this game, expecially if you liked mass effect in terms of combat. You actually HAVE to control your team, issue orders regularly, ask yourself which guy to bring along each time, and how to approach situations etc.
Higher difficulties, as in ME, bring forth the robustness and fun out of the combat system. Therefore, don't bother with lower difficulties since those don't give any incentive to playing the "commander role", because you can pretty much solo everything.
The story holds a major twist that's actually brilliant and excellently done with in my opinion, very, very good voice acting, and a nice '60s theme to pack everything into a nice, enjoyable package.
It gets repetitive after a while, because of low enemy variety, that's true : the game's biggest problem right there.
All in all, disregard the metascore and have fun.

Lost Planet 3 tells the story of Jim Peyton, a blue collar family man from Earth, sent to a remote colony on planet E.D.N. III, 50 years after the events of the first game.  As the story unfolds, Jim learns that mega-corp NEVEC has been up to no good, and that he is embroiled in a conspiracy a generation in the making.  The art, sound and voice direction in this game are truly top notch not only making the story line unfold like a feature length film, but giving nuance and style to the gameplay itself.  In addition to a third person shooter, Jim can take control a utility mech, giving the player some compelling puzzle solving and innovative combat along the way.  The game supports Steam Trading Cards, Widescreen modes as well as the Xbox controller, but unfortunately is lacking any Steam Achievements.  Barring that one minor flaw however, Lost Planet 3 is truly a game not to be missed by even casual fans of the sci-fi genre.  I highly recommend this game to almost anyone.

Quake's 20th anniversary is here and I started playing the singleplayer campaign again. I played Quake when it originally released and it still holds up today. Quake's legacy might be its multiplayer, but Quake 1's campaign is great. It's all about the creepy atmosphere. It's not a game where you quickly mow through legions of demonic creatures. It involves exploration and some minor puzzle solving (mostly just finding keys or pressing a panel to open a wall, etc). You're wandering around a dark, subterranean castle-like environment which is in stark contrast to the sci fi settings of the sequels. This is by far the best setting out of the Quake series and I wish they'd do a modern take on the original setting, instead of all the sci fi Strogg nonsense that came after it. None of them captured the eerie horror setting and atmosphere of the original which is a shame. There is a basic story and lore to the game you can read about, but its not really presented in the game. You don't need to read anything to enjoy the game though. Similar to how Doom had a basic plot, but the game itself just involves you navigating levels and shooting stuff.
You must play this game with the Ultimate Quake Patch installed. It restores Trent Reznor's (of Nine Inch Nails) original soundtrack which was a creepy atmospheric masterpiece. To play the game without it is doing yourself a serious disservice. In addition to the soundtrack, it adds support for new resolutions. I personally don't think it needs any high res texture pack, playing it at a higher screen resolution is enough. It might look primitive by today's standards but id Software did a superb job with the limitations they had at the time.
Multiplayer is all but dead. While servers still exist, good luck finding anybody to play with. I had loads of fun with the multiplayer when the game was new, the Headhunters mod was particularly entertaining. You're not going to be playing this game today for the multiplayer, but for its singleplayer where it really shines.

The game is good but with no option to reload a game if you make a mistake (No save scumming), a few flaws in the game becomes major game breakers. If these get fixed, I'll be happy to recommend the game, but for now it remains an excersize in frustration. (Yes it's meant to be difficult, yada yada difficulty =/= frustrating experience)
The game isn't intuitive and doesn't adhere to normal RTS "rules" - Double clicking a unit or building will select all of those units/buildings on your screen. In fact it selects everything in the entire map of that type. This means that if you're used to RTS game that does it the normal way (Select all of that type showing on your screen) you'll be kicking yourself every time you accidentally try to upgrade or delete every single building of that type on the map, instead of the ones on your screen that you intended. With no option to reload a save, that will lose you games. (I deleted all my turrets...)
Making command groups seems to have a life on it's own. ctrl + 1-9 is supposed to work, but it only registers with about 50% accuracy. This doesn't appear to be an issue with my keyboard. You can imagine how annoying that is. Always having to double check.
No way to make waypoints when units patrol (And patroling is important to stay alive) - It's from A to B only. No shift/ctrl+click in order to make more waypoints.
No "Guard area" to have units automatically detect and defend an area larger than their viewrange. Both waypoints and "Guard" should be a must in a game so focused on making sure certain areas remain safe.
You will lose a lot. No problem in that. But you will lose to stupid things. You will lose to a single infected hitting a tent 2-3 times and instantly spawning 4 new infected - If that initial building falls, it's game over. The 4 new infected only need to hit the next house together once for 4 new infected to spawn. The domino effect is so bad you might as well quit right away.
Even if you have units ready to kill the newly spawned infected, it simply cannot be done in time.
This means that you will lose games to a single infected slipping past your patrols / walls A LOT - Only to get notified once it's already hitting a building.
Sure this makes the game difficult, but it works as an instant failurestate you can not come back from. A good game would be designed in such a way that one could fight his way back from an event like that. This game doesn't.
This flaw could be eased by making buildings less susceptible to infection (More HP), or delaying the spawn of new infected from a recently infected building by 5 or 10 seconds. to make up for easier difficulty the building could continue to spawn 4 new infected every 10 seconds until the area around the building is cleared. That way one coudl have buildings infected but still be able to clear them in time, if one was prepared well enough. Spacing out buildings to avoid spreading infection isn't an option. The game has 2 mechanics in place to limit your expansion rate (Teslatowers and idle zombies everywhere on the map that you haveto clear to make space. And there's a lot of them).
This results in the game forcing you to focus excessivly on making sure there are absolutely no gaps in your perimeter ever. If there is, you lose the game.
Another issue is the random generation of maps. There's no guaranteed spawn ressources. Meaning that you can spawn somewhere where you can't begin to gather ressources without first building teslacoils to expand your network. There should be a basic check for ressource spots around the command center when generating a map. Expect to re-generate maps in order to get  playable spawn location.
I hope the devs will take the early access time and use it to fix some of these issues and allow for more a exciting game. There's nothing exciting about losing a game because you missed a single infected when there's a billion of them.
Edit: Keys and mouseclick not registering sometimes seems to be consistent no matter the action.
The game really needs "Your stuff is being attacked" alert for when things currently on your screen is being attacked. I'm losing tons of games to buildings falling without alert because it was slightly in the corner of my screen (And if it's on screen there's no alert given). This is made worse by zombies being so indistuingishable from normal population. Constantly pressing ALT to check if it's a zombie or not (No way to show health bars permanently. Another flaw)

This game, is okay.
That being said, It did not feel like xcom, at least not enemy unknown. I think it would have done much better not being tied to the xcom name. While there are similarities, I think they would have been better off trying to go its own way. The Outsiders do not really fit into the mythos created by enemy unknown. At the very least, they should not have resorted to using the sectoids and mutons if they wanted to make it seem more original. Also, given that the Titan was prevelant in most of the early previews, I was a little dissapointed that it only showed up once, and that we didn't get a chance to control it like they had been hiting at in the early stages of the game's development.
The story itself was interested, though seemed to fall apart at the end a little too fast. The cold war theme fit in well with the characters, but the characters themselves seemed a little, artificial at some points. A little more information and scenes on how the war was progressing while at the base would have fleshed it out a bit more. But other then the map, you really didn't get a feel for how things were going across the nation.
The levels themselves were very linear, with interesting little combat zones thrown inbetween. It would have been much better to keep them more open level so one could retrace their steps across the map, but that's just me.
Perphaps the biggest dissapointment was the squaddies. While the idea was good, but it would have  greatly helped if they could shoot worth a damn, as the only way they tended to kill things was with their abilities, and not the guns you gave them (Sad when a soldier can't kill a Sectoid with a plasma rifle . . .). Particularly in the later levels, it made them moving targets at best, reload checkpoint at the worst. I wasn't expecting them to have a better kill count then me, but I was at least hoping they'd get on the board without handing them the kills.
Over all though, this was a decent game that suffered from some short comings due to its predecessors in the series. I would recommened it to others, just don't set your expectations too high. Another interesting little tidbit I also enjoyed, were the live action trailers also put out. In some ways, they were better then the game . . .

This time I won't walk through the technical aspects of the game. Shallowly I'm gonna say that everything is good--from the sound effects, the atmosphere, to the graphics and optimization--, but I won't dive into any deep details of the game itself.
Instead, this time, I'll introduce this game to you with a different approach:
.
Now that I have your attention, let's do this.
Back in 2012, during a weekday, I was at work when this Dishonored came out. I hadn't heard about it until its release on Steam, and was surprised by it because the publisher behind is very famous, Bethesda, and I used to follow their work since Fallout 3.
For this same reason--being a well-known publisher--, I was convinced to learn more about what this piece is up to. The more I knew, the more I wanted to buy it. You may ask why I just didn't wait for a sale and went ahead... well, that's exactly what I did. The first sale it came with a good discount was the one I bought it. The year was 2013.
I started playing Dota 2 in 2011 and was still playing in 2013, and when my spare time wasn't being taken by its single map and game mode, then my girlfriend, which, by chance, is now my ex, was the one draining my attention.
Contrary to what I used to be a few years earlier, while playing Dota 2, I didn't feel motivated to play singleplayer adventures anymore. Not patience enough. Moreover, I felt that I was becoming unskilled at Dota and becoming weaker than my friends--as if it mattered.
Addicted to Gaben's latest bet and driven by an illusion of "something missing when not playing Dota", I was not having fun at all. That pursuit to be good was unstoppable. I'd say that 80% of that precious time was being a waste with stressful matches and brainless people, and behold my eyes I saw myself becoming one of them. Not because I was being transformed into a creepy, internet-badass, toxic guy, but because the few hours I had to have fun was turning into ashes.
And it goes beyond: my girlfriend was suffering as well. Too addicted to the game to stay with her. Finally, when we once had a break, I decided to rethink "fun".
The break was game changing.
It was a cold and rainy, dark and silent Friday night of July. I had nothing to do but stare at my computer. Dishonored was dwelling quietly in my library until a sudden pain in my consciousness began to poke, "you bought this game and never played it before", a voice whispered inside my head, and instinctively I was lead to start downloading it.
Unfortunately, was very late. I mean it, 5 AM. And even with the progress bar almost reaching its end, I was tired and my eyes couldn't take any longer.
was the hour I woke up with the sound of the downpour, "half of the day fell by the wayside," I thought, but surprisingly mistaken I was.
When I got to my computer Dishonored was ready to play. I was not excited. Not even 1%. The laziness had taken over me and the idea of beginning a solo run gave me goosebumps, especially because perhaps this journey could stand only an hour or two, tops.
I took a deep breath and went to the door to close it. Looked back to the computer and approached my old office chair, sitting, chilling. Headphones up and running at maximum volume, the "start" button was tapped.
Suddenly I became Corvo, thrown into a hostile world as gray as that Saturday, with a long way ahead, just pursuing the typical feeling of a sinner: vengeance.
"<someone> is now playing Dota 2" popped up from time to time, with an annoying notification noise, but happily they were mostly all ignored by my best version of me, the unchained one. Sincerely not because I wanted to, but because I wanted to want to. The experience of that game was fulfilling the needs of my brain to make itself immersed into something, and I didn't want to disturb it.
Along with this immersion, a different sensation just showed up. Though I knew I had it before, I couldn't give it a name. But it's okay because I was also too busy to think about it. My concentration was trying to save Corvo's skin from enemies' dirty hands.
Those hours weren't only about that steampunk universe though. During what remained of the noon I paused a few times to make sure my vital signals and sanity were untouched by peeing and eating. Good stuff, all okay. The best finally came, but at night: as soon as the darkness embraced my room, I knew that the apex of the game would be lying shortly thereafter.
The only light in that room was from the surface of my screen. Of course, it wouldn't do any good to my eyes, but caring was out of the question at that moment.
Yes, I was delivered as I suspected. Completely not noticed when the clock ticked 4 AM. Knowing that I couldn't proceed with the same level of immersion I was experiencing before, I decided to have some sleep. When I reached my bed, my phone screams a message notification. My girlfriend.
August. Sunny Sunday noon, still cold. 2 months after starting playing Dishonored and life changed a bit. It's weird to compare a game to our lives, isn't it?
Look, I'm not comparing, but it somehow affected it. Getting back in time a little, let's drive our brains to that rainy Saturday once again. So, it was the responsible one for stopping me from playing Dota 2. It remembered how video games are supposed to entertain, the right way.
Also, as a side coincidence, my girlfriend and I were back together, again, and with a blow, the game was completed.
The pace was the one I have chosen, with no pressure, rush or even having to deal with kids dictating how the game is meant to be played.
When the credits were rolling the screen, a curious relic came up in my mind: that Saturday's feeling. An entire memento took form, including the smell of a mix of fresh tree leafs, the ones next to the wall of mom's house, with rain drops. Really hard to describe.
This feeling. This feeling we're all looking for, all the time.
Now I can name it.
Fun.

A lot of the negative reviews on this game are from people who have played it for 2-3 hours and I can understand why but I think they need to give it a bit more time because it is a real fun strategy game if you can get over the initial hump, which is the 3rd level. It took me a few attempts to beat it and a couple of hours but when I did it was a Eureka moment in terms of how to play.
Each ship shoots in a different way and moves in a different way so none are alike in terms of how you should attack with them and certain weapons do damage to shields or hull so you do have to think about placement but once you get your head around the game mechanics it is not that difficult. It does require you to think strategically and plan your actions but it is a strategy game so I'm not sure what people expected.
A lot of the reviews have focused on no undo button but again it's a strategy game not a trial and error game!
To me, it's kind of like the Sid Meier's Ace Patrol series but if that game had a full squadron of many different airplanes that you would take to the skies. Or a battle isle/Historyline game (for the older gamers!)
If you like something that requires you to think about your actions and consequences on a chessboard type arena then you will like this. If that kind of stuff frustrates and you don't have the patience to fail then you will not!
The Negative side is that the tutorial missions are a bit week and there is no help guide, which would have really sped up my understanding of how the game mechanics work and how the ships work! So the first few missions require some trial and error in understanding how to play, which will put people off (because of the lack of an undo button) but once you get past that it's a great strategy game.
Is it worth £14.99? Depends how much you like strategy games. I bought it on sale and I'm not sure I would have taken a gamble on it given the negative reviews on here. I have really enjoyed playing it so would probably pay full price knowing what I know now! Or chuck it on your wishlist and wait till a sales on!

Well.. I thought for a while about giving up on this game but i still got write this review only 3.8 hours into it...
This is a Turn base, Battle chess, space sim, Strategy game...
The concept is simple.. you control a space fleet against other space fleet. You have to suruvive the enemy onslaught and fulfill certain object each maps...
Exterior of this game is really good.. I enjoy the music tone in the background and i have no trouble with the indie graphics. And battles in space is always better then people wacking each other with a sword..
I been playing this kinda of games since good old shiny force one.. but for the 200-300 different turn base battle chess i played so far.. This is probably the hardest one I have ever encountered...
The AI don't cheat but they do move very smart each turn. The Movment and facing of your starships are weird and hard to get use to.. There are many maps and some really really grand battles that require you to survive 100 turns and etc.
The developer Dave Toulouse made a post about this game at his blog.
It sums up quite well the success and failure of this game...
AS it is..
70% of people that try this game give up on the very first mission because of the unforgiving 1 shoot kill your trasnporter... 25% gave up after all the training map becaues of the difficulty spike onto other missions... 4.9999% gave up after they cannot reach 3 troopy for each map which yield no achievements. Only 0.0001% of people would take the pain of restarting maps over and over again and enjoy it...
3 things can be done to lower the difficulty and fix the game...
1. Add a undo button... it's a extinction simulator.. not a real battle.. just let me take that move back so i don't have to restart mission...
2. Add a save function for each map.. well.. same as undo.. Need the magic button to reset mistakes..
3. I can turn my spaceship without moving? I will gladely pay 1 move for it...
Anyhow.. Desite i Enjoy a challage of a unforgiving rogue like space turn by turn.. I will have to gave up on this one because of above reason..
6.5/10 .. would gave it a 8 if there is just a save... Only recommend people that loves the turn by turn battle chess and willing to restart each maps .. many many many many many many times.....

I have played over 500 hours on this game on the 360 and i dont regret any of those hours, as this is my favourite game ever made, but dont get me wrong, there are some downsides to it.
Lets jump straight into the pros and cons.
Pros:
1: Extensive and engaging storyline.
2: Very good soical racer in its time.
3: Lots of things to do after you have completed the storyline, with friends or without friends.
4: An insane amount of cars.
5: An installable "Unoffical Patch" that grants you even more cars.
6: MASSIVE open world all there for the taking
7: In its time it had a great community.
Cons:
1: Impossible for new players, as registering an account is very difficult, and if you are on windows 10, theres a 50/50 chance you will or will not be able to play.
2: Atari and Eden games were dead many years ago, so dont expect any new updates or customer support.
3: No email verification, so if you forget your password, your save data and your entire account are done for.
4: Some glitches and bugs that can be frustrating, but do not happen very often.
5: Pretty hefty price tag for a game that is this old and may or may not work.
6: Graphics are very outdated, but that is to be expected from a early 2011 game.
7: Servers that are practically dead, in my past few days of playing i have not found one online player, which is very frustrating in my opinion.
Sugguestions to beat the cons:
1: DO NOT BUY IF YOU ARE ON WINDOWS 10, and research on a way to make an account, im sure there is a way.
2: Install the unoffical patch, as this grants many new cars to play around with.
3: Write your password down.
4: If these glitches do happen, for example hitting a stop sign in some areas will flip your car, do not get frustrated! You can always dodge or overcome these glitches.
5: Buy this game when it is on sale. It goes down to around 4.99 USD occaisonally.
6: Not really a fix for this one, but maybe there is some kind of mod out there that can give you a better graphics experience.
7: Find some friends that are playing! Post in the community discussions and look for people that are already playing the game.
Overall, this is my favourite game ever made. If one day i become a billionare, i am going to buy out atari and eden games and make a tdu3. Thanks for reading and i hope this helped you make your decision on whether to buy the game or not.

HOI4 is a dismal failure.
As a pure gaming experience, it is overdone, overly complicated, and wrought with potential left unfulfilled. As an historical simulation, it is abysmally off-target and misdirected. And before anyone says, “It is only a game, get over yourself,” may I retort? First, and most importantly, anyone who would submit that HOI4 is not an historical simulation of the run-up and exposition of World War Two (1939-1945) is in deep, deep, denial. Every fiber of this game’s design is an attempt at historical relevancy. That it falls short is more a statement of today’s billion-dollar computer gaming industry than a statement about the dedication, industry, and skills of the HOI4 development team.
Full disclosure: I am not generally a fan of Paradox Game design philosophy, although I own quite a few. I believe that their game designs often confuse ponderous and monotonous detail mechanics as a substitute for strategic and operational decision-making that leaders (read: players) should be making as a conscious decision to express the location of the player as the Man-in-the-Loop. Yet, I have put down hard currency for quite a few of their releases.
I have been playing wargames for 57 years. I was Vice-President of R&D for the Avalon Hill Game Company in the 1970s and a game designer for the Department of Defense in the 1980s. I was an original founder of the Game Designer’s Guild in the 1970s. I have designed many games and quite a few successful historical simulations. I have been a student of the game design process for many years. My thesis is basically this: There is little or no difference between the elements of successful design in a board wargame and a computer wargame. The only difference is that the capabilities of a computer allow for automation of logistical bookkeeping, hidden movement, fog of war, and simultaneous movement. At its heart, however, good game design is good game design, apart and separate from coding, simulation engine design, and artificial intelligence.
HOI4 is a wargame. If you think it is not, you are either much younger than I (by half a century) with a very narrow experiential base or very pedestrian in your philosophical concept of what constitutes a “game.” As such, it is a failure. But, bear with me as I explain:
I have invested more than 40 hours into a game that I want so badly to succeed. I love the dedication of the development team. I think the portrait graphics are stunning. I am entranced by the sprite animations that absolutely infest the Graphical User Interface, GUI, (“game space,” to the literalists). The development and technology mechanism is challenging and first rate. Unfortunately, the historicity or “What If” potential of the “front end” build-up of the 1936 scenarios is wasted when the AI and the player finally go to war. What ensues is wild science fiction and not “What If” historical possibility.
Exhibit A: I am the Brits in the 1936 scenarios (by far the most interesting). I reconstruct an historical development track aimed at the eventual replay of radar, Spitfire, BEF, Dunkirk, and defense of the home island. Pointless. When war finally erupts in June, 1939, the ITALIAN Army successfully invades southern England by sea and air owing to ITALIAN and German air superiority over the English Channel (to which the Spitfire-rich RAF and the robust Royal Navy appear totally impotent). To top it off, that same ITALIAN Army (who historically lost 250,000 men to Gen. O’Connor’s Western Desert Force approximately one-fifth its size) destroys the Royal Navy's Eastern Med fleet and the British Army in the Middle East, eliminates a significant RAF contingent (without having any aircraft carriers!), and invades the Nile Delta, captures the Suez Canal, and takes Jerusalem. What is WRONG with this picture?
Exhibit B: I am the German side in another 1936 scenario. I follow an historical blitzkrieg buildup. I avoid a Poland War option and watch the Russians and Poles form an early alliance. By the time war breaks out in June, 1940, 170 Polish and German divisions pour across the frontier and destroy the panzer-infused Wehrmacht within DAYS. What is WRONG with this picture?
Exhibit C: I try the Germans again, this time in the 1939 scenario to test whether the fault lies with the long R&D and build-up mechanics of 1936 or the AI. I aggressively follow the “kill Poland” national focus, develop a powerful tactical Luftwaffe and bleeding edge panzer and mechanized divisions. When the balloon finally goes up in August, 1939, the Luftwaffe loses badly (“You have lost Air Superiority over Eastern Germany”) to the Polskie Siły Powietrzne, armed with the obsolete PZL P.11 air superiority fighters. Meanwhile, the Polish Army is kicking butt. What is CRAZY wrong with this picture?
At first, I thought the problem is with the HOI4 game system’s artificial intelligence algorithms. A truly effective AI would be able to construct “event gates” to corral the movement, resources, and combat outcomes to conform to certain specific event horizons. Combat effectiveness is clearly suspect. The AI seems much too productive and powerful. But, after further play, I am simply not sure. The AI is clearly failing, but it is not clear as to why it falls so short. Are other game  mechanics at play to a lesser or greater extent to distort historical possible outcomes?
As good as the national focus, R&D, production, GUI, and resource features appear to work in the 1936 scenarios, the game system, as a whole, falls flat when it comes to producing even vaguely probable outcomes when the fighting starts. It appears that our code-crunching development team has only the most superficial familiarity with historical reality. Trust me, if the simulation game mechanics cannot produce a facsimile of actual history, the designers have missed the mark.
It may appear that I am unduly harsh, but this critique needs to be stated. I think the development team is doing some awfully nice things in HOI4--a definite improvement over HOI3. They clearly have dedication, heart, and skin in the game. But, it is all too easy in the Computer Age to forget that the long-term value of any game is its DESIGN, not its mechanical implementation. Code-writing is implementation. Concept, mechanics, and outcomes are the soul of DESIGN. HOI4 implementation is currently a failure. BUT, it is a magnificent failure.
My ancient recommendation to the development team is this: Read more WW2 history and, more importantly, incisive and deep historical analysis (Wikipedia is NOT your friend). Seriously evaluate the effectiveness of the AI. Stop with the over-priced and under-valued DLC add-ons: you are putting lipstick on a pig that will never cure the underlying flaws of the AI. Then, take a deep breath and carefully consider how the design could more closely align itself with history. Next, TEST it for its approximation to historical events. Finally, release HOI5 to high praise and adulation from your peers and dedicated fans. And me!

To be blunt, don't buy this game. Even for the sale price I paid ($16.79 CAD) I regret it.
To expand on why I feel that way, let me explain further. The game you see in the gameplay trailers is vastly edited to make this game appear to be something it's not. It makes you think you're going to get a nice looking game with some action moments, some decent combat and exploration as you survive all while running nicely. Sure there might be some resource grinding but that's fine. But what you actually get is a game that feels slow and sluggish while looking okay and running pretty poorly. The combat? The alien creatures are derpy at best with their movements and you're going to spend more time dealing with attacks out of nowhere than you are doing all that lovely base building. That's not a joke either. Turn your back for a moment to harvest a resource and be ready for something to hit you from behind despite the landscape being clear as far as your eye can see.
Let's go back to the poor performance. I'm running on a system that's only about 3 months old. I have an GTX 1060 6GB, i7-7770, 16GB RAM, etc. And yet the game struggles to hold a stable 45FPS on the lowest settings. I could understand if the game was the most beautiful game out there but it's not. I can run games like The Witcher 3 on maxed out settings and get a stable 60FPS. Sure it's an older game but it looks 10x better as well. This game just doesn't run well at all.
The gameplay itself, well as I said its slow and sluggish. It feels clunky, that's about the best word I can think of. The movement of your character feels extremely stiff. I'm going to assume they are trying to use the idea of the planet having different gravity but it's been poorly done. So much so that the game goes against itself at times. Stiff, slow movement? That must be an attempt to replicate higher gravity correct? But then why does my jumping (and use of a jetpack/jump boost) make it appear as if the gravity is lower? Essentially there is no consistency. Which then makes me believe it's just poor coding. But it's not just the player movements. Something as simple as picking up a resource. You get a prompt to "press f" to collect something. Only you need to hold that key or press it then move your mouse. Why is there a delay in picking up a resource I've already performed an action to gather?
The game also does everything it can to make the early experience as frustrating as possible. You get started at your crash site with limited tools and resources, that's fine. You spend some time gathering the resources around, dealing with the pick up delay, then the random attacks start. No problem, you have a pistol. Only it has very limited ammo. So limited in fact that depending on the attacking enemy and your ability to aim, you'll kill 1-2 enemies at most before you're out. With no way to restock any time soon. So you're left attempting to melee with your chisel or other tool. All while the random attacks continue the moment you turn your back to gather resources.
It also appears as if some features have been removed or disabled without any update to the videos. I could also do without the long developer watermark in the upper left corner of my screen the entire time. We know who is making the game, you said so at the start. Don't add more useless text to my screen.
All in all, don't spend your money. I stated what price I paid above but even $10 is too much for the game in it's current state. Alpha or not, you're misleading the early supporters with the trailers you currently have playing. In fact this game feels like something before Alpha.

In honor of Quake's 20th birthday and Quake Champions announcement, I feel it's relevant to say how great this gem of a game has aged.
As id's leap into 3D, and one of the first truly 3D polygonal shooters I can recall, Quake is still as much fun in 2016 as it was in 1996. The game oozes a dark, eeire and ominous atmosphere, with an interesting blend of gothic fantasy and gritty sci-fi for a really one of a kind look. The 3D graphics, though obviously very dated, are still rather charming. This is too speak nothing of Trent Reznor's fantastic soundtrack, which deeply enhances the creepy atmoshphere.
If you enjoyed Doom 2016, this would be right up your alley. It makes me very happy to say how well Quake holds up.
This is the best game ever made.

Draughts or Checkers, whatever you want to call it, it's a pretty simple but still tactical board game.
You move each piece diagonally around the board gobbling up your opponents men, get a piece to the farthest row from you and it gets an "upgrade" to a king, a piece with a super power, it can move backwards!
It's not the most complicated game in the world, but I used to love playing it as a kid, it was strategic and tactical but still pretty simple to learn.
Chess, now that's a game on a whole other level, sure, it's pretty much the same checkers board you're used to but gone are the uniform pieces with their identical moves, now there's a small army of characters you can move across the board, each type having its own special movement and area of attack.
If checkers is a junior tactical game then chess is checkers  with a high school education.
Now, imagine a game of chess, but replace the chequered board with the star speckled blanket of space, change the knights, bishops, kings and queens into space vessels with different movement capabilities and areas of attack, digitize the game onto the PC, give it some animated visuals and atmospheric sounds then  throw in a narrative to keep things interesting.
You know what you've got? Human Extinction Simulator, a turn based, tactical  space title from Machine 22.
Human Extinction Simulator sees  humanity struggle to survive an alien attack, each scenario pushes the story forward as humanity defends and retreats against the alien onslaught.
Whilst the narrative is a little dry and only delivered in flavour text at the start of each scenario, (don't get expecting whizzy cut scenes, it's not that sort game) it does do a good job of setting a "Battlestar Galactica" type tone to the proceedings as your military struggles to protect transports full of evacuees and slow down the aggressive destruction wrought by the evil Navassian fleet.
The game is comprised of seven scenarios, each with several missions (simulations) which play out another chapter of the story, you'll be defending transports, saving key personel and launching daring raids into the heart of enemy territory,
The initial scenario serves as a tutorial and introduction to the story.
It does a pretty good job of introducing you to the game mechanics, which as I mentioned, is a lot like a game of chess.
In Human Extinction Simulator you control a fleet of ships, both big and small, each ship type has its own weapons systems with their own unique ranges and fields of fire.
These areas of attack might not necessarily fall in front of a ship, dependent on the weapons attached, the fields of fire can fall to the sides of a vessel too.
Some weapons are more powerful than others, so keeping ships at the right range from their target to do the maximum amount of damage is one of the many considerations you'll need to make whilst playing.
Another important part of the tactics in this game is coverage, much like the game of chess, you're going to want to try and keep ships covered by other units, the enemy will think twice about moving to take out a squadron of fighters if he knows that it will leave him vulnerable to volley from a battleship on the next turn.
Along with the different weapon ranges and damage types, you'll also need to think about ship movement.
Human Extinction Simulator adopts a hex based approach to movement, different ship types can move a different number of hexes each turn and can have different turning arcs depending on their size and speed.
Taking into account turning arcs to line up shots, anticipating where you think the enemy will ships will move to and how you should move your own to ensure they'll be pointing in the right direction to respond requires a keen tactical mind.
This is a game that will challenge you.
You will lose, you'll replay a mission, you'll lose again, this can become frustrating but when you finally do achieve your goals in a given mission you get such a feeling of accomplishment it's worth all the effort.
Challenge is what makes victory worthwhile, without it winning is meaningless, and winning in Human Extinction Simulator means A LOT!
Visually, it's a top down, hex affair, which always limits graphical showmanship somewhat, but flashy graphics aren't what this type of game is about.
The backdrops are pretty and the ships themselves are crisp, detailed and show damage as their condition deteriorates throughout a battle.
The interface is clean and intuitive and firing ranges are shown clearly on the hex grid when you select a ship which is a huge help.
Sound is also perfectly serviceable from the zaps of little lasers to the beefy bangs of a ship you really couldn't afford to lose exploding into pieces.
The AI is spot on, it doesn't cheat, but it is clever,
The Navassians are crafty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, even if you've got a handle on all the ship movements and weapon ranges, you'll still find them doing something unexpected, it refreshing (and frustrating) to have such a worthy artificial foe, this is all the more important as Human Extinction Simulator is a single player only game, but the AI is likely to be a tougher opponent than your friends would have been anyway!
At the start of this review, I compared checkers to chess, well if chess is checkers with a high school education then Human Extinction Simulator is Chess with a PHD.
Human Extinction Simulator is both a highly frustrating and highly rewarding tactical game.
Whilst some will find the game too challenging and its top down hex based style unappealing, fans of hex based strategy shouldn't hesitate to give Human Extinction Simulator a look.
Yes, it's a tough game, but how you face defeat is more the measure of a man than a thousand victories.
