RIFT in and of itself is a decent game. However, there's some things about it that make it really hard to recommend.
Pros:
- Graphics are relatively good (better than Everquest 1/World of Warcraft but not as good as Elder Scrolls Online)
- Invasions are a regular thing that can take over a zone and kill quest NPC's. In some cases you have to participate in the invasions to get them out of your way to do other quests.
- Content is split up into solo content (open world), group content (mostly instanced things) and raid content (instanced with a few in the open world)
- in group or raid content only 1 person has to enter the instanced and it'll offer to pull everybody else in the group or raid into the instanced as well.
- Once you ignore somebody it ignores their entire account (the character, any name changes and all present/future characters on the account)
- The wardrobe system is awesome. Whenever you achieve a weapon or armor graphic by having an item in your inventory it's added to a permanent account-wide list. From this list you're able to choose what weapon and armor graphics you want your character to have.
- Guild quests are an interesting concept that I haven't seen in any other game. The fact that your entire guild can be sent on 1 objective is a cool idea. The perks gained from leveling your guild up through these quests also can increase quality of life greatly in game.
Cons:
- On the note of invasions they can also be a con because they kill quest NPC camps. Sometimes there can be so many invasion mobs in one camp that it looks like a herd of cattle except their all stacked on top of each other.
- The community. A good portion of the community has made it to my ignore list due to how they act in groups, PVP or in general chat. On the bright side, the game seems more pleasant when you get all the bad apples on ignore.
- To do random dungeons to get the daily reward bonuses you HAVE to have a full group. Therefore even though it would probably be possible for me and 2 buddies to complete a dungeon we still have to get into queue and gather 2 more people.
- Dailys and Weeklys. You find yourself doing the same 10 repetitive quests because that's how you receive currency to achieve new armor/weapons. Somebody once asked me in a group what they missed because they've been gone 7 months from the game. I responded with "about 7 months worth of dailys".
- The wardrobe system also has some downsides. To get all of the graphics for armor and weapons you, in theory, have to do raids as well. Some of the raids require a number of people to even enter the instanced even though the content itself would otherwise be soloable in future expansions.

RIFT COSTS MORE AND DELIVERS LESS THAN EVER BEFORE
I loved Rift dearly for many years, but the publisher has killed it.  It was a wonderful game, and still is, but I can't recommend it.  Spending money on RIFT now is a bad investment.  Even if 4.1 hits the mark it is already too late and has been for some time.  From heavy-handed community management to stealthy and steady removal of content and features, to say nothing of the pitifully non-functional state of the expansion content, this game is circling the drain and everyone knows it.  I don't recommend this game for a new player as it simply has no future and at this point I don't think that can be changed.  After playing daily for three years and thousands of hours, it's time to call it quits.  Starfall Prophecy is so awful I started making excuses not to log in, and after a few months of that I didn't even feel a pang of regret when I uninstalled what Trion has the nerve to call an 'expansion.'
The old content of the original game is still worth playing if you love varied zones, crafting, collecting pets and costumes, and adventuring solo - you can still do all of it for free.  The player housing feature, called Dimensions, is actually the only part of the current game that is both functional and satisfying.  But if you are looking for challenging group content from a trustworthy publisher with a long and healthy future ahead of it, look elsewhere.  RIFT has become a single player game and frankly there are better single player games out there.

I'm torn on this game.  It's decidedly better than Enforcer (though it does make me wonder if Alliance would have been bad) and at times it tries really hard to be a good game, but several glaring flaws come close to ruining it altogether for me.  First, the movement is a bit awkward.  I played the game clear through on the hardest difficulty and I never could master the controls on it.  Combat was alright.  Nothing special as far as tactical shooters go but the AI's movement felt pretty well natural with my squad even giving enough space to avoid the entire team being wiped by a single grenade (most of the time).  What almost kills the game for me though is the dialog and "choices" in the game.  I don't know if it's a bug or just bad writing but throughout the game the choices I made seemed to be ignored for a standard plot line.  Spoiler:
Additionally, the dialog jumps as characters will use a term or reference an event that they haven't heard yet or wouldn't have known which breaks any chance at becoming immersed in the game.  Beyond that, I'm at a loss for where this game fits in with the XCOM universe.  I honestly think that after hearing the game pitch, someone at Take2 said, "Hey, cool alien invasion game idea.  You know what, we have the XCOM license, let's slap that on for some extra sales."  It's the only explanation I can come up with that doesn't place this game into a different universe as Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within due to inconsistencies in plot lines, how different certain species are portrayed from one to the next, and no feigned attempt at explaining why we don't start Enemy Within with plasma guns and UFO technology.
Despite the flaws, I don't regret the purchase.  I would be highly selective on which friends I'd recommend it to since it will take a forgiving player to like the game and even then I'd say wait till it's on sale.  Since I can't recomment it to the general public, I have to give this game a thumbs down.
Edit:  A quick note, I have an older machine and the core game played fine with the physX stuff turned off, but the DLC was unplayable for me as it used a different set of shaders on the enemies that caused the framerate to drop to unplayable unplayable levels.

Nevertheless the game shows promise, the fact that you're a soldier of XCom and seeing things from a close up view is a nice twist and had me interested. Furthermore the combat seems nice in concept, having various soldiers with different abilities. There presentation and atmosphere of the game is kind of neat in a way but only when the game actually kind of works.
Honestly, I don't recommend this game.

Bought it immediately because I was a big fan of To The Moon and wanted to support the dev. Cannot recommend A Bird Story at full price as a standalone game, nevermind as a follow-up to previous works.
Art assets and music are as strong as they've ever been and if you are going to buy the game, I STRONGLY suggest getting the bundle.
The real emphasis should be placed on the story and gameplay, and I don't think there's enough here to justify a purchase. The emotional impact of the game is undermined by the relative predictability of the story and certain elements (characters?) are introduced solely to create some arbitrary sense of conflict and urgency. There is little sense of exploration, and gameplay consists mostly of following corridors that may/may not open up and the odd bit of interaction.
There is some decent animating with the sprites to convey without dialogue, but the limited scope of the plot in general keeps that potential leashed. To The Moon's dialogue was a major strength in engaging the audience, and while it represents a considerable experiment for an author to communicate without it, it didn't do much for me.
The game caps at roughly an hour of length; I cannot recommend it at its full pricetag, as much of the experience was simply going through the motions to tell what amounted to a very basic story and a preview of the actual sequel to To The Moon.

If I've learned one thing from To the Moon and A Bird Story, it's that Kan Gao really knows how to make me cry. Each project is more beautiful than the last.

Hidden Folks also does a great job of mixing things up. The meat of the game comes in the form of gigantic, complex scenes with around a dozen items or characters to find. They’re big enough that even playing on an iPad Pro I had to constantly zoom in and out, and pan around to find things. There are also much smaller scenes, like a simple campfire or farm, as well as one-off interactive vignettes. One such level has you helping a villager navigate a perilous path by removing obstacles.
This creates a satisfying flow, so you’re not just doing the same thing — staring at a screen — over and over. Hidden Folks also removes a lot of frustration by not forcing you to find everything before you can move on to the next scene. There are no times in the game, and no punishment if you make a mistake or struggle to find something. Instead, Hidden Folks is laid back and serene, while still challenging enough to make actually finding things feel satisfying. It’s a game you can play for a few minutes or an hour and still feel a sense of gratification. And it’s the perfect companion for that Sunday morning coffee.

You are provided with several "maps" in addition to smaller transitional maps inbetween the larger ones.
You have a list of people or objects to find which come with a not-too-obvious clue, which makes it nice and challenging. The clues are pretty funny as well.
Not only do you have to find these people or objects, most of the time you will have to interact with the map to open doors, curtains and other things (dont't want to spoil too much) in order to find them.
Along with the game being highly interactive, you are provided with sound effects made by the mouth which are highly entertaining and had me constantly chuckling. I think the zipper sounds on the tents or the advertisement signs rolling up and down were my personal favorite.
The maps are fairly large and there are tons of things going on in them. The artwork remains pretty simple but there are ever so slight differences between the people which adds to the challenge of finding characters!
With the goofiness of the game, you can spend hours just enjoying looking around the map being nosey checking out what all of the people are doing while trying to find your objects. The game is challenging but never frustrating as it's just too entertaining and funny.
PROS:
Graphics - Very simplistic style but perfect! Works very well for a search game as many   characters look similar and there are tons of things going on in the maps!
Sounds - Freaking funny and different. Loved it.
Gameplay - Very interactive, not just looking for items or one-click interaction.
CONS:
Not enough to play. Need more. :(
What I'd like to see: I got through the game in about 6 hours, but each map has so many things going on, I feel that there's room to add new search lists for pre-existing maps, as well as new maps(which I know they're already working on, yay!) There's so many things you can dink around with and objects to find, they could easily do new lists. I want to play more!
I highly recommend giving it a go. It's very funny and they brought life to a "Waldo" like cramped world where you just want to enjoy all the little areas and see what people are doing.

A proper modern Rogue. Not a rogue-like, but a game that teaches you every time you fail. It's never ambiguous why you got ♥♥♥♥ed, and it's rarely unfair. Some maps are like "here, have 6 trees" which FeelsBadMan, but isn't likely the reason you sucked so bad. If you lose, it's because you didn't push enough, didn't take raids seriously, tried to cheat the game, cut corners, wasted resources.
It's difficult to recommend this game enough. There are plenty of rough edges that affect quality of life more than gameplay though:
* unit control - they take the shortest path, which at your walls tends to be through the standing horde; also, the attack move command also doubles as an attack target command so in tense moments you may tell your units to attack themselves
* tutorial - there isn't one, which is alright given it's a Rogue, but not explaining that you can pause feels a bit cruel
* information - it's not always clear what the effects of actions will be (especially mayors); it's not really clear what the rule for how houses block each other is either
* the escape key - doesn't cancel the selection
However, it's Early Access and all that is polish, the core gameplay is great and leaves you often fearing "what did I ♥♥♥♥ up this time?"

Drifting Lands is a side scrolling bullet hell shooter.  If that doesn't interest you then maybe you should look elsewhere, otherwise dive right in.  A word of warning, the beginning stages are a tad monotonous while the game eases you into the flow of things.  From what I've read, the game does get more enjoyable then settling back towards monotonous for the home stretch.  With a game boasting over one-hundred levels, I guess I'm not too suprised?  I wish I could say I put in more time with this title, but I was looking for the instant gratification a la Gradius so the slow build up turned me off from the title.
The developers decided to spicen up things by adding a rougelike system where you get random salvage from enemies that can be fitted to your shift so you can make your ship the deadliest in all the galaxy.  The UI felt a tad overwhelming in item menus, trying to compare stats and figure out what weapon tickles your fancy, but you learn the basics pretty fast considering the developers were insightful enough to add the beloved "green upgrade" "red downgrade" coloring when swapping engine bits.  Post mission feels like a bit of an item torrent which kinda reduced the good feelings of getting drops, but I would imagine that changes as you progress farther into the game and get nicer loot.
A story was actually written for this game, which is something I can't say for many attempts at this genre.  It's even decent too, for a video game.  Characters have motivations and goals, and they're all rather well drawn as well.
Ultimately, if you're curious about the genre, it is a pretty nice stepping stone into side-scrolling shooters and bullet hells.  Grabbing it on sale would be your best bet I believe.

The skill tree ... the first thing I unlock in Mechanic is the ability to make a pipe?!? seriously? Of which I only use when making the damn shovel to grind science!
Put machines and recipes behind other machines and recipes, not behind some ♥♥♥♥ed up skill tree progression system. You are forcing us to make stuff, invest points in, things we have no need or desire to build.. like flares.. who cares... seriously... 20 points?!?!?
If you want to do a skill tree.. make it so were better at something, like mining, do more dmg in combat, or whatever, but dont lock recipes behind a tree scheme.

Long Review
Alright, this game is rough.  It's like the developers of Mass Effect wiped their♥♥♥♥♥with the extra funding they had from the ME series, and churned out a♥♥♥♥♥♥show of a game called The Bureau: XCOM Declassified.
This.  Is.  Rough.  The worst part is, you can often times see the potential this game has.  It's a game that WANTS to be good, WANTS to be a fan service... But it falls flat so, so early.  The main character is a boring, rude, monotone agent who constantly bounces between "caring", and "shut up, we have a job to do".  His "personality" actually adds to the overall failure of this game, I feel.  The cover system is atrocious.  You are either super glued to your cover, or you can't get into cover, on a game solely based around Third-Person Cover Shooting.  Like I said, Mass Effect with a pennies worth of funding.  That gets really infuriating when you're on the highest difficulty and some of the enemies advance to flank you, and you're bashing the multitude of buttons to get off cover and nothing is happening.  The abilities are boring and unimagitive...  Once again, comparing to Mass Effect, they pretty much ripped off the abilities.  Lift, Pulse Wave, Weaken...  Jeeeeeeeeeeeez.  The guns are all boring, with little personality in each one.  I could beat the game using the M1911 pistol, to be honest, since it seems to deliver one hell of a headshot.  In fact, most of the guns feel like they do NOTHING.  You're tickling a Sectoid with your Scatter Laser.  wat.  Running around the HQ QUICKLY becomes tedious.  You have to run back and forth, back and forth, etc. etc.
Pros:
XCOM Lore
A nice "old school" feeling... They did somewhat decent on that
Interesting view into some of the aliens
Killing an alien every now and then results in some funny physics
Decent graphics and audio
Cons:
Terrible controls
Boring abilities and guns
Tedious legwork in the HQ
Sticky or repelling cover
Repetitive gameplay to the maaaaaaaax.  Trying out new guns, new squaddies, or new ability combos don't add at to the experience at all.
Go play XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within, or any of the older XCOM's.  They'll probably offer the same lore in a different style, and they will actually be good.

The Bureau, I find, falls into an unfortunate category of games that is just solidly and frusteratingly mediocre. It clearly had enough production effort to be a full fledged title, and to that extent, truly does meet all the minimum specifications for what makes a game full and complete. And yet it remains less than excellent.
Graphics/Visuals are good. Very distinctive art style similar to LA Noire, seeming to aim for that 1940's television appearance with enhanced special effects. Fun and interesting, but loses points for lack of originality and frequent repetition. Protagonist facial expressions are cycled through faster than infomercials at 2 am and the entire direction of the art is tried and dull. It's the same exact set up from virtually every alien sci-fi film/tv show throughout the 70's plus a few others. In short, boring.
Music: Uninspired. Unoriginal. Nothing special. In fact, even while writing this I can't actually recall any of the music because of how unimpressed I was.
Story: Exactly what you'd expect. Aliens invade. The military "secretly" tries to fight back with loud explosions.♥♥♥♥♥♥happens. Again, nothing special.
Overall I stand unimpressed. I play the broken record by repeating that over and over but it's true. I liked it but not enough to play it beyond the several hour mark.

Alright, some people like this game, yeah, but me personally... I do not reccomend.
Let's start out at the beginning.
I bought the game, and was excited for it- Makers of Terraria, looked fun, had pirates- what's not to like?
Then, the game loaded.
The first thing you'll notice about Pixel Piracy is it has a weird come-and-go soundtrack. On the main menu, it's almost completely devoid of sound, besides an occasional "Ahoy there!" sound blip when you click certain things. (By the way, this "ahoy there!" will become the bane of your existence by the time we're finished.)
Sound isn't the only part of a game though- I mean, you can play minecraft on mute and still have a great time. So, I start a new game, with Captain Yar Har Ho. (I have no idea why I named him that.)
My game started. I attempted to walk around, and only succeeded in whipping the camera around. Turns out you control your captain by clicking him around. Once i figured this out, I directed the captain off his ship onto a town he was parked next to. The game was still pretty quiet, until I directed the Captain into the town's tavern. Once inside, I was assaulted in sound by a pixel-ey pirate singing a folk song. It was not pleasant.
I looked around the town, and eventually deduced A. I could hire one crew member, and B. The game was confusing me too much to figure out what the rest of the merchants actually did. So i took on some fat oaf I found in the town, and we headed back to the boat.
Next question: how do I sail this thing?
Well, the crew is controlled via real-time clicking and such, so is the boat the same way? Or maybe you get full control of the boat! Like a real-life pirate ship captain! That'd be fun!
Unfortunately, this is not the case.
Instead, you get to open your map. And then click on one of many pre-determined spots. Then, you get to sit around and do nothing whilst your ship sails to it in real time. During the trip (or at least my trips) there are no random encounters or things to spice it up- you just sit there and stare while the seagulls fly above you and the captain yells "Ahoy there!" for the god freaking thousandth time.
It's not very fun and the closest it is to adventure is the music the game suddenly pulled out of nowehere.
My one crewman and I traveled to one of the nearest destinations- an island! Everyone knows there are adventures to be had on unexplored islands, with man-eating natives, fierce beasts, and buried treasure!
The fat oaf and I died to a bush.
I'm not kidding. We killed a native or two, and then walked into a bush, which then killed us instantly.
You be the judge of that.
So far, the adventure has consisted of several thousand "Ahoy there!" phrases, some bad singing in a bar, and being murdered horribly by a rather large fern. Luckily, the game prompts a save every time you travel, so it wasn't the end- we could try again!
By this point, I had discovered a help menu in the game. Although most of the text came across as rather confusing to me, trying to explain without any visual aid and also making jokes at the same time, I still deduced that early on in the game, you're advised to attack other ships rather than explore islands. I've always loved that in games, having an area made extremely accesable but being told "Don't go there, you're probably gonna die!"
So, Fat Oaf and the Captain Board their small-but-proud vessel once more. and set sail! To become true pirates, pillaging and fighting and.... well, It ain't gonna happen.
We encounter an enemy ship! Do we fight or flee?
"Fight!" Yells the captain!
The game loads up a stretch of sea, with the Captain's ship on the left, and a fearsome pirate one the right!
I command the Fat Oaf to attack first!
The other pirate immediately knocks him into the ocean where he is eaten by sharks and never seen again.
I sigh, then command Captain Yar Har Ho to attack.
After a somewhat anticlimactic fight, Yar Har wins. He takes some gold, and a watermelon, and then sails away.
I sigh again, and close the Pixel Piracy Window.
To summarize.
Pixel Piracy isn't necessarily a bad game- it has some unique ideas and the trailers all look cool. But thanks to confusing menus, lackluster combat and crew control, and huge chunks of time where you are doing nothing but sailing, this game just becomes very meh. I've said it's not a bad game, but it's just not a good game either. If I had to reccomend, don't buy Pixel Piracy. Unless they make some drastic changes, it's probably a better choice to buy Terraria, or even Goat Simulator.
And I swear to god if I have to hear "Ahoy there!" one more time I'm going to hit someone with a frozen ham.

If you don’t know how to play a seek-and-find then I’m not entirely sure how, but you must have skipped right over your childhood years and were born as an adult. Jokes aside, the name of the game is self-explanatory: you are given a list of objects, ranging from animals to pickup trucks, and you have to spot them amongst a smattering of other people and objects that form an interactive scene.
That sounds simple enough, but the task becomes akin to finding the metaphorical needle in the haystack due to large, detailed scenes that are chock full of objects. Your list features hints that will allow you to (hopefully) pinpoint the location of a critter, object, or person
Once you’ve found an object, you click on it and it is checked off of your list. You can also use the mouse to click and drag so that you can pan around the scene or alternatively you can use your WASD keys. The game also allows you to choose between a sepia and a night mode so that you can ease the strain on your eyes, which is a thoughtful option setting.
The game is divided into four thematic sections, each of which has its own theme: forest, dry lands, city, and factory. In each, you can find objects that you’d associate with the setting; in the forest, you’ll find lush trees, monkeys and pandas, farm land with the appropriate animals, and camping grounds with RVs and people aplenty—and so on and so forth.
While the sheer number of stuff jammed into each scene is impressive, the organization of those scenes is doubly so, zooming out and viewing the scene as a whole may be a little daunting, but you’ll soon notice groupings of stuff that makes sense thematically. I’m not sure how, but Hidden Folks manages to avoid appearing cluttered. The game allows you to zoom in and take the scene in a bit at a time, which is not an invaluable search tool, it allows you to truly appreciate the little touches; the loving attention to detail.
Where Hidden Folks really shines is its atmosphere. From the constant chatter of monkeys in the first stages to the purr of car engines in the city levels, every single sound in this game comes from the mouth of an actual person. The thought alone made me giggle when clicking on an alligator and hearing it roar, which happened to be one of my favourite sound effects. These non-invasive utterances not only set the atmosphere, they also act as auditory cues that help you find what you’re looking for amidst the scores of other objects. The vast majority of objects you interact with have their own sounds and they also react to your clicks; bushes get cut down, fixed objects that obscure the hidden folk behind them can be moved aside, and birds will scatter. These neat little touches make the time spent diligently searching worthwhile.
For those of you who are hungry for more, there are an additional three levels in the works and they will be available for free to anyone who owns the game.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
Hidden Folks takes a very classic style of gameplay and adds a creative spin that improves it in every way. There’s a lot to like here for gamers of all skill levels, though I think those who have a preference for puzzle games will really appreciate the finer details of the hint system and cues created by sounds. This is a game for players of all ages and a charming addition to anyone’s library.

Nominally a first-person stealth game, Dishonored happens to provide the player with numerous tools – mostly in the form of quasi-magical abilities – that make murder a lot more fun than avoiding enemies altogether: a short range teleport, a swarm of rats, the ability to summon a powerful gust of wind (perhaps most satistfying to use against enemies standing at the edge of a cliff or a railing), a gun with a satisfyingly loud bang, a melee attack that results in hefty amounts of blood and gore. Coupled with level design that emphasizes a certain degree of freedom in what route to choose (both horizontally and vertically!), the game seems arguably influenced not only by Thief, System Shock, and Deus Ex, but also by Crysis, that other murder-simulator defined by copious access to overpowered superpowers. Sadly, the creators elected to implement a moral system – which measures the amount of "chaos" the player leaves behind – that is somehow even more pointless than similar systems found in games by Bioware (Knights of the Old Republic) or Bethesda (Fallout 3). The perfunctory story, utterly predictable in its beats, as well as the trite worldbuilding also align the game more closely with titles such as Fallout 3. How much one will enjoy this game, then, will depend largely on how much enjoyment one derives from traversing city blocks sneakily before descending upon a platoon of guards in a brothel like a wrathful demigod – without much of an overarching storyline that would make such murder feel particularly poignant.

Have about 25 hours in so far and probably won't be stopping anytime soon. Some good RTS mechanics with a horde survival twist. It's still in beta, but the updates have been fast and frequent. The maps randomly generate with each playthrough, so you'll have to adjust your strategy accordingly. Keeps it fresh imo. There's 4 map environments, but you'll need to complete the 1st map type requirements to unlock the 2nd and so on. This gives long term goals as I just unlocked the 2nd environment.
As for the experience itself, if you're a fan of SC or WC, then you'll feel right at home. The game doesn't pull any punches either as I had to lower the base difficulty while getting accustomed to the upgrade paths and expanding mechanics. Letting a single zombie through WILL result in you restarting your run. If a zombie destroys a building(most non-defensive building have low HP) all worker required to run that building will spawn as zombies and cascades from there.
A few issues I've had are the following(remember still in Beta):
-I've had one crash, but the game saved my progress.
-No tutorial, so be ready to do a lot of trial and error.
-When you load into a saved game, it will appear like the game locked up, but it's simply paused. Press the SPACE bar to pause and unpause at will. Really nice once you know it exists.
-When you have units hotkeyed, quickly switching from one selected unit to another via hotkey and giving a command within .5 seconds will result in giving that command to the previously selected unit instead of the one you now have highlighted. Now since this is player vs AI, it's not that big of a deal and you usually have more then enough time to correct the falsely given command, but still annoying early on when trying to scout the area using multiple units.
+-A successful playthrough can take 2-4 hours depending on difficultly. You are able to save your game at any time and come back, but just keep in mind if you tell your spouse "I'm gonna get one more game in", that one more game could takes hours.

Drifting Lands is an Action RPG that mixes shoot ‘em ups with a dash of bullet hell. While the game does a great job on the shoot em’ up part, it drops the ball on the bullet hell part.
Graphics
Graphically Drifting Lands looks nice, it has a nice bright 3D models on 2D background ascetics and well done animations, but unfortunately the art style doesn’t always mix well with gameplay.
At time visual effects would blend with the background and because enemies sometimes use the same colors of attack as the player it becomes a mess to know what’s what when the difficulty starts to crank up and more enemies enters the fight.
Sound
The sounds in Drifting Lands is near arcade like, and by that I mean you will hear all of the music and sound effects in no time, so much so it’s easy to actually forget the music is playing. Heck sometimes the game would forget that it was supposed to be playing a level’s theme music and would delay playing it.
The sound effects are passable, it’s nothing special, just the same old generic laser blaster sound effects. No matter what weapon you choose they nearly all have the same sound, the biggest difference being that some are played faster than others.
Gameplay
The biggest draw to any shoot em’ up is the fun fast paced gun play and Drifting Lands drops the ball on one end but has fun gun play, where it fails at is the fast paced part. At times the game will throw dozens upon dozens of enemies at you, just to slow everything back to a crawl for the majority of a mission.
The game tries to create a learning curve that could fit any and all players, there are two different difficulty setting and all three ships have their own strengths and flaws. This may sound complicated for anybody new to this genre of shooters, but Drifting Lands does a great job of making things easy to get into for newer players, while veteran players will feel left out, this is due to the game being far too forgiving.
The two modes mentioned earlier are Normal mode and Forgiving Mode.
Normal mode Is meant for players well versed in shoot em’ ups, upon death players could lose valuable loot or even their entire ship.
Forgiving Mode is exactly as it sounds, players will never lose their ships and instead of losing items they’re simply broken and can be repaired for a price.
Both modes feel the same, playing on normal won’t change the amount of damage enemies cause nor will it add in special enemies or increase the number of enemies on screen. The only real difference in the modes are the things that players can lose.
The loot players get from finishing levels plays an important part in progressing the game, players may pick up new weapons, shields, thrusters and other items to make their ship stronger.
Like any loot system everything is random, playing a certain level won’t grant you certain gear, but the game also supplies loot items through a store that players can visit before and after every mission. The shop will sell upgrades that can only be applied if the ship meets a certain criteria, such as structure or power.
The upgrades is where the RPG elements come in, players don’t gain experiences while playing levels, instead they gain credits that can be exchanged to power up their ships. All three ships have three different attributes; Structure, Power and Navigation.
Upgrades will change how much health or shield a ship has, while gears can also upgrade these stats some will actually degrade a section in order to power up another.
For every little thing Drifting Lands does right it fumbles something else. The game boasts over 100 levels, but doesn’t do anything interesting with those levels, players will face the same types of enemies over and over again.
Final Score
For a shoot em’ up Drifting Lands is painfully slow, veterans of the genre will become bored with the gameplay quickly, while new players may like the slower pace. New players will have fun with the game’s simplicity, while more experienced players will feel as if there’s a great bullet hell game stuck within a decent shoot em’ up.

Drifting Lands is a fun game.
On the surface it might seem ARPG + Roguelike + side-scrolling shooter is a weird and possibly even ill-advised combination, but Drifting Lands makes it work. The game leans heavily on the shooter side of things, so the other aspects are more like spices the devs have sprinkled in rather than the focus of the game, so don't go in looking for Diablo 3 The Side-Scroller or anything.
What it boils down to is you playing a series of side-scrolling shooter levels where the enemies come at you fast and at times the screen seems to consist mostly of bullets. It's not as hectic as proper bullet hell games but at times it does get very frentic. The roguelike + ARPG mechanics come in through your ship upgrades and skills. Blowing up enemies gets you both random loot drops and money, which you can use to buy new skills and upgrades with between missions. The system works and there are enough options to cater to a wide array of playstyles. I hit upon my own favourite style fairly early on, after which point I experienced the classic mild RPG frustration of not getting many meaningful upgrades for the style of weapons I wanted to use while having to vendor junk I didn't like, so I guess the devs nailed that part of it!
People who are way into bullet hell style nightmare shooters, will probably find Drifting Lands too casual for their tastes, but anyone looking for a unique idea backed up with  good gameplay and nice graphics could do a lot worse than taking a look at Drifting Lands.

The game offers a good mix of shmup / random loot mechanics and I can confidently recommend it to those of you who enjoy shmups and don't mind some grind.
Drifting Lands is an interesting take on a SHMUP genre that involves adding random item generation and levelling, think of a mix between Diablo and Raptor: Call of the Shadows.
The game starts by revealing that the world as you know it has been destroyed due to some disaster. The pieces of earth float together, so most of the life happens to take place on those shards. (Hence the name, Drifting Lands).
The process is pretty straightforward: you have to fly through the levels, destroy enemies, pick randomly generated loot most of the time. There are some alternatives like smuggling, you need to drop some cargo on a specific area of the level, which brings some variety to a traditional gameplay.
After the level ends – you can upgrade your ship, sell the items you won’t be using or purchase a new ones.
Shoot-Em-Ups are very reliant on the core gameplay loop: destroying enemies and dodging bullets, and I’m happy to say that Drifting Lands delivers on that. A good addition to the gameplay are usable player skills: you can select and take 4 out of 30+ skills into battle. Skills like flame burst that damages everything before you, special shield that absorbs bullets for 2 seconds, all sorts of dashes, various weapon boosts, mines, passive abilities that affect the loot and money earned. Needless to say, this introduces a great variety and makes player adapt to the style. The loot system also helps with that: there are lots of stats and weapons / items can contribute greatly to boosting the ones you want.
I remember that I thought that it’s impossible to make a beautiful 3d SHMUP, and I’m glad that I was wrong. Drifting Land introduces amazing graphics and colorful effects, the game feels very alive because of that. Shining bullets, colorful explosions, great player ship animations – all this adds to the immersion of the game.
First, it’s the backgrounds. Don’t get me wrong, they are drawn very well, but they still remain somewhat unremarkable and unnoticed. One thing that is often seen in good shoot-em-ups is a varying landscape on every level. After you play the level a few times, you remember how it was, what obstacles and enemies can be encountered. Background plays a big role in that: if the level has enemies after mountains, those mountains help you understand and improve on next playthrough, because you know where to anticipate such enemies. No such thing here: I understand that the game relies on random generation a lot, but most of the levels I’ve played were simply floating rocks in the background. Sometimes there were tornadoes. The colors and gamma change occasionally, but there are rarely any remarkable landmarks that can be seen. Because of that, there is the repetitive feeling, like when you are moving in the same place.
Second, the levels often offer randomly-generated enemy sequence, but there are too many levels and too few enemies. In the end, it starts to feel like a grind. I’ve played the game for about 5 hours and I still enjoy it, but I think this is one of the few times when I wanted a good game to be a bit shorter and more focused on its objective / plot instead of asking to do similar missions with similar enemies multiple times.
Overall, while having a few noticeable flaws, Drifting Lands does a lot of things right. The gameplay is action packed and challenging. The management layer that comes from items, ship upgrades and abilities makes the gameplay much more engaging. If you enjoy shoot-em-ups and are not afraid of replaying similar levels multiple times – I can recommend the game to you.

First let me make something clear, if your on an OS other than windows 7, you'll most likely encounter so problems with the game constantly crashing.
For those of you still on Windows 7, I would definately recommend this game. It is an old game as of writing this review so it doesn't run flawlessly, you'll find the UI a bit difficult to navigate considering its a port from consoles, BUT hear me out.
Graphics: 7/10
For a game from 2011 the games graphics are still good, I haven't seen any graphical glitches, the textures are a little low on detail and the shadows lacking in some areas but thats to be expected from older games.
Sound: 8/10
The only thing I can think of thats dragging down the sound quality of this game would be the poor voice acting, they definately did not spend much on the voice actors at all. Its a shame since the cars sound pretty good, I've heard most of these cars in real life and they are actually pretty close to the real thing. Only compaint would be the poor voice acting.
Models: 9/10
Car models are excellently well done, nice amount of detail put into all the cars in the game, player models are also great.
Damage model: 4/10
Well, I guess the damage model is good for those looking for a driving game instead of a simulator, but to put it simply your car is invincible aside from the front bumper and scratches on the side of the car.
Driving mechanics/physics: 10/10
Not much to say here, these are pretty realistic, on the hardcore difficulty with full clutch + Hshifter that is. Each car has its own fine tuned driving style and difficulties. Example being the Aston Martins having alot of torque and rear while drive gives them alot of wheel spin and difficulty when accelerating out of a corner, meanwhile cars such as the Nissan GTR being 4 wheel drive are very stable through corners at high speeds and while accelerating, this is accurate to real life.
Ultimately if your looking for a racing game that has an expansive free roam, this is a very good buy, it doesn't take long to get money, theres a choice for either persistant online free roam, or you can create another seperate profile for offline free roam. The race events are well designed and the courses you race on are well made also.

As far as games go, I can't think of too many that are more demonized than this one. Most people went into it thinking they were going to get some sort of polished up grid-style xcom team FPS and the reality is that while this game doesn't quite fall into that category, it isn't exactly the worst thing ever either.
The game itself has a fairly interesting storyline that fits in “ok” to the XCOM universe despite not making a whole lot of sense until late game. Most levels consist of you running from point A to point B and collecting whatever tidbits of information (if any) and special items/weapons in addition to killing anything in your way.
The combat is a bit frustrating at first as your cohorts movement commands are issued in a way relative to their position which makes using their abilities a bit difficult if they happen to be out of range. Also, they seem to be incredibly bad at dodging anything so expect to have to babysit them for the entirety of the game. As far as strategy goes, I managed to find a sweet spot with scout and commando but other class mixes are viable all the way until the last few battles (your experience may vary).
Overall, the game came off as a bit tedious and I kind of sloughed through the last few hours of "level plus multiple respawns". Additionally the plot revolving around the main character (Carter) is pretty nonsensical and random which made it kind of difficult to get “into” the story. I would only recommend this game for diehard fans of XCOM who want to see another take on the popular franchise.

XCOM : enemy unknown turns into a real time third person shooter strategy game. This game puts seemingly difficult RTS commands and simplifies them just enough to make the game play as smooth as possible.
XCOM is known for it's suspenseful cinematics and storyline incorporating an unknown attacking alien species. The story unfolds with special agent Carter who rendez-vous with other members of the "Bureau" aka people who deal with alien affairs. He attempts to deliver a package to a general then suddenly the general is shot by another agent. Shocked, Carter quickly turns to the other agent ready to take action when she quickly points out the change in eyes and behavior of the general who was under alien mind control.
XCOM fans will be familiar to the play area as it will give friendly reminders that you've sort of been here before. It gives me a warm fuzzy feeling going from an RTS view to first person. The grid system sort of is there, but the command system is absolutely on point. By holding B (on a 360 controller), a command menu opens up and slow down times slightly as you make a selection of what to do. Player can choose from numerous actions such as move, pin down, and shoot while certain characters have specialized abilities (that can be unlocked by gaining experience). One character, for example has the ability to set up an auto turret while another can scope enemies with his sniper. The game is nothing short of exciting when it comes to game play as there can be a lot going on. Some players will like this as you will need to quickly command your troops where to go while ensuring you're doing your part to keep the enemy suppressed. Nonetheless, the command system is quick and efficient in it's means. Players won't have a problem designating commands. The shooting itself is alright with nothing exceptionally special and there is an option to scatter/throw a grenade. Any game that has that as an addition is greatly welcomed.
There is also a melee feature players can use which is basic at best. It would have been nice to see them incorporate ways to capture aliens and maybe somehow incorporate what they did with Enemy Unknown, that way maybe you could upgrade or change your melee weapon. Basic movements are all there as you can take cover, roll, jump, and sprint. Although a little stiff, it's nice they put it in. When finishing a mission players will find themselves in the XCOM base where they can sort of roam freely talking to NPC's or managing their staff. The player may recruit new soldiers and send them off to missions or take those soldiers with them on a mission.
make me feel like I'm PC gaming back in 2008 but don't interfere with game play. Pause menus are nice and user friendly. People actually move their mouths while they speak in game which I found a neat feature.

Overall a good game and would highly recommend it for those who seek a FPS / RTS sort of hybrid. I support it for this reason but cannot guarantee everyone will be satisfied with it's shooting/action styles.

is an action-tactical, third-person shooter that incorporates cover systems, tactical pausing, and squad commands to make for riveting combat scenarios.  The story is fairly enthralling and while the characters are definitely cliché, I thought they were diverse and interesting enough, with the exception being the unquestionably boring main character.  It is far from perfect, but I enjoyed it, that much I know.  I think if you like games in this style, then you will probably enjoy it too; but if you’re someone who easily dislikes things that aren’t absolutely perfectly crafted, you may want to reconsider trying this.
This game is not like other X:COM games you may have played; rather it is a different type of game altogether that is simply set in the X:COM universe.  Evidently, this bothered many people; but I find it hard to understand why some people feel the core gameplay is so absolutely terrible.  The style of play is very similar to the
series.  You combat in third-person shooter style, with the ability to use tactical pausing and to issue commands (move, target, use ability) to squadmates.  There is an XP and leveling system for both your main character and squadmates, with a handful of different squadmate classes to work with.  It certainly doesn’t have the most refined, expansive, and exemplary combat/gameplay mechanics out there, but I thought it was good enough and enjoyed playing the game.
The story is somewhere between mediocre and good.  I liked the atmosphere and setting of an alien invasion in 1960s America.  The narrative and characters are undoubtedly cliché at times, but I felt it was all intriguing enough to hold my interest as I played through the game.  Some of the plot developments do come out of nowhere, but ultimately I thought they actually helped to make the story more interesting.
I didn’t experience any jarring bugs or glitches and I thought the graphics and soundscape were pleasant.  Some of the cutscenes had a grainy look to them even after I turned film grain off, but it wasn’t the end of the world— the in-game graphics were still crisp and attractive.  For me, the most egregious negative aspect of the game was the checkpoint autosave system.  I don’t like playing a game on a PC in this day & age and not have the option to quicksave and/or make multiple saves.  (You can, however, also load up the start of any level and continue playing from there, if you missed something).  But, to be honest, the checkpoints were extremely frequent and never really caused any true frustration.

Another game I do not regret buying! Brink is sort of like a mixture between Team Fortress and Modern Warfare, with the ability to traverse the battlegrounds using Parkour. The action is fast and furious with an emphasis on completing objectives and assisting team-mates rather than notching up individual kills. You have the option of customizing your characters cosmetically and there is a simple and uncomplicated skill leveling system. There are just a handful of weapon classes so its not a diverse range, but each handles differently.
Graphics are great! Maps look excellent and "feel" very natural, soundtrack is bloody excellent and evocative, adds a lot of atmosphere to the game, storyline and themes show a depth rarely explored in games. Voice acting is very good and creates very vivid characters just by that alone. Single player campaign is short, shorter than those of other FPS'es, and mostly for the story. A good team for multiplayer play is recommended.

If you don't press the correct sequence of movement keys (W,LShift, LShift, for example) you can't do anything (shoot, move, command others). You just stand there getting killed while you try to figure out what keys you are supposed to press that will unfreeze you. Tool tips and commentary appear in various areas of the screen so you don't reallly know where to look. The tutorial, such as it is, flashes by the screen so quickly you often miss the instructions.
Perhaps it plays better if you connect a game pad to your PC... I don't know because I don't use a game pad.
The story line is decent. For a TPS game the field of view is very limited and, once again, the keyboard controls are an abortion. On top of all of that, even when you do get the right key sequence, the game software is VERY slow to respond (I have an i5 quad core and an Nvidia GTX750, so I don't think it's my gear).
Ambitious project. Major FAIL.  Major disappointment.

Previously I enjoyed this game but with some of the more recent updates the game is nearly unplayable.
Below are some of my gripes:
1. Melee hitboxes are ridiculous.
- The game forces you into melee combat right off the bad which is ok for most games but here it is difficult to hit anything that isn't on level ground. I'm looking at you wall climbing skeliopods.
2. Mobs spawn way too often when mining and resource gathering.
- I understand that adding difficulty will increase the experience but it is immersion breaking when you so much as tap a banana leaf with your tursty rock and have two mobs pop up out of nowhere whereas the area was clear not even 2 minutes prior.
3. Progression is grindy and not really fun for me.
- I love tech trees. They give you something to work towards...  however, when I have to smack a tree for 10-15 minutes to get the points I need to get a 3d printer something has got to give. Don't get me wrong, I might be missing something, but it takes away from the experience if you have to grind for something you don't even need just to get the points required to stop yourself from dieing.
4. Why the hell did the pistol get nerfed? Why don't Engineer and Scientist spawn with one?
- The pistol was perfect before. Unlimited ammo and a painfully slow recharge between shots. Now that it requires ammo (which requires a boatload of science) and a 3d printer (also requires a lot of science).  With the state of melee combat as it is,  janky as hell, a pistol is pretty much required. Ammo is ok, but having it locked behind so much research is a bad choice at this time.
5. Why am I constantly stubbing my toes?
- When navigating up and down the many hills in this game I seem to stub my toe often which causes me to freeze in place for a couple of seconds. When trying to chase down a mob THAT YOU CANNOT HIT or, more often, running away, having to stop to contemplate your navel really gets bothersome.
I have more gripes about the game but these 5 are the major issues I have with the game.
In closing, in it's current state I don't believe I'd pay full price for it. Does it have the content to cover the full price? Yes.However, the gameplay issues and design choices far overshadow the current available content.

TL;DR: A game i use to love is simply not fun anymore. I can't reccommend this game at this point in time unless drastic changes are made.
Osiris: New Dawn is a sandbox survival game that I use to hold dear to my heart. Key words "use to". In its current stages the game is trying entirely to hard to be a hardcore game. I absolutley can not reccommend this game to anyone as is. Osiris use to be a nice space survival game that I could play and have fun with my friends. Now its just feels to difficult as well as to clunky to enjoy. Minning something, for example, has a chance to spawn in an "alien". This mechanic coupled with the need for a vast amount of resources, means that you are constanly fighting off waves of mobs. I can hear you asking now: "Well whats that matter?". Well Jimmy, if you ever attempt to enter combat with anything, hitting the bloody thing is near impossible and on top of that weapons snap like a twig in early game so thats pointless. The monsters also dont have any "attack" animation, so upon contact you take a large amount of damage. Bandages are sparse and making them doesn't really equal out to the effort of getting the mats for bandages (considering the spawn while gathering issue). The class system is also a mess and seems a bit thrown together. The very start of the game is very slow and difficult considering the previously attributed complaints as well as all of the classes "starting items". (if you can call them that.) I could drone on about the other issues I have but I think you, the reader, get the jist. In the end, a game that i held dear to my heart had fell away and fallen into the pile of "why would I play that". Hopfully the dev team takes this game back on the right path but until then, I simply cant reccomend it (which really really makes me sad).

Anyone familiar with Where’s Wally will know the reference at the top of the review, those that aren’t aware of the series of books, essentially you are tasked with finding Wally in the page of the book as well as finding other items throughout the world. It is this game mechanics that Hidden Folks is all about. You get given a list of items to find before allowing you to move onto the next area. The areas themselves  are absolutely ginormous, with you moving around using your mouse, zooming in as you go. Each item you are tasked to find comes with a clue, which gives you an idea to where you can find it on the level.  These clues are invaluable as some of the more congested areas would make it difficult for you to find a pair of sunglasses without a rough indication as to their location. As you progress through the levels they get more and more congested, at one stageI had to take a 10 minute break to give my eyes a rest from all the action going on at once. In between some levels you are given a smaller area to look through as a kind of interlude and to give your eyes a rest, included is also a section where you have to clear the path  for the character, allowing them safe passage through the level.
The game is a fantastic example of what an independent developer can achieve, the game just works. My personal favourite level is the desert level, which has areas of a festival where you can switch on the music and watch the characters dance around, then scroll to the east and you stumble across a Mad Max style area. Its these little nods to popular culture that also add a great little aside, finding Q-bert was a great addition.
Overall, this is a game that will appeal to people who like both hidden object games, as well as someone looking for a bit of light relief. With its low price point at £5.99 I don’t think it’s a game you can pass up on if you are a fan of Where’s Wally.

This absolutely unforgiving game has great potential. I do recommend this game if you have some money to spare and dont mind losing (all the ♥♥♥♥ing time). One of the best Indies I have played, ever. Normally I dont like early access games but this one was great.
Easy mode, 22%, 150 days.
Day one. I spot a few zombies around my compound. No biggie, I quickly eliminate them and at the same time start building up my colony.
Day 20, the first wave of zombies arrives from the West. My one tower filled with rangers was able to fend off the attack with ease. Well this was easy, I thought, I might make it to day 150.
Day 60, the second wave of zombies arrives from the west again. I managed to build up my defenses, got a nice wall of fortification around my settlement. A few towers with 1 sniper each and 3 rangers. Snipers set to strongest target and one arrow shooting tower to complement it. The horde never got through the walls.
Day 90, the third wave arrives from the north. I do not have many defenses there, other than two stone towers filled with the 1 sniper 3 ranger combo. I quickly build two rows of walls and place an executor tower. The wave almost got through, but I managed to hold them off losing one tower.
Day 91, I decide I need to expand. I thought of this game like "Attack on titan" and decided to make rings of defenses. I did the same setup. Two rings, this round . First row has a few executors, 1 row of stone walls and some produce buildings inside of those walls. Farms, stone, iron, oil, etc. The second row is heavily defended by Thanathos units, executors and even a few Titans. To complement this I placed two rows of stone walls and several fully stocked stone towers. Nothing gets through here.
Day 110, Another wave of undead arrives form the North, got through the first ring. Mowed down on the second. They never stood a change. I rebuild the first ring and was ready for the last wave.
Day 140, the announcement pops up, THEY ARE BILLIONS!. They come from all sides. I got this, I totally got this. I have spent all of my income on defensive buildings and units. The first ring gets sacrificed, that was already the plan. I quickly destroy all produce buildings to limit the amount of undead spawns from my buildings.
Day 141, here they come. My PC starts lagging, my PC with a i7 6700HQ and Geforce 970 6GB and 64GB of DDR4 starts lagging. Not by much, but it does lag. Masses of undead pound down the walls. My first ring falls. No problem, I got another, bring it on! But while I was concentrating on the West horde, the one ins the North breaks through. I thought the chokepoint I created there would hold them with ease. It did not. My units die, my executors fall, my walls crumble. The undead destroy my buildings, more undead spawn. Everybody dies.
I felt sad that I lost, yet proud, that I lasted this long. We survived for 143 days. Only 7 days short. 120 days longer than my first attempt. There is progress, albeit slow, I will one day beat this game.

Drifting Lands is a arcade shoot’em’up which combines the classic gameplay with RPG elements and tries to do something different. It instantly reminded me of the old and classic games like Thunder Force III which were fun but somewhat lacking in satisfaction. Can Drifting Lands manage to infuse the old school gameplay with a modern day twist? Let’s find out:
The most impressive thing about Drifting Lands is the amount of customization options present in the game. You can change the layout of your ship completely by upgrading its weapons, armour and much more. Sure, to upgrade your ship you need to grind in the levels and replay previous levels to get the required loot.
This also lends to some increased replayablity factor to Drifting Lands. The loot that you don’t require inn upgrading you shop can be sold to the shop and the same can be used to buy a plethora of new gizmos to attach to your ship. This is easily the most unique prospect of Drifting Land and that is why it is also one of key selling points of the game.
Most of the time games of this genre does not bother with a story or at most have a half hearted attempt at it. Drifting Lands, on the other hand, tries harder than most to keep players invested in its story of the post apocalyptic world and its new survivors. It tells the story of how a world got destroyed and the land masses now simply float in the air.
The remaining humans live on a massive ship called the ARK and they send out their pilots to fight back against the robots taking over the world. While it is uninspired and kind of clichéd, it just did enough to keep me hooked for a while and create a believable world.
The game has a lot of content available for the players. While not necessarily good or meaningful, it boasts over 100 stages and a number of enemy varieties to support them. It does feel like that it is being padded out after some time and you will be tired of the game before its completed and it is a good thing for some players who want their game to have some meat on its bones.
The major flaw with Drifting Lands is the fact that it gets repetitive way too quickly. There are no varied mission objectives or anything that makes you keep going. Even the backgrounds start repeating themselves after a while and nothing new is left to see after that.
A huge number of stages can be good but they need to be freshened up after a while and Drifting Lands fails completely on that front. It will only take you over 5-6 hours before you start getting bored of its repetitive nature and move on to something else.Remember how the game has an impressive amount of customization options and stuff. Well, all of that is hidden behind a wall of grinding which serves no other purpose than make the game feel more repetitive and padded out for the most part.
When it is minimal and you have just started, getting good loot and gear feels rewarding. But combining that with the repetitive nature of the game, replaying old levels just feels like a wasted opportunity when you already have a huge number of levels going forward. The grinding slowly builds up and all the sense of satisfaction is drained out by the end of it.
Colourful, Vibrant and full of energy, Drifting Lands sports a visuals style that is pleasing to the eyes and flashes off some great art style. Everything from the enemy design to the UI of the game feels neat and fresh. The maps are very well detailed and provide a great backdrop to the ongoing battles. The screen does gets crowded from time to time and it is expected but Drifting Lands manages to pull it off with a certain level of flair.
Complimenting its great visual design is the enamouring sound design of Drifting lands. The soundtrack is brilliant with its ambient design and the sound effects are done very well. While it is nothing that you have never heard before, it is a very good sound design for its worth.
There is no denying that Drifting Lands is a good game. It tries to create a new experience and somewhat succeeds at it. But due to the grinding nature, it neither feels as satisfying as the old games nor does it has enough depth to carry forward as a RPG. If you can ignore its flaws and you want a fresh take on an arcade shoot’em’up, then Drifting Lands is worth the somewhat steep price.

In UN Squadron you had 3 lives and that was it. If you died, you had to start over with no weapons, no ships, no credits.

ships with more health if you didnt grow up playing these games or are dying a lot.  Even if you're halfway decent, pick the Interceptor b/c you can eventually make it have just as much health, with the right equipement, as the maurader and it gets double the weapon damage modifier. Yea you dont get as much focus, but you kill more things, so credit take is about the same.
All in all, great addictive mix of shooting stuff till it goes boom and grinding for gear. Totally worth the price, I'm sure I'll get lots of hours out of it.

This game gives me mixed emotions, but they're ultimately positive.
First off, the game looks and plays great. Overall the game has a feeling of polish in just about everything. So keep that in mind while I gripe about things that may or may not put you off from it.
Anyhow, the biggest complaint I have is weapon variety and feel. Even with the skills you're given, the ways you have to attack something start to feel very same-y. Thus far I've only really encountered a couple of "types" of primary weapons. You've got your bullet types and your laser types. The bullet type weapons consist of a handful of spread options for spewing bullets in various directions and patterns. Laser types shoot a beam in various directions and duration. And they all feel very similar. For example, the "minigun" and "autocannon" weapon types both go "pew-pew-pew" and deal damage. The only real difference is the angle of attack and frequency. Any of those types can be dealing different elements of damage, but it's going to feel the same regardless. There's no visceral feedback at all. There's no blood thirsty rush from keeping the trigger down and rushing almost into a collision with a minigun. Almost everything has a plinky feel to it. Even the railgun, a slow single shot laser type weapon, somehow manages to feel kind of like a flashlight.
Which is a bummer since everything else in this game is very pleasant. And maybe that's part of the problem? The smoothness present in everything almost seems to have seeped into the combat. Combat gets fast and hectic, but never carnal like Steredenn, for example. No matter what is happening, it's all very smooth.
All that said, it's a good time. I just wish the primary weapons had a little more personality.

Drifting Lands is an unusual attempt at combining two genres that have remained separate for long. Taking the persistence and gear of an ARPG and combining that with the fast-paced frenetic action of a Shmup. While it doesn't hit the absolute highs of either genre, this is still a great treat for fans looking for something a little different.
The story of Drifting Lands follows the world being destroyed, with the remaining land masses now floating in the air. The last free humans now live on a massive ship called the ark and send out pilots to patrol and fight back against robots, cults and more.
The game itself is mission-based. The most common objective is to survive an entire section while battling enemy ships. What makes the game so different comes after you're done with a mission.
Drifting Lands features procedurally generated loot much like in an ARPG. You can equip different weapons, thrusters, armor and more. Gear comes at different rarities that affect passive bonuses. For a different touch, gear will feature flaws that act as a price for using that specific piece.
Just like other Shmups, the different weapons have different firing arcs; with all the popular ones included. Credits are the game's currency, and are used for buying new gear as well as upgrading your ship.
You have three stats: Power, Navigation and Structure. Higher tier gear will require you to meet the pre-requisite of the chosen stat or stats. As you progress through the game, you'll be able to buy higher class ships that allow you to put more stat points on them.
Besides gear, you can assign six skills to your ship to use in combat; four active and two passives. One passive allows you to automatically retreat from combat if your ship is destroyed. If you turn that off on normal mode, you will essentially be playing hardcore mode for the game where you can lose your ship if you die.
Going through the game will unlock new grades of difficulty; up to 10. Going up in grade will raise the number of enemies, loot quality and overall difficulty. So far Drifting Lands sounds amazing, but the game can't manage to bring it all together for a satisfying experience.
Drifting Lands has a great gameplay loop of completing missions to earn better gear, but it's not enough to sustain the game over the many, many levels. By the time I reached grade 3 of 10, I was already starting to feel bored with the game. The story content actually ends at the end of grade four; leaving the rest of the experience for just gear grinding.
Actual new content and progression are doled out very slowly. The developers should have taken a page from the Diablo 3 redesign and try to give the player something new at each grade. The same goes for the different skills. Due to the limited number of skills and slots, you'll quickly find your favorites and will never want to take them off.
Despite the ARPG design, there really isn't as much loot as I was expecting. The game can overwhelm you with passive attributes, but it becomes easier once you get used to it.
The level design is possibly the worst part of the game, because there is no level design. Every stage takes place in an open environment. The sections that you fly through are hard-coded in terms of enemy ships, but randomly placed. However, the environment itself has no bearing on what you do. There were cases where the same section repeated twice in a single level. There are only three factions of enemies, and they share a lot of similar ship designs.
For fans of challenging shmup design, expect to navigate densely packed areas of bullets, lasers and more. It's very easy to go from full to dead if you're not paying attention to what's around you.
The last problem with Drifting Lands is a surprising one: A general lack of polish.
Drifting Lands comes with a lot of general flaws and problems that seemed to have been missed. There are spelling errors and general quality of life issues. One big issue is that there are sections where the backgrounds are the same color as the enemy bullets; making it impossible to see incoming shots. The game feels like it could have used one more round of play testing to make sure that everything was all shipshape. This isn't damning, but when combined with the short campaign leaves the game feeling unfinished.
Drifting Lands has what it needs to be amazing, but it lacks the polish and content to make it a serious contender as a rogue-like, Shmup or ARPG. I hope the game does well enough to warrant more development, but at the moment, the design just isn't firing on all cylinders. If more content is released to expand on the progression curve, this would be an easy recommendation.

Osiris: New Dawn used to be THE Early access title for me. Sure there has always been placeholder items that you can build and they have no use and sure at one point it was super easy.  I could build everything up for my base in a few hours with my friends. That was TOO easy. Still, it was fun and had some amazing ground work laid for it. With what I experienced with a few hours of play after coming back to the game it's rediculous.
No matter the danger setting for alien spawns you can easily get overran by aliens from mining a single node. Pick up on items is frustrating due to the new animation to the point that it felt like, sometimes, I had to press quite a few times just to pick something up.
As for survivability when you start getting overran well...you can use pretty much all the starter health and food items you got and you may survive it or just let them kill you. health items barely restore much and now the fall damage alone could kill you if you get a lil too excited with your hovering and fly too high.
I know someone will probably read my review and just say 'well get good' or they 'like the challenge' that comes with it being so tedious and unneccesarily frustrating to start out and that's fine. Everyone has different tastes but I, personally, felt like Osiris had a lot going for it in the begining and had a bright future and, now, I don't really find the build up fun in the slightest. You'd find it quite difficult to start up on your own considering how things are spread across the skill trees. Also goodluck getting pretty much ANY resource without being trambled by a dozen aliens. Also, unless you go with a combat class you don't really get a true weapon to start out with and gear wear is a bit too fast for my tastes as well as the speed at which your light burns out.
Honestly, I would say just to wait for the full release of the game. My review could be biased or just based on frustration so make your own choice, but I would recommend waiting. At the very least, wait until more updates have come out.

Like everything from Freebird Games, "A Bird Story" made me cry. I went in expecting it.
The best way to describe it is it feels like Gone Home or Dear Esther, a minimal gameplay experience with a story that is told entirely without words. This was risky given the nature of pixel art, but Kan Gao makes it look easy.
What some people might be wondering though is, how does it compare with "To the Moon", Kan Gao's last commercial release? They're two different gameplay experiences, both emotional and both great stories. It feels much shorter, maybe an hour and a half or so, but much more well made. However, I think "A Bird Story" is less intrusive with its gamey elements than "To the Moon"; oftentimes, puzzles in TtM felt more like a strange side game than a natural extension of the game. Gao's beautiful music returns and often is worth the price of admission alone, flowing effortlessly along with the visuals.
While the story felt more experimental and Studio Ghibli-esque, I'm hoping the proper "To the Moon" sequel returns more to the form of the first game. And while it may not be readily apparent, there is a connection to the world of "To the Moon", and now I'm left waiting for one day to come with a bucket of my own tears.
DARN YOU FREEBIRD GAMES!

The game is good but it has some major flaws that I hope are addressed later.
The biggest issue in the game is that given that it's a strategy game, a lot is left up to the RNG world generation rather than the difficulty settings that ultimately establishes if the game is easy or even winnable.
You can end up with a map where you cannot secure enough oil without overextending, are not able to place housing around a bank or marketplace due to limited space.
Or you can end up in a map where you start in an area that is easily secured, has farm land, iron and oil literally within sight of the HQ.
I don't mind a challenge but the inability to save and the fact that you can get a profoundly unfavorable start make these starting locations simply not worth playing as you just get one shot at them - I mean do you really want to sink in 3-4 hours before you get wiped out without a chance to try that again?
So what that means is that if you are playing to win, your first 5 minutes of the game is rushing around the map scouting as much as you can to figure out if you want to attempt the map. It took me 4 attempts to beat the game the first time. First 3 times I refused to "cheese" by restarting till a favorable start. 4th time I restarted until I got a start where my HQ was in a large area that was secured by 3 natural choke points that were trivial to defend. Easiest game by far and a trivial victory.
With that said - the game is pretty and fun - I just wish they got rid of the dependency on map layout. Really just having warehouses, banks and markets not be proximity based would fix so many of the issues.
Either way it's a neat take on tower defense and has outstanding quality for an early access title.

1996's state-of-the-art FPS.

There could not have been a better time for a game like Quake to be launched than its own. Feeding upon the virtues and vision of Doom and Doom II, it reaches even farther confines of first-person gameplay, something it excels at, even if  compared to games of the same genre from years later. It is outstanding how well this behemoth of 1990s shooters has aged, since its frantic and well-balanced action gives way to countless reruns should the player wish to have some more of the Quake elixir. That could be explained by its advanced mechanics - quick strafing, jumping, recoil, plurality of enemies and plurality of ways to face them, among other gameplay qualities.
It could also be explained by its unparalleled level design, which may very well be the game's utmost asset. Here, names such as Tim Willits, John Romero, and American McGee spring to mind. Throughout Quake's four episodes, the player is challenged with labyrinthine keeps, gloomy catacombs, unforgettable halls... all of them filled with key areas that quickly swarm with just enough creatures to keep the protagonist busy and trigger-happy at all times. The bridges, narrow corridors, staircases, secret passages, underwater ruins, all respond to the player's arrival and can be revisited in punctual moments during the progression of the stage. Not to mention that each level has its own mechanisms of completion, often related to the acquisition of keys that open gates that give way to advanced rooms in the map. Never will a room, corridor, or any piece of game space feel redundant or undistinguished, as the game will give the player a purpose and leverage to keep progressing through the areas, using each level's singular rationale. Play maps like The Crypt of Decay (E2M3), The Vaults of Zin (E3M2), or The Wind Tunnels (E3M5), and have a wee glance at how memorable level design is here. Also multiplayer, still in its baby steps back then, provided great fun with maps like The Dark Zone (DM6). It is no Tokay's Tower, but it offers satisfactory deathmatch action.
This Steam version comes with four different applications that will behave distinctly depending on the system being used (two of them dedicated to QuakeWorld). Some resolution and colour issues hinder the experience more often than not, which is why the player should make sure to search for optimisation mods and patches online, such as the extremely efficient Ultimate Quake Patch v1.11, which works in perfect unison with the GLQuake application.
I find it nearly impossible not to value the game's momentous contributions to an almost perennial genre. It is unique in its techno-Gothic aesthetics and its veer towards an all-Lovecraftian story - with references spanning even post-Lovecraft Cthulhu Mythos bestiaries, such as the Chthonians - while staying simplistic and not bothering the player with plotline complexities, which is understandable, considering the forthrightness of old-time shooters when it comes to writing. It is heart-warming to notice that almost twenty years have not stained the delight of mouse-and-keyboard frenzy that Quake inspires.
